Dutch economy grew by 0.6% in Q2, faster than initially thought
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Dutch economy grew by 0.6% in the second quarter of 2026, more than the national statistic agency CBS’s initial assessment.
The CBS said higher export volumes and stronger household spending were the main reasons for the revision. The second, more detailed assessment is published around 85 days after the end of the quarter.
Over the 12-month period GDP grew by 1.6%, its fastest rate since the first quarter of 2025. That figure was also revised upwards from an initial 1.3%.
The labour market improved, with an additional 15,000 employees and registered freelancers in the second quarter. The initial assessment said the total number of jobs had dropped by 8,000.

‘I had never heard of Eswatini’: Deported by the US to a country that rejects them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
06:56:42 UTC
15:56:42 KST

‘I had never heard of Eswatini’: Deported by the US to a country that rejects them
From our southern Africa correspondent – Migrants previously convicted by US courts have been imprisoned in Africa’s last absolute monarchy, Eswatini, over the past several months. Since being deported from the US, they have found themselves in a country about which they know nothing, and where local residents look on these “criminal” arrivals with suspicion. Their abrupt journey to the small southern African kingdom stems from a secret deal struck by Trump administration as part of his programme of mass deportations investigated by “The Deportation Project”, undertaken by Forbidden Stories and a network of 72 journalists across 15 countries.
Protests are rare in the small southern African kingdom of Eswatini, and largely repressed. But that didn’t stop more than a hundred women from gathering on July 18, 2025 in front of the US embassy in Manzini, the economic capital of the country still widely known by its former name of Swaziland.
“Come out, ambassador! Come out and talk with us!” they shouted.
What the women wanted to talk about was the secret arrival of foreign “criminals” who had just been transferred to Swazi prisons. Fearing for the safety of their children, the demonstrators were demanding that these prisoners be sent back to the US – where they had just been deported from.
Over the course of a year, four planes have discreetly touched down in Eswatini carrying 32 migrants deported by the administration of US President Donald Trump. Wedged between Mozambique and South Africa, this country is preparing to host 160 deportees in total.
Watch moreICE, Trump and Africa: Secret deals, broken lives
All of them will be held in the central prison of Matsapha, not far from Manzini. In a country where daily life is still largely shaped by tradition and where few dare to question the decisions of King Mswati III, the secret arrangement with Washington has nevertheless set off an outcry of rare force.
“If South African media hadn’t announced it, we never would have known,” said Sibusiso Nhlabatsi. Determined to meet these migrants face-to-face, the lawyer has been turned away from the prison five times. A well-known attorney and human rights specialist as well as a former colleague of Thulani Maseko, a human rights lawyer shot dead in 2023, Nhlabatsi is not taking no for an answer.
He took his case to the Supreme Court, which ruled in his favour in 2025. The government appealed the decision. In March 2026, the High Court of Mbabane finally authorised the detainees to see him.
“They had been transported like a bag of potatoes – and even with a bag of potatoes, if you transport it from one country to another, there are concerns that you have to go through, there are standards that must be met,” Nhlabatsi said. “They’ve been thrown in prison, despite the fact that they have never committed a crime in Eswatini.”
‘Whether we sign or not, we're still going to get left here’
Nhlabatsi has since travelled every week to the brand-new wing of the high security prison in Matsapha. The detainees’ cases can be hard to untangle, as the detainees come from as far afield as Vietnam, Laos, Yemen, Cuba, Ethiopia, the Democratic Republic of Congo or Jamaica.
The only thing they have in common is having been previously convicted by US courts – though Nhlabatsi stressed that they were not the monsters they were being made out to be.
“Most of them have been rehabilitated, most of them have rehabilitation certificates,” the lawyer said. “It’s not like they were taken straight from jail in the United States of America and then deported. They have been living in American society.”
The feeling of injustice is keenly felt behind the bars of Matsapha’s high-security prison. But not every detainee has the same strength left to fight for their return to their families in the US.
As part of a consortium of 26 media outlets coordinated by Forbidden Stories, RFI and FRANCE 24 spent six months investigating the secret deals struck between the administration of US President Donald Trump and several African countries. These “third countries” have agreed to host undocumented migrants detained by ICE and deported from the US.
From Ghana to Cameroon and Eswatini, our journalists spoke to the people deported to countries utterly unfamiliar to them.
Those who were the first to arrive are the most beaten-down by their fates.
“I had never heard of Eswatini,” said Vietnamese deportee Dung Nguyen in an exclusive interview with FRANCE 24 and Forbidden Stories. "They ... asked us to sign some papers, and I refused to sign the papers. And they said, whether we sign the papers or not, we're still going to get left here."
Nguyen was convicted of rape in 2011, and released in 2015. He has since married, bought a house and found work. Nguyen was living as a free man when he was arrested and bundled onto a military plane on July 16, 2025.
Despite his newfound detention, he said, he is not subject to the same strictures of Swazi inmates – he watches TV, eats better meals and has access to social media. Under the supervision of prison staff, he can even leave the prison to go to the nearest shopping mall.
The ‘Coca-Cola king’
Like Nguyen, most of the migrants held in this prison had never heard of King Mswati III, who has ruled the country since 1986. Over that time, he has earned another name for himself – the “Coca-Cola king”.
It’s not hard to see why. Not far from the prison, the largest Coca-Cola factory on the African continent stretches across more than 6,500 square metres. A wholly owned subsidiary of the Coca-Cola Company, Conco Ltd is the kingdom’s single largest source of foreign currency.
The royal family controls a 40 percent stake in Eswatini Coca Cola Beverages – the authorised bottler – through the Tibiyo Taka Ngwane sovereign wealth fund set up by king Sobhuza II in 1968.
Read moreInvestigation: In Cameroon, the victims of Trump’s deportations face uncertain fates
‘An evil deal’
The US and Eswatini have seemed to enjoy a good relationship for decades. But according to Siboniso Mkhabela, the national organising secretary of the opposition People’s United Democratic Movement (PUDEMO), that relationship has taken a turn since Trump came to power.
He described the agreement on migrant deportations struck between the US and Eswatini as “an evil deal".
"Before Trump came into the White House, we were this close to achieving a milestone in our struggle," the opposition activist said. "This resolution was simply saying those who were involved in the killing of a human rights lawyer and many others during the unrest in June 2021 must be held accountable."
But for many people, Washington has since kept its eyes firmly closed in the face of a regime that grows more repressive by the day in a monarchy that has never been so absolute as it is now.
Watch moreLawyers and activists in Eswatini challenge government for accepting US deportees
Mkhabela said that he can no longer wear a PUDEMO tee-shirt in public. Many opposition party supporters remain behind bars as a result of expansive counter-terrorism laws.
Critics of the agreement between Washington and Mbabane point out that the deal was negotiated during the period when the second Trump administration was dismantling its USAID programme, on which Eswatini heavily relied – more than half of the kingdom’s national budget for its AIDS programmes were financed by the US. Backed into a corner, the government may have had little choice but to make a deal.
While Swazi authorities have confirmed having received people deported from the US, the details of the deal have never been made public. But FRANCE 24 was able to obtain a copy of the document, signed on May 14 by Prime Minister Russell Dlamini. The agreement states that Eswatini will receive 160 migrants deported from the US, as well as the sum of $5.1 million “for reinforcing border and migrant migration capacity”.
‘How long are they going to stay?’
"The Nation is assured that these inmates pose no threat to the country or its citizens," government spokesperson Thabile Mdluli said, adding that the deportees were only “on transit” through the country. Justice Minister Prince Simelane insisted that the detainees would not be treated as prisoners, but as “guests of the king”.
These statements have done little to stem the rising anger in Eswatini’s population, with many people expressing shock that the detainees are allowed to walk around the Matsapha shopping centre.
“Why do they have better living conditions than other prisoners?” “How long are they going to stay in Eswatini?” “What’s going to happen if they have children with our women”? These are just a few of the questions that have been asked in Eswatini’s parliament in recent months.
Mzwandile Masuku, the son of opposition leader Mario Masuku, has another question to add: what’s happened to the $5 million?
“Our minister of finance is on record as having said that he had not seen the funds,” he said. “We cannot point to where the money was received and where those funds have ended up.”
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Questioned in parliament, ministers have given contradictory answers. Prime Minister Dlamini has stated publicly that there was no financial compensation, but that the agreement was intended to foster “better relations” between Eswatini and the US.
The finance minister later clarified to say that the funds had been deposited into an account belonging to the National Disaster Management Agency, to which he does not have access.
Government spokesperson Mdluli rejected repeated requests for an interview, saying that the information already shared with the public was sufficient.
Masuku, whose father has been imprisoned on multiple occasions, knows that he has to be careful. But he has been working tirelessly with his colleagues for months now to have the deal overturned before all 160 deportees arrive in Eswatini.
Whether he’s successful or not, the fact remains that Eswatini can’t keep these people behind bars indefinitely – and only five have returned to their home countries. Others hope to be granted permanent residency in the country they now find themselves in.
But they’ll first need to shake off the image of “criminals” that the US has imposed on them. In Matsapha, the detainees know that their future no longer depends on the US justice system, but on the goodwill of a kingdom they had never in their lives imagined setting foot in.

Israeli forces raid several West Bank areas, arrest Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
06:54:58 UTC
15:54:58 KST

Ikrame Kouachi
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
Israeli forces raided several areas across the occupied West Bank early Wednesday, arresting at least two Palestinians, according to the Palestinian official news agency WAFA.
Israeli occupiers also damaged Palestinian property and vehicles.
Ten military jeeps were used to raid the village of Beit Duqqu, northwest of occupied Jerusalem.
Troops deplpyed across the village raided several homes and arrested a number of residents before withdrawing, sources said.
The number and identities of those detained were not immediately known.
In Nabi Saleh, northwest of Ramallah, Israeli forces raided and searched a home and arrested a 19-year-old Palestinian.
Israeli forces also raided the city of Tubas and the nearby town of Aqaba in the northern West Bank, raiding several homes and deploying infantry units in several neighborhoods.
Israeli forces raided the town of Janata and Aida refugee camp east and north of Bethlehem. No arrests were reported.
In the northern Tulkarem area, Israeli forces raided the towns of Attil and Deir al-Ghusun early Wednesday with several military vehicles and infantry units.
Local sources said troops patrolled the towns, raided and searched several homes and damaged their contents.
Residents of several homes were subjected to field questioning and interrogation amid a heavy military presence.
The forces also arrested a Palestinian man from his home in Deir al-Ghusun, according to the sources.
In the Masafer Yatta area south of Hebron, occupiers damaged property in Khirbet Aqawwis early Wednesday. This came a day after they set fire to a workers’ vehicle near the village of Umm Qussa in the Yatta countryside after chasing its occupants.
WAFA quoted local sources as saying that such attacks have been repeated over recent days and months as part of ongoing assaults targeting Palestinians and their property in Masafer Yatta.
The occupied West Bank has witnessed an escalation in Israeli raids and arrests since October 2023, alongside increasing occupier attacks, movement restrictions, and closures of entrances to Palestinian towns and villages.

Death toll from capsized ship in Indonesia rises to 20
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:52:42 CST
15:52:42 KST

JAKARTA, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- The death toll from a passenger ship that capsized and sank in Indonesia's Java Sea rose to 20 on Wednesday, with 115 people still missing and 108 survivors, according to the National Search and Rescue Agency.
The Virgo Transport 8 departed Surabaya in East Java on Sept. 12 for Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan. It encountered bad weather during the voyage and lost contact at around 2 a.m. local time on Sept. 13.
Rescuers have since found bodies inside the ship and along the coast of Central Kalimantan province.
Divers are focusing their search on the ship's cabins, but poor underwater visibility and strong currents have hampered the operation, the agency said.
Indonesia, an archipelagic country with around 17,000 islands, relies heavily on ferries and other forms of sea transportation to connect its islands and facilitate travel. Maritime accidents occur from time to time due to factors including weather conditions, sea conditions and vessel safety. ■

Venezuelan acting president concludes meeting with Trump in New York
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:52:29 CST
15:52:29 KST

CARACAS, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Venezuelan acting President Delcy Rodriguez said Tuesday that she had concluded a meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump.
Rodriguez said on X that the talks covered strategic areas from strengthening bilateral relations to advancing cooperation in energy, mining and security.
The meeting took place on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, marking the first meeting between the two leaders since the U.S. seizure of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.
Venezuela severed diplomatic relations with the United States in January 2019 amid tensions over what Caracas described as U.S. interference in its internal affairs. U.S. diplomatic personnel left the embassy in Caracas in March that year.
On Jan. 3, U.S. military forces launched a large-scale strike against Venezuela and forcibly seized Maduro and his wife before transporting them to New York.
On March 5, the two countries said that they had agreed to restore diplomatic and consular relations. ■

S. Korea's August domestic migration hits 53-year low amid housing slowdown
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:52:20 CST
15:52:20 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's August domestic migration hit a 53-year low amid a long-term population decline and a housing market slowdown, statistical ministry data showed Wednesday.
The number of those relocating to new homes shrank 4.5 percent from a year earlier to 471,000 in August, marking the lowest for August since 1973, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics.
The population mobility rate, or the number of movers per 100 people, sank 0.5 percentage points to 10.9 percent in August.
The sluggish migration was driven by structural demographic changes combined with a slowdown in both housing transactions and supply.
The number of housing transactions in June and July fell 4.4 percent year-on-year to 132,000, while the number of completed apartments, a key indicator of housing supply, plunged 29.1 percent to 43,000 in the two months.
Six provinces and cities recorded a net influx of residents, led by Gyeonggi province with 4,486, Incheon with 2,270 and North Chungcheong province with 562.
Ten municipalities saw a net outflow as Seoul posted the largest fall of 2,901, trailed by South Gyeongsang province with 1,230. ■

Feature: Seeing is understanding -- Hong Kong, Macao students explore country's development firsthand in Beijing
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:52:04 CST
15:52:04 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- In the Chinese capital, groups of Cantonese-speaking students from Hong Kong and Macao made for a distinctive sight as they journeyed from iconic landmarks to cultural and technological venues.
The students, totaling around 1,000, are members of flag-raising teams from schools and universities across the Hong Kong and Macao special administrative regions (SARs). They wrapped up their five-day visit to Beijing on Tuesday, with paying tribute to the national flag as its central theme.
The itinerary took them to the Great Hall of the People, the Palace Museum, the station of the Chinese People's Liberation Army guard of honor, as well as schools, companies, and science and technology sites -- offering them a firsthand look at the Chinese capital and a deeper understanding of their homeland.
Dyun Jeoi Ming, a student from Zheng Guanying Official School in Macao, gathered with his peers at Tian'anmen Square at dawn on Sunday for the national flag-raising ceremony. They stood in silence as the guards marched into view and joined in the national anthem as the five-starred red flag was slowly raised.
Though having watched the ceremony countless times on television and on the phone, Dyun said seeing it in person was an entirely different experience. "Standing here today, I am moved beyond words," he said.
For many of the students, raising the national flag is already a familiar part of school life in Hong Kong and Macao. Since their respective returns to China in the late 1990s, the two SARs have retained their capitalist systems and ways of life under the "one country, two systems" principle, but national flag-raising ceremonies and national security education have increasingly become an established part of school life.
In recent years, a wide range of initiatives have also helped young locals forge a better understanding of the country, from joining live "Tiangong Class" space lectures delivered by Chinese astronauts in orbit, to visiting Chinese naval vessels docking in Hong Kong, and taking part in study and exchange programs on the mainland.
As the students set off for Beijing this time, Kong Chi Meng, director of the Education and Youth Development Bureau of the Macao SAR government, said the trip was of "great significance," as it would help the participants strengthen their sense of national identity.
Over the past few days, the students visited historical sites including the ruins of the Old Summer Palace, or "Yuanmingyuan" in Chinese, and a tunnel warfare site, gaining a firsthand glimpse into China's painful wartime history and its resistance against foreign aggression.
Other experiences, from marveling at masterpieces of ancient Chinese bronze craftsmanship to exploring deep-sea laser spectroscopic probes and watching robotic arms swiftly operate along auto production lines, left the students in awe.
"Seeing firsthand what cannot be found in textbooks, I have come to better appreciate the wisdom behind the saying, 'One needs to not only read 10,000 books, but also travel 10,000 miles to know the world around us,'" said Cheung Wing-sam, from Cognitio College in Hong Kong.
Divided into groups, they also visited a dozen primary and secondary schools and universities in Beijing, where they talked and performed with their mainland counterparts.
Xu Xiangyue, deputy head of the Peking University flag guard team, said that students from Hong Kong and Macao come from different campuses and have different life experiences, but "when the national anthem plays and the national flag rises, our eyes naturally turn in the same direction."
For some, the trip may also open a window onto future possibilities, allowing them to align their personal aspirations with the country's broader development.
A senior student surnamed Chan at City University of Hong Kong said that an increasing number of university students in Hong Kong are considering pursuing career opportunities on the mainland after graduation.
"This event gives me a valuable opportunity to see for myself what the mainland is like," said Chan, who plans to share the experience with fellow students after returning to Hong Kong. ■

Vilnius marks autumn equinox with traditional Doors celebration – photos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
06:52:00 UTC
15:52:00 KST

Vilnius residents and visitors gathered on Stalo Hill late Tuesday to mark the autumn equinox, which heralds the astronomical beginning of autumn and the gradual return of longer nights.
The annual celebration has become a tradition in the Lithuanian capital, drawing on customs associated with welcoming the darker part of the year. This year’s event, titled Doors, was organised by the Vilnius Centre of Ethnic Culture in the city’s Kalnų Park.
The celebration featured songs, poetry, a dance performance and a fire show. Students from Vilnius schools helped create the atmosphere by arranging patterns made from candles.
Flame-adorned sculptures by artists Rytas Jonas Belevičius and Rūta Ona Čigriejūtė illuminated the symbolic path of the departing sun as it began its seasonal journey toward the winter period of rest.
The autumn equinox marks the point when day and night are approximately equal in length. After the equinox, nights gradually become longer than days in the Northern Hemisphere.

New Zealand introduces bill to strengthen border security
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:51:55 CST
15:51:55 KST

WELLINGTON, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- The New Zealand government introduced a bill to strengthen customs' ability to combat organized crime and growing border threats, a senior official said Wednesday.
The Customs and Excise (Border Security) Amendment Bill aims to update legislation to address changes in the border threat environment, including a "massive increase" in illicit drug seizures, Customs Minister Casey Costello said in a statement.
The volume of drug intercepts more than quadrupled from 1.5 tons in 2018 to 6.5 tons in 2024, while transnational, serious and organized crime groups are exploiting technology, legitimate trade and travel systems, and people with access to secure border areas such as baggage handlers, Costello said.
The bill would strengthen security requirements in customs-controlled areas and export storage facilities, increase penalties for serious offending, provide customs with additional operational powers, modernize information-sharing and digital border capabilities, and enhance officer safety, according to the statement.
Customs also needs improved powers to address the growing trade in child exploitation material, the minister said.
"When the original Customs and Excise Bill was passed in 1996, the main border issues involved individuals, offensive material in magazines and on videos and people trying to bring in extra cartons of duty-free cigarettes," she said, adding that customs is now dealing with criminal cartels involved in serious, high-value crimes backed by threats, intimidation and violence.
The bill recognizes customs' role in protecting national security and establishes a framework for information sharing with industry partners, Costello said. ■

A craftswoman airs mooncake-shaped Hui ink sticks at an ink workshop in Shexian County, Huangshan City, east China's Anhui Province, Sept. 9, 2026.
The Hui ink sticks are primarily composed of the soot produced by burning pine trees or tung oil, with glue as the main ingredient, supplemented by various minerals and Chinese herbal ingredients in the formulation. It undergoes a meticulous crafting process involving dozens of steps.

US Democrats lead over Republicans by 8.6 points: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
06:50:13 UTC
15:50:13 KST

Emerson and Marquette surveys also show a clear Democratic edge as control of Congress approaches a decisive test, Newsweek reported.
Candidates in competitive House and Senate races face a political climate shaped by dissatisfaction with the country’s direction and President Donald Trump’s low approval.
National generic-ballot polls measure which party voters prefer for Congress rather than testing named candidates.
They offer a broad view of the political environment, but local campaigns, district boundaries and turnout will determine who wins.
Quantus Insights’ survey of 1,389 likely voters, conducted September 15 to 18, found 50.3 percent supporting the Democratic candidate in their congressional district and 41.7 percent favoring the Republican.
Another 6.3 percent were undecided and 1.7 percent selected another candidate. The design-adjusted margin of error was plus or minus 2.9 percentage points.
Democrats retained an advantage among habitual voters.
Respondents who participated in the 2022 midterms favored the party 50 percent to 43.9 percent, while people who voted in all four general elections from 2018 through 2024 broke 50.3 percent to 43.9 percent.
Several demographic divides help explain the overall result.

Poland would help evacuate civilians from Lithuania, says Warsaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
06:49:00 UTC
15:49:00 KST

Poland would help evacuate civilians from Lithuania in case of an attack by Russia, Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Tuesday.
"Poland will help. Poles will help, state institutions will help," he answered a question from reporters during his visit to the Polish-Ukrainian border.
He pointed to Poland’s experience of taking in Ukrainian refugees following the February 2022 invasion.
"If any of the Baltic states, such as Lithuania, Latvia or Estonia, were attacked, we would call for Article 5 to be invoked," he said, referring to NATO’s collective defence clause.
Lithuania approved an evacuation plan in case of an emergency in July, with Vilnius having such a plan in place from 2025.
Baltic officials maintain there’s no immediate threat of a military conflict. However, recent intelligence reports, released publicly, show an increased threat of Russia launching more sabotage or other attacks as it is increasingly bogged down in Ukraine.

World leaders want to strengthen control over AI, while Trump is betting on &quot;superintelligence&quot; - media

World leaders want to strengthen oversight of AI, while Trump is betting on "superintelligence" - media
Kyiv • UNN
UN leaders call for stronger oversight of AI and the creation of global safeguards. Trump opposes regulation and supports the term "superintelligence".
Artificial intelligence has become one of the main topics of the UN General Assembly following cases in which the technology escaped human control, while warnings from industry representatives sparked global alarm and calls for stronger state oversight of the sector. Euronews reports, writes UNN.
Details
UN Secretary-General António Guterres opened the speeches by world leaders at the General Assembly with a call for stronger oversight of AI, issuing a vivid, though somewhat grim, warning about what could go wrong.
Let us agree that decisions on which life and death depend must never be delegated to machines. Killer robots must have no place in our future
He had also warned about AI in his first address to the General Assembly ten years ago.
Saying that the world needs to "create the conditions for the responsible development of AI and the additional safeguards needed to counter the risks," the UN will discuss at the Security Council on Wednesday how to establish a degree of control over the technology. Some of the industry's best-known representatives will take part in the meeting.
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump reaffirmed his firm opposition to AI regulation, saying that the word "artificial" diminishes the significance of the technology, and expressing hope that the rest of the world would adopt the new term.
"Super Intelligence" "sounds much better" and is "much more accurate," he said.
Trump wants to rename artificial intelligence as "superintelligence"22.09.26, 19:15 • 4252 views
He also compared warnings from AI safety advocates with warnings about climate change, whose anthropogenic nature is confirmed by the overwhelming majority of the scientific community.
Other countries call for safeguards
Ahead of the UN General Assembly, leaders of more than 20 predominantly European countries called for mandatory safety measures for advanced AI, warning that the development of the technology could outpace people's ability to control it.
China and the United States, the global leaders in AI, did not support the idea.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that during the UK's presidency of the G20 in 2027, the country would begin work on establishing global standards in the field of AI. He also announced a partnership with Washington in the defense sector aimed at detecting cyberattacks on critical infrastructure.
French President Emmanuel Macron proposed creating AI technology independent of the major powers.
I do not want anyone to become a vassal of one of the major powers. Our investment capabilities must be pooled to create an advanced open-source AI model that we can share. We must not depend on anyone else
The American tech giants themselves are increasingly calling for global coordination on AI safety issues. Sam Altman of OpenAI is expected to address the UN Security Council on Wednesday.
France, which holds the presidency of the Security Council this month, initiated the meeting, believing that the threat posed by AI to international peace and security has so far been insufficiently discussed at the UN.

Control of space will decide this century, says Streeting
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
07:43:59 BST
15:43:59 KST

Control of space will determine security in this century in the way that control of the seas did in the nineteenth and control of the air did in the twentieth, the Defence Secretary will say today in a keynote address to the first UK Space Power Conference.
Wes Streeting is due to address the conference as the Royal Air Force announces the formation of No. III Space Effects Squadron, its first unit dedicated to disrupting, degrading and denying hostile activity in orbit.
He will say: “Britain has to keep pace in the new space race. Control of the waves was the essential ingredient in 19th century deterrence. That is why Britain built the finest naval power in history. In the 20th century it was control of the skies, and so we built a world class air force to protect us. This century will depend on control of space.”
On why the domain has become contested, he will say: “Our dependency on space is precisely why it is increasingly under threat from our adversaries. That threat is growing in scale, speed, and sophistication. And challenges in space increasingly mirror the geopolitics on Earth.”
Setting out what he takes his own responsibility to be, he will say: “My job is to make sure that our deterrence in space is as strong as it is on Earth, and to modernise our armed forces so that they are ready to deter and, if necessary, defeat any adversary, in any domain.”
The comparison he draws carries an implication about scale, given that Britain built the Royal Navy and then the Royal Air Force as the principal instruments of national defence in their respective eras, and applying that logic to space invites a question about how large a space force the argument requires, against current investment of £880 million between 2026/27 and 2029/30 in space-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance and space control activities.
That sum forms part of the £7.8 billion committed to space until 2030 in the UK Space Strategy published earlier this month, of which more than £3 billion is directed at defence capabilities in orbit. The strategy also allocated £2.8 billion towards connectivity including the SKYNET military satellite communications programme, and £149 million to the European Space Agency’s Vigil mission alongside £85 million for the National Space Operations Centre.
Streeting said at the time that national security depends on freedom of action in space and, if necessary, the ability to protect British and allied space assets, and that as threats in orbit grow more sophisticated so must the ability to detect and respond to them.
The Strategic Defence Review stated that the ability to operate in, from and through space underpins British security, prosperity and daily way of life, and the department says challenges in the domain increasingly mirror those on Earth as hostile states develop capabilities to jam, disrupt or disable space assets.
Britain has formally ruled out destructive anti-satellite missile testing and continues to work through the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space on norms of responsible behaviour in orbit.

Techritory 2026 in Riga to explore ways to protect Europe’s data and digital infrastructure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
06:43:50 UTC
15:43:50 KST

Europe’s ability to control and protect its data, digital services and critical infrastructure has become an economic and security issue. More than a thousand technology leaders, entrepreneurs, experts and policymakers will discuss ways to strengthen Europe’s digital sovereignty at Techritory 2026, the ninth digitalisation and connectivity forum, held at ATTA Centre in Riga on 21–22 October.
This year’s forum theme is “Security and Prosperity Through Digitalization and Connectivity”. European countries and businesses remain significantly dependent on technology platforms, cloud services and digital infrastructure developed outside Europe. Data, cloud services, artificial intelligence, connectivity and digital identity have also become part of the infrastructure underpinning the economy and national security. Digital sovereignty therefore extends beyond the technology sector: it shapes Europe’s ability to protect critical services, society and the economy, while retaining the freedom to act during crises.
“European digital sovereignty means genuine control over critically important data and services. Global cloud services can be part of a company’s infrastructure, but they need to be complemented by local or regional primary or backup infrastructure that is not only located in Europe but also owned by European companies. This reduces geopolitical risks, improves transparency and preserves the ability to move between solutions. In Europe, including Latvia, we have the knowledge and capability to build advanced infrastructure ourselves for artificial intelligence and other business needs,” says Andris Gailītis, Chairman of the Board of DELSKA.
The forum programme will focus on the development of data centres across Europe, defence technologies, digital sovereignty and resilience, the future of European digital network regulation, satellite connectivity and cybersecurity. Separate discussions will examine Latvia’s opportunities to increase exports of digital services and become an important European partner in data, connectivity and security infrastructure.
Participants in Techritory 2026 will include Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs; OECD Deputy Secretary-General Yasushi Masaki; Tomas Lamanauskas, Deputy Secretary-General of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU); Michelle Iliev, State Secretary at Moldova’s Ministry of Economic Development and Digitalization; DELSKA CEO Andris Gailītis; LMT Group President Juris Binde; Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braže; Latvian Minister of Smart Administration and Regional Development Edgars Tavars; and other senior representatives of the public and private sectors.
Techritory 2025 attracted 2,098 participants from 63 countries in person and online, including 883 who attended in person. More than 100 speakers took part in the event.
Attendance is free. The forum’s working language is English, and advance registration is required at techritory.com.
Techritory 2026, the digitalisation and connectivity forum, will take place for the ninth time this year. It is organised by SIA Elektroniskie sakari. Its strategic partners are SIA Latvijas Mobilais Telefons, the Nordic Council of Ministers, SIA DELSKA and the Ministry of Smart Administration and Regional Development.

Russia is “setting the stage” to annex Georgia’s breakaway region of South Ossetia, with Moscow’s calculations increasingly tied to uncertainty over the future of its military base in Armenia, a Senior Associate at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace think tank has told TVP World.
Paul Goble, a former CIA analyst and longtime specialist on Russia and the former Soviet Union, was speaking to TVP World’s Eastern Express after Moscow-backed authorities held a presidential election in South Ossetia.

Armenia changes the calculation

Estonian MFA: Rumors of impending Russian attack blown out of proportion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
06:39:00 UTC
15:39:00 KST

Estonian MFA: Rumors of impending Russian attack blown out of proportion
Recent media reports suggesting an imminent Russian attack on NATO and the Baltic states are unfounded, Foreign Ministry Secretary General Jonatan Vseviov said.
European Union countries will extend sanctions against Moscow, but under pressure from several member states, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman will be removed from the blacklist. This means the two Russian billionaires may soon once again be able to operate more freely in Europe.
Foreign Ministry Secretary General Jonatan Vseviov said the choice was inevitably between a bad decision and an even worse one.
"With regard to these two individuals, this is certainly a failure, but that failure was the price that had to be paid to keep the other 3,000 names under sanctions. Estonia, of course, opposed removing these two names from the list, but as in real life, we do not make choices between good and bad options, but between bad and even worse ones," Vseviov said.
By Tuesday evening, Estonia had added Usmanov and Fridman to its own sanctions list. One positive aspect of the situation, however, is that sanctions that previously applied for six months will now remain in force for three years. According to Vseviov, the decision provides certainty that a similar dispute will not have to be fought again for some time.
"This is quite an important victory. It does not mean that our battles are over. We are now immediately going to start considering the next sanctions. Kaja Kallas has proposed adding around another 1,600 people to the lists and I have no doubt that those battles will sometimes be just as dirty as they were this time. But we will not give in and will go as far as we possibly can. The main objective is to ensure that the price of aggression continues to rise and, unfortunately, the reality is that in this process you sometimes have to choose between bad and even worse options," the Foreign Ministry secretary general said.
Vseviov said that, in the bigger picture, the most important objective is to inflict pain on Russia and increase the cost of its aggression.
"In this case, it was clear that if we had allowed the decision to fall through — and every one of the 27 member states has that option — then today we would not be discussing just two people being released from sanctions, but all 3,000 of them. That was something we did not even want to consider, so while the situation is bad, in the bigger picture sanctions on the other 3,000 people are now in place for three years. Those countries that demanded political exemptions will certainly hear a great deal more about this. I very much hope they also hear these questions from their own journalists and have to explain themselves why they did what they did — let them explain it," Vseviov said.
Vseviov was critical of the Russian elections held over the weekend, but noted that there had been concern within the Kremlin.
"Those elections were, of course, about as far removed from elections as anything can possibly be. For some reason, however, Russia's leadership was deeply concerned about them, was tense and worked intensely to ensure that the result was exactly what the scriptwriters had envisioned," Vseviov said, adding that Russia may now return to issues that it had previously not dared to address.
"Of course, keeping an authoritarian state's boat on course, or simply keeping it afloat, is not merely a matter of getting through election day. Dictators are generally afraid — they are afraid because there are no guarantees of any kind, because laws do not apply and there is no rule of law. The regime's power and stability more broadly simply rest on its strength. If the perception emerges that it does not have enough strength, absolutely everything can collapse at any moment. That is something that can never happen in democracies," Vseviov said.
According to Vseviov, Putin's regime wobbles every day as the country's fuel shortages, the continuation of the war in Ukraine and Ukrainian long-range strikes directly on the Russian capital Moscow undermine the dictator's image.
In recent weeks, however, there has been a great deal of media discussion about a Russian attack on NATO, which the secretary general said is the result of various circumstances coming together.
"Although Russia ultimately seeks, of course, to change the entire European security architecture, its top priority at present is still resolving the Ukraine issue. It very much needs to turn European countries against one another or paralyze us with fear — in any case, to divert us from the Ukraine policy we have pursued so far. Fear can infect us in many ways," Vseviov said.
According to the secretary general, a bombshell story about an imminent attack sells better and it is also possible that the views of well-intentioned people, analysts or political scientists have simply been taken out of context.
"But when you look at the narrative that has emerged from all this, you find facts that are true in themselves but have been blown completely out of proportion. For example, Russia makes some adjustments on the other side of the Narva River and now everyone across NATO is losing their heads and hyperventilating over it. Or claims are made that every one of us knows are untrue. For example, that Lithuania is currently making actual preparations to evacuate the population of Vilnius to Poland. These claims appear side by side and no one really delves that deeply into each specific, separate fact, but the overall narrative is one that leaves people breathless," Vseviov said, adding that there is no reason to believe Russia is about to attack NATO countries.
"I am pleased to confirm that there is absolutely no reason to believe that Russia is imminently going to launch a military attack on NATO, Estonia or the Baltic states. We can see beyond our borders. It is somewhat surprising to find ourselves, as representatives of Estonia, in a situation where, after years of explaining to our Western colleagues that Russia poses a strategic threat — and I assure you, it remains a strategic threat because it wants to fundamentally change the way Europe is organized — we now have to tell them: listen, friends, calm down, keep a cool head and breathe normally," Vseviov said.
The secretary general said there is no benefit in panicking or becoming paralyzed by fear. Instead, the situation should be assessed calmly and consideration given to what can be done.
"People talk about what happens if Russia tests NATO's collective defense. Well, what then? We need to make sure we successfully pass every conceivable test. And this is not a communications exercise where we think about how best to arrange our words. It is a question of where our forces are, what our readiness is and whether our allies remain politically and militarily united with us, including in other areas. These are practical matters that can be worked on and that is the work we are doing. So to everyone who is worried, I say: let's not worry, let's act instead," Vseviov stressed.
"If a situation arises in which we really do have to cry wolf, you can be absolutely certain that Estonia will do so. We do not intend to consider the option of silent surrender even in theory," Vseviov said.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski, Johanna Alvin

Minab schoolchildren send message to US students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
06:38:53 UTC
15:38:53 KST

The ceremony took place on the morning of the start of the school year in Minab county, at the site of the Shajareh Tayyebeh school. One student from the county read the letter on behalf of all Minab students.
Here is the full text of the letter:
Dear students in America,
We don't know your names, and you don't know ours. But as you begin another school year, we wanted to write to you, student to student, before anything else gets in the way.
All of us know the feeling of the first day of school: a new notebook, the smell of unused pages, seeing friends again. We imagine your first days feel much the same — a little nervous, a little excited. These are small things. But they are what make a childhood feel safe.
On February 28, one of our schools did not get to have that ordinary day. Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in Minab was full of children just like you, sitting at their desks, when it was struck in a military attack. More than 120 children never went home. In total, across the recent wars our country has endured, 277 students never got to finish their education. Their notebooks are still on their desks in some homes.
We are not writing to make you feel guilty. You did not choose this, just as we did not. We are writing because we believe you deserve to know what happened to children your own age, in a place you may have only heard about on the news — if at all.
We have one simple question: shouldn't a school always be a safe place? In every country, a classroom is supposed to be one of the safest places in the world for a child. That is not political. It is something all of us, as students, should agree on without argument: children in war must never be targets. Striking a school is not a strategy — it is a crime. The United Nations itself has said there are reasonable grounds to believe war crimes were committed in the attacks on our schools.
We ask you to sit with that question for a moment — not to feel sad for us, but to ask whether it could ever be justified. We believe the answer is no.
We also want to ask something else, gently: get to know us — not through headlines, but through history. Iran is one of the oldest civilizations on Earth, home to poets like Hafez and Rumi, to ancient cities that were centers of learning, to a culture of hospitality and family that has endured for thousands of years. We are not only a headline about war. If you ever get the chance to study a country beyond your own, we hope you'll learn about ours — not the Iran distorted by American media and politicians, but the Iran of Persepolis and poetry, of children who, just like you, love their school and their future.
Today, our school bells are ringing again. We are returning to rebuilt classrooms, to seats some of our classmates should have filled. It isn't easy. But we choose to return, because that is what our friends would have wanted for us.
Wherever you are, whenever your bell rings this year, we hope you'll think — just for a moment — of children far away who deserved, as much as you do, the safety to simply be students.
With hope for a world where no school is ever a target again,
The students of Minab, Iran

====================================================================================================

Could Europe’s start-ups help solve the power problems created by the AI boom?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
06:38:49 UTC
15:38:49 KST

Euronews Next looked at startups in Europe that are trying to make better use of existing grid capacity, reduce the electricity used for cooling and put waste heat to work.
Europe’s push to build its own artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure is intensifying a debate over whether its electricity system can keep pace.
Data-centre electricity consumption across the continent is projected to rise from 96 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2024 to 236 TWh by 2035, according to UK-based energy think tank Ember.
Europe needs more data centres to expand its AI capacity, but they add further demand to already strained electricity grids. That power crunch is, in turn, making it harder to connect and build new facilities.
But some startups in Europe are pitching ways to tackle the region’s power crunch.
Euronews Next took a look at their efforts to reduce the electricity used for cooling, manage demand with batteries and put waste heat to use.
Startups rethink cooling with sensors, simulations and liquid
Servers generate a lot of heat, which must be removed to stop them from overheating.
Rather than relying on cooling equipment alone, UK startup EkkoSense places wireless sensors inside data-centre rooms to monitor temperature, airflow, power and cooling capacity.
Its software turns the readings into a three-dimensional view, helping operators identify equipment receiving too much or too little cooling.
In 2024, EkkoSense deployed its system across 20 data-centre sites operated by Virgin Media O2, one of the UK’s largest telecommunications companies.
The system cut cooling energy by an average of 15%, according to Virgin Media O2, saving more than £1 million (about €1,166,588) annually and the equivalent of 760 tonnes of carbon dioxide under location-based accounting.
While EkkoSense watches what is happening inside the room, German startup etalytics recreates the cooling system in a simulation.
Its software tests how chillers, pumps and heat exchangers would perform under different conditions. It then calculates how they could operate while using less electricity and keeping temperatures within safe limits.
Last year, Japanese technology company NTT tested etalytics’ simulation software at its data-centre facility in Bonn.
The electricity used by its chillers fell by 19.1% during the first months of a trial, with NTT expecting savings to reach as much as 25% over a full year.
Spanish startup Submer takes a different approach by changing the cooling hardware itself.
Its systems immerse servers in a non-conductive liquid that carries heat away directly, reducing the need for energy-intensive fans and air conditioning.
“The solution developed by Submer uses a new liquid cooling technique to increase energy efficiency by up to 50%, reduce carbon emissions from the use of refrigerant gases, reduce the footprint and improve the total cost of ownership (TCO) of data centres,” said Submer’s client Spanish telecommunications company Telefónica, in a blog post.
Software gives data-centre batteries a second job
Data centres use batteries to keep servers running during an outage. Some startups are now using those same batteries to help manage when a facility draws electricity from the grid.
Irish energy-technology company GridBeyond has developed software that controls when batteries charge and discharge in response to conditions on the electricity network.
The batteries can charge when electricity is abundant. When demand rises, they can supply some of the facility’s power, reducing the amount it needs to draw from the grid at that moment.
Its software has been installed at two Dublin data centres owned by Singaporean company Keppel DC REIT, providing a combined 8 MW of flexible capacity, according to GridBeyond.
Turning server heat into heating
Other startups are focusing on the heat produced by computing equipment.
UK start-up Deep Green places compact computing facilities next to organisations that need heat, such as swimming pools and district-heating networks.
Liquid warmed by the servers carries that heat into the neighbouring building’s heating system.
In a trial in southwest England, Deep Green told a local newspaper that donating heat to a swimming pool would cut its gas use by 62%, save more than £20,000 (about €23,331) a year and reduce its annual carbon emissions by 25.8 tonnes.
"By moving data centres from industrial warehouses into the hearts of communities, our ‘digital boilers’ put waste heat to good use, saving local businesses thousands of pounds on energy bills and reducing their carbon footprint,” Mark Bjornsgaard, CEO of Deep Green, told Exmouth Journal.
"Pools are just the start and around 30% of all industrial and commercial heat needs could be provided by this technology."
However, greater efficiency and flexibility cannot replace physical expansion. As AI demand grows, Europe will ultimately need more electricity generation and stronger grids.
According to the International Energy Agency, new grid infrastructure can take between five and 15 years to plan, approve and complete.
Still, the work of these startups could ease pressure on Europe’s power system while that infrastructure is being built.

IDF probes suspected Haredi draft-dodging scheme using mental health exemptions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
06:38:48 UTC
15:38:48 KST

The IDF is examining what military officials describe as a recurring method for obtaining exemptions from military service on mental health grounds, after identifying dozens of requests linked to the same clinics and psychiatrists and containing similar wording and reasoning.
According to information gathered by the military, the psychiatrists involved have signed dozens of documents recommending exemptions. The requests are then submitted through law offices rather than directly to the IDF.
The military says the phenomenon has increased since draft orders were sent to all eligible Haredi men and as arrests and other sanctions connected to draft avoidance have intensified.
Against that backdrop, the IDF has begun discussions with the Health Ministry over suspicions that psychiatrists may be helping young men prepare professional opinions recommending military exemptions even when they do not actually meet the relevant criteria.
The military is also expected to discuss the matter with police.
Yedioth Ahronoth and ynet previously reported that organizations opposed to Haredi enlistment have advised young men receiving draft orders to consider seeking exemptions on mental health grounds. Those groups have also told them that information provided to the IDF would not be passed on to other authorities and therefore would not affect their ability to obtain a driver’s license, pursue studies or find employment later.
Similar wording, same submission pattern
The IDF says it identified a pattern both in the wording of the psychiatric opinions and in the way they were submitted.
Military officials also stress that the phenomenon is not limited to the Haredi community.
Because the IDF does not have enforcement authority over civilian actors, it has approached the Health Ministry and police and asked them to examine whether an investigation should be opened.
The military has also changed the procedure for submitting psychiatric opinions following a separate phenomenon in which documents seeking exemptions were submitted on behalf of prospective recruits by someone else.
According to the IDF Spokesperson’s Unit, the protocol for granting an exemption from service on mental health grounds is based on professional standards. The documents are reviewed by a professional and classified for further handling according to medical criteria.
The military says the screening system was designed to streamline the process, shorten waiting times and avoid harming prospective recruits who genuinely suffer from mental health problems.
IDF warns psychiatrists over suspected false opinions
The IDF says it is also aware of cases in which prospective recruits received exemptions without their knowledge after documents were submitted in their names.
According to the military, Medical Corps officials have held warning conversations with psychiatrists suspected of providing false opinions, and broader warning notices have also been distributed to psychiatrists.
Military professionals are also in regular contact with several Haredi organizations working to combat the phenomenon. The IDF says those groups provide reports about psychiatrists suspected of issuing false opinions and cooperate with the military in handling individual cases.
Following the discovery of such cases, the IDF issued a directive allowing a prospective recruit who challenges a false psychiatric opinion submitted on his behalf to move immediately from an exemption to medical profile 97, based solely on an examination by a military psychiatrist.
The change is intended to allow prospective recruits who say a false opinion was submitted for them to cancel the exemption and enlist as quickly as possible.
“The phenomenon of opinions that do not correspond to a prospective recruit’s medical condition and are submitted in the names of prospective recruits is known and is being addressed by the IDF,” the military said.
“In addition, the IDF is cooperating with Israel Police in order to eradicate the phenomenon.”

Estonia Probes Sabotage After Fire at Building Used by Milrem Robotics
Latvia has handed over to Estonia three Latvian nationals suspected of setting fire to a Tallinn building used by defense company Milrem Robotics, and a court has ordered all three detained.
This was reported by Estonian public broadcaster ERR on its official website on September 22. According to ERR, the handover took place at the end of the previous week.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
State Prosecutor Gardi Anderson told ERR that Estonia's Internal Security Service (KAPO) questioned the suspects before they were brought before Harju County Court. Based on the evidence collected so far and the questioning, the judge found their detention justified, Anderson explained.
"At present, they are suspected under the section on damaging and destroying property, but this may change during the investigation," the prosecutor stated.
Anderson added that prosecutors have spent the past month working with the Police and Border Guard Board and KAPO, ERR reported. The aim was to establish the circumstances that led to the arson and identify the suspects.
The prosecutor emphasized that evidence gathering remains ongoing and that sabotage is one of several versions under examination, not an established finding. "We are checking all versions, including whether it was sabotage," Anderson told the broadcaster.
Milrem Robotics, majority-owned by the UAE defense group EDGE, is an Estonian manufacturer of autonomous and unmanned ground vehicles.
Its unmanned ground systems have been delivered to Ukraine for battlefield logistics, reconnaissance, and explosive ordnance tasks. In June, the company launched a production line in the Netherlands, with Dutch funding covering 100 additional vehicles for Ukraine.
The building on Betooni Street in Tallinn's Lasnamäe district caught fire over the weekend in August, ERR noted. After the incident, Prime Minister Kristen Michal stated that the state was investigating the theory that Russia was behind the arson.
Now that the suspects are in Estonia, investigators will continue to collect and analyze evidence, Anderson indicated in comments to ERR.
The handover caps an investigation that began in August, when the fire broke out overnight into a Saturday after a local resident had reported suspicious activity near the site. No one was injured.
By August 18, Estonian authorities had identified suspects and requested their arrest, with prosecutors leading the case while the Internal Security Service and the North Prefecture examined the circumstances.
Michal warned at the time that if the arson was intended to intimidate Estonia or to end its support for Ukraine, it would not succeed.

US President Donald Trump confronted CNN journalist Kaitlan Collins at the United Nations on Tuesday, questioning why she was covering his appearance days after his administration barred CNN and two other major news organisations from the White House.
“You should not be here covering me. You said you weren’t going to cover me. You shouldn’t be covering me,” Trump told Collins at UN headquarters in New York.
Collins responded that CNN had been credentialed by the United Nations to cover the 81st General Assembly.
She had asked Trump when the war on Iran would end, prompting his response before the exchange turned to the media-access dispute.
Later, Trump criticised Collins and CNN in a post on Truth Social, accusing the network and its journalists of being overly focused on his presidency and using disparaging language against them.
UN credentials remain separate from White House access
The confrontation came after the Trump administration revoked press access for journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico, preventing them from entering the White House complex.
The three outlets filed a federal lawsuit on Monday challenging the restrictions, arguing that the move violates First Amendment protections for freedom of the press.
A federal court hearing on their request for temporary relief is scheduled in Washington.
The outlets have continued covering Trump outside the White House, including his UN appearance, using United Nations credentials rather than White House credentials.
The distinction was central to Tuesday’s confrontation, as CNN journalists remained authorised to report from the General Assembly despite the separate White House restrictions.
Media standoff moves into the courts
The dispute has widened beyond the three affected outlets. Major television networks suspended participation in the White House television pool after CNN was excluded, disrupting a system used to distribute live presidential coverage to news organisations.
Trump has defended the White House restrictions, accusing the targeted outlets of publishing what he describes as false or misleading reports.
On Tuesday, he also indicated he would probably restore their access if a court ruled against his administration.
The legal battle now puts the administration’s control over White House access and the press’s constitutional protections at the centre of the dispute, with the court proceedings expected to shape the next stage of the confrontation.

Finnish President Alexander Stubb said Ukraine is in a stronger position militarily, politically and financially than it was a year ago, arguing that Russia is not winning the war and that the next step should be bringing Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table.
Speaking to Bloomberg Talks, Stubb said peace negotiations had recently resumed, with US presidential envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff traveling to Moscow before heading to Kyiv. He said the renewed diplomatic activity could lead to a partial ceasefire before winter.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I think we’re in a much better place in general than we were a year ago,” Stubb said in an interview, published Wednesday, Sept. 23, adding that Ukraine is currently “on top” on the battlefield.
Stubb argued that Russia is failing to make decisive territorial gains despite continuing its offensive.
“This year the Russians have acquired 900 kilometers (560 miles) of land from Ukraine. But Ukraine has taken 800 km (500 miles) back,” he said, describing the situation on the ground as a stalemate in terms of territorial gains.
He also cited what he described as a current “killing ratio” of one Ukrainian soldier to five Russian soldiers, while acknowledging that the comparison was “morbid.”
“So I think the message that we have to the Russians is that listen, you guys are not going to win this. So let’s try to end it,” Stubb said. “Zelensky wants peace. Trump wants peace and now we need to get Putin to the peace table.”
Europe Warned It Is Running Out of Time to Prepare for Wider War With Russia
Stubb backs reciprocal energy ceasefire
Stubb also addressed Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries and Moscow’s calls for a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure. He said any agreement to stop attacks on energy infrastructure would need to be mutual.
“If Ukraine doesn’t hit oil refineries, then Russia should not hit energy and electricity installations in Ukraine, especially as winter is coming,” Stubb said.
He acknowledged that Russia’s record in such arrangements has been poor, adding that Moscow continues to strike Ukrainian targets while Ukraine has focused some of its long-range attacks on Russian oil refineries and logistics centers.
Stubb said he understood the reasoning behind Ukraine’s attacks, describing Russian oil refineries and logistics centers as important sources of revenue and support for Russia’s war effort.
Ukraine needs air defense, energy support and money
Stubb said Ukraine’s immediate needs remain largely unchanged from those he outlined during a NATO meeting in July: air defense, support for energy infrastructure ahead of winter, and financial assistance.
“There are three things that Ukraine needs. One is air defense and second one is energy installations for the winter and the third one is money,” he said.
Finland recently provided a package worth about €300 million ($343 million), which Stubb said was focused on critical air defense, but he acknowledged that more support would be necessary.
He specifically pointed to the need for Patriot and other anti-ballistic systems, saying countries that possess such systems should help Ukraine.
Stubb was also asked about efforts to allow Ukraine to produce Patriot missiles domestically. He said he did not have the latest information because he had not yet spoken with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky following his latest meeting with US President Donald Trump.
However, Stubb said he viewed meetings between Trump and Zelensky positively because they allow the US president to receive a direct assessment of the battlefield and Ukraine’s needs.
Trump could take stronger role in negotiations
Stubb said Trump’s decision to allow his negotiators to become involved again in the peace process could indicate that the US president is preparing to take a stronger role in negotiations.
“The president of the United States is extremely active,” Stubb said, adding that Trump is simultaneously dealing with issues in the Western Hemisphere, domestic politics, the Middle East and Ukraine.
“But it seems to me that he’s of course allowing his negotiators to get involved again, which would indicate to me as well that President Trump will take an even stronger role now in the peace negotiation,” he said.

India news: El Nino heat could kill 15,800 by Feb — report
September 23, 2026
What you need to know
- El Nino-driven heat could cause nearly 16,000 deaths in India by February, a new Climate Impact Lab report says
- Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi to visit Canada in December, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says
Here are the biggest headlines from India on Wednesday, September 23:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
El Nino-driven heat could kill thousands in India by February: report
This year's powerful El Nino phenomenon, which is driving global heat to record levels and contributing to severe droughts, wildfires and water shortages, is likely to cause 15,800 deaths in India by the end of February, according to a research report released on Wednesday.
The warning, released by the University of Chicago-based Climate Impact Lab, said as many as 451,000 more deaths between June and February of next year could be attributed to El Nino, when compared to typical heat-related deaths in a year.
El Nino is a natural climate phenomenon that occurs every two to seven years, toward the end of the year. It comes in various strengths — depending on the prevailing conditions.
El Nino patterns are considered strong if the surface temperature of the water off the west coast of South America is over 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above average. In July this year, the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) was already observing temperature increases ofgreater than 3 degrees Celsius in the eastern and central Pacific.
The Climate Impact Lab report said the powerful heat this year was most dangerous in places that are already hot and relatively poor. It projected that the Global South will see more heat-related deaths.
What could help prevent deaths?
Heat warnings, hydration outreach, cooling centers and a plan to cope with the heat are all ways governments can help protect people, the report said, adding that they should also expand hospital capacity and chalk out anticipatory financing.
Abhiyant Tiwari, a heat expert at NRDC India who was not involved in the study, said the report's projections should serve as a call to action rather than be another reason for alarm.
But while it's one thing to have well thought-out plans — as India does — implementing these plans remains a challenge, he said.
"The real measure of our preparedness is not how many heat warnings we issue, but how effectively we protect people and reduce preventable deaths," Tiwari said.
Welcome to our coverage!
Hello! and welcome to DW's India new blog.
This is Mahima Kapoor reporting from the national capital, where the mood is somber, even a little angry, over the recent incidents of alleged rape against minors and women.
A minor was reportedly gang-raped near a temple in southeast Delhi on Monday evening and the authorities have arrested at least one of the three accused. Today, a renowned women's college in the vicinity said it would switch to online classes to keep students safe.
Continuing on the somber front, a new report by the Climate Impact Lab said that El Nino-driven heat could kill over 450,000 people across the world by the end of February and that nearly 16,000 of those are projected to be from India.

The 'EU Kids Act' targets addictive apps to protect children online
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
06:33:21 UTC
15:33:21 KST

The European Commission has proposed a single EU-wide rulebook to govern how children experience social media, video platforms, games and AI chatbots. Watch the video!
President Ursula von der Leyen first announced the "EU Kids Act" during her State of the Union address.
The Act, officially presented on September 17, responds to a patchwork of protections across the bloc, like no common minimum age for social media, addictive features like infinite scroll and autoplay, and inconsistent or missing age checks.
The proposal centres on "safety by design," requiring platforms to prove their products are safe before children use them. It splits childhood into bands: 3- to 13-year-olds get only child-friendly platforms under adult supervision; 13- to 15-year-olds get restricted, feature-limited access with parental controls; and 15- to 18-year-olds have full access under continued safety rules.
National rules, like France's push to restrict under-15s, would remain, though Paris wants Brussels to harmonise them. Enforcement would follow the Digital Services Act, with Brussels policing major platforms directly and funding this through supervisory fees.

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,522,440 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
06:32:54 UTC
15:32:54 KST

Russia has lost around 1,522,440 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Sept. 23.
The number includes 1,560 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,367 tanks, 25,387 armored combat vehicles, 152,553 vehicles and fuel tanks, 50,216 artillery systems, 2,152 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,665 air defense systems, 442 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,723 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs).
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

Eleven killed in South Africa as gunmen open fire on Durban homestead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
06:30:34 UTC
15:30:34 KST

The attackers forced the victims into a single room before opening fire, leaving only two survivors and a community in shock.
Eleven people, among them a pregnant woman, were shot dead late on Tuesday when armed men burst into a house in a township in Durban, South Africa, provincial officials said.
The victims had gathered at the homestead shortly before 11pm (local time) when the attackers entered and began shooting, according to Thamsanqa Ntuli, premier of KwaZulu-Natal, the province whose largest city is Durban.
Speaking to AFP on Wednesday, Ntuli said two people survived. Police have not yet identified a motive.
Ntuli said the killings had left residents "in profound shock and grief."
South African broadcaster eNCA reported that the gunmen herded everyone into a single room before opening fire, and torched a car belonging to one of the victims.
One resident told the channel he had grown up with some of those killed and had never seen anything like it in the area, likening the scene to something out of a film.
Mass shootings are a recurring feature of violent crime in South Africa, where both legally held and illegal guns are widespread. Attacks are frequently linked to gang feuds or to disputes between competing informal businesses.
The country has one of the highest murder rates in the world, with roughly 60 people killed every day in a population of about 62 million.
President Cyril Ramaphosa has called crime one of the gravest threats facing the nation, and in March soldiers were sent to violence hotspots nationwide to reinforce the police.

Art professor: Only dictators have erected triumphal arches in the past century
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
06:29:00 UTC
15:29:00 KST

Art professor: Only dictators have erected triumphal arches in the past century
Estonian Academy of Arts professor and architectural historian Mart Kalm told ERR that the era of building triumphal arches is over and that the U.S. president's desire to build one offers a glimpse into his aspirations.
Kalm noted that building triumphal arches is a tradition dating back to ancient Rome. "In fact, they began erecting them in Rome as early as the Roman Republic (sixth to first centuries B.C.). It was a gate-shaped monument through which an army returning victorious to Rome would pass, along with its spoils of war, slaves, animals and everything else," Kalm explained.
U.S. President Donald Trump recently confirmed his plans to build a triumphal arch in Washington, D.C.
"To tell the truth, the era of building triumphal arches is essentially over. The last ones may have gone up around a hundred years ago and since then only dictators have built them. Trump apparently just has this dream of becoming an emperor, but he ended up in the wrong country: a republic. He would like to be an emperor and that seems to be the thinking behind it. The initial designs synthesize elements from all sorts of different triumphal arches."
The arch is planned to stand 86 meters (282 feet) tall, a few meters taller than the Olümpia Hotel in Tallinn. "Distances are so vast in Washington that it is understandable, in terms of proportion, that something that large could be there. I understand the logic, although of course it is pointless gigantomania. If you've already got that affliction, at least this is a professional solution," Kalm said.
Kalm considers the Arc de Triomphe in Paris the most famous triumphal arch. "And with good reason! Do you know of any wars Trump has won? Napoleon had plenty of military victories. Later, of course, everything went the other way and half of Europe is full of triumphal arches inspired by victories over Napoleon."
One of the most recent arches is in North Korea. "It was erected to commemorate the struggle against Japan. It was built in 1982 by a thoroughly authoritarian regime, although Russia is trying to give them some semblance of legitimacy. The fact that this is one of the newest arches also shows who Trump wants to be like," Kalm emphasized.
The Estonian Academy of Arts professor also noted that building an arch has been considered in Estonia as well. "Architect Edgar Kuusik, in 1944, before the end of the war when the Russians were already here, designed a victory monument to the Soviet army. It was to be built next to the Tallinn Art Hall, which Kuusik himself had designed 10 years earlier, on the site of St. John's Church in Freedom Square. Can you imagine that the same man who came up with something so insane was a recipient of Estonia's Cross of Liberty?" Kalm said.
--
Editor: Neit-Eerik Nestor, Marcus Turovski,
Source: "Ringvaade"
