====================================================================================================

Glimpses into lives of Roman surburbanites in Bath revealed in rare finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
06:00:19 UTC
15:00:19 KST

The restoration of a Georgian building in Bath once frequented by Jane Austen has unexpectedly provided a tantalising glimpse into the life of the city’s Roman suburbanites.
A network of Roman ditches containing pottery, coins, glassware and a fragment of a military helmet has been found beneath Bath Assembly Rooms in the north of the city.
Experts say the finds expand the known extent of Roman occupation in Bath and suggest further remains are likely to lie under neighbouring Georgian buildings and streets.
The Roman baths that give the city its modern name are one of the best preserved ancient sites in northern Europe, attracting more than 1 million visitors a year.
Previous archaeological finds have revealed that in Roman times there were suburbs around the baths complex and, further away, comfortable country villas.
But relatively little had been found in an area north of the city, partly because the city’s Georgian buildings and streets are so solid – and well-protected by conservation laws – that the sort of construction project that might unearth remains rarely takes place.
Marek Lewcun, of Wessex Archaeology, said this made it all the more exciting when Roman artefacts were discovered beneath Bath Assembly Rooms. “There was a gap in our knowledge and this helps fill in a missing link,” he said.
Lewcun said the finds suggested the residents of this part of Bath were the sort that might live in the outskirts of a modern city: “So we’re probably looking at the ordinary folk that you might find in a modern suburb today, people who had small shops supplying pottery, bread, things like that.
“We are looking at people who had gradually integrated with those who had come from all over the Roman empire. Before they arrived we were living in mud huts, more or less. We’ve gone from that to living in buildings that have got roofs, heating, water.”
Lewcun said people with more money or status, such as retired military leaders, were probably living further up the hill in villas. “That may have been the equivalent of retiring to somewhere in the sun today.”
The archaeologists found almost 60 fragments of Roman pottery, glass vessels, animal bones, roof tiles, Roman coins and a limestone tessera which may once have formed part of a mosaic floor.
Among the most intriguing discoveries was a fragment of a Roman military helmet. This is seen as further evidence that military personnel were involved in the construction of the settlement. A slot for a beam was also found, showing that a Roman building had once stood here.
Lewcun and the team were helped by the fact that the builders of Bath Assembly Rooms in the late 18th century did not create deep foundations, knowing the thick clay was strong enough to support the structure. It meant the Roman ditches were left untouched for the 21st-century archaeologists to probe.
The bath complex was built by the Romans around mineral-rich hot springs after the defeat of the British queen Boudica in AD60 and 61.
Known as Aquae Sulis (the waters of the goddess Sulis), it became a place of pilgrimage for people seeking healing in the apparently curative water.
Jane Austen lived in Bath in the early 19th century and visited Bath Assembly Rooms, where dancing, coffee-drinking, billiard-playing and gambling took place.
Unsurprisingly, beauty products, wig curlers, wine bottles and tobacco pipes from the rooms’ heyday have been found during the restoration project but the Roman remains are regarded as a joyful bonus.
Tatjana LeBoff, the National Trust project curator at Bath Assembly Rooms, described the Roman discoveries as significant. “It’s so wonderful to find Roman remains under our Georgian building,” she said.
The £20m restoration project includes refurbishing the upper rooms heavily damaged by bombing in the second world war and conserving 10 original Georgian chandeliers. The building is due to reopen next year with a new Georgian visitor experience and a place for 21st-century assembly.

====================================================================================================

London buses in decline? Why public transport in global cities is slowing to a crawl – visualised
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
06:00:18 UTC
15:00:18 KST

Experts warn that slower buses risk driving passengers away: research cited by Transport for London (TfL) suggests a 10% fall in speed leads to a 6% drop in demand.
Passenger journeys in London have already fallen by more than 300m a year, or 16%, since 2013, despite the city’s population growing by almost a million people.
The city’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, does not play down the issue. “We’re really concerned about bus usage. One of the reasons, when you speak to commuters, is a lack of reliability. And why is it they lack reliability? Because of bus speed.”
A congested city, with ever more demands on road space, has left London facing difficult choices over which modes of transport to prioritise. But when passengers turn away from slower buses, the service frequencies and even routes are liable to be cut.
The fear is, as one industry figure puts it, “a vicious circle of decline”: slower buses; fewer passengers; and increasing pressure on services.
Recent research has also pointed to this trend being recorded in other global cities such as Paris, Brussels, Lisbon and beyond.
The growing wait for the London bus – in data
Guardian analysis of data from TfL, which runs London’s road and rail public transport network, reveals several indicators that the capital’s bus services have slowed, become truncated or less reliable. The Covid-19 pandemic had a sharp and obvious impact on the data, but there are clear downwards trends cutting through that period.
Across the network as a whole, the average speed in 2025-26 stood at 9.18mph – the lowest speed since comparable records began in 2013-14, and a 4.8% drop over this period.
Bus timetables have long been adjusted to reflect London’s traffic. A snapshot of routes analysed by the economist Alexander Jan, a veteran of transport planning in the capital, found scheduled journey times are now, on average, 30% longer than they were 50 years ago.
Yet even with that extra time built in, buses are increasingly failing to meet expectations. Delays have worsened: on high-frequency routes – those running more than five buses an hour – passengers now wait 22% longer than expected, up from 18% in 2018.
If unreliability is, as Khan argues, deterring passengers, the latest ridership figures are concerning.
Last year saw the first fall in bus journeys since the post-pandemic recovery. Between 2010 and 2019, annual passenger numbers consistently exceeded 2 billion; in 2024, they fell to 1.8 billion.
At the same time, the size of London’s bus network has shrunk. Between 2010 and 2019, TfL buses travelled an average of 487m km (303m miles) a year. Over the past three years, that figure has fallen to about 460m.
Across the network buses are slower, passenger numbers are falling, services cover fewer miles and waiting times are rising.
Those slower journeys come with a financial cost. Because drivers’ wages account for the largest share of operating costs, slower buses mean more vehicles and more staff are needed to provide the same level of service.
According to analysis by the Confederation of Passenger Transport, making London’s buses 10% faster would bring in an extra £70m a year in fares and cut operating costs by £214m.
Delays and cuts also hit the poorest in society, who are more likely to rely on buses for shift work, lower costs or lack of a car. In London, a bus into the centre costs less than half the peak tube fare, and housing costs increase with proximity to underground stations.
A global trend
London is far from the only city whose buses are slowing down.
A 2026 report by the Transport Strategy Centre (TSC) at Imperial College London found a “persistent decline in bus speeds” in the past decade in 15 networks in Europe, Asia and North America.
London’s slowdown is modest compared with other cities: in Paris, Istanbul, Kuala Lumpur and Singapore, bus travel is more than 10% slower than before the pandemic.
Local factors vary, but the TSC report identifies a pattern: growing traffic and congestion and less space for buses, “diminished in part to the expansion of road space for cycling and walking”.
In Barcelona, the redevelopment of Plaça de les Glòries Catalanes pushed traffic on to surrounding roads, at lower speed limits, with no priority for buses. Journey times rose by more than 25%.
In New York, widening the protected cycle lane on Sixth Avenue reduced general traffic lanes from four to three; morning-peak bus speeds fell by 8% over the following year.
When buses are fast and reliable, as the TSC report concludes, passengers “respond with increased use, strengthening the viability of the system; when speeds decline, ridership suffers, undermining sustainability goals”. In other words, making buses better is, the TSC says, “a primary lever for achieving equitable, low-carbon, and resilient cities”.
Why are London buses getting slower?
In London, the persistent slowdown comes despite successive London mayors championing buses and bringing in better technology and vehicles. There was a great leap forward in bus performance in the early 2000s through Ken Livingstone’s congestion charge and investment in infrastructure such as GPS tracking, which massively improved reliability.
Livingstone’s fleets of new bendy buses were phased out by his immediate successor, Boris Johnson, a self-professed enthusiast – even if his signature New Routemasters proved controversial.
Since then Khan, famously the son of a bus driver, has brought in the Hopper fare, allowing multiple bus connections for the price of one journey, and is aiming for a fully electric bus fleet by 2030. Passengers on many routes now enjoy cleaner, quieter, cheaper buses, not least on the electric doubledeckers pioneered on the 63 route with better seats, skylights, wood-effect flooring and charging points – a nicer environment, at least, to wait in traffic.
Again Khan does not play down the issues: “We’re really concerned about bus usage. I’m fully aware that it’s poorer Londoners that rely on buses because they’re cheaper.”
Geoff Hobbs, TfL’s director of public transport service planning, says travel patterns have changed since Covid, with more home working, fewer trips to high streets and shifting demographics reducing demand in some areas. The growth of online shopping has also brought more delivery vans on to London’s streets, adding to congestion.
“School rolls in some parts of London are getting smaller and some schools are even closing. And it’s youngsters that make heaviest use of buses,” he says.
There is also “the double whammy of many more deliveries and delivery vans: you make less trips to town centres; and those same vans stop at places we’d rather they didn’t, blocking traffic”, Hobbs adds.
A Guardian reporter’s journey on the 22 bus was slowed – and often stopped – by many of these obstructions. On the 1 hour 47 minute journey, long single-lane queues around Putney and various lane and road closures from roadworks in Mayfair kept the bus still for 40 minutes in total.
But TfL and operators identify two factors above all others: growing pressure on road space and the sheer volume of roadworks.
Graham Vidler, the chief executive of the Confederation of Passenger Transport, says: “There are too many vehicles wanting to use the roads at popular times. You can account for that in timetabling.
“But what you can’t account for are unplanned and uncoordinated roadworks. And that’s probably the biggest thing that’s moved the dial. The number of roadworks seems to be mushrooming.”
Seb Dance, London’s deputy mayor for transport, agrees: “The biggest impact is roadworks and particularly unplanned roadworks. We’ve got a problem in London where we’ve got old infrastructure, whether it’s sewage, water, electricity, gas.”
A post-pandemic rebound in utility works, alongside road redesign projects and repairs to weather-damaged roads, has left more than 1,000 roadworks obstructing London’s streets on an average day.
Roadworks impinge on an increasingly limited road space, with five times as much of London now covered by cycleways as a decade ago – 450km compared with 90km. The conversion itself has meant lengthy works to build separate lanes – as well as move pavements and relocate bus stops – for surging cycling and e-bike use.
Hobbs says bus performances has had to come second to other considerations, including safety and the general city environment: “There are trade-offs to be done … London has become a more walkable city. There are more cycle lanes. There have been all sorts of schemes that make London, a better place to live. You go back far enough, Trafalgar Square was a sort of giant roundabout.”
Pedestrianisation of that square, once a key bus interchange, will be followed at Oxford Street, another important bus route.
Operators believe buses are at the raw end of such trade-offs. Vidler says the cycle lanes built in recent years “serve a really important purpose – but if the politicians decide to give more space to one mode it follows that others will get less. And if you’re putting in more cycle lanes, it means it’s harder for bus passengers to travel.”
Dance resists this interpretation. “Mainly there are just too many cars. So moving people out of cars to more efficient spaces such as public transport, buses and bikes is part of that solution,” he says.
Demand from other types of vehicles is growing, whether Lime bikes, e-scooters or the embryonic robotaxi fleets from the likes of Uber. But technology can also help buses find a way through. The next wave of TfL’s Fusion programme – “basically computers on all the traffic lights across London”, says Dance – will link the capital’s thousands of signals to speed up flow and give more buses priority where possible.
A lane rental scheme, charging companies by the day for the roadworks they carry out, was pioneered on TfL’s roads and is being extended to boroughs, incentivising work to be coordinated and completed quicker.
“We’ve got to make our buses more reliable,” says Khan. “Which means them going faster.”
The hot summer of 2026 is likely to have further affected bus performance. The mayor told bus drivers to take breaks and even to stay in the depot rather than operate a vehicle without functioning air-cooling systems. Contractual penalties for poor performance will be suspended during extreme heat, which is likely to be more common.
And for speed as heat, safety remains priority. Road speed limits across London are decreasing, with more 20mph routes and the 50mph on major suburban roads planned to be cut to 40mph before 2030 – potentially affecting even the express Superloop buses established by Khan.
For now, those orbital bus routes in the outer boroughs, rebranded and remapped under Khan, are seen as a success story. Instead of a doom loop of slower buses and fewer passengers, he says, “the Superloop has shown we can increase bus usage. If you provide a good product, people will use it.”
Claire Wright, TfL’s head of streets performance, says that despite the “marginal decline” in speeds, the bus network remains the most popular form of public transport in the capital, “helping people get around affordably while also delivering public health and air quality benefits from fewer people driving”.
She adds: “We’ll continue to closely monitor network performance to ensure the bus network serves Londoners as effectively as possible.”

Bolognina: make tracks for Bologna’s bustling former rail workers’ quarter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
06:00:17 UTC
15:00:17 KST

Why go now?
Located just north of the Centrale train station, Bolognina neighbourhood is more than just a Little Bologna. It is a completely different world from the medieval maze of palaces, churches and towers that define the city’s “Centro Storico”, which is increasingly filled with crowds of tourists as Bologna joins the big league of Italian getaway destinations.
There is an immediate visual difference as narrow cobbled lanes give way to wide, tree-lined avenues, pastel-coloured low-rise apartment blocks, spacious parks and piazzas. Bolognina sprang up at the beginning of the 20th century, initially to house families of workers from the railway, then from nearby manufacturing industries.
Today, the quarter is home to a diverse multi-ethnic population and remains a stronghold for militant leftwing politics, with the local community committed to avoiding gentrification. Tourists are certainly made welcome, and it is a delight to feel part of genuine local life.
Where to eat and drink
Eating out here makes a refreshing change from the city centre. Of course there are still spots serving traditional freshly made tagliatelle al ragù such as the atmospheric old-school trattoria La Golosità di Nonna Aurora. But you can also sample Georgian cuisine at Pane Georgiana, a sharing plate of Ethiopian and Eritrean dishes at Ristorante Africano Adal, spicy Sichuan cooking at Ba Hot Pot, or handmade tortellini and tortelloni stuffed with halal meat at the innovative Brodellini.
For vegetarians, the perfect spot is Piazza Martino, a cantina and deli owned by a nearby farm in the Bolognesi Hills that practises a “first we grow, then we eat” philosophy, transforming their organic produce into delicious aubergine parmigiana, vegan pepperoni lasagne, and courgette and potato polpette (balls).
Bolognina’s prime foodie street is Via Luigi Serra, symbolised by the fiercely independent Trattoria di Via Serra. The restaurant’s three small, rustic salons are always packed and getting a reservation isn’t easy as they don’t take bookings through social platforms and rarely answer the phone or emails. Chef Tommaso Maio and co-owner Flavio Benassi used to have a restaurant up in the hills nearby, but 13 years ago decided to come to the city, choosing Bolognina rather than the city centre for their new venture. “Our aim then, and still today, is to offer the locals here an old-fashioned neighbourhood trattoria where they can still order a comforting bowl of tortellini in capon broth, lasagne and freshly baked crescenti biscuits,” they explain.
If there is no free table at the Trattoria, then the street offers plenty of options, from hearty plates of cold cuts and cheeses at the deli-diner La Vecchia Bottega, cocktails, spritz and craft beers at the hip Fermento bar, or local wines at La Petite Enoteca. To finish the evening, there is often live music at the bars in Piazza Lucio Dalla, named after Bologna’s local hero, an iconic Italian singer-songwriter.
Cultural experiences
Leave historic Bologna behind by walking from the central train station across the Matteotti bridge and you immediately come face to face with a striking Holocaust memorial, an austere, minimalist monument of two narrowly separated 10-metre high steel walls. Just opposite stands the massive Chiesa del Sacro Cuore di Gesù, dating back to 1912 when Bolognina was first being built. It is worth visiting just to marvel at the soaring 60-metre-high dome.
Hidden away in the backstreets in a former tram shed, La Memoria di Ustica Museum is a unique homage to a commercial flight between Bologna and Palermo that was mysteriously shot down in 1980 with no survivors. French artist Christian Boltanski has meticulously reconstructed the wreckage of the downed airliner and assembled the personal items belonging to the victims, creating an immense, intensely moving installation.
Checkpoint Charly is a thriving alternative art and artisan cooperative occupying a former lingerie warehouse. Workshops include ceramics, printmaking, photography, graphics and music, with a dozen cultural events presented each year. The DLF – Dopo Lavoro Ferroviario – is a sprawling park behind the station originally created in the 1920s for after-work activities for railway workers. This green lung has been saved from abandonment and now houses the laid-back all-day Kinotto Bar, the Vecchia Orsa DLF craft brewery and beer garden, a pizzeria, the Puccini concert arena and the Locomotiv Club, a live indie music venue.
Where to shop
Although this essentially residential neighbourhood may not be a shopping paradise, bargain hunters should plan to visit on the first Sunday of the month when the Piazza Lucio Dalla is transformed into a huge flea market. Over in the daily Mercato Albani, Ilario di Lorenzis has recently opened Intelligenza Artigianale, an atelier showcasing his funky hand-crafted bags, T-shirts and caps, while cycling fans should head for Bolognina Bike Shop, whose friendly owner, Dario Brunetto, repairs bikes and recycles vinyls, retro decor and collectible vintage cycling jerseys.
Don’t miss
Since opening in 1934, Mercato Albani has been the beating heart of Bolognina. Running down the middle of a shady tree-lined avenue, locals gather each morning for their daily shopping from bustling stalls selling Bologna’s speciality mortadella (pork salami) and prosciutto, fish, cheese and organic veggies. Then there is a complete change of personality from 5pm till around midnight when shuttered stands open up as lively cocktail and craft beer bars, the natural wine enoteca, Vineria Punk, plus casual diners serving pizza and pasta, vegan dishes and Greek cuisine. Giuseppe Agrello the owner of Bollore, a cool vermouth bar, explains that “when we were invited to open in the mercato, we insisted that during the day it should stay as it is and not become just another tourist food court. So we only begin in the evening and also organise concerts, art exhibitions and cultural events for the community.”
Where to stay
Hotel Il Guercino is a delightfully quirky, family-owned hotel, extravagantly decorated with a mix of baroque and Asian influences, with a spa featuring sauna, hot tub and steam bath. Doubles from €150.
This trip was provided by Bologna Welcome and Emilia Romagna Turismo

The Trump-Xi summit: Why Europe has so much at stake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
06:00:17 UTC
15:00:17 KST

From tariffs to rare earths and AI, the agenda for US President Donald Trump's summit with China’s President Xi Jinping in Washington will have an impact on Europe.
As Chinese President Xi Jinping lands in the US on Wednesday for a three-day summit with US President Donald Trump, Europeans will be watching closely for any decisions that could directly affect their economic interests.
Trump and Xi's second meeting in a year will cover issues ranging from trade to AI and rare earths. This latest summit follows their crucial meeting in October 2025, where the two sides agreed on a trade truce after weeks of trade tensions.
The EU, meanwhile, began crucial negotiations with Beijing in June aimed at reducing its €1 billion-a-day trade deficit, setting a looming October deadline for tangible progress.
Since their China-US summit last year, the Iran war has erupted, triggering a surge in energy prices and ramping up pressure on the US President ahead of the November midterm elections. On China’s side, shipments to the US surged by 34.4% in a year, widening China's trade surplus to about $29.2 billion, according to Chinese data.
"Xi Jinping arrives in Washington with the upper hand, even on American soil," Alicia García Herrero, an expert at Brussels-based think tank Bruegel, said.
Several issues on the table for Xi and Trump directly concern the EU. So what can Europeans expect from the US-China summit?
Tariff cuts
The trade truce, due to expire on 10 November, will be on the agenda, a year after it ended a trade war between the two with tit-for-tat tariffs exceeding 100%. For the Europeans, US tariffs on China are always a wrong signal, as they reroute Chinese exports to the EU market.
However, this week's summit might lead to stabilisation between Washington and Beijing.
According to US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, China and the US will make “some announcements on agriculture and non-tariff barriers.” A mutual tariff reduction covering $30 billion in goods is also expected.
“What we expect is for Trump to gain a sort of a win that he can sell for the midterm elections, and China to simply buy some more time to strengthen its industrial base,” Ivano di Carlo, an expert from the European Policy Centre (EPC), told Euronews.
Europe squeezed on rare earths
The trade truce also included exports of rare earths. During last year's trade war, Beijing had blocked global exports of the strategic materials, key for EU industry, for which it holds a monopoly of production and processing.
The issue was raised last week by EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič during a video call with his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao. But Washington has far greater negotiating power than Brussels when it comes to securing access to the materials, García Herrero told Euronews.
“The US will negotiate for Europe and Europe will have to pay a price for that,” García Herrero said.
Europe non-existent on AI
The two powers are also expected to discuss artificial intelligence, amid growing calls for international safeguards. Two weeks ago, Jacob Coxon, who has worked as a researcher at both AI heavyweights OpenAI and Anthropic, said on X that both companies are “gambling with our lives” and that people building AI “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” raising global concerns around this technology.
Several incidents were also reported over the summer, including OpenAI agents hacking another AI company, Hugging Face’s platform.
Both China and the US have expressed concern about the risks surrounding AI development, but they are also locked in an intensifying technological competition. On Sunday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng discussed an “AI hotline” proposal, which would be a “notification mechanism” between Washington and China to warn each other when an AI incident becomes serious enough to threaten national security.
“This AI dialogue that is going to become like a red button during the nuclear race is only shared by the US and China,” García Herrero said. “So it really leaves Europe as non-existent in terms of being a pole.”
According to the expert, the summit will “confirm the G20 nature of the world.”

My mother set up NatWest First Saver accounts for my children when they were born. The accounts are held in trust for when they turn 18 and my parents have paid into them monthly to help fund them through university.
My mother is now in the final stages of Alzheimer’s and I have registered financial power of attorney for her.
My daughter began university last year and my son starts this month, but I have been unable to access the £20,000 in their respective accounts. I was told my mother has to give consent for the children to access them, but she’s not in a position to do so.
I’ve been variously advised to set up online banking in my mother’s name without her consent, to request a one-off payment of less than £1,000 and, upsettingly, that it would be easier if my mother were dead.
As a consequence, we’ve had to take out a bank loan to cover my daughter’s expenses.
  SW, Worcestershire
NatWest blames “lack of colleague awareness” of a “complex process”. We’re talking here of numerous colleagues in call centres and in branches who, over the best part of a year, have been unable to fathom what should be a standard procedure.
This appears to be a training issue and it’s hardly reassuring that “learning from your experience” will be used to “inform future improvements”.
Your children now have access to their funds and compensation has been paid to reflect the delays.

Former treasurer says economic reform in Australia will take 'financial crisis'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
05:59:27 UTC
14:59:27 KST

Former treasurer says Australia needs 'financial crisis' for economic reform to happen
In short:
Former treasurer Joe Hockey says voters will not back meaningful fiscal reform unless there is a "financial crisis".
He says a major problem is government spending with "no restraint" in order to be re-elected.
As global interest rates rise, governments are under pressure to reduce spending.
With federal government debt surpassing $1 trillion, and future generations bearing the burden of the growing interest bill, the clamour for budget repair is growing.
But last night, Australian treasurers past and present delivered some insight into the difficulty of getting any kind form of meaningful reform across the line, one before an audience of power brokers and the other on ABC's The Business.
Joe Hockey, former treasurer in the Abbott Coalition government, knows full well the difficulty of introducing any kind of fiscal reform.
In his first budget, shortly after coming to power in 2013, Mr Hockey up-ended a raft of assurances during the election campaign with a series of wide-ranging spending cuts and user pay fees that enraged the electorate.
The Abbott government ended up backing away from most of the swingeing cuts in the face of that opposition.
When asked by The Business host Kirsten Aiken whether any meaningful fiscal reform was even possible if it cost voters money, his answer was an emphatic "no".
"There's going to have to be a crisis now. There's going to have to be a financial crisis,"
"And people will only take the medicine when they, you know, feel really ill about it. And I think this is coming right across the world."
'Whatever it takes to get re-elected'
His sentiments were echoed by current Treasurer Jim Chalmers in his address to an Australian Financial Review gathering on Tuesday.
"Power is much more effective right now in the distorting and blocking than the building or reforming,"
Mr Hockey pointed to an inflection point occurring across the developed world in government finances where income tax, the biggest source of government income, is about to be exceeded by welfare payments.
Loading...
"The problem is governments have no restraint when it comes to expenditure," he said.
"They're so focused on populism, they'll spend whatever it takes to get re-elected and that's particularly acute now that … one side of government isn't getting 50 per cent of the votes."
The fragmenting of political parties and voting patterns has made the task even more difficult as temporary coalitions of divergent parties are formed.
"You're going to be populist because you're trying to win the votes of some minority over there," Mr Hockey said.
"It's terrible."
'Not entirely powerless'
The phenomenon may now be more acute, but it certainly is not new.
As treasurer, Mr Hockey philosophically was more aligned with the school of thought pushing for lower taxes and less spending.
He oversaw the dismantling of a key aspect of the Henry tax reforms by abolishing the resources rent tax and the carbon tax, which significantly reduced the federal government's tax haul.
When combined with his ditched spending cuts, the end result was a decade of deficits during the greatest resources boom in Australian history.
Earlier this week, Mr Chalmers delivered the seventh and latest Intergenerational Report, which laid out the challenges of ever delivering a balanced budget over the long term.
An aging population with ever greater costs associated with health and aged care and with a smaller proportion of workers supporting them points to an ongoing and possibly permanent structural deficit.
Yesterday, the treasurer pointed to the escalating debt and ongoing deficits amongst the world's most powerful economies, which in recent months have sent global interest rates higher, adding to the already substantial financial strains.
"We are not entirely powerless in the face of all this," he said.
"We have advantages, we are better placed and better prepared and we have a better plan than other countries.
"But the point remains that something as consequential as the world's ability to finance its budgets is, to some degree, hostage to decisions taken in Washington and on Wall Street."
It was a point that Mr Hockey concurred with.
"You can't keep borrowing hoping that it'll just go away. And the United States is no different."

Two-state solution is being erased ‘before our eyes’: Guterres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
05:57:10 UTC
14:57:10 KST

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Tuesday warned that international support for a two-state solution must move beyond diplomatic statements, saying developments in the occupied Palestinian territories are increasingly undermining the prospect of a viable Palestinian state.
“For Palestinians and all those who care about peace in the Middle East, support for two states must go beyond words,” Guterres told a high-level ministerial meeting on the Two-State Solution and the Comprehensive Peace Plan for Gaza on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly in New York.
Guterres said the conditions needed for an independent, democratic, contiguous and sovereign Palestinian state were being systematically eroded, citing illegal Israeli settlement activity and other policies in the occupied West Bank, as well as attacks by illegal Israeli settlers.
Guterres warns of threat to Palestinian territorial continuity
The UN chief specifically raised concerns over planned construction in the illegal E1 settlement plan, a strategically important area of the occupied West Bank.
Advancing the projects, he warned, “would deal a deathblow to the prospect of a contiguous and viable Palestinian State.”
Guterres said the expansion of illegal Israeli settlements constitutes a violation of international law and stressed that a lasting peace requires two states living within recognised borders based on the pre-1967 lines, with Jerusalem serving as the capital of both.
“There is simply no alternative, and time is running out,” he said, linking the two-state framework to wider regional stability.
Costa calls for Gaza peace plan to be implemented
European Council President Antonio Costa said the international consensus around a two-state solution had yet to translate into sufficient action on the ground.
Costa recalled that 142 countries endorsed the New York Declaration on the Two-State Solution last year, while UN Security Council Resolution 2803 provided an operational framework for a Gaza peace plan. Yet, he said, the situation had “barely improved” over the past year.
He called for the roadmap for Gaza to be implemented, while warning that the two-state solution was being jeopardised daily across the occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem.
“Preserving the pathway to peace” requires urgent collective action to establish an independent and sovereign Palestinian state living alongside Israel in security, Costa said.
The meeting came during the high-level week of the 81st UN General Assembly, where the two-state solution and the future of Gaza remain prominent issues on the international agenda.

Türkiye, partners condemn disinformation targeting aid workers

Foreign ministers of MIKTA countries meet on the sidelines of the 81st U.N. General Assembly.
Türkiye and its MIKTA partners condemned false and harmful claims targeting humanitarian workers and organizations, warning that they can incite violence, undermine trust and obstruct aid operations.
The foreign ministers of Türkiye, Mexico, Indonesia, South Korea and Australia issued the joint statement following their 30th meeting in New York on Sept. 21, on the sidelines of the 81st U.N. General Assembly. Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan attended the meeting.
“Humanitarian personnel save lives. Misinformation, disinformation and harmful narratives put them at risk. This must stop,” the ministers said.
They warned that advances in digital communications, social media and artificial intelligence had enabled harmful content to spread at unprecedented speed and scale, threatening humanitarian work during armed conflicts, disasters and other emergencies.
The ministers condemned efforts to create, coordinate or spread false claims that misrepresent aid organizations and personnel, encourage violence or discrimination against them, or hinder their activities.
They called on countries, parties to armed conflicts and other actors to respect and protect humanitarian personnel and operations, including in the information environment.
The group reaffirmed its support for U.N. Security Council Resolution 2730 and the Declaration for the Protection of Humanitarian Personnel, urging their effective implementation.
The ministers said tackling misinformation, disinformation and hate speech targeting humanitarian work was a policy priority.
MIKTA members would continue working with the U.N., aid organizations and civil society to strengthen protection, they added.

Officials also pointed out that the law governing the Election Commission, as well as a Supreme Court judgment, provides that decisions should, as far as possible, be taken unanimously. Where unanimity is not possible, the majority view prevails.

‘Genocide,’ ‘concentration camp,’ ‘war crime’: Israel faces barrage of criticism at UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
05:50:23 UTC
14:50:23 KST

The Gaza war took center stage on the opening day of the UN General Assembly’s annual high-level debate in New York, as leader after leader used the global platform to deliver some of the sharpest criticism yet of Israel’s conduct in Gaza and the West Bank.
The language ranged from accusations of “war crimes” and “forced displacement” to “genocide” and “concentration camp,” underscoring the growing diplomatic challenge facing Israel as the conflict approaches its third anniversary.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres set the tone. He condemned Hamas’ October 7 attack as an “abhorrent terror attack,” but said what followed was an “onslaught on Palestinians in Gaza” involving killing and destruction on a scale unlike anything he had witnessed during his tenure. He also warned that violence, displacement and settlement expansion in the West Bank were “raising the spectre of ethnic cleansing.”
One of the most strident speeches came from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who described Gaza as “the world’s largest graveyard for children” and went on to call the enclave “the most inhumane, most shameful concentration camp of our time.” He urged countries that have yet to recognize a Palestinian state to do so and called for greater international pressure on Israel.
Erdogan also criticized Washington’s decision to prevent Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas from traveling to New York, saying Turkey would continue to give voice to the Palestinian cause from the UN podium. The Israeli delegation, including Ambassador to the UN Danny Danon, walked out during his speech, while Palestinian delegates applauded.
Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani used equally stark language. “What has happened in Gaza is genocide in every sense of the word, and a stain of shame on the conscience of humanity as a whole,” he told the assembly. He accused Israeli leaders of openly promoting the departure of Gaza’s population and called on Israel to end its military activity, withdraw from the enclave and lift restrictions on it.
Israel has repeatedly rejected accusations of genocide, saying its military campaign is directed against Hamas and that the terrorist group operates from within civilian areas.
Jordan’s King Abdullah II, whose country has maintained a peace treaty with Israel since 1994, also delivered a sweeping indictment of Israeli policy.
Abdullah argued that destruction in Gaza and what he described as the “de facto annexation” of parts of the West Bank were part of an attempt to erase the Palestinian presence and make a future Palestinian state impossible. He described the forcible removal of Palestinians from their homes as “forced displacement” and a “war crime,” and accused Israel of an “appetite for expansion” that threatened the wider region.
The Jordanian monarch urged governments not to treat Gaza and the West Bank as separate crises, arguing that they were two elements of the same Israeli strategy.
He also pointed to the 2002 Arab Peace Initiative, which offered Israel normalization with Arab and Muslim states in exchange for an agreement with the Palestinians, arguing that the proposal had remained available for more than two decades.
Criticism spreads to Western allies
Israel’s challenge, however, is not limited to criticism from Turkey, Qatar or other Arab states. French President Emmanuel Macron, delivering his final UN General Assembly address before his term ends next year, sharply criticized the situation in Gaza and also claimed that Hamas does not operate in the West Bank, despite the terrorist group maintaining local infrastructure there that has been involved, among other things, in carrying out attacks against Israelis.
Macron directly challenged the way U.S. President Donald Trump portrayed his plan to end the war. He said that despite declarations of peace, not a single humanitarian corridor had reopened, asking: “Are we simply standing by and watching a spectacle that should shame us all?” He also criticized Israeli policy in the West Bank, arguing that developments there were making the establishment of a Palestinian state less possible with each passing day. Those who believe that violating the sovereignty of neighboring countries will make Israel more secure, he said, are mistaken, and are in fact “weakening its security, today and in the future.”
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham likewise began his UN address by condemning the October 7 Hamas attack as “utterly horrific” and saying Britain stood with Israel and Jewish communities worldwide in the face of continuing threats from Iran. “But this does not justify the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza or the West Bank,” he said.
Burnham said Britain would not “stand by” as suffering continued and the prospect of a two-state solution came under threat. He singled out Israeli plans for construction in the E1 area east of Jerusalem, saying the project could put a viable Palestinian state beyond reach.
He also defended his government’s move to restrict dealings with Israeli settlements, arguing that continuing to voice support for two states without taking action would further undermine public trust in politics.
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva also accused Israel in particularly severe terms, saying “generations of Palestinians” would carry the pain and trauma of what he called the “genocide of women and children” carried out by Netanyahu’s government in Gaza.
At the same time, Lula said Israeli civilians had paid the price for the “radicalism and intolerance” of Hamas’ terrorist attack. He also criticized measures targeting the International Criminal Court and warned that continued settlement expansion was making a two-state solution increasingly difficult.
Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa added his voice to the criticism outside the General Assembly hall, speaking at an Atlantic Council event on the sidelines of the gathering ahead of his own UN address.
Asked about the trauma caused in Israel by the October 7 attack, al-Sharaa said he understood what had happened to innocent civilians but argued that one historical event could not determine an entire country’s policy.
He said October 7 should not dictate Israel’s approach toward Syria and warned that such a policy would create new security threats. “If you want to protect your security, you have to respect the security of others,” he said.
Al-Sharaa accused Israel of creating new problems around itself rather than solving existing ones and criticized Israeli strikes and military activity inside Syria. He contrasted Syria’s improving relations with the United States, Britain, Gulf states, Iraq and Lebanon with its relationship with Israel. “I believe the problem is with Israel, not Syria,” he said.
The Syrian president also disclosed that direct talks with Israel, which he said have been underway for nearly a year with US involvement, had at one stage reached “almost 90%” agreement. “There were several sessions of negotiations with Israel, and we almost reached 90% of agreements,” he said, adding that Israel subsequently withdrew or introduced additional conditions.
According to al-Sharaa, Damascus is first demanding that Israel return to the lines established under the 1974 disengagement agreement. Only then, he said, could the sides move toward broader security arrangements and potentially discuss a lasting peace.
The succession of speeches is far from over. Representatives of Syria, Iran and Spain are among those expected to address the General Assembly as the debate continues, with Palestinian and Irish representatives also due to speak later in the week.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is scheduled to address the assembly on Thursday and has already signaled that he intends to use the podium to push back against international criticism. “I’m going to tell the truth about our heroic soldiers,” Netanyahu said before the gathering, while also promising to confront New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani over his fierce criticism of Israel.
Beyond speeches, pressure turns into policy
The criticism heard inside the General Assembly is increasingly being matched by diplomatic and economic measures.
Foreign ministers from Qatar, Egypt, Jordan, the United Arab Emirates, Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia met in New York and expressed “deep concern” over continuing humanitarian suffering in Gaza. They called on Israel to meet outstanding commitments under the first phase of the current plan, including facilitating humanitarian aid and the rehabilitation of critical infrastructure.
Earlier this month, 12 Western countries, including Britain, France, Canada, Spain and several Nordic states, announced that they had introduced, supported or were considering restrictions on trade involving Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
Britain, France and Canada said they intended to introduce national measures banning trade in settlement goods, while other European countries have already taken steps of their own. The same joint statement reaffirmed the countries’ commitment to Israel’s security and condemned Hamas’ October 7 terrorist attack.
The result is a UN gathering in which unusually harsh rhetoric toward Israel is increasingly accompanied by concrete policy measures, while Netanyahu prepares to take the same podium and make Israel’s case before the world.

====================================================================================================

What to expect from Trump-Xi meeting in Washington?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
05:47:37 UTC
14:47:37 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping is visiting Washington from September 23 to 25 for a state visit and talks with US President Donald Trump, while skipping this year's UN General Assembly in New York. Beijing says the visit will include discussions on bilateral ties and “world peace and development”.
The more immediate question is whether Xi and Trump can prevent their countries' strategic rivalry from escalating, analysts say.
Xi and Trump are due to meet at the White House on September 24, their second face-to-face encounter this year after Trump's May visit to Beijing. Trade, Taiwan, technology, Russia sanctions, Iran and artificial intelligence (AI) are all expected to feature as the two powers try to preserve a fragile detente.
With the current trade truce due to expire on November 10, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng held “very successful” talks on Sunday, laying the groundwork for the summit, with tariff reductions, critical minerals and a proposed US-China AI safety mechanism on the agenda.
For Xi, the visit is about consolidating what Beijing calls "constructive strategic stability". For Trump, it offers a chance to secure economic gains while keeping relations with America's principal strategic competitor from sliding back into confrontation.
"I see the visit as an anchor — a real bedrock — for further US-China relations," Henry Huiyao Wang, founder and director of the Beijing-based Center for China and Globalization and a former Counselor to China’s State Council, told TRT World.
But the summit will also expose the limits of that stabilisation.
From trade truce to strategic stability
The May meeting between the two leaders in Beijing produced understandings aimed at reducing immediate pressure in the relationship. Since then, officials have sought to turn them into longer-term arrangements covering trade, investment, technology and critical minerals.
Henry Wang said the leaders' diplomacy provides a "guiding compass" for the relationship, while Chinese geopolitical analyst Gao Jian said Beijing wants to consolidate the "constructive strategic stability relationship" agreed in May through more predictable communication and mechanisms to manage differences.
The immediate test is economic. At the May summit, the two sides floated a proposal to reduce tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods imported from each other.
Henry Wang said this proposed mechanism for tariff-free imports from each side could provide a starting point. "$30 billion tariff-free imports for each side would be a good start," he said, suggesting it could eventually expand.
Chinese investment in the US could form another pillar. Sourabh Gupta, head of the trade and tech programme at the Washington-based Institute for China-America Studies, said he will be watching for an investment framework allowing Chinese capital into selected areas of America's industrial expansion.
James Borton, a senior fellow at Johns Hopkins SAIS, said the bigger question is whether Trump and Xi can turn temporary truces into a "durable mechanism" for managing competition.
"A sweeping strategic settlement is unlikely," Borton said.
AI: competition with guardrails
AI is becoming a major arena of US-China competition, spanning advanced chips, computing power and frontier models.
But unlike some other disputes, both sides have an incentive to prevent the technology race from producing uncontrolled security risks.
Borton describes the emerging model as "technological rivalry alongside narrow cooperation — competition with guardrails rather than technological detente".
Henry Wang puts it more bluntly: "We do not need an AI arms race; we need global AI governance."
Gupta said a framework or announcement on AI safety would be one of his three key indicators of whether the summit produces meaningful progress.
The likely outcome is therefore not an end to technology competition, but an attempt to put boundaries around it.
Russia sanctions law tests the truce
Trump's signing of a Russia sanctions law on September 18 has introduced another potential fault line.
The law gives the president authority, under specified conditions, to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on major buyers of Russian energy, including China and India, while giving him discretion over whether to apply or waive them.
Borton said the summit will show whether Russian energy becomes "a bargaining chip" or is kept separate from the US-China trade talks.
Gupta takes a different view of the immediate risk. Applying the 100-percent tariff to China, he argues, would directly undermine the existing US-China arrangement, which limits tariff escalation and seeks to keep critical-mineral flows stable.
It could also invite Chinese retaliation over rare earths.
Gupta therefore expects Trump to use his waiver authority to exclude China, rather than jeopardise the broader trade understanding.
That makes the Russia issue a test of Washington's ability to compartmentalise its pressure on Moscow from its effort to stabilise ties with Beijing.
From Beijing's perspective, Wang Hanyi, a research fellow at Shanghai International Studies University, said China opposes unilateral sanctions and what it considers extraterritorial pressure.
“If the US further pressures China with tariffs and sanctions, it will only complicate bilateral relations,” she told TRT World, adding that “the two sides should properly handle differences through dialogue and consultation on the basis of mutual respect and equality.”
Iran, Hormuz and the Houthi-Saudi flashpoint
The Middle East could provide an unexpected test of whether Washington and Beijing can cooperate where their interests overlap.
The Iran conflict has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, while fighting has intensified around Yemen and the Red Sea. Houthis have advanced towards the Bab al Mandab Strait and launched missile and drone attacks towards Saudi Arabia, further threatening regional energy and shipping routes.
The developments have already drawn Beijing deeper into the diplomacy.
After Saudi Arabia appealed to China for help, Beijing privately urged Iran to use its influence over the Houthis to restrain the group, according to reports. China is heavily dependent on Middle Eastern energy and has a direct interest in keeping both the Bab al Mandab and Hormuz routes open.
That gives Trump a reason to test what influence Xi can exert over Tehran, say analysts.
"China is the biggest guarantor, supporter and stabiliser that Trump can have," CCG’s Henry Wang said, pointing to Beijing's relationships with Iran and Gulf states.
Gupta sees room for China to act as a diplomatic bridge, noting its relationships across the region and its earlier role in facilitating the Saudi-Iran rapprochement.
But he cautions against expecting Beijing to become Washington's regional troubleshooter. China has limited leverage over Israel and little interest in coercing regional actors, he said.
Borton similarly said China is unlikely to become a US intermediary, though it could serve as a diplomatic bridge.
The shared interest is clearer on energy and shipping. Prolonged disruption of Hormuz or Bab al Mandab would hurt China and the wider global economy.
The question is whether that common interest can translate into practical diplomacy.
Taiwan remains the hard limit
If trade and AI offer room for practical arrangements, Taiwan remains one of the hardest limits on US-China accommodation.
Beijing considers Taiwan part of China and opposes US interference. Washington maintains its longstanding policy while continuing defence cooperation with Taipei.
Henry Wang said Beijing could welcome Trump's earlier statements opposing Taiwan independence and expressing reluctance to station US forces thousands of miles from the US.
Gao Jian said China wants Washington to respect its core interests and avoid actions that increase tensions. At the same time, Wang Hanyi described Taiwan as "the most important issue" and "very core of China's core interests".
For Washington, however, any perceived shift in Taiwan policy would carry significant strategic and domestic consequences.
That makes presidential language on Taiwan potentially as important as any formal agreement.
What would count as progress?
Zhiqun Zhu, professor of political science and international relations and director of the China Institute at Bucknell University, cautions against expecting breakthroughs on Iran, Taiwan, advanced technology or Asian security.
A cordial meeting that extends the trade truce and stabilises bilateral relations, he said, could itself be meaningful.
Gupta is looking beyond immediate tariff concessions. His three watchpoints are an investment framework, an AI-safety arrangement, and progress on arms control, strategic stability and additional military-to-military channels for handling emergencies.
Those measures would not resolve the fundamental disagreements between Washington and Beijing, analysts say, but they could reduce the risk of miscalculation as competition intensifies.
That may be the realistic measure of the summit.
Most analysts believe that the Washington meeting is unlikely to transform US-China relations. Its significance will lie in whether Xi and Trump can build mechanisms that allow their countries to compete without repeatedly sliding into confrontation.
From Taiwan and Russian energy to Iran, Hormuz and the Houthi attacks around Bab al Mandab, analysts say Washington and Beijing are increasingly encountering one another in theatres far beyond their own borders.
The choice is not necessarily between cooperation and rivalry, according to experts on both sides. It is whether the two powers can build enough guardrails to manage both at the same time.

'More dangerous': The numbers on this sign raise a bigger question
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
05:46:45 UTC
14:46:45 KST

in brief
- Australians are paying more at the bowser than they have in months due to global disruptions.
- Energy shocks could become the new normal as geopolitical tensions grow.
Australians are being warned that the high prices currently being paid at fuel stations could be "the new normal" as a resumption of the full fuel excise combines with a flare-up in the Middle East.
Escalation in the war, which has dragged on since the end of February with little end in sight, has pushed oil prices to their highest level since April, driving Australian fuel costs back toward their peak.
Alison Reeve, program director of energy and climate at the Grattan Institute, told SBS News that the broader issue is volatility.
While Australians can "adjust to a new normal" of sustained high fuel costs, it's "volatility that's actually more dangerous to the economy than a price that goes high and stays high", she said.
While Australians may be able to adjust to higher prices, fluctuating prices make it more challenging for governments, industry, and households to plan ahead.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"Volatility feels like it's going to be the new normal because we're just in a much more geopolitically disrupted age," she said.
Why are fuel prices so high?
Australia imports around 90 per cent of its refined and crude oil, making it heavily exposed to global market dynamics which are currently being driven by conflict around the world.
In recent weeks, Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen seized control of the vital Bab al-Mandeb strait and disabled the crucial Saudi Arabian East-West pipeline, significantly hampering the key oil producer.
Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil facilities have caused a diesel shortage worldwide, which could well be exacerbated by United States President Donald Trump's threat on Wednesday to cut US diesel exports.
While Saudi Arabia has reportedly restarted the East-West pipeline, the combination of global disruption and a weak Australian dollar has left consumers facing the steepest price for a full tank in months.
The NRMA's latest petrol report found that regular unleaded in Sydney climbed more than 20 cents in the past week, with diesel rising 24 cents, to averages of 237.8 and 286.1 per litre.
On Saturday, Energy Minister Chris Bowen said consumers should expect the "crisis" in Saudi Arabia and Iran to "flow through to prices here".
Bowen also noted that the country has more fuel on-shore now than it did at the outbreak of the conflict.
The new normal?
The government has ruled out further cuts to the fuel excise after the Opposition floated the idea of an automatic halving for two weeks whenever oil topped US$100 ($140) a barrel.
Brent crude reached US$104 ($146) on Monday, just behind its May peak of $114 ($160).
A widely accepted rule of thumb is that every US$10 (about $15) increase in the price of an oil barrel adds 10c to the cost of fuel in Australia.
A fuel excise cut which came into effect at the start of April and ended at the start of August cost the Treasury an estimated $2.95 billion in foregone revenue.
"This is not something that we have been considering," Finance Minister Katy Gallagher told ABC Radio on Monday.
"We've shifted and including in the budget to providing more permanent cost of living arrangements, including through the tax system."
The federal budget handed down in May forecast oil prices to return to US$80 ($117) by mid-2027; however, some experts now predict that oil could climb as high as US$150 ($220) a barrel as global stockpiles are depleted.
Trump initially promised when he launched strikes on Iran that the conflict would be over in four or five weeks. More than six months later, he has told the UN he is debating whether to keep talking or "drive them into hell with no chance of survival".
Addressing the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, the US leader said he believed Iran would make a deal after the midterm elections at the start of November.
He also called on the world to "stand united" in economically isolating Iran, saying its defeat would drive oil prices "plummeting down even lower than they were at the start of the conflict".
'Better solutions' on offer
Money markets and all four of the big banks now expect the Reserve Bank of Australia will raise interest rates once again at its September meeting, following critical comments from governor Michele Bullock in recent weeks.
Stubbornly high inflation, driven by the war in Iran, housing shortages, and a tight labour market, is compounded by rising petrol and diesel costs, which are included in the consumer price index.
"Almost everybody buys petrol," Reeve said.
However, "second-order flow-throughs" mean the knock-on effect of high fuel costs on agriculture, shipping, and transport also trickle into daily prices.
"Everything that's on your plate spent a fair amount of time on a truck at one point to get to you," Reeve said.
While the government has previously announced it will commit to boosting domestic fuel reserves to 50 days, up from the normal 40, to buffer future shocks, doing so during a crisis is challenging.
Reeve said a "better solution" would be to reduce national reliance on fuel.
"Can you get more people into electric cars? Can you get more electric trucks on the road? Can you get the mining sector to switch to using solar and batteries off-grid, rather than using diesel?" she asked.
"Once you've done that, it matters a lot less what's going on internationally."

In a 42-second clip that currently has nearly 50 million views on Instagram, social media comedian Frankie LaPenna can be seen squaring off with the “Rekbot”, a machine resembling the T-800 from the Terminator franchise inside a mixed martial arts-style cage in San Francisco, California.
The 29-year-old, who has over 20 million followers online, is better known for comedic pranks and daredevil antics involving over-the-top physical stunts, like riding a motorcycle into an office desk and playing cards near a raging bull.
A man can be heard telling LaPenna just seconds before he traded blows with his adversary: “I’m scared for you, man”.
The clip shows the comedian landing several punches before the robot sends him backwards with a powerful push kick. Another kick knocks him to the ground, and that seems to be the end of it.
The Sept 18 cage match was organised by robotics startup REK to promote its virtual reality game, which pits humans against remote-controlled humanoid robots like the Rekbot.
“Last night was a turning point in history, a striking moment to behold. Thank you everyone for coming!” the company posted on X.
And while REK claims that the match was “the first Human VS Terminator robot fight”, there had already been previous skirmishes between man and machine.
In December, for instance, the CEO of a Chinese robotics company, wearing protective pads, squared off with his own T-800 creation. He was kicked hard in the torso and knocked down.
Still, REK’s publicity stunt stirred commentaries online about human folly and the AI-fuelled march towards human extinction, with references to end-of-times movies like The Matrix, Blade Runner and I, Robot.

REK seems to be keen on taking that dare. It said on X that the Rekbot “wasn’t even the final boss”, and teased “more” to come “soon”.

“As of 8 a.m., air defense units had shot down or neutralized 119 enemy UAVs of various types,” the Air Force said, according to preliminary data.
Russian drones were recorded striking 18 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at eight locations, as per the Air Force.

George Lucas planned three more "Star Wars" films but "decided to step away" from directing
Kyiv • UNN
Lucas wanted to make three more "Star Wars" films, but after "Revenge of the Sith," he left directing to focus on his museum. The museum opened in Los Angeles.
George Lucas, creator of the legendary "Star Wars" franchise, said that he intended to make three more films, but instead decided to step away from directing after the release of "Star Wars: Revenge of the Sith" (Episode III: Revenge of the Sith) in 2005. UNN reports this with reference to The Hollywood Reporter.
Details
In a recent interview with CBS Sunday Morning, Lucas and his wife and business partner Mellody Hobson spoke about the creation of the new Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles.
After Hobson noted that the "level of detail" Lucas put into the museum "nearly killed him," the director added: "Well, I'm 82 years old, so there's a limit to everything…"
"When I was doing it," Lucas continued, referring to the creation of the museum, "I decided to leave the movie business, which was a big deal, because I needed to make three more Star Wars movies. But I realized that I was running out of time, and I really wanted to create this museum, and I had spent a lot of time developing digital technologies for the film industry. You know, all art depends on technology."
How many Star Wars films Lucas directed
Lucas directed four Star Wars films during his career, beginning with the first installment in the franchise, "Star Wars: A New Hope" (Star Wars: Episode IV – A New Hope), in 1977. Although he handed directing duties to Irvin Kershner and Richard Marquand for the next two films in the original trilogy, respectively, he still wrote the screenplay and served as executive producer on those films before returning to the director's chair for the prequel trilogy.
In 2012, Lucas sold Lucasfilm and the "Star Wars" franchise to Disney for $4 billion. In addition to the sequel trilogy, Disney continues to expand the universe through television series. The franchise's next film, "Star Wars: Starfighter" (Star Wars: Starfighter), starring Ryan Gosling, will be released next year.
The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art opened to the public on Tuesday.

Brent crude fell in early Asian trading after Donald Trump said US and Iranian representatives had held what he called “very productive” talks. Reports that Saudi Arabia is restarting a key oil pipeline also weighed on prices.
Oil prices fell on Wednesday after US President Donald Trump said American and Iranian representatives had held talks at the United Nations.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, was trading at $98.41 a barrel in the morning in Europe. US benchmark West Texas Intermediate cost $95.21 a barrel for next month delivery. Brent has repeatedly risen above $100 since the Middle East war began in February.
The three-hour meeting was “very good” and “very productive”, Trump told reporters during a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. He said another meeting was planned soon.
His comments came hours after he told the UN he faced a “big decision” on whether to reach a deal with Iran or “annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly”.
The US and Iran remain at an impasse. Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz closed, while the US has maintained a blockade of Iranian ports. Fighting involving Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen has also disrupted energy exports through the Red Sea.
“The three-hour US-Iran meeting matters because it shifts the market from pure escalation pricing toward a genuine diplomatic process, even if a final deal still looks distant,” said Stephen Innes of Quintex Intel.
Prices also fell following a report that Saudi Arabia had restarted operations along its East–West Pipeline. The route allows Saudi crude to reach the Red Sea without passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia said this month that drones launched from Iraq had forced it to close the pipeline.
The kingdom hopes to resume exports later this week, Bloomberg reported, citing a source. Saudi Aramco has reportedly told Asian refiners that they may soon be able to collect crude from the Red Sea port of Yanbu. European refiners, however, have reportedly been told they will receive no Saudi crude under their October supply agreements.
Global stocks edge higher ahead of Trump–Xi meeting
European stock markets looked set to open higher on Wednesday. Futures for the Euro Stoxx 50 and Germany’s DAX rose 0.3%, while FTSE 100 futures gained 0.2% early in the European morning.
Asian shares mostly rose. South Korea’s Kospi gained 1.2%, with Samsung and SK Hynix both up more than 2%. Taiwan’s Taiex rose 0.9%, according to the Reuters report you supplied. The MSCI index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan gained 0.5%, its sixth consecutive daily rise. Japan’s stock market was closed for a holiday, although Nikkei futures traded higher.
On Wall Street, the Nasdaq rose 0.5% to a record close on Tuesday. The S&P 500 was little changed, while the Dow fell 0.4%.
In currency markets, the euro traded at $1.1429, near a two-month low, as investors considered the possibility of another US interest rate rise. The dollar also edged up against the yen to 157.60 yen.
Gold traded at $4,379 an ounce. US Treasury futures rose slightly as oil prices eased, keeping the yield on the 10-year government bond below 5%.
Investors were also looking ahead to a meeting on Thursday between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Trade and competition over AI are expected to be on the agenda.
Kyle Rodda, a senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, said the war in the Middle East could prove more consequential for markets, including whether the US could persuade China to use its influence with Iran.

In a meeting with leaders and foreign ministers from the anti-cartel alliance, Trump on Tuesday urged member countries to join the US in targeting 24 criminal organisations, which he earlier described as the “ISIS of the Western Hemisphere”.

He said he was asking “all nations in the Shield of the Americas to formally designate narco-terrorists as common threats to stability and apply crushing sanctions” against all of the groups. The meeting took place on the sidelines of the annual United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York City.
The coalition’s 15 governments later issued a joint statement saying they intended to impose asset freezes and visa restrictions on members and supporters of the groups and to pursue criminal charges against them.
At the top of the list are two groups that have been declared “terrorist” organisations by Washington: Mara Salvatrucha (MS-13) – one of Central America’s most powerful criminal gangs – and Tren de Aragua, a Venezuelan gang that is also active in Colombia, Peru and Chile.
The list also includes major Mexican cartels, Colombian armed groups such as the National Liberation Army, Brazil’s Primeiro Comando da Capital and Comando Vermelho groups, and Peru’s Shining Path.
Al Jazeera’s Alessandro Rampietti, reporting from Bogota, Colombia, said the statement was largely symbolic for now, because each country must follow its own legal procedures.
“For example, here in Colombia, it will require a law to pass in Congress. We understand that the government here has asked Congress to move forward in drafting such a law. So while the consequences may not be immediate, this is clearly an important step towards building what the US has been trying to do in Latin America [through] this alliance,” he added.
The coalition is made up of governments closely aligned with Trump, including Argentina, Ecuador and El Salvador, whose leaders he has praised or endorsed. Colombia and Peru joined after Trump-aligned presidents took office in recent months.
Brazil and Mexico have not joined.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also attended, praised “the emergence of strong leaders who are committed to the challenge of taking on transnational terrorism”.
The gathering was the administration’s latest effort to rally the region behind a more aggressive approach to drug trafficking. Since returning to office last year, Trump has designated cartels as foreign terrorist organisations and ordered dozens of strikes on boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific that US officials say were carrying narcotics bound for the US.
The strikes have killed more than 223 people, and UN experts say they violate international law and could amount to crimes against humanity.
The Trump administration’s National Security Strategy, released late last year, laid out plans for a revamped Monroe Doctrine, the 19th-century policy asserting US primacy in the hemisphere that critics associate with decades of US intervention.
Trump has also spoken of retaking the Panama Canal and annexing Greenland and Canada. On Tuesday, he signed an agreement on Greenland that stopped short of his demand that the island become US territory.
The focus on the hemisphere has raised concerns across the region.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, in his UN speech, bristled at the approach, warning countries in Latin America and the Caribbean of “renewed hegemonic temptations”.
“Brazil is nobody’s back yard,” Lula said.

"U.S. troops in Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland guarantee our security and also send a very clear message to Russia that it should not entertain any thoughts of aggression," the foreign minister added.
The U.S. is continuing its military presence in Estonia.
