‘We’re all carrying this war on our backs’: Elite Paratroopers unit marks 70 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
02:15:00 UTC
11:15:00 KST

The Paratroopers Reconnaissance Unit, one of the IDF’s elite combat units, is marking 70 years since its establishment. Seven decades after its founding, the unit remains heavily involved in combat operations, with its soldiers moving repeatedly between fronts.
“We’re now moving from Gaza and heading up to the West Bank, to Jenin. We’ll be there over the holidays,” said Lt. Col. N., the unit’s commander, who, like the other officers interviewed for this article, can be identified only by his initial under IDF information security rules.
“We’ve all been in continuous combat since Oct. 7,” he said, referring to the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, that triggered the war in Gaza. “We carried out operations and took part in hostage missions. We operated in most areas of Gaza, including incidents connected to the hostages. From there, the unit moved to Lebanon and then Syria. There, in a single night, we seized the security zone and destroyed capabilities. From there, we went back down to Gaza, to Khan Younis. Operations night after night. Last week, we marked the unit’s 70th anniversary, a significant and special day with the veterans.”
‘The unit was my dream’
Asked what best captures the unit’s character, its deputy commander, Maj. A., pointed to fighting in Bint Jbeil, a Hezbollah stronghold in southern Lebanon.
“For me, it was mainly Bint Jbeil,” he said. “We went in initially and took commanding positions, and on the third day we operated alongside the Givati Brigade. We began identifying movement in the sector and brought the entire system into action. Fifteen terrorists were killed that morning, and it was a major event. There were six different positions, each operating as effectively as possible.”
“There was a lot of drive from the soldiers, and it wasn’t simple,” he said. “We had to gain control of the Silvester Ridge, and we identified the enemy withdrawing.”
“I grew up in this unit,” A. added. “The Paratroopers Reconnaissance Unit was always my dream. I went through my training here, served as a team commander, and on Oct. 7 I deployed with the unit.”
The prolonged fighting has put the unit’s defining characteristics to a daily test.
“First and foremost, the unit’s DNA is initiative,” said another Maj. A., a company commander. “We encountered all kinds of situations. We established positions when the attack began on Oct. 7, including a position from the sea, and all of that was initiated by the company’s soldiers through creative thinking. It reflects the values that come from the unit they grew up in.”
He recalled one encounter in which members of the unit were wounded.
“We had an encounter that didn’t go particularly well, with casualties, and that story explains what the Paratroopers Reconnaissance Unit is about,” he said. Rather than allowing the incident to develop into a crisis, he said, battalion and company commanders focused on drawing lessons from what had happened and determining how to move forward.
“The soldiers’ spirit changed over the course of the fighting, but it remained very strong throughout,” he said. “It’s really not something to take for granted — continuing to push, carrying out relevant operations, going through sleepless nights. I want to emphasize that there were crises and it was difficult, but it never broke them.”
Some soldiers who served under him during their mandatory service later returned to fight alongside him as young reservists in Lebanon, he said.
“Our ability as a system and as a reconnaissance unit is to support the soldiers after every encounter,” he said.
Maj. M. recalled another moment from the fighting in southern Israel that illustrated the unit’s experience on Oct. 7.
“Someone sitting here had just learned that his brother had been killed,” M. said, referring to one of the unit’s company commanders who was present during the interview. “Meanwhile, we heard gunfire and understood that someone had been wounded.”
“I’ve never told anyone this, but it’s a story that illustrates what the Paratroopers Reconnaissance Unit is and what the people of Israel are,” he said. “We were fighting near the Gaza border when we learned that his brother had been killed. He was next to me when he received the news, and then they started shooting at us. I’m telling you, it happened literally minutes after we understood what had happened to his brother. It was still the beginning, and without thinking too much, we charged forward and fought.”
M. said the young soldiers joining the unit today arrive with a different outlook after years of war.
“The soldiers enlisting today are different soldiers,” he said. “You see it in every aspect of the exercises. You see the way they talk to one another, with a real understanding. They simply understand what it means.”
“The fear exists, but in the end it isn’t paralyzing fear. It’s a sense of solemn responsibility,” he said. “By the end of the exercise, the soldier really understands what is required of him. They see the teams, both those that suffered casualties and those that didn’t. You see an incredible cohesion here and an inseparable bond, and they talk about it a lot.”
Maj. Y., who commanded a training company on Oct. 7 and was later appointed the reconnaissance unit’s operations officer, recalled being wounded that morning.
“I’ve been here for four months as commander of the Orev anti-tank company,” he said. “During the war, I was a training company commander at the brigade training base, and then I came here as operations officer.”
He said he was wounded by shrapnel in his leg after a group of company commanders from the Paratroopers Brigade training base gathered in the southern city of Sderot on Oct. 7.
“There was an encounter involving the deputy commander of Maglan, and before I understood what was happening, I got hit,” he said, referring to another elite IDF unit.
“Maj. A. here, to his credit, played a huge role in keeping me alive,” Y. said. “Without getting into politics, Noam Tibon also took part in rescuing me.”
Tibon, a retired IDF major general, independently headed south on Oct. 7 and joined fighting against Hamas terrorists while trying to reach his son and his family at Kibbutz Nahal Oz.
Y. said his lengthy rehabilitation left him struggling with the feeling that the war was continuing without him.
“I experienced the beginning of the fighting as a spectator,” he said. “For a long period, I personally knew everyone fighting in the field, but I felt like I was ‘sitting in the stands.’”
‘We are not fighting machines’
Maj. A. said the unit’s repeated moves among Gaza, Lebanon, Syria and the West Bank have created their own challenges.
“First of all, we are not fighting machines and we are not mercenaries,” he said. “All of this moving from one front to another is rooted in Zionism.”
From a professional standpoint, however, he said many of the combat challenges are similar.
“With many of the challenges we encountered in the north, we relied on existing combat doctrine and methods,” he said. “You make adjustments for every sector, but it isn’t overly complicated.”
The most difficult transition, he said, is between Gaza and the West Bank.
“The work in Jenin is very intensive, but you know that there are still hostages in Gaza, and that is not an easy mental challenge,” he said.
Maj. S. recalled the morning of Oct. 7, when the unit was rushed to communities near the Gaza border as Hamas-led terrorists attacked Israeli towns, military bases and a music festival.
“I really remember that on Oct. 7, you felt like they were looking for you and trying to hunt you,” he said. “Very quickly, the unit tried to reverse that equation so that we would be hunting the enemy.”
“In my opinion, the drive to engage the enemy is what distinguishes us from other units in the IDF,” he said.
S. said his older brother had commanded the unit’s reconnaissance company six years earlier.
“I remember how much he loved the position and the unit, for exactly the same reasons,” he said. “Wherever the unit is needed, that’s where it will go.”
S. began fighting at Kibbutz Re’im before moving to the area around Kibbutz Holit, another community near the Gaza border that was attacked on Oct. 7.
“At around 8 in the morning, we were in the orchards north of Holit,” he said. “As soon as we entered, we encountered them. The deputy battalion commander was wounded first, then another officer and I were hit. It was a complicated encounter.”
Beyond his personal experience, S. said the battle demonstrated the importance of how the unit responds under fire.
“In the end, the reconnaissance unit produces operational results even in an encounter like that, and the way you operate is critical,” he said. “That drive to engage the enemy was evident everywhere we operated.”
Looking back on the unit’s 70-year history, Lt. Col. N. said the years since Oct. 7 have left their mark on everyone serving in it.
“I feel it myself, and I see it in everyone who has been here from the first day,” he said. “We’re all carrying this war on our backs.”

oversized flowers, terrazzo, and pop references ornament zyva studio’s paris showroom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
02:10:14 UTC
11:10:14 KST

Zyva Studio builds Paris apartment around ornamentation
Paris-based Zyva Studio has turned the apartment of its founder, Anthony Authié, into the showroom of the studio. Across 60 sqm, ornament is not a finishing layer but a starting point that challenges Adolf Loos’s claim that ’ornament is a crime’ and instead opens space for imagination. The 20th century had settled the matter: form follows function, and decoration would be a lapse of taste. With no nostalgia and no pastiche, the studio would rather ask the question differently. What if ornament did not come last, to dress an architecture already finished, but first, as a starting point? It then adds nothing superfluous; it opens a fiction.
flowers and colorful interior motifs shape the apartment
Within Zyva Studio’s Paris apartment, spiky flowers rise from floor to ceiling, green stems ringed with yellow and red corollas. Above them, monumental chains in red, blue, and yellow hang like a child’s toy shifted in scale. None of these pieces decorates something that was already there; each one is both the object and its ornament. In the bedroom, the clay bed leans against a metal headboard where the ventilation ducts remain exposed, like an engine room. What is usually hidden becomes the motif. The coffee table, designed with Mosaic Factory, sets a terrazzo top on a tubular structure borrowed from the pipes of Mario Bros. A noble material, a pop reference, and no hierarchy between the two.
kitchen and mezzanine, terrazzo running from floor to wall
patterned surfaces create a continuous material thread
One motif runs through the apartment: the aggregate. It spreads across the terrazzo floor, tightens in the granite of the round table, returns in the kitchen worktop, and reappears in the terrazzo of the coffee table. Four densities, four grain sizes, one ornament declined. Answering this mineral thread are the printed hides, the cowhide rug on the floor, the Dalmatian curtains at the windows, the star-shaped handles, and the doors perforated with crosses and dots. This apparent chaos is held together by a thread; each motif calls the next and ends up building one single world.

In brief
- Queensland is still refusing to sign onto a government plan called Thriving Kids.
- The plan would help the government shift NDIS spending to the states.
A plan to shift billions of dollars worth of NDIS spending to the states is snagging on one holdout jurisdiction as a minister also warns criminal gangs have penetrated the scheme.
Queensland is the only state or territory still refusing to take responsibility for autistic and developmentally delayed children with low-to-moderate support needs under the government's new Thriving Kids program.
States have agreed to chip in a combined $4 billion into Thriving Kids over five years, helping prop up Labor's sweeping efforts to curtail what it calls runaway NDIS spending.
But Canberra and Brisbane still appear divided on the issue despite the looming 1 October deadline for jurisdictions to sign up, angering Health Minister Mark Butler.
"I'm a little frustrated they haven't signed because all other states and territories, Liberal and Labor alike, CLP government in the NT has signed on," he told ABC Radio on Wednesday.

Queensland Premier David Crisafulli was shirking a responsibility he had previously promised to accept, according to Butler.
"I can't imagine a Queensland government that, for the next 15 months, would sit on its hands and pretend it does not have a very serious obligation to follow the rest of the country," he said.
"Frankly (it should) implement commitments that the premier made at the National Cabinet meeting earlier this year."
Queensland was losing time to bring its Thriving Kids program online, according to Butler, with the state expected to take up development checks, support programs, workforce capability preparation along with a suite of other obligations under the new framework.
The state has reportedly raised red flags over insufficient assurances about the welfare of Queenslanders relying on the NDIS.
The stern rebuke from the minister comes the day after Australia's most important security partners were warned organised crime syndicates were feasting on government programs, in an address by NDIS minister and senator Jenny McAllister.
McAllister said the government had saved $2.1 billion through NDIS fraud crackdowns since 2022, before US, New Zealand, Canadian and British representatives in a Sydney meeting of the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing partners.
On Wednesday, McAllister described the NDIS as having been a "very soft target" and nearly defenceless against criminal gangs.

Romania’s political deadlock risks handing power to far right, PM nominee warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
02:02:00 UTC
11:02:00 KST

Siegfried Mureșan participates in an exchange of views with European Budget Commissioner Piotr Serafin in Brussels on Jan. 29, 2025. | Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
Romania’s center-left opposition must urgently decide whether to support a new pro-European government or be blamed for the far right gaining control, warned the country’s potential next prime minister.
In an interview with POLITICO, European lawmaker Siegfried Mureșan said he would ask the Social Democratic Party (PSD) to back his center-right National Liberal Party (PNL) in a new vote “by the end of next week,” even though the PSD’s leadership has so far refused to do so.
“Romanian socialists are facing a moment of truth — they need to decide whether they behave as responsible European social democrats and support a pro-European government or whether they are intensifying their cooperation with the radical right, the anti-European populistic extremist party here,” said Mureșan, who is the third person tasked with forming a government since the ruling coalition lost a no-confidence vote in May.
Advertisement
Another failure in Bucharest would set up a divisive early election in the EU’s seventh-most-populous country, where the far right is leading the polls at a moment when populist-nationalist parties are surging in countries around Europe.
Mainstream parties in Romania — a key strategic NATO ally that has suffered some spillover from Russia’s war in Ukraine — have barely fought off the far right in a series of parliamentary and presidential elections that began in winter 2024.
PSD leader Sorin Grindeanu said on Monday that the group will not vote in favor of Mureșan’s government and would only support the formation of a government it forms part of. He has not, however, closed the door to a coalition with the far-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR), which has courted confrontation with Brussels and supported pro-Russian candidates. The PSD and AUR voted together to bring down the previous government earlier this year.
Mureșan called on the EU’s center-left S&D group leadership in Brussels to prevent that from happening, arguing they “are obviously responsible for what their member parties are doing” and arguing they “will have a very significant problem of credibility, shall they continue to be silent about their Romanian members partner cooperating closely with the far right.”
“As long as the European socialists are not acting to prevent this in a very credible way from happening, we cannot exclude socialists in other countries going this way, unfortunately, as well,” he added.
Grindeanu, however, has suggested that his PSD could be convinced to enter discussions with Mureșan if he agrees to include ten policy proposals identified as core for the PSD. Among them are a new push for energy infrastructure, a defense and national security uplift, public services reform and investment in education and healthcare.
Advertisement
However, if the proposed cabinet and policy program is rejected, President Nicușor Dan will gain the constitutional power to order new elections — the first since 2024, when the AUR made major gains and became the second-largest party in parliament. Mureșan acknowledged that the far-right faction is now polling at around 35 percent, compared to just 21 percent for his own center-right PNL.
“Early elections are not my preferred option,” said Mureșan. “I believe that we should try to form a pro-European government now. But should this not be possible, I think they should not be ruled out.”
The request from Dan, who last year beat the AUR’s controversial candidate George Simion in the race for the presidency, comes at an awkward time for Mureșan. Currently serving as a member of the European Parliament, he is one of the chief negotiators on the EU’s €2 trillion long-term budget, which the bloc’s leaders want to see finalized by the end of the year.
According to him, though, the far right taking control of Romania would make that job far harder because “any anti-European government around the table would want Europe to be weaker. They know that the budget is an important tool to keep Europe strong, and they would basically vote against an ambitious and realistic [budget].”
On top of that, “we would have a government which would be very friendly to Russia, and all of this would be bad for the people of Romania, for the European Union.”

One of America’s largest reservoirs just hit a record low
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
02:01:16 UTC
11:01:16 KST

One of America’s largest reservoirs just hit a record low
- Date:
- September 22, 2026
- Source:
- NASA Earth Observatory
- Summary:
- Lake Powell has fallen to its lowest level on record after an exceptionally dry and warm winter left the Colorado River Basin with little mountain snow to melt. Lake Mead also reached record lows, raising concerns for a river system that supplies water and power to more than 40 million people. Federal officials have taken emergency steps to stabilize Lake Powell, including sending in water from another reservoir and reducing releases downstream.
- Share:
Snow drought and unusually warm conditions across the Colorado Basin in 2026 sharply reduced water flowing into major reservoirs across the U.S. West.
By summer, the effects of the weak 2025-2026 mountain snowpack in the Upper Colorado Basin had reached Lake Powell. With far less snowmelt than usual feeding the Colorado River, inflows dwindled, and the second-largest reservoir in the United States fell to record-low levels in late August and early September.
Lake Powell Falls Below Its Previous Record
Satellite images captured the dramatic change in Lake Powell near Glen Canyon Dam. The images were collected by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) aboard the NASA-USGS Landsat 8 satellite on September 1, 2017 (left), and September 10, 2026 (right).
In the 2026 image, Lake Powell's water surface stood at 3,517.24 feet. Roughly a month earlier, the reservoir had already fallen below its previous record low of 3,519.92 feet, which was set on April 13, 2023. Water levels continued declining into early September.
The 2017 image provides a striking contrast, showing Lake Powell during one of its highest water levels of the past decade.
Lake Mead Also Reaches Record Lows
The Colorado River first flows into Lake Powell before continuing downstream toward Lake Mead. In August 2026, Lake Mead also reached record-low levels.
The river system, managed by the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation (USBR) and other agencies, is a critical source of both water and electricity across the Southwest. More than 40 million people depend on it, including residents of Las Vegas, Phoenix, Los Angeles, and San Diego. The river also supplies water to roughly 5 million acres of farmland.
Why Snow Matters So Much to the Colorado River
Much of the Colorado Basin is arid or semi-arid, which makes mountain snow especially important. A substantial share of the Colorado River's annual flow begins as snow that accumulates at high elevations during winter and melts during spring and early summer.
The Upper Colorado Basin, along with many mountainous regions across the U.S. West, received unusually little snow during winter 2025-2026. The shortage amounted to a snow drought.
Periods of record warmth made conditions worse by further reducing the snowpack. As a result, the spring snowmelt delivered far less water to reservoirs than it normally would, providing little relief for already depleted lake levels.
Emergency Steps to Protect Lake Powell
In April 2026, the USBR began taking measures to stabilize Lake Powell and prevent the reservoir from dropping below the elevation required for hydropower generation.
Without intervention, the agency considered that possibility realistic by August 2026.
To help support Lake Powell, USBR began releasing additional water from Flaming Gorge Reservoir in northern Utah and southern Wyoming. At the same time, officials reduced the amount of water being released from Lake Powell into Lake Mead.
The agency also canceled a "controlled flood" planned for April that was intended to rebuild sandbars used as fish habitat. In August, officials also skipped a "cool mix" release designed to help protect native species.
A Megadrought Continues to Strain the Southwest
Drought in the U.S. Southwest has persisted since around the beginning of the 21st century. Experts have described the prolonged dry period as a megadrought, and it continues to place intense pressure on the region's limited water supplies.
NASA-supported projects and monitoring systems are giving water managers and other decision-makers across the Colorado Basin more detailed information about drought conditions and how they are changing.
At the Colorado River's headwaters, for example, a dashboard built around the Western Land Data Assimilation System (WLDAS) provides real-time visualizations of soil moisture, snow water equivalent, and evapotranspiration. The information helps support Colorado's drought task force and contributes to weekly U.S. Drought Monitor maps.
Satellite Data Helps Track Drought Across the Basin
Closer to Lake Powell, the Drought Severity Evaluation Tool, co-developed with the Navajo Nation, allows leaders to track localized drought indicators, precipitation patterns, and vegetation health across tribal lands. (With funding from NOAA's National Integrated Drought Information System, its adoption expanded to Oklahoma's Chickasaw and Choctaw Nations in 2025.)
Another resource, the Colorado River Integrated Assessment tool, was developed by Arizona State University researchers in partnership with the Central Arizona Project. It brings together improved modeling with NASA-satellite-validated measurements of snowpack, surface and groundwater storage, soil moisture, and other conditions throughout the Colorado River Basin in a single interactive system.
Story Source:
Materials provided by NASA Earth Observatory. Original written by Lindsey Doermann. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Burnham passes his first Trump test — but papers over the cracks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
02:00:43 UTC
11:00:43 KST

Burnham passes his first Trump test — but papers over the cracks
Britain’s newbie prime minister got through an hour with the U.S. president mostly unscathed. But the immediate differences were on show more than with Keir Starmer.
Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham shakes hands with U.S. President Donald Trump during a meeting on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly on September 22, 2026 in New York City. | Toby Melville/WPA Pool/Getty Images
NEW YORK — Before Andy Burnham’s meeting with Donald Trump, a senior U.K. government figure noted wryly that they were looking out for one thing — whether the U.S. president would claim that Burnham was better than the last guy.
After nearly an hour together in a cramped, low-ceilinged room in the United Nations basement, Trump did exactly that.
The president said U.K.-U.S. relations were “more up now than they were with your last prime minister.” Moments later he put the boot into Keir Starmer again, claiming the ex-PM’s tough rhetoric on Russia had been “too tough.”
Advertisement
That final comment will please Starmer, who welcomed Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy to Britain after Trump berated him in the Oval Office. But it also shows how far his relationship with Trump fell after his initial attempts to please the president in early 2025.
Burnham had the benefit of a fresh start, and ahead of his first meeting with Trump, British officials insisted he would take a less fawning approach than his predecessor. He could afford to do so, they said, because Trump’s presidency is almost at the midway point and there is less to lose.
Yet there were similarities to Starmer’s early days. Both leaders were on their best behavior, straining not to upset each other in public.
They each gave the other a free pass. Burnham sat expressionless as Trump talked about “fake news” media, while Trump did the same as Burnham talked about Britain’s recent sanctions on West Bank settlements.
Burnham raised the salience of immigration, an issue Trump invoked against Starmer, while Trump even praised Burnham’s “great election win.” (Burnham has not won a general election, merely a special election for the parliamentary seat of Makerfield.)
But some things were different. The splits between the two nations were closer to the surface than in Starmer’s first trip — and even in those cordial words for the cameras, the divides broke into the open.
Advertisement
Trump seized on a Daily Telegraph journalist’s invitation to condemn the long-stalled British plan to hand sovereignty of the Chagos Islands, a strategically vital archipelago in the Indian Ocean, to Mauritius. His words were little surprise on their own, but Burnham’s response — in which he repeatedly refused to rule out reopening the terms of the deal to satisfy Trump’s concerns — formed a genuine shift in U.K. policy.
It remains unclear how any deal could satisfy the demands of Mauritius and the U.S. at the same time.
Then there was the gulf between the two leaders on AI regulation.
Andy Burnham used his speech to UNGA to put his appeal to domestic cost-of-living issues on a world stage. | Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
Burnham used a breakfast Tuesday in New York with business figures, including Apple’s Tim Cook, to call for an agreed global set of standards on the technology.
Burnham spent almost an hour in a room with the leader of the free world (and an eight-strong delegation on each side), yet appears not to have raised AI with Trump at all. Downing Street repeatedly refused to say he brought it up and there was no mention of it the official readout.
Advertisement
After it was all over, Burnham used his speech to UNGA to put his appeal to domestic cost-of-living issues on a world stage.
He also announced a “national center for information defense” (with little detail) that would counter disinformation; he portrayed Britain as an “honest broker” on controlling AI. But Britain’s decision not to back a declaration by 22 countries on global AI controls earlier in the week meant it could be sidelined. (Burnham said Britain would look at multiple initiatives, including that one.)
There were other potential wrinkles. Burnham said he would speak in defense of the Falkland Islands, weeks after Trump gave fuel to Argentina’s long-standing claims on their sovereignty by suggesting he would not help if Argentina tried to invade.
Burnham also revealed that he made a plea to Trump about U.S. tariffs and their effect on a particular factory in the northeast of England (he would not say which one). Despite the carve-outs that Starmer won, British industry — especially the automobile sector — is still being hit by Trump’s tariffs.
But so much that could have gone wrong, didn’t — at least for now. Trump did not use the time before the cameras to bring up Britain’s difficult progress toward spending 3.5% of GDP on defense, and did not hit out over the pace of the decision to allow oil and gas drilling in the North Sea.
The newbie prime minister looked buttoned-up during the moment for the cameras with Trump, relaxing only when he was asked about Manchester, where he spent nine years as mayor. The world stage is still new to him.
Advertisement
And in that context, his aides will be chalking the first meeting up overall as a win — just as Starmer’s aides did on the way back from New York two years ago this week. Trump praised Burnham as a natural businessman, a man who “gets it.” The vibes, in this relatively easy opening period, were good.
He will need to maintain the influence if he can. Burnham later said he lobbied Trump to press for an “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia. Pressure on the U.S. to release more air defense missiles to Ukraine ahead of the winter will only increase.
While Burnham didn’t invite him to the U.K. on Tuesday, they did pave the way for another visit to one of Trump’s golf resorts. “I said I was having second thoughts about playing golf with him, given a recent performance of my own was probably not up to the right standard,” Burnham told broadcasters.
For the man who wasn’t going to bend the knee to Trump, flattery will get him everywhere.

South Sudan’s Kiir dissolves government ahead of first national elections

South Sudan’s Kiir dissolves government ahead of first national elections
President’s move clears hurdles to long delayed election and raises concern he can now wield unchecked power.
South Sudan’s President Salva Kiir has dissolved the country’s transitional unity government and appointed a caretaker administration as the country prepares for its first-ever national elections.
The decree on Tuesday ended a power-sharing arrangement set up under a 2018 peace deal that halted years of civil war, and raised concerns that Kiir could now wield unchecked power.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Colourism in South Sudan
- list 2 of 3What’s behind the renewed violence on South Sudan’s border with Sudan?
- list 3 of 3Will South Sudan’s latest peace deal last?
The decree, read out by the national broadcaster, said all vice-presidents, ministers and local administrators have been removed and that the national and state assemblies have been dissolved.
The judiciary and security institutions remain in place, while Kiir will stay in office “during the election period until the next elected president assumes office”, it said.
The decree came a day after the parliament approved changes to the National Elections Act that allowed Kiir to stay in power during the election period, while removing all vice presidents, who were appointed under the 2018 peace deal.
The changes mean that South Sudan can move towards elections scheduled for December 22, without first completing a permanent constitution or census – two processes that were previously tied to the transition.
The main opposition alliance has rejected the changes.
Elections were initially expected in 2022 but have been postponed twice.
Tasks still outstanding under the 2018 peace deal include drafting a permanent constitution, registering voters and unifying the armed forces loyal to rival parties.
That agreement followed five years of civil war that killed about 400,000 people and displaced millions, according to the United Nations.
Amnesty International, a prominent rights group, called Kiir’s decree a “decisive step” towards the country’s first-ever elections. But Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International’s regional director for East and Southern Africa, urged the authorities to “ensure that a conducive environment exists for people to vote and stand in elections”.
Analysts meanwhile warned that the changes offered Kiir unfettered control.
“Kiir will be the only person in power, without vice-presidents, without the executive, without the parliament,” Michael Wani, a lawyer and former member of the constitution drafting committee, told the AFP news agency.
Independent analyst Machot Amuom told AFP there was a lot of “ambiguity” in the legal changes. “The new law gives the president full powers … He can decide even not to go for elections for another year or another two years,” Amuom told AFP.
Last week, Kiir also replaced the head of the elections commission without giving a reason. South Sudan Broadcasting Corporation (SSBC) said the new chief, Gabriel Bol Deng Majok, had been given a “fresh mandate” to oversee preparations for the polls.
The preparations come as Kiir’s longtime rival Riek Machar, who leads the opposition Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-in-Opposition (SPLM-IO), remains under house arrest. He is on trial on charges including treason and murder, which he denies.
The transition is also taking place under tight security.
AFP reported checkpoints and road closures around the government complex in the capital, Juba, while security personnel were ordered to remain on heightened alert for three days.

Artworks reveal Chinese rulers and Cixi loved role-playing long before modern cosplay
What Emperor Qianlong did with his court painters is the 18th century equivalent of digital photo manipulation and Photoshop
The Qing dynasty’s Empress Dowager Cixi is renowned as a cosplay enthusiast, leaving behind photographs and paintings of herself embodying the Buddhist Goddess of Mercy, Guanyin. However, she was not the first to engage in such role-playing while on the throne.
Long before Cixi (1835–1908), the Qing dynasty’s emperors Yongzheng (1678–1735) and his son, Qianlong (1711–1799), indulged in role-playing, as evidenced in numerous paintings.
Yongzheng, whose reign lasted 13 years, was known as a strict and relentless workaholic. Thus, the contrast of his playful side revealed in the role-playing paintings often surprised many.
He left behind two albums titled The Album of the Yongzheng Emperor in Costumes, each featuring paintings of him portraying various characters, including a Taoist priest, a Buddhist lama, a Han intellectual, a peasant, and even a European figure.

LONDON — Britain is preparing to release thousands of prisoners early to free up space in its overcrowded prisons. Its European neighbors are getting worried.
Five EU diplomats told POLITICO that their countries are particularly concerned about this change, with some saying they fear their nationals could be returned with little or no advance warning or communication.
“It’s very risky sending back criminals without any prior information,” said one EU diplomat, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive ongoing discussions.
Advertisement
The policy risks becoming another hurdle in Britain’s efforts to reset relations with the bloc, as the two sides prepare for a major summit to progress trade talks.
Britain is on course to release over 2,500 offenders by the end of the year under the scheme, with a further 700 due to be freed on Oct. 1.
But from January 2027, the government will also remove the requirement for foreign offenders to serve a minimum period in a British prison before being deported.
A U.K. government spokesperson said: “We will continue to engage with European partners on this issue. … The most serious offenders are excluded and, where there is evidence someone plans to commit future crimes, they will stay behind bars.”
Poor communication
Communication has so far, the diplomats say, been limited.
A second diplomat told POLITICO: “[The U.K. government] keeps saying that they cannot inform us. There should be some sort of collegiality among police forces, to let us know they’re letting [someone] out. We should be warned.”
Advertisement
The diplomat added embassies are also frustrated by the lack of coordination between departments on the issue.
“The FCDO always says talk to the Home Office,” the person said. “The Home Office says we should speak to FCDO — and the Cabinet Office says it has nothing to do with them.”
A third diplomat called it “a tricky situation,” saying European capitals are worried prisoners fresh out of “British jail can just pop to an airport in their home country, and are allowed to walk freely.”
A member of UK Border Force patrols at Heathrow Airport on July 16, 2019. | Daniel Leal/AFP via Getty Images
They said capitals would want more “information about the person being transferred,” but that the “Brits treat it as if there is nothing to confirm with us, and that it’s just a unilateral deportation.”
But prison reform campaigners point out that many of these offenders would face deportation at the end of their sentences anyway. The changes bring forward the point at which foreign prisoners become eligible for removal, as opposed to the outcome.
“It is up to the receiving country to decide if the prisoner should serve any prison time,” said Mark Day, deputy director at the Prison Reform Trust. “Some foreign nationals who are deported may not be required to serve any form of sentence. For others, the sentence served may be more punitive than the one they would have experienced in the U.K.”
Advertisement
Day said deportation also remains subject to legal and practical constraints, including where removal breaches the European Convention on Human Rights or the Refugee Convention.
Foreign nationals make up around 12 percent of the U.K. prison population, according to the latest Ministry of Justice figures. The biggest groups include nationals from several EU countries, such as Poland and Romania, as well as from the EU candidate country Albania.
Under the current post-Brexit trade deal, there are mechanisms where the U.K. notifies a European country when its national is convicted of a crime in Britain. The government is currently exploring whether additional measures could further support public safety.
Testing the reset
The issue is yet another test of the Labour government’s pledge to move on from Brexit and “reset” relations with its European allies.
The U.K. and EU are expected to hold a joint summit later this year, finalizing agreements to make trade smoother, travel easier, and climate cooperation tighter.
But the two sides are yet to agree on a date for the meeting amid concurrent disputes over EU trade protectionism and tuition fees.
Advertisement
The U.K. wants a carve-out from the EU’s “Made in Europe” policy and is pushing for British companies to get preferential treatment under EU industrial and procurement rules.
Meanwhile Brussels says the U.K. must cut tuition fees for European students studying in Britain if it wants a deal — which the British university sector says it can’t afford.
The latest row over prisoners is unlikely to make finding a solution easier.
“If somebody does something terrible after being flown to any of the member states … it can become a major diplomatic spat,” the second EU diplomat quoted above said. “There should be the U.K.-EU summit in November. You can imagine the juicy headlines.”
They added: “It’s really about basic trust. How would you excuse the British government for not telling us? We have the U.K. asking for trusted partner status [which would give British companies preferential access to EU procurement rules]. This is a ticking bomb.”

Trump’s Greenland deal, explained
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

US President Donald Trump shakes hands with Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen as Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen looks on during the signing ceremony for their trilateral security agreement in New York on Sept. 22, 2026. | Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images
Eight months after Donald Trump almost destroyed NATO by threatening to annex Greenland — by force, if necessary — he signed what he called a “fantastic” new deal that would give the U.S. all the control and military access it needs over the Danish territory.
European allies were so alarmed by Trump’s apparent determination to take the territory at the start of the year — and his threat of 25% tariffs on anyone who got in his way — that they began talking about a future for the West without America. In many ways, the transatlantic relationship has not been the same since.
Tuesday’s agreement on security in the Arctic and North Atlantic, signed at the United Nations by Trump and the prime ministers of Greenland and Denmark, ends the dispute. But what exactly is in the deal? Who will pay for it? And who are the winners and losers from months of high-stakes talks?
Advertisement
Here’s POLITICO’s guide:
What exactly is the deal?
This new agreement, which still needs ratification by Danish and Greenlandic lawmakers, is not, in fact, completely new. Instead, it sets out to “amend and supplement” an earlier deal between the U.S. and Denmark dating back to 1951. Many experts have been saying for months that this earlier agreement gave Trump most of what he said he wanted in terms of more or less unfettered freedom to set up military bases and police the region’s security.
One key difference this time is that Greenland itself is a signatory.
What is in the deal?
The opening part of the text reaffirms the signatories’ commitments to abide by international law, respect Danish territory, fulfill NATO’s responsibilities, and uphold the rights of Greenlanders. Much of the rest of the text focuses on American military and civilian access to Greenland and plans to establish U.S. military facilities there.
Trump promised to build two “very major” bases in Greenland. According to the text released by the Danish government, the two touted new American bases aren’t entirely new either, at least in terms of their locations.
One will be at Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland, which was the former American Bluie West One base that closed in the 1950s. And the other is Mestersvig in eastern Greenland, which is currently home to Denmark’s Sirius Dog Sled Patrol unit and would be refurbished.
Advertisement
Under the deal, the U.S. military will have “free access” to air, land and sea routes on and around Greenland between the two bases. Greenland is already home to the U.S. Pituffik Space Base, where about 150 American troops are stationed to operate a ballistic missile monitoring site to protect North America from long-range missile attack.
The deal also sets out how the U.S. could establish new drone warfare facilities — “unmanned military installations” — in Greenland with fast-track approval processes from the Danish and Greenlandic authorities. But Denmark and Greenland will have the final say on where such facilities should be located, or whether they are built at all.
Locking out the enemy
What’s also new are several clauses designed to stop potential rivals and adversaries taking a military or economic stake in Greenland in the future. It states that no non-NATO nation can open a base on the island or mine for critical minerals or rare earths without the agreement of the three signatories.
The HDMS Ejnar Mikkelsen, a Royal Danish Navy patrol vessel, sails in the waters of the Nuuk fjord, Greenland, on March 6, 2026. | Florent Vergnes/AFP via Getty Images
Trump has often spoken about Chinese and Russian military activities around Greenland, claiming earlier thisyear that, “if you take a look outside of Greenland right now, there are Russian destroyers. There are Chinese destroyers … there are Russian submarines all over the place. We’re not going to have Russia or China occupy Greenland, and that’s what they’re going to do if we don’t.”
NATO officials have quietly pushed back against those claims, with one diplomat saying “we’re not seeing any Chinese activity” around Greenland, while Russian movements in the High North haven’t changed significantly and there’s little, if any, Russian presence near Greenland.
Who pays?
In a recent social media post, Trump said “there will be no cost to the United States,” for rebuilding bases and expanding the U.S. presence in Greenland.
Advertisement
It’s unclear how that would work since the one base mentioned in the agreement was closed by the U.S. in the 1950s and the other is a small Danish installation that currently houses sled dogs.
It depends on what the Pentagon would want to use the bases for, but most likely projects are new air defense and radar installations, which would come with large construction costs. Nothing in the agreement specifies cost-sharing mechanisms between the three parties to the deal. The Pentagon didn’t respond to a request for comment.
Who won?
At the start of this year, Denmark faced the threat of losing the territory entirely. While Europeans’ trust in the U.S. as an ally has taken a long-term hit, the immediate risk to Danish territory has now gone, according to the legal text.
Instead, the deal explicitly reaffirms Danish sovereignty and Greenland’s right to self-determination — including choosing independence from Denmark, potentially. For what it’s worth, the deal also explicitly recognizes the need to protect the “pristine” environment of the territory and Greenlanders’ cultural, social and economic rights.
“Reading it, one wonders why so much fuss for so little, when this could have been done from the start,” said Grégoire Roos, program director for Europe at the Chatham House think tank in London. “I also think it’s well played from Denmark — clean and diplomatic. Some might call it the European touch.”
Speaking before the deal was published, the Atlantic Council’s Daniel Fried, a former U.S. ambassador to Poland, said the deal gave Washington something it could call a win, and “allowed the U.S. to walk back from its damaging and pointless threats of aggression.”
Advertisement
Will it last?
One persistent concern among European diplomats and Danish officials over the past year or so has been that even when Trump wasn’t always talking about Greenland, he had not forgotten his ambitions for the U.S. to take ownership of it.
In the past, Trump has not always stuck to the deals he’s made, if he felt he could get better terms — another persistent source of anxiety in European diplomatic circles.
It’s possible that the biggest consideration will be White House bandwidth. With so many other priorities — from Iran, to the mid-term elections, to the next presidential race — will Trump or his allies have the time and headspace to give to re-examining these amendments to a 75-year-old deal?

Friedrich Merz has a Friedrich Merz problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

BERLIN — The trouble with Friedrich Merz is that when things get difficult, he can make them even more difficult.
At a press conference this week, the German chancellor had barely begun addressing yet another disastrous set of election results when he stopped to rebuke a man moving in front of the cameras. “Haven’t you found a seat? Because you’re blocking the view for a lot of other people.”
The icy tone was fleeting, but telling. In the face of crushing political pressure, Merz is trying to convince Germans that he can revive the economy, reform the welfare state, and halt the flight of voters to the political extremes, such as the far-right Alternative for Germany party and the Left party, both of which clinched victories in state elections over the weekend.
Advertisement
Yet his combative public manner repeatedly gets in the way of the message. The irony is that the Merz I’ve seen away from the cameras can be engaging and capable of laughing at himself. His political problem is that too few voters ever see that side of him.
Criticism of Merz’s manner is no longer just about style. His personal manner is cited as one of the reasons the Christian Democrats fared so badly in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania: For the first time in the party’s postwar history, they failed to clear the 5% threshold for entering a state parliament.
Aloof, confrontational and lacking in empathy — these have been frequent accusations as Merz has taken to the airwaves during the regional election season to fight his corner, sometimes making matters worse.
One encounter earlier this month was particularly damaging. In a televised roundtable, pediatrician and influencer Bea Merscher attacked his record on health spending as “inhumane.” Merz angrily told her she was “going too far,” described doctors as “beneficiaries” of the health system, and added: “You are doctors. You couldn’t get by without this health system.”
Fact checks found Merz largely right on the substance of health spending and reform — but he lost on tone. The public tends to prefer doctors to politicians in a bare-knuckle prime-time fight.
“His problem is that he argues with opponents as though they are another politician or a board member,” a person who worked with him in opposition told me, confidentially, so as not to draw the chancellor’s ire. “He doesn’t think about how it looks from the sofa in front of the TV.”
Advertisement
Yet there is another, more surprising Merz — one I have encountered over years on the international circuit, in brief conversations, small dinners and events where, once he loosens his tie, a more personable character emerges.
When we first met, at a dinner in 2022 to discuss Germany’s laggardly response to the war in Ukraine, I pressed Merz — then opposition leader — on why he had not pushed then Chancellor Olaf Scholz harder to send longer-range weapons to Kyiv. His answer was evasive. Over a glass of Sekt afterwards, I risked saying so.
It could have gone either way. Merz can end conversations sharply if he feels he is being treated badly. But he can also have a wry charm. He joked that I was being “very testing,” before explaining that he did not want to appear to be backseat-driving the government as the conflict intensified.
Supporters participate in a Christian Democratic Union event in Berlin on Sept. 17, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
I had another go when our paths crossed at an Airbus factory in the U.K. in 2025, where he appeared with then Prime Minister Keir Starmer — who, to Merz’s amusement, called him simply “Friedrich,” an informality unusual in German politics. Again, Merz wavered on the sensitive question of supplying Taurus missiles to Ukraine. Again, I pressed him on the omission.
He saw the funny side. “You again!” he observed the next time we met.
There was another glimpse of that Merz when I asked whether he planned to congratulate former Chancellor Angela Merkel on her birthday. The question forced him into elaborate good wishes for the predecessor with whom he has had a famously testy relationship, after she bested him in the struggle for control of the CDU and, in his view, steered the party too far to the left.
Advertisement
“Of course! We should all do that!” he replied — and laughed.
These moments matter because Merz’s public image has hardened around a very different figure: formal, wealthy and remote from the instincts of many voters. A former corporate lawyer and BlackRock Germany chair, he has never made much effort to disguise the fruits of success in a country that tends to prefer its wealth worn with stealth.
For years, that included his private plane and a taste for expensive cars. Since becoming chancellor, he has toned down the high life. Paradoxically, that may have made him appear more desiccated, not less: the Merz who is enjoying himself is often more engaging than the Merz who is trying hard to look chancellor-like.
Merz’s instinct under pressure is to answer with more detail and more reform. A 34-point plan to revive Germany invited mockery for its complexity, while the AfD campaigned hard against his proposal to raise the retirement age to 67 and was rewarded at the ballot box.
Now he needs to not only move faster, but also better sell his case: that state reforms will create new jobs and make pensions affordable in the future. Right now, many Germans think reforms will simply take something away from them.
Andreas Rödder, a leading German political historian and Christian Democrat who once ran for chancellor, has long warned that Merz’s “firewall” against the far right would fail. He thinks the chancellor’s strategy of continuing and hoping the reforms eventually pay off is doomed.
Advertisement
He argues that Merz lacks the courage to break with the Social Democrats and pursue reforms that are being slowed by tensions inside the coalition. Like others who have had on-off relations with Merz, Rödder also points to an oversensitivity to criticism and a tendency to discard people he has fallen out with rather than win them round.
“Just saying, ‘I am staying where I am’ is not an answer here,” Rödder told me. “The question is why he doesn’t see that. He announces swathes of reforms and yet it is unclear how he can really deliver them in this coalition, so people stop believing what they hear.”
It is, as Rödder puts it, a paradox: Merz had the courage and toughness to run for the CDU leadership three times. Yet the relaxed and self-aware Merz visible in private has remained largely hidden from the voters he now needs to persuade. He is a hard-working, pragmatic chancellor who knows many of the cues are suddenly uncertain, which the economic giant of a country needs.
The question is whether he has the means and agility to learn what has gone wrong — and learn to speak to Germans anyway, winning over hearts and minds — when both have sorely deserted him.
Anne McElvoy is a Global Reporter for the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network.

‘Sweden is back’: Magdalena Andersson has big plans for Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

STOCKHOLM — After four years in opposition, Sweden’s former Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson is about to retake power — and she aims to use it to fortify Europe’s place in an unstable world.
Andersson is in the middle of coalition talks as she prepares for a second stint as prime minister at the head of a left-leaning government, after winning a tight election against the right and far-right earlier this month.
In an exclusive interview with POLITICO conducted on election day, the Social Democrat leader set out her mission to refocus Swedish foreign policy — and to give the EU more muscle.
Advertisement
“We need a strong European Union in the world we live in today,” she told POLITICO. “With Russia still waging war in Ukraine, we have an unpredictable United States, and we have China trying to step forward — we really need the European Union to be strong.”
Sweden has an influential voice in European affairs, with an enviable economic record and numerous successful businesses, including tech successes Klarna and Spotify and manufacturing giants Volvo and Saab. If she is confirmed as prime minister, Andersson will be one of the few voices from the left among the EU’s 27 leaders, alongside Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen and the embattled Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.
When it comes to beefing up the EU, Andersson’s priority is to overhaul its decision-making processes, especially at the sometimes quarrelsome European Council leaders’ summits. Andersson was in office at the time of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and remembers the difficult dynamic during sanctions discussions, when Hungary’s former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán threw obstacles in the way of agreements that required unanimous support.
The “number one” issue for giving the EU a strong voice is whether the bloc’s 27 leaders “can actually agree on things” when they sit “around the table,” she said. “Having a strong Europe — finding unanimity, how important that is for us to be strong — I think that’s the key.”
To that end, Andersson wants to scrap the rule granting a veto right to every EU member country on foreign policy. “I think it should be qualified majority … on foreign policy,” she said, adding that when Ukraine and other countries — such as candidates in the Western Balkans — join the EU, “there will be changes one way or another, and then I think this should be one of the issues discussed at that point in time.”
Raiding Russian assets
One area where EU leaders tried — and famously failed — to get a unanimous agreement was on whether or not to use Russia’s financial assets, lying immobilized in a Brussels depository, to help fund Ukraine’s mounting costs of defending itself. Efforts to secure a deal foundered last year on legal concerns from Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever.
Advertisement
The debate was revived in recent weeks by a group of countries led by Germany. What does Andersson think should happen to the assets? “Take them, use them,” she said.
For “frugal” Sweden, this is “a better way” than adding to the EU’s multi-year budget, which she wants to limit. As for Belgium’s legal worries over seizing assets from the depository in its jurisdiction, she is blunt: “Solve the legal questions, then.”
Such assertiveness is still new for Sweden, which had been studiously neutral until Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Russian leader Vladimir Putin changed that, and Sweden joined NATO in 2024, a decision that now enjoys wide domestic support.
Ulf Kristersson speaks with journalists in front of a polling station in Strängnäs, Sweden on Sept. 13, 2026. | Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP via Getty Images
In the closing days of the election campaign, Ulf Kristersson, the center-right leader and outgoing prime minister, accused Andersson’s left bloc of being an unreliable partner to NATO because two of the four parties in it did not initially support membership. Andersson insists that is wrong. “Both the Left Party and the Green Party have declared clearly: Now we are members of NATO, we should be active and strong members of the alliance,” she said.
The Carney model
Sweden has long been one of the EU’s most passionate advocates for free trade. With U.S. President Donald Trump weaponizing tariffs, Andersson is clear that “trade and technology” have become “part of our security.” But Trump’s trade war with Canada has not dampened her enthusiasm for Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, whom she’s known since her days as a finance minister when he was a central banker.
“He’s doing a great job,” she said. It is clear Andersson supports efforts to forge closer ties between Canada and the EU, and wants Europe to follow Carney’s lead in treating Trump with a firm hand. “Standing up for Europe is something that we should do. I think that’s a good way to handle politicians like Trump,” she said. And Carney’s prescription for “middle powers” to work together chimes with Andersson’s analysis of what the EU must do to be “strong.”
Advertisement
“For a country like Sweden, with our big export companies, the U.S. is an important partner,” Andersson said. “But also, Swedish companies create a lot of jobs in the U.S. … We need a close and strong relationship with the U.S., but at the same time, we shouldn’t be naive.”
Andersson wants Europe to look beyond its own borders for alliances elsewhere — with the likes of Japan, Australia, Canada and former EU member Britain. “We spend a lot of time trying to solve our internal problems, but for [the] European Union to be strong in the world, I think we have to also work more outside.”
She criticized Kristersson for, in her view, focusing too much on the Baltic region and ignoring “the global south,” where Europe needs allies. “I want my government to be active in the global scene. Sweden is back,” she said.
Cancel Brexit
Andersson also wants closer collaboration with the U.K., which also has a new leader of a center-left government in Andy Burnham. Her message to Brits: “We would prefer you to be part of [the] European Union — Sweden is the country who has lost our closest ally in European Union when you left. No country is as sad and miss[es] you as much as we do.”
Burnham, she believes, has “the potential” to be “a very successful prime minister.” Although she doesn’t know him, she says she is “really looking forward” to meeting him.
Under Kristersson’s outgoing right-wing government, some British-born, long-term residents living in Sweden were forced to leave. Andersson promised to review the situation.
Advertisement
“This is one of the things we have to look into. I mean, people from Britain have been living here for decades,” she said. “And some of them, they have become senior citizens, and they’re not allowed to stay anymore.”
Would she like Britain to rejoin the EU? Almost before the question is finished, she shoots back: “Yes. Please. Tomorrow.” She added: “But I know it’s up to you, and you have had your referendum. We respect it, but we miss you.”
Unfinished business
Andersson became Sweden’s first female prime minister in November 2021, but lost power at the election less than a year later, and she clearly feels she has unfinished business. She had to watch from the opposition while Kristersson ran the country for four years with the support and influence of the far-right, anti-immigration Sweden Democrats.
Andersson wants Europe to look beyond its own borders for alliances elsewhere. | Tim Ross/POLITICO
This month’s election was a critical test for the country’s appetite for even greater far-right involvement in the government. In his election pitch, Kristersson promised ministerial posts to Sweden Democrats for the first time, if he were re-elected. Andersson sought to make crossing that Rubicon a central question in the campaign.
She insists restoring the notion of a “firewall” or “cordon sanitaire” — in which mainstream parties promise not to collaborate with the far right — is not undemocratic.
“How could it be undemocratic? I mean, parties decide who they want to work together with, and people vote for them or they don’t vote for them,” she said. “If you’re clear on how you will act and people vote for you, I mean, that’s how things work. And for the Social Democrats or a party like mine, of course we will never work with a [party] like the Sweden Democrats. The labor movement has always been the largest opponents against right-wing authoritarian, populist parties.”
Advertisement
At times the intense campaign spilled over into violence. The worst moments, she said, were “the occasions when party members campaigning have been attacked, which happened several times — physically attacked.”
Election day began early for Andersson, voting alongside her husband in a school sports hall. Then she held a rally at party HQ in central Stockholm, where ABBA legend Benny Andersson endorsed her on stage with a rendition of Mamma Mia (the audience sang along, changing the words to “Magdalena”).
For the rest of the day, her red campaign bus toured the outskirts of the city, as she hopped on and off to meet residents and party volunteers in an 11th-hour push to get the vote out. Knocking on doors has been “fantastic,” she said, and it’s obvious how much she enjoys being out on the stump meeting voters. “You always learn something new.”
Andersson said the secret to staying well on a punishing schedule is “good food” and exercise — though her usual biking, hiking and kayaking had to give way to walking and a gym during the campaign. And getting enough rest, of course, is vital. “I always sleep well,” she said. “I’m very good at power napping.”
With the world the way it is, that could be the most useful skill of all.

ShinyHunters hackers say they breached FBI, stole data on bureau employees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
01:55:00 UTC
10:55:00 KST

ShinyHunters hackers say they breached FBI, stole data on bureau employees
- ShinyHunters hackers claim to have breached the FBI and stolen data on nearly all current and former FBI agents, including sensitive personal details.
- The FBI acknowledged investigating unauthorized activity affecting its job site and applicant portal, which were disrupted following the breach.
- Experts warn such leaks can cause long-term harm to agents, as stolen information can be used to harass or pressure them.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The digital extortion group known as “ShinyHunters” said on Sept 22 that it had breached the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and stolen data on a huge number of current and former FBI employees.
Later, the FBI said in a statement that the agency “is aware of claims regarding unauthorised activity affecting FBIjobs.gov and is currently investigating”.
In a statement posted to its dark-web site and during an online chat with Reuters, ShinyHunters said it had targeted the FBI in response to a May 2026 agency announcement that detailed ShinyHunters’ methods and advised targets not to pay.
It said it had stolen data “on almost ALL FBI Agents, and individuals who filed an application with the FBI for a job”.
As proof, the group offered what it said was a screenshot of a vandalised FBI job site and what the group said was information on roughly 5,000 agents it said was a sample of the overall stolen data set.
Job site disruption
Reuters could not verify the authenticity of the screenshot, but the job site did appear to have experienced recent disruption. A message posted to the site on Sept 22 said that both it and the FBI “Special Agent Applicant Portal” were “currently unavailable”.
The data sample appeared to contain information about FBI agents’ names, home addresses, Social Security numbers, their assignments and, in at least some cases, the names of their family members.
Reuters was able to partially verify the authenticity of the information by running the details, including the Social Security numbers, against credit bureau records and previously breached data preserved by the dark-web intelligence firm District 4 Labs.
In at least 10 instances – including in the case of FBI Director Kash Patel – Reuters found details that appeared to match. A person familiar with the matter said that the job descriptions in the data also matched in at least some cases.
However, the news agency could not establish where the data came from, or whether it had been stolen from the FBI’s internal systems as the hackers claimed. Attempts to reach the people whose details were in the sample data were unsuccessful.
Past thefts were harmful
Cynthia Kaiser, a former FBI official, said breaches like the ones claimed by ShinyHunters were “incredibly harmful” because they could be used by criminals to expose and put pressure on the people investigating them.
Kaiser, now senior vice president at cybersecurity firm Halcyon, noted that an old leak dating back to 2016 was still occasionally used today to harass FBI agents. “Once that information is stolen, it is used forever,” she said.
ShinyHunters is one of the world’s most notorious and attention-seeking hacking crews.
Its recent break-ins include the purported theft of millions of business records from video game developer Rockstar Games, the maker of Grand Theft Auto, and a May intrusion centred on education tool Canvas that caused widespread disruption across US schools.
Earlier in September, AI company Anthropic said it had caught ShinyHunters-linked hackers trying to use its tools.
On Sept 20, the group told Reuters it had gone to war against another notorious cybercrime group, cl0p, in a rare bout of public score-settling.REUTERS

India, EU &amp; Canada unite to defend multilateralism; express concern over power politics
Unknown

01:54:33 UTC
10:54:33 KST

India joined the EU, Canada, Australia and several other countries in co-sponsoring a declaration expressing a joint commitment to multilateralism, international law, peace and prosperity, while expressing concern over escalating conflicts, trade disruption, power politics protectionism and coercion.The declaration followed the announcement of a new initiative titled Partners for Multilateralism (P4M) on the margins of the UN General Assembly that aims to make multilateral bodies more “representative, effective, legitimate and trusted” through middle-power cooperation, amid growing fragmentation and violations of international law.Drawing attention to geopolitical tensions, conflicts and extreme competition, foreign minister S Jaishankar said multilateralism will be best served when international law, rules, and norms are scrupulously observed.Other declaration co-sponsors included Brazil, Barbados and Kenya, making P4M a diverse group of countries that bridges – unlike the G7 and BRICS - the gap between the West and Global South. After the co-sponsors, 16 other countries signed off on the declaration that flagged increasing use of economic interdependence as a source of leverage, disrupting trade, supply chains, investment and development finance in messages directed at both US and China.
The declaration stressed reform of multilateral institutions, including the UN, to promote fair trade, prevent conflicts and protect rule of law, while backing fair, open, resilient, predictable and inclusive economic cooperation, including more diversified and resilient global supply chains.The declaration said that the multilateral system founded on the UN Charter remained indispensable, as it had helped provide a framework for peace, decolonisation, prosperity, and human dignity. However, the declaration also said that it must now respond to a world that is more interconnected and complex, more contested and more multipolar.“We affirm the need to uphold and enforce the rules, principles and commitments that remain essential to international order, while renewing and reforming the multilateral system so that it is more effective, representative, inclusive and fit for purpose,” said the declaration, while stressing the joint commitment to sovereign equality, territorial integrity, peaceful settlement of disputes and prohibition of the threat or use of force.The inaugural meeting was co-hosted by European Council President Antonio Costa who said that the P4M will serve as a global network for dialogue, coalition-building and practical cooperation, helping us coordinate our response to shared challenges, with the UN at its core.As he underlined the need for multilateralism to assert itself strongly in these times, Jaishankar also pointed to the issue of terrorism. “The future of peace and international security, of climate action and climate justice, of emerging technologies and development finance ,of countering terrorism and strengthening supply chain, and of ensuring disaster resilience and preparing for pandemics, all depend on a will to cooperate,” he said.
The minister also flagged the 4F crises of fuel, food, fertilizer and finance cannot be left to itself, saying where new capabilities and concerns arise, there is a very powerful case for frameworks and guardrails.“Where there is a threat of chokepoints dominance and disruption, de-risking and diversifying must be encouraged. And where there is a compelling cause or a powerful case, the like-minded must have the confidence to come together,” said Jaishankar, stressing the need for reformed multilateralism.

US halts Obamacare enrollment for over 760,000 enrollees, claiming fraud

US halts Obamacare enrollment for over 760,000 enrollees, claiming fraud
- The US government halted Obamacare enrollment for over 760,000 people due to suspected fraud, aiming to save $2.2 billion in taxpayer money through an anti-fraud task force.
- CMS cancelled 315,000 plans in August for unverified citizenship or immigration status and froze new broker registrations for six months due to high fraud rates.
- Experts warned the broker freeze might reduce enrolment and hurt insurers, while CMS called the fraud issue "the tip of the iceberg" with potential improper spending of $6.6 billion.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The Trump administration is halting enrollment in Obamacare health plans for more than 760,000 enrollees it believes were fraudulently signed up, Vice President JD Vance said on Sept 22, part of an anti-fraud effort he estimated would save US$2.2 billion (S$2.81 billion) in taxpayer money.
The US Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services cancelled about 315,000 plans in August, citing unverified citizenship or immigration documentation and suspected improper enrollments.
The agency will bar 569 brokers it accused of submitting “statistically implausible rates of plan year 2026 applications” without necessary applicant information such as a Social Security number.
The plans, created by Democratic President Barack Obama’s signature Affordable Care Act, offer income-based subsidies.
Republican President Donald Trump sought unsuccessfully in his first term to overturn the law and has proposed changes that would make the plans less comprehensive.
Millions dropped coverage in 2026 as rising medical costs and the expiration of extra Covid-era subsidies made monthly premiums unaffordable.
Vance described the cancelled group as “a mix of both phantom people, but also real people who just don’t meet the eligibility requirements”, including some he said who were signed up by brokers without their knowledge.
Vance said the administration would further verify between 419,000 and 450,000 more people to confirm they are legal US residents meeting income thresholds.
CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz said the enrollees were treated as “phantoms” because officials believe most either do not exist or were unaware they had coverage, having never filed a claim and being unreachable despite repeated contact attempts.
Broker registration freeze
The administration is using an emergency-style rulemaking process to impose an immediate, industry-wide freeze on new Obamacare broker registrations, bypassing the usual advance notice-and-comment period.
Oz called it a “temporary national moratorium” for six months, saying most fraud was concentrated among such agents.
CMS said some brokers have allegedly enrolled people without genuine consent, changed people’s plans without permission, used inaccurate information, or created questionable applications to receive commissions.
The agency said brokers without a 2026 registration will be frozen out until Feb 1, 2027.
The freeze could weigh on insurers that rely on brokers to sign up customers, analysts said.
Enrollment impact warning
Because brokers are key to how people enroll, the freeze “may negatively affect enrollment and potentially margins related to higher risk pool in a market that is already contracting” as enhanced subsidies expire, said Morningstar analyst Julie Utterback.
A blanket moratorium “would punish legitimate professionals instead of targeting the bad actors responsible for fraud”, said Mychal Walker, president of the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals, a trade group that urged CMS to adopt targeted safeguards instead.
CMS said unauthorised Obamacare enrollments could cost up to US$6.6 billion in improper federal spending for the 2026 plan year.
The cancellations were led by Vance’s anti-fraud task force, which includes Health Secretary Robert Kennedy Jr., Oz and Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson.
CMS said it expects a return of about US$2.2 billion in advance payments of the premium tax credit for the cancelled enrollments.
Oz said the figure would climb, calling it “the tip of the iceberg”.
An HHS report released early 2026 estimated nearly half of new Obamacare enrollments between 2021 and 2024 may have been improper, phantom or fraudulent.
CMS said more than 1 million enrollees received coverage without providing a Social Security number. REUTERS

Belgium calls for equal application of international law, protection of civilians

Melike Pala
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot called Tuesday for international law to be applied consistently across conflicts, stressing that sovereignty, territorial integrity and the protection of civilians cannot depend on geography.
Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Prevot said the principles underpinning the international order must be upheld not only in Europe but also in conflict zones including Palestine, Sudan, Myanmar, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Haiti.
He said the circumstances of conflicts around the world may differ, but the principles of international humanitarian law remain applicable.
"No human life is worth less than another. Civilians remain civilians. They must be protected," he said.
He also called for humanitarian aid to be allowed to reach civilians in conflict zones, arguing that assistance should not be treated as "an optional expense, a reward or a bargaining chip."
Prevot also linked the principle of equal application of international law to the ongoing war in Ukraine, warning that allowing borders to be changed by force would make borders elsewhere less secure.
"The same standard must guide us when it comes to international humanitarian law. Its rules do not apply only when they suit us," he said.
UN reform, AI
Prevot also called for reform of the United Nations while cautioning that reform should not undermine the organization's ability to perform its core functions.
He further urged for reforms to ensure better representation for every region of the world.
He also addressed the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), saying governments face the challenge of benefiting from technological innovation while ensuring adequate protections for people.
"We must neither hold back innovation out of fear nor assume that it will regulate itself," he said.
Prevot also used his address to defend the independence of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court.
Both courts, he said, are based on the principle that "power cannot be its own judge."
"When judges or staff members of an international court face sanctions or pressure for carrying out their mandate, Belgium will always stand with them to protect them," he said.
