She said if birth rates remained low, it would put pressure on services and public finances.
Japan's PM has 'frank' discussions with Trump on China and North Korea
Japan's Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae has said her meeting with US President Donald Trump was an opportunity to "demonstrate to the world" how "robust" the US-Japan alliance is in an "increasingly severe security environment".
Japan would be particularly keen to send that message to China, ahead of President Trump's meeting with Xi Jinping, Thursday local time.
Diplomatic relations between Japan and China are at a significantly low ebb, after Takaichi indicated an attack or blockade or Taiwan could potentially prompt a military response from Japan.
In her opening remarks Takaichi expressed gratitude for Trump's "very, very powerful commitment to the Japan-US Alliance".
In a social media post following the meeting, Takaichi said she "engaged in frank exchanges of views with President Trump on issues including China and North Korea."
North Korea has launched at least 15 missiles since the start of the year, according to Japan's defence minister, compared to five missiles in 2025.
Japan has ramped up its defence spending in the face of increased tensions in the region, which has drawn the ire of China and Tokyo was reportedly keen to ensure Takaichi met with Trump before the US-China summit.
In the meeting Takaichi reassured Trump that key Japanese ministers who worked closely with the US, including in defence and foreign affairs, had been retained in a recent cabinet reshuffle, saying the "person-to-person counterpart relationship" would drive "policy coordination" and "deepen" the alliance between the countries.
Takaichi also pointed to "economic security" on areas like "AI, semiconductors, and critical minerals" which she said was "steadily advancing".
Trump praised Takaichi as "very highly respected" and said she was doing a "great job" and the country is "doing very well".
In the aftermath of the meeting the US Ambassador in Japan tweeted that the meeting between "two visionary and determined leaders" represented a "dynamic and unbreakable alliance" with focuses including "upgrading and strengthening our shared deterrence".
National emergency-style response needed to violence against women and children: Lib
As many of us gear up to celebrate the AFL grand final this weekend, women's shelters and crisis hotlines are readying themselves to try and help even more women and children than usual.
According to the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics, domestic, family and sexual violence surges around major sport events. Shadow Minister for Families Melissa McIntosh says the federal government should be treating this crisis in a similar way to a bushfire or flood.
"We know how to deal with oncoming crises, bushfires, floods," she says.
"We are prepared for a pandemic, why aren't we prepared for what is now declared as a national crisis when it comes to women and children's safety?"
Specifically, she'd like to see a "women and children's safety war room", similar to the kinds of control centres set up during a natural disaster.
While this exact approach isn't something experts and advocates have asked for, there have been sustained calls for this crisis to be treated with more urgency and coordination by federal, state and territory governments.
Domestic, Family and Sexual Violence Commissioner Micaela Cronin has repeatedly said a national watchdog with teeth is needed to hold all levels of government to their commitments and ensure they enact the hundreds of recommendations already made by royal commissions, inquests and reviews.
At its last meeting, national cabinet agreed to prioritise action to stop violence against women and children by tasking their ministers to focus on areas like alcohol reform and holding perpetrators to account.

In an interview with the ABC today, NDIS Minister Mark Butler denounced Queensland’s Liberal National government over being the only state not to formally sign up to deliver Thriving Kids, a week before the first phase of the program is set to begin.

Digital duty of care bill not in national interest: Taylor
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has repeated his criticism the government's digital duty of care bill amounted to "political censorship".
The proposed bill would force platforms to take actions to mitigate and respond to harms caused by digital platforms.

Speaking to reporters on the Central Coast, Taylor said the bill wasn't in the national interest.

"It's not in our national interest to give a blank check to the minister on political censorship, which is what the bill does right now."
The Coalition has previously ruled out support amid concerns the laws would hand the minister too much power to determine what constitutes online harm.
Coalition releases eight-point energy plan
Angus Taylor has also been asked about the Coalition's energy policy.
The opposition today released an eight-point plan, officially jettisoning many of the key climate policies trying to push down emissions or speed up the renewable rollout.
It includes scrapping laws committing Australia to net zero, laws requiring heavy industry to cut emissions, and removing laws requiring car makers to import more fuel-efficient and electric vehicles. The plan also includes the push to end a ban on nuclear power.
So does this mean the Coalition is formally abandoning the renewable transition? Taylor says that choice should be left to Australians.
"We should have all the energy sources available. Our coal, our gas, our nuclear, our household solar — where we lead the world. I mean all of these should be available and we shouldn't restrict it in the way that [energy minister] Chris Bowen does," he says.
"What we'll continue to see is technologies emerging with lower emissions that Australians want to choose, and that's fine.
"I put faith in the Australian people on this because they get it, they understand it."

It also recommends new independents and new parties should be allowed to spend up to $1.2 million on their campaigns, while keeping an $800,000 electorate limit for established candidates.

Princess Diana joked about her own funeral two months before her death
Kyiv • UNN
On her 36th birthday, Diana joked that her home resembled a funeral parlor. Two months later, she died in a car crash in Paris.
Shortly before her death, Princess Diana made a joking remark about a funeral that took on a sinister undertone after her death. Her brother Charles Spencer recounted the episode in his new book, "A Swan Song: Diana, My Sister," E! News reports, writes UNN.
Details
For her 36th birthday, Diana received many flowers. In a thank-you letter to one of her relatives, she joked: "I’m so lucky! My house is so full of wonderful flowers that it looks like a funeral parlor!"
Two months later, on August 31, 1997, the princess died in a car crash in Paris. Spencer recalled her words while preparing a speech for his sister’s funeral.
The brother’s last meeting with Diana
Spencer also said that he last saw his sister approximately two months before her death. They happened to meet at the Tate Gallery in London and spoke only briefly.
Neither of us had any idea that the other would be at the event. We spoke only briefly, never to see each other again
In the book, Spencer also claims that after Diana’s death, then-Prince Charles told him: "Be assured, we will forget her soon."
Commenting on these claims, Buckingham Palace stated that prolonged grief can affect a person’s judgment and memories.

AMIA bombing: Why Argentina is charging Iran and Hezbollah suspects, 32 years later
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
21:03:41 UTC
06:03:41 KST

- i24NEWS
- International
- Latin America
- AMIA bombing: Why Argentina is charging Iran and Hezbollah suspects 32 years later
AMIA bombing: Why Argentina is charging Iran and Hezbollah suspects 32 years later
A new Argentine indictment names seven Iranian officials and a Hezbollah operative accused of roles in the 1994 attack on Buenos Aires’ Jewish community center
More than three decades after a bombing destroyed Argentina’s Jewish community center and killed 85 people, an Argentine judge has formally charged seven Iranians and a Lebanese national over their alleged roles in the attack.
The decision on Monday brings the country one step closer to a potential trial in absentia in one of the world’s longest-running terrorism investigations.
But what happened at the AMIA Jewish community center, who does Argentina hold responsible, and why has it taken 32 years for the case to reach this point?
Argentina’s Jewish community
Argentina is home to Latin America’s largest Jewish community, with an estimated 170,000 to 180,000 Jews, most of them living in Buenos Aires. The community has roots in waves of Jewish immigration from Europe, as well as longstanding Sephardic communities from the Middle East and Mediterranean.
Over generations, Argentine Jews built a strong network of synagogues, schools and community organizations. AMIA was one of its central institutions, making the 1994 bombing not only a mass-casualty attack, but a devastating strike at the heart of Jewish life in Argentina.
What happened in the AMIA bombing?
On July 18, 1994, a suicide bomber drove a van packed with explosives into the Argentine Israelite Mutual Association, known by its Spanish acronym AMIA, in Buenos Aires.
The blast killed 85 people and injured 151, destroying much of the seven-story Jewish community center.
The attack was the deadliest antisemitic attack outside Israel since the Holocaust.
It came just two years after another major bombing in Buenos Aires: the 1992 attack on the Israeli Embassy, which killed 29 people.
No one has ever been convicted of carrying out the AMIA bombing.
Who does Argentina say was behind the attack?
Argentina has long accused Iran and Hezbollah of orchestrating the bombing.
According to Argentine prosecutors and courts, the decision to attack AMIA was made by senior Iranian officials and was then carried out by Hezbollah, Iran’s Lebanese proxy group.
In 2024, an Argentine court formally ruled that Iran and Hezbollah were responsible for the attack.
Judge Daniel Rafecas’s latest ruling says the decision to attack AMIA was made in August 1993 by the highest levels of the Iranian regime and entrusted to Hezbollah. The group then allegedly organized a regional and local support network to prepare and carry out the bombing.
Iran has denied responsibility for the bombing.
How was the attack carried out?
According to Rafecas’s reconstruction, the attackers purchased a Renault Trafic van on July 10, 1994, just eight days before the bombing.
The vehicle was then modified and loaded with approximately 300 kilograms of ammonal and TNT.
The van was eventually driven onto the sidewalk outside the AMIA building and detonated, causing the massive explosion that killed 85 people and injured 151.
Who has now been charged?
Monday’s decision formally charged seven Iranian nationals and one Lebanese national, all of whom are outside Argentina and could face trial in absentia.
Judge Daniel Rafecas divided the defendants according to their alleged roles in the attack.
Four senior Iranian officials were charged as “indirect authors” of the bombing: Ali Fallahijan, who was Iran’s intelligence minister at the time; Ali Velayati, then foreign minister; Mohsen Rezai, then commander of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard; and Ahmad Vahidi, who commanded the Quds Force.
Rafecas also charged three other Iranian nationals as necessary accomplices: Hadi Soleimanpour, Iran’s ambassador to Argentina at the time; Mohsen Rabbani, the Iranian Embassy’s cultural attaché; and Ahmad Asghari, identified in the ruling as a Revolutionary Guard intelligence agent.
The eighth defendant is Salman Raouf Salman, also known as “Samuel El Reda,” a Lebanese Hezbollah operative whom Rafecas says coordinated the final stages of the attack.
The eight charged suspects are not in Argentine custody.
Why is there a trial in absentia?
The AMIA investigation has faced a fundamental problem for decades: the people Argentina accuses of organizing the attack have remained outside the country.
In June, Rafecas ruled that the Iranian and Lebanese suspects could be tried in absentia.
Argentina introduced a legal framework for trials in absentia in 2025. Under the system, defendants accused of certain serious crimes can be tried without being physically present, provided their rights to a defense and other due-process guarantees are protected.
The decision does not mean a trial will begin immediately.
The indictments can still be appealed, and additional procedural steps must be completed before a trial can move forward.
Why has the investigation taken so long?
The AMIA case has been plagued by allegations of political interference, corruption and obstruction of justice.
In 2004, prosecutor Alberto Nisman was appointed to investigate the bombing. He spent years building a case that Iran and Hezbollah were responsible.
But in January 2015, Nisman was found dead in his Buenos Aires apartment, just hours before he was due to present allegations that then-President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner and other senior officials had participated in an alleged cover-up of Iran’s role in the AMIA attack.
His death was initially ruled a suicide.
Argentine authorities later determined that Nisman had been murdered.
His death became another major controversy surrounding an investigation that had already deeply divided Argentine politics and society.
What happened to officials accused of obstructing the investigation?
The AMIA case has also led to criminal proceedings against Argentine officials accused of interfering with the investigation.
Former President Carlos Menem, who was in office during both the 1992 Israeli Embassy bombing and the 1994 AMIA attack, was tried over allegations that he helped cover up aspects of the investigation. He was ultimately acquitted and died in 2021.
Former intelligence chief Hugo Anzorreguy was sentenced to four and a half years in prison for obstructing the investigation.
Former AMIA investigating judge Juan José Galeano was also convicted. In 2019, he was sentenced to six years in prison for concealing evidence and violating his duties.
In 2024, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights also held the Argentine state responsible for failing in its duty to properly investigate the AMIA bombing.
Could the AMIA and Israeli Embassy bombings be connected?
Monday’s ruling also raised the possibility of formally connecting the two Buenos Aires attacks.
The Israeli Embassy bombing in March 1992 killed 29 people, while the AMIA attack two years later killed 85.
Both attacks have been linked by Argentine investigators to Hezbollah and Iran.
Rafecas has asked Argentina’s Supreme Court to weigh in on whether the two cases should be connected, potentially allowing investigators to examine the attacks as part of a broader campaign. (infobae)
What does this mean for Argentina’s Jewish community?
The AMIA bombing remains one of the defining tragedies in the history of Argentina’s Jewish community.
For decades, relatives of the victims have demanded accountability, while successive Argentine governments and courts have struggled to bring those accused of orchestrating the attack before a courtroom.
Monday’s indictment does not resolve the case.
But it represents a significant new legal step toward a trial, potentially one that could take place even if the accused never appear in Argentina.
President Javier Milei, a strong supporter of Israel who has made the AMIA investigation a prominent issue, welcomed the decision.
“Morality as state policy,” Milei wrote on X.
For the families of the 85 people killed in 1994, however, the central question remains the same: after more than three decades, will anyone ultimately be held accountable for the attack?

Guterres pleads for 'world built on interdependence' in final General Assembly address
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
21:02:47 UTC
06:02:47 KST

Guterres pleads for 'world built on interdependence' in final General Assembly address
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres pleaded for “a world built on interdependence” Tuesday as he made his final address to the annual gathering of world leaders convening to face a formidable menu of challenges, from climate change and war to inequality and the rise of artificial intelligence.
In a no-nonsense farewell speech, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urged global leaders Tuesday to respond to the defining challenge today: Will the world continue on its path to fragmentation, or cooperate to tackle the existential threats from climate crisis, runaway artificial intelligence and intensifying inequalities?
Read more'No peace without justice,' Macron tells UN General Assembly
The UN leader has long implored leaders not to give up on cooperation and shared decision-making in the face of accelerating global challenges and increasing great-powers competition. Tuesday’s message at the UN General Assembly took on additional urgency because he leaves office at the end of this year.
“The fault lines in our world are widening,” he said, citing raging wars, rising temperatures and artificial intelligence, among other matters. Instead of letting the future continue to veer toward fragmentation, transactionalism and mistrust, he called for “a world built on interdependence – and sustained by a dense web of economic, political, social and technological connections”.
His speech opened the main portion of the world's biggest diplomatic meeting of the year. Leaders from the UN's 193 member countries address each other and the international community and air their hopes, plans and grievances.
Guterres also rebuked might-makes-right thinking, telling superpowers to recognise “that their power isn’t so super”. Recent years have made it clear that “military power alone cannot secure peace,” he said.
Yet about an hour after Guterres spoke, US President Donald Trump offered a different and equally frank view of power.
Read moreIran, AI and the ICC: Trump makes threats, touts policies at UN General Assembly
“While others have promised strength, I have used it to make America the most powerful country in the world,” Trump said, touting his country's economic, technological and military footprint.
He reiterated his view that the UN has “great potential” but rebuked it for what he called “imposing the far-left agenda of globalist bureaucrats”. He went on to criticise such bodies as the International Criminal Court, to which the US is not a party.
The annual high-level gathering at the UN General Assembly will be consumed with wars in Iran, Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan, DR Congo and Myanmar and a persisting question: Can the leaders do anything to end them?
And what can they do about the relentless rise of global warming threatening the future of the planet, the growing inequalities within and among nations, and shocks to the global economy as blocked shipping routes and supply chains increase the cost of living?
The future of the United Nations itself will also be on the agenda. At 81, its powers are still the victorious nations from World War II, not the 21st century’s major global players. Member nations have agreed to a wide-ranging reform package that includes updating key institutions such as the powerful UN Security Council, where the US, Russia, China, Britain and France hold inordinate sway because of their veto power. Reform, however, is easier said than implemented.
Behind the scenes, there will be speculation about who will lead the UN next. Guterres’ second five-year term ends on December 31, and no clear successor has emerged. Guterres closed his speech by acknowledging the forthcoming departure and vowing to “never, ever give up” on the values for which the UN stands.
“Wherever I will be, whatever I will be doing, I will keep championing the conviction that peace is possible,” he said, before leaving the rostrum amid a sustained, standing ovation. He put his hand on his heart.
There is still no question that the UN remains the key gathering place for its member nations and their leaders. Some 130 heads of state and government are expected to speak at the General Assembly, along with dozens of ministers.
Among the headliners Tuesday: Trump and French President Emmanuel Macron. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky and Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian speak Wednesday.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – whom New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani wanted arrested for his treatment of Palestinians in Gaza until he learned he has no such authority – will address the assembly on Thursday. For a second year, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas won’t be coming to the UN because the US refused to give him a visa. He will nonetheless address the assembly by video the same day.
Read moreUS again denies Palestinian leader visa for UN General Assembly
The United States, under its agreement with the UN to host the organisation, is required to allow diplomats from all member nations to attend meetings.
Equally telling is who else isn’t coming. China’s President Xi Jinping is meeting Trump in Washington on Wednesday, yet he is skipping – some diplomats say snubbing – the UN gathering and sending a vice president instead. Russian President Vladimir Putin isn’t coming either, and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has backed out.
France's UN ambassador, Jerome Bonnafont, said ahead of the gathering that it is “extremely critical” for world leaders to support the UN as the place where the world’s nations meet – especially at a time of such polarisation.
“We believe in multilateralism," he said, "and we believe that the high-level week is the occasion for countries in the world to reaffirm that they prefer cooperation and dialogue to confrontation”.
There is no doubt it’s been a tough year for the world body. It has been pushed to the sidelines when it comes to its key responsibility of ensuring international peace and security and trying to end major conflicts in the Mideast and Ukraine. The US failure to pay billions of dollars in outstanding arrears has left the organisation’s finances in rocky shape.
“While the world still trusts the UN, the global public is eager for change," said former UN deputy secretary-general Mark Malloch-Brown, a United Nations Foundation board member.
The future of artificial intelligence has pushed to the forefront of global concerns, with its speeding advances and the dawning recognition that there are no industry controls, let alone any global guardrails for a technology that has many advantages but also many disadvantages and unknowns.
Days before the global gathering, leaders of three major AI companies warned about the technology getting out of human control and called for a pause, but Trump dismissed their concerns as “a hoax”, and urged continued advances to keep the US ahead of China.
Read moreTrump calls concerns over rogue AI a 'hoax' promoted by a ‘sick conspiracy’
The UN Security Council added a meeting on AI to its agenda on Wednesday afternoon, a sign of the growing apprehension and need to address the issue. It was already slated to hold a high-level meeting on Ukraine with Zelensky on Wednesday morning.
(FRANCE24 with AP)

NATO member moves closer to lifting nuclear weapons ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
21:01:42 UTC
06:01:42 KST

NATO member moves closer to lifting nuclear weapons ban
Lithuania’s parliament has backed a constitutional amendment that would lift a ban on nuclear weapons, thus bringing the NATO member a step closer to hosting them on its territory. Russia has warned the Baltic country, which borders its Kaliningrad Region, that such a move would have significant security implications.
The proposal was backed by 99 lawmakers on Tuesday, with 13 voting against and five abstaining. Two more votes are required, scheduled for October 6 and January 12, 2027. At least 94 of Lithuania’s 141 MPs must support the amendment in each vote.
The measure would remove Article 137 of the Lithuanian constitution, which prohibits weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases on the country’s territory. Supporters argue that the provision no longer reflects Lithuania’s security needs, while opponents have raised concerns over sovereignty and called for the issue to be put to a referendum.
President Gitanas Nauseda has backed removing the restriction, while Lithuanian officials have argued that allowing nuclear weapons would strengthen deterrence against Russia.
Moscow has repeatedly rejected claims that it intends to attack NATO countries.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova last week called the proposed change “absolutely irresponsible,” accusing NATO members of pursuing provocative policies and treating Lithuania as a potential staging ground against Russia.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has warned that Lithuania could become a target of Russian nuclear weapons if it allowed foreign nuclear arms to be deployed on its territory.
The debate comes amid broader discussions in Europe over nuclear deterrence. French President Emmanuel Macron unveiled changes to the country’s nuclear doctrine in March that included the possibility of temporarily deploying French nuclear weapons in other European countries.
Finland has since joined the French initiative after lifting its own restrictions on hosting foreign nuclear weapons, while Latvia announced on Tuesday that Paris had agreed to open talks on its participation.
NATO already operates a nuclear-sharing arrangement under which US nuclear weapons are stationed in several member states, including Belgium, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, and Türkiye. The Financial Times reported in June that Washington was considering expanding deployments to additional NATO countries in Europe.

Ecuador: Militarization Continues and the Armed Forces Still Refuse to Cooperate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
20:54:57 UTC
05:54:57 KST

One year after the publication of the report “It was the military. I Saw Them“, which documented the enforced disappearance of 10 people from the Ecuadorian coast, including six children, in the context of President Daniel Noboa’s so-called “Plan Fenix”, some progress has been made. Nevertheless, the lack of cooperation by the Armed Forces in the criminal investigations and the deepening of the policy of militarization of the public security continue to be the main obstacles preventing all victims’ families from obtaining truth, justice, and reparation, and from ensuring the non-repetition of these crimes, Amnesty International said today.
“The progress achieved over the past year demonstrates that it is possible to respond to the demands for truth and justice made by the families, civil society, and international mechanisms. Yet this progress remains insufficient as long as many of those families continue not knowing what happened to their loved ones and the military authorities continue to withhold essential information for the investigations,” said Ana Piquer, Regional Director for the Americas of Amnesty International.
The progress achieved over the past year demonstrates that it is possible to respond to the demands for truth and justice made by the families, civil society, and international mechanisms.”
Ana Piquer, Regional Director for the Americas of Amnesty International.
In December 2025, a court of first instance convicted 16 military personnel for the enforced disappearance of four boys from the Las Malvinas neighborhood, in the south of the city of Guayaquil. In February 2026, the Constitutional Court issued a landmark ruling requiring the Air Force commander to issue a public apology to the boys’ families in an event that was broadcast live. In May 2026, a judge ruled that Dave Loor and Juan Santillán had been victims of enforced disappearance, as part of a decision on a habeas corpus petition filed by their families, which had been appealed by the Armed Forces.
Between January and August 2026, following precautionary measures issued by the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights in favor of 26 disappeared persons and six women searchers, the Prosecutor’s Office established working groups in the provinces of Guayas and Los Ríos, where the highest number of enforced disappearances in the country are concentrated. The purpose of these working groups is to facilitate dialogue between various authorities and the victims’ families, in order to expedite the search for the disappeared people and criminal investigations. The advocacy efforts of the victims’ families, the support of the local organization Permanent Committee for the Defense of Human Rights (CDH Guayaquil), and international mobilization have been key to achieving all these measures.
Despite this progress, the whereabouts of the vast majority of victims of enforced disappearance remain unknown, and their families continue to wait for answers. The main obstacle continues to be the lack of cooperation by the Ministry of Defense with the criminal investigations being conducted by the Prosecutor’s Office. In particular, the Ministry has refused to share information regarding the security operations after which the victims disappeared, claiming that such information is confidential.
The CDH Guayaquil filed an appeal before the Constitutional Court in September requesting the declassification of the information. Amnesty International supports this initiative and recalls that the classification of information related to human rights violations is contrary to the obligations under international law assumed by Ecuador and to international standards, as it violates the right of victims and their families to know the truth.
For their part, families constantly face challenges in having their rights respected and have suffered further violations. Several have reported harassment and acts of intimidation by the Armed Forces, even when most of them are part of the Prosecutor’s Office’s victim and witness protection system.
In addition, during 2026, Ecuador deepened its military and security cooperation with the United States in efforts to combat drug trafficking. This has led to new allegations of possible serious human rights violations and crimes under international law in joint operations and in operations allegedly led by U.S. authorities. Amnesty International documented an attack on an Ecuadorian vessel in this context, in which the whereabouts of its crew members remain unknown.
“The State must guarantee truth, justice, and reparation for all victims and their families, and reverse a militarized security strategy that has proven ineffective in reducing crime rates and has been accompanied by serious human rights violations. Only through full respect for everyone’s rights can a safer Ecuador be built,” said Ana Piquer.
The State must guarantee truth, and reparation for all victims and their families, and reverse a militarized security strategy that has proven ineffective in reducing crime rates and has been accompanied by serious human rights violations.”
Ana Piquer, Regional Director for the Americas of Amnesty International.
Amnesty International reiterates its call on Ecuadorian authorities to guarantee access to truth, justice, and reparation for all families affected by enforced disappearances, recalling that this is a crime under international law. The organization also reiterates its call to reverse the militarized approach to public security. This approach has not been effective in reducing violence in the country and, on the contrary, has facilitated the commission of serious crimes under international law and human rights violations.

====================================================================================================

No evidence of a 'wage-price spiral' in Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
20:48:14 UTC
05:48:14 KST

analysis
No evidence of 'wage-price spiral' in Australia, RBA board member says
Iain Ross, a member of the Reserve Bank's monetary policy board, gave a very interesting speech last night.
He rejected the idea that Australia had almost experienced runaway wage growth in recent years that could have fed into damaging inflation.
"I want to talk about wage-price spirals," he said.
"The threat of rising wages has been a persistent theme in the financial press since inflation began rising sharply from mid-2021.
"A number of media commentators have raised the risk of a wage-price spiral, pointing to the 1970s when the oil price shock collided with large pay rises flowing through the economy.
"[But] the labour market framework of today is very different to that of the 1970s and 1980s.
"There is no evidence of the emergence of a wage-price spiral in the present circumstances and recent data suggest such an outcome is unlikely."
The formation of wage-price spirals
Ross is a former president of the Fair Work Commission, a former judge of the Federal Court and Supreme Court of Victoria, and a former assistant secretary of the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU).
Nobody on the RBA's nine-person monetary policy board has as much practical experience with Australia's labour market and wage-setting institutions.
It is rare these days to hear a speech from an RBA board member that focuses so heavily on the reality of Australia's modern wage-setting institutions and the decline in workers' power to challenge the idea that our economy can experience a "wage explosion" any time soon.
What is a "wage-price spiral"?
According to the idea, Ross explained, after an increase in aggregate demand or an external cost shock, businesses raised their prices, which pushed up inflation.
Workers then want higher wages to maintain their real wages, and if they think inflation will remain high, they may push for particularly large wage increases (so expectations play an important role in the process).
Those higher wages then feed into higher costs and prices and so on, which amplifies the inflationary effects of the original shock, and round and round we go.
Australia's economy experienced episodes of rapidly rising prices and wages in the 1970s and 1980s.
But Ross explained those events occurred in a very different Australia.
He said our modern labour and wage-setting institutions, our modern financial system, our extremely diminished union movement and much tougher sanctions for unlawful industrial action, and the broader industrial structure of our economy, were significantly different from 50 years ago.
He said our modern industrial relations system limited how frequently workers could revise their wage claims, and how easily higher wage claims could spread through the economy these days.
"These changes in Australia's wage-setting mechanisms have made the wage-price dynamics of the 1970s much less likely to recur," he said.
A 'substantially different' wage bargaining environment today
It's worth reading his entire speech, if you're interested in learning more about the big differences between the 1970s and today.
He talked about the old concept of "comparative wage justice", which held that employees doing the same work for different employers or in different industries should receive the same amount of pay, irrespective of the capacity of their employers or industry.
He said that concept helped to spread large wage rises through Australia's economy 50 years ago.
And he discussed the old practice of indexing wages to the consumer price index every three months, which tied rising wages with rising prices in a rapid inflationary feedback loop in the 1970s.
"The situation is very different today," he said.
"Comparative wage justice no longer plays the pervasive role it once did, and quarterly indexation is not a feature of the current system.
"The current enterprise bargaining arrangements, in particular, effectively operate as a shock absorber by constraining the bargaining capacity of those who are the subject of enterprise agreements.
"Such employees are unable to pursue claims for increased wages until the enterprise agreement to which they are subject has passed its nominal expiry date," he said.
Does the RBA think the unemployment rate is still too low?
His speech was delivered at a fascinating time.
The RBA board will hold a highly anticipated meeting on Monday and Tuesday next week to discuss what to do with interest rates.
All four major banks and the bulk of money market traders expect the RBA to raise rates next week, given inflation and economic activity have been stronger than anticipated in Australia recently.
Inflation is still a global problem, and central banks in comparable countries have been lifting rates again.
RBA governor Michele Bullock also made a public appearance yesterday (a few hours before Ross delivered his speech).
She warned that Australia's jobs market was probably still a bit too tight at the moment and putting upwards pressure on wages, business costs, and inflation more generally.
Australia's unemployment rate is currently 4.5 per cent.
"I think between 4.5 and 5 [per cent unemployment] will probably take enough heat out of the labour market that it'll ease pressure on inflation," Bullock said.
Loading...
Will the RBA board members vote as one next week?
Whatever the RBA board does with interest rates next week, it will be interesting to see if its decision will be unanimous.
Under the board's new voting regime, which began in early 2025, there have been 12 meetings.
Of the 10 meetings where unattributed votes have been published, there have been split votes 30 per cent of the time:
And two of the three meetings in which the board's nine members have failed to vote as one have occurred this year.
Will next week's meeting record another split decision?

Scientists discover largest new impact crater in the solar system ever—on our moon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
20:46:46 UTC
05:46:46 KST

The moon has no shortage of craters. But a newly discovered pit discovered by NASA scientists has proven to be the cosmic equivalent of a needle in a haystack.
Each month for the past 17 years, the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) has surveyed the entire moon, producing vast amounts of images and data that reveal how the lunar surface changes over time.
Robert Wagner, an image processing specialist at the private space company Intuitive Machines, was assigned to look at LRO data. When he compared images of the eastern edge of the moon that were taken in May 2024 with photographs of the area from the month prior, he was stunned to see a brand-new crater, 222 meters (728 feet) across and 43 meters (141 feet) deep.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
By moon standards, that’s big—and so rare that it’s estimated that an impact of that size only occurs once every 132 years. In fact, as Wagner and his colleagues describe in a recent Science Advances paper, it’s the largest newly formed crater ever discovered in our solar system.
“I just stopped, dropped everything, and started looking into what that spot was,” Wagner said in a statement.
The impact area has been dubbed McGetchin Crater, after former Lunar Science Institute director Tom McGetchin, who died in 1979.
Unlike Earth, the moon has relatively little atmosphere and no liquid water or major plate tectonic system. That means the surface changes relatively little over time—unless it gets hit from something outside. That makes it a great place to study impacts from asteroids, comets and meteorites, not to mention human-made objects, because the areas that have been hit tend to be much better preserved than they would be on the solar system’s other planets and moons.
Scientists used a heat-sensing instrument onboard the LRO to probe the region of the new crater in more detail. They found that while the middle of the crater glows red, the area around it is 16 degrees F cooler than the surrounding area at night. Those finding were published in a separate paper in the same journal.
The scientists surmised that this occurs because lunar dirt, called regolith, that piled up around the crater as a result of the impact is less dense and therefore less able to retain heat.
The knowledge of how lunar craters form and evolve could prove useful as humans plot their return to the lunar surface for the first time in more than half a century. In particular, plans to develop long-term moon bases could benefit from the information. The data collected from studying the crater could help scientists develop technology that would better allow astronauts to brave and traverse the hostile environment.

Viral NATO video falsely framed as ‘war propaganda’ against Russia
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
A viral NATO video is being falsely framed online as “war propaganda”, with users accusing the Alliance of sharing a “promotional video” designed to prepare the public for imminent war with Russia. But the footage is not new: NATO published it in July 2024 for its 75th anniversary, and it’s been stripped of its original context. The claim comes as European leaders warn of growing Russian hybrid threats, including alleged drone, cyber and sabotage activity. Vedika Bahl explains in Truth or Fake.
Moscow is facing growing accusations of targeting NATO countries with its hybrid campaign, as a growing number of European leaders have warned Russia may be preparing attacks to test the Alliance’s commitment to supporting Ukraine.
But amid those tensions, a different claim is spreading online: that NATO is preparing the public for an imminent war with Russia.
Pro-Kremlin accounts have been sharing a video they describe as NATO “propaganda” or “promotional material” for a future conflict with Moscow, and some posts have been viewed hundreds of thousands of times, if not millions.
The video was also shared by the Russian embassy in the Netherlands, which accused NATO of trying to “inspire the youth to be ready to die for the elites”. It was also amplified in the United States by conspiracy theorist Alex Jones, who made further “white genocide” claims about the video’s portrayal of diversity.
However the video is not new footage, and it wasn’t produced to promote an impending war with Russia. The video was created to celebrate the Alliance’s 75th anniversary, and NATO published the video on its official social media accounts in July 2024, ahead of a summit in Washington marking the date.
The footage has since been downloaded, stripped of that context and recirculated online as supposed evidence that NATO is preparing the public for war with Russia.
Whilst the video is being misinterpreted online, it does not mean tensions between NATO countries and Russia are not intensifying.
European leaders have increasingly warned of late about Russian hybrid threats and possible attempts to test NATO’s commitment to supporting Ukraine.
Last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said intelligence indicated Russia could be planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on NATO’s eastern flank. French President Emmanuel Macron also warned of intensifying Russian hybrid attacks and said he had ordered plans to protect critical infrastructure.
Macron also pointed to a recent drone incident at Germany’s Leipzig airport, which German officials attributed to Russia. There have been other incidents involving Russian aircraft: NATO jets recently shot down a Russian drone that entered Lithuanian airspace, while a Russian warship was accused of firing flares at a Danish military helicopter.

Melbourne man accused of spreading propaganda for Islamic State group arrested
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
06:42:48 UTC
15:42:48 KST

In brief
- The accused is a 65-year-old retiree.
- The AFP alleges the man pledged allegiance to the IS group between 2018 and 2020.
A man accused of being a member of the self-proclaimed Islamic State (IS) group has been arrested by counter-terrorism agents over allegations that he instructed people on how to plan and conduct mass-casualty attacks from his base in Australia.
The Melbourne man, whom the Australian Federal Police (AFP) alleges was a propagandist for the extremist group, is accused of sending about 10,000 documents, messages, images, videos and audio files relating to executions and torture.
The 65-year-old retiree allegedly pledged allegiance to the IS group between 2018 and 2020.
The man, a Somali-born Australian citizen, is alleged to have acted on the behalf of the terrorist group without travelling to the territory it controlled during conflict in the Middle East.
Police said his role was significant.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The scale of extremist material the man was accused of spreading put him among the top propagandists on the encrypted messaging platform he used, AFP acting assistant commissioner Paula Hudson said.
"The material allegedly shared by this man glorified acts of extreme violence and promoted a terrorist organisation, spreading a hateful ideology that's designed to radicalise others," Hudson said.
The videos, photographs, audio files and documents he allegedly sent contained messages relating to "abhorrent content", including executions, mass murder and torture.
"Terrorist organisations like ISIS rely on online platforms to distribute propaganda and recruit supporters," Hudson said.
"Their content is specifically designed to radicalise individuals, encouraging them to adopt extremist beliefs and commit acts of violence."
The man was arrested at a home in Carlton, in Melbourne's inner-north, on Wednesday morning.
Counter-terror officers will also allege that the man shared information about avoiding detection from law enforcement, along with instructional guides on planning and conducting mass-casualty attacks.
He is expected to be charged with being a member of a terrorist organisation, possessing violent extremist material, and using a carriage service to cause offence.
How the man came to be radicalised was expected to emerge in court, Hudson said.
The arrest followed an investigation that began with a referral from the Australian Border Force, which intercepted the man and searched his luggage at Melbourne Airport in November 2020 as he left for Egypt.
A search of his mobile phone allegedly turned up suspicious content.
Agents seized the device but allowed the man to continue on to Egypt, where he stayed for a six-month period.
Investigators believe the man had compassionate grounds to leave the country, as was required during COVID-19 travel restrictions in place at the time.
There is no evidence the man travelled to any declared no-go zones at the time.
An additional search warrant was executed in 2024.
Police do not allege the man continued to distribute extremist material after his initial interception in 2020.
Authorities believe that more than 200 Australians have joined the IS group since 2012, some of the more than 50,000 fighters the group was thought to have attracted from overseas.
Police have not ruled out further arrests but said there was no threat to the community.

Trump’s U.N. Address Offers a Doctrine of Peace Through Force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
20:38:58 UTC
05:38:58 KST

In his speech to the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, President Donald Trump spun a familiar web of rhetoric regarding U.S. foreign policy—one that highlights force as a method of achieving peace.
In a speech that moved from Iran to Venezuela, Cuba, and beyond, Trump presented something approaching a foreign-policy doctrine: American military might is not the alternative to diplomacy but the leverage that makes it possible.
David Satterfield, Director of Rice University's Baker Institute for Public Policy, tells TIME that the speech Tuesday demonstrates a position held by the Trump Administration that “force is the only currency of value.”
“The strong do as they will and the weak suffer as they must,” he says, further characterizing the approach.
In Trump’s telling, strength is not merely a deterrent. It is something to be used—through military action and economic isolation—to force negotiations or impose an outcome.
How Trump defines ‘peace through strength’
Trump has repeatedly distilled his foreign policy strategy into three words: “peace through strength.” The examples he gave of this policy in action illustrate how he may see the U.S. functioning as a global enforcer going forward.
His definition of the phrase has previously been suggested by its use in Department of Defense ads and in his online endorsements of fellow Republicans. He recently credited this approach for the joint U.S.-Israel strikes that initiated the current conflict with Iran, posting to Truth Social in March: “PEACE THROUGH STRENGTH TO PUT IT MILDLY!!!”
Trump’s approach also encompasses economic coercion. In the case of Iran, he said the U.S. had initially offered economic cooperation, turned to military action when Tehran refused, and was now seeking its “complete economic isolation” to push it back toward negotiations.
Trump grouped Cuba among those affected by U.S. economic pressure campaigns on Tuesday. He described a government under mounting strain and predicted political change, declaring that Cuba was a “failed” nation but that “freedom will be coming.” Cuban delegates departed in protest.
Yet Trump presented such coercion as compatible with his role as a global peacemaker. He claimed credit for resolving eight wars since returning to office, although that claim has been widely disputed.
In tandem, these elements suggest that Trump sees taking action as a superior means of enacting change. He proposes the approaches as being almost diametrically opposed: While others only speak of making a difference, he acts.
“While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace. While others have ignored threats, I have confronted them,” Trump said in front of the General Assembly. “While others have talked of courage, America has shown it.”
Satterfield says that this speech is mostly “old wine rebottled” for Trump. But it clarified how the President is applying his longstanding ideas today: using military action and economic coercion not merely to deter adversaries, but to force negotiations and shape political outcomes.
Trump defends military force against Iran and drug cartels
While Trump sees Iran as an example of his “peace through strength” ethos, the conflict is ongoing, and it remains to be seen how it fits into the pattern that he is hoping to establish.
Addressing the topic seemed all but unavoidable heading into the General Assembly. In doing so, Trump said that he had a choice ahead of him: Move forward with a peace deal or “annihilate the Islamic Republic.”
The comments came amid stalled negotiations in the war that the U.S. and Israel launched in February.
“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world?” he asked. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”
Members of Iran’s delegation walked out during Trump’s remarks, an immediate demonstration of the gulf between his coercive message and the adversary that he may hope to persuade by it.
In his speech, he also issued threats against cartel leaders, defending his campaign of drone strikes against suspected drug boats in the Caribbean. These strikes have been criticized by international organizations, legal experts, and human rights groups, which state that the military actions violate international law and constitute extrajudicial killings.
“The cartels are the ISIS of the Western Hemisphere—not good people,” he said. “Like ISIS, they should be killed, exiled, or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release, which is what we’re doing.”
But while these messages are largely meant to promote the very strength that Trump relies upon in his endeavors, the potency of his remarks may be dwindling amid contested claims of success.
Venezuela is Trump’s ‘peace through strength’ model. But Iran is testing its limits
Kristian Coates Ulrichsen, a fellow for the Middle East at the Baker Institute, tells TIME that Trump’s speech seems “consistent with the narrative of American dominance” that he has long used to justify military action.
Trump suggested Tuesday that he considers Venezuela a leading example. In January, the U.S. military launched Operation Absolute Resolve—a nighttime raid in Caracas that captured Venezuela’s president Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores. Both were transported to New York City to face federal drug-trafficking indictments.
The move paved the way for a transition of power in Venezuela, with former Vice President Delcy Rodríguez ascending to the role of acting President. It also led to an August agreement giving a U.S.-linked venture a controlling stake and long-term development rights in fields containing an estimated 65 billion barrels of oil. Trump said the deal “more than doubles” American oil reserves.
“We’re working closely with the leaders of Venezuela to forge a much better future for the Venezuelan people,” Trump said in his speech. “Last month we signed the largest oil deal in history, covering 65 billion barrels of oil, which will benefit both Venezuela and the United States enormously.”
Trump also suggested that U.S. actions had established peace and a route to prosperity for Venezuelans. However, with an acting President who is yet to be elected making deals that may take years to reach fruition, and are likely to draw legal challenges in the meantime, the full picture remains to be seen.
But there is one thing the Venezuela operation might have helped accomplish, which is to establish a potential pattern of a U.S. foreign policy that is defined by unilateral intervention. Following a large show of force, Trump has been quick to claim victory, even while the impact of U.S. involvement is still playing out for the people whom it directly affects.
Another example is the conflict between Israel and Hamas. In his remarks, Trump gave himself credit for ending the war in Gaza, even though key aspects of the peace deal Trump helped broker in October 2025—including Hamas’s disarmament, a long-term governance plan, and the delivery of needed humanitarian aid in Gaza—are largely stalled.
Perceived success in Venezuela “arguably triggered the overreach that we saw in the decision to begin military operations against Iran without a Plan B if initial objectives were not achieved,” Ulrichsen says.
But the limitations of such rhetoric are most “visible” in the Iran conflict, according to Ulrichsen, who says the U.S. has not been able to “translate rhetoric into gains on the ground.”
Trump has repeatedly predicted that the war would end after the November midterm elections, saying last week that it would end “immediately after” them. He endorsed this belief on Tuesday, as well. Trump initially told reporters that U.S. envoys had held a “very good” three-hour meeting with “mediators of Iran."
“They had a very good meeting, and we'll see how it turns out. But certainly, it's to their advantage to make a deal, and we can do that,” he said.
Negar Mortazavi, a senior nonresident fellow at the Center for International Policy, emphasized the point that concrete outcomes in the Middle East may prove critical for Trump.
“President Trump’s ‘peace through strength’ approach has yet to produce the agreement he wants with Iran,” Mortazavi says. “Trump’s argument leaves a central question unanswered: How does further destruction secure an agreement on Washington’s terms when the pressure so far has not?”
“For now, Trump can point to the damage U.S. forces have inflicted, but the war’s central political disputes remain unresolved,” she adds.
The outcomes of these most recent efforts—and whether they moved the needle on peace efforts—remain undetermined. Subsequently, Trump turned to the same takeaway that he shared in his speech, which is that Iran is facing either “potential greatness or obliteration.”
“It does seem as if such rhetoric is producing diminishing results as his tone gradually loses its shock value,” Ulrichsen observes.

Details
Total exports of major grain types during this period fell from nearly 1.6 million to 381,000 tonnes. Barley shipments decreased 9.9-fold, to 21,900 tonnes, while corn shipments fell 3.3-fold, to 11,800 tonnes.
Olena Tyurina, director of the analytical department of the Russian Grain Union, forecasts that Russia will export no more than 1 million tonnes of wheat in September as a whole. For comparison, the figure stood at 5.7 million tonnes in September last year.
Exports through Novorossiysk collapsed nearly tenfold
Shipments through Black Sea ports declined particularly sharply. A total of 72,500 tonnes of grain was handled through Novorossiysk—9.6 times less than last year—while Tuapse handled 6,100 tonnes, 9.3 times less.
The number of countries buying Russian wheat fell from 29 to 8. Supplies to Egypt decreased 3.6-fold, to 81,000 tonnes, while Turkey purchased only 6,100 tonnes, compared with more than 200,000 tonnes a year earlier.
The Russian Grain Union notes that countries reducing purchases of Russian and Ukrainian wheat are beginning to seek alternative suppliers—from Europe to Australia.
At the same time, the price of wheat for Russian producers fell to $105.7 per tonne, compared with $129 in September 2025. According to Tyurina, September prices this low have not been recorded in Russia over the past eight years.

new zealand’s world of wearableart designs art around the act of being watched
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
20:35:30 UTC
05:35:30 KST

World of WearableArt begins with an object, but the competition is structured around everything that happens after that object reaches a body. In Wellington, finalist garments enter an arena where distance and movement become design constraints, while stage lighting changes what remains visible from a seat.
The 2026 edition, titled GLO!, brings 108 finalist works by 134 designers from 18 countries to the TSB Arena. Its strongest critical question sits inside that format: what happens to an artwork when it has to perform for an audience?
The event began on a much smaller scale. Suzie Moncrieff staged the first WOW show at Nelson’s William Higgins Gallery in 1987, asking designers to ‘take art off the wall and adorn the body.’ Around 200 people attended. Today the Wellington production reaches more than 60,000 people across its season. As the audience expanded, the viewing conditions changed with it. A garment that once moved through a gallery-scale setting now has to be legible across an arena.
WOW makes that requirement explicit. Its judging criteria state that a garment should ‘look as good up close, as it does from a distance,’ with construction strong enough to handle choreography. Judges later see the finalists again under full show lighting, with music and the full cast in place. The process treats visibility as part of the design brief. Surface detail still counts, but so does silhouette. Movement can alter the object, and distance decides which gestures survive.
The 2026 works often make that pressure easy to see. Joe Blanck’s Lophii swallows the wearer inside the profile of a deep-sea anglerfish, its illuminated lure projecting beyond the body. Cecilio Castrillo’s Artemis stretches outward through a pale, winged structure that reads almost diagrammatically against the dark stage.
Kayla Christensen’s Sacred Nightfall, winner of the 2026 Supreme WOW Award, works through a different kind of scale: an intricately stitched tapestry becomes a figure once wrapped around the performer. The body turns each of these objects from a construction into an image that can travel across the room.
Modernist art critic and art historian Michael Fried supplied one of the twentieth century’s most famous warnings about art becoming dependent on its viewer and surroundings. In his 1967 essay Art and Objecthood, he wrote: ‘Art degenerates as it approaches the condition of theatre.‘ Fried was arguing against an art whose meaning depended on duration and the beholder’s physical encounter.
WOW takes almost the opposite position. Here, dependence on the stage is built into the competition. The garment is expected to change once somebody steps inside it.
Performance theorist Erika Fischer-Lichte offers another way to understand that shift. She argued: ‘a performance comes into being through the bodily co-presence of actors and spectators.‘ A wearable artwork complicates the relation further because the object sits directly on the performer, the body gives it scale and motion, and the audience supplies another condition through which it is seen. At WOW, the garment bridges sculpture and event, with its full form emerging through use.
There is another audience waiting beyond the arena. Caroline Evans, writing about fashion after the rise of digital media, observes that ‘we now consume fashion as image as much as we experience it as material object.‘ The photographs coming out of Wellington demonstrate this idea. Viewed as a still image, music disappears and choreography becomes a frozen pose. Movement has to be suggested by the position of a limb or the sweep of a material caught mid-motion.
The same garment therefore has to work through two very different kinds of viewing. Onstage, its appearance changes from one second to the next as the performer moves through light and space. In photographs, all of that is compressed into a single image that reaches far more viewers than the live production itself. Large silhouettes and forms that can be understood almost immediately tend to survive that transition especially well. And so, the qualities that make these works readable from the back of an arena also make them easy to carry onto a screen.
Spectatorship is an active process during which viewers select and interpret what they see, connecting it to their own experience. WOW gives them unusually direct material to work with. The designs often begin with recognizable forms, then enlarge or distort them until recognition itself becomes part of the encounter.
Shing Hei’s My Ugly Duckling places the bird around the body, while Rachel Poole and John Fitzgerald’s Ripe for the Pecking turns fruit into exaggerated wearable volume. These references arrive quickly from across the room.
The useful critical question around WOW concerns the pressure that spectatorship places on form. Its garments are built to reach someone sitting far from the stage and a camera positioned closer to it, then continue onward as still images. That sequence favors scale and instant legibility, while movement supplies another layer once the wearer enters. It also explains why the body remains so central. Once art leaves the wall here, the viewer enters the design brief with it.
This article is part of designboom’s SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE chapter, asking how wonder gets built, presented in partnership withSolidNature, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away. Discover more stories that turn onlookers into participants, alter perception and disrupt the everyday here.
happening now! effe and patricia urquiola design baluar, a sauna and hammam collection translating medieval bastion geometries into wellness architecture.
the first stop of our new travelling series brought together designers, architects, collaborators, and friends for a week of conversations and hands-on activities.

US President Donald Trump said Tuesday that talks with Iran have gained momentum and could lead to a deal, but warned that the US could take additional military action against Iranian nuclear facilities if necessary.
Trump made the remarks during a multilateral meeting with Gulf Cooperation Council countries, including Türkiye, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
"It's an honor to be here with some of America's greatest and closest friends, allies, and partners to continue our effort toward a safer and more prosperous Middle East," said Trump.
He said US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had held a "productive meeting" with mediators involved in efforts to engage Iran.
"I think there's a lot of momentum for them to make a deal. That's what we are hearing from everybody," said Trump.
He said the US’ objective in the war had largely centered on preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, claiming that Iranian nuclear sites had been destroyed.
He also referred to the Iranian facility known as Pickaxe Mountain, saying the US could strike the location if it detected significant activity there.
"We may have to blow up another one, Pickaxe Mountain," he said. "We're not seeing a lot of activity there, but if we do, we'll blow it up immediately."
Trump also discussed the Strait of Hormuz, saying oil flows through the strategic waterway had increased significantly since the war began.
He said he believed the situation with Iran could end after the US midterm elections in November, or potentially earlier.
"We think that the situation with Iran could end right after the midterm elections and maybe before. I don't know. You never know," he said.
Trump said the war would ultimately result either in a deal or a rapid end to the fighting.
"Look, it's going to go one way or the other. It's either going to -- we're going to make a deal, or it's going to end very, very quickly," he said.
Reflecting on discussions held last year on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Trump said many of the same leaders had gathered to discuss efforts to end the war in the Gaza Strip.
"Exactly one year ago, many of our nations met here on the sidelines of the United Nations to discuss how we could end the bloody war in Gaza, and almost the same faces were here, including my friend right over here from Turkey," Trump said, referring to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
"He's a tough cookie. Don't mess around with him," said Trump, adding that he hoped his remarks were being properly translated.
"He's fantastic. Fantastic guy, right, my friend," he added.
Following the meeting, Erdogan told reporters outside UN headquarters that eight countries have come together.
"We are striving to overcome the difficulties in the Gulf. We want to see the fruits of our efforts as soon as possible," said Erdogan.

Russia’s Invasion Hits Ukraine’s Lifelines, Threatens Global Food and Energy Chains
Unknown

- Category
- World
Russia’s Invasion Hits Ukraine’s Lifelines, Threatens Global Food and Energy Chains
UN Secretary-General António Guterres condemned Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine as a “blatant violation” of the UN Charter during his General Assembly address on September 22.
The Guardian reported that Guterres described the invasion as a war imposed on a sovereign country and warned that civilians continue to bear its consequences.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Russia’s full-scale invasion has subjected a sovereign country to a brutal war in blatant violation of the charter,” Guterres stated. He added that homes, energy and water systems, and transport infrastructure have repeatedly come under attack, threatening global food and energy supply chains.
Guterres also addressed escalating conflicts across the Middle East and called for an end to hostilities and unrestricted humanitarian access. He warned that military, economic, and technological power alone cannot provide lasting peace, stability, or security.
The UN chief separately compared the risks posed by artificial intelligence with the nuclear threat confronted during the Cold War.
“Back then, it was nuclear weapons. Today, artificial intelligence demands the same clarity of purpose and sense of urgency,” Guterres stated.
The remarks formed part of Guterres’ broader defense of multilateral institutions as geopolitical divisions deepen. He argued that a more representative UN system remains necessary to address conflicts, technological risks, and other global challenges that individual powers cannot resolve alone.
The targeting of Ukraine's energy infrastructure has emerged as a central concern for international officials.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that Russia is preparing strikes against the national power grid during the coming winter and stated that Ukraine is prepared to respond in kind if such attacks occur, emphasizing that while Kyiv seeks to avoid humanitarian crises, it retains the capability to retaliate.

Trump says US-Iran officials held 'productive' talks in New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
20:31:29 UTC
05:31:29 KST

Breadcrumb
Trump says US-Iran officials held 'productive' three-hour meeting in New York
President Donald Trump told the United Nations on Tuesday he was deciding whether to "annihilate" Iran, before revealing that US and Iranian officials had held talks for the first time in months.
Trump's carrot-and-stick approach came as he delivered a speech to the UN General Assembly in New York focused heavily on his stalled war against the Islamic Republic.
"I have a big decision to make -- will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country?" the 80-year-old said in his speech, during which all but one member of the Iranian delegation walked out.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival?"
Trump said he believed Iran would make a deal immediately after November's midterm elections.
But just hours later, Trump revealed that Iranian and US representatives had met for "very good" talks on the sidelines of the UN gathering.
Iranian state media later confirmed that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met US special envoy Steve Witkoff in New York, saying the meeting took place at Witkoff's request.
Trump said the talks lasted three hours and that Witkoff and his son-in-law Jared Kushner were part of the US team that met the Iranian delegation.
"They had a very good meeting, a very productive meeting -- they have another one scheduled in the very near future," Trump told reporters.
"I can't imagine why they wouldn't want to do it. It's potential greatness, or obliteration."
Witkoff told reporters that "I feel very good right now" about the Iranian meeting but would not give further details.
According to Iranian state broadcaster IRIB, Araghchi accepted Witkoff's request for a meeting in order to reiterate Tehran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Those conditions include the immediate lifting of the naval blockade, the release of all frozen Iranian assets and an end to the war on all fronts, including Lebanon.
It is believed to be the first face-to-face meeting between Iranian and US officials since US Vice President JD Vance met senior Tehran officials in Switzerland in June.
Trump promised when the US and Israel launched the war on February 28 that it would be over in four or five weeks, but the conflict is now grinding on well into its sixth month.
A ceasefire agreed in April broke down within weeks and negotiations have since stalled, with Iran refusing to cede control over the Strait of Hormuz shipping lane.
Trump has sought to justify the economic pain of high fuel prices caused by the war by saying that Iran cannot be allowed to develop a nuclear weapon.
Despite the belligerent tone of much of his speech, Trump portrayed himself as a peacemaker who was acting in America's interests, declaring: "While others have ignored threats, I have confronted them."

Saudi Arabia’s King Salman slams targeting of Mecca by ‘terrorist’ Houthis

Saudi Arabia’s King Salman slams targeting of Mecca by ‘terrorist’ Houthis
Saudi monarch’s rare condemnation hints at sense of urgency in the kingdom amid ramped-up attacks from Yemen.
Saudi Arabia’s King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud has branded Yemen’s armed Houthi movement a “terrorist militia” and accused the Iran-allied group of repeatedly targeting the holy city of Mecca.
The 90-year-old Saudi monarch made the comments during a cabinet meeting on Tuesday, the official Saudi Press Agency (SPA) reported.
It was a rare sharp intervention in current affairs by the king, as most day-to-day affairs are led by his son, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
Deadly Houthi attacks this month have marked one of the greatest threats to Saudi Arabia’s security in years.
King Salman called the suspected Houthi targeting of the holy city a “heinous crime” and a provocation against Muslim sentiment worldwide, according to SPA.
Last week, Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted a drone launched by the Houthis towards Mecca, an accusation that the Houthis strongly denied, with Houthi leader Abdel-Malik al-Houthi calling the Saudi claims “a heinous lie”.
It was the first time in nearly 10 years that a security alert had been activated in Mecca, home to the Kaaba, Islam’s holiest site.
The Saudi monarch commended the military and security services for “defending the homeland and resolutely confronting any aggression against the holy sites, pilgrims, citizens and residents of the Kingdom”.
Saudi cities targeted
King Salman also cited a meeting between the crown prince and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi in Cairo last week, as well as his conversations with French President Emmanuel Macron on “efforts to enhance regional stability and ensure the security and freedom of maritime navigation”.
Houthi missile and drone attacks increasingly target Saudi cities, energy infrastructure and shipping, opening another front in the wider regional conflict that began with the United States and Israel’s war on Iran in February.
On Saturday, Saudi-led coalition forces in Yemen said they had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards the Saudi capital Riyadh, sending a dark column of smoke from a fuel storage area at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.
The escalation has also raised the stakes for global energy supplies, as Houthi fighters expanded their control to Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast, which has been used as an alternative route for Saudi oil exports amid the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
Amid growing regional tensions, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan last month signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, which treats an armed attack on any of its three member countries as an attack on all three.
