Europe Warned It Is Running Out of Time to Prepare for Wider War With Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
20:26:12 UTC
05:26:12 KST

Europe may already be losing the hybrid war with Russia – and could face a real war on the continent if it fails to turn its economic and military strength into political action, speakers warned at a Paneuropa Ukraine conference in Kyiv.
The conference “A Vision of a United Europe: Shared Defense, Diplomacy, and Geopolitical Agency” was held in Kyiv on Sept. 18, bringing together Ukrainian and European politicians, diplomats, researchers and security experts to discuss Europe’s ability to respond to Russia’s war against Ukraine and growing geopolitical challenges.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A recurring message throughout the conference was that Europe cannot continue relying on assumptions that a major war is impossible on the continent.
Several speakers argued that Russia’s war in Ukraine should be viewed as part of a broader confrontation with the European security order, while others warned that Europe is already losing, or has nearly lost, the hybrid conflict being waged against it.
The conference is set to continue in Vienna from Oct. 2-4, when a Paneuropa Congress will take place. A draft Vienna Declaration has already been prepared and is expected to be presented after the two events.
Ihor Zhaloba, head of Paneuropa Ukraine, said the decision to hold the first conference in Kyiv was itself meant to send a political signal.
“Paneuropa is not afraid, Ukraine is not afraid; we are working and considering how to resolve the various issues facing us today,” Zhaloba said.
Trump Says Putin Is Willing to Meet as Diplomatic Momentum Continues
                                                                                                                                                                         
He argued that Europe must develop the political will to use its economic, technological and geopolitical strength.
“This is not merely about Russia’s war against Ukraine; it is about Russia’s war against Europe. And, on a broader scale, a conflict between the democratic world and the totalitarian world,” Zhaloba added.
That broader framing was echoed throughout the conference.
Europe cannot afford to assume war is impossible
Reinhard Kloucek, president of Paneuropa Austria, said a generation of European politicians had grown up believing that war was something that happened elsewhere rather than on the continent.
“That makes you lazy,” he said.
Kloucek argued that the international order is already changing and that Europe needs to become an independent geopolitical actor rather than remaining dependent on the US, China or Russia.
He warned that failure to act could leave future generations living in a drastically different Europe.
“If we do not realize in the European countries that now we have the chance because of the challenges we are facing, then our children and grandchildren will live in a Soviet Union 4.0,” Kloucek said.
Kloucek also added that Ukraine is central to Europe’s ability to develop such a geopolitical role.
“The clear point is if we, as Europe, want to play a geo-political role, we need Ukraine,” he said, adding that Russia’s success in conquering Ukraine would demonstrate its ability to divide Europe despite the continent’s greater economic potential.
                                                                                                                                                                         
‘The EU has nearly lost’ the hybrid war
Juraj Mesík, an independent researcher of global trends and risk management from Slovakia, identified Russia as the main threat to Europe and argued that Europe possesses the industrial and technological capabilities needed to confront Russia but lacks the political will to use them.
Mesík described “learned helplessness” and Europe’s reliance on the US as major obstacles, arguing that Russia interprets Europe’s defensive posture as weakness.
“Russia is weak and vulnerable – the main strength of the Kremlin is political impotence of democratic Europe,” he said.
Halyna Yanchenko, a Ukrainian lawmaker, went further, saying Europe should stop treating real warfare as an abstract or secondary threat.
“It seems it is time for us to stop talking about hybrid or cognitive warfare and start talking about a real threat. Russia is waging a direct and aggressive hybrid war in Europe. And as of today, it is winning this war – or perhaps has nearly won it already,” she said.
Yanchenko argued that Russian influence is being amplified by populist political forces in Europe and warned that the transition from hybrid conflict to conventional warfare could become the most dangerous stage.
“The most frightening thing is the transition from hybrid war to actual war; few realize that probably only three countries in the world are prepared for actual war – Russia, China, and Ukraine – simply because the latter has no other choice.”
She also said Ukraine’s experience demonstrates the consequences of delayed military assistance, adding that earlier deliveries of weapons could have changed the course of the war.
“There are only two things that constitute real security guarantees for Ukraine – and it is not NATO, but a strong Ukrainian army and a robust defense-industrial complex.”
Experts warn a real war in Europe is possible
Valeriy Pekar, chairman of the board of the NGO Decolonization, offered one of the conference’s most detailed scenarios for how a wider European conflict could begin.
He argued that Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 should not necessarily be viewed as the model for future Russian military action. Instead, he pointed to what he described as Russia’s concept of “liminal war” – a conflict designed to create uncertainty over whether and how an adversary should respond.
Pekar said a future confrontation could begin with a combination of missile and drone strikes, sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation, political influence operations and covert activity, potentially without the immediate deployment of ground forces.
He used Poland as a hypothetical example, saying a combination of attacks and infrastructure disruption could create a refugee crisis and undermine European decision-making.
His broader warning was that Russia could seek to destabilize European countries through relatively limited but coordinated actions rather than immediately launching a conventional invasion.
Hans Petter Midttun, a nonresident fellow at the Centre for Defence Strategies and a Kyiv Post author, similarly argued that Europe must recognize the strategic nature of Russia’s war.
“NATO is no longer deterring Russia. And that’s the main purpose of NATO. It’s not to fight a war and win it,” Midttun said.
He added that Russia is fighting not merely for Ukrainian territory but to restore great-power status and achieve strategic parity with China and the US.
According to Midttun, Ukraine is therefore an objective within a much broader Russian strategy, while the West itself represents the fundamental obstacle to Russia’s ambitions.
Ukraine’s role in a stronger Europe
Yaroslav Yurchyshyn, a Ukrainian lawmaker and chair of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Freedom of Speech, said Ukraine should already be regarded as part of the Western democratic world.
He argued that Europe needs stronger institutions to counter cognitive warfare and proposed an EU-level platform involving Ukraine, Norway and the UK, saying the countries face essentially the same security threat.
“Criminal elements are traditionally united, whereas we are not,” Yurchyshyn said.
He added that Europe needs its own security policy, whether developed alongside NATO or independently, and that such a policy would be ineffective without Ukraine.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Yehor Chernev, head of Ukraine’s permanent delegation to the NATO Parliamentary Assembly and chair of the Rada’s Committee on National Security, focused on Europe’s practical military weaknesses.
He said Europe remains heavily dependent on the US for security and on both the US and China for critical defense supply chains.
He said European countries can take five to seven years to introduce or field a new type of weapon, while Ukraine has developed significant combat experience and defense-sector expertise during the war.
Chernev also highlighted European dependence on China for critical raw materials, including rare-earth metals, and argued that Ukraine’s experience could help Europe reduce bureaucratic and industrial bottlenecks.
Ukraine’s path into Europe
Ivanna Klympush-Tsintsadze, chair of the Rada’s Committee on Ukraine’s Integration into the EU, focused on Ukraine’s European integration.
She said public support for EU membership in Ukraine remains high but has fallen from around 90% in 2022 to roughly 73–75%, making it important to maintain and deepen public understanding of the integration process.
She argued that Ukraine’s eventual EU membership should be made as irreversible as possible through legal and institutional mechanisms, while acknowledging that Ukraine must continue its internal reforms even during wartime.
Oleksandr Khara, director of the Centre for Defence Strategies, said Europe’s existing political structures were largely designed for peacetime and are not sufficient to address the current combination of threats from Russia, China and broader geopolitical instability.
“We need a more united Europe, not less,” Khara said.
Yevheniia Kravchuk, a Ukrainian lawmaker and chairperson of the PACE Committee on Culture, Science, Education and Media, similarly stressed that security has become inseparable from human rights and European institutions.
She added that Ukraine’s support for EU integration remains considerably higher than in many EU countries, calling this a paradox that Europe should consider.
Belarus and Europe’s wider neighborhood
Svitlana Shatalina of the Coordination Council of Democratic Belarus described Belarus as remaining within Russia’s orbit and called for greater European support for Belarusians living abroad.
She highlighted difficulties faced by Belarusians unable to renew passports without returning home and argued that treating Belarusian citizens abroad as full members of European societies would strengthen their ability to resist Alexander Lukashenko’s regime.
Pavlo Zhovnirenko, chairman of the Center for Strategic Studies, described the war as existential for both Russia and Ukraine and rejected the idea that a simple compromise could resolve the conflict.
He warned that if Russia is not stopped in Ukraine, its military and demographic gains could eventually be turned against Europe.
“In other words, if Europe fails to help Ukraine win, Ukraine’s potential could eventually be turned against Europe itself,” Zhovnirenko said.

Kyiv requires more interceptor missiles ahead of winter -- Macron at UN

Kyiv requires more interceptor missiles ahead of winter -- Macron at UN
French President Emmanuel Macron emphasized this on Tuesday during the general debate of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York, according to a Ukrinform correspondent.
“Russia has been waging a brutal war against civilians in Ukraine for almost five years and occupying the territory of a sovereign state. France will remain unwavering in its support for the Ukrainian peopl’s legitimate aspirations for peace, security, and a future,” Macron said.
France will also do all it can to ensure that meaningful negotiations between Ukraine and Russia begin as soon as possible, he added.
“We must protect Ukrainians more than ever. As winter approaches, we must protect them on the energy front. We must provide them with more interceptor missiles and protect civilians,” the French president stressed.
Macron called for the introduction of what he described as a “dual moratorium” — on strikes against energy and civilian infrastructure, as well as on hostilities in the Black Sea, which would allow Ukraine to resume grain exports.“
This will help address food security challenges, which are of enormous importance to many transition economies and developing countries. Such a dual moratorium is a necessity. Let us put it on the negotiating table and force Russia to face this reality,” he said.
The French president also recalled the Coalition of the Willing established together with the United Kingdom, which brings together countries prepared to guarantee peace and stability in Europe.
Speaking about the state of the world in general, the French president noted the return of imperialism, arrogance, and the “unrestrained use of force that recognizes no rules.” According to him, some states are seeking to undermine the international order, expand their borders, and deprive peoples of the right to determine their own future.
“The question we must answer is very simple: do we want to live under a return to the law of the jungle, or do we seek to live in a civilized international society?” Macron inquired.
He urged states not to give in to fatalism or to the belief that might must inevitably prevail.
“We must learn the lessons of the 20th century. Those who have forgotten these lessons are making both a moral and a political mistake. This applies to the situation in the Middle East, Ukraine, and Africa,” the French president stressed.
Macron said the world had entered a “new era of barbarism,” marked by the mass destruction of civilian infrastructure, human rights violations, and the effective dismantling of the safeguards established by the Geneva Conventions.
According to him, France will continue to provide political and practical support to international mechanisms for gathering evidence and establishing accountability for crimes, including the work of the International Court of Justice.
“There can be no peace without justice. We cannot simply accept a new order of impunity that some are seeking to establish,” he stressed.
Macron also advocated reforming the UN Security Council, including expanding it to include new states and regions, particularly Africa. He backed the Franco-Mexican initiative to limit the use of the veto in cases of mass atrocities, which 128 countries have already joined.
“The world is gradually becoming increasingly divided. Rhetoric of defeat paves the way for empires that abuse their power, threaten the sovereignty of states, and monopolize production capacities, technological capabilities, and wealth,” he warned.
As a reminder, France will strengthen Ukraine’s air defense by supplying radars and interceptor missiles.
As reported, the war in Ukraine will have far-reaching consequences for the entire world, as the issue of respect for international law is being decided there.

The U.S., Greenland and Denmark Agreement: What It Entails and How It Will Change Security in the Arctic
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
23:21:55 EEST
05:21:55 KST

The U.S., Greenland and Denmark Agreement: What It Entails and How It Will Change Security in the Arctic
Kyiv • UNN
The U.S. will build two bases and expand Pituffik. The agreement strengthens NATO in the Arctic and limits the influence of non-allied states.
The United States, Denmark and Greenland have signed a new security agreement that will allow Washington to establish two new military bases on the island and expand the existing Pituffik Space Base. The document also limits the military presence and investments of states that are not NATO or EU members or Alliance partners, Reuters reports, writes UNN.
Details
The new U.S. bases are planned for Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and Mestersvig on the east coast. At the same time, the agreement does not specify the number of U.S. military personnel or the timeline for their deployment.
U.S. aircraft and vessels will have the right to move across Greenland’s territory and its territorial waters in accordance with the provisions of the agreement. The document supplements the 1951 U.S.-Danish treaty on the defense of Greenland.
Greenland to remain in NATO even if it becomes independent
The document provides for strengthening NATO’s presence in the Arctic, while Denmark undertakes to continue strengthening its own defense capabilities in the region.
If Greenland becomes an independent state in the future, Denmark and Greenland must ensure that it retains its NATO membership, including by submitting an application for membership if necessary. Countries that are not members of the Alliance will be prohibited from maintaining a permanent military presence on the island.
At the same time, the agreement enshrines respect for Greenland’s right to self-determination and obliges the United States to take into account the Greenlandic way of life and the characteristics of the local society.
What the document provides for
The document does not grant the United States any separate rights to Greenland’s mineral resources. At the same time, investors from countries that are not NATO members, Alliance partners or EU members will not be able to control or exercise significant influence over the island’s strategically sensitive sectors.
For the agreement to enter into force, it still must be approved by the parliaments of Denmark and Greenland. The document is concluded for an indefinite period and may be amended only by mutual consent of the parties.

F-16 Crashed at U.S. Base in Spangdahlem, Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
20:21:48 UTC
05:21:48 KST

An F-16 fighter jet crashed at the U.S. Spangdahlem Air Base in the Eifel region.
This was reported by the German media outlet Südwestrundfunk (SWR), citing base officials.
The pilot ejected. He received medical attention. The cause of the crash is under investigation.
A squadron of F-16 fighter jets, consisting of about 20 aircraft, is stationed at Spangdahlem Air Base. In recent months, numerous U.S. transport aircraft have also been spotted at the base.
The German Air Traffic Control Authority reported that the crash occurred following training exercises.
Local residents saw a large plume of smoke following the crash. Firefighters and police are on the airfield.
According to SWR sources, two aircraft took off from the base in the afternoon of September 22, one of which crashed.
U.S. military personnel are stationed at approximately 20 locations in Germany, primarily in the south and southwest of the country.
If smaller military facilities are included, the total number rises to about 40.
The most important are the Ramstein and Spangdahlem air bases.
Ramstein, located in the federal state of Rhineland-Palatinate, is the largest U.S. military base outside the United States. It is the largest logistics hub for the deployment of troops, equipment, and cargo to the Middle East, Africa, or Eastern Europe.
The U.S. Air Force has been stationed at Spangdahlem Air Base since the mid-1950s. During Donald Trump’s first presidential term, there were plans to withdraw U.S. troops from this air base, but those plans were put on hold in 2021. In 2026, Poland announced that it was ready to accept U.S. troops withdrawn from Germany.

The PMO records also detail almost 18,000 shekels in spending on makeup, hair styling and medical accompaniment for the prime minister and his wife.
Makeup and a makeup artist for Benjamin and Sara Netanyahu cost $1,498, approximately 4,600 shekels, while hair styling cost another $1,485, also about 4,600 shekels.
A doctor from Sheba Medical Center accompanied the prime minister during the trip at a cost of 8,887 shekels, including VAT. The service was contracted through Sheba’s research and health services fund.

“The Prime Minister’s Office repeatedly ignores responses to Freedom of Information requests concerning the use of public funds, and once again the information can only be obtained by filing petitions with the courts,” Negev said.
“This is not only about public oversight of the ministry’s use of funds, but also about reporting obligations under the law. Elected officials need to know that public money is not theirs to use without accountability.”
The court petition was filed by attorney Dan Rosenthal.

Trump, who first disclosed the talks to reporters, later met Arab leaders and representatives gathered in New York and struck an optimistic tone about the diplomatic effort.

Trump has repeatedly raised the possibility of striking the site amid concerns about Iranian nuclear activity.

In Israel, officials continue to assess that Trump does not want a major new escalation with Iran before the U.S. midterm elections. The renewed diplomacy in New York is viewed as an attempt to exhaust the diplomatic track, but the underlying assessment remains that Washington and Tehran are still far apart.
Israeli officials assess that Iran is unlikely to accept Trump’s terms and that the U.S. president is equally unlikely to accept Tehran’s demands, with each side viewing the other’s conditions as requiring unacceptable concessions.
Israel is therefore preparing for several possible outcomes, including a rapid collapse of the talks, while officials say it remains unclear whether the renewed diplomatic push will ultimately produce an agreement.

In Lower Saxony, investigators discovered suspicious materials just a few meters from the wreckage of a drone found last week near the Bundeswehr air base in Wunstorf. According to NDR, WDR and Süddeutsche Zeitung, the possibility that the aircraft may have been equipped with explosives is currently being investigated, UNN reports, citing Bild.

The German Public Prosecutor General's Office and the Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) are already handling the case. Investigators are examining a possible connection with the drone containing explosives discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August.
The aircraft found near Wunstorf bears similarities to the drones from Leipzig: it is not a mass-produced commercial model, but a specially constructed aircraft. At least one component was probably manufactured using a 3D printer.
In addition, analysis of the wreckage indicates that the drone may have lain near the military facility for a very long time, possibly up to two years. On Tuesday, the find was discussed at a meeting of the heads of Germany's intelligence services in an official setting attended by the chancellor.
Wunstorf is home to Germany's entire fleet of Airbus A400M military transport aircraft. The air base is considered the most important hub for the deployment of troops and military cargo.

Arms makers in Ukraine sign first 26 deals in program that lets them lease equipment for 5% of cost, with state paying other 95%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
20:11:49 UTC
05:11:49 KST

Ukraine's defense makers have signed the first 26 deals under a program that lets them lease or rent new equipment, with the right to subsequently purchase it into ownership, while the state covers most of the bill. The preferential-leasing scheme has channeled about $2 million so far, with producers paying just 5% of the leasing fee and the state covering the rest, the Defense Ministry said.
For many Ukrainian arms makers, the bottleneck is not orders but the cash to expand fast enough to fill them, Deputy Defense Minister Hanna Hvozdiar says, and the program is the state's answer.
Producers can lease equipment, machinery, automation equipment, transportation, and even factory space, paying 5 percent per year while the state subsidizes the rest, up to about $11 million per contract over five years.
The state covers most of the cost
Beyond capping the borrower's rate at 5 percent, the contracts can defer lease payments for up to a year, easing the squeeze while new equipment is bought and installed.
Only companies that hold "critically important" status in the defense sector, a label the state gives firms it deems essential to the war effort, can take part. The 26 deals are only the first, the ministry said, with the program still open to new applicants.
Three banks run the leasing
The Defense Ministry launched the program in April and named Ukreximbank, PUMB, and MTB Bank as the first authorized lessors, it said. In August, it spelled out what producers can lease, from machines, mobile production platforms, and technological gear to the non-residential real estate a plant needs to run.
Ukraine races to scale production
The leasing program is one piece of a broader drive to get money flowing to Ukraine's defense industry so it can produce more, faster. The government has been building financing tools around the sector, including a push by former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov to raise the country's largest defense-tech venture fund.

apple opens 600-capacity music venue inside london’s battersea power station
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
20:11:48 UTC
05:11:48 KST

Apple has opened Apple Music Hall inside London’s Battersea Power Station, introducing a 600-capacity live music venue that doubles as a recording studio, broadcast facility and production space. Set along the River Thames, the venue is conceived for intimate performances that can simultaneously become Spatial Audio recordings, multicamera films and global livestreams. In other words, Apple has designed a concert hall where the show does not necessarily end when the lights come back on.
The interiors look to the industrial language of the historic power station rather than attempting to compete with it. Heritage brickwork, fluted arches and bronze balconies reference elements found across the restored building, while a large glass wall opens the venue toward the concourse and the river beyond. The result places Apple’s typically controlled visual world inside a considerably rougher architectural shell, allowing traces of Battersea’s industrial past to remain part of the experience.
Apple Music Hall opens inside Battersea Power Station | all images by Apple
48 SPEAKERS WRAP SOUND AROUND 600 LISTENERS
Inside the auditorium, the scale remains deliberately compact. A 38-foot-wide stage can shift between conventional front-facing concerts and more immersive, in-the-round configurations, while a 48-speaker spatial sound system surrounds the audience. Apple says the setup is intended to combine the closeness of a small venue with the technical infrastructure normally associated with much larger productions, giving artists more control over how a performance is staged and heard.
Things become considerably more elaborate behind the curtain. Two dedicated recording and mixing studios allow performances to be captured as multitrack recordings and mixed in Spatial Audio either live or afterwards. The hall is also hardwired for 16 or more cameras feeding into a dedicated broadcast control room, with infrastructure allowing iPhones to capture footage alongside traditional broadcast cameras. A single performance can therefore leave the building as a finished audio recording, broadcast-ready mix and multicamera video — quite an efficient afterparty.
the new venue has capacity for 600 people
FROM LIVE SHOW TO GLOBAL BROADCAST
Performances staged at Apple Music Hall can also be livestreamed internationally through Apple’s platforms, extending a 600-person room far beyond Battersea. The opening is accompanied by new Apple Music Radio studios within the same London complex, from which the service’s London-based presenters and programs will now broadcast live. Together, the spaces bring performance, radio, recording and video production under one roof rather than treating each as a separate stage in the process.
The project continues Apple’s long relationship with music, from the iPod and iTunes era to Apple Music and its current push into immersive audio. But Apple Music Hall gives that largely digital ecosystem a very physical address. Here, architecture becomes part venue and part production apparatus: brick arches and bronze balconies frame the audience out front, while studios, cameras and mixing desks quietly prepare the same performance for everywhere else.

At least four dead and six missing in Japan day after Typhoon Dujuan made landfall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
20:09:10 UTC
05:09:10 KST

Authorities announced a revised, higher death toll on Tuesday after search and rescue crews located the bodies of two more people. Six others are still reported missing.
Typhoon Dujuan left at least four people dead and 22 injured in Japan, while thousands of houses near Tokyo were without power after the storm swept through the region, authorities said on Tuesday.
Officials warned that the death toll may continue to rise as six people remain missing, noting that search and rescue operations were underway to locate them.
The typhoon moved away from Japan's coast and out into the Pacific by the morning, allowing authorities to lift or downgrade most heavy rain and landslide warnings.
Dujuan had already led to the early closure in the capital of one of the world's biggest video game trade fairs.
Japan often sees strong typhoons in the late summer and early autumn, with other storms this season disrupting some events at the Asian Games being held in the country.
The Fire and Disaster Management Agency said three people died in Chiba prefecture and one in Kanagawa region, both near the capital, Tokyo.
Entire areas were completely submerged by floodwaters, causing considerable damage and bringing many critical services, major roads and public transportation to a standstill.
More than 45,000 households in Chiba near Tokyo were still without electricity on Tuesday afternoon, while over 460 houses suffered varying degrees of damage.
Although Dujuan weakened as it moved northeast, it dumped record rainfall in parts of the Tokyo area.
Oshima, an island about 120 kilometres south of central Tokyo, recorded 832 millimetres of rain over a 48-hour period, more than double its average rainfall for the whole of September, public broadcaster NHK reported.
Rainfall in Tokyo's Edogawa Ward reached a record 282.5 millimetres over 24 hours.
Scientists say human-driven climate change is intensifying the risk posed by heavy rains because a warmer atmosphere holds more water.

Saudi Arabia restarted the 7-million-barrel-per-day oil pipeline after drone attacks

Unknown Publisher

Saudi Arabia restarted the 7-million-barrel-per-day oil pipeline after drone attacks
Kyiv • UNN
The East-West oil pipeline was restarted at low capacity after three pumping stations were damaged. Full restoration will take up to 8 weeks.
Saudi Arabia has resumed operations of the East–West oil pipeline, which was shut down on September 11 following drone attacks. The kingdom is preparing to resume oil exports from the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, Reuters reports, citing three sources, writes UNN.
Details
The pipeline is currently operating at low capacity. Saudi Aramco plans to gradually increase throughput to 4 million barrels per day, while the route’s maximum capacity is 7 million barrels.
According to the sources’ estimates, reaching 40% capacity will take several days. Full restoration of operations may require six to eight weeks.
Three pumping stations were damaged in the attack
Satellite imagery and data from Reuters sources indicate that three pumping stations were damaged in the drone attacks. The pipeline has 11 pumping stations in total, as well as two pressure-release stations.
After operations resume, the pipeline will once again supply oil to Saudi Aramco facilities on the Red Sea coast. On September 22, a shipment of oil was already scheduled to be loaded in Yanbu for delivery to China.
The East–West oil pipeline has gained particular importance due to disruptions in the transportation of oil through the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia uses this route to redirect about 4 million barrels per day to Yanbu—an amount equivalent to approximately 4% of the global oil supply.

Macron urges world to 'stand firm' against 'abuse of power by empires' in final UN speech
French President Emmanuel Macron used his last address before the UN General Assembly as France's leader to urge the world's nations to stand alongside the United Nations in the face of a resurgent "law of the jungle". Macron also called for a moratorium on strikes on civilian and energy infrastructure in the Russia-Ukraine war and an "open-source" model for frontier AI independent of China and the US.
French President Emmanuel Macron called Tuesday for countries to recommit to international laws and the UN system over a resurgent "law of the jungle".
Read moreUN live: 'No peace without justice,' Macron tells General Assembly
Macron, giving his last speech to the UN's signature annual diplomatic gathering as president, also railed against the humanitarian situation in Gaza while calling for a moratorium on strikes against civilian and energy targets in the Ukraine-Russia war.
"The question put to us, in very simple terms, is whether we want to live in this state of nature, with a kind of return to the law of the jungle, or in a civilised international society," he said.
"My message is to stand firm. Do not yield to the situation which is developing ... The rhetoric of defeat that is giving way to abuse of power by empires, threatening the sovereignty of some nations," Macron said.
The French president, who has been a long-standing supporter of Ukraine and raised the country's case in a meeting with US President Donald Trump on Monday, called for Moscow and Kyiv to agree to a moratorium on striking civilian and energy targets.
'Barbaric acts'
"We've seen the destruction of civilian infrastructure, human rights violations. It's a new era of barbaric acts," he said.
"We must protect the civilian population, and this is why we'd like to express our support for a double moratorium, a moratorium on strikes on energy and civilian infrastructure," he added. He also called for a moratorium of attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea, a crucial sea route for both countries' grain exports.
Macron at one point hammered the rostrum as he spoke about the humanitarian crisis in the devastated Gaza Strip.
"What is our credibility worth if we remain inactive on Gaza? Some claim that peace has been achieved, but this has not opened up humanitarian deliveries. It is a spectacle that shames us all," he said.
Watch moreTrump's world? Leaders navigate consequences of US policy
In a stark contrast to Trump's rejection of global AI regulation in his own address hours before, the French president called for countries to work together on building an open-source frontier artificial intelligence model independent of the "great powers" – China and the United States.
"I don't want anyone to become the vassal of one of the great powers. Rather, we must come together to build an open-source frontier model, a cutting-edge model," he said.
"We should not depend on somebody else."

Zelenskyy: Removal of two Russian oligarchs from EU sanctions lists shows how difficult it is to maintain unanimity
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

23:05:13 EEST
05:05:13 KST

The removal of Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Friedman from the EU sanctions lists shows that it is very difficult to maintain unanimity, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
"This shows that maintaining unanimity is very difficult. And this will be of great significance – whether through the courts, through legislation, through sanctions, or through business," Zelenskyy said at a press conference in New York on Tuesday.
The president said he had discussed this issue today with several European officials.
As reported, the ambassadors – the permanent representatives of EU member states – following a discussion that had lasted the past few weeks, finally decided to extend the sanctions for violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity for three years instead of six months, as had been the case previously, but this came at the cost of excluding Usmanov and Fridman from the sanctions list at the request of Slovakia, France, and Luxembourg.
Ukraine imposed targeted sanctions against Russian oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman on October 19, 2022. As the Ukrainian Ministry of Economy noted at the time, sanctions were imposed that day against 256 individuals – oligarchs from the Forbes list and their associates. The list included Friedman's partners at Alfa Group – Petr Aven, German Khan, and Alexei Kuzmichov – as well as Vladimir Lisin, Leonid Mikhelson, Arkady and Boris Rotenberg, Mikhail Prokhorov, Suleiman Kerimov, Elena Baturina, Yuri Kovalchuk, and others.
A major asset of Friedman and his partners – Sense Bank (formerly Alfa-Bank) – was nationalized by Ukraine in the summer of 2023. In 2022, ARMA also took control, by court order, of the corporate rights and other assets of IDS Ukraine – a group linked to Friedman and the country's largest producer and distributor of mineral water.
In September 2024, the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine filed a lawsuit with the High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC) seeking to forfeit the assets of IDS Ukraine and other Ukrainian assets linked to Friedman to the state. Specifically, the case involved shares and stakes in the Myrhorod Mineral Water Plant, Morshyn "Oscar" Mineral Water Plant, Industrial and Distribution Systems, Alfa Insurance, and Alfa-Leasing Ukraine. Hearings in this case are still ongoing.
As for the Ukrainian assets of Usmanov and his business partners – the Skoch and Streshinsky families – in 2024, the High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC), acting on a lawsuit filed by the Ministry of Justice, had already ruled to forfeit them to the state. According to information from then-Deputy Minister of Justice Inna Bahatykh, the assets in question include more than 165,000 metric tonnes of iron ore products with an estimated value of over UAH 2 billion, as well as 100% of the charter capital of Peter-Service Ukraine LLC – an IT company previously controlled by Usmanov.

A nearly 70-page consent order, provided to Al Jazeera by the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP), found the San Francisco, California-based delivery giant failed to pay some of its workers the minimum amount required by law between December 2023 and June 2026.
The city expected some of those underpayments to continue through November before corrective measures go into effect, according to the order.
DoorDash confirmed that roughly $6.6m in payments never reached its delivery drivers and that there were more than $5.7m in late payments. A spokesperson for the company told Al Jazeera that it will notify the affected workers in the coming weeks.
The city echoed DoorDash’s statement and said it has already identified the affected workers using DoorDash’s records.
“When a worker earns a wage, they deserve to be paid that wage — not tomorrow, not after a lawsuit, but on time and in full,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at a news conference on Tuesday.
The city government said that underpaid workers would receive 200 percent of what they were originally owed.
“A worker who was owed $1,000 but received no payment will receive $3,000. A worker who was paid $1,000 later than allowed under the law will receive $2,000,” a news release announcing the settlement said.
‘Put money back in people’s pockets’
The city began cracking down on delivery driver underpayments under Mamdani’s predecessor, Eric Adams.
His administration established a first-of-its-kind minimum-pay rule for app-based delivery workers in 2023.
Delivery companies, including DoorDash, Grubhub and Uber, were required to meet a minimum pay rate for covered work.
The rule initially called for a minimum pay rate of $17.96 per hour and was set to increase to $19.96 per hour when fully implemented in 2025.
Samuel Levine of the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) said that the settlement is a result of the Mamdani administration expanding its enforcement capabilities after increasing staff when he took office in January.
“What we’ve been able to show, particularly over the last nine months of the Mamdani administration, is that by investing directly and bringing in the best lawyers, investigators, data scientists, and economists to the government, we can cut through a lot of the noise, identify violations when they happen, and put money back in people’s pockets,” Levine told Al Jazeera.
New York is not the only city in the US to attempt to address delivery driver underpayments.
Seattle, Washington has also adopted a minimum-payment system. Starting in 2024, the city began using data from delivery platforms in an effort to enforce it.
In August, Uber Eats agreed to pay nearly $4.4m to settle allegations that the platform violated the city’s minimum-pay rules for delivery workers, affecting 14,000 workers.
Seattle’s Office of Labor Standards (OLS) said Uber Eats failed to provide required minimum payments for some cancelled orders, including instances when a driver had already arrived at a restaurant to pick up food.
Seattle also alleged that Uber Eats failed to provide minimum payments when either the pick-up or drop-off location was outside of the city limits.

French President Emmanuel Macron sharply criticized Israel at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, saying Hamas had “never caused trouble” in the West Bank and arguing that Israeli policies there were undermining both Palestinian rights and Israel’s own security.
In the UN’s simultaneous English interpretation, Macron was rendered as saying: “Look at what is happening in the West Bank, where every day violations are taking place. In the name of what? Hamas has never caused trouble in the West Bank!”
The assertion contrasts with documented Hamas activity in the territory. Israeli security authorities have for years reported Hamas cells and operatives in the West Bank, including plots to carry out attacks. In one recent case, Israeli officials identified Qadri Samara, accused of killing Netanel Shakron at a spring near Neve Tzuf on the eve of Yom Kippur, as a Hamas operative. The suspect was captured several hours later at a medical facility in Ramallah.
During Yom Kippur, Israeli forces also arrested two Palestinians in Qabatiya whom the IDF said were preparing an imminent attack. The military did not publicly identify them in its initial account as Hamas members.
Israeli authorities have separately uncovered Hamas-linked infrastructure and alleged attack plots in the West Bank over the years. The Shin Bet, for example, has previously announced the disruption of Hamas cells that it said were directed from abroad to carry out attacks.
Macron’s broader argument focused on Israeli settlement policy and settler violence, which France says threaten the possibility of a Palestinian state. Earlier this month, France, Britain and Canada announced plans for measures targeting settlement-related activity, saying settlement expansion and increasing settler violence pose an “urgent threat” to a two-state solution.
Macron told the General Assembly that developments in the West Bank were making a viable Palestinian state increasingly difficult to achieve.
He argued that Palestinian statehood was not only a matter of Palestinian rights but also a condition for Israel’s long-term security.
“Anyone who claims that Israel’s security depends on violating the sovereignty of all its neighbors is making a fatal mistake,” Macron said. “They are weakening Israel’s security.”
Macron also condemned the rise in settler violence in the West Bank, saying it was undermining Palestinians’ legitimate right to national existence.
Macron takes veiled swipe at Trump over Gaza
The French president also appeared to criticize U.S. President Donald Trump’s claims of having brought peace to Gaza.
Macron recalled that France was among a group of countries that recognized a Palestinian state a year ago and acknowledged criticism that recognition had changed little on the ground.
“I hear the cynicism of some people: ‘Recognition on paper, look at the reality,’” he said.
But, he argued, the international community’s credibility was equally at stake if it remained passive over conditions in Gaza.
“There are those who boast of a supposed ‘peace,’ but that peace did not open the humanitarian corridors even for a second,” Macron said. “Should we simply watch this spectacle that shames us all? Never.”
Macron has made the two-state solution a central element of France’s Middle East policy. France formally recognized a Palestinian state at the UN in September 2025, while at the same time condemning Hamas’ Oct. 7 attack and calling for the group to be disarmed and excluded from governing a future Palestinian state.
France has also repeatedly stressed that its criticism of Israeli policy does not alter its commitment to Israel’s security. In a joint statement this month, Macron and the British and Canadian prime ministers reiterated support for “a safe and secure Israel, living alongside a safe and secure Palestine.”

Colombia has withdrawn from South Africa's genocide case against Israel in the International Court of Justice, the court announced Tuesday.
In a statement, the ICJ said Colombia informed the Court that it had decided to withdraw the Declaration of intervention that it had filed under Article 63 of the Statute of the Court on 5 April 2024 in the case concerning Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in the Gaza Strip (South Africa v. Israel).
Colombia's Foreign Ministry then confirmed the withdrawal, but said the decision does not change Colombia’s status as a State Party to the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, nor does it affect the validity, scope or binding force of the international obligations assumed under that instrument.

Colombia, Israel ties revitalized in recent months
"The friendship between Israel and Colombia is stronger than ever," Sa'ar said.
Israeli ambassador to Colombia Vivien Aisen echoed the remarks, saying Colombia chose "the right side of history" and made "a brave and responsible decision that we deeply appreciate."
The move comes as part of a wider effort by the administration of President Abelardo De la Espriella to undo some of the hostilities of the previous president, and restore ties with Israel.
After being sworn in at the start of August 2026, de la Espriella announced the immediate resumption of full diplomatic relations with Israel, underlined by a landmark commitment to move the Colombian Embassy to Jerusalem.
Colombia also recognized Israel's sovereignty over the Golan Heights.
South Africa’s Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO) has not officially issued a public statement responding to Colombia's formal withdrawal, but has previously said that it would not cause South Africa to drop its legal challenge.

Antagonistic narcissism is linked to cold feelings toward psychologists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
20:00:52 UTC
05:00:52 KST

People with certain narcissistic traits tend to hold negative views about seeking mental health treatment, often because they harbor cold feelings toward psychologists and psychiatrists. A recent survey analysis reveals that a specific antagonistic form of narcissism acts as a psychological barrier to pursuing therapy, while a more self-promotional form of narcissism does not. These findings were published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences.
Many people who experience severe mental health issues never seek professional treatment. Psychologists refer to this discrepancy between the prevalence of psychological distress and the use of services as the treatment gap. While some people readily seek assistance, others avoid clinics entirely even when their daily functioning is severely compromised. Finding ways to bridge this treatment gap requires untangling the specific beliefs and emotional reactions that keep people away from mental health care.
To understand why some individuals avoid therapy, researchers examine the psychological traits and social attitudes that shape decisions about care. Narcissism is one personality dimension that influences how people navigate interpersonal situations and personal vulnerabilities. Psychologists divide grandiose narcissism into two distinct dimensions. Narcissistic admiration involves a self-promotional strategy where individuals seek social approval, project confidence, and focus on personal success. Narcissistic rivalry is a defensive and antagonistic strategy where individuals protect an inflated self-image by devaluing other people and acting with hostility.
To measure these dimensions, psychologists typically ask people to rate how much they agree with specific statements. Statements like being a very special person gives me a lot of strength capture the essence of narcissistic admiration. Statements such as I want my rivals to fail capture the hostility of narcissistic rivalry.
Engaging in psychotherapy typically requires personal disclosure, accepting a vulnerable position, and opening up to an expert’s evaluation. For someone high in narcissistic rivalry, this uneven power dynamic can feel highly threatening. Marta Rogoza, a researcher at the Polish Academy of Sciences, led a team to investigate how these two facets of narcissism relate to views on mental health services. The researchers wanted to know if a person’s specific type of narcissism alters how they perceive mental health professionals.
By testing their hypotheses in both the United States and Poland, the researchers aimed to see if the emotional mechanisms underlying these attitudes persist across distinct social environments. Mental health services are widely utilized and somewhat normalized in the United States. In Poland, seeking psychological help remains heavily constrained by stigma and structural barriers.
The research team conducted three separate survey analyses to test their ideas. In the first analysis, the researchers surveyed 1,622 adults in Poland using an online questionnaire. The participants answered questions designed to measure their levels of narcissistic admiration and narcissistic rivalry. They also rated their attitudes toward seeking professional psychological help, evaluating how useful or acceptable they found mental health services.
The results of the first analysis revealed a divergence between the two facets of narcissism. Narcissistic rivalry was associated with less positive attitudes toward seeking psychological help. Conversely, narcissistic admiration was linked to more favorable views of mental health treatment.
For the second analysis, the researchers recruited 556 adults in the United States to see if the pattern held across different cultures. In addition to measuring narcissistic traits and general attitudes toward therapy, the team asked participants to rate their emotional reactions using a feeling thermometer. This tool required participants to rate how cold or warm they felt toward mental health professionals and toward individuals diagnosed with mental disorders.
The American sample yielded results consistent with the Polish sample, while offering new insights into emotional reactions. Narcissistic rivalry was linked to cold feelings toward both mental health professionals and people with mental health conditions. Narcissistic admiration was associated with warmer feelings toward mental health professionals.
When the researchers ran statistical models, they found that cold feelings toward mental health professionals accounted for the association between narcissistic rivalry and negative attitudes toward seeking help. In the context of psychological help, professionals occupy positions of expertise and evaluative authority. Seeking their help requires stepping into an asymmetrical power dynamic.
The statistical models suggest that negative emotional reactions toward these specific authority figures are directly tied to decisions about whether therapy feels acceptable. Cold feelings toward people diagnosed with mental disorders did not have this same statistical relationship with help-seeking attitudes. Perceptions of other patients might reflect abstract social categorizations, making those feelings less relevant to a person’s own decisions about seeking care.
In the third analysis, the team surveyed 647 adults in Poland to look closer at specific types of mental health professionals. Instead of asking about a general group, the researchers asked participants to rate their feelings toward psychologists, psychotherapists, and psychiatrists separately.
Once again, narcissistic rivalry was associated with colder feelings toward all three groups of professionals, as well as toward people with mental disorders. These cold feelings toward the professionals statistically explained the link between narcissistic rivalry and negative attitudes toward seeking therapy. On the other hand, narcissistic admiration was linked to warmer feelings specifically toward psychotherapists, which in turn predicted slightly more positive attitudes toward seeking psychological help.
The survey analyses rely on self-reported data collected at a single point in time. Because the research is observational, it cannot prove that narcissistic traits directly alter a person’s attitudes or feelings. The statistical models show relationships between variables, but experimental studies would be needed to establish causality.
The research focused entirely on people’s reported attitudes rather than their actual behavior. Expressing negative views about therapy on a survey does not guarantee that a person will refuse help in a real crisis. The findings also highlight that grandiose narcissism is not a uniform trait. People with high levels of narcissistic admiration might actually view therapy positively, perhaps seeing it as an opportunity for self-improvement or personal development.
Future research could track individuals over time to see if changes in how they view mental health professionals precede changes in their willingness to seek therapy. Investigators might also explore qualitative interviews to understand exactly why individuals high in narcissistic admiration evaluate psychotherapy favorably. Learning whether this openness represents a genuine desire for growth or a superficial pursuit of status could guide efforts to make mental health care more accessible.
The study, “Only the weak need help? The role of narcissistic rivalry in attitudes toward psychological help,” was authored by Marta Rogoza, Marta Marchlewska, Zuzanna Molenda, and Dominika Adamczyk.

Unknown

EU plotting new ‘scheme’ to steal Moscow’s frozen assets – Russian intel
The EU is working on a new scheme to “steal” Moscow’s frozen sovereign assets to bankroll Ukraine, Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) said in a press release on Tuesday.
Around $300 billion in Russian sovereign assets was frozen by Kiev’s Western backers after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. Roughly $240 billion is still being held at the Belgium-based clearing house Euroclear.
According to the SVR, EU leaders have “a vital interest in stealing Russian assets,” because they fear they will not be able to indefinitely finance “the thieving Kiev regime” without appropriating the funds.
Eurocrats are now “in a hurry” to pull off the seizure before elections in several EU states in 2027, the agency stated, arguing that future governments in the bloc could be less willing to back further financial support for Ukraine.
The EU has already redirected profits generated by the immobilized funds to Ukraine but has been unable to seize the underlying assets due to strong political and legal resistance.
According to the SVR, experts in Brussels are now discussing the creation of a new supranational structure that could take control of Russian central bank funds after they are moved outside of Belgian jurisdiction.
Belgium has repeatedly blocked proposals to seize the assets, with Prime Minister Bart De Wever warning that outright confiscation would expose his country to legal and financial retaliation. Euroclear has also said it could sue the EU if the funds are seized.
Last week, Belgium’s top administrative court also struck down a government decision not to release the assets of Russia’s BCS Bank, which were frozen alongside Moscow’s sovereign assets in 2022. The court found that Belgian authorities had mishandled the case and ruled that the bank could seek a fresh review, potentially setting a precedent for other entities whose requests were rejected under similar circumstances.
Moscow has long denounced any attempt to appropriate its sovereign assets, calling it “theft” and warning that confiscation would trigger retaliation, potentially including measures against Western assets held in Russia.
The SVR has also warned that confiscating Russia’s sovereign funds would damage trust in European financial institutions among major foreign investors, including China, India, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Singapore.

“Therefore there is no analogy with the obstructionist policies pursued by Viktor Orbán.”
The latest dispute adds pressure to an already strained diplomatic relationship.
Hungary has repeatedly blocked progress in Ukraine’s EU accession process, including cluster negotiations, while citing concerns over the rights of the country’s ethnic Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia.
Budapest’s position has also affected Moldova, whose accession pathway remains linked to Ukraine.
Magyar had previously sought to distinguish his government from Orbán’s approach, including through a June agreement with President Volodymyr Zelensky on the educational, cultural, linguistic and political rights of Hungarian communities in Ukraine.
Yet Budapest has continued to withhold support. By Sept. 8, Budapest has blocked the start of negotiations on clusters 2 and 3 four times and refused to disclose which legislative steps it expects Ukraine to take in order to lift the ban.
The country had also delayed a joint EU letter on Ukraine’s and Moldova’s bids that required unanimous approval from all 27 member states.
The Hungarian Foreign Ministry continuously points to minority-rights concerts as justification for such decisions – a line first used by Orbán during his tenure, whose government stalled opening the initial “Fundamentals” cluster for 17 months over the status of ethnic Hungarians in Transcarpathia.

Prosecutors in France probe secret filming of women with smart glasses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
19:55:42 UTC
04:55:42 KST

Prosecutors in France probe secret filming of women with smart glasses
- Paris prosecutors have launched investigations after complaints about women being secretly filmed on the street using smart glasses without consent, highlighting privacy violations and social media misuse.
- The e-Enfance association reported around 20 such cases, mostly involving Meta glasses, where women were filmed to provoke reactions and then subjected to online abuse.
- French law punishes non-consensual filming with up to two years in prison and fines; prosecutors also explore related cybercrimes, urging stronger oversight and platform responsibility.
AI generated
PARIS - Paris prosecutors said on Sept 22 they had opened several probes after receiving complaints concerning women filmed on the street without their consent using smart glasses.
Anyone wearing smart glasses can take photos, film videos, listen to music, make phone calls, translate text or interact with an AI assistant.
Meta’s smart spectacles, developed in partnership with Ray-Ban maker EssilorLuxottica, have become a commercial success.
Meta sold seven million pairs in 2025.
Other companies, including Google and Snap, are also preparing to roll out AI-powered glasses.
Calls have grown in Europe for action against what campaigners call “pervert” smart glasses after secretly filmed footage of girls and women has appeared online, with a petition in Britain demanding a ban on their sale.
In France, the e-Enfance association, which operates the national hotline for victims of online abuse, earlier this month sounded the alarm about videos recorded with camera-equipped glasses and shared online.
The Paris public prosecutor’s office said on Sept 22 it had received “complaints relating to violations of privacy linked to the use of smart glasses”.
Prosecutors did not say which brands were involved.
Prosecutors pointed to a “growing trend on social media involving women being filmed on the street with smart glasses without their consent and the videos being published online”.
Under French law, such an offence is punishable by up to two years in prison and a €45,000 (S$65,000) fine.
Prosecutors said that in some cases investigations had also been opened for sexual assault when “the acts are accompanied by non-consensual sexual contact”.
The Paris prosecutor’s office said its cybercrime division “tested smart glasses in September in order to identify the commission of other cybercrime-related offences”.
Such offences could include the theft of a cryptocurrency wallet’s recovery phrase, enabling criminals to steal the funds.
‘Humiliating strangers’
The e-Enfance group said it had received around 20 reports from women as of Sept 8, most involving Meta glasses.
“We need to strengthen oversight of these devices from the design stage,” said the association’s Veronique Bechu.
“And when creators make a business model out of humiliating strangers, platforms must adopt a zero-tolerance approach and suspend repeat offenders,” she added.
According to the association, the cases reported to its hotline tended to follow a recurring pattern: a content creator approaches a young woman or girl in a public place and discreetly films her using smart glasses.
The aim is to “provoke a reaction, make her uncomfortable or place her in an embarrassing situation” before sharing the footage on social media, mainly TikTok.
Those filmed often become the target of ridicule, misogynistic insults and even threats, the association said, citing the case of a teenage girl filmed in Paris during an annual French street music festival.
After approaching her, a man wearing Meta smart glasses filmed her and posted the video on TikTok, Instagram and X, where it went viral. The teenager subsequently received “hateful comments and death threats”.
Meta has said it has taken multiple steps to prevent tampering with a blinking LED light on its glasses designed to indicate when recording is taking place. AFP

BlueBird Tech Starts Production of New Ukrainian Antennas for Drones and UAVs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
19:52:57 UTC
04:52:57 KST

The Ukrainian company BlueBird Tech has launched production of two new in-house-developed antennas—the CLOVER 3.5–4.5 GHz and the PCB VeeDip 1.2 GHz.
As the company told Militarnyi, both antennas were designed and manufactured in Ukraine and are intended for use in communication systems, unmanned aerial vehicles, and drone detectors.
The CLOVER omnidirectional clover-type antenna operates in the 3.5–4.5 GHz band and is designed for video transmission on FPV drones and for detecting enemy UAVs.
Thanks to its extended signal reception range (3.0-4.9 GHz), the antenna can detect not only FPV drones but also aircraft-type UAVs, such as the Molniya.
The VeeDip PCB planar V-shaped dipole antenna is designed for the 1,150–1,300 MHz range and can be mounted on drones, mobile repeaters, or ground stations.
Weighing just 11 grams, the antenna is designed to transmit and receive video, telemetry, and control signals without adding unnecessary weight.
As of September 20, 2026, the CLOVER antenna costs 600 UAH, while the PCB VeeDip costs 336 UAH.

Trump admin asks top US court to reverse pro-Palestinian scholar’s release
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
19:52:16 UTC
04:52:16 KST

Trump admin asks top US court to reverse pro-Palestinian scholar’s release
Debate over Badar Khan Suri’s release sparks a renewed legal clash over authority between US federal courts and Trump’s immigration system.
The administration of United States President Donald Trump has asked the US Supreme Court to overturn the decision to release a Georgetown University scholar who had advocated for Palestinian rights and opposed Israel’s war in Gaza.
Georgetown scholar and postdoctoral fellow Badar Khan Suri was released last year after a judge heard claims that his detention violated his due process and free speech rights under the US Constitution.
On Monday, the US Department of Justice (DOJ) petitioned the high court to consider whether federal immigration law barred the lower-court judge from ordering Suri’s release.
Suri, an Indian citizen, was first arrested by masked US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers outside his home in Rosslyn, Virginia, in March 2025 amid the Trump administration’s targeted crackdown and mass deportation campaigns of foreign nationals and visa holders engaged in pro-Palestinian activism across college campuses.
At the time, critics accused the Trump administration of targeting him based on his familial ties. His wife is the daughter of Ahmed Yousef, a former adviser to assassinated Hamas political leader Ismail Haniyeh.
Suri was brought to Texas after his detention and freed in May 2025 on the orders of a district court judge, on the grounds that he was likely to succeed in proving his arrest was in retaliation for his constitutionally protected speech.
The Trump administration has argued that the judge should not have interfered in the case.
In July, the Virginia-based US Circuit Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit ruled in a 2-1 decision that nothing prevented a lower-court judge from hearing a challenge to someone’s allegedly unconstitutional detention, even if it related to deportation proceedings pending before the immigration courts.
Solicitor General D John Sauer argued that the Fourth Circuit’s ruling threatened nationwide immigration enforcement by letting detainees bypass immigration courts to contest their deportations.
“That is all practically disastrous,” Sauer said.
Sauer noted that a different appeals court had reached the opposite conclusion earlier this year, overturning a ruling that freed pro-Palestinian activist and former Columbia University student Mahmoud Khalil, who had been released on bail in June last year after spending more than 100 days in ICE detention.
In January, the Third US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that lower federal district courts lacked subject matter jurisdiction to hear immigration or detention challenges while active removal proceedings are ongoing. While the order did not influence the core First Amendment arguments in Khalil’s case, it stripped away crucial procedural safeguards.

Trump says relations better with Burnham than Starmer after first face-to-face meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
19:50:36 UTC
04:50:36 KST

Donald Trump has asserted his relationship with the UK is “more up” with Andy Burnham than under Keir Starmer despite tensions between the two countries on a range of thorny issues including regulation of artificial intelligence, the Chagos islands and the war in Iran.
At their first face-to-face meeting, the US president praised Burnham, who sat nervously alongside him, as a “natural businessperson”, saying he thought he had “lots of assets on his side” and would be a “great” prime minister.
Burnham, who was joined in the talks by Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, and Jonathan Powell, his national security adviser, said he and Trump had built on the “good connection” they established early on, in an effort to shore up relations which had splintered over Iran.
UK officials reacted with relief that the talks appeared to have gone according to plan. But despite the warm words at the UN general assembly in New York, there were still signs of difficulties ahead.
On his way to the US, Burnham had revealed he would urge the US president to de-escalate the Iran conflict, with turmoil in the Middle East pushing up global energy prices, putting the UK economy under intense pressure.
Much of the summit has been dominated by geopolitical turbulence, with Trump using his speech to double down on his strategy. The president repeated his threat to “annihilate” Iran, adding he would “drive them into hell” if they did not back down and sign a peace deal with the US.
Asked later whether he had any sympathy with allies which were feeling pain over the cost of living as a result of his actions, Trump claimed that “as soon as the war is over the prices are going to come way down”.
Trump, who has suggested Iran could agree to a deal after the US midterms in November, said “people understand” the need to prevent Tehran obtaining a nuclear weapon, even if that meant price hikes at the petrol pumps and in shops.
In his own UN speech, Burnham was expected to push for greater international control over AI. He revealed to business leaders that he wants a “single set of global principles and standards” to guard against rogue AI, saying the issue would be a main focus of the UK’s G20 presidency next year.
But Burnham’s ambition for the UK to be an “honest broker” between countries in that could set him on a collision course with Trump, who has called warnings about AI’s existential threat to humanity a “hoax” and gave a defiant speech in which he intensified his criticism of attempts to regulate the emerging technology.
“The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now. We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in,” he said.
“Americans have never been a nation that retreats from a frontier or shrinks from a challenge, no matter how great or how daunting that challenge may be … I’m not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution.”
Burnham is also under pressure to sign up to an initiative being led by Finland and Norway – and backed by more than 20 countries – to bar AI companies from launching their models commercially without submitting them for safety testing first, amid growing concerns over the risks.
In another schism between the two countries, Trump was scathing about the UK’s deal to give away sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, while paying for a lease of the military base of Diego Garcia.
“I don’t support it. I think it’s terrible. It was a terrible deal. [Mauritius] all of a sudden say they have ownership. Somebody has ownership that never showed up before after decades and centuries. I think it’s ridiculous,” he said.
But he suggested that Burnham may reconsider the deal. “It’s amazing how strategic it is, and I think the prime minister is going to be looking at it,” he said, to which the UK leader nodded and said “yeah”.
However, Trump avoided commenting on the UK’s decision to ban trade with West Bank settlements, leaving it to the prime minister to answer the question. He is also understood to have agreed to a request from Burnham to bring up the case of imprisoned Hong Kong dissident Jimmy Lai in talks with China’s Xi Jinping on Thursday. British officials in the meeting suggested Lai could live in the UK.
UK officials had been somewhat nervous about the meeting, as Trump had previously dismissed Burnham as “extremely liberal” and described the former mayor of Greater Manchester as the “mayor of a town”. However, his demeanour towards Burnham was mostly cordial.
But it appeared to have gone to plan for both sides, with Trump praising US-UK relations, saying: “I think you’re up. Well, they’re more now than they were with your last prime minister, let me put it that way.
“I think right now, based on my relationship with your prime minister, Andy, I think we’re doing very well.”
Later in the press conference, Trump hit back at reporters questioning why he has banned some journalists from the White House, leading to a wider boycott by media organisations. The president claimed he had a “right to clean out fake news”.
In his UN speech, Trump promised there would be peace between Ukraine and Russia “more quickly than people understand”. After talks with Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, he warned that Starmer’s rhetoric had been “too tough” towards Moscow and that London “needs to be a little bit careful”.
Many of Trump’s talking points were contradicted, however, by the UN secretary-general António Guterres, who used his speech to warn about the consequences of international conflict, climate change and AI over the past decade.
“Geopolitical divides have deepened. Inequalities have intensified. Trust has frayed. The climate crisis went from distant warning to daily reality. And artificial intelligence moved at a speed that has blindsided even those who created it,” he said.
Without naming Israel, he added that what followed the Hamas attack of October 2023 “was an onslaught on Palestinians in Gaza, with a scale of killing and destruction unlike anything I have witnessed in all my years as secretary-general”.

US to get free access to Greenland’s airspace and territorial waters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
19:47:46 UTC
04:47:46 KST

WASHINGTON, September 22. /TASS/. Under the agreement with Denmark and Greenland, the United States will gain unrestricted access to the airspace and territorial waters of the Arctic island for its military aircraft and ships, the new security agreement on the island, which is autonomous and part of Denmark, said.
"With a view to ensuring a secure and effective operation of the Defense Areas, the United States of America shall enjoy, for its public vessels and aircraft and its armed forces and vehicles, the right of free access to and movement between the Defense Areas through Greenland, including the Territorial Waters, by land, air and sea. This may also apply to unmanned military installations subject to agreement by the Parties on the modalities at the time of establishment," the agreement, released by the White House, says.
"United States aircraft may fly over and land in any territory in Greenland, including the Territorial Waters, and United States public vessels may have undersea access to and movement within the Territorial Waters, without restriction except as mutually agreed upon by the Parties."
The agreement was signed on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York by US President Donald Trump, as well as the Prime Ministers of Denmark and Greenland, Mette Frederiksen and Jens·Frederik Nielsen.

EU drops sanctions for Russian oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
19:43:00 UTC
04:43:00 KST

EU drops sanctions for Russian oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman
September 22, 2026
The European Union on Tuesday reached a compromise to prolong sanctions for around 3,000 Russian individuals, entities and companies — but it also resulted in the lifting of sanctions on two Russian oligarchs, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman.
It all comes after lengthy negotiations ahead of a Wednesday deadline to extend the sanctions, which required unanimity among EU countries to be approved.
"The compromise will involve an extension of the regime for 36 months, until 22 September 2029," a spokesman for Ireland, which holds the EU's rotating presidency, said.
"The decision was also taken to delist certain individuals under the regime," it added.
Previously, the sanctions were subject to six-month extensions, so Tuesday's agreement allows the EU to avoid another squabble over the sanctions for three years.
Ukraine denounced the EU's removal of oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman from its Russia sanctions list as "shameful and unjustifiable."
"Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on social media.
"Wars end through resolve and strength, not concessions to the aggressor's entourage," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on social media.
Zelenskyy did say he was "grateful" to EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen for "her readiness to work on adding more Russian names to the EU sanctions list".
Kyiv has called on EU countries to impose "national" sanctions on the two oligarchs.
France and Luxembourg sought exemptions
France was one of the countries demanding the removal of Russian-Uzbek billionaire Usmanov from the sanctions list.
Officials in Paris explained the decision as having to do with "national security" concerns. The French government has not provided any additional details.
According to AFP, diplomatic sources say the demand was linked to a potential prisoner release deal involving French nationals held in Azerbaijan, whose regime is close to Usmanov.
Meanwhile, Fridman's sanctions exemption was put forth by Luxembourg.
Sources say the move comes as Fridman sues Luxembourg for €15 billion ($17 billion) over his frozen assets, due to EU sanctions.
Who are Usamov and Friedman?
Usmanov and Fridman are two of Russia's best-known oligarchs, and both have a net worth of $14 billion and 16 billion, respectively. They both are known to have close ties to Vladimir Putin.
The Uzbek-born Usmanov made his fortune in the metals industry and in telecom. He currently owns the USM holding company, as well as MegaFon, one of Russia's main mobile phone operators.
For his part, Fridman, has made his fortune as founder and one of the shareholders of Alfa Group, which includes Alfa Bank, Russia's largest and most important private commercial bank.
Fridman also co-founded investment firm LetterOne in Luxembourg and stepped down from its board of directors in 2022 after being targeted by European Union sanctions.
