I think I'm autistic. I don't know whether a formal diagnosis will help or hinder me
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
19:38:34 UTC
04:38:34 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
As medical technology advances and our awareness of good mental and physical health grows, it's never been easier to get a diagnosis. But is putting a label on what's happening in our body always a good thing? Or can it lead to harm? Watch Insight episode 'Overdiagnosed?' On SBS On Demand.
I never suspected I had autism, but after a recent dinner with a psychologist friend of mine, I took an online screening test that suggested I might. Now, I am figuring out whether I want to seek a formal diagnosis and know for sure.
I've always felt 'different'. I don't say that to boast; it's just that my early life was informed by the near-death experience I had as a baby.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
When I was five months old, I developed bacterial meningitis and ended up in hospital for 10 days with apnoeic episodes and a seizure. Doctors were unsure how much my brain would recover. They told my parents I would likely be Deaf or have significant brain damage, but luckily neither of these would come to pass.
Still, I've wondered whether the brain trauma I sustained had consequences for who I am. And now, after taking that test, I also wonder whether it is because I might be autistic.
In primary school, I found it hard to make friends, and I spent most lunchtimes on my own — imagining I was a movie star and the sixth member of British pop bands Spice Girls or Steps.
That was until a switch flipped in me one day when I was 10 years old, and I decided to join the other kids in a game of handball.
I underwent a lot of occupational and behavioural therapy over the years in my meningitis recovery as my general development was affected — particularly when it came to social skills.
And it was like the years of therapy finally activated, and I developed self-awareness.
Somehow, I was instantly cognisant of my personality differences and determined to course-correct as quickly as possible.
So, I hid my daydreaming and blended in when my friends wanted to play Xbox or the playground game Capture the Flag. I wasn't necessarily good at copying their behaviour, but I could cope with it.
Looking back, I see that many of the techniques I'd learnt in therapy probably helped me mask the traits I felt made me different — such as my fixation on pop music.
Building emotional walls
When I realised I was gay at 13, I had to mask even more so.
My emotional barriers came with me wherever I went. It's hard to 'be yourself' when you're always on high alert for being asked that question. Consequently, I hated sleepovers or hanging out without a clean end time.
Someone asking me at the last minute to hang out was my worst nightmare ... didn't they know I needed to emotionally prepare for that?
But when you're used to operating with defences up, you eventually forget that they're there and socialising becomes even harder.
The imaginary world of being a pop star still hums in the background of my adult life.
It's been particularly useful to escape boredom on an ordinary day or when I'm exercising. Over the years, I've come up with many hypothetical albums and tours while doing cardio.
And I've channelled my fixation on pop music into co-hosting a podcast about my favourite band Steps, which I do outside of my career in advertising.
Autism or brain trauma?
When you pair these traits with the results of the online screening for autism I did a couple of months ago, one would think it'd be a pretty open/shut case of autism. But my childhood brain trauma complicates it.
My screening score was consistent with autism, specifically in the areas of circumscribed interests and social relatedness.
You could say that my dedication to pop could be an autistic trait, but maybe I've also just had more time to dedicate to fandom? My scores regarding 'social relatedness' could be autism, but they could also be linked to the social dysfunction heavily prevalent in childhood brain trauma survivors.
I've investigated the cost and time it would take to try to figure out the cause of my traits, but to what end? It's not like I can take a pill to be less awkward or less interested in pop music.
Guilt and social stigma
I also feel some guilt about potentially receiving a formal autism diagnosis, as I don't think 'autism' can fairly represent everyone on the spectrum; I know others with autism have much more profound traits.
I would never want to claim that title and take away resources from people in my life who need them more than I do.
I'm biased, but I wouldn't say people look at me and think I need lots of support or fit under the label — I've got a high-pressure job and a large social network.
I also have some apprehension about receiving a formal diagnosis because of potential social stigma.
I would worry about telling my boss and putting it on my Tinder profile.
Would a diagnosis impact the way others see me? I do worry about it a lot.
'Can't I just be a pop super fan?'
Ultimately, I'm not planning on seeking an official diagnosis right now. Instead, I'm going to go back to therapy to figure out what this all means for me.
I know a diagnosis can be very helpful to neurodivergent people, and I acknowledge I might be on the autism spectrum, but I'm not in any rush.
After so many years of having walls up, I'm finally able to tell people what my interests are, and I'm not keen to have them re-diagnosed as an autistic trait. Can't I just be a pop super fan?

The $400 reason a smaller Australia may not be much poorer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
19:38:26 UTC
04:38:26 KST

in brief
- Treasury data suggests lower migration barely impacts individual Australian wealth.
- Experts warn smaller migrant numbers increase fiscal burdens for retirees.
Australian living standards would not collapse if population growth targets are not met in the future, Treasury forecasts predict, with households revealed to be just a few hundred dollars worse off even with a drastically different size.
The difference between a high migration and a low migration scenario in the next 40 years, may only pan out to affect GDP per capita by about $400, the figures suggest.
However, experts caution that governments will need to make "tough decisions" around funding if fewer migrants were to arrive in the country, as a shrinking tax base would have to support a growing dependent population of retirees.
Some of the government's political opponents have cited the results of the Intergenerational Report (IGR) to claim that migration levels need to be cut further than current government projections.
Published by the federal government every three years since 2002, the IGR outlines Australia's economic and budgetary outlook over the next 40 years.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The forecasts in the reports are predictions, some of which have fallen far off the mark, such as the first report projecting that Australia's population would reach 25 million in 2042 — a milestone reached 24 years earlier in 2018.
Its release comes amid an ongoing public debate over optimal net overseas migration figures, which the Coalition and One Nation parties argue should be reduced.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has defended the government's forecast that annual migration to Australia will drop to 225,000 people by 2028.
He said migration is "a force for good in our economy and in our society".
"We will continue to make the case for getting that net overseas migration down in the most responsible way, that balances all of the key considerations in our economy and in local communities," Chalmers told the ABC's 7.30 program on Monday.
While fewer people in the country may alleviate some structural pressures on housing, infrastructure, and public services, Dr Liz Allen, senior lecturer in demography at the Australian National University, told SBS News that migration cannot be separated from its broader impacts on society.
"There's no optimal population size. That's just the reality," she said. "We need to look at what's going on underneath."
What the data tells us
Data in the IGR, released on Monday, shows that under a low migration scenario of 185,000 annually, GDP per capita would shrink by just $400 in 2066, compared with the baseline assumption of 235,000.
Under a higher migration scenario of 285,000, gross national income per capita (GNI) would be just $100 more, despite adding some 2 million people over the 40-year projection period.
GDP per capita refers to a country's total economic output, divided by population. GNI refers to total earnings by a country's people and businesses.
The country's population would climb by roughly 5.5 to 6 million, from around 36 million under a low-migration scenario, to around 42 million in a high-migration scenario by 2066. However Australians would only be up by $500 annually.
Allen said that while individual slices might remain virtually identical, the size of the cake as a whole would be smaller.
"With a shrinking relative working-age population, living standards could go backwards as the government needs to do more with less money," she said.
The fiscal drag of ageing
While per capita GDP and GNI remain virtually identical, national GDP growth drops from 1.6 to 1.3 per cent with fewer migrants as the projections reveal the country would face substantial challenges if migration numbers do not match the forecasts.
Under the low-migration scenario, gross debt as a percentage of GDP would rise by 4.8 per cent while total payments on aged care, the NDIS, healthcare, and other spending would increase by 0.6 per cent.
The old-age dependency ratio — the number of people aged 65 or over for every 100 workers — is projected to rise from 27.4 to 40.2. With fewer migrants, that burden climbs to 43, but with more, it drops to 37.8.
Erin-Lea Brown, economic prosperity deputy program director at the Grattan Institute, said higher migration would help to alleviate issues of an ageing population.
"You have this softening of the ageing population effect," she said. "Our population would still absolutely age over that time period, and it would be a major structural trend in our economy, but it would be to a lesser degree."
Productivity over population
The IGR finds that changes in productivity would be far more significant to national wealth.
The Treasury's baseline productivity is assumed to be 1.2 per cent of GDP, but it also modelled it to be as low as 0.8 or as high as 1.6.
Under a high-productivity scenario, GNI per capita surges from $149,500 to $172,000 in 2066, and gross debt falls from 27.4 per cent of GDP to just 2.4 per cent of GDP.
Labour productivity growth — the ability to "do more with less" — has driven growth in real GDP per person over the past 40 years, Brown said.
As population growth slows and the boost to participation driven by women entering the workforce over the past 40 years levels out, it will become "even more important for labour productivity to do the heavy lifting", Brown said, to "ensure that we continue to have economic growth into the future".
Paying for the future
Australia is far from the only country with a fertility rate — the number of babies born to each woman — below the 2.1 needed to keep the population stable.
More than half of countries have a birth rate below the replacement level, while countries such as Italy, South Korea, China, and Japan have rapidly shrinking populations.
Given that government fiscal policy relies largely on taxing its working population, Allen said a reconsideration of taxation is needed given the long-term demographic shifts Australia is facing.
On Monday, Chalmers ruled out making changes to GST while also rejecting proposals to implement an inheritance tax.
Allen, however, said tax reform can come from elsewhere by "taxing corporates, taxing other entities, and taxing the non-renewable products of the earth from Australia".
"Unless we see some major change to the way that taxation and government funding is conducted in this place, future governments are going to have to make tough decisions."
Intergenerational reports, experts note, are useful because they force governments to "lift their eyes" from the next election to think about long-term planning. Rather than trying to predict the future, they try to capture the impact of present policies in 40 years time if nothing changes.
"In a way, a successful IGR may actually be one whose forecasts never eventuate because it exposed an unsustainable path and forced a change of some kind," Brown said.
Allen added that politicians should not be using the report to "stoke fear" but to rally together to work on the "scary" problems of the future.
"We fix these things by making the future more hopeful, so that folks have greater certainty, and tomorrow looks promising."

Polish Guards Call Police After Drone Spotted Over Redzikowo US Missile Shield Facility
An unauthorized drone breached the perimeter of the strategic US Aegis Ashore missile defense base in Redzikowo, Poland, Polish news outlet Onet reported on September 21.
This prompted Polish military guards to call a civilian emergency hotline rather than neutralizing the threatm Onet wrote.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The incident occurred on the afternoon of September 15. Poland’s Ministry of National Defense (MON) confirmed the breach, stating that reconnaissance systems detected the unmanned aerial vehicle operating approximately 500 meters from the facility for roughly five minutes.
The Redzikowo installation is a cornerstone of the US and NATO missile defense shield in Europe, Onet noted.
While American personnel operate the advanced radar and interceptor systems, the Polish military holds primary responsibility for the physical security of the base and its surrounding airspace, deploying a specialized subunit for this exact purpose.
According to Onet, rather than engaging the drone with electronic warfare jammers or kinetic countermeasures, the Polish military unit initiated civilian protocols, reporting the incident to the 112 emergency dispatch and local police.
The defense ministry stated that authorities successfully identified the location from which the operator was flying the drone, but declined to specify if any military anti-drone systems were activated during the breach, citing operational security.
The incident has raised severe concerns regarding the Polish Armed Forces' readiness to defend critical infrastructure. Despite the prominent role of cheap, tactical drones used for reconnaissance and explosive delivery in neighboring Ukraine, military sources told Onet that Polish installations remain highly vulnerable.
Security experts warn that even heavily guarded ground facilities are functionally defenseless from the air without modernized, localized anti-drone defense grids.
Russia has been deliberately escalating its hybrid warfare against Europe by flying military drones directly into NATO airspace. These incursions into Poland, Romania, Latvia, Germany, and other countries are designed to probe Western radar networks, test political red lines, and normalize airspace violations without triggering a direct military response.
Poland had recently scrambled military jets and placed ground-based air defense and radar systems on high alert in response to Russian airstrikes targeting neighboring regions in Ukraine.
The Polish Armed Forces Operational Command described the activation as a preventive measure to secure NATO's eastern flank airspace.

How Fake Movie Casting Calls Became Part of Russia’s Foreign Recruitment Network

How Fake Movie Casting Calls Became Part of Russia’s Foreign Recruitment Network
Russia-linked recruiters are using fake movie auditions targeting African men as part of a broader online operation to recruit foreigners for Russia’s war against Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to an investigation by Politico on September 22, citing research by Code for Africa, a nonprofit African network of digital democracy and data journalism labs, one advertisement presented itself as a “global casting” call seeking African male actors for a new film project.
Code for Africa traced the advertisement, which featured an AI-generated image of Black men dressed as soldiers, to a Facebook page based in Germany.
The supposed movie casting was one part of a much larger recruitment network targeting people across Africa and Asia, as well as Belarus. Researchers identified 89 websites, seven social media accounts, including on Facebook, and 39 accounts or channels on messaging platforms linked to the operation.
Another advertisement reviewed by Politico, attributed to a group called IRC Russian Bear, showed a soldier wearing Russian flag patches and offered recruits $15,000 after signing a contract, followed by a monthly salary of $3,000.
According to the investigation, the campaigns primarily target young men facing unemployment or unstable employment, offering salaries substantially higher than what many could earn in their home countries.
Politico reported that the recruitment network also relies on Western technology. Its main recruitment brand was hosted on a server in Amsterdam, while associated websites used AI tools developed by companies in the US and Sweden. Software from an Austrian company collected applicants’ personal data before it was transferred to Russia.
Code for Africa said Meta had already removed more than 300 advertising campaigns linked to the recruiters. Researchers also found that online searches for Russian military contracts for foreigners could direct users to recruitment websites.
Nationals of India, Sri Lanka, Cuba, Kenya, Nepal, Botswana, South Africa and other countries have previously been reported among foreigners recruited to serve with Russian forces in Ukraine.
Earlier, Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War reported that more than 28,000 foreign nationals had signed contracts with the Russian military, with at least 5,149 killed in combat. The recruits came from more than 48 countries, primarily across Asia, Africa, and Latin America.

U.S. to welcome up to 17,500 more White South Africans as refugees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Trump administration to welcome up to 17,500 more White South Africans as refugees
The Trump administration is planning to welcome up to 17,500 additional White Afrikaners from South Africa as refugees over the next 12 months, according to a notice sent to Congress on Tuesday and obtained by CBS News.
The State Department informed congressional officials that the Trump administration is planning to allocate 17,500 refugee spots for fiscal year 2027, and that they will "primarily" go to Afrikaners, who President Trump has claimed are being oppressed for being White. Fiscal year 2027 starts in October.
While the second Trump administration has effectively shut down the U.S. refugee resettlement program for most people fleeing persecution and violence around the world, it has made an exemption for Afrikaners, resettling thousands of them over the past year and a half.
Trump administration officials have portrayed Afrikaners as victims of racial oppression in post-apartheid South Africa. The South African government has consistently denied persecuting the ethnic minority, made up of descendants of European settlers, mostly from the Netherlands.
"Afrikaners face the seizure of agricultural property without compensation; government policies designed to dismantle equal opportunity in employment, education, and business; and hateful rhetoric fueling disproportionate violence against racially disfavored minorities," the State Department said in its notice to Congress.
Last week, the U.S. imposed new sanctions on South African officials who it said were responsible for discriminating against Afrikaners.
The Afrikaner resettlement effort is projected to cost the U.S. government $500 million, the notice to Congress said.
"The United States anticipates that Afrikaners from South Africa will fully assimilate into the United States in a manner that preserves taxpayer resources for U.S. citizens and does not anticipate other countries resettling Afrikaners," the notice read.
Mr. Trump has alleged that Afrikaners face a "genocide" in South Africa. In a tense Oval Office meeting last year, he confronted South African President Cyril Ramaphosa on the claims, showing him a video that spotlighted murders of farmers in the country.
Those claims have been strongly disputed. A "60 Minutes" report earlier this year featured Afrikaners who rejected the notion that White people are facing a "genocide" and said murders on farms were linked to a broader crime problem in South Africa that harms members of all races.

Hurricane &quot;Polo&quot; is intensifying near Mexico and threatens flooding

Hurricane "Polo" is intensifying near Mexico and threatens flooding
Kyiv • UNN
Hurricane "Polo," with winds of up to 270 km/h, is intensifying off the coast of Mexico. The storm threatens flooding and landslides in coastal states.
According to the U.S. National Hurricane Center (NHC), Hurricane "Polo," which reached Category 5 strength (the highest possible) earlier on Tuesday, continues to intensify off Mexico’s Pacific coast, posing a threat of life-threatening flooding, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
The NHC said that, despite its proximity to land and the expected heavy rainfall, "Polo" will likely move slowly along the coast over the next few days before changing course and moving away from shore.
"The storm is expected to turn northwest and west-northwest tonight and on Wednesday," the NHC warned. "According to the forecast, the center of ‘Polo’ will remain near the coast of southwestern Mexico over the next few days, although it is expected to remain over ocean waters."
With sustained winds reaching approximately 270 km/h, the storm is likely to strengthen further overnight into Wednesday. It was also reported that an aircraft operated by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)—the so-called "hurricane hunter"—is already heading to the disaster area to study "Polo."
"Polo," which the NHC classifies as "extremely dangerous," is currently located approximately 335 km south of the resort city of Zihuatanejo.
According to the NHC forecast, rainfall in the coastal states of Guerrero and Michoacán could cause life-threatening flooding and landslides; less intense rain is also expected in coastal areas of the states of Oaxaca, Colima, and Jalisco.
Mexican authorities warned of heavy rainfall in the western and southern regions of the country, which could cause rivers to overflow.
Private weather service AccuWeather said the storm’s impacts could extend to tourist destinations such as Acapulco and Puerto Vallarta, while the southern part of the state of Baja California Sur (including the Los Cabos area) could face storm surges and strong wind gusts by Sunday.
The storm could later move inland toward the United States, but its movement will be affected by interaction with Tropical Storm "Odalis"; this could keep the hurricane farther offshore and limit the intrusion of tropical moisture into the southwestern United States.
Strong winds and rain caused by "Polo" are also expected to reach the country’s main ports—Lázaro Cárdenas and Manzanillo. "The information currently available indicates that (Storm ‘Polo’) will not make a direct landfall; it will pass offshore (...) particularly past the states of Jalisco, Colima, and Michoacán. And I urge everyone on the Pacific coast to remain vigilant," President Claudia Sheinbaum said during her regular morning press conference.
In 2023, Acapulco was hit by a devastating natural disaster—Hurricane "Otis," considered the most powerful tropical cyclone ever to make landfall on Mexico’s Pacific coast. According to the Guerrero State Attorney General’s Office, the storm that struck the region in late October claimed the lives of at least 68 people, while the damage it caused was estimated by Mexican business associations at approximately $16 billion.

Trump also pointed to Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refining capacity, saying the strikes appeared to have seriously affected Russia’s refining operations and diesel prices.
“I think they (Putin and Zelenskyy) both want to see the war end,” Trump said. “To be honest with you, it’s time. A lot of people are being killed, and they don’t want that.”
On possible Patriot missile production in Ukraine, Trump said Washington and Kiev were discussing the issue, describing Ukraine as having “very capable production” and “very capable people”.
Zelenskyy said he hoped the war could end with Trump’s help, adding that an agreement was needed “as quick as possible before winter”.

Experts: Affordable Munitions Could Help USAF in Taiwan Conflict, but More Is Needed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
19:29:22 UTC
04:29:22 KST

A new think tank report calls for a buildup of U.S. drones and munitions needed for a potential fight against the Chinese military over Taiwan, thought other experts argue the report is missing some nuance in the munitions equation.
The Center for a New American Security’s report, “Drones, Missiles, and the U.S. Munitions Shortage: The Role of Affordable Mass in a Taiwan Conflict,” released Sept. 18, makes the case for increased long-range weapons to strike Chinese military targets to thwart a takeover of Taiwan.
The report, authored by Philip Sheers and Stacie Pettyjohn, notes a gap between the number of targets the U.S. would need to strike and its diminishing stockpiles, given the ongoing use of such weapons in the conflict with Iran.
“In a U.S.-China conflict over Taiwan that is likely to become protracted, the inventory depth and disruption that lower-cost systems can provide will be invaluable to reversing U.S. disadvantages and stopping China from achieving its operational objectives,” Sheers and Pettyjohn write.
To close the gap, the report recommends both stockpiling high-end missiles and massing cheap drones and munitions to overwhelm a Chinese attack. Other recommendations include:
- Multiyear funding and contracts so manufacturers can expand weapons production capacity and the Pentagon can rebuild long-range missile stores
- Funding for cheap, long-range anti-ship and land-attack weapons to quickly fill inventory gaps.
- Standardized shared components across airframes to lower costs and scale production.
- Pairing inexpensive drones with advanced missiles to drain enemy air defenses.
- Prioritizing easily built designs rather than over-engineering
- Routing updates and briefings to Congress on these issues
The White House and Pentagon have taken steps to boost munitions production this year, especially low-cost weapons.
In July, the Pentagon announced multiyear framework agreements with Anduril, CoAspire, and Zone 5 Technologies to mass-produce missiles for the Air Force, followed by a Sept. 17 announcement that Lockheed Martin would expand production of the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile.
The former announcement is part of USAF’s Family of Affordable Mass Missiles program, unveiled in the fiscal 2026 budget with plans to ramp up such production to hit 5,300 missiles a year by 2028 and reach nearly 8,000 missiles a year by 2031.
The current projected five-year budget for FAMM is more than $12 billion for nearly 27,000 missiles.
Retired Air Force Col. Mark Gunzinger, now with AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the CNAS report’s call for more munitions is necessary. But he cautioned that the report’s focus on making weapons affordable needs to be tweaked.
“It should not be about buying cheaper weapons; it should be about how to optimize cost per effect in the battlespace,” Gunzinger said.
The Air Force must fight asymmetrically and maximize the effect of each strike, regardless of munition or platform, and there’s a middle ground for weapons and platform development and procurement, Gunzinger argued.
Precision-guided, specialized weapons such as the Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile and the platforms that deliver them are pricey, and lower-end, short-range munitions for stationary targets have their place, but Gunzinger said defense planners can often make too much of a tradeoff if they focus too much on price to the detriment of capability.
“Now you’ve got something that, ‘OK, you hit a price point, but is it going to survive long enough to do its mission?’” Gunzinger said. “Is it going to be able to shoot its weapon before it dies?”
A Numbers Game
The CNAS report’s operational and tactical focus is countering a People’s Liberation Army attack on Taiwan with strikes against PLA ships—destroyers and amphibious assault ships—and hitting airfields on the periphery of the country, close to the Taiwan Strait.
But it does not include a plan to hit the Chinese mainland interior.
“The paper focuses on denying a PLA joint island landing campaign without considering strategic attacks to deny sanctuaries to the PLA and collapse China’s ability to maintain the offensive,” Gunzinger said. “This risks reducing a conflict with the PLA over Taiwan to a force-on-force math problem, like how many weapons and aircraft are needed to attack PLA forces located in the Taiwan Strait and coastal China. It risks becoming a numbers game.”
Because striking mainland China in a Taiwan invasion scenario might be required, Gunzinger said the current 500-nautical-mile limit of most affordable strike options undermines the CNAS report’s conclusion that more mass will equate to victory.
“China has the capability to project outer and inner rings of airborne and sea-based air defense sensors and shooters to defend its cross-Strait forces and operations,” Gunzinger said.
And using nonstealthy drones to approach the Chinese coastline to then launch affordable missiles doesn’t work either, he said. “This would likely result in losses of the aircraft and their weapons.”
“We win part of the battle,” Gunzinger said. “They win the war.”
Breaking a Stalemate
The numbers-on-numbers approach is what has led to a stalemate in the Russia-Ukraine War, said retired Navy Cmdr. J. Michael Dahm, now a senior fellow for aerospace and China studies at Mitchell.
“Just because you can generate mass doesn’t mean that you’re going to achieve your effects,” Dahm told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “You may be able to keep your adversary off balance, but if you’re not going to then judo throw him into what you want him to do, you’re just engaging in this kind of protracted, endless warfare.”
Throughout the history of the modern Chinese military, it has mostly been defense-oriented, Dahm said. The PLA has airfields dotting its landscape and hardened sites to pull and rotate forces from, as well as a layered air defense network.
What could overwhelm the Chinese defenses, however, is what the U.S. has seen poke through its defenses recently in the Middle East, Dahm said. Iranian air attacks have used a combination of low-end munitions and cheap drones with more expensive and capable missiles fired from various angles, locations, and at varying rates of speed to confuse and defeat air defenses.
This aligns with one of the report’s recommendations—for the Pentagon to develop new operational concepts that pair cheap and high-end weapons for mixed attacks.
“Using low-cost drones in the opening wave to identify air defenses, consume interceptors, and relay targeting data to follow-on missiles offers a promising and sustainable way to create repeated air base disruption,” according to the report. “High-end weapons should be preserved for more challenging targets, while affordable mass should be integrated into strike plans to service soft targets and to saturate air defenses.”
“The Iranians have figured out how to be effective: … send a whole bunch of slow-moving drones with a couple of cruise missiles and a couple of ballistic missiles,” Dahm said.
That’s because modern air defenders must set their systems to track certain ranges, altitudes, and speeds of whatever is in the airspace. And they can’t track everything effectively all at once.
“I don’t want a flock of birds showing up on my radar, so I set the speed gate for higher speed, but how high do I set it for? 100 knots or do I set it for Mach 3? What am I looking for? Range. How far am I looking? Altitude. Am I looking high? Am I looking low?” Dahm said.
Those factors mean an air defense system can’t stop everything.
“The way you overwhelm even the most sophisticated air defense system is you send some slow stuff, you send some medium stuff, and then you send these ballistic missiles that are screaming in from the upper atmosphere at Mach 3-4-5,” Dahm said. “It is hard for any modern air defense system to deal with all those inputs.”
While Iran is using that method against the U.S., Dahm advocates the U.S. use the same strategy in a Taiwan scenario against the PLA.
“That is absolutely what we should be doing,” Dahm said.
For example, to strike a Chinese military ship, such as a cruiser, Dahm said U.S. or coalition countries wouldn’t only send the same type of missile from one direction. They would simultaneously target the ship from air, land, sea, and subsurface platforms with a variety of projectiles at varying speeds and ranges, though the centerpiece of the assault might be an LRASM.
“You might send two LRASMs, but you need to accompany that with some of these more cost-effective missiles,” he said. “It is the reason we need the cost-effectiveness and the affordability, because we shouldn’t have an expectation that all of those weapons are going to work.”

Russian FSB to feature in new TV show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
19:19:52 UTC
04:19:52 KST

Some of Russia’s highest-profile counterterrorism operations have been dramatized in a new television show produced with input from FSB officers, who advised its creators on real cases and operational details.
The 16-part series ‘Pros’ was previewed behind closed doors at an FSB cultural center in Moscow on Tuesday by veterans and serving officers, some of whose identities remain classified.
REN TV chief and general producer Vladimir Tyulin explained what motivated the project.
”The country needs heroes, children need heroes they could look up to,” he said.
The series follows a fictional team of seven FSB special forces officers through cases based on real events, including the 2009 bombing of the Moscow-St. Petersburg Nevsky Express train, the 2011 attack at Moscow’s Domodedovo Airport and counterterrorism operations in the North Caucasus, Izvestia reported on Tuesday.
Security personnel served as consultants during production, helping the writers incorporate operational details previously known only to those directly involved.
One episode focuses on the operation against Doku Umarov, the Islamist militant leader who claimed responsibility for several deadly terrorist attacks. These included the Domodedovo bombing, which killed 37 people, and the 2010 Moscow Metro bombings, which left 40 dead.
Tyulin said the actors underwent special training before filming, learning to use tactical gear and move as a unit.
Sergey Shavrin, a decorated Hero of Russia and veteran of the FSB’s Vympel special unit, praised the series’ authenticity, including its portrayal of officers keeping the realities of their work from their families.
Terrorism researcher and Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO) lecturer Alexander Smirnov also weighed in on the series.
”The film is simply magnificent, it keeps you in suspense,” he said. “And most importantly, the real work is shown very authentically.”
’Pros’ is due to premiere on REN TV on October 18.

Call it a win: boredom but no temper tantrums in Burnham’s first face-to-face with America’s King Baby
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
19:18:40 UTC
04:18:40 KST

How do you deal with a problem like The Donald? The simple answer is that you don’t. You can’t. The normal rules of political engagement don’t apply. The US president is like a five-year-old child with the world as his set of toys: a King Baby.
Nothing is ever constant or predictable. What’s agreed one day can be forgotten the next. Any deal can be interrupted with a temper tantrum at any time. Trying to second-guess Donald Trump is a fool’s errand.
So the primary aim of Andy Burnham’s first face-to-face meeting with Trump was to get out alive with his – and the UK’s – self-respect intact. To take no incoming damage. And whatever he did, not to offer the president a third state visit. Keir Starmer never really lived that one down. Putting out on the first date only encourages the other person to think you’re a pushover.
The hoped-for result was a pleasant and almost forgettable bilateral meeting at the United Nations general assembly in New York. It was only scheduled to last 30 minutes, so more like speed dating – one step up from two world leaders shooting the breeze while getting to know each other. Where differences could be acknowledged without causing a major diplomatic incident.
All of which falls pretty comfortably within Burnham’s skill set. Andy’s stock in trade is an easy-going self-confidence. He’s comfortable in his skin in a way that Keir never was. Or maybe the artifice is just better concealed. He understands that trash-talking is all in a day’s work for most politicians. In the past, he may have called Trump all sorts of things. Poisoned politics. Someone who would be unwelcome in Manchester. Well, that was then, this is now. Things change. Just like Trump. Now he would be welcoming the US president to the G20 in Manchester next year. Who would have guessed?
And it all looked to have gone pretty much to plan. Maybe Trump also wanted this meeting to go well. His poll ratings in the US are dire, the midterm elections look like trouble and The Donald needs all the friends he can get – even if he had just tried to lose a few more of them in his speech to the UN earlier. A speech that had been even wilder and madder than many of his previous ones. Still, at least he hadn’t threatened to invade a Nato country this time. And it’s always good to learn of countries you never knew existed. Anyone for “Kazakhistan”?
Taking questions with Trump afterwards, Andy didn’t look quite as self-assured as usual – he seemed very much on edge – but who could blame him for that? This was his first time as prime minister at the UN and The Donald always has it in him to blow any meeting out of the water.
It was Andy who went first, trying to remember what they had just talked about. It had all been a bit of a blur. That was it – they had talked about Iran. In his earlier speech, The Donald had suggested it was a toss-up whether he came to a deal with Iran or whether he annihilated it. On the whole, Andy was in favour of a deal. Quickly if possible. The war was causing a massive hit to the cost of living. He chose not to highlight the irony of Trump calling on Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop bombing Russian refineries as it was playing havoc with the cost of oil. Pots and kettles and all that.
Burnham then bigged up the deal with Saudi Arabia. The one where we send one plane to refuel Saudi fighters that don’t need refuelling because their targets are only a few hundred miles away. Finally, he mentioned the Falklands. By now The Donald was looking a wee bit bored. Unsure where the Falklands are or why they had been talking about them. Perhaps he was wondering why he was looking even more orange than usual.
Then came the actual questions. Was Andy a man with whom Trump could do business? Sure he was, said The Donald. Andy was a “great businessperson”. Really? And by the way he was a lot nicer and a lot more talented than his predecessor. Poor Keir. Not only is he no longer prime minister, but he’s still getting rubbished at meetings he would have been attending. He really can’t buy a break. But that’s Trump for you. Andy shouldn’t relax too much. That will be him getting trashed one day.
On we went. Immigration. Burnham deftly trying to give credit to the immigrants working in the NHS while going on to condemn illegal immigration. Trump was just dreaming of walls and border guards. What about patriotism? Which did the prime minister prefer: Manchester or Manhattan? By now Andy was feeling a bit more self-assured that the whole thing wasn’t about to go tits up, so he joked about the president calling Manchester “some town”. Trump just shrugged. It still is just some town to him, but he wasn’t going to labour the point. He was trying to be on his best behaviour. For a five-year-old.
Then a question on the sanctions imposed on illegal settlements in the West Bank. Trump looked bewildered. Had never heard of them. Andy insisted he had personally called the White House to inform the president of the UK’s intentions. It had been done to maintain the possibility of a two-state solution and to restore trust in politics. This was more like the authentic Burnham. Standing up for what he believed. Trump said nothing. Maybe he actually did recognise the prime minister as an equal.
There was just time for a mention of the proposed handover of the Chagos Islands – It’s a terrible idea,” said Trump unhelpfully, to which Andy gulped “We’re looking at it” – before we closed with Trump insisting relations with the UK had never been better and that Britain was a country on the up. Some of us could distinctly remember The Donald saying the UK was on the slide only last week. But who’s counting?
Then a minder called the impromptu presser to a close and kicked everyone out of the room. Trump looked blank. He often does. Burnham looked relieved. He had got out of his first encounter with the president alive. Both he and the UK were still intact. Chalk this one up as a win.

Macron says 'credibility' at stake on 'shameful' situation in Gaza
Unknown

Melike Pala, Seyma Erkul Dayanc and Necva Tastan Sevinc
22 September 2026•Update: 22 September 2026
French President Emmanuel Macron said Tuesday that the international community's "credibility" is at stake if it remains inactive on the situation in the Gaza Strip, describing the continued restrictions on humanitarian aid as “shameful.”
Macron told the UN General Assembly that claims that peace has been achieved in Gaza had not been matched by an increase in humanitarian deliveries.
"Some claim that peace has been achieved, but this has not opened up humanitarian deliveries. The spectacle, it is shameful. Shame on all of us," he said.
He questioned the credibility of states that recognized Palestine but fail to take action on the humanitarian situation in Gaza.
"But what is our credibility worth if we remain inactive on Gaza?" he asked.
Macron also condemned what he described as continuing violations in the occupied West Bank.
"Look at what's happening in the West Bank, where day in, day out we are seeing violations, and in the name of what? Hamas was never very active in the West Bank," he said.
He said the international community must uphold the "legitimate rights of the Palestinian people," including their right to exist, while stressing France's commitment to Israel's security.
Macron warned, however, against arguments that Israel's security requires violations of the sovereignty of neighboring states.
He also urged respect for Lebanon's sovereignty, saying a fully sovereign Lebanon would be necessary to address the presence of Hezbollah and restore security.
"Sovereignty for Lebanon and its people. Sovereignty for Palestinians. Their very basic and most basic rights are once again being violated," he said.
Turning to Syria, Macron said France would continue supporting the country's sovereignty and unity.
"The revolution should not turn into a disappointment," he said.
International law, UN reform, AI
Macron also warned that international humanitarian law and the Geneva Conventions were facing a serious challenge amid conflicts around the world.
"War crimes have been industrialized. We've seen the destruction of civilian infrastructure and human rights violations. It's a new era of barbaric acts," he said. "The Geneva Conventions offered a protective framework, but it is being dismantled.”
He also reaffirmed France's support for the International Court of Justice, saying Paris would continue to back its “central role.”
"We cannot simply accept this new order of impunity, which some are trying to erect," he said.
The French leader also urged reform of the UN Security Council, saying France supports measures aimed at making the body more effective. “We must open up to new members, new regions.”
He also urged greater international engagement on artificial intelligence (AI), warning against allowing the technology's future to be determined by only two major powers or a handful of economic actors.
"We must hold fast and not yield on artificial intelligence," he said.
"There are some who wish to make us believe that only two powers, the US and China, will be making the decisions. They want us to believe that just a few economic actors will make all the decisions," Macron added.
He said countries should not accept a situation in which a small number of powers or companies determine the direction of technological innovation and its consequences.

Always the Victim, Never the Bigot: the Zionist campaign against Abdul El-Sayed doubles down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
19:07:03 UTC
04:07:03 KST

The U.S. has spent the last few years supporting one of the worst atrocities on the planet, largely because we are told that Israel shares our alleged wonderful values. Israel’s most passionate supporters say it hasn’t done anything wrong in Gaza, deny the testimony of Palestinians and the analysis of experts, and accuse Israel’s critics of dishonesty, hatred, and bigotry. And most critically, if you criticize them for this, they claim victimhood.
Support for Israel and Zionism, we are told, is a central part of the Jewish religion and Jewish identity, and if we criticize that, we are bigots.
No one should be impressed by that argument. The world is full of people who make a collection of religious or ideological beliefs part of their identity, and if some of those beliefs are factually wrong or even immoral, they can cause problems. The list of examples here is endless and includes cases that are very different from support for Israel, but the underlying principle is the same. There are people who believe their clergy couldn’t be pedophiles. There are people who believe the Bible is a science textbook or that people who oppose their beliefs are heretics whose rights should be suppressed. There are people who still think the Confederacy was fighting for noble principles and people who thought the Soviet Union was a workers’ state.
People have the right to their beliefs, but they don’t have the right to suppress criticism, and if they claim to be victims if their beliefs are criticized, they are simply wrong. Furthermore, if they deny atrocities or downplay them or dismiss testimony by the victims of their favored state, they are morally wrong and quite often guilty of bigotry themselves.
We see this controversy playing out in Abdul El- Sayed’s senate campaign in Michigan, in which he has been attacked in bad faith from all different angles largely over his criticism of Israel, with Zionists demanding apology after apology.
An aside: To be fair, in my opinion, there was one important point where his critics were correct and El- Sayed apologized. In response to the March attack on a synagogue in Michigan, in which the alleged attacker, a Lebanese man, had recently lost family to Israeli bombs, El-Sayed had said: “ hurt people hurt people.” While often true, I believe this was not the appropriate thing to say when, in this case, the Jewish community was justifiably horrified by what had happened and fearful of further attacks. But that is only a part of the criticisms aimed at El- Sayed. The majority of the attacks are unfounded and bigoted.
Cue the latest controversy surrounding El-Sayed, Israel critics, and Israel defenders.
The mainstream media has, in recent weeks, become obsessed with the story of leftist social media commentator Hasan Piker and his support for El-Sayed. Since El-Sayed’s defeat of Hailey Stevens and the more than $30 million of Israel lobby spending that came with her, the establishment (both Democratic and Republican politicians, as well as the media) has zeroed in on Piker’s & El-Sayed’s relationship as evidence of El-Sayed’s so-called antisemitic beliefs (i.e., his criticism of Israel).
Commenting on El-Sayed’s relationship with Piker, New York Times columnist Michelle Goldberg, suffering from a serious attack of pundit brain, said that El-Sayed should do what then-Senator Obama did in 2008 with his pastor, the Reverend Jeremiah Wright (also a vocal critic of Israel), and throw Piker under the bus. Goldberg’s entire argument falls into the trap of making El-Sayed responsible for everything Piker has said or supposedly said. Would that win over his critics? No, as we will soon see.
For context, when Obama’s associations with Wright and his sermons (which included criticism of U.S. foreign policy against Palestinians, and domestic policies against African Americans, among others), Obama called Wright’s comments “divisive,” “racially charged” and “views that denigrate both the greatness and the goodness of our nation.”
In Goldberg’s memory, Obama’s speech was a fair and wonderfully balanced response to the pressure he faced to distance himself from Wright. In reality, Obama was pandering to Israel supporters in a period where the majority of Americans were paying little or no attention to Israeli apartheid.
And Obama’s speech was not simply the wonderfully fair and balanced production that Goldberg remembers. Here is what Obama said in that speech about Wright’s comments on Israel and Palestine:
“But the remarks that have caused this recent firestorm weren’t simply controversial. They weren’t simply a religious leader’s efforts to speak out against perceived injustice. Instead, they expressed a profoundly distorted view of this country — a view that sees white racism as endemic, and that elevates what is wrong with America above all that we know is right with America; a view that sees the conflicts in the Middle East as rooted primarily in the actions of stalwart allies like Israel, instead of emanating from the perverse and hateful ideologies of radical Islam.
As such, Reverend Wright’s comments were not only wrong but divisive, divisive at a time when we need unity; racially charged at a time when we need to come together to solve a set of monumental problems — two wars, a terrorist threat, a falling economy, a chronic health care crisis and potentially devastating climate change — problems that are neither black or white or Latino or Asian, but rather problems that confront us all.”
There is a lesson to learn here, not about a great speech pulling us together, but about who gets thrown under the bus, and it’s not just Wright or Piker. It’s the entire base that voted for El-Sayed, in part due to the shared belief that, yes, Israel is committing a genocide, and America should not be funding it.
Further proof that the solution Goldberg offered would not actually satisfy El-Sayed’s critics, is the “nonnegotiable” petition that has since been launched by a coalition of Michigan rabbis and Jewish leaders, which makes it quite clear that the issue isn’t some Twitch streamer— it’s anti-Zionism. And contrary to what Goldberg wrote in her piece, it isn’t just about Zionists not feeling welcome— it is about what Zionists in the Democratic Party have always wanted, which is to make anti-Zionists unwelcome.
Michelle Goldberg was worried that Zionists wouldn’t be allowed in the Democratic Party. The petition is not asking for a big tent with Zionists and anti-Zionists uneasily allied to defeat the Republicans. They want anti-Zionism expelled and treated as antisemitic.
The petition demands that everyone accept and embrace a political ideology (Zionism) because some people have made it a central part of their identity and religion. As an argument, it has no force. As a political threat, it might have some.
El-Sayed is in a difficult position because at least some Zionist democrats are willing to support his republican opponent, Mike Rogers, and therefore Trump, if El-Sayed does not capitulate. But if he does what they want, he shows he is just another cynical politician with no integrity.

It remains unclear whether Eisenkot will scale back his own campaign to make Yashar! the largest party, but he agreed during the meeting that strengthening the broader bloc should come first.

Ukraine anger as EU removes Russian oligarchs from sanctions list
- Published
The European Union is to remove sanctions on two oligarchs imposed after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, according to reports, prompting anger in Ukraine.
France had campaigned for Russian-Uzbek billionaire Alisher Usmanov to be taken off the list, citing "national security concerns". Luxembourg called for the removal of Russian-Israeli businessman Mikhail Fridman, who is suing the country for the release of frozen assets.
Latvia initially opposed the deal but agreed to a compromise, part of which involved extending sanctions on nearly 3,000 other individuals and entities for three years.
Ukrainian officials said the move was "unacceptable" and sent the wrong signal to Moscow.
"Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans," Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said on X.
He urged all EU member states to instead announce national sanctions on the two individuals. Latvia has already said it would do so.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov earlier welcomed the prospect of the two oligarchs being taken off the list, claiming the EU's sanctions were illegal and all Russians should be removed.
Usmanov founded USM Holding company, an investment group that owns iron, steel and copper suppliers, and the Megafon telecommunications company. He has in the past had ties with the English Premier League clubs Arsenal and Everton.
The EU froze his assets in 2022, describing him as "a pro-Kremlin oligarch with particularly close ties to Russian president Vladimir Putin". Usmanov said the decision was "unfair".
It has been reported that France's initiative was linked to a prospective prisoner release deal with Azerbaijan.
Fridman, a Russian-Israeli citizen born in Ukraine, is the founder of the Alfa Group investment conglomerate, with key interests in energy and banking. The EU has described him as a top Russian financier and enabler of Putin's inner circle.
Fridman himself said at the time of Russia's full-scale invasion that the conflict should end as soon as possible, but avoided outright condemnation of President Putin.
His Russian-Latvian business partner Pyotr Aven was stripped of Latvia's highest civilian honour in 2022 for failing to condemn the invasion of Ukraine.
This may have influenced Latvia's opposition to the move, vetoing it in a vote by EU ambassadors on Monday.
However, on Tuesday it changed its vote to an abstention as a compromise was reached. The new deal involved extending sanctions on some remaining 2,600 individuals and entities to three years. Until now, sanctions had to be renewed every six months.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs also announced that France had agreed to start talks with Latvia about joining a French nuclear deterrence initiative and strengthen its military presence in Latvia.

Jorge Palma (1950-2026): the songs that will never die
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
19:05:26 UTC
04:05:26 KST

On Tuesday, Portugal woke up in mourning: Jorge Palma died at 76 following a cardiorespiratory arrest. His songs remain. Euronews asked artists from Herman José to António Zambujo for their favourite song.
Jorge Palma, one of the most influential singers, songwriters and composers in contemporary Portuguese music, died on Monday at the age of 76 in physical years, even if metaphorically he had lived more than a hundred thousand, as he sang on Encosta-te a mim, a track from the 2007 album Voo Nocturno. The music video, in which Palma appears surrounded by lifelong friends and recent companions, will live on. Palma may have left us, but his songs will forever be part of Portuguese culture and soul.
On Estróina, a track on his most recent album, Vida (2023), he sings: "Whoever my undertaker may be, make sure I am properly dressed." There could be no finer attire than the many farewell words already dedicated to him, alongside the many he himself wrote.
And, as he went on singing, "and since life is meant to be lived live and in full colour, let us raise a glass to pleasure, with no false modesty." That is exactly what we will do. Euronews spoke to several people close to the singer, to Portuguese culture and to his work, all unconditional admirers of his legacy, to understand what remains after his passing and which songs they will never forget.
Herman José - Actor and comedian
For Herman José, who crossed paths with Jorge Palma many times and in many different settings, his death "leaves a silence that will be hard to fill".
One of his most cherished memories with the singer goes back to 1974. "I was one of his musicians, alongside the great Pedro Osório. It is one of those memories that time does not erase and that today returns with particular strength. We were all much younger, in a Portugal that itself was embarking on a new life, and even then Jorge's extraordinary musical personality was already there – restless, free, unpredictable, fascinating," he recalls.
The comedian says Jorge Palma was an "utterly unique musician", one of those who "never needed to resemble anyone else to be recognised from the very first chord, the first word, the first inflection of that voice".
From all the work Jorge Palma leaves behind, Herman José chooses Deixa-me Rir (from O Lado Errado da Noite, 1985), "perhaps because in it I find so much of Jorge: the intelligence, the irony, the mistrust of certainties, a certain melancholy hidden behind the smile. And that rare ability to say serious things without ever losing his irreverence," he concludes.
António Zambujo - Singer and songwriter
For the singer from Beja, choosing just one Jorge Palma song is "unfair" because "his body of work is immensely rich". Even so, he accepted Euronews' challenge and picked the song O Meu amor Existe, from the voice-and-piano album Só, released in 1991.
"I consider this record the best in the history of Portuguese music, and whatever I might say about Jorge Palma would never be enough, given the dimension I believe he has," he said.
Gabriel Gomes - Musician and composer
"I have lost a friend, a hero," Gabriel Gomes, accordionist and former member of Madredeus and Sétima Legião, tells us to begin with. He quickly adds: "But I gained so much from his presence in my life."
Earlier this year he shared the stage with Jorge Palma and, at the Artes à Vila festival in the Batalha Monastery, presented his first solo project.
"The emptiness hurts, but his memory and his work will eventually fill it. It was quick, as he deserved," he sums up.
Gabriel Gomes chose the song Passos em Volta, from the album Bairro do Amor, which they played together on stage so many times and in which, just as in the lyrics, Jorge Palma "opened the window and flew away".
Tiago Cação - artistic agent
With a long career in the music, live entertainment and artist management industries, he confided that he had never wanted to meet Jorge Palma.
"I never wanted to meet Jorge. I never wanted to get close to him. I always wanted to keep Jorge in an intangible place, alongside the great poets and great musicians I have always admired. On Friday, my father (much younger than Jorge), whom I thought knew nothing about music, said: 'I would not like to die without seeing a Jorge Palma concert. Because with artists like Jorge, we always think they do not die. And they do not'," he shared.
For Tiago, the song he will never forget is Sonhadores inatos. "I identify with the simple idea of never stopping dreaming, despite the inevitabilities that come with being alive."
Fernando Vendrell - Film director
The filmmaker admits that today he can only think of Frágil (Bairro do Amor, 1989). "Tonight I feel so fragile," he paraphrases.
Director of films such as "Aparição" and "Sombras Brancas", Fernando Vendrell remembers Jorge Palma as "an extraordinary writer of songs".
"In my view, they are among the most perfect songs ever written in Portugal. His gaze and his writing were agile, his melodies graceful and unique. They brought with them a world we belonged to or wanted to be part of," he says.
Ana Margarida de Carvalho - Journalist and writer
When she heard the news of the singer's death, the song that came to her mind was Na Terra dos Sonhos, for its melody and because it was written by a "sceptical optimist".
Ana Margarida de Carvalho says she knows all the albums, songs, acoustic versions and live recordings, where his "virtuosity on piano, acoustic guitar or electric guitar" always stood out: "He had enormous versatility, a powerful voice that stood the test of time," she recalls, referring to the many concerts she attended. Jorge Palma's voice also became part of her everyday life. "He is always on my car playlist..." she says.
Among the many songs by Jorge Palma, the journalist also highlights Portugal, Portugal, which she considers "an anthem", and Estrela do Mar, whose chords "sound like waves, or the string quartet, in which he pays tribute to Durrell's Alexandria Quartet".
However, she told Euronews she was choosing Eu Fui um Lobo Malvado (Acto Contínuo, 1982). "With lyrics that are naïve, perhaps, but which in my view make it a song that turns back on itself and becomes the most beautiful declaration of welcome, a song about friendship and reconciliation, ultimately – and I know it by heart, and so do my children."
"I have not yet wielded a weapon that did not ricochet / and the scar always outlives even the neatest bandage / but whenever you want you are welcome in my castle / which perhaps because it is old and wrinkled / does not need painting," she quotes.
Luiz Carvalho - Photographer
The author of the cover photo for this article (kindly made available for publication) recalls his first encounter with the singer: "I have known you since that afternoon in 1980 in Paris when I photographed you singing in the Saint-Michel metro station. Afterwards we went for a drink, I think Graça Lamy was there too. The damned negative exists but I just cannot find it. I love your work and, above all, your attitude to life: free, non-conformist, polite, a musician with classical roots, at times too wild for the body to be able to keep up. I would have loved to make a documentary about you, something alive, handheld camera, direct sound... You will always be in my heart and in my ears, for as long as I still have road ahead of me."
The song he has chosen is O Lado Errado da Noite, "a striking melody, very much in tune with part of his own journey".
Finally... the choices of the authors of this piece
Ana Filipa Palma: A Gente Vai Continuar is not only one of his greatest songs, it is also one of the most listened to today and, above all, a promise that his voice will remain "for as long as there are winds and sea".
The tribute to Palma at the latest edition of the Play awards ended with the whole audience singing A Gente Vai Continuar.
Ricardo Figueira: I choose Bairro do Amor because it is comforting to believe there is a place drawn in coloured pencil by people who have suffered for not having anyone, a country with no prisons and no hospitals, where the sun seems bigger and there are waves of tenderness in every look. Even if that place exists only in songs.

How is the US trying to ground Iranian airlines worldwide?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
19:04:59 UTC
04:04:59 KST

Breadcrumb
How is the US trying to shut Iranian airlines out of global aviation?
The US has issued an ultimatum to countries and companies continuing to provide services to Iranian airlines.
In the latest salvo under the Trump administration's "Operation Economic Outcast", Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has announced that organisations that continue to have ties to the country's airlines after Wednesday risk being frozen out of the global financial system.
Here's what we know about Washington's bid to shut Iranian airlines out of international aviation.
What has the US done?
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said this week that, from 23 September, the US will impose secondary sanctions on airports and aviation service companies that continue to work with Iranian airlines.
Companies that continue to deal with Iranian carriers after this date risk being locked out of the dollar-based financial system.
That includes airport operators, cargo service providers, ground handlers and fuel suppliers.
"On 23 September all Iranian airlines will be shut down around the world," Bessent told CNBC.
"How do we do that? That if they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets, or you will be knocked out of the dollar system," he said.
This follows a decision by the Treasury on 8 September to slap sanctions on 27 Iranian airlines and another nine aviation service companies.
"Let this be a warning to anyone doing business with Iran's remaining airlines: You are at risk of being cut off from the global financial system," Bessent said at the time.
How have countries responded?
Several countries have announced restrictions in the days since the sanctions were announced.
Mahan Air announced it had suspended flights to Istanbul and Ankara at the request of Turkish authorities on 21 September. A few days earlier, the carrier halted its Tehran-Muscat route.
Georgia has also introduced a blanket ban on Iranian carriers using the country's aviation sector.
Meanwhile, AFP reported that Iraq is expected to comply with the US measures, citing several sources, including a senior Iraqi government official.
However, Baghdad had not formally announced the restrictions as of Tuesday, while online flight data seen by The New Arab continued to show Iranian-operated flights available to Baghdad and Najaf.
The uncertainty has already caused disruption for Iraqi travel agencies, particularly in Najaf, where many businesses depend heavily on flights carrying pilgrims between Iraq and Iran.
Some agencies have stopped taking flight bookings or begun switching customers to land routes, while others have warned that the restrictions could cause major losses. Travelling overland can also significantly increase journey times, particularly for elderly passengers and Iraqis travelling to Iran for medical treatment. A journey to the holy city of Qom, for example, can take more than 12 hours from the border.
Mahan Air routes to key countries, including the United Arab Emirates, China, Russia, India, Pakistan and Thailand, also do not appear to have been affected so far.
Beijing sharply criticised the measures as "illegal".
"China consistently opposes illegal unilateral sanctions that lack a basis in international law or authorisation from the UN Security Council," foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters.
How will this impact Iran's aviation industry?
Iran's aviation industry has already been severely degraded after years of US sanctions that have made it extremely difficult to modernise and maintain its ageing civilian aircraft fleet.
Airlines have struggled to obtain crucial spare parts and components needed for repairs and maintenance, raising longstanding concerns about the safety and reliability of the country's ageing aircraft.
The impact of the latest measures will depend largely on how many countries and aviation companies comply with Washington's threat of secondary sanctions.
The most immediate effects will be felt by carriers operating international routes. The bulk of Iran's overseas routes are handled by three airlines - state-owned flag carrier Iran Air, Mahan Air and Qeshm Air - while smaller carriers operate short-haul routes to Iraq and Gulf countries.
If airports, fuel suppliers, ground handlers and ticketing companies comply with the US measures, Iranian carriers could find it increasingly difficult to operate abroad even in countries that have not formally banned them.
Why is the US doing this?
The sanctions are part of the Trump administration's so-called "economic D-Day", which aims to further isolate Iran from the global economy.
Aviation was among five sectors the administration said Tehran was using to circumvent existing US sanctions, move money and provide military support to its allies in the region.
"Iran continues to use its supposed 'commercial' airlines, many of which are controlled by the regime and the IRGC, to ferry fighters, ship weapons and sensitive technologies, and move gold and hard cash to its proxies," the Treasury wrote.
The return to economic pressure comes amid continued deadlock after almost seven months of war.
Concerns about munitions stockpiles, souring public opinion and limited military options have left the White House hesitant to return to open conflict but unwilling to negotiate a peace deal.
The deadlock comes at a particularly sensitive time for Trump, less than two months before the crucial US midterm elections, with polls showing declining public support for both the war and his presidency.

US military power a ‘Wizard of Oz’ illusion – ex-CIA analyst (VIDEO)

US military power a ‘Wizard of Oz’ illusion – ex-CIA analyst (VIDEO)
US military might has turned out to be an illusion in the style of ‘The Wizard of Oz’, former CIA analyst Larry Johnson has said.
The myth of American dominance in the defense sector was shattered by the Ukraine and Iran conflicts, Johnson said in an interview with RT’s Sanchez Effect on Monday.
Before the escalation between Moscow and Kiev in February 2022, “Russia had the perception that the US was very powerful militarily, that it had strategic depth, that its industrial base was such that it could support and sustain a modern war,” he said.
However, the opinion in Moscow has changed since then as Russian forces were able to “solve and defeat” all of the systems supplied by Washington to Kiev’s military, the former CIA analyst told host Rick Sanchez.
“I’m calling this ‘The Wizard of Oz effect’... just like in ‘The Wizard of Oz’ at the end when the curtain gets pulled back and the great and powerful Oz turns out to be this little old guy with a drinking problem behind the curtain. That’s the US,” he said.
Johnson mentioned a recent report by the Pentagon’s inspector general, which sounded the alarm over “shortfalls” in munitions and a bottleneck in resupply of key weapons.
It was also “an embarrassment” when in August General Dynamics lost a $530 million contract with the Department of War to manufacture shells, the former CIA analyst said.
“They produced exactly zero. Meanwhile, Russia is producing as many artillery shells in one month as all of NATO does in a year,” he stressed.
According to Johnson, Iran has also delivered “enormous damage” to US capabilities in the Middle East since the American-Israeli attack on the country in early February.
Rebuilding the US Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain, which was crippled by Iranian strikes, “doesn’t make economic sense” as Tehran has shown that it’s capable of hitting it again at any moment, he said.
”The US has been effectively expelled from the Persian Gulf,” the former CIA analyst noted.

Should alcohol have more explicit health warnings? These experts think so
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

Push for more detailed alcohol labelling, after low uptake of voluntary system
In short:
An analysis of labels from 6,037 different alcoholic drinks sold in Australia has found just one in four included a voluntary warning label.
The study's lead author says this indicates harms are not being communicated clearly and wants labels to be more specific, warning consumers about the risk of cancer and liver disease.
What's next?
The UK and Ireland have committed to introducing mandatory health warning messages on alcohol labels to include conditions such as cancer, but there are no plans to upgrade current mandatory labelling requirements in Australia beyond pregnancy warnings.
Alcohol use is widespread in Australia, with about three in four people aged 14 and older consuming it over the course of a year.
But public health experts say harms associated with drinking, even at low levels, are not being communicated clearly enough to consumers.
Drinking alcohol is one of the leading risk factors for the burden of disease in Australia, and is linked to several types of cancer as well as liver disease, heart disease and stroke.
While it's mandatory in Australia to include a pregnancy warning on drinks containing 1.15 per cent alcohol by volume, additional warnings about alcohol-related harm are voluntary.
Australian research published today in the Australian and New Zealand Journal of Public Health analysed labels of 6,037 alcoholic drinks sold in Sydney stores to determine how many products included one.
The researchers found just one in four products included a voluntary warning label, most of which targeted specific groups, such as drivers or underage drinkers.
Two in three products included a responsible consumption message such as "drink responsibly".
But study lead author Asad Yusoff, of the George Institute for Global Health, said separate research suggested responsible consumption messages were "ineffective" and often "confusing" to consumers.
"There's no real definition around what it means to drink responsibly,"
Australian guidelines recommend healthy adults drink no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than four standard drinks on any one day.
Although the percentage of Australians consuming more than this amount was decreasing, Mr Yusoff said many people did not realise that even low-level drinking could cause harm.
"One to two standard drinks per day significantly increases your risk of developing both breast and colon cancer," he said.
There is no safe level of alcohol consumption, according to the World Health Organization.
Warnings need to be prominent and explicit
Mr Yusoff said there needed to be clear and prominently placed warning labels on all alcoholic drinks sold in Australia, explicitly telling people about specific harms associated with drinking, such as cancer or liver disease.
Current warnings were mostly small, dull in colour and tucked away where people were "unlikely to view them", he said
"For a warning label to be effective it really needs to be on the front of the package."
Eric Hadinata, an addiction medicine specialist who did not contribute to the study, noted that government-mandated pregnancy warning labels typically included the words "alcohol can cause lifelong harm to your baby" next to a pictogram.
Dr Hadinata wanted this warning to be more prominent and placed on the front label.
Terry Slevin, chief executive of the Public Health Association of Australia, who did not contribute to the study, said the low uptake of these voluntary labels was "not a surprise".
Like Mr Yusoff, Mr Slevin said warnings on alcohol packaging needed to be more detailed about the exact harms drinking could cause to have an impact.
This, he said, would give people "full, informed consent" about what they were consuming.
"We have that expectation for all the products we use and all the products that we buy; I think it's fair that we have that expectation of alcohol,"
Australia's Food Standards Code outlines what information manufacturers need to include on their packaging, which varies depending on alcohol content.
UK, Ireland mandate health warning labels
The United Kingdom and Ireland have both committed to introducing mandatory health warning messages on alcohol labels.
The Irish laws, to be implemented in late 2028, will require labels to include calorie content as well as warning consumers about the dangers of drinking while pregnant and warnings about liver disease and cancer.
Both Mr Yusoff and Mr Slevin would like the Australian government to introduce similar legislation.
Dr Hadinata, who co-chairs the Alcohol and Other Drugs Committee at the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners, also wants more detailed warnings, but suggests plain packaging similar to tobacco products will also improve health outcomes.
Alistair Coe, executive director of Alcohol Beverages Australia, said labelling in Australia already contained useful information and guidance, including alcohol content, the number of standard drinks and pregnancy warnings.
"Australia has one of the world's most comprehensive and transparent alcohol regulatory systems, supported by clear government guidance that considers all the evidence," he said.
"Policy efforts should remain targeted at the minority of people who need support, not the vast majority of responsible drinkers."
A spokesperson for the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing said alcohol labels were part of a "multi-pronged response" to increase awareness about and respond to alcohol-related harm, alongside other initiatives.
They did not comment on whether the department would seek to introduce additional mandatory health warning labels.
