Sharing Thoughts: Philosophical Perspectives on Intersubjectivity and Communication
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:48:00 UTC
01:48:00 KST

This welcome collection addresses the question of how to individuate thoughts and their constituents, concepts, to explain intersubjective phenomena such as communication.[1] The book contains an illuminating introduction by Verdejo and Valente, followed by thirteen original essays. For reasons of space and thematic unity, I will not discuss three excellent essays by Bermúdez, Longworth, and Peacocke.
To introduce the topic of this collection, pre-theoretical characterizations of several intersubjective phenomena appeal to thoughts shared between different subjects.[2] According to a natural view of disagreement, subjects A and B disagree just when A accepts a certain thought that B rejects. And according to a natural view of communication, communication succeeds just when the hearer grasps the thought expressed by the speaker. But what might thoughts be, such that they can be shared?[3]
Of course, external truth-conditions can be shared across subjects. But an individuation of thoughts in terms of their external truth-conditions will not yield the right results. Subject A can accept the thought that George Eliot wrote Middlemarch while subject B rejects the thought that Mary Ann Evans wrote Middlemarch, and although George Eliot is Mary Ann Evans, A and B do not really disagree. Relatedly, when a speaker utters ‘he’, pointing to a man who just appeared on television, and her interlocutor misses the pointing gesture and takes ‘he’ to refer to the man they had previously been talking about, communication can fail even if the man on television turns out to be the man previously talked about (Loar, 1976).[4]
It further proves difficult to individuate thoughts in a fine-grained way (more fine-grained than reference) while vindicating both thought-sharing views of intersubjective phenomena and other individuation constraints. There is a well-documented conflict between the thought-sharing view of communication and Frege’s constraint, according to which thoughts t1 and t2 are distinct if t1 is accepted and t2 rejected by the same subject without irrationality (Schiffer, 1978).[5] Communication as thought-sharing is also in conflict with Campbell’s criterion, which tells us that mental tokens occurring in an inference are tokens of the same concept just when their coreference is assumed (‘traded on’) across premises (Campbell, 1987). Yet another conflict arises between the thought-sharing view of communication and a principle connecting thought and action, according to which two identical sets of propositional attitudes lead to the same actions under the same circumstances (Perry, 1977).[6]
One possible reaction to these conflicts is to uphold the relevant intersubjective constraint and reject another constraint. In this volume, Prosser revises the thought-action principle to uphold communication as thought-sharing. Another option is to reject the relevant intersubjective constraint, as Pollock does with the thought-sharing view of (dis)agreement in her essay. Providing revisionary accounts of the phenomena that initially seem to demand shared thoughts can free us from making thoughts shareable.
Yet another option is to uphold all our constraints but regard them as constraints on different notions of thought. Some measure of unity can be retained by defining one notion in terms of the other, for example, by defining shared thoughts as equivalence classes of private thoughts (Cumming, 2013; Dickie & Rattan, 2010).[7] Unfortunately, this compromise is unstable because the relation that underlies intersubjective phenomena seems to be intransitive, as explained by Goodman in this volume.[8]
Interestingly, however, intransitivity allows one to regain theoretical unity in the following way. The relation that underlies intersubjective phenomena can be identified with the relation whose absence or presence is at stake in Frege’s constraint and Campbell’s criterion, respectively, and this unique relation R can be made intransitive. Since R is not an equivalence relation, it cannot hold in virtue of its relata bearing a further relation to a third entity or in virtue of a shared intrinsic property. This non-reducibility of R characterizes so-called relationist views of thought (Fine, 2007; Gray, 2017).
The non-reducibility to shared properties of thought-tokens does not mean that R cannot be positively characterized. All extant characterizations of R invoke the notion of coreference or conditional coreference, as in the condition that if both tokens refer, then they corefer. Some characterizations of R make R entail (conditional) coreference, as in representationally required coreference (Gray, this volume). Other characterizations do not yield this entailment, as in presupposed coreference (García-Carpintero, this volume).[9]
Here is then a unificationist, relationist view of thought. The absence or presence of the same intransitive and irreducible (in the relevant sense) relation R between thought-tokens explains not only the rational believing of a material contradiction by a single subject and her trading on the coreference of tokens, but also communication and (dis)agreement between different subjects.[10]
With this background in place, we can delve deeper into the contributions to this volume. Prosser and García-Carpintero both develop a unificationist, relationist individuation of thought, with an intransitive relation R that does not entail coreference. While Prosser defines R by the very ability to trade on coreference, García-Carpintero considers this trading as a manifestation of R, which he defines as the presupposed (conditional) coreference of tokens. The case of the Schroeters is slightly different. They also develop a unificationist account that employs an intransitive relation based on Campbell’s criterion. This relation is an immediate and epistemically basic appearance of coreference that does not entail coreference. However, there is an additional ingredient to the Schroeters’ account: coreference itself. This additional ingredient yields an equivalence relation of ‘strict concept identity’.
Embracing a unificationist perspective in terms of an intransitive R, Gray focuses on the logic of this relation. Characterizing R as representationally required conditional coreference, Gray devises a formal language similar to predicate logic, except that constants may receive no interpretation, and (conditional) coreference between constant-tokens is encoded by an intransitive syntactic relation between constant-types, rather than by the identity of constant-type. The resulting logic is a three-valued one, and Gray claims that expected patterns of validity given an intransitive R are captured by a non-standard consequence relation called ‘Strawson entailment’.
In their respective essays, Goodman and Recanati both express skepticism about explaining intersubjective phenomena in terms of a relation based on Campbell’s criterion. Goodman compares a view of communication that invokes an intransitive relation R of encoded coreference based on Campbell’s criterion with a view that demands coreference reached through the right kind of process. Since it seems possible to explain communication without invoking encoded coreference, Goodman asks why one would invoke it. She argues that while encoded coreference is needed to stop a vicious regress in the intrapersonal case, there is no such motivation in the interpersonal case. This leaves the encoded coreference view of communication at a dialectical disadvantage. As for Recanati, he argues that Campbell’s criterion cannot be used to define notions of persisting or shared thoughts, because this criterion is about inferences, which Recanati claims are fundamentally synchronic and subjective. Recanati goes on to present his own account, fine-tuning variants of Frege’s constraint for each of the subjective, diachronic, and intersubjective cases.[11]
Disunified accounts of thought in terms of one relation explaining intrapersonal phenomena and another relation explaining interpersonal phenomena are not represented in this volume. However, several contributors reject thought-sharing views of interpersonal phenomena, which is another way of renouncing the unificationist ambition. Although he operates in a specific framework that treats communication as a signaling game and thought-content as information, Onofri’s main points are that successful communication does not require the sharing of anything more than referential content, and yet successful communication requires more than merely sharing referential content. It follows from this package of views that successful communication is not thought-sharing. According to Onofri, what successful communication requires beyond coreference is that coreference also obtains in a set of non-actual possibilities.
The account of successful communication offered in Dickie’s contribution may be paired with a rejection of the thought-sharing view. For communication with non-empty terms, Dickie’s account demands coreference reached through a process of the right kind. According to Dickie, a process of the right kind is one that makes coreference luck-free in relevant nearby situations, although it need not make coreference luck-free in the actual communicative situation.
As for Pollock, she revises the pre-theoretical account of (dis)agreement, in view of a holistic and internalist individuation of concepts, according to which a subject’s concept is defined by its relations to all her other concepts. This individuation does not allow thoughts to be shared, which makes the revision necessary.[12] Pollock further targets advocates of a ‘sociolectal’ externalist individuation of a subject’s concepts in terms of her relation to her linguistic community. Pollock argues that the sociolectalist too must reject the pre-theoretical view of (dis)agreement, despite the easy shareability of sociolectally individuated thoughts. For example, the sociolectalist is forced to grant the following possibility: A accepts the thought that C’s party is in a fortnight, B rejects this very thought, but A and B intuitively do not disagree. This can happen, for example, if A believes that a fortnight is 14 days, B believes that a fortnight is 10 days, and both believe that C’s party is in 14 days.
Sawyer’s essay is a response to Pollock’s. Sawyer argues that the sociolectalist can still explain (dis)agreement in terms of accepting and rejecting shared thoughts. In our example above, Sawyer claims there is disagreement simpliciter between A and B, since one rejects and the other accepts the thought that C’s party is in a fortnight. But there is a further agreement ‘relevant to coordination in behavior’ between A and B, which is a matter of them both accepting another shared thought, i.e., that C’s party is in 14 days. This further agreement explains the intuitive absence of disagreement between A and B.
I came away from this book with several worries about unificationist accounts of thought using a relation based on Campbell’s criterion. My first worry does not concern their unificationist aspect. It is rather about the capacity of a relation based on Campbell’s criterion to explain the intersubjective phenomena of interest. Assumed coreference (or appearance of coreference, or trading on coreference) can be present when a speaker refers to one thing and a hearer refers to another, but in such cases communication fails.[13] Worse still, the conjunction of assumed coreference with coreference itself does not guarantee communicative success. This is suggested by cases such as the one presented at the start of this review, in which speaker and hearer not only assume coreference but also corefer, and yet communication fails (Loar, 1976).
In view of this shortcoming, a characterization of R as knowledge of (conditional) coreference seems more promising.[14] Since knowledge is more demanding than true belief, knowledge of coreference is more demanding than a true assumption of coreference. Knowledge of coreference might then be the mark of successful communication. However, as shown by Dickie in her essay, not all views of knowledge will support this thesis. Dickie argues that successful communication tolerates a certain kind of luck which knowledge does not tolerate. If this is right, knowledge of coreference is not necessary for successful communication (Tamburini, 2025).[15]
It is further unclear whether a relation based on Campbell’s criterion can fulfill the unificationist ambition. Some characterizations of the relation do not obviously support this ambition. Take García-Carpintero’s presupposed coreference. García-Carpintero regards presuppositions as requirements on the common ground of a conversation. This notion of presupposition does not seamlessly extend to thoughts, whether of a single subject or of different subjects.[16] Turning to Gray’s representationally required coreference, his formal language suggests a natural sense in which coreference may be representationally required: non-semantic relations between symbols are recruited as markers of coreference by the relevant representational system. While this view can make sense of relations between the thoughts of a single subject, it is unclear how it could extend to interpersonal phenomena.
Can we regard several thinkers as forming one representational system whose symbols are subject to the same rules?
The unificationist may reply that the marking of coreference by non-semantic relations between symbols is just one way in which coreference could be representationally required. In the same vein, unificationists such as García-Carpintero and the Schroeters contend in this volume that different cognitive mechanisms implement the same relation R in subjective and intersubjective cases. However, it seems to me that this appeal to implementation mechanisms does not help. To begin with, it is not obvious that the mechanisms supposed to implement R in the intersubjective case can really do so. For Prosser, who is the most explicit on this issue, the assumption by conversational participants that they are using shared words of a shared language allows them to trade on coreference.[17] Prosser’s idea seems primarily designed for communication with words that carry reference-fixing meaning conventions. But there are words whose conventional meaning does not determine reference, such as demonstrative and personal pronouns. To trade on the coreference of pronoun-tokens, speaker and hearer must further converge on a way of identifying the reference of the tokens, as acknowledged by Prosser. Now, if non-reference-fixing conventions are the norm in natural languages, an account of intersubjective trading on coreference in terms of shared linguistic conventions has limited application.
Talk of different implementations of the same relation further raises the distinct possibility that we might be dealing with different relations. Assume that, in the case of a single subject, explanation bottoms out in non-semantic relations between mental symbols. And assume that, in the interpersonal case, explanation bottoms out in a type of interpretive process. An opponent to the unificationist project might not be impressed with an abstract characterization of a unique relation R that is variously implemented; she may insist that radically different ‘implementations’ are just a sign of distinct phenomena.
Although there is much more to say, I must stop here for reasons of space. I strongly recommend this collection. It is essential reading for anyone interested in how the individuation of thoughts relates to intersubjectivity.

"We have gotten our content through, and that's usually rewarded,” Mika Aaltola said at POLITICO's Brussels Playbook Live event in Brussesl on Sept. 22, 2026. | Davis Baatzsch for POLITICO
The center-right European People’s Party won’t rule out voting with the far right to deliver its policy agenda, even as Social Democrats and Liberals increase calls for an ironclad centrist coalition deal, according to Finnish EPP delegation chief Mika Aaltola.
“I’m not saying that there should be anything to be ashamed of in our track record. Actually, I’m saying the opposite. We have gotten our content through, and that’s usually rewarded,” Aaltola said at POLITICO’s Brussels Playbook Live event.
He added he is against putting up a firewall to keep out far-right forces “because it leads into badly behaving kids on the other side of the fence.”
Advertisement
“We should go beyond that. On some issues, I think that they [the far right] are relatively sane. On some other issues, there’s insanity,” he added, while insisting a majority of votes in Parliament will involve the mainstream parties.
Since the 2024 EU election, the EPP has repeatedly passed legislation with support from right-wing and far-right groups, particularly on migration and green policy — topics where the centrist groups have the widest gaps between them — sidelining its traditional centrist and center-left partners.
Liberals and Social Democrats are now pushing for binding, coalition-style commitments among the three centrist forces to prevent the EPP from turning to the far right.
“We need to step up also our game in the center … if we don’t find compromises within files, we have to find it across files,” said René Repasi, head of the German Social Democrats in the Parliament, who was taking part in the panel debate with Aaltola. “We need to not to dilute everything in compromises, but give everybody their wins, and that is the point: You need to have this in an agreement with a binding governance structure that includes many other members than simply the leaders in order to increase ownership.”
However, Aaltola pushed back against the idea, arguing that the Parliament’s political reality is more diverse. “That’s kind of a Soviet election result type of politics, there’s always going to be diversity,” he said. “That’s what democracy is all about, and so we cannot hammer out that coalition agreement that would be millimeter tight, and no voter will buy it from us.”
Renew Europe Vice Chair Gerben-Jan Gerbrandy, who was also on the panel, argued that centrist unity is essential to tackle Ukraine, geopolitics, climate change, and the cost-of-living crisis, warning that fights over the far-right firewall are distracting from more pressing concerns for EU citizens.
Advertisement
“I sincerely hope that EPP stops fooling around and comes back to the center where we can concentrate on the real challenges,” he said.
He argued that passing positions with the far right weakens Parliament’s hand in negotiations with EU governments over legislation.
“Now you see positions being adopted in Parliament, with the extreme right as part of it, that we go into a trilogue [three-way EU talks] and we’re completely, completely being outpaced by Council because they don’t take that position seriously anymore,” he said. “I even heard about Commission proposals that they don’t dare to put on the table because they fear what might happen with the anti-European forces in Parliament.”

Ukraine and Romania have signed a memorandum of understanding under the Carpathian Economic Forum (C8 Summit), based on an updated Strategy for the Development of Cross-Border Infrastructure between the countries that takes into account transportation needs for both freight and passenger traffic.
According to a statement by Ukraine's Ministry for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport, the document was signed by Minister Mykola Kalashnyk and Irinel Ionel Scrioșteanu, State Secretary of Romania's Ministry of Transport and Infrastructure.
Under the memorandum, the countries are expected to work on modernizing and developing road border crossings and access roads, strengthening rail connections, as well as simplifying border control procedures and expanding opportunities for transshipment of Ukrainian cargo at Romanian ports.

"The signed memorandum sets out specific areas for this work. The ministry said that the next stage would be to move toward implementation of the relevant projects and attract financing for their execution.

Spinoza on the Human Perspective
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:44:00 UTC
01:44:00 KST

In the 1960s, Alexandre Matheron and Louis Althusser portrayed Spinoza as an anti-humanist thinker who rejected the idea of a specific human nature. A strong monistic interpretation also implies marginalizing human essence as distinct from the essence of other finite things since modes are united with the substance. This collection of essays shifts the focus to show that Spinoza’s philosophy was indeed about human nature. Spinoza on the Human Perspective contains papers by leading international scholars who analyze Spinoza’s concern with human life.
Part I addresses the following questions: Is there a unified, specific concept of human essence? Did Spinoza develop a new “metaphysics of form”, as Pierre-François Moreau argues? Do we need additional concepts, such as “lifeform” to better understand the peculiarities of Spinoza’s conception of humanity? In “The Identity of Indiscernibles and Human Essence in Spinoza’s Ethics”, Michael LeBuffe analyzes three puzzles about humanity in the Ethics: Is human essence real or imaginary? Is Spinoza’s ethics based on egoism or humanism? And why is rational conflict among human beings impossible? LeBuffe notably claims that there is a unified human essence, even though humans can differ as individuals due to external causes. He also argues that Spinoza’s ethics is both humanistic and egoistic, and that rational conflict would be a conflict of a thing with itself.
In “Spinoza on the Notion of a Human Form”, Sarah Tropper focuses on the concept of “form” as applied to human nature. Her approach differs from that of François Zourabichvili in A Physics of Thought. She claims that the Spinozian concept of form is similar to that of Aristotle, except it is a non-substantial form, while Zourabichvili supported a materialistic interpretation of Spinoza’s concept of “form”, rooted in the “little physics”. She also explains how the concept of the human form permits changes within certain limits in the context of a gradualistic ethics. In “Non-Essentialist, Activity-Grounded Lifeforms”, Barnaby R. Hutchins imports the concept of “lifeform”, which is generally used in biological contexts, to understand Spinoza’s conception of humanity. While this concept is usually associated with essentialism, Hutchins attempts to show that a realist, nonessentialist concept of “lifeform” applies to Spinoza’s concept of human nature. It implies that “it is not that species grounds agreement; rather, agreement is what grounds species” (50). However, this reasoning is based on effects rather than causes. Agreement in nature could be seen as conditioned by a set of aptitudes belonging to a species.
Part II of the volume focuses on the model of human nature. Does Spinoza’s philosophy offer a real or a nominalist conception of human nature? In “Human Nature in Spinoza’s Philosophy”, Julie R. Klein follows Alexandre Matheron’s argument that Spinoza never defines what characterizes human nature, despite speaking of it. She advocates for a nominalist interpretation of human nature, positing that agreement in nature is based on likeness rather than a shared substantial form or essence, as in the Platonizing interpretation.
Another question raised in Part II of the volume is: How does this definition of human nature relate to our interactions with others? In “Homo homini Deus, & Homo homini Lupus: Spinoza on Human Nature and Human Relations”, Steven Nadler offers first a reading of why, for Spinoza, “Man is a God to Man” for selfish, rather than altruistic motives, which is consistent with views he has developed elsewhere. He also argues that “Man is a wolf to man”, not only due to passions, but also due to human nature itself, as we may be driven to desire the same goods in the same social space. However, one might object to this Hobbesian interpretation of Spinoza on the grounds that we only contradict ourselves to the extent that we are powerless against our passions (E4p33-34), rather than due to human nature as defined in positive terms (E4p32d). It is impossible to agree with other human beings in nature when acting under the influence of passions since passions are negation and it is impossible to agree with something else if negation is involved (E4p32s).
Part III focuses on knowledge and the human lifeform. It addresses the following questions: What is unique about human beings? How do they distinguish themselves from other beings in Nature? In “Living as a Human Being and Self-Interpretation”, Lia Levy rejects the idea of human nature being described as an essence or species. She considers the model of human nature as a regulative being of reason that serves a practical purpose. According to Levy, we are constantly self-interpreting our existence in terms of the model of human nature that we are trying to emulate.
In “The Idea of the Idea, Consciousness, and Human Experience in Spinoza’s Ethics”, Oliver Istvan Toth argues that, if Spinoza’s philosophy is primarily a philosophy for humans, it is “a philosophy of consciousness rather than a philosophy of being” (121). In his interpretation, Spinoza develops the idea of what is referred to in analytic philosophy as “access consciousness”, which is distinct from phenomenal consciousness. This concept plays a determining role in shaping the self of the human mind. In “Belief as an Essentially Human Attitude”, Ursula Renz challenges the Hegelian view that Spinoza’s philosophy leaves no room for finite subjectivity. She sets out a metaphysics of belief and demonstrates that opinion and belief necessitate the existence of a human subject. As human beings evolve in particular social environments, these beliefs and opinions express a certain perspective on human life.
Part IV delves into the nature of the human body, examining its ability to affect and be affected by other bodies. It begins with “Axiom Four of Part Two of the Ethics Deserves Paparazzi”, in which Noa Shein explores E2a4, where Spinoza claims that we sense our body being affected in various ways. This axiom refers to the way in which we experience our existence as finite modes: we perceive a multiplicity of bodily affections and realize that our body is affected by other bodies, as well as it affects other bodies. Through the sensory experience of our body being affected, we can also have a sense of the existence of other bodies, and, therefore, extension.
In “Spinoza and the Galenic Idea of the Human Body”, Beth Lord claims that Galenism plays a determining role in understanding the body, soul, and desires in the Short Treatise. In her view, in the Ethics, Spinoza would adhere to Galenism regarding living bodies but not human experience and motivation, primarily due to the concept of conatus. However, one could argue that Spinoza uses the concept of ingenium as a substitute for the concept of temperament in the Ethics, thereby distancing himself from the Galenic notion of temperament and its associated ideas of body equilibrium and organic fate.
Part V addresses the socio-political relevance of the human lifeform. It explores themes such as friendship, human laws, and religious toleration. In “The Authority of Humanity. Human Living and Intellectual Friendship in Spinoza”, Mogens Lærke demonstrates that private “authority to teach and advise”, as exemplified by the Epistles of the Apostles in the TTP, is connected to the notion of humanitas. This concept lies at the core of Spinoza’s conception of intellectual friendship. In “Spinoza’s Conception of Law from a Human Perspective”, Philip Waldner shows that although Spinoza appears to dispense with teleology, the normativity of human laws entails such a teleology. From a practical perspective, they cannot be reduced to efficient causation. But one could argue that laws based on human decisions (type II) necessarily involve human nature, which obeys to the universal laws of nature (type I) that rely on efficient causation. In “Ingenium and the Argument for Religious Toleration in Spinoza”, Daniel Garber argues that, while there are universal dogmas to which all religions should ascribe, differences among religions should be tolerated based on the ingenia of groups of people.
Part VI is devoted to human life from an eternal perspective. In “Becoming One: Theology and Philosophy, Will and Intellect, Mode and Substance in Spinoza”, Michael Della Rocca emphasizes unification as a condition of human existence in the Ethics. He argues for the unity of a rationally founded religion and philosophy, which is perceived due to the unity of the will and the intellect. He also highlights the unity of modes and substance and contends that Spinoza “carries out some kind of stripping away of distinctions between mode and substance” (245) by adopting a “purified, negation-less concept” of mode (254). After all, even the strong monistic view adopts a certain perspective on human existence. However, this raises the question of whether there is anything particular about human essence if we are all modes united with the substance. It is interesting to note that a volume that tends to challenge the monistic view gives voice to integral monism in its final part. It thus incorporates a certain degree of polyphony.
In conclusion, I highly recommend reading this collective volume. It leaves no doubt that Spinoza does indeed have a conception of human nature worthy of study and discussion. This new insight into Spinoza’s philosophy should be welcomed in the scholarship as a reinterpretation of Spinoza as a thinker of the virtues and trials of humanity—or, should I say, humanitas. One might then question whether Spinoza could, in fact, be considered as a humanist thinker in his own way, since his approach is to understand humankind rather than laugh at it.

The second Concert for Peace is scheduled for October 3 in Maputo, organized by the Italian Embassy as part of the Mozita 2026 cultural festival.     
   The event, at 6:30 p.m. at the Cine-Teatro Scala, commemorates the General Peace Accords signed in Rome in 1992, which brought an end to the Mozambican civil war.
                                    
                                       
				   Performing on stage will be Italian musicians from the Luigi Boccherini Conservatory in Lucca, led by maestro and composer Girolamo Deraco, alongside the Xiqitsi orchestra and choir, conducted by maestro Kika Materula. The program includes opera arias from the Italian repertoire, orchestral pieces, and—in its world premiere—an original composition dedicated to Mozambique and peace, written by Deraco and titled “United We Sing,” with lyrics by Eyal Lerner.
                                    
                                       
				   Also by the same composer, “Nubes sunt pulchrae”—based on a text by Alessandro J. Bianchi—will be performed to mark the 800th anniversary of the death of St. Francis, patron saint of Italy. Also on the program is a premiere by composer Gabriele Marchetti, dedicated to the Xiqitsi Orchestra and selected as the winner of an internal competition within the composition class at the Boccherini Conservatory led by Deraco.
                                    
                                       
				   Admission is free, and the event is open to the general public.

Ottawa and Brussels will announce a comprehensive set of partnerships within the coming year, but the shape of the future relationship is still up for discussion, Canada’s ambassador to the EU said Tuesday.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced during her State of the Union speech last week that the door would be open to Canada becoming “the first associate member” of the EU. But Ottawa has played down the formal nature of that arrangement.
“It was enormously gratifying for Canada to hear that from the president because I think it reflects the fact that Europeans see Canada in the same way that we see Europe,” Jonathan Wilkinson told POLITICO’s Brussels Playbook Live Summit.
Advertisement
“Ultimately, I’m less fussed about what we end up calling it. I’m more fussed about that we have initiatives that are really going to drive prosperity, economic security, and a range of things moving forward,” he said.
The EU and Canada are in the process of identifying areas to upgrade their partnership, including critical raw materials, AI, research and innovation. Asked when those deals could be signed, Wilkinson said they would be coming “pretty soon,” with several planned for the joint EU–Canada summit in October.
“This is not something that you commit to do, and it’s five years later. This is something that we’re looking to do within the next 12 months,” he went on. “I’m not sure what you’re going to call it, but a much deeper and closer relationship.”
However, two EU officials, granted anonymity to explain the arrangement, said it was a way to brand a new kind of partnership that goes deeper than existing trade, research and defense agreements.

EU agrees to lift sanctions on 2 major Russian oligarchs: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22

01:41:05 KST

Melike Pala and Burc Eruygur
22 September 2026•Update: 22 September 2026
European Union member states agreed Tuesday to remove Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from its sanctions list, according to diplomatic sources cited by the Politico news outlet.
EU capitals reached the agreement after France pushed for the removal of Usmanov, while Luxembourg had previously sought the delisting of Fridman.
The decision followed more than a week of disagreements among EU member states on the renewal of individual sanctions against roughly 3,000 people and entities linked to Russia.
Slovakia and France favored lifting sanctions against Usmanov, but Slovakia, Hungary and Luxembourg favored lifting sanctions against Fridman, according to reports.
Five diplomats told Politico that the agreement was reached after Latvia, which had opposed the move, agreed to abstain.
The sanctions list is expected to remain in place for three years, effectively postponing further discussions on individual listings until 2029.
France had backed Usmanov's delisting, citing a "specific national security issue," according to a French diplomatic official cited by the Washington Post.
Earlier Tuesday, Estonia's Foreign Ministry Deputy Secretary General Kerli Veski told the ERR broadcaster that there was no justification for removing the two men from the EU sanctions list.
Veski also said Estonia, Latvia and most other EU member states opposed removing the billionaires from the sanctions list.
Usmanov and Fridman are Russian billionaires with extensive business interests in Europe.
Usmanov made his fortune in metals, mining, telecommunications and technology. Russian-Israeli Fridman built his wealth through banking, energy and investments.
Both have faced EU sanctions since the start of the war in Ukraine.
Their assets in Europe have been affected by the sanctions, and both have challenged restrictions through legal and political channels.
Commenting on the decision on US social media company X, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha defined the move as "shameful and unjustifiable," urging all EU member states to announce that they will impose their own national sanctions on the men.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said at a media briefing that Moscow viewed the sanctions on Usmanov and Fridman as “illegal” and that sanctions should be lifted for all Russian citizens.

It is tough being a small economy in an AI boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:44 UTC
01:39:44 KST

You have to feel sorry for the Philippines. An economy that was doing nicely has once again become Southeast Asia’s straggler, even though officials are doing many right things. Painful as it is, they should stick to their guns.
Faced with a run on the currency, the central bank has forgone the kind of aggressive intervention that Indonesia and Japan have favored. That makes sense, given the massive foreign-exchange market dwarfs the Philippines’ ability to effectively combat the slide. Nor has Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr sought to scapegoat the head of the monetary authority or the finance secretary by pushing them out. He is standing by their fairly orthodox approach to the multiplying challenges.
However, it is not easy to watch. The Philippine economy is geared more toward domestic demand. Decades of underinvestment are again making themselves felt. The artificial intelligence (AI) boom is threatening to widen the gap.
An analysis from Bank of America was bullish on the overall benefits of AI spending for Southeast Asia, but cautioned that not everybody would prosper to the same degree. Malaysia, an export and semiconductor powerhouse that is the site of a big data center buildup, is well positioned. While it is a standout winner, Indonesia and the Philippines are laggards.
Manila’s more pressing issues are close to home. Growth has been set back by a graft scandal involving procurement for flood relief measures. The furor has curbed spending on public works. The peso is the worst performer in Asia this quarter, down about 2.3 percent against the US dollar and hovering at record lows. It has also posted some of the biggest declines among emerging markets, a move that is exacerbating a significant inflation problem.
The combination of plummeting growth and quick inflation is forcing policymakers to pick their priorities. While it is probably too soon to diagnose a case of stagflation, it is troubling that the word has even entered the conversation.
In the years before the COVID-19 pandemic, and immediately afterward, the Philippine economy was a star. The expansion was so hot it compared favorably with China. Today, it is a different story.
With GDP growing far slower than anticipated last quarter, it is one of the worst performers in Asia and far behind Malaysia and Singapore, whose numbers have been boosted by exports and the surge in demand for semiconductors. These neighbors spent the 1970s and 1980s enmeshing themselves in global supply chains and pouring money into infrastructure and education. They were right to do so.
Manila would have to just hope it can ride out the current difficulties and, then, take a step back and develop a long-term strategy that resembles the one undertaken by regional peers in less arduous times. At the moment, the alternatives to orthodoxy are unappealing.
Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Governor Eli Remolona is left to smooth some of the sharper declines in the currency. He has told lawmakers that trying to strengthen the peso to 60 per greenback (it traded at 62 on Friday) or more only risks burning through reserves. Imposing capital controls as Malaysia did in 1998 would be unwise. That was a time of acute crisis in emerging markets and, while the radical steps put a floor under the ringgit, the country did pay a price — the government got a reputation for inconsistency that took many years to wear off.
Remolona has raised interest rates, mostly to curb inflation that is still well above the central bank’s target because of the Iran war. The Philippines is especially vulnerable, importing almost all the oil it requires.
Not everything is grim. Last month, the World Bank upgraded the archipelago to upper-middle income status. It has a relatively young, mobile workforce with high proficiency in English — although that edge might be slipping — and AI is as much a threat as an opportunity to the Philippines’ outsourcing industry, which has been a crucial source of jobs and growth in recent decades.
Central bankers are not in the job to be popular. Paul Volcker, who crushed inflation in the 1980s as US Federal Reserve chair, was sent timber by home builders put out of business by high rates. Ben Bernanke, one of his successors, kept a plank in his office as a reminder that hard times were what he trained for. It is up to Marcos to sell the necessary pain and, while doing so, stand by Remolona.
There is not a lot of choice, but maybe doing the right thing should offer some consolation. At some point, it will be noticed. Hopefully, it would not be too late.
Daniel Moss is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asian economies. Previously, he was executive editor for economics at Bloomberg News. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

ASRock says new order would drive its momentum far

Photo: Meryl Kao, Taipei Times
The shipments are expected to continue through the end of this month, with second-stage shipments likely to start in the first quarter of next year, he said, adding that the customer has positioned the project as a long-term deal.
Revenue growth this year would also be supported by the company’s latest artificial intelligence (AI) box, the AI BOX-A395, which was launched last month and is suitable for enterprise teams of about 10 to 20 people as a lower-cost alternative to larger AI server platforms, Lee said.
ASRock Industrial is initially marketing the product in Taiwan, saying it has received inquiries from schools and universities for research and teaching purposes, he said.
Customers in Japan, South Korea, India, Southeast Asia, Europe and the US have expressed interest in the product, he added.
ASRock Industrial does not operate its own factories, working with electronics manufacturers in Taoyuan, China’s Guangzhou and Vietnam, company president Handsome Tzeng (曾瑛俊) said.
The Guangzhou and Vietnam facilities focus mainly on motherboard production, while Taiwan is in charge of system-level products and higher-value-added projects, he said.
However, the company continues to face shortages of key components, with central processing units and memory chips continuing to face price increases and longer lead times, chief operating officer Kenny Chang (張晃華) said.
To address this issue, the company is validating alternative components and suppliers while striving to secure components for products set for production next year, he said.
ASRock Industrial reported revenue rose 24.75 percent year-on-year to NT$1.83 billion and net profit increased 10.15 percent to NT$228 million last year, while earnings per share rose to NT$3.68 from NT$3.32 a year earlier.
The company, a subsidiary of motherboard maker ASRock Inc (華擎), is slated to debut its shares on the Taiwan Stock Exchange later next month.

Street dancer teams up with robot dancers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:42 UTC
01:39:42 KST

Chinese street dancer Wu Yufei (吳宇飛) has spent most of his 13-year career performing solo, but this year, he found some new partners — a crew of robots with sleek moves.
The 27-year-old Sichuan native, together with his fellow robot performers, has made it to the final of America’s Got Talent (AGT), a stage he had been hoping to reach for years.
A longstanding science-fiction fan, Wu said in Pasadena, California, that dancing with robots in the group Homies gave him a “very magical feeling.”
Photo: AFP
After months of training with them, his robot dancers now feel like more than just “cold, lifeless machines,” he said.
“It almost feels as if there’s a kind of team spirit there,” Wu said, as he and the dance crew of humanoids — made by Chinese robotics group Unitree — prepared for the AGT final this week.
Robot dancing has become a huge craze in China after Unitree robots performed in a breakout performance at China’s annual Spring Festival gala performance, the country’s most-watched television extravaganza.
Businesses and event planners across the country have since rushed to hire robots to perform and attract visitors.
Training robots to dance involves capturing intricate human movements, running computer simulations, and then transferring results to the robots, industry insiders said.
For Fang Zhenghua (方正華), the art director behind Wu and Unitree’s AGT performances, training a robot to dance resembles “creating a soul.”
“The impact of AI [artificial intelligence] on dance performances, or the impact of robots on dancing — I was quite against it all at the beginning,” he said.
However, over time, working with the skilled engineers — who he describes as the “mothers” of the robots — changed his perspective.
Training robots requires input from human dancers and relies heavily on engineers to troubleshoot problems, particularly in real-time during performances.
“It takes a lot of fine-tuning,” said Liu Zhiquan (劉志全), commercialization lead at robotics motion-capture firm BridgeDP.
A 30-second dance routine could take days, sometimes weeks, to perfect, and performers need to be willing to compromise, he said.
“If the dancers are not tech-savvy, there will be a lot of retakes,” he said.
Wegers Wei (魏唯), from Shanghai-based dance studio Limit Crew, said that when he designs routines for robots, he avoids movements that he knows would be difficult for them.
“If we find that some routines don’t look good for robots or if they look like the robots are making mistakes, we would change them,” said Wei, whose robots won first and second places for street dance at this year’s World Humanoid Robot Games.
Robots are good at rotating moves, or what street dancers call power moves, Wei said, as it is “just a matter of adjusting the motor power and the torque of the arms.”
However, routines that require body flexibility are extremely difficult for robots, he said.
Another blind spot is musicality.
Robot dancing is mostly scripted playback. Unlike humans, the machines cannot improvise or “make on-the-spot adjustments” if the music changes suddenly, Wu added.
While the general public in China mostly sees robot dancing as entertainment, industry insiders see it as a chance to show off robotic designs, capabilities and reliability.
“That’s why everyone is keen to perform these kinds of high-skill dances,” said Guo Renjie (郭人傑), founder and CEO of robotics engineering company Zeroth.
A recent Morgan Stanley report forecast that China’s humanoid robotics market could reach US$2 billion in value this year.
Accounting for more than 97 percent of humanoid robot shipments in the first half of this year globally, the Chinese industry also faces increasing scrutiny from investors and policymakers.
Many companies are struggling to find commercially viable uses for their humanoids beyond entertainment.
Executives at humanoid robotics companies have publicly acknowledged that the industry is still years away from its own “ChatGPT moment” — the point at which robots become useful to ordinary people.
“I think everyone should give this industry time to reach its full potential,” Guo said.
Unitree made a blistering debut on the Shanghai stock market last month, surging 629 percent through the first day’s trading.
Its market capitalization has since fallen by about half from its peak.
At the AGT filming studio in Pasadena, Wu pointed to another robot benefit — how quickly his robot crew could learn routines.
“Their knowledge can be replicated extremely quickly,” he said. “Not only does a single robot learn quickly, but they can all learn the same things at the same time, which is quite terrifying.”

====================================================================================================

The political earthquake from Germany’s China shock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:37 UTC
01:39:37 KST

Sept. 6 could mark a turning point in Germany’s post-World War II political history. In the Saxony-Anhalt state election, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party came within three seats of an absolute majority, winning 43.8 percent of the vote — more than twice its share in the 2021 election. The AfD’s gains came at the expense of the center-right Christian Democratic Union, the state’s incumbent governing party and the party of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, which won just 17.2 percent, down from 37.1 percent in 2021.
There is no shortage of explanations for the surge in support for the AfD in parts of Germany. Immigration, cultural conflict and distrust of the political establishment are among the most cited — and for good reason. However, the economic factors fueling the AfD’s rise have so far received much less attention.
Saxony-Anhalt has endured profound economic challenges in the past few decades. Reunification brought the collapse of East Germany’s industrial base, destroying millions of jobs and causing large numbers of younger workers to relocate, leaving the region with one of the country’s oldest and fastest-shrinking populations.
Illustration: Mountain People
After more than three decades of economic deterioration, Saxony-Anhalt appeared to be recovering. That upturn has stalled. Saxony-Anhalt’s economy has contracted since 2021, bringing GDP close to its 2013 level.
Intensifying competitive pressure from Chinese exporters is threatening to make matters much worse. Saxony-Anhalt’s imports from China increased 87 percent in 2024, reaching 20 percent of the state’s total imports, and by a further 46 percent in the first nine months of last year.
The China shock is not confined to Saxony-Anhalt. Germany’s economy has stagnated since 2019, with output increasing by only about 0.12 percent annually, on average, from 2020 to last year. During that period, Chinese producers claimed an expanding share of the global market for advanced manufacturing products, such as automobiles and machinery, which were once central to Germany’s export model.
However, the effects are not felt equally across regions. Consider the southwestern state of Baden-Wurttemberg, home to automotive giants such as Mercedes-Benz and Porsche, major suppliers such as Bosch, a dense network of specialized engineering companies, and globally competitive Mittelstand companies, including the laser technology group Trumpf and the engineering company Durr. While Baden-Wurttemberg remains one of Europe’s most important industrial regions, many of the mainstays of its economy are directly exposed to intensifying Chinese competition.
The western state of Rhineland-Palatinate — a hub of chemical and pharmaceutical production, exemplified by companies such as BASF and Boehringer Ingelheim, as well as automotive suppliers and machinery manufacturers — is similarly exposed. At a time of weak domestic demand, high energy costs, structural changes in the automotive industry and a global trade slowdown, neither state can afford the added pressure generated by China’s growing dominance in the industries that have long formed the backbone of their economies.
Baden-Wurttemberg and Rhineland-Palatinate look very different from Saxony-Anhalt, economically and demographically, but the prosperity of all three depends heavily on industries exposed to Chinese competition. It is then probably no coincidence that the AfD has also made major electoral gains in Baden-Wurttemberg, nearly doubling its vote share to 18.8 percent in March, and in Rhineland-Palatinate, securing 19.5 percent of the vote two weeks later.
Not surprisingly, support for the AfD was higher among industrial workers than among the broader electorate: 61 percent in Saxony-Anhalt, 37 percent in Baden-Wurttemberg and 39 percent in Rhineland-Palatinate. The center-left Social Democratic Party, long the party of Germany’s industrial workers, suffered major losses. In Rhineland-Palatinate, it was ousted after 35 years in government, while in Baden-Wurttemberg it only narrowly retained parliamentary representation.
For most of its history, the AfD had been viewed as a creature of eastern Germany, and the party’s eastern roots might go some way toward explaining why it made its biggest breakthrough in Saxony-Anhalt. However, in view of rising support in western Germany, that outcome should be viewed as a warning, not an outlier. Industrial crisis, exacerbated by an intensifying China shock, creates fertile ground for political extremism.
None of this is to say that Chinese imports automatically lead to votes for the AfD. Economic decline is only one of many forces that shape electoral outcomes, but the pattern is too striking to ignore, especially as it has precedents elsewhere. Empirical research has shown a causal link between the China shock the US experienced in the early 2000s and US President Donald Trump’s 2016 electoral victory, underscoring the political salience of trade-induced economic dislocation.
Against this backdrop, treating the China shock as simply an economic story would be a mistake. For decades, Germany’s stability rested on an implicit bargain: A high-value manufacturing would provide good jobs, strong export revenues and broad-based prosperity, which political institutions would translate into social cohesion. Competition from China shakes that bargain to its foundations.
The risk is not simply that Germany loses market share in automobiles, chemicals or machinery. It is that the regions most exposed to the transformation will lose faith in the political system that has for so long maintained stability.
Dalia Marin, professor of international economics at the School of Management of the Technical University of Munich, is a research fellow at the Centre for Economic Policy Research and a nonresident fellow at Bruegel.
Copyright: Project Syndicate
Taiwan’s democracy and high-tech economy play a crucial role in global affairs and are central to the world’s embrace of a raft of next-generation technologies, including AI. It is underpinned by a security relationship with the United States that’s existed in several iterations since 1949 and the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) retreat from China. Taiwan was not subjected to any “downgrading” during at an APEC ministerial meeting in China and was granted the same rights as other members, Minister of Labor Hung Sun-han (洪申翰) said yesterday.
“During our participation in the meeting, we did not encounter any so-called downgrading,” Hung told reporters after arriving at Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport yesterday afternoon.
Hung was returning from the eighth APEC Human Resources Development Ministerial Meeting in Nanjing, where he became the first ministry head in President William Lai’s (賴清德) administration to travel to China.
Photo: CNA
Speaking after the three-day trip, Hung said that “through our continued insistence and with the assistance of the APEC secretariat, the Chinese side granted us rights equal to those of other members in accordance with APEC rules.”
That was consistent with Taiwan’s insistence on “reciprocal dignity,” Hung said, referring to a principle he had laid out before departing for China for APEC, one of the few major international forums in which Taiwan is a formal member.
The minister also confirmed that he neither applied for nor used a “Taiwan compatriot permit” — a travel document issued by China to Taiwanese, whose passports Beijing does not recognize for travel to China — for the trip.
“We followed the usual practice and entered China using an invitation letter,” Hung said, referring to the arrangements for Taiwanese officials attending APEC meetings in China.
Asked whether the nameplate reading “Chinese Taipei” in front of him at the meeting constituted downgrading, Hung reiterated that Chinese Taipei is Taiwan’s formal membership name in APEC.
“What we really need to insist on is that, as a formal APEC member, we enjoy the same rights as other members,” he said.
The trip drew attention as a rare cross-strait visit by a Cabinet-level official from the Democratic Progressive Party amid strained ties between Taipei and Beijing.
Ahead of Hung’s trip, China’s Taiwan Affairs Office on Sept. 2 said that Beijing would handle Taiwan’s participation according to its “one China” principle, APEC memorandums and established practices.

Erdogan at UN: Gaza is 'most inhumane, most shameful concentration camp' of our time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:37 UTC
01:39:37 KST

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has called for Gaza's reconstruction to begin without delay and urged the international community to increase pressure on Israel.
Addressing the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Erdogan said efforts to rebuild Gaza should start as soon as possible.
"We need to begin the reconstruction of Gaza without wasting any time. In this regard, I call on you to exert greater pressure on Israel," he said.
Erdogan said Türkiye remained committed to the agreement signed in Sharm el-Sheikh a year earlier and would continue to follow up on its implementation.
He said attempts to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state would ultimately fail.
"Everyone should now understand and accept this: Attempts to strangle the state of Palestine will end in failure," he said.
He expressed hope that an independent Palestinian state with territorial integrity, based on the 1967 borders and with occupied East Jerusalem as its capital, would eventually be established.
"We will, God willing, see those beautiful days when an independent and territorially integrated State of Palestine, within the 1967 borders and with East Jerusalem as its capital, will come into being," Erdogan said.
Palestinian state, Abbas' absence from UN
Starting his address, Erdogan expressed his sadness that Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas has been unable to participate in the UN General Assembly for two consecutive years.
"Palestinian President Mr. Abbas has been unable to be in this hall for two consecutive years. This injustice against our Palestinian brothers and sisters wounds consciences," he added.
Erdogan said Türkiye would continue to speak on behalf of an independent and sovereign Palestinian state despite Abbas' absence.
"Although Mr. Abbas cannot be here in person, just as we did last year, we will be the voice of a free and sovereign state of Palestine," he said.
Erdogan called on countries to recognise a Palestinian state. "Today, once again, I call on all countries that have not yet recognised the state of Palestine to reconsider their decisions," he said.
Humanitarian situation in Gaza
Addressing the situation in the Gaza Strip, Erdogan said the enclave had become the world's largest cemetery for children and the region with the world's highest rate of child amputations.
Erdogan said 74,000 Palestinians, most of them women and children, had been killed in Gaza over the past three years, describing them as victims of "Israel's state terror."
He said Palestinians continued to search for loved ones beneath the rubble and recover the bodies of their spouses, children and parents, while children who lost limbs in Israeli attacks were trying to return to school and continue their lives with wooden prostheses.
More than 70 percent of generators in Gaza's hospitals were currently out of service because of fuel shortages, Erdogan said.
"Gaza is the most inhumane and shameful concentration camp of our age," he added.
Erdogan said more than 1,500 Palestinians had been killed even after the October 2025 ceasefire was reached through the efforts of US President Donald Trump and with contributions from Türkiye and other countries.
He said that although the Palestinian resistance movement had agreed to move to the second phase of the peace plan, the Israeli government was unwilling to end the occupation.
Turning to the occupied West Bank, Erdogan said the territory was experiencing its worst period of settler violence, while Muslims and Christians were being prevented from accessing holy sites in Jerusalem.
He also said that the UN agency for Palestinian refugees UNRWA was being targeted.
"We are facing a genocidal mindset that cannot get enough of killing," Erdogan said, adding that no one with humanity, mercy, compassion and conscience could turn a blind eye to the situation.
He stressed that the issue was not a personal matter for him but "a humanitarian issue" and "a matter of conscience for all of us."
UN reform
Erdogan said the situation showed that the UN, founded 81 years ago to maintain peace and security, had been rendered unable to fulfill its responsibility.
He said people in Palestine, Lebanon, Sudan and other crisis regions who had placed their hopes in the UN were deeply disappointed.
"One day, everyone will have to seek refuge in humanity's common conscience," he said, warning that although people may currently feel safe and live far from conflict zones, no one knows what the future may bring.
Erdogan said he considered this year's General Assembly theme, which focuses on rebuilding trust in the international system, particularly appropriate and voiced support for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres' reform efforts, including the UN80 Initiative.
He said trust in the UN could only be restored when children in Gaza could live safely, Palestinian children could look to the sky and see kites rather than warplanes and drones, children in Lebanon did not wake to the sound of bombs, workers were not exploited, and people in Africa could look to their futures with confidence.
Erdogan also renewed his call for reform of the UN Security Council, saying a structure in which the will of more than 190 countries depends on five countries is neither fair nor capable of fully establishing trust.
"The Security Council must be reformed in accordance with the principle that 'the world is bigger than five,'" he said.
International law, diplomacy and global inequality
Erdogan said the international community must change an approach under which international law is applied differently to powerful and weaker states.
"An international system in which wrongdoers get away with what they do and impunity becomes normalised is doomed to decay," he said.
Outlining principles for a more equitable international order, Erdogan said regional ownership should be used when international efforts to resolve crises reach an impasse, citing the Black Sea Grain Corridor as an example of an initiative that contributed to regional and global security.
He also called for cooperation and open diplomacy to be placed at the centre of interstate relations, arguing that history had repeatedly shown that politics built on distrust produces no winners.
Erdogan called for a new paradigm to address widening global income inequality, saying shared development, solidarity and connectivity were key to a greater peace and stability.
He also warned against "techno-polarisation" and "digital hegemony," saying technological development should remain human-centred and should not create new divisions between those with access to technology and those without it.
Türkiye's regional diplomacy
Erdogan said Türkiye sought a more just and humane international system not only through rhetoric but also through its policies.
Referring to a defence alliance established with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, he said Türkiye aimed both to strengthen solidarity and to develop regional solutions to regional problems.
He said Ankara was continuing efforts with relevant actors to bring an end to conflict in the Gulf and warned against attempts to spread regional fighting to neighbouring areas.
Syria, Iraq and Ukraine war
Turning to Syria, Erdogan said the country had entered a new phase since December 2024 after 14 years of suffering.
He said Syria, under President Ahmed al-Sharaa, was moving toward becoming a secure and peaceful country despite internal and external challenges, and that Türkiye would continue to stand by the Syrian people.
On Iraq, Erdogan said Türkiye fully supported efforts to strengthen state authority and consolidate stability and was working with Baghdad on strategic transportation and energy projects, particularly the Development Road Project.
Addressing the Russia-Ukraine war, Erdogan said Türkiye sincerely wanted the conflict to end with Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity ensured.
He said Ankara remained in contact with the parties to restore navigational safety in the Black Sea, ensure food security and prevent the war from spreading to a wider region.
Erdogan also condemned recent attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea, saying such attacks were "unacceptable regardless of who carried them out."
Eastern Mediterranean, Cyprus
Erdogan said Türkiye believed freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz must be preserved.
On the Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean, he said existing disputes should be resolved on the basis of good-neighbourly relations and international law, adding that Türkiye's proposal for an Eastern Mediterranean Conference could help establish common ground.
Erdogan also reiterated his call for the recognition of sovereign equality and equal international status of the Turkish Cypriot people and for an end to their international isolation.
He called on the international community to recognise the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus and establish political, diplomatic and economic relations with it.
Türkiye's role in European security
Erdogan described Türkiye as an "island of stability" amid regional conflicts, citing its defence industry and the economy, saying the country continued to play a significant role in European security and prosperity.
Referring to the NATO summit hosted in Ankara in July, he said the meeting demonstrated Türkiye's commitment to common security.
"It is not possible for a Europe that excludes Türkiye from its security architecture to become stronger or safer," Erdogan said, adding that Ankara expected the European Union to adopt the same strategic vision in its relations with Türkiye.
Balkans, South Caucasus and Turkic states
On the Balkans, Erdogan highlighted Türkiye's historical, cultural and human ties with the region and said joint steps were being taken through the Balkan Peace Platform to deepen cooperation.
In South Caucasus, he voiced support for lasting peace between Azerbaijan and Armenia and praised Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan for their will to reach a solution.
He said Türkiye was also continuing its normalisation process with Armenia.
Erdogan said the Organization of Turkic States had developed into an exemplary regional cooperation model, that the 13th leaders' summit, scheduled to be held in Ankara on October 30, would open new opportunities for the organisation.
He said the fourth Türkiye-Africa Partnership Summit, due to be held in Libya in December, would symbolise more than two decades of institutional partnership between Türkiye and Africa.
Commenting on South Asian affairs, Erdogan said disputes including the Kashmir issue should be addressed through dialogue within the framework of relevant UN provisions and resolutions.
"When a constructive approach is adopted, every problem can be resolved," he said.
Africa, Asia-Pacific and Latin America
Coming to Africa, Erdogan voiced Türkiye's support for ceasefire and lasting peace efforts in Sudan and for measures to strengthen security, development and institutional capacity in Somalia.
He said maintaining stability in Libya remained a priority and stressed that the reconciliation process should proceed under Libyan leadership and ownership.
Erdogan said Türkiye would continue strengthening relations with Asia-Pacific partners through its Asia Anew Initiative, and described the elevation of ties with ASEAN to Dialogue Partner level as a concrete result of that policy.
He said Türkiye was also developing relations with Latin American and Caribbean countries on the basis of mutual respect, partnership and a win-win approach.
Climate change and COP31
Turning to climate change, Erdogan said the world faced serious environmental threats affecting air, water, soil and living species, while developing countries and the Pacific region were struggling to access the financing needed to confront the climate crisis.
He said Türkiye would host the COP31 summit in Antalya in November and would seek to put climate justice at the centre of the gathering.
Erdogan said Türkiye's partnership with Australia aimed to make COP31 an "implementation COP," where financing pledges were fulfilled, technology transfer was accelerated and commitments were translated into concrete steps.
He highlighted the Zero Waste Movement launched by first lady Emine Erdogan in 2017, saying it had grown into a global awareness campaign. He described the initiative as a key bridge connecting different methods of combating the climate crisis.
Food waste and global food security
Erdogan warned that excessive consumption and a growing culture of waste posed a threat comparable to climate change.
He said 5.8 trillion servings of food, amounting to more than 2 billion tons, were wasted globally every year, while hundreds of millions of people searched for food in garbage.
Türkiye was ready to contribute to efforts to reduce waste and strengthen global food security, he said.
Erdogan also announced that Türkiye had nominated Mehmet Mehdi Eker for the post of director-general of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization and asked member states for their support.
Islamophobia, discrimination and social media
Addressing emerging social threats, Erdogan said hostility toward Islam was spreading in Western countries and that Muslim women and girls had increasingly faced discrimination.
He criticised headscarf bans in schools in some countries, describing them as an attack on women's fundamental rights.
Erdogan said xenophobia, cultural racism and antisemitism were harmful trends that required determined action.
He criticised "gender-neutralisation policies," saying Türkiye would continue initiatives aimed at protecting the family and children.
Erdogan also identified the spread of disinformation on social media as another threat to social peace, and said defending the truth had become more important than ever.
Call for international AI framework
On artificial intelligence, Erdogan called for a common international legal framework, saying the time for such regulation had already arrived.
He urged accelerated work toward preparing and bringing into force a UN international convention on artificial intelligence.
'We will not remain silent in the face of injustice'
Concluding his address, Erdogan said the positions he had voiced would disturb some actors but that Türkiye would continue speaking out on behalf of those facing injustice.
Quoting the late Turkish poet Sezai Karakoc, Erdogan said that even if people remained silent, "history will not" and "the truth will not."
He pledged to continue defending what he described as the rights of the oppressed, victims and those without a voice for as long as he remained able to do so.
"If necessary, we will endure hardship; if necessary, we will pay a price. But we will not remain silent in the face of injustice, and we will never consent to oppression," Erdogan said.
He said the world faced two possible paths: allowing fear, conflict and isolation to deepen uncertainty, or building the future through justice, solidarity and common will.
Türkiye, he argued, has chosen the second path and would continue along it, calling on those listening at the UN and around the world to support a shared vision for the future.

EDITORIAL: Getting the GDP to workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:35 UTC
01:39:35 KST

Fueled by robust economic growth and rising inflation, Taiwan is set to raise its statutory minimum wage to a new high for the 11th consecutive year during an annual review scheduled for tomorrow.
However, the constant hikes of the minimum wage mask the core issues of real-wage stagnation and a growing imbalance of wealth distribution.
The increase in the wage floor is weakly correlated to the average wage, while the spillover effect is limited to a small group of people. The only significance of the wage-hike policy is to show that the government is committed to protecting low-wage earners and their families.
Taiwan’s economic growth is projected to accelerate at an annual rate of 11.48 percent this year, the fastest in 39 years, while consumer prices are expected to climb to 2.03 percent year-on-year, exceeding the central bank’s 2 percent target, the central bank has estimated.
However, the economic benefits remain out of reach for the majority of workers due to uneven growth. Many are struggling to make ends meet as wage growth stagnates amid persistent inflation.
The median monthly wage — which is considered a more accurate gauge of standard income, as extremely high or low wages do not skew it — rose 3.37 percent annually to NT$41,054 in the first seven months of this year, Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS) data showed.
That marked the second consecutive year of growth of at least 3 percent in median monthly wage, but far below the regular average wage of NT$49,491 in July, the data showed.
For the first time, more than 70 percent earned less than the average, the agency said.
The trend is evident, as the proportion of workers earning less than the average has risen over the past few years, with 66.81 percent earning less than the average in 2021, the DGBAS data showed.
The agency attributed the surge in regular average wage to sharp pay increases within the technology sector, particularly among artificial intelligence (AI)-related companies.
Driven by explosive demand for AI chips and servers, employees at electronics and components companies — such as semiconductor manufacturers — were paid on average NT$48,310 and NT$44,374 per month respectively, significantly surpassing the NT$37,803 paid to workers in the overall manufacturing sector in the first seven months of this year, the data showed.
The result highlights uneven wage growth in the manufacturing sector, with the traditional industries lagging even further behind.
It seems that a decade of government-mandated minimum wage hikes has failed to effectively raise overall local wages.
The minimum wage has increased more than 47 percent since 2016, when it was NT$20,008, reaching NT$29,500 per month this year.
The real average wage, in which the impact of inflation is deducted, only edged up 1.12 percent in the first seven months of this year, entering a third year of a growth streak following a 1.4 percent annual expansion last year and a 0.58 percent increase in 2024.
The government has to implement a better approach to address anemic income growth — something other than hiking the minimum wage.
Some economists have suggested that the share of GDP going to workers should be increased to curb a decline over the past few years. In 2024, about 43 percent of the nation’s GDP went to workers, dropping from 46.54 percent in 2008, the DGBAS data showed.
That compared with an upward trajectory of the share of GDP that went to operating surplus, which rose to 35.06 percent of GDP from 31.57 percent over the same period.
That might be a viable option, as Japan and South Korea have labor shares of GDP of 50 percent and 47.5 percent respectively.
Taiwan lacks a union-led mechanism to push for annual wage adjustments such as Shunto, or the Spring Wage Offensive, an annual collective bargaining process in Japan in which unions and management negotiate wage increases and working conditions.
Addressing Taiwan’s wage problems requires structural reforms and supporting measures rather than just raising the minimum wage.
Taiwan’s democracy and high-tech economy play a crucial role in global affairs and are central to the world’s embrace of a raft of next-generation technologies, including AI. It is underpinned by a security relationship with the United States that’s existed in several iterations since 1949 and the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) retreat from China. A central pillar of that security relationship is the American willingness to sell arms to Taiwan. Indeed, since 1979 it has been embedded in US law, with the Taiwan Relations Act (TRA) charging the US with helping to improve the island’s ability to deter an attack from

North Korea’s Kim Jong-un praises ‘new-type weapon’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:33 UTC
01:39:33 KST

North Korean leader Kim Jong-un oversaw the test of a “new-type weapon” system, touting it as evidence of the country’s advancing military technology, state media reported yesterday.
The announcement came two days after South Korea and Japan said Pyongyang launched two short-range ballistic missiles into waters off its east coast, which the countries condemned as threats to regional peace and security.
North Korea has legally enshrined its status as a nuclear-armed state, with its leadership repeatedly declaring the country’s atomic arsenal permanent and irreversible.
Photo: Korean Central News Agency via AFP
The nuclear-armed country’s missile bureau “successfully tested a new type of weapon” on Sunday in the presence of Kim, the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said.
Pyongyang did not specify what the weapon system entailed, but said Kim praised the launch as an “undoubtedly a striking demonstration of ultra-modern defense technology.”
The North Korean leader warned that the advances would give adversaries “an incurable headache and a very cruel and unavoidable blow,” KCNA said.
The Sunday launches came eight days after North Korea fired multiple short-range ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan (known as the “East Sea” in South Korea and the “East Sea of Korea” in North Korea) as part of a joint firepower drill.
That exercise involved long-range artillery and missiles, with the weapons “hitting the targets with 100 percent accuracy,” state media reported.
In yesterday’s KCNA report, Kim linked the Sunday test to the country’s military preparedness, saying: “To acquire such a technology is of weighty significance in the state’s readiness for war and the future development of the armed forces”.
Seoul condemned the launches as a violation of UN Security Council resolutions and urged Pyongyang to halt its ballistic missile activities. Japan lodged a “stern protest” with North Korea over the launches, calling them as a threat to regional peace and security.
Last week, Pyongyang rejected a resolution adopted at the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) demanding it halt its nuclear activities, saying that its nuclear weapons status was “irreversibly and permanently fixed” by its laws.
The North Korean Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson said the IAEA resolution has no effect on its position as a nuclear weapons state.
