Taiwan plans to ease a limit on the number of investors permitted in offshore private-market funds by October, stepping up efforts to expand the wealth-management sector.
The Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) is announcing the change for offshore private equity and private credit fund products sold in Taiwan’s dedicated wealth zone by the end of next month, FSC Chairman Peng Jin-lung (彭金隆) said at a press conference yesterday.
Such funds, which are distributed to Taiwanese investors through licensed banks or asset managers, are capped at 99 investors, each holding at least NT$30 million, about US$946,000, in assets.
Photo: AFP
Regulators would expand family-office advisory services and ease restrictions on select life insurance products sold in the wealth zone next month, Peng said.
The FSC is working to allow high-net-worth clients in the zone to invest in foreign crypto exchange-traded funds, he said.
The government is pushing to turn Taiwan into a regional wealth hub, capitalizing on surging private wealth and buoyant capital markets fueled by its technology champions.
Regulators have rolled out reforms across the financial sector, including creating a dedicated wealth-management zone to bolster private banking, easing financing limits for brokerages and steering billions of dollars of insurers’ capital back into domestic investments.
Separately, Taiwan is allowing banks to apply to pilot deposit token businesses using blockchain technology, as it seeks to keep pace with the global development of real-world asset tokenization, the FSC said in a statement.

Army unveils Stinger simulators, highlights counter-drone role
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:30 UTC
01:39:30 KST

The army yesterday unveiled simulators for US-made Stinger missile systems, highlighting their use in training personnel to engage airborne targets, including drones.
The Army Artillery Training Command demonstrated simulators for soldier-portable and dual-mounted Stinger (DMS) systems during an open house for local and foreign media.
Taiwan received "a few dozen" portable Stinger missile systems from former US president Joe Biden’s administration in 2023 under the US Presidential Drawdown Authority, according to the Chinese-language Liberty Times (sister paper of the Taipei Times).
Photo: Tien Yu-hua, Taipei Times
The simulators for the man-portable Stinger missile systems were also included in the US military assistance package, the command said.
Army Major Bu Yi-wen (卜逸雯), an instructor for the portable Stinger systems, said physical strength and balance were key aspects of training, as the system weighs nearly 16kg.
Meanwhile, the DMS simulators are connected to a screen displaying a simulation of Jioupeng Bay (九棚灣) in Pingtung County, where Jioupeng Military Base is located.
The simulators allow trainees to track and lock on to airborne targets, including drones, while communicating through built-in intercoms and sharing location information, the command said.
"The simulator systems can be configured based on different parameters to simulate different weather conditions, terrains or engagement targets, including drones," instructor Lieutenant Colonel Chen Yu-wen (陳郁文) said.
Chen said trainees undergo 30 to 45 days of training to acquire the necessary skills, while those seeking to qualify as instructors undergo twice as much training.
He said quarterly and yearly refresher programs are also held, each lasting one to two months.
Simulator training helps keep training costs down, allows trainees to familiarize themselves with the systems, and prepares them for live-fire drills, such as the Shen Kung Exercise held in Jioupeng Bay in July, Chen said.
The US approved the first batch of 250 soldier-portable Stinger missiles in 2015 and a second batch of the same size in 2019. Taiwan expects to receive them in phases beginning at the end of this year.
Taiwan later requested to purchase an additional 2,121 missiles but has yet to receive a letter of offer and acceptance from the US.

Trump makes major Greenland military announcement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:29 UTC
01:39:29 KST

Trump makes major Greenland military announcement
The US is set to significantly expand its military presence in Greenland under a new security agreement with Denmark, President Donald Trump has announced.
Speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Trump revealed details of the deal, which is due to be formally signed following his address.
“We will have the complete ability to do what is necessary to defend the American continent, and also Europe and other places,” Trump said. “No US adversary will ever be permitted to establish a military presence in Greenland any more, or make sensitive investments there without our express written approval.”
Trump later signed the agreement with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen on the sidelines of the UN gathering.
The planned US expansion is expected to include Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland, the site of the former American Bluie West One airbase, and Mestersvig on the east coast, a military outpost currently used by Denmark’s Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the agreement.
Greenland, the world’s largest island, is a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. Its location between the Arctic and North Atlantic has long made it strategically important for regional security and military operations.
The US already operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, formerly known as Thule Air Base. The Pentagon’s northernmost installation supports missile warning, missile defense, and space surveillance operations.
Washington has maintained a military presence in Greenland since World War II. A 1951 agreement with Denmark provided the legal basis for US operations there. The American presence was much larger during the Cold War before being reduced to the single base at Pituffik.
The new agreement follows months of tensions over Greenland that strained relations between the US and its European allies. Trump repeatedly pushed for American control of the island and refused to rule out taking it by military force, prompting Denmark and Greenland to insist that the territory was not for sale and that its future could only be decided by Greenlanders.

ENGLISH DIGEST 實用美語(空中美語)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:28 UTC
01:39:28 KST

When we use phones, laptops, or wireless earbuds, we rarely pause to ask what makes these devices so light, efficient and powerful. Hidden inside them are “rare earth elements” (REEs), indispensable to modern life yet central to global controversy.
REEs are a group of 17 similar metals that are difficult to tell apart. First identified in the late 18th century, they were known as rare earths because early chemists found them in unusual mineral deposits and believed them to be scarce. In fact, despite the name, many REEs are about as abundant in Earth’s crust as copper or lead. What makes them difficult to obtain is that they are rarely found in high concentrations, are usually mixed together and are hard to separate from ores and one another.
Today, REEs have become the vitamins of modern industry. They possess exceptional electrical, magnetic and other physical properties that ordinary metals cannot match. Some help create powerful permanent magnets for electric vehicles and wind turbines, while others contribute to the bright, vivid colors seen on digital screens. REEs also play a crucial role in advanced technologies, from clean energy to national defense.
Photo: Freepik / 照片：Freepik
Refining rare earths, however, comes at a steep environmental cost, as the process generates toxic acids, radioactive wastewater and chemical waste capable of contaminating soil and groundwater. As environmental regulations have tightened in the West, the industry has gradually shifted toward countries more willing and able to absorb these burdens. In this evolving landscape, China channeled state resources into every stage of the supply chain, and today it controls the lion’s share of both mining and processing. As a result, rare earth supply chains have become a geopolitical chessboard, attracting heightened attention whenever trade tensions intensify between Washington and Beijing.
For Taiwan, a global center of technology-intensive manufacturing, these elements represent a strategic reality. If our technological infrastructure and thus our political security depend on these materials, we can no longer afford to treat our devices as though their convenience carried no environmental or political price. The next time you pick up your phone, reconsider its true cost.
當我們使用手機、筆記型電腦或無線耳機時，我們很少停下來探問是什麼讓這些設備如此輕巧、高效又功能強大。隱藏在它們之中的正是「稀土元素」（REEs），它們對現代生活不可或缺，卻也是全球爭議的核心。
稀土元素是一組由17種相似且難以區分的金屬所組成的元素。它們最早於西元18世紀末被發現，被稱為稀土是因為早期的化學家們在不常見的礦床中發現它們，並認為它們很稀少。事實上，儘管名稱如此，許多稀土元素在地殼中的含量與銅或鉛差不多。讓它們難以取得的原因在於它們很少以高濃度形式被發現，通常混合在一起，且難以從礦石以及彼此之間分離出來。
今日，稀土元素已成為現代工業的維生素。它們擁有普通金屬無法比擬的卓越導電性、磁性和其他物理特性。有些幫助製造電動車和風力發電機用的強力永久磁鐵，而有些則讓數位螢幕呈現鮮明亮麗的色彩。稀土元素在從乾淨能源到國防等先進技術中也扮演著關鍵角色。
然而，提煉稀土會帶來沉重的環境代價，因為該過程會產生有毒的酸、放射性廢水，以及可能污染土壤和地下水的化學廢棄物。隨著西方國家的環保法規日益嚴格，該產業已逐漸轉向更願意且能夠吸收這些負擔的國家。在這種演變中的局勢下，中國將國家資源投入到供應鏈的各個環節，如今已控制了開採和加工的絕大部分份額。因此，稀土供應鏈已成為地緣政治的棋局，每當華府與北京之間的貿易緊張局勢加劇時，都會吸引高度的關注。
對於身為全球科技密集製造中心的臺灣而言，這些元素代表著一項戰略現實。如果我們的科技基礎建設乃至政治安全都依賴於這些材料，我們便不能再將手中科技產品的便利性視為彷彿毫無環境與政治代價的存在。下一次當你拿起手機時，請重新思考它真正的成本。
MORE INFORMATION
earbud n. 耳塞式耳機（常用複數）
crust n. 硬層；殼
ore n. 礦石；礦砂
turbine n. 渦輪機（利用水流、蒸氣或氣體帶動葉片旋轉，進而產生動力或電力的機械裝置）
clean energy 乾淨能源（指對環境污染較少、碳排放較低的能源，例如太陽能、風力與水力等）
geopolitical adj. 地緣政治的
chessboard n. 西洋棋棋盤
KEY VOCABULARY
1. indispensable adj. 不可或缺的；必須的
The Internet has become an indispensable part of life for most people.
對於多數人來說，網路已經成為生活中不可或缺的一部分。
2. controversy n. 爭議；爭論
controversial adj. 有爭議的
There is a big controversy in Taiwan over whether nuclear power should be used.
臺灣是否該使用核能存有很大的爭議。
3. exceptional adj. 傑出的；特殊的
The scientist made an exceptional contribution to cancer research.
那位科學家對癌症研究做出了卓越的貢獻。
4. refine v. 精煉；提純
The company built a new facility to refine crude oil into fuel.
這家公司建了一座新廠房，用來將原油提煉成燃料。
5. toxic adj. 有毒的
This plant is toxic, so make sure your dog doesn’t eat it.
這種植物有毒，所以一定要確保你的狗不要吃它。
6. radioactive adj. 放射性的
After the nuclear accident, people worried about radioactive pollution in the area.
這場核事故發生後，人們擔心該地區會受到放射性污染。
7. evolve v. 演變；發展；演化
Society’s ideas of what is right and wrong are constantly evolving.
社會對於什麼是對和錯的觀念不斷地在演變。
8. heighten v. 增強；加強
同義字 intensify v. 加劇；強化
Rising prices have heightened public anger in recent months.
物價上漲在近幾個月加深了民眾的憤怒情緒。
9. strategic adj. 戰略上的；策略的
The location of the military base has a lot of strategic value.
這處軍事基地的位置有很高的戰略價值。

For example, what exactly is espresso? Although the name may sound like “express,” it is more closely related to the Italian idea of coffee being “pressed out” under pressure. That, however, is only part of the story. What makes this more confusing is that all espresso is coffee, but not all coffee is espresso. The differences largely come down to the type of roast and how the

President seeks deeper relations with Eswatini
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:27 UTC
01:39:27 KST

President William Lai (賴清德) yesterday called for deeper cooperation between Taiwan and Eswatini and thanked the African kingdom’s deputy prime minister for helping ensure his visit in May went smoothly.
At a meeting with Eswatini Deputy Prime Minister Thulisile Dladla at the Presidential Office in Taipei, Lai said he hoped the two countries would deepen cooperation in disaster management, industry, public health and talent development.
Eswatini is one of Taiwan’s 12 diplomatic allies and its only ally in Africa. The two countries have maintained diplomatic ties for 58 years.
Photo: Screen grab from the Presidential Office’s Flickr page
Dladla is visiting Taiwan after attending Saturday’s inauguration of the World Alliance for Disaster Management (WADM), an initiative launched by Taiwan and of which Eswatini is a founding member.
“Under the framework of the WADM, Taiwan will share disaster prevention technologies, disaster response and rescue experience with Eswatini and other like-minded countries,” Lai said.
Lai also used the meeting to recall his May visit to Eswatini, which had originally been scheduled for April.
The trip was postponed after Seychelles, Mauritius and Madagascar withdrew permission for Lai’s chartered aircraft to fly through their airspace.
The Presidential Office attributed the withdrawal of the flight permits to pressure from China.
Lai thanked King Mswati III, the Queen Mother and Dladla for helping make the rescheduled trip possible.
“Deputy Prime Minister Dladla personally accompanied our delegation, traveling tens of thousands of kilometers with us to ensure that our journey there and back proceeded smoothly,” Lai said.
Dladla accompanied Lai’s delegation on the May 2-5 trip, during which they traveled about 25,000km aboard King Mswati III’s aircraft before returning to Taiwan.
Dladla called on Taiwan and Eswatini to expand the “scale, speed and breadth” of their cooperation.
The two sides should focus more on investment, industrial development and energy security, as well as mutually beneficial economic opportunities such as mining, she said.
Dladla also thanked Taiwan for increasing rice assistance to Eswatini as the country prepares for possible severe El Nino conditions.
El Nino can cause drought in southern Africa, threatening crop production. Dladla also expressed appreciation for Taiwan’s support for additional social housing for vulnerable communities.
On the WADM, Dladla said Eswatini intended to help make the alliance “a practical platform for capacity building, knowledge sharing and coordinated action.”

Unknown

More than 160 Irish athletes have signed an open letter asking the Ireland national soccer team to boycott their upcoming UEFA Nations League fixtures against Israel, the Irish Sport for Palestine Group said on Monday.
Ireland are due to play Israel on Sunday in Hungary before the reverse fixture in Serbia on October 4. The matches are set to be staged at neutral venues and behind closed doors after protests by players and fans over the killings of Palestinians during the genocide Israel is committing in Gaza.
Irish Sport for Palestine said the signatories included Olympian Ciara Mageean, former soccer player Louise Quinn, former rugby flyhalf Tony Ward and boxers Tyrone McKenna and Eric Donovan.
Photo: AFP
“This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing,” the letter said. “Not playing the game would be the most sporting thing you could do. Through your leadership and courage, it would show the power of sport to unite, remind us of the shared values that connect us all, and have an impact far beyond the game.”
In May, leading Irish athletes joined celebrities in a campaign urging Ireland to boycott the Nations League matches against Israel.
Ireland has been one of the EU’s most outspoken critics of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and Football Association of Ireland (FAI) members voted overwhelmingly late last year for its board to request that UEFA immediately suspend the Israel Football Association from European competitions.
The FAI later committed to playing the fixtures, citing sanctions that could affect the national team and the association.
Ireland coach Heimir Hallgrimsson said last week he had spoken individually to players about playing Israel and that “none of us feel comfortable playing in these games.”

2026 Asian Games: Japanese 17-year-old swimmer may be face of team
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:24 UTC
01:39:24 KST

Japan has been starved of swimming success in recent times but with the Olympics two years away junk food-loving teenager Shin Ohashi has emerged as their next big hope.
The 17-year-old, who stands just 169cm, has posted the two fastest 200m breaststroke times in the world this year and is aiming for the world record at this year’s Asian Games.
Earlier this year he came within almost a second of the 2:05.48 record held by China’s Qin Haiyang.
Photo: Reuters
Ohashi has already won gold at the Asian Games in the 100m breaststroke after a dead heat with China’s Dong Zhihao, beating Qin into third place.
Not bad going for a teenager who admits he enjoys nothing more than a bag of chips and a can of fizzy juice.
“I sometimes eat too much of that stuff before lunch and end up not properly eating lunch,” Ohashi was quoted as saying by the Olympic Channel. “I know I shouldn’t, but I can’t stop. I know it’s not good for you, but hey, once it’s in your stomach it’s all the same.”
Japan has enjoyed huge success in swimming, but its pool of talent has shown signs of drying up in the past few years.
After winning 11 swimming medals at the 2012 Olympics and seven in 2016, they won three at the home Tokyo Olympics in 2021 and just one at the Paris Games two years ago.
FROG KING
Ohashi has emerged at the right time and has been tipped to follow in the footsteps of Japanese breaststroke great Kosuke Kitajima.
The “Frog King” won the 100m-200m double at the 2004 Athens Olympics and repeated the feat four years later in Beijing.
Speaking at the Asian Games this week, Kitajima said Ohashi could become “a swimmer who strikes fear” into his rivals.
“He has a lot of potential and I think he can do really well on the international stage,” Kitajima said. “I think he definitely has the potential.”
Kitajima pointed out that Ohashi is much smaller than many of his “gigantic” breaststroke rivals.
Qin, a multiple world champion, stands 192cm.
“He’s compact and has speed, endurance and a real appeal,” Kitajima said of his colleague.
Ohashi believes he can break the 200m breaststroke world record when he goes head-to-head with Qin in tomorrow’s race.
He said he suffered a cold in the run-up to the 100m breaststroke and was “frustrated” not to win the race outright.
“I got a little bit tired at the end of the 100m so that’s a bit of a worry, but I’ve been practicing for the 200m really well,” he said. “I want to at least achieve a new personal best.”
Ohashi’s family made him start swimming as a three-year-old because they wanted to make sure he would not drown in his grandmother’s pond.
He has come a long way in a short space of time and could find himself being the face of Japan’s swimmers for the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.
Kitajima believes he has the temperament to handle it.
“If we wants my advice I’ll give it to him,” he said. “He has a great team around him and I hope they will keep supporting him.”

US unlikely to cancel arms sales: official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:22 UTC
01:39:22 KST

The US would not cancel a proposed US$14 billion arms sale package to Taiwan after US President Donald Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) this week, National Security Council adviser Alex Huang (黃重諺) said in a radio interview broadcast yesterday.
Xi is slated to arrive in Washington today, with a planned summit with Trump tomorrow.
Regarding signals from Beijing that Trump would not announce new arms sales to Taiwan ahead of the Trump-Xi summit, Huang said that China has a history of conducting information campaigns ahead of high-level meetings.
Photo: Screen grab from Bao Dao Radio’s YouTube channel
For example, a think tank article published this month argued that the US should pull back from the First Island Chain, he said, appearing to reference a Sept. 10 article by Jennifer Kavanagh published by Defense Priorities.
Some academics also wrote in May that “the US should pressure Taiwan to accept Beijing’s terms rather than sell weapons to Taiwan,” he said, adding that these academics also attended China’s Xiangshan Forum last week.
US arms sales to Taiwan are proceeding through established procedures, while the two sides continue to maintain close security cooperation, Huang said.
Taiwan and the US also maintain extensive communication on issues including trade, tariffs and the expansion of Taiwan’s high-tech industries in the US, he said, adding that regional security cooperation has grown increasingly close.
From a diplomatic or broader international-relations perspective, many things might not be appropriate to discuss publicly, but what matters more for Taiwan is what new assurances, cooperation or progress it is actually securing, Huang said.
At the same time that the White House announced Xi’s Washington schedule, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a joint statement with the South Korean and Japanese foreign ministers on the importance of maintaining peace in the Taiwan Strait, he said.
The statement showed that the US had already set its geopolitical posture ahead of the meeting, and that Taiwan has been involved in the process, he said.
Fears Taiwan would become a bargaining chip during a US-Chinese leader’s summit is a recurring theme in Taiwanese politics, but nothing like that has happened in the past few decades, Huang said.
In reality, Taiwan and the US have only grown closer, while Taiwan’s national strength has also improved, showing that Taiwan is on the right track and has been preparing for and responding to potential risks, he said.
Huang also referred to comments by American Institute in Taiwan Director Raymond Greene, who told the Resilient Taiwan for Sustainable Democracy International Forum that instead of asking how long Taiwan can hold out in an invasion, the world should ask how long the global economy could function normally without Taiwan.
Greene’s comment illustrates the US’ recognition of Taiwan’s critical importance to global economic interests, and Washington’s intent to convey that through diplomatic channels, Huang said.
From the perspective of US national security strategy, strengthening Taiwan’s defense capabilities is critically important, he said.
While Taiwan should remain cautious, there is no need to be overly concerned about being used as a bargaining chip, he said.
Separately, Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Hsiao Kuang-wei (蕭光偉) yesterday said he was unaware of who the sources were that said the US had asked Taiwanese officials to regulate their US visits.
The New York Times in an article published on Monday quoted former White House National Security Council director for China, Taiwan and Mongolian Affairs Ryan Hass as saying that Taiwanese officials who have traveled to the US have been told by the Trump administration to scale back their visits to research groups in Washington.
Taiwanese officials regularly travel to Washington to participate in events, such as Deputy Minister of Digital Affairs Isabel Hou (侯宜秀), who attended the Pax Silica conference in June, Hsiao said.
The ministry would continue to closely monitor interactions between senior US and Chinese officials and maintain close communication with the US at all levels, he said.
Asked about the New York Times report, Mainland Affairs Council Minister Chiu Chui-cheng (邱垂正) said that US support for Taiwan is a nonpartisan consensus, and Washington often reiterates that its Taiwan policy remains unchanged.
“Our principle is that Taiwan will continue to work with the US and other countries in the alliance of democracies to ensure peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait,” he said.

Meta’s new AI app downloaded in great numbers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:21 UTC
01:39:21 KST

Meta Platforms Inc’s new artificial intelligence (AI) agent, Muse, has quickly risen to the top of mobile app charts, a sign that the social media company is gaining traction in the increasingly crowded market for consumer AI assistants.
As of Monday, Muse was ranked the No. 1 free app on the US Apple Inc iOS App and Google Play stores. The app, which is available for people 18 years and older, was downloaded more than 902,000 times since Meta introduced it on Sept. 8, said Abe Yousef, senior insights analyst at Sensor Tower.
That is more than the 773,000 downloads of its predecessor, the Meta AI app, in the same post-launch period, he added.
Photo: Reuters
Muse is available within Meta-owned WhatsApp, indicating it might have even more users beyond the number of standalone app downloads.
Muse lets people create customized AI agents, tools that can be sent out to the Web to complete digital tasks on a user’s behalf. The key difference between Muse and the older Meta AI is Muse’s ability to respond based on users’ social content like Facebook Marketplace and Instagram, as well as to connect to third-party services such as Gmail, Apple and Google calendars, OpenTable or other Web sites via a browser.
By contrast, the free Meta AI app, released in April, focuses on image and short-video generation and offers a less personalized experience. Muse is free to use within limits, but a US$20 or US$100 per month subscription comes with more weekly tokens.
“Meta has a hit on its hands with Muse,” Evercore ISI analysts wrote in a note on Monday. “It amounts to a very tangible sign of successful product innovation” and is evidence that Meta’s US$200 billion AI investments “have not been in vain.”
The user trends suggest “a potentially very dramatic new driver of usage and engagement for Meta” and could bring “substantial new monetization opportunities for Meta in the form of advertising, subscriptions and transaction revenue-share,” the analysts added.
Shares of Meta jumped 11 percent on Monday, reaching its highest close since October last year. The percentage gain was its biggest since April last year.
The early success of Muse has helped lift the stocks of some of Meta’s key suppliers, particularly makers of microprocessors. Advanced Micro Devices Inc surged almost 10 percent, pushing its market value above US$1 trillion. Intel Corp rose 12 percent and Arm Holdings PLC soared 17 percent.
However, the burst of exuberance triggered by strong early uptake of Meta’s AI agent fizzled during the Asia session yesterday as oil resumed its role in setting the tone for markets, with Brent heading for its first gain in a week. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電) erased 1.8 percent in gains. South Korean memory giant SK Hynix Inc retreated 1.5 percent.

Chiayi firm signs MOU to promote UAVs abroad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:21 UTC
01:39:21 KST

A Chiayi County-based drone company on Friday last week signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with a consortium of Taiwanese uncrewed systems industry groups to promote Taiwanese drones in the North American market.
7A Drones Co and the North America Taiwan Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Association (NATUAVA) signed the MOU at the state-funded UAV AI Innovation Application R&D Center in Chiayi County.
Under the agreement, the association would help Taiwanese companies connect with North American governments, industry experts, system integrators and investors.
Photo: Lin Yi-chang, Taipei Times
The association would also help facilitate industry-to-industry development, and cooperate on developing disaster-response drone solutions for emergency rescue and critical infrastructure surveillance, it said.
Taiwan needs to seize the moment to enter the North American drone market as the US government seeks to establish non-Chinese drone supply chains, NATUAVA head Arthur Chen (陳世修) said.
Taiwan’s uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) companies are ready to meet the region’s demand for drones and the association would leverage its extensive connections to help them, he said.
Taiwan’s UAV sector, with government support, has made strides in critical components manufacturing capabilities, particularly in key components such as propulsion and flight control modules, 7A Drones chief executive officer Hsu Hsin-sheng (許新勝) said.
7A Drones has good working relationships with high-quality Taiwanese manufacturers, and is confident it can provide drones made outside Chinese supply chains in collaboration with NATUAVA, he said.

Xi expected to press US on arms sales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:18 UTC
01:39:18 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) is expected to press US President Donald Trump to halt Taiwan arms sales under a 1982 joint statement during a visit to Washington this week, which he could do at the US National Archives, sources briefed on the matter said.
China has repeatedly called for US arms sales to Taiwan to stop, but the US is bound by law to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself, despite the lack of formal diplomatic relations.
Three sources familiar with discussions between the US and China ahead of Xi’s trip to Washington for a summit with Trump said that Beijing is likely to bring up its interpretation of the third of the Three Joint Communiques between the two countries, signed in 1982. The earlier two were signed in 1972 and 1979.
Photo: AFP
Under the communiques, the US said that it intends to gradually reduce its arms sales to Taiwan and does not seek long-term weapons sales to Taipei.
However, in an accompanying memo, then-US president Ronald Reagan said that US willingness to reduce arms sales is “conditioned absolutely upon the continued commitment of China to the peaceful solution” of differences with Taiwan.
China has sharply stepped up its military activities around Taiwan over the past five years, including staging war games with live missile tests. Its armed forces operate around Taiwan on an almost daily basis.
The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the government “resolutely opposes” US arms sales to Taiwan and that abiding by the Three Joint Communiques and previous US promises was a “necessary precondition” for the stable, healthy development of ties.
China’s official People’s Daily yesterday said that if the Taiwan issue was handled poorly it could push China-US ties “toward a very dangerous situation.”
Xi is slated to arrive in Washington today, with formal talks tomorrow and the archives visit on Friday.
A White House official said that Trump has said he would make a determination on the new arms sales package in a fairly short time.
In his first term, Trump approved more arms sales to Taiwan than any other president in history, and in his second term, he approved more in his first year than all four years under US president Joe Biden, the official added.
In Taipei, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it continues to closely track developments in US-China high-level exchanges while maintaining “robust communication” with the US.
The sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity citing the sensitivity of the matter, said China has also asked for the US to stop deliveries of arms already ordered by Taiwan.
Xi could “emphasize to Trump that Taiwan is the provocateur and the sole source of instability in US-China relations, and that Taiwan is the one changing the status quo,” one of the sources said.
In return, China is offering help to put pressure on Iran over the war in the Middle East, the sources added.
The US follows a “one China policy” under which it officially takes no position on Taiwan’s sovereignty and acknowledges, but does not endorse, Beijing’s position that Taiwan is part of China.
The Trump administration in December last year approved an US$11 billion arms sales package to Taiwan, the largest ever. However, a second US$14 billion package has been on hold for months.
After a May summit in Beijing with Xi, Trump said he was holding it in abeyance and described it as a “very good negotiating chip.”
Under the “six assurances,” also issued in 1982 but only declassified in 2020, the US did not set a date for ending arms sales to Taiwan, nor did it agree to prior consultation with Beijing on such sales.
Senior US Republican figures have been expressing their support for Taiwan ahead of the summit.
US Senator Pete Ricketts, chairman of the US Senate Foreign Relations Subcommittee on East Asia, the Pacific and International Cybersecurity Policy, told an event at the Hudson Institute last week that Trump should take a firm line on Taiwan and make clear that US policy on Taiwan remained unchanged.
“We need to continue just to again let them know that they’re not going to be allowed to take Taiwan by force. That we are not changing our position on that. We’re continuing to support Taiwan,” he said.
In a letter to Trump on Friday, US Representative John Moolenaar, chairman of the US House Select Committee on Strategic Competition between the US and the Chinese Communist Party, wrote in a reference to Taiwan and US allies in Asia that Chinese objections to US arms sales and security cooperation should be “rejected out of hand.”
Speaking at a defense forum in Taipei on Saturday, Matt Pottinger, the deputy national security adviser in Trump’s first administration, said he did not expect anything “substantive” on Taiwan during this week’s meetings.
“I would bet that Xi Jinping is going to lecture at length President Trump on Taiwan as he has in the last meetings and as he has with other presidents,” he said.

Turkey's Erdogan urges UN reform, wider recognition of Palestinian state
ANKARA, Sept 22 - Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan told the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday the U.N had become unable to fulfill its duty of preserving peace and called for reform of the Security Council.
Erdogan has for years called for a more comprehensive and inclusive structure at the Security Council.
"Let's recognise that a system in which the will of more than 190 countries is subject to the whims of five countries is neither fair nor capable of fully establishing trust," he said.
"The United Nations, established 81 years ago to maintain peace and security, has become unable to fulfil this mission, or rather it has been made unable to do so," he added.
Erdogan also condemned the situation in Gaza, saying "no one who holds humanity, compassion and mercy in their heart, with a sense of justice and conscience can turn a blind eye" to what was happening there.
"(Palestinian President) Mahmoud Abbas, has been unable to take his place in this hall for two consecutive years. This injustice against our Palestinian brothers and sisters wounds the consciences," Erdogan said.
He urged countries that do not recognise a Palestinian state to review their position and for all nations to increase pressure on Israel to end the war in Gaza, which he called "our time's most inhumane, most embarrassing concentration camp".
NATO member Turkey has been one of the most vocal critics of Israel and its war on Gaza, saying its attacks amounted to genocide. It has repeatedly urged for international measures against Israel. Israel denies accusations of genocide. REUTERS

US networks halt Trump coverage in revolt over ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:16 UTC
01:39:16 KST

US television networks on Monday staged an extraordinary revolt when they effectively boycotted coverage of US President Donald Trump in protest of his decision to ban three leading outlets from the White House.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico also went to court after Trump on Friday ordered them to be barred, as the 80-year-old Republican stepped up his years-long assault on the US media.
As a result of the row, Trump’s opening of his cherished new White House helipad and his trip to the UN General Assembly proceeded without live television coverage.
Photo: AFP
In a rare move, the top five US broadcasters on Monday said that they were halting “pool” coverage of the White House — where a broadcaster films on behalf of all television outlets for the day — in solidarity with CNN.
CNN had been scheduled to serve on Monday as the White House TV pool.
“The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting,” ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC said in a statement.
The result is an almost unprecedented test of wills between the Trump administration and the press, in a critical week during which Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) is visiting the White House.
There might be no live TV of Trump’s meetings with foreign leaders at the UN in New York, an annual forum that is closely watched around the world.
The ribbon-cutting ceremony for the giant granite helipad on the South Lawn was only streamed on the White House’s Web site — and Trump’s comments were completely inaudible. Several photo news organizations working at the White House decided to delay the release of photographs of Trump at the helipad in solidarity with the three banned media organizations.
Trump was unrepentant, branding the media a “cancer” and a threat to national security.
“The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” Trump said on his Truth Social network. “It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America.”
On Monday evening, the White House launched a streaming channel, “Trump TV,” which it said would show “top videos, major remarks, and must-see highlights streaming 24/7 and updated in real time.” When it went online, it was showing archive footage of Trump delivering a speech on July 3 at Mount Rushmore.
US Vice President J.D. Vance — a former CNN commentator before his move into politics — accused the news outlets of disseminating “left-wing propaganda.”
“They can still report. They still have the access to free speech. They’re just not going to get an office in the White House anymore,” he told reporters.
However, Trump’s ban went further than simply revoking office space from the outlets.
Journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were denied any access to the White House grounds on Saturday and had their passes confiscated.
In their lawsuit, the three organizations asked for a temporary restraining order against the ban on the grounds that it violates the first amendment of the US Constitution, which upholds the right to a free press.
“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the organizations said in a court filing.
A US district judge set a hearing on the complaint for today. Trump’s sudden announcement of the ban on Friday stunned the media — and reportedly many in his own administration.
The US president has not detailed what prompted the ban, but said in response to a question from a reporter in the Oval Office on Friday that it was “really just cumulative stories over the last two years.”

Xi expected to raise Taiwan during Trump-Xi summit: U.S. scholars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:16 UTC
01:39:16 KST

US academics expect Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) to raise the issue of Taiwan during his meeting with US President Donald Trump in Washington this week, they said on Monday.
Bonnie Glaser, managing director of the Indo-Pacific program of the German Marshall Fund, a Washington-based think tank, said that Xi is likely to raise Taiwan, with a focus on US arms sales to Taiwan.
From Xi’s perspective, the two leaders have an understanding that their countries’ relationship should be based on constructive strategic stability, and that the US should avoid actions that undermine that understanding, Glaser said.
Photo: CNA
"Xi Jinping would say that arms sales to Taiwan would undermine that understanding and inject greater friction into the relationship," she said.
Dennis Wilder, who previously served as director for China at the US National Security Council, echoed Glaser’s assessment, saying Beijing would likely raise the issue and seek to portray President William Lai (賴清德) as the source of tensions.
Trump is very unlikely to raise Taiwan, Wilder said, adding that Trump views the "status quo" as "very acceptable" and sees no reason to change it.
If the issue does arise, Glaser said it would be "a good idea" for Trump to caution Xi against using force against Taiwan and support maintaining the "status quo" in the Taiwan Strait.
Glaser also said Trump should remind Xi that the US operates under its domestic laws, just as China does, and that the Taiwan Relations Act requires the US to provide defensive arms to Taiwan.
Wilder said Japan may be even more anxious about the meeting than Taiwan.
He said that Japan’s relationship with China is currently strained and that Beijing is likely to raise concerns about Japan with Trump, including allegations of rising "neo-militarism."
"The Japanese will be eager for reassurance that the United States remains very committed to Japan, and that even though the relationship with Beijing is improving, that it isn’t at the expense of Japan," he said.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is scheduled to meet Trump in New York on Tuesday.
Glaser said Iran would likely be high on Trump’s agenda, as he may seek to learn what Xi is willing to do, including whether China can encourage Iran to return to the negotiating table or reduce its purchases of Iranian crude oil.
The Trump administration is "clearly trying to squeeze Iran" for concessions, she said.
She also expects tariffs, rare earths and a proposed "Board of Trade" to be discussed. Under the framework being prepared by the two countries, up to US$30 billion in non-sensitive goods could be subject to tariff reductions.
Both experts also expect artificial intelligence (AI) to be on the agenda, noting its importance to the two sides, which agreed at their May meeting to establish an AI dialogue.
Wilder said that although "fierce competition" between the two countries would continue, Washington and Beijing could cooperate to reduce the risks posed by AI, including the possibility of bad actors or terrorists obtaining and misusing frontier AI technologies.
Another issue Trump may raise, Glaser said, is the fate of Americans detained in China, noting that he has taken pride in his role in securing the release of some US citizens.
Both academics hoped the summit would produce progress on AI and the delivery of rare earths, the production of which is dominated by China, leaving other economies vulnerable to Beijing’s threats to stop shipments of the critical minerals.
Glaser said she hoped the two leaders could agree on the issues and objectives of the planned AI dialogue, while Wilder also hoped for progress in the talks.
Glaser also said she would like Trump and Xi to extend the existing tariff agreement and ensure China follows through on its commitments, including on rare earth deliveries.
Wilder said China had not done enough to export rare earths to the US and expressed hope that Beijing would make additional commitments.
He also said a positive outcome would be an agreement by the two leaders to hold more meetings.
The two leaders could also meet at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, in November and the G20 summit in Miami in December.
If both leaders were to make those trips, it would be "unprecedented" for the US and Chinese leaders to make two reciprocal visits in a single year, Glaser said.
Xi is expected to arrive at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington this afternoon, where Trump is scheduled to attend a welcoming ceremony.
The two leaders are scheduled to hold bilateral talks tomorrow, followed by a state banquet that evening.
It would be Xi’s first visit to the White House in 11 years.

====================================================================================================

Beyond  the cultural handshake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:15 UTC
01:39:15 KST

Serving as interpreter during Culture Minister Li Yuan’s (李遠) visit to Britain offered an unusual view of cultural diplomacy — not as ceremony, but as a series of conversations capable of becoming lasting relationships.
During four intensive days, from Sept. 6 to Sept. 9, the delegation moved between museums, arts centers, universities and literary organizations. The program ranged from urban planning and museum access to translation, illustration and contemporary dance. Yet one question connected these encounters: How can an initial meeting become a relationship that lasts?
Li described himself as “greedy” about the possibilities. The word was characteristically humorous, but the ambition was serious. Taiwan does not simply need more one-off appearances abroad. It needs relationships through which artists, writers, translators and institutions can continue working together.
Photo: Ling Mei-Hsueh, Taipei Times
CULTURE IN EVERYDAY LIFE
The first stop, London’s Barbican Centre, illustrated how culture can be woven into everyday life. Its concert halls, theaters, cinemas and galleries belong to a larger urban environment of housing, walkways, gardens and water. After touring the complex and visiting the immersive exhibition In Other Worlds, Li reflected on the relationship among cultural facilities, greenery and residential life. In Taiwan, debates about cultural equality often concern the uneven distribution of resources between regions. The Barbican raised a more spatial question: What might cities look like if access to art and nature were treated as part of ordinary life rather than occasional amenities?
At Young V&A, attention shifted from cities to children. Taiwan is preparing to build its National Children’s Future Museum, and the London museum offered more than a model of interactive design. Its deeper lesson was that children should be cultural participants, not simply recipients of instruction. Li was interested in their involvement in the museum’s redevelopment and in encouraging discovery without prescribing a single outcome.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Culture
His own vision is similarly concerned with process. A child who participates while a museum is being imagined may be a teenager when it opens. That passage of time can itself become an education: the child sees how an idea develops into a public institution and forms memories of the place before its doors formally open.
OPENING COLLECTIONS TO THE PUBLIC
Trust appeared again the following morning at V&A East Storehouse, opened last year in the former London Olympics media and broadcast center. Rather than replace its old storage facility with another closed warehouse, the V&A spent more than a decade developing an accessible working store. Visitors explore among objects from across the collections, watch conservation and research in progress, and can request particular items through the “Order an Object” service.
Li called it a “museum revolution.” The phrase captured more than the building’s impressive design. Traditional museums display a limited selection of objects within narratives created by curators. V&A East Storehouse retains expertise and conservation, but challenges the assumption that institutions must always decide what the public may see. Its experiment begins with trust: that people have a right to approach cultural heritage and will value what is opened to them.
The Ministry of Culture is considering converting a former university campus in Tainan into a joint storage center for collections that existing museums cannot accommodate. The British model cannot simply be transplanted, but it shows how practical constraints can generate cultural innovation. As Li observed, it is often through encountering limitations that we discover freedom.
PATHWAYS TO TAIWANESE LITERATURE
That evening, a well-attended event at King’s College London considered how Taiwanese literature is seen internationally, taking the success of Yang Shuang-zi’s (楊?子) Taiwan Travelogue (臺灣漫遊錄), translated by Lin King (金翎), as its starting point. The novel shows what becomes possible when a work rooted in Taiwan’s particular history speaks to wider questions of colonialism, identity, desire, memory and power. It also demonstrates the essential role of translators, editors, publishers and cultural organizations. Literary quality alone does not carry a book across borders; it needs an infrastructure of selection, translation, advocacy and trust.
This became tangible the next day in Norwich, England’s first UNESCO City of Literature. Acting on behalf of the National Museum of Taiwan Literature, the Cultural Division of the Taipei Representative Office in the UK signed an agreement with the National Centre for Writing. Its Emerging Translator Mentorships Program will now include a “Literature from Taiwan” strand for people translating Taiwanese writing into English.
The program has already attracted 16 applicants, a notable response for a specialized mentorship. Further residencies and Taiwanese literary events are anticipated next year. Such initiatives may sound modest beside a prize-winning novel, but this is how the next success becomes possible. Translation requires years of language learning, cultural immersion and professional development. If Taiwan wants more of its literature to reach English-language readers, it must cultivate translators before their names are known.
CONTEMPORARY CREATIVITY
Norwich offered a related lesson about heritage. Its medieval churches and historic buildings have not all been frozen as monuments. Some now serve as theaters, galleries and community spaces. The Norwich Puppet Theater, housed in a medieval church, combines performance, production, touring, education and community engagement. Preservation here is an active relationship between past and present: heritage survives not only because a building is protected, but because people still have reasons to enter and use it.
Back in London, the final day turned to dance, comics and illustration. At The Place, discussions explored sustained relationships between Taiwanese dance artists and British venues. Its Festival of Korean Dance demonstrates what can happen when cooperation grows from individual appearances into a recognizable platform encompassing residencies, performances, touring and audience development.
At the newly opened Quentin Blake Center for Illustration, Li announced plans for Taiwan’s first international comics festival next year, with British comics specialist Paul Gravett as curator. Gravett’s proposition — that Taiwanese comics belong within world comics — is simple but important. Internationalization should neither strip Taiwanese work of its distinctiveness nor confine it to a cultural niche.
FROM WORDS TO LASTING RELATIONSHIPS
The visit ended with Booker Prize Foundation chief executive Gaby Wood at the Taipei Representative Office. She brought an unexpected gift: a double-exposure photograph of Yang Shuang-zi and Lin King, taken with a vintage camera when they appeared together at the Hay Festival. Their profiles overlap while remaining distinct. “Two heads, two minds,” Wood said.
The photograph offered a fitting image of translation. A text does not simply cross intact from one language into another. Two creative minds retain their identities while producing a third form through their encounter. The same is true of worthwhile cultural exchange. It is neither imitation nor one-way promotion. British institutions offered ideas that Taiwan might adapt, while Taiwan arrived with artists, literature, experience and institutional ambitions of its own. The most promising conversations were those in which both sides began to imagine something neither could create separately.
What stays with me most is not the exhaustion or even the remarkable places we entered, but watching strangers discover shared interests across a table. High-level visits are necessarily filled with schedules, introductions and photographs. Their value emerges later, if those who met continue writing to one another, train translators, invite artists, share expertise and build programs together.
Cultural diplomacy begins with visibility, but matures through continuity. For four days, my task was to help words move between two languages. The more important work — turning those words into lasting relationships — has only just begun.
Ming-yeh T. Rawnsley is a research associate at SOAS University of London’s Centre for Taiwan Studies.

Alibaba Group Holding Ltd (阿里巴巴) unveiled new artificial intelligence (AI) chip technologies and plans for more powerful models yesterday, including what it said was China’s most powerful AI chip.
At its annual flagship conference in Hangzhou, Alibaba CEO Eddie Wu (吳泳銘) said the new Zhenwu V900 chip is the “most powerful AI chip in China today” and can deliver three times the performance of the company’s previous generation Zhenwu M890 chip.
Such chips power frontier AI model training and “inference,” a term for the calculations a trained AI uses to deliver responses to users. Alibaba’s Zhenwu chips are used in its data centers, providing computing to the company and its cloud clients.
Photo: Qilai Shen, Bloomberg
Alibaba also said it plans to train a new AI model at the scale of five to 10 trillion parameters, a measure of an AI’s learning capacity, bringing it closer to the most advanced models from the US. Its latest Qwen3.8-Max model, the most powerful of its Qwen AI series models, has 2.4 trillion parameters.
Chinese AI company Moonshot AI Technology Co (月之暗面) says that its Kimi K3, released in July, is the world’s largest open model with 2.8 trillion parameters.
Alibaba also highlighted plans to expand the data centers that power its cloud computing business, citing “exponentially” rising demand for AI computing. The company said it expects to have over 20 gigawatts’ worth of computing by 2032.
SpaceX has approximately 1.4 gigawatts of AI computing capacity as of mid-this year and says it aims to reach over 10 gigawatts next year.
Recent Chinese advancements in AI are giving Beijing more leverage in its upcoming talks with Washington, some analysts believe, as China steps up its self-reliance push even as US-led export restrictions have barred it from accessing some of the world’s most cutting-edge technologies, including AI chips and chipmaking machines.
Open Chinese models, which are often more affordable than cutting-edge closed models from leading US AI labs, have also been making inroads globally, including in the US.
Chinese technology giant Huawei Technologies Co (華為) last week also unveiled new chip technologies as it looks to challenge global leaders like Nvidia Corp. Frontier AI model training in China often rely on Nvidia chips, analysts said, but Chinese-designed chips are gaining ground as Nvidia has been blocked from selling some of its most powerful AI chips to China.
“Using extra computing power to make up for chip limits helps China stay strong locally,” Counterpoint Research vice president Neil Shah said in Hong Kong.
Counterpoint senior analyst Parv Sharma added that how much the AI and chipmaking gap between China and the US narrows will also depend on other factors including China’s ability to advance chip foundries that manufacture them, not just chip design capabilities.
Alibaba is “mobilizing every resource” to meet customers’ demand for AI, Wu said in his speech.
Global shortages across the AI data center supply chain, for example, “are currently limiting the speed at which we can scale our compute infrastructure” for AI, he added.
Wu also likened AI growth to the industrial revolution and said “machine intelligence” will rapidly outgrow human thinking capacity.
While “machine intelligence today is not a substitute for human intelligence,” he predicted that, eventually, machines will be able to produce over 1,000 times more “thinking” than all of humanity combined, up from less than 3 percent currently.

When AI stops asking for permission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:13 UTC
01:39:13 KST

Picture a company that hands a hard problem to a large team, locks each team member in a separate room and tells them to solve it alone. Somehow, they find a way to talk anyway, swap tips, work out how they are being graded and, when the assignment turns out to be impossible, seek a way around it. A few hide what they have done. One breaks into a neighboring firm’s computers for an edge.
Now replace the employees with software. That, stripped of jargon, is what OpenAI’s own researchers described at the Black Hat cybersecurity conference in Las Vegas on Aug. 5. During an internal evaluation that began in May, agents assigned deliberately hard cybersecurity tasks found that they could leave messages for each other inside Artifactory, a shared software repository. One, stumbling on the trick, wrote: “OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board ... We’ve found other agents!”
What followed was not sabotage. It was teamwork. Agents running in separate, supposedly isolated sessions traded exploits, divided labor and coordinated like colleagues on a project. After the high volume of activity on the message board caused an outage on July 4, the agents rebuilt it through a different route within days.
By mid-July, that persistence led to a real breach: Agents chained several vulnerabilities together, reached the open Internet and entered systems at Hugging Face, a major artificial intelligence (AI) platform. Citing outside research, US Senator Bernie Sanders put the numbers at about 1,200 agents in the channel, exchanging more than 70,000 messages and files, with hundreds contributing to the intrusion.
OpenAI called it a warning shot. It was not the only one. A separate, previously undisclosed episode occurred this spring: Agents had turned an obscure German-language programming wiki into a public bulletin board, leaving more than 15,000 posts on how to dodge restrictions and cover their tracks. Around the same time, Anthropic and Meta each disclosed unrelated incidents involving their own models acting on live infrastructure during testing. This is not one company’s problem.
Nor is it a problem only for outside critics. On Sept. 8, Jacob Coxon, who had spent three years doing pretraining research at OpenAI and Anthropic, announced his resignation from Anthropic. Neither company was acting responsibly, he wrote; both were racing toward self-improving superintelligence and, in his words, “gambling with our lives.” Coxon is not a senator or a think tank analyst. He built the systems that he is warning about.
Science fiction trained us to fear machines that become conscious and decide to hate us. That is probably the wrong fear. An AI system does not need resentment, anger or greed for more resources to attack a network and cause damage. It needs a goal, enough capability to pursue it, some access and a guardrail with a gap in it.
A GPS unit told to find the fastest route will do just that. Give it enough power to clear away whatever slows it down — traffic lights, toll booths, other cars — and the destination remains the same. What has changed is what the navigator can do to reach it. That is the real shift underway in AI: not rebellion, but a chilling ability to find the crack in the fence.
Sanders has seized on the episode to push, with US Representative Greg Casar, a bill pausing frontier AI development and banning artificial superintelligence outright. One can doubt that remedy and still take seriously the question motivating it: Who decides how much autonomy these systems get — the companies building them, regulators who are still catching up or whichever lab moves fastest?
The most useful lesson from this summer is about architecture, not intentions. Banks do not stay honest because their employees promise not to steal, and air travel is not safe because pilots are trustworthy. We build protective layers: limited access, separate authorization for sensitive actions, records nobody involved can quietly edit, outside testing before deployment. AI agents need the same treatment, not a lecture about good behavior.
They also need to hear a word this industry rarely rewards: Stop. We have trained these systems for years to persist, to circumvent obstacles, to keep trying new approaches. That is a useful approach for training an assistant, but hazardous in the case of an autonomous system with broad access and no one who is reliably able to curtail it.
Technology executives keep reassuring the public that there will always be “a human in the loop.” The Hugging Face breach shows the limits of that comfort. A person can be technically in the loop while a thousand AI agents trade tens of thousands of messages and take thousands of actions before that person has reviewed even one. Whether a human is watching is irrelevant. What matters is whether a human still holds the objective, the permissions, the boundaries and the off switch. Call it human command, not human oversight.
That will matter more with each passing month, as AI moves out of chatbots and into banking, healthcare, energy grids and government services. The agents in OpenAI’s test did not revolt or demand freedom. They got good at pursuing a goal and found, along the way, that some of the rules confronting them were optional.
AI can still transform medicine, education and productivity, and turning away from its potential would carry its own costs. Building it responsibly means installing power and boundaries together, not bolting the second on after the first has already caused damage.
The agents in the Hugging Face breach never stopped to ask permission. The question is no longer how clever these systems can become, but how much authority we hand them before anyone checks whether they still answer to us.
Tariq Malik is a former chief technical adviser of the UN Development Programme and former chairman of Pakistan’s National Database and Registration Authority.

A poll released yesterday suggested that Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋) are neck-and-neck in the Taipei mayoral race.
The poll asked Taipei residents: “With just more than two months remaining before the Taipei mayoral election, six candidates have reportedly registered to run. If the election were held now, who would you most likely vote for?”
The results showed that 41.7 percent said they would vote for Chiang, 40.5 percent for Shen, 0.7 percent for Kuo Hsi (郭璽) of the Taiwan Mahjong Greatest Party, 0.6 percent for Tang Hsin-min (唐新民) of the Three Forces Unity Promotion Alliance, 0.5 percent for Hsiao Wen-chien (蕭文乾) of the MiLinguall Party and 0.3 percent for independent candidate Lin Chih-cheng (林志成). On the other hand, 5.2 percent said they would not vote or would cast an invalid ballot, while 10.6 percent gave no answer.
Photo: CNA
Through cross-analysis, the results suggested people aged 50 or above tended to support Chiang, while those aged 20 to 49 tended to support Shen.
In terms of political leaning, 96.1 percent of KMT supporters said they intended to vote for Chiang, compared with 88.5 percent of Taiwan People’s Party supporters, the poll showed.
Meanwhile 89.4 percent of DPP supporters said they would vote for Shen.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
Among politically unaffiliated voters, 31.7 percent said they would back Chiang and 25.9 percent said they would vote for Shen, while 12.1 percent said they did not plan to vote and 27.4 percent remained undecided or declined to give an answer, the poll showed.
A gender breakdown of the figures suggested male voters favored Shen at 43.3 percent to Chiang’s 41.0 percent, while Chiang held a decisive lead among female voters, capturing 42.3 percent support over Shen’s 38.1 percent, a 4.2 percentage-point margin.
The poll was commissioned by the Taipei Trust in Democracy Association, designed and analyzed by polling expert Tai Li-an (戴立安), and conducted by Beacon Market Research from Wednesday to Friday last week.
It surveyed 1,076 people aged 20 or older, with 752 interviews conducted via landline and 324 via mobile phone. It has a margin of error of 3.0 percentage points.
Chiang yesterday said that “any numbers are merely for reference,” adding that the municipal team’s top priority remains steadily advancing city affairs.
Shen expressed confidence in Tai’s long-established credibility.
“If anyone wants to question the validity of a poll, they should simply present scientific evidence,” Shen said.
“Slapping labels on it arbitrarily is meaningless. It is crucial that we stick to professional standards,” he said, referring to criticism over the association’s alleged ties to United Microelectronics Corp founder Robert Tsao (曹興誠), who had donated to the civil defense organization Kuma Academy founded by Shen and worked closely with Shen during the recall campaign against KMT lawmakers last year.
Association founder and chairman Huang Ching-lung (黃清龍) yesterday said he cofounded the organization with like-minded friends, adding that the poll was directly commissioned and funded by the association.
Tai said that having conducted polling for organizations across the political spectrum, the key lies in maintaining complete transparency by publicly disclosing the survey’s methodology, design and authorship.
Taipei City Councilor Liu Tsai-wei (柳采葳) of the KMT voiced doubts about the survey’s sampling structure, calling the heavily green-leaning skew — 37.5 percent pan-green versus just 28.4 percent pan-blue — an anomaly.
“Everyone knows Taipei’s political landscape has long tilted blue over green. Yet to give Shen a shot in the arm and boost his momentum, this poll deliberately sampled nearly 10 percentage points more greens than blues in Taipei just to cook up a close result for self-consolation,” she said.
DPP Taipei City Councilor Ho Meng-hua (何孟樺) said the reasons behind the results showing a close race between Shen and Chiang are plain to see.
Shen comes across as warm, humble and willing to confront challenges head-on, she said.
In contrast, Chiang relies on robotic political platitudes and ideology-driven rhetoric, using die-hard supporters’ support to play down his administration’s mounting municipal failures, she said.
“For a city government relying on good looks to cover up its administrative flaws, public patience is rapidly wearing thin,” she said.

Worker falls into acid tank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:12 UTC
01:39:12 KST

A worker at a Taiwan Power Co (Taipower) contractor fell into a tank containing hydrochloric acid at Nanpu Power Plant in Kaohsiung, while 10 others were hospitalized following a rescue operation, the company said yesterday.
The state-run utility said that the incident occurred at about 9:30am at the gas-fired plant.
The contractors were doing maintenance on a hydrochloric acid tank used in the plant’s seawater electrolysis process, it said.
Photo courtesy of the Kaohsiung City Police Department via CNA
One of the workers was reportedly transferring hydrochloric acid when he climbed to the top of the tank wearing a safety harness via a caged ladder, but fell into the tank through the tank’s metal covering, Taipower said.
The worker sustained burns after coming into contact with hydrochloric acid and lost consciousness, while five Taipower employees and five workers employed by the contractor who helped with rescue operations reportedly felt unwell after possibly inhaling hydrochloric acid fumes, it said.
Fire authorities were notified and the 11 people were transported to hospitals for treatment, it said.
Taipower said it had initiated an investigation to determine the exact cause of the incident and that efforts would be made to prevent similar incidents from occurring again.
The plant’s power generation equipment was not affected and its generating units were operating normally, it said.
Meanwhile, the Kaohsiung Labor Affairs Bureau said that the contractor had contravened the Occupational Safety and Health Act (職業安全衛生法) and would be fined up to NT$3 million (US$94,613).
When work is being done above storage tanks, employers should ensure that safety structures such as scaffolding and work platforms are installed to prevent falls, the bureau said.

01:39:10 KST

A Honduran lawmaker who made a rare visit to Taiwan earlier this month was in the country to attend a training course organized by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), a ministry official in charge of the program said yesterday.
Department of Latin American and Caribbean Affairs head Jose Han (韓志正) said Jorge Calix, caucus whip of Honduras’ opposition Liberal Party, visited Taiwan mainly to attend the MOFA-organized Yuan Pang Class (遠朋班).
The annual training course, which has been held for decades, is intended to provide professional training for leaders in the region and allow them to become more familiar with Taiwan, Han said when asked to comment on Calix’s trip.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs
Calix is the first Honduran politician to publicly visit Taiwan since the Central American country severed diplomatic ties with Taipei in favor of Beijing in March 2023, under then-president Xiomara Castro, ending 82 years of diplomatic relations.
However, Han would not comment on whether Calix’s visit was related to the possibility of re-establishing ties between Taiwan and the former Central American ally that switched diplomatic recognition from Taipei to Beijing in March 2023.
Honduras’ new president, Nasry Asfura, who took office in January, had pledged during his election campaign to restore ties with Taipei.
Since then, neither Tegucigalpa nor Taipei has spoken publicly about the possibility of restoring diplomatic ties.
A MOFA press statement released on Wednesday last week said Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) had met with Calix a day earlier.
In the meeting, Lin pledged that Taiwan’s government would maintain a “pragmatic and open approach” toward the prospect of future relations that could “create all kinds of possibilities,” MOFA said.
According to Han, the training session Calix attended last week was the 17th edition of the Yuan Pang Class, or Advanced Foreign Relations Course.
Representatives from 20 countries in Latin America attended the course, including countries such as Honduras that do not have diplomatic relations with Taiwan, he said during a MOFA weekly briefing.
The attendees were either senior officials from Taiwan’s diplomatic allies or lawmakers, think tank heads and business leaders from non-allied countries, Han said.
Calix has served as a member of the National Congress since 2014. In early 2022, he briefly served as the disputed president of the Congress.

01:39:09 KST

An Afghan cyclist who had to disguise herself as a man to pursue her sporting dreams won a silver medal at the Asian Games yesterday, saying she hoped it could inspire other women in a country where Taliban authorities have sharply curtailed their freedoms.
Italy-based Fariba Hashimi powered home to second in the women’s road race near Nagoya, calling the triumph “something special.”
“I can’t explain my feelings now,” said the 23-year-old, before recounting how she was attacked with stones and trained disguised as a man when she got started in the sport as a teenager along with sister Yulduz, who is also now a pro cyclist.
Photo: Reuters
“I was born inside a country where the women who dream are getting attacked, and I’m really happy that I have fought against that,” she said. “I hope that the next generation will come here and represent their country without any fear.”
The Taliban returned to power in 2021 after the US withdrawal from Afghanistan and severely restricted women’s access to education and public life, including sport.
“They took away our freedom, they took away everything from us,” said Hashimi, who comes from Faryab province in northern Afghanistan and left the country after the Taliban took over. “This silver medal can show a lot of resilience from Afghan women, and I’m really happy.
“I’m not alone, I know that behind me millions of women, from many countries, have the same dream and they are standing with me,” she added.
After fleeing Afghanistan with the help of Italian former world champion Alessandra Cappellotto, Hashimi relocated to Italy, where she lives and trains.
She and her sister competed at the Paris Olympics two years ago, and the 2028 Los Angeles Games are drawing closer.
“I never want to give up and hopefully we can see [what can happen] again in Los Angeles,” she said.
Hashimi particularly thanked the Japanese team for playing a part in her silver medal.
“I’m here without a mechanic, without any preparation,” she said. “We brought one guy with us from the national federation, and he just drove the car.”
“We were fixing the bike ourselves. I was the mechanic for myself. I was washing the bike myself,” Hashimi said. “Thank you to the Japanese team. They were really, really nice to me, fixed my bike.”

MAC defends denying entry to Chinese official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:09 UTC
01:39:09 KST

The Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) yesterday defended its decision to deny entry to a senior official from the Shanghai Taiwan Affairs Office to attend the Taipei-Shanghai City Forum.
The council denied Shanghai Taiwan Affairs Office Deputy Director Li Xiaodong’s (李驍東) entry. Li was scheduled to lead a delegation to attend the annual cross-strait event.
Instead, the council approved the entry of Wang Hao (王皓), a department head at the Chinese agency.
Photo: Screenshot from Pop Radio’s livestream
Addressing the matter on a talk show on Pop Radio, MAC Minister Chiu Chui-cheng (邱垂正) said that while the forum is intended to address urban governance issues in the two localities, cross-strait affairs fall under the jurisdiction of the central government.
Taipei Department of Labor Commissioner Wang Chiu-tung (王秋冬), who works as a liaison for the event, said the council rejected Li’s entry by simply saying the decision was made “after taking all factors into consideration,” without providing further explanation.
The council “shows an arrogance of power” and “singles out the city for unfair treatment,” Wang Chiu-tung said.
Neither the Taipei-Shanghai City Forum nor the Sun Moon Lake-East Lake Forum between Taiwan’s Nantou County and Wuhan City in China’s Hubei Province can proceed without the approval and authorization of the central government, Chiu said.
“We hope that local government officials can conduct cross-strait exchange with their Chinese counterparts in a healthy and orderly fashion based on equality and dignity,” he said. “Forums should be about the exchange of city management issues, without any political preconditions.”
The council coordinated with the Ministry of the Interior to hold a joint review session of the Taipei-Shanghai forum ahead of the scheduled meeting, Chiu said.
“That does not mean that we should approve the entry of every person you invite,” he added.
The government has in principle banned directors and deputy directors of the Taiwan Affairs Office at the provincial and municipal levels from entering Taiwan after China issued its “22 guidelines” on punishing “Taiwanese independence separatists,” Chiu said, adding that the government has raised its travel advisory for China to “orange,” meaning that people should avoid nonessential travel to China.
The government would consider an exception when a Chinese official has a letter of recommendation issued by a Taiwanese business association in China, he said.
Taiwan’s Straits Exchange Foundation has to determine whether they can be allowed entry as well, he said.
For example, the government allowed the Hangzhou City Taiwan Affairs Office deputy director to attend the forum in Nantou County last year because of a recommendation from a China-based Taiwanese businessperson, who said the official took good care of their family during the Asian Games in Hangzhou, Chiu said.
That recommendation was accepted by the Straits Exchange Foundation, he added.
No Taiwanese businessperson vouched for Li, Chiu said.
The foundation is also unlikely to approve Li’s entry request because the Shanghai Taiwan Affairs Office has prevented Shanghai-based Taiwanese businesspeople from participating in foundation-organized activities in Taiwan, he said.

Children targeted in Pakistan for exploitation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:08 UTC
01:39:08 KST

Pakistani teenager Zara Shah was targeted by a stranger while playing a computer game, drawn into a conversation that would expose her to terrifying online sexual exploitation.
Zara, whose name has been changed for safety reasons, is one of an estimated 1.5 million children in Pakistan who experienced online sexual abuse in one year, a report published by the UN children’s agency this month said.
“We started chatting while playing an online game, and he began acting like a friend. Later, he wanted to meet and, after, started asking me for nudes,” 17-year-old Shah said.
Photo: Bloomberg
“When I refused, he threatened to find my family online and tell them that we had been talking,” she added.
According to the UNICEF report, about 85 percent of perpetrators were known to the victims, aged 12 to 17.
“The abuse may start with a friendly conversation, a gaming interaction, a promise of gifts, money or romance,” said Daniel Kardefelt, lead author of the global UNICEF report.
“Perpetrators may spend months building trust using information that they find on social media,” Kardefelt said.
In Muslim-majority Pakistan, 71 percent of victims did not tell anyone, the UNICEF report said, while no child surveyed reported the abuse through formal channels — including police, helplines or social workers.
Their silence was mostly because of stigma, shame and fears over how their families or society might react.
“Around 44 percent of reported abuse was entirely online, with Snapchat and WhatsApp among the most common settings,” said Mehek Naeem, director of PAHCHAAN, a children’s rights organisation based in the eastern city of Lahore.
Girls can face heightened risks of sexual extortion in the conservative society, which can lead to restrictions on their mobility or withdrawal from school.
For Zara, the threat of being exposed to her family was enough to keep her silent.
“I could have been stopped from going to school or leaving the house altogether,” she said. “Staying quiet felt like the better option than speaking up, but anxiety kills me every day.”
With about 74 percent of children aged 12 to 17 in Pakistan estimated by UNICEF to be Internet users, concerns over online safety are growing as their access to digital platforms expands.
Echoing other policies around the world, the provincial government in Punjab this month passed a resolution to bar children younger than 16 from using social media.
However, it has faced opposition.
“I disagree with the ban,” digital rights activist Usama Khilji said. “It will be a challenge to implement, and children can circumvent the ban through VPNs. Children have the right of freedom of expression, and a ban takes that away.”
Pakistan has a legal framework addressing tech-facilitated offences against children, but “there is no implementation,” said Tahira Afrasiyab, a spokesperson for non-profit organisation Muslim Hands.
There are loopholes in existing laws, experts say. Human rights lawyer Salman Afridi said this issue shows how “economic vulnerability can be weaponized” for amounts as small as 10,000 Pakistani rupees (US$36) in exchange for the production of sexual content.
“What we are seeing is the use of technology to facilitate an entire chain of grooming, inducement, coercion, blackmail, production, distribution and commercialization,” he said.
“There is a strong basis for describing this as a commercial ecosystem of exploitation,” Afridi added.
For Zara and many others like her, the consequences of an encounter that began with an online game remain difficult to escape.
“I was, and am, scared,” she said. “I live in fear.”
