Labor ministry to appeal voiding of official’s dismissal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:07 UTC
01:39:07 KST

The Ministry of Labor yesterday said it would appeal an administrative court ruling that voided its dismissal of a branch chief who was accused of bullying following a worker’s suicide.
On Sept. 3, the Taipei High Administrative Court ruled that the ministry’s disciplinary proceedings against former Workforce Development Agency (WDA) branch head Hsieh Yi-jung (謝宜容) had “violated due process” and made “erroneous” findings.
On those grounds, Hsieh’s challenge to her dismissal was well-founded, the court said.
Photo: Lee Chin-hui, Taipei Times
The ruling struck down her dismissal. Prosecutors earlier declined to indict her over the death of the worker, finding no causal relationship between her leadership and the suicide.
Hsieh, who headed the WDA’s northern regional branch, was accused of workplace bullying following the suicide of a 39-year-old subordinate, surnamed Wu (吳), in his office in New Taipei City on Nov. 4, 2024.
Amid an uproar surrounding the case, the ministry issued two major demerits at a performance review on Nov. 20, 2024, resulting in the high-ranking civil servant’s dismissal from office.
The Chinese-language tabloid Mirror Media yesterday published portions of the 205 responses the ministry received to a questionnaire distributed as part of its investigation into Hsieh’s conduct.
Employees reported having experienced or heard about Hsieh’s alleged bullying, Mirror Media reported, adding that they accused her of calling subordinates “idiots” and calling their work “garbage.”
The ministry in a statement later yesterday said that it disagreed with the court’s first-instance ruling and had instructed legal counsel to prepare to appeal to the Supreme Administrative Court within the statutory deadline.
Hsieh was also found guilty of corruption by a criminal court, impeached and referred for disciplinary action by the Control Yuan, the ministry said.
As those cases are pending before the Supreme Court and the Disciplinary Court for civil servants respectively, Hsieh will remain suspended from duty and will not be reinstated at this time, the ministry said.
Hsieh was sentenced to four years and six months in prison on corruption charges in September last year. The Taiwan High Court in April upheld the prison sentence, although it slightly reduced her deprivation of civil rights to two years from three.

Tangled web of local factions as vote nears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:06 UTC
01:39:06 KST

On Thursday last week, Changhua County Council Speaker Hsieh Dien-lin (謝典霖) and his father were taken into custody and denied access to visitors or communications in connection with a June banquet that authorities allege constituted vote-buying and embezzlement of public funds.
The incident has dealt a severe blow to the protective umbrella that has long shielded powerful local political families from scrutiny.
It also makes the barrage of denials and excuses offered by the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) after foreign media shone a light on vote-buying allegations look utterly self-defeating.
However, the comments by foreign journalists pale in comparison to the evidence emerging from judicial authorities. Hsieh and others allegedly organized more than 10 banquet tables as part of a planned vote-buying operation while using pretexts to fraudulently obtain public funds from the county council to foot the bill. Local politicians have apparently become so brazen that they no longer feel the need to pay out of their own pockets; they simply treat the council as a private ATM, using taxpayers’ hard-earned money to keep their political families in power.
Corrupt systems, in which public institutions are treated as private property, are commonplace across areas governed by KMT-aligned local factions.
On Sept. 1, six current and former KMT Taitung County councilors, including Deputy Speaker Lin Tsung-han (林琮翰), were investigated over alleged abuse of their positions to benefit the family of Taitung County Council Speaker Wu Hsiu-hua (吳秀華) to develop and widen a farm road leading to a private resort owned by the Wu family.
In Hualien County on Sept. 9, Sioulin Township (秀林) Mayor Wang Mei-kuei (王玫瑰) of the KMT and her husband were arrested over alleged contraventions of the Public Officials Election and Recall Act (公職人員選舉罷免法), accused of using community feedback funds to organize banquets and distribute cash.
Meanwhile, Chang Chia-hao (張家豪), the KMT’s candidate for mayor of Yilan County’s Jhuangwei Township (壯圍), has has been implicated in alleged vote-buying involving the use of his official position to organize banquets and distribute gifts to voters to secure their support. Chang was detained on Sept 10.
Within the tangled web of KMT local factions, local self-government has long since degenerated into a predatory production line that turns public funds into private gains.
In the eyes of local faction leaders, public power is not a responsibility, but a family money tree.
There is an even more serious challenge in the implications for national security. The local political networks that have long depended on enormous flows of money to operate might be more concerned with personal interests than loyalty to their country.
As Beijing’s “united front” infiltration of Taiwan becomes increasingly aggressive, there are systematic efforts to cultivate ties with Taiwan’s grassroots communities, village networks and local political families. Some factional politicians who covet public funds and crave campaign cash could potentially become amenable local entry points for Chinese capital.
November’s local elections are near. Votes should not be rubber stamps for corrupt politicians to recoup public funds, or free passes for hereditary factional fiefdoms. If Taiwanese cannot use their ballots to sweep away such practices, society will never escape from the shadow of factional patronage and political corruption.
Yang Chih-chiang is a teacher.

A central pillar of that security relationship is the American willingness to sell arms to Taiwan. Trump says US to build two 'very major' bases in Greenland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:39:02 UTC
01:39:02 KST

The United States will build two major military bases in Greenland under a deal with Demark to be signed on Tuesday, President Donald Trump told the UN General Assembly.
"We will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations. We'll be building two very major military bases," Trump said in a speech, adding Washington would have a much more secure relationship with Greenland and Denmark
Photo:AP
The US plans to re-establish a Cold War-era military base in southern Greenland and set up another on the east coast, now used by the Danish dog sled patrol, according to three people familiar with the matter.
The sites are Narsarsuaq, whose population has dwindled to a few dozen people since the US closed its Bluie West One military base in the 1950s, and Mestersvig, a military outpost used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, a Danish special forces unit said.
Denmark, Greenland and the United States are expected to sign their new agreement at the United Nations General Assembly in New York City at 10:30 a.m. ET (1430 GMT) on Tuesday.
The text of the agreement has not been made public and the three people familiar with the deal, speaking on condition of anonymity, said its details will not be finalized until it is signed.
The governments of Denmark and Greenland did not immediately respond to a request by Reuters for comment.
White House spokesperson declined to comment on the details of the agreement, repeating an earlier statement that its signing on Tuesday would "secure and defend the security of Greenland and the United States."
Denmark says the agreement puts Arctic security under the watch of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, the military defense alliance, rather than leaving it solely to the US and Denmark.
The deal follows months of pressure from US President Donald Trump, who has long said he wants the US to control Greenland and has at times refused to rule out military or ?economic force to acquire the semi-autonomous Danish territory. The idea has been rejected by an overwhelming majority of Greenlanders, polling shows.
Trump's threats, which peaked in January, triggered a diplomatic crisis within NATO and pushed Denmark and Greenland into negotiations with Washington aimed at defusing the pressure.
During the Cold War, the US maintained 17 military installations and more than 10,000 personnel in Greenland. Today only Pituffik Space Base remains, with some 150 US military personnel.

Export orders cross US$100bn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:38:57 UTC
01:38:57 KST

Export orders surpassed US$100 billion for the first time last month, driven by strong demand for artificial intelligence (AI), high-performance computing and cloud service applications, as well as rising international raw material prices, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said yesterday.
The strong order performance reflects better-than-expected demand for custom chips — known as application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) — from major cloud service providers, the ministry said.
Last month’s orders rose 71.4 percent year-on-year to a record US$102.96 billion, the 19th consecutive month of increases and surpassing the ministry’s forecast of 61.4 to 64.8 percent growth.
Photo: CNA
Cumulative orders in the first eight months of the year grew 55 percent to US$704.99 billion, a new record for the period, the ministry said in a report.
Export orders — including those received by Taiwanese firms and produced domestically or abroad — indicate product and component shipments to overseas markets one to three months before customs clearance.
Last month, firms produced 45.7 percent of all orders overseas, up 2.3 percentage points from a year earlier, as makers of information and communications technology (ICT) products boosted production abroad, the ministry said.
Orders for ICT products (including servers, networking products and industrial PCs) increased 100.5 percent, and electronic products (including ICs and thermal components) grew 83.9 percent year-on-year last month, driven by the rapid development of emerging technology applications, the ministry said.
Conversely, orders for optoelectronic products fell 5 percent due to weak demand for flat panels, it said.
In traditional industries, semiconductor firms’ continued capacity expansion and rising copper demand amid the AI boom boosted orders for machinery and base metals by 28.3 percent and 26.8 percent respectively, the ministry said.
Orders for chemicals grew 15.4 percent due to high pharmaceutical and industrial demand, and those for plastic and rubber products rose 6.7 percent on higher raw material costs, it said.
By destination, orders last month from the US registered the largest annual increase of 88.9 percent, followed by increases of 70.5 percent from ASEAN and 58.2 percent from Europe, the ministry said.
Orders from China (including Hong Kong) grew 47.7 percent, and those from Japan were up 41.1 percent, it said.
The ministry said the booming development of AI and emerging technology applications, the promotion of AI infrastructure by various countries and increased capital expenditure by cloud service providers, coupled with the Taiwanese semiconductor and server supply chains’ key position in the world, could support growth in export orders this month, despite geopolitical risks and trade policy uncertainties.
The ministry-compiled diffusion index of export orders — a gauge of manufacturers’ order expectations for the following month — climbed above the neutral level to 52.1, suggesting that firms remain confident in their outlook.
Orders for this month are forecast to increase 50.7 to 55.1 percent year-on-year to between US$106 billion and US$109.1 billion, and the full-year figure could top US$1.1 trillion if monthly orders stay above US$100 billion from this month to December, it said.

Man shot by ICE, sent to jail with bullet inside him
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:38:56 UTC
01:38:56 KST

A Venezuelan national shot and wounded by a US immigration agent in Texas was jailed with the bullet still inside his body, his lawyer said on Monday.
Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, told reporters he was delivering an order for DoorDash on Sunday when his vehicle was rammed by a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent and he was shot.
“I’m in a lot of pain, because the shot fractured my clavicle, and at the hospital where they took me they couldn’t remove the bullet, because it’s close to the spinal cord... I’m not doing very well, I still have the bullet inside,” he told reporters by phone.
Photo: AP
The shooting in Austin, Texas, marked the latest instance of violence by ICE agents tasked with enforcing US President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.
Homeland Security Investigations, which is a part of ICE, is leading the investigation into the shooting with the assistance of the FBI, the US Department of Homeland Security said.
Garces Perez had “illegally entered our country under the [former US president Joe] Biden administration and had a final order of removal,” the department said on social media.
However, Garces Perez’s attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, maintained he was in the US “legally with a work permit.”
She told a news conference that he was transferred from a hospital to a detention center in Pearsall, about 215km southwest of Austin.
“He was shot here in his back, and they didn’t take the bullet out, and they didn’t give him pain medication, and they transferred him to ICE, to a processing center where he spent the night without a bed,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said.
Garces Perez on Monday confirmed that account.
“I was on my way with an order from the DoorDash app, and then a truck pulls up next to me. It doesn’t turn on its lights or anything, it just tries to hit me,” he said.
Then a black pickup cut him off, and an agent got out and demanded his documents, Garces Perez said. Garces Perez asked to be allowed to pull over from the middle of the road, but agents refused.
“I made a U-turn and that’s when he started chasing me, thinking I was going to run away, but I was looking for a place to leave my car safely,” Garces Perez said. “That’s when he hit me twice and shot me.”
He does not know how many shots were fired at him.
“There is absolutely zero justification for having shot him,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said. “This is why we’re calling for a stop to ICE traffic stops. ICE officers are overarmed, overpaid, undertrained and violent.”
Garces Perez said after he was shot, an ambulance arrived and he could not move.
At the hospital, he said he was told tests were being run to prepare for surgery, but the operation to remove the bullet was halted.
“A doctor comes in and tells me: ‘no,’ because they were in a hurry to discharge me and have me taken” to the detention center, Garces Perez said.
“I told the doctor: ‘How are you going to leave the bullet in there if it still hurts?’” he added.
He maintained he did not receive adequate medical care at the hospital.
In the early morning, a nurse gave him a painkiller, he said.
Then he was taken to a room with no bed at the detention center, he said.
A makeshift shrine with flowers, candles and a sign reading “Justice 4 Wilber” was placed near the site of the shooting.
On Monday, a work crew painted over expletive-laced graffiti nearby, which expresses local outrage about ICE and the ongoing immigration crackdown.
About 51,000 undocumented migrants were arrested in the US last month, according to the department’s figures.
Ruben Ray Martinez, 23, was shot by ICE in March last year, in what the Texas Tribune said was the first known killing by immigration agents of a US citizen in Trump’s second term.
More recently, a Mexican man, Lorenzo Salgado, died in July after he was shot by an ICE officer in Houston, Texas.
Two US citizens — Renee Good and Alex Pretti — were shot and killed by federal immigration agents in separate incidents in Minnesota during a crackdown on undocumented migrants in the northern state earlier this year.

Flu epidemic continues as deaths and cases hit new high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:38:55 UTC
01:38:55 KST

The Centers for Disease Control (CDC) yesterday said that 165 severe flu cases and 30 flu-related deaths were reported last week, the highest weekly numbers in this flu season, and that cases might continue to increase, urging people to take precautions.
Medical visits for flu-like illnesses increased by 1.4 percent to 141,374 last week, with 11.8 percent being emergency visits, showing that the seasonal flu is still in its epidemic period, CDC Epidemic Intelligence Center Director Guo Hung-wei (郭宏偉) said.
From Tuesday last week to Monday, 165 severe flu cases and 30 flu-related deaths were confirmed, the highest weekly numbers since October last year, and also the highest numbers of the same week in five years, he said.
Photo: Hou Chia-yu, Taipei Times
Of the accumulated 1,586 severe cases and 304 flu-related deaths in this flu season, 65.8 percent were people aged 65 or older, and 83.2 percent had chronic diseases, he said, adding that elderly people with underlying conditions have the highest risk of developing severe illness.
Among the latest confirmed flu deaths, the youngest was a five-year-old boy who did not have underlying health conditions, but also did not get vaccinated, CDC physician Lin Yung-ching (林詠青) said.
The boy began having flu-like symptoms late last month and first sought treatment at a clinic, but as he later developed recurring fever, altered consciousness and convulsions, he was referred to a hospital for emergency treatment, Lin said.
At the hospital he was confirmed to be infected with influenza A virus and showed signs of encephalitis, he said.
The boy remained unconscious for more than two weeks in an intensive care unit and died of influenza-induced acute necrotizing encephalopathy combined with sepsis, he said.
Contact tracing found that a person living with the boy had also contracted the flu late last month, Lin said.
Guo said medical visits for COVID-19 increased 20.6 percent to 14,462 last week, and 48 severe cases and nine deaths were confirmed from Tuesday last week to Monday.
Among the deaths was a man in his 30s, who had multiple chronic health conditions, and he died of cardiogenic shock and septic shock about two weeks after hospitalization, Lin said.
As transmittable respiratory diseases typically become more active when temperatures drop, the CDC urge people to practice hand and respiratory hygiene, he said.
Infected high-risk people, including young children, people with chronic conditions and older people, should also seek medical attention as soon as possible, especially if they develop symptoms such as difficulty breathing and altered consciousness, he said.
Flu cases are expected to rise to a peak of 150,000 to 160,000 weekly medical visits, CDC Deputy Director-General Lin Min-cheng (林明誠) said.
There is an increased infection risk as people congregate during the upcoming Mid-Autumn Festival, Lin Min-cheng said.
As for a cluster of 11 acute hepatitis C cases that was traced to a clinic in New Taipei City’s Banciao District (板橋), Lin said two new cases were confirmed last week among the 1,118 people who received injections from January to last month and were notified that they could get a free blood test.
A total of 1,111 people has been informed by the local health department, and seven could not be reached, he said.
Of the 418 people who have been contacted but have not received the free blood test, 36 refused to get tested, four had died, and 32 reported receiving a blood test on their own, he said, adding that the positivity rate of the tested people so far was 3.08 percent.
The CDC would look into the causes of the four deaths to determine if the deaths were connected with hepatitis C infection, and a meeting would be held with the New Taipei City Department of Health on the case, he added.

HPA’s tokens program partners with businesses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:38:51 UTC
01:38:51 KST

The Health Promotion Administration’s (HPA) Health Token program, which is to launch next week, has partnered with major convenience stores and supermarkets, HPA Director-General Shen Ching-fen (沈靜芬) said yesterday.
FamilyMart, 7-Eleven and PX Mart, as well as World Gym, Fitness Factory and Curves are participating in the first phase of the program, Shen said.
The program is to launch on Thursday next week for National Health Insurance (NHI) cardholders aged 18 or older, including foreign residents, with tokens redeemable from Dec. 1, she said.
Photo courtesy of the Health Promotion Administration
The tokens are modeled on a similar program in Singapore and would reward healthy behaviors, such as getting medical checkups and vaccinations, with rewards including healthy food and beverages, discounted access to gyms and sports facilities, reduced healthcare costs and health insurance benefits, she said.
People can earn tokens via an app for publicly funded health checkups and cancer screenings and publicly or self-funded vaccinations, including COVID-19, influenza and pneumococcal vaccines, Shen said, adding that those actions would earn 800 to 1,350 tokens.
The HPA estimates that people could accumulate 3,700 to 13,150 tokens in two years, depending on age group and health risks, she added.
The program is a collaboration between the public and private sectors, with supermarkets and convenience stores, pharmacies, medical institutions, sports venues and insurance providers involved, she said.
At 7-Eleven, FamilyMart and PX Mart, people can redeem fresh produce, drinks and dried goods, while World Gym, Fitness Factory and Curves would offer discounts on monthly passes and exercise-related products, she said.
The HPA has also partnered with pharmacy chains, including Great Tree and Wellcare, to offer medical devices and nutritional supplements in exchange for tokens, she said.
Participating life insurance providers include Taiwan Life Insurance Co, Cathay Life Insurance Co, Fubon Life Insurance Co, Nanshan Life Insurance Co, KGI Life Insurance Co and BankTaiwan Life Insurance Co, she said.
About 26 Ministry of Health and Welfare hospitals would allow people with NHI cards to redeem tokens for self-paid health examinations, vaccinations and anesthesia, she added.
From next week, people can earn 200 tokens the first time they log into the health token section of the NHI’s app and 100 tokens for completing the lifestyle assessment, she said.
People do not need to keep receipts or apply for tokens individually, as all records would be automatically credited through the system, she said.
From Oct. 1, people could link their accounts on the NHI app with the Health GO App to begin redeeming health-related products, Shen said.
Redemption requires at least 1,000 tokens, she said.
Moreover, those who download both apps between Thursday next week and Nov. 30, and complete identity verification and registration can enter a lottery to win NT$200 digital merchandise vouchers, she said.
The lottery would run for eight consecutive weeks, with 3,600 winners selected each week, she said.
A year-end bonus draw on Dec. 7 would select 200 people from those who completed account linking from Nov. 26 to 30 to win an Apple Watch, she added.
The health token program is to be extended to school-age children in later phases, Minister of Health and Welfare Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) said.

Unemployment steady, low and seasonal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:38:50 UTC
01:38:50 KST

Taiwan’s unemployment rate rose for a third straight month last month as graduates entered the job market, but the increase was largely seasonal, with the jobless rate for the month remaining the lowest in more than two decades, government data showed.
The unemployment rate climbed to 3.41 percent from 3.39 percent in July, the lowest August reading since 2001, the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS) said.
On a seasonally adjusted basis, the rate edged down to 3.32 percent from 3.33 percent, indicating that underlying labor-market conditions remained firm, the DGBAS said.
Photo: CNA
“The rise in unemployment is seasonal, as the labor-force participation rate is growing and the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate is declining,” DGBAS Census Department Deputy Director Tan Wen-ling (譚文玲) said at a news conference.
The number of unemployed people rose by 2,000 to 411,000, as the number of first-time job seekers increased by 3,000 during the month, Tan said.
With more people entering the workforce, Taiwan’s labor participation rate rose to 59.69 percent, the highest for August since 1995, driven by increased participation among women and middle-aged or older workers, she said.
The rise in participation is significant for an economy facing a shrinking workforce as low birthrates and rapid population aging put pressure on labor supply, she said.
The government has sought to encourage women and older people to remain in or return to the workforce to help ease labor shortages, and “the increase indicates that government efforts are bearing fruit,” Tan said.
Young workers continued to face the highest unemployment, as the jobless rate among people aged 15 to 24 was 11.74 percent, reflecting the large number of young people entering the workforce after graduation. The rate was 5.88 percent for those aged 25 to 29 and 3.35 percent for people aged 30 to 34, the DGBAS data showed.
By educational attainment, people with university degrees had the highest unemployment rate at 4.56 percent, followed by those with graduate degrees at 3.16 percent and those with senior high school or vocational high school education at 3.13 percent, the data showed.
Broader measures of labor market slack remained stable, as the number of people working fewer hours than they wanted fell to 119,000, suggesting there was little change in underemployment, the DGBAS said.
Taiwan’s headline unemployment rate remained above those of neighboring Japan and South Korea, where the rates were 2.4 percent and 2.7 percent respectively.
Tan said the gap partly reflects differences in employment structures, adding that non-regular workers accounted for about 36.5 percent of employees in Japan and 38.2 percent in South Korea, compared with only 7.6 percent in Taiwan.
The increase in unemployment rate last month is unlikely to signal a deterioration in the labor market, as unemployment typically falls in September when new graduates find jobs and summer workers return to school, Tan said.

Typhoon Dujuan left at least four people dead and 22 injured in Japan, while thousands of houses near Tokyo were without power after the storm swept through the region, authorities said yesterday.
The typhoon moved away from Japan’s coast and out into the Pacific Ocean by morning, allowing authorities to lift or downgrade most heavy rain and landslide warnings.
Dujuan had already led to the early closure in the capital of one of the world’s biggest video game trade fairs.
Photo: Kyodo via Reuters
Japan often sees strong typhoons in the late summer and early autumn, with other storms this season disrupting some events at the Asian Games being held in the country.
The Japanese Fire and Disaster Management Agency said three people died in Chiba Prefecture and one in Kanagawa region, both near Tokyo.
Search operations were continuing for six people missing after landslides triggered by torrential rain, the agency said.
More than 45,000 households in Chiba were still without electricity yesterday afternoon, while more than 460 houses were damaged.
Although Dujuan weakened as it moved northeast, it dumped record rainfall in parts of the Tokyo area.
Oshima, an island about 120km south of central Tokyo, recorded 832mm of rain over 48 hours, more than double its average rainfall for the whole of September, public broadcaster NHK reported.
Rainfall in Tokyo’s Edogawa Ward reached a record 282.5mm over 24 hours.
Scientists say human-driven climate change is intensifying the risk posed by heavy rains because a warmer atmosphere holds more water.

People who vandalize or climb the Danjiang Bridge without authorization could face fines of up to NT$300,000, the Highway Bureau said yesterday.
The bridge, which connects New Taipei City’s Tamsui (淡水) and Bali (八里) districts, officially opened to traffic on May 12. Its surrounding scenery has also become a popular spot for taking photographs and checking in on social media.
The Northern Region Branch of the Highway Bureau said in a statement that the bridge is an important transportation landmark linking Tamsui and Bali.
Photo: Chen Yi-kuan, Taipei Times
Graffiti or other damage, as well as unauthorized climbing is prohibited throughout the bridge area, including the main bridge, approach roads, pedestrian facilities and bicycle paths, it said.
Graffiti and other acts of vandalism damage public facilities, and undermine the bridge’s visual appeal and surrounding environment, the branch said, adding that it would step up patrols in cooperation with police and use surveillance equipment to monitor the area.
People found using highway land or facilities without authorization, or causing damage would be fined NT$60,000 to NT$300,000 as stipulated by Article 72 of the Highway Act (公路法), the branch said.
People should help protect the bridge and its facilities, as the landmark serves transportation and recreational purposes, it said.
People who witness vandalism or other illegal acts should immediately report them to authorities, it added.

Panama opens a door for Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:38:48 UTC
01:38:48 KST

When Panama severed diplomatic relations with Taiwan and recognized China in 2017, Beijing achieved one of its most important diplomatic victories in Central America.
However, nearly a decade later, Panama is demonstrating that diplomatic recognition does not necessarily eliminate Taiwan from a country’s political system.
Panama and Taiwan had diplomatic relations for more than 100 years and the goodwill between the countries was displayed last week when Panama’s National Assembly established an interparliamentary exchange group with the Legislative Yuan.
Forty-five of the assembly’s 71 lawmakers joined the group, representing more than 60 percent of the legislature. Its members include National Assembly President Shirley Castanedas and both vice presidents, Manuel Cohen and Manuel Cheng.
The significance of the new alliance extends beyond the number of lawmakers involved. Panama formally recognizes Beijing and accepts its “one China” policy, yet a clear majority of its elected legislature has created an institutional mechanism for maintaining exchanges with Taiwan.
That exposes a weakness in China’s strategy of diplomatically isolating Taiwan: Beijing can persuade governments to withdraw formal recognition, but it cannot necessarily prevent other democratic institutions within those countries from maintaining relationships with Taipei.
The process did not begin with the creation of the friendship group. More than 20 Panamanian lawmakers have visited Taiwan over the past six months. In November last year, a nine-member cross-party delegation traveled to Taiwan, the first delegation from Panama’s National Assembly to do so since 2017.
Panamanian President Jose Raul Mulino stressed that foreign policy was the responsibility of the executive branch and said the lawmakers’ visit had not been authorized by his administration.
Meanwhile, the Panamanain Ministry of Foreign Affairs accused the Chinese embassy of interfering in the country’s internal affairs after Chinese officials reportedly pressured lawmakers to cancel the trip.
The dispute illustrated the limits of diplomatic recognition in a democratic political system.
Mulino’s government controls Panama’s formal diplomatic relations and has given no indication that it intends to restore recognition of Taiwan, but the National Assembly is an independent branch of government. Its lawmakers can travel, establish parliamentary groups and develop political relationships that do not necessarily correspond perfectly with the foreign policy preferences of the executive.
For decades, Beijing’s campaign against Taiwan’s diplomatic allies has been built around a relatively binary proposition: A country recognizes either Beijing or Taipei. Once a government switches recognition to China, Taiwan closes its embassy, formal cooperation programs are terminated and Beijing expects the political relationship with Taipei to largely disappear.
However, a country can recognize China while legislators maintain exchanges with Taiwan. Those exchanges can potentially create relationships involving universities, businesses, local governments and civil society without immediately challenging formal diplomatic recognition.
For Taiwan, that could provide an alternative strategy in countries that have already switched recognition to Beijing.
Rather than treating the loss of diplomatic relations as the end of meaningful engagement, Taipei could expand parliamentary diplomacy and gradually rebuild relationships below the level of formal recognition. Such a strategy would not require governments to immediately choose between China and Taiwan.
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed concern about Chinese influence surrounding the Panama Canal. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio chose Panama as the first destination of his first overseas trip after joining the White House and pressed Panamanian officials over Chinese involvement in the country.
Soon afterward, Panama announced that it would leave China’s Belt and Road Initiative, which led China to accuse the US of interference. Panama was the first Latin American country to join the initiative in 2017, only months after establishing diplomatic relations with Beijing.
The decision did not mean Panama was preparing to abandon relations with China, but it did demonstrate that decisions once presented as evidence of Panama’s long-term alignment with Beijing can be reversed when domestic interests and geopolitical circumstances change.
Taiwan’s expanding parliamentary relationship should be understood within this environment.
Panama is not restoring diplomatic relations with Taiwan, but the political space available to Taipei is clearly larger than it was several years ago. More importantly, the space is being created by Panamanian institutions themselves.
Honduras, which severed diplomatic relations with Taiwan in 2023, is experiencing a different but related process. Honduran President Nasry Asfura campaigned on reconsidering the decision to recognize China and argued that Honduras had been better off economically when it maintained formal relations with Taiwan.
Since taking office, his government has been reviewing agreements signed with Beijing before making what Asfura has described as a final decision regarding Honduras’ relationships in Asia.
The Honduran National Congress has also become increasingly involved. Lawmakers have requested reviews of agreements signed with China, while congressional leaders have publicly questioned whether the diplomatic switch delivered the benefits that had been promised.
Panama and Honduras are following different paths, but both challenge the assumption that establishing diplomatic relations with China permanently removes Taiwan from a country’s political landscape.
Honduras is reconsidering the economic and political rationale behind its diplomatic switch. Panama is demonstrating that even without reconsidering formal recognition, elected institutions can rebuild direct relationships with Taiwan.
Taiwan has only a small number of formal diplomatic allies and competing with China financially for recognition would be extraordinarily difficult. Parliamentary diplomacy offers a different approach because it does not require Taiwan to immediately win the diplomatic contest.
If lawmakers visit Taiwan, universities establish exchanges, businesses identify opportunities and civil society organizations cooperate, relationships can develop before diplomatic recognition ever becomes part of the discussion.
That does not guarantee that Panama, Honduras or any other country would eventually restore relations with Taiwan. Beijing retains enormous economic and diplomatic leverage, and governments would have to consider substantial consequences before making such a decision.
However, Panama’s new parliamentary group demonstrates that diplomatic recognition is not necessarily the final stage of the competition.
China can convince a government to recognize Beijing. Preventing Taiwan from rebuilding relationships with the democratic institutions inside that country might prove considerably more difficult.
Juan Fernando Herrera Ramos is a Honduran journalist based in Taipei. His work on Taiwan-China-Latin America relations has been published in Nikkei Asia, The Diplomat and the Taipei Times.

It is underpinned by a security relationship with the United States that’s existed in several iterations since 1949 and the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) retreat from China. A central pillar of that security relationship is the American willingness to sell arms to Taiwan. KARATE
Photo: Reuters
The women’s team kata squad and men’s kumite competitor Chung Meng-yu won bronze medals yesterday.
The 34-year-old Chien Hui-hsuan, who won bronze in the women’s individual kata event on Sunday, was joined by 22-year-old Tien Hsin-erh and 23-year-old Hung Chih-hsuan for the team competition.
The Taiwanese trio defeated Macau by a 5-0 decision in the quarter-finals, but lost 5-0 to Vietnam in the semi-finals, sending them into a bronze-medal contest against Nepal.
They secured the medal with another unanimous 5-0 victory, earning Taiwan’s seventh medal of the Games and third in karate.
Kata is a demonstration of choreographed offensive and defensive movements before judges, unlike kumite, in which athletes face each other in sparring bouts.
Later yesterday, Chung added another bronze medal for Taiwan in the men’s kumite under-84kg division.
He lost 4-1 to Jordan’s Mohammad al-Jafari in the quarter-finals but remained in medal contention through repechage, which gives athletes defeated by finalists another route to a bronze-medal bout.
Chung faced India’s Chetan Bhatt for the medal, and their bout finished 1-1 at the end of regulation, but Chung was named the winner on “senshu,” meaning he scored a point using a valid scoring move before his opponent did.
Chung’s result gave Taiwan’s karate team their fourth bronze medal in three consecutive days of competition.
Chien opened the run with bronze in the women’s individual kata on Sunday, while Shih Cheng-chung claimed bronze in the men’s kumite under-67kg division on Monday.
WUSHU
Taiwanese wushu athlete Liu Chang-min won bronze in the men’s nanquan-nangun.
Competing at the Aichi Prefectural Martial Arts Hall, Liu scored 9.720 points in the nanquan portion during the morning session and 9.710 in the afternoon’s nangun routine. His combined score of 19.430 placed him third overall.
China’s Li Jianming won gold with 19.563 points, while Hong Kong’s Lau Chi Lung took silver with 19.456.
Taiwan’s Huang Wen-sheng narrowly missed the podium. Huang placed seventh in nanquan with 9.703 points before finishing second in nangun with 9.726, giving him a combined score of 19.429 — just 0.001 behind Liu.
Although Liu placed fifth in both portions of the competition, his consistent performances across the two routines were enough to secure bronze. The event’s final standings were determined by the athletes’ combined nanquan and nangun scores.
Liu’s bronze was Taiwan’s second wushu medal at this year’s Asian Games, following Johnny Sun’s silver in the men’s taijiquan and taijijian event on Monday.
BASEBALL

Taiwan scored six runs in the first inning, including Chen Min-sih’s two-run homer, before Liu Ji-hong added another two-run shot in the second to extend the lead to 8-0.
Chen Hsiao-yun went 3-for-3 with three RBIs. His two-run hit with the bases loaded in the bottom of the sixth gave Taiwan a 15-run lead and ended the game under the tournament’s run-ahead rule. Taiwan finished with 10 hits.
Three Taiwanese pitchers combined on a two-hit shutout.

Anuchit Lungloek and Nattapon Chaichuay were the only Thai batters to record hits, singling in the third and fifth innings respectively. Thailand did not draw a walk.

US President Donald Trump on Monday said he was working on a “massive” deal to buy fertilizer from Belarus, pivoting away from main supplier Canada toward an ally of Russia.
Trump’s announcement on purchases of potash comes as Washington pursues dialogue with Minsk despite its repression of dissidents and support for Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
At the same time, Trump has stepped up a trade war with North American neighbor Canada, a long-term US ally and top trading partner.
Photo: AP
“The United States is working on a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus,” Trump said on his Truth Social network. “The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers.”
The US imports the vast majority of its potash — a chemical salt used to manufacture fertilizer. Prices soared after the Ukraine war.
In 2024, 79 percent came from Canada, 11 percent from Russia and 4 percent from Belarus, the US Geological Survey said.

Authoritarian symbols on campus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:38:47 UTC
01:38:47 KST

Ten years ago, when I was an undergraduate at National Chung Hsing University (NCHU), there was a referendum on whether to remove a statue of Chiang Kai-shek (蔣介石) from the campus. I wrote to the Liberty Times (the Taipei Times’ sister newspaper) urging faculty, staff and students to vote for its removal. Eventually, the statue was removed from the university.
Today, I am filled with emotion at seeing students at Soochow University democratically remove their own statue of Chiang, a figure of authoritarian rule, after it was on display for 48 years
The timing is noteworthy, with the nine-in-one local elections approaching. Education providers at all levels have been promoting “campus neutrality,” including administrative and educational neutrality, but the presence of symbols of party-state authoritarianism undermines transitional justice and campus democracy, while making political neutrality impossible.
During my time at NCHU, I often heard the seemingly plausible argument that staying “neutral” meant the university was avoiding the question of whether to remove the statue.
However, an institution of learning should be the last place to preserve symbols of worship to a political party or figure, or party-state symbols that harmed political dissidents.
Removing the statue was the only way for the campus to achieve genuine political neutrality.
Authoritarian statues carry powerful political symbolism and historical traumas. Erecting the image of a dictator from the White Terror era on a university campus is, in essence, a political imposition on a public space dedicated to education. It infringes on academic independence and freedom of thought, and is tantamount to the university’s endorsement of a kind of political authoritarianism.
That is the definition of non-neutrality and failure to distinguish between party and university.
Removing such statues does not deny the existence of the historical figures they depict; rather, it removes the artificially imposed cult of personality from educational institutions.
By separating party and university, a teaching and learning environment free from political oppression is created.
Whether at NCHU or Soochow, the deeper significance of universities doing away with Chiang statues lies in their educational and ethical role as models for a democratic society. The demonstrations of social responsibility enable higher education to move beyond the ivory tower and make a substantive contribution to deepening the country’s democracy.
Lai Yen-cheng is the executive secretary of a youth civil society group.

A fragment of the oldest peace treaty has been identified in Turkey
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22

01:38:19 KST

A fragment of the oldest peace treaty has been identified in Turkey
Kyiv • UNN
The fragment of the Treaty of Kadesh corresponds to Articles 12–20 of the treaty between Ramesses II and Hattusili III. It was found in modern-day Turkey.
The Ministry of Culture and Tourism of Turkey announced the recent identification of a fragment of a cuneiform text corresponding to Articles 12–20 of one of the first peace treaties in history. It concerns the Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty, also known as the Treaty of Kadesh. Popular Science reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
Around 1259 BCE, after two centuries of intermittent fighting over Kadesh, Egyptian Pharaoh Ramesses II and the Hittite king Hattusili III concluded an agreement that became the oldest known proclamation of peace in human history.
The treaty was signed approximately 15 years after the Battle of Kadesh.
Archaeologists have carefully documented fragments of the treaty preserved on Akkadian cuneiform tablets and in hieroglyphs on the walls of Egyptian temples, but the recently discovered section, found in what is now Turkey, carries a significant message even 3,200 years after it was written
The publication also recalled that the first fragments of the Treaty of Kadesh were discovered during excavations in the early 20th century, and that copies of the document were even included in UNESCO’s Memory of the World Register in 2001.
This heritage, preserved from millennia ago to the present day, reminds us of our responsibility to protect human life and dignity. We wish you a future in which all people, especially our Palestinian brothers, will live in safety, peace, and tranquility
We remind you
In Egypt, archaeologists discovered the intact tomb of an official named Sekhentiu-Ptah containing ritual objects.

Ukraine strikes Russian drone storage and launch site in Oryol Oblast, damages 5 launchers
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian site used to operate attack drones in Oryol Oblast on Sept. 21, damaging five launchers, Ukraine's General Staff said on Sept. 22.
The strike targeted a facility near the settlement of Tsymbulova in Oryol Oblast, roughly 150 kilometers (93 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
At least three drone storage warehouses were hit and caught fire, a launch site used for jet-powered strike drones was damaged, and five launchers were also damaged, according to the General Staff.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the extent of the damage.
"Ukraine's Defense Forces systematically and as a priority target sites used to store, prepare, and launch attack drones in order to reduce Russia's ability to strike civilian targets in Ukraine," the General Staff said.
The strike came amid a broader wave of Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure. Overnight on Sept. 22, Ukrainian forces also struck the Kuibyshev oil refinery in Samara Oblast. The refinery processes around 7 million metric tons of oil annually and supplies fuel products used by Russia's military-industrial sector and armed forces.
Ukraine frequently targets facilities connected to Russia's drone, missile, and energy infrastructure in an effort to reduce Moscow's capacity to sustain attacks against Ukrainian cities and support its war effort.

Romanian Ex-Presidential Candidate Held in €1.1M Fraud Case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22

01:37:00 KST

Romanian prosecutors have asked a Bucharest court to place former presidential candidate Călin Georgescu and businessman Ionel Rusen in pretrial detention for 30 days over an alleged organized criminal group and a 1.1 million euro ($1.26 million) fraud.
According to a prosecution filing reviewed by OCCRP, investigators allege Georgescu, Rusen and Italian businessman Massimiliano Arena persuaded a Romanian businessman to transfer money as a guarantee for a foreign credit line that never materialized. Prosecutors say Georgescu initiated the arrangement and introduced Rusen as someone capable of securing the financing.
The victim first transferred 1 million euros and later another 100,000 euros after being told the loan could be increased from six million euros to 15 million, the filing says. Prosecutors detained Georgescu and Rusen for 24 hours following searches that uncovered electronic devices, signal jammers and documents suspected of being false. The filing also cites secretly recorded conversations in which Georgescu discussed buying property in Italy and seeking political asylum, which prosecutors cited in arguing that he posed a flight risk.
Georgescu’s campaign team previously told Digi24 it had no information about the case and Rusen told Digi24 that he was not Georgescu’s business partner, had not participated in his presidential campaign and declined to comment on the fraud allegations. Arena told IrpiMedia that he had learned about the Romanian complaint from journalists and would comment only after receiving official notification from the competent judicial authorities.

Netanyahu to cut short NYC trip amid protests, Mamdani threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:33:35 UTC
01:33:35 KST

Breadcrumb
Netanyahu to cut short NYC visit amid protests, Mamdani arrest threat
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has dramatically shortened his visit to New York for the UN General Assembly, amid planned protests, heightened security and tensions with Mayor Zohran Mamdani over the International Criminal Court warrant for his arrest.
Netanyahu is expected to arrive in the US on Thursday morning, address the General Assembly at 2pm New York time and leave for Israel later that evening, according to Israeli media reports.
The Israeli leader is not expected to spend a single night in the US, cutting what had initially been planned as a longer visit to just several hours. He has also cancelled a planned stop in Texas to meet billionaire Elon Musk and will not take Israeli journalists aboard his official "Wing of Zion" aircraft.
Israeli media cited planned protests and security concerns among the reasons for the unusually brief visit.
According to Ynet, Netanyahu's plane is expected to avoid New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport and instead land in neighbouring New Jersey.
The outlet linked the arrangements partly to tensions with Mamdani, who has repeatedly called for Netanyahu to face arrest over the ICC warrant.
Other Israeli reporting, however, has attributed the decision to avoid JFK to logistical and security considerations surrounding Netanyahu's aircraft.
Mamdani has been an outspoken critic of Netanyahu and previously pledged to have the Israeli leader arrested if he travelled to New York, citing the ICC warrant issued against him in November 2024.
The mayor acknowledged in July, however, that New York City does not independently possess the legal authority to enforce the warrant.
"It is clear that we do not have the independent legal authority to enforce this warrant," Mamdani said at the time, while calling on the US federal government to join the ICC and execute it.
He has nevertheless maintained that Netanyahu is not welcome in New York and has continued to describe him as a war criminal over Israel's actions in Gaza.
The ICC issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Israeli defence minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024, saying there were reasonable grounds to believe they bore criminal responsibility for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during Israel's war on Gaza.
Israel rejects the allegations and does not recognise the court's jurisdiction. The US is also not a member of the ICC.
US President Donald Trump said in July that Netanyahu would not be arrested in the United States.
Heavy security and protests expected
Netanyahu is expected to receive unusually heavy security protection during his brief stay, with US Secret Service involvement in preparations for the visit reportedly greater than usual.
Large demonstrations are also expected in New York during his visit.
Haaretz reported that Netanyahu is preparing for a hostile reception both on the streets and inside the General Assembly, where Israeli officials anticipate that ambassadors and other delegates could walk out or stage protests during his speech.
A mass walkout took place when Netanyahu addressed the General Assembly last year.
Mamdani has said he does not plan to participate in protests against Netanyahu during the visit and has been coordinating with the New York Police Department over security surrounding UNGA.
Netanyahu is not expected to meet Trump during the trip, and a meeting with Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also not been confirmed.
His address comes around a month before Israel's general election, with Israeli media reporting that the speech is expected to focus heavily on Iran while also being aimed at a domestic Israeli audience.
Israeli officials are meanwhile hoping protests inside the General Assembly will be smaller than last year, amid international attention on the war with Iran and Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Israel continues to occupy most of the Gaza Strip and carry out deadly air strikes, shelling and gunfire despite the October 2025 ceasefire.
More than 73,900 Palestinians have been killed and nearly 175,000 wounded since October 2023, including around 1,400 killed since the ceasefire took effect.
Most of Gaza's roughly 2.1 million people remain displaced, while Israeli restrictions continue to impede the entry of critical humanitarian and reconstruction supplies.

Trump signs Greenland security deal allowing US to expand military presence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:32:59 UTC
01:32:59 KST

The agreement will enable the US to expand its military presence on Greenland through the modernisation and enlargement of its current Pituffik Space Base and the establishment of new defence areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig.
US President Donald Trump has signed a new Greenland security deal with Denmark and the island territory.
Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, and Greenland PM Jens-Frederik Nielsen signed the agreement on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday.
Under the terms of the deal, shared online by the Danish Foreign Ministry, the US will be permitted to expand its military presence on Greenland through the modernisation and enlargement of its current Pituffik Space Base and the establishment of new defence areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig.
It will also allow the US "free access to and movement between" defence areas across Greenland, "including the Territorial Waters, by land, air and sea." American aircraft may also fly over and land in any territory on the island, it states.
Trump previously said the deal - which also reaffirms the "sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark" and recognises Greenland's "right to self determination" - would see Washington take "permanent control" of the island's security.
"From now on, no U.S. adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval," he wrote in a post on Truth Social on Friday.
Both Frederiksen and Nielsen have welcomed the agreement - which stops short of Trump's wish to seize the territory for the US, a move he had argued was essential for the US' "national security."
In a statement on Friday, Frederiksen said the deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic Area," while Nielsen said it was "to the benefit of us all."
The US is reported to have had 17 military facilities and over 10,000 troops on Greenland at the height of the Cold War. It currently operates just one base on the island, the Pituffik Space Base - the US Department of Defense's northernmost installation.
Pituffik is used for missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance missions, per the US Space Force.

U.S. fighter jet crashes at air base in Germany, injuring pilot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

U.S. fighter jet crashes at American air base in Germany, injuring the pilot
An American military aircraft crashed at a U.S. air base in western Germany on Tuesday, injuring the pilot, the American military said.
In a statement, the U.S. Air Base Spangdahlem said that the pilot ejected and was receiving medical care. It also said the plane, which was an F-16 Fighting Falcon, crashed around 2:30 p.m. local time, and that the cause of the crash was being investigated.
The local German district, where Spangdahlem is located, had said earlier that fire and emergency teams responded to the incident.
Spangdahlem is home to an F-16 fighter jet squadron with about 20 aircraft, the German news agency dpa reported.
The squadron, which supports U.S. Air Force and NATO missions worldwide, is the centerpiece of the air base. The base has about 5,000 military and civilian employees, plus their family members, according to the latest figures. The U.S. air base also employs between 700 and 800 Germans.
Spangdahlem Air Base is home to the U.S. Air Force's 52nd Fighter Wing, which provides airpower and support for NATO operations in Europe and beyond.
The U.S. Air Force has maintained a presence in Spangdahlem since the mid-1950s. Along with Ramstein near Kaiserslautern in southwestern Germany, Spangdahlem Air Base is considered one of the most important airfields for the U.S. military in the region.
Another F-16 crashed less than a week ago, this one in Grand Traverse County, Michigan. The pilot, a member of the 149th Fighter Wing of the Texas National Guard, ejected and was in stable condition, a spokesperson said. The Texas Military Department said the pilot had been on a routine training mission when the incident occurred.
The crash remains under investigation. No injuries on the ground were reported.

- list 2 of 3Two ex-Sri Lanka officials sentenced to death over 2019 Easter bombings
- list 3 of 3At least 26 people killed in Sri Lanka prison clashes
What does the verdict say?
The three-judge bench in Sri Lanka’s High Court has found that 14 of the accused were guilty on all charges, which included murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism and possessing firearms and explosives under the Prevention of Terrorism Act.
A 15th defendant was found guilty of only some of the charges, while nine others were acquitted of any charges related to aiding and abetting the suicide bombers.
Twenty-five men were originally charged, but one defendant died in custody.
Police had filed more than 23,000 charges against the suspects, all of whom denied involvement.
The presiding judge told the court that sentencing would be delivered later on Tuesday.
What happened in the bombings?
Six almost simultaneous bombings struck churches and hotels on Easter Sunday in 2019, killing 279 people and marking the deadliest attacks in Sri Lanka since the end of its civil war in 2009.
At least 450 people were injured, with officials in the aftermath blaming a local armed group for the suicide bombings.
Most of those killed were Sri Lankan and died in three churches where worshippers were attending Easter Sunday services. Three other bombings struck luxury hotels – the Cinnamon Grand, the Kingsbury and the Shangri-La – located in the heart of the capital, Colombo, killing at least 45, including foreign nationals.
Among the dead were Japanese, Dutch, Chinese, British, US and Portuguese tourists.
All of the accused are from Sri Lanka’s minority Muslim community.
How did the legal case unfold?
The prosecution in the case, which opened in November 2021, named Naufer Moulavi as the main architect of the attacks.
Moulavi had submitted what they said was a voluntary confession to the court in which he had admitted his role.
While the court accepted the confession, Moulavi later told the court that he had not been shown what he was signing, leading him to retract his statement and reject the allegations against him.
Moulavi was ultimately one of the 14 found guilty of all charges by the court on Tuesday.
During the trial, more than 2,300 people gave evidence for the prosecution.
There were also 2,076 pieces of evidence, including explosives, swords and firearms.
Last month, Former Police Chief Pujith Jayasundara and former Defence Ministry Secretary Hemasiri Fernando were sentenced to death by the country’s High Court, which found them guilty of criminal negligence. Chaminda Athukorale, lawyer for the two men, said they would appeal the ruling.
What did the Supreme Court rule in 2023 about the government’s role in the bombings?
Sri Lanka’s Supreme Court ruled that former President Maithripala Sirisena and four other top officials failed to prevent the bombings despite having prior intelligence about them, and ordered them to pay compensation to the victims.
The court ordered Sirisena to pay 100 million rupees ($273,300) from his personal funds to family members of victims who brought the civil case before the court.
Former Police Chief Jayasundara, two top intelligence officials and former Defence Ministry Secretary Fernando were ordered to pay a total of 210 million rupees ($574,000).
The seven-judge bench ruled that Sirisena had failed to take adequate measures to prevent the attacks, despite receiving solid intelligence warnings that they were being planned two weeks earlier.
In addition, the court ruled that Sirisena, who also served as defence minister and commander in chief of the armed forces, had failed to hold regular meetings of the national security council and had omitted key personnel from meetings he did hold.
What else has been discovered about these bombings?
In February this year, Retired Major-General Suresh Sallay, the country’s former intelligence chief, was arrested for his connection to the bombings.
Sallay, who was promoted to State Intelligence Service (SIS) chief in 2019 after Gotabaya Rajapaksa became president, has been accused of involvement in the coordinated suicide bombings – a charge he has denied.
“He was arrested for conspiracy and aiding and abetting the Easter Sunday attacks,” an investigating officer told the AFP news agency at the time of his arrest. The investigation into his role in the attack is ongoing.
A 2023 investigation by the British broadcaster, Channel 4, found that Sallay was linked to the bombers and had met them before the attack.
A whistleblower told the network that he had permitted the attack to proceed with the intention of influencing that year’s presidential election in favour of Rajapaksa.
Two days after the bombings, Rajapaksa declared his candidacy and went on to win the November vote in a landslide after promising to stamp out violence.
Rajapaksa’s government was rocked three years after the bombings by mass demonstrations about the economy in Sri Lanka.
Sri Lanka’s Catholic Church has regularly criticised the government’s investigation into the Easter Sunday bombings and petitioned the United Nations for an international probe.
In a 2022 address to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, Cardinal Malcolm Ranjith demanded a mechanism to probe the attacks, which had been blamed on local Muslim groups.
“The first impression of this massacre was that it was purely the work of a few Islamic extremists,” Ranjith said at the time. “However, subsequent investigations indicate that this massacre was part of a grand political plot.”
Other investigations also faulted the authorities for failing to act on warnings from an Indian intelligence agency that an attack was imminent.

At least 555 Ukrainians have faced treason and espionage charges from Russia during full-scale invasion, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:31:57 UTC
01:31:57 KST

Russia has accused at least 555 Ukrainian citizens of treason, espionage, and related crimes since the start of the full-scale war, accounting for nearly 38% of all known defendants in such cases. Of those, 266 had been listed in Ukraine’s official register of missing persons, according to a study by the human rights group Pervy Otdel (lit. “Department One”) and Parubets Analytics, which based their findings on court records, law enforcement statements, media reports, information from lawyers and relatives, and open-source investigations.
People are entered into Ukraine’s missing-persons register as the result of reports from relatives or fellow service members. As of Aug. 8, 2026, 249 people covered by the study remained on the register, another 17 had previously been listed as missing but were later removed, seven were taken off the list after being released in prisoner exchanges, and one was officially declared dead.
Nearly 90% of the known disappearances (239 out of 266) occurred in Ukrainian territories that are under Russian military occupation. The most common last known locations were Melitopol, Nova Kakhovka, Kherson, Donetsk, Berdiansk, Enerhodar, Tokmak, Oleshky, and Skadovsk. Overall, 454 of the 555 people in the study — 81.8% — were first detained in Ukraine. Another 100 were detained within Russia’s internationally recognized borders, and one was taken into custody in Kazakhstan.
As of the time the study was completed, Russian courts had sentenced 402 Ukrainians on treason, espionage, and related charges . Courts in occupied Ukrainian territories handed down 241 of those sentences — 60.1%. Among individual courts, the Southern District Military Court in Rostov-on-Don issued the largest number of convictions, with 65.
Sentences are known in only 382 of the cases. Of those, seven received life terms, while the rest were sentenced to prison terms ranging from five years to 27 years and nine months. The median sentence was 14 years. In cases where treason or espionage charges were combined with terrorism or sabotage charges, the median sentence rose to 18 years.
In 323 cases, researchers from Pervy Otdel and Parubets Analytics were able to determine certain specifics of the accusations. Just over half of those cases — 176, or 54.5% — involved allegations of collecting and passing information to Ukraine about Russian troops, military equipment, and infrastructure. Another 37 people were accused of preparing or carrying out terrorist attacks, making assassination attempts, or successfully carrying out a killing. Additionally, 34 were accused of providing financial assistance to Ukraine, 15 of sabotage targeting transportation or infrastructure, and another 15 of serving in or attempting to join the Ukrainian armed forces or other Ukrainian formations.
As of the time of the study, 534 of the 555 people remained in custody, though researchers were able to determine the exact place of detention for only 360 of them. Of those whose locations were known, 236 were being held in facilities inside Russia and another 124 in pretrial detention centers and penal colonies in occupied Ukrainian territories. Researchers said Ukrainians have also been transferred to prisons in Siberia, the Russian Far East, and the Far North.
The report’s authors stressed that 555 is not a complete count. They estimated that the names of about 30% of defendants in such cases remain unknown due to the fact that proceedings are closed and court records often omit identifying information. The study’s data are current as of Aug. 8, 2026.

US to gain permanent control over Greenland’s security — Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:31:51 UTC
01:31:51 KST

UN, September 22. /TASS/. Under the US-Denmark agreements, Washington will gain permanent full control over the security of Greenland, President Donald Trump said.
"As I announced just days ago, the United States has also reached an unprecedented agreement regarding the northern frontier of North America, the large and strategically vital piece of land known as Greenland," he told the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.
According to Trump, the United States is gaining "permanent control over security and all other needs on that territory. We will have the complete ability to do what is necessary to defend the American continent and also Europe and other places."
The ceremony to sign the documents with the participation of Trump as well as representatives of Denmark and Greenland is currently taking place on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Earlier, Denmark, of which Greenland is an autonomy, categorically rejected the US president’s intention to gain control over the island. Trump has repeatedly said that Greenland should join his country to ensure security. Even during his first term, he proposed buying the island, while in 2025, he promised to annex it, threatening Copenhagen with trade duties in case of refusal.
In 1951, Washington and Copenhagen, in addition to their alliance obligations under NATO, signed the Greenland Defense Treaty. Under it, the United States undertook to defend the island against possible aggression. It is home to the American space base Pituffik responsible for the missile warning system and monitoring the Arctic zone.

EU budget talks face deadlock despite push for year-end deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:31:05 UTC
01:31:05 KST

Member states have spent months reiterating their negotiating positions, fuelling frustration within EU institutions that are pushing for faster progress. Reaching an agreement only in December would mean that negotiations remain largely deadlocked until the final stage.
European affairs ministers met in Brussels on Tuesday for another round of negotiations on the EU’s next seven-year budget. Despite a shared ambition to reach a deal by the end of the year, negotiations appear to have stalled, with significant differences still unresolved.
"This is my fourth [Multiannual Financial Framework] negotiations, so I have to admit that some of the discussions come with a large sense of déjà vu," European Commissioner for the Budget Piotr Serafin said during a debate with EU ministers on Tuesday.
“Many positions are quite predictable, as they have been consistently repeated over the last decades,” the commissioner added.
The next key stage in the negotiations will come at the European Council in Brussels in mid-October. Ahead of that meeting, the Irish government, which is currently chairing negotiations among the member states, will present a compromise text for leaders to consider.
“There is a general agreement to reach a deal by the end of the year,” Irish Minister for European Affairs Thomas Byrne told journalists on Tuesday, referring to discussions among the EU’s 27 member states.
October's text would mark the penultimate stage before a final compromise is expected in December, when EU leaders will need to bridge their differences and find a workable trade-off to break the deadlock.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa have repeatedly called for an ambitious budget, backed by new EU taxes and sufficient spending to match Europe’s ambitions in strategic sectors such as AI and defence, while preserving adequate funding for traditional areas such as agriculture and fisheries.
EU institutions want to avoid a repeat of the previous budget negotiations, when member states ultimately failed to agree on new sources of EU revenue, known as “own resources.” This time, however, growing global uncertainty and the Commission’s push to strengthen Europe’s competitiveness on the global stage have made the need for additional EU revenue to invest in strategic sectors even more pressing.
The €2 trillion proposal presented by the Commission in July 2025 reflected this trend. It provided increased funding for competitiveness, security, and defence, alongside significant cuts to agricultural and regional funds, compared with the current budget.
The two camps
Two main camps have emerged among member states in recent months. One, made up of 17 countries and known as the “Friends of Cohesion,” is pushing to preserve funding for agriculture and regional development.
Another group, including Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Finland, Sweden and Denmark, is calling for cuts of “several hundred billion euros” across the budget, while prioritising spending on defence and competitiveness. They refer to themselves as the “modernisers,” although they are also commonly described as the “frugals.”
Germany is leading the group of frugal countries and used the occasion on Tuesday to escalate its rhetoric, even in opposition to the position of EU institutions. Targeting Costa in particular—who has been outspoken against major budget cuts—German Minister Gunther Krichbaum said he had lost touch with reality. “You have to ask yourself whether Mr. Costa has now completely lost his grip on reality,” the minister told journalists on the sidelines of the meeting, as Germany continues to push for substantial cuts.
The “Friends of Cohesion” generally support the introduction of new “own resources,” while the frugal countries remain more sceptical.
They argue that, as net contributors, they will bear a disproportionate share of the cost of the next budget, noting that they already account for around 40% of contributions to the current one.
The budget is likely to be financed through a combination of contributions based on a percentage of member states’ gross national income (GNI) and new “own resources.” Member states will have to agree on the share of GNI to be allocated to the EU budget and determine which own resources should be mobilised to make up the remaining funding.
"I see many different ways of computing national contributions. It seems that there is a competition going on between capitals to come up with numbers that show that their national contribution increases the most. This is not really helpful," Serafin said during the debate on Tuesday, calling EU countries to build a "common understanding on the actual numbers" to present in the most objective way.
Byrne told journalists on Monday that the Irish presidency would put forward a set of proposals on own resources as part of the text to be presented in October.
To reach a deal, all the 27 member states have to agree on the new budget.
The final deal will also require the backing of the European Parliament, whose position on the budget differs significantly from that of the member states.
EU lawmakers are calling for a 10% increase in funding across the main budget headings and want the repayment of the Recovery Plan loans, issued in 2020 to support the economy following the COVID-19 pandemic, to be kept outside the regular EU budget.
During the discussion on Tuesday, leading MEPs asked the member states to avoid cuts.
"If we reduce the EU budget, EU countries will have to address these challenges separately at national level, and likely at a higher cost," said Romanian MEP Siegfried Mureșan, who is co-leading the negotiations on behalf of the European Parliament alongside Portuguese MEP Carla Tavares.
Tavares also urged member states to step up the negotiations.
"The clock is ticking, and we need to make progress if we are to reach an agreement on the next MFF in time. Parliament is ready to work towards the conditions needed for its consent, but the Council still needs to move forward as well, particularly on new genuine own resources," she said.

EU agrees to lift sanctions on Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

EU agrees to lift sanctions on Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman
EU member states’ permanent representatives have agreed to remove two Russian billionaires — USM Holdings founder Alisher Usmanov and Alfa Group co-founder Mikhail Fridman — from the sanctions list, according to Reuters and Euronews.
The Russia sanctions list includes about 3,000 individuals and entities. It had previously been renewed every six months with the consent of all 27 EU members. EU representatives have now agreed to extend the sanctions regime for three years. Under the deal, the businessmen would be removed from the sanctions list in exchange for extending it for three years.
The sanctions list was due to expire overnight on September 15. On September 14, EU representatives managed to extend it by just one week. At the time, reports said restrictions on Usmanov had caused disagreements among the bloc’s members. Slovakia, followed by France, demanded that the sanctions against him be lifted. The other 25 members disagreed. Luxembourg then also asked for Fridman to be removed from the sanctions list.
France said its request was based on national security considerations. According to EUobserver and the Financial Times, Paris pushed for Usmanov’s removal from the sanctions list as part of a prisoner-release agreement with Azerbaijan. The deal may involve the return of French businessman Martin Ryan to France. In March, a court in Baku sentenced him to 10 years in prison on charges of gathering information about the military during the conflict in Nagorno-Karabakh. In addition to Azerbaijan, Turkey and Uzbekistan, where Usmanov was born, had also lobbied for his removal from the sanctions list.
Luxembourg’s support for Fridman, meanwhile, has been linked to the $16 billion lawsuit he filed against the country’s authorities in 2024 over the freezing of his assets. The businessman later filed similar lawsuits against the Netherlands and the United Kingdom.
As of September 22, Latvia was the only EU member still opposed to lifting sanctions on the Russian businessmen. “The situation is complicated. […] Extending the sanctions for 36 months would be the right move. However, the price should not simply be removing two people from the sanctions list,” Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said.
According to Euronews, Latvia ultimately lifted its veto and “opted for a constructive abstention,” allowing the agreement to be reached. It will take effect once EU representatives confirm the previously agreed-upon decision in writing. Riga has nevertheless imposed national sanctions on Fridman and Usmanov.
The European Union sanctioned Usmanov and Fridman in 2022, shortly after Russia began its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. EU authorities concluded that both billionaires belonged to Vladimir Putin’s inner circle. As a result of the sanctions, Fridman resigned from the board of the investment group LetterOne and sold his stakes in Alfa Bank and Alfa Insurance.
Usmanov and Fridman sought to challenge the restrictions and enlisted lobbyists in the West to push for the sanctions to be lifted. Hungary, for example, demanded that the businessmen be removed from the EU sanctions list as early as 2025. In March 2026, Hungary and Slovakia also tried to block the renewal of EU sanctions on Russia, demanding that Usmanov and Fridman be removed from the sanctions lists.
In 2023, Leonid Volkov resigned as chairman of the board of ACF International (the Anti-Corruption Foundation) because he had signed a letter in support of Mikhail Fridman.
