Gaza mother speaks out on family torn apart by Israel’s genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:02:03 UTC
01:02:03 KST

Breadcrumb
‘My heart breaks’: A Gazan mother’s account of a family torn apart by Israel's genocide
After leaving Gaza so her daughter Qamar could receive medical treatment, Palestinian mother Huda Al-Kurdi is now living in the United States (US) with her two children, including Qamar and her son Omar.
The need for treatment came after Qamar was seriously injured in an Israeli attack on 4 December 2023, the day she turned six. Her leg was amputated about a week later, on 12 December, after a lack of necessary treatment and medication led to severe infections.
"The amputation was not the result of the critical injury but of the lack of necessary treatment and medication, which led to severe infections in the leg. We waited more than a year for a medical evacuation that would allow Qamar to receive treatment," Huda tells The New Arab.
In sharing this, Huda notes that while Qamar was eventually able to leave Gaza and receive the treatment she needed, her six-year-old daughter Taleen, who was also injured in the attack, was not allowed to leave with them and remains in Gaza with her father.
What happened in Gaza
To understand the extent of what Huda and her children went through, Huda first recalls their life in Gaza before Israel’s genocide.
Like many families in Gaza, Huda lived a relatively stable life with her husband and their three children in Jabalia, northern Gaza. She had specialised in mathematics, while her husband studied law at the Islamic University of Gaza, but neither worked in their fields because of unemployment and the Israeli blockade.
After the genocide began, Huda and her family were forced to flee to one of the shelters run by the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA) because of the heavy bombardment. They remained there for about four months.
However, overcrowding and the lack of privacy forced her to return home from time to time to cook or collect some belongings. It was during one of these visits that Huda was with her sister and their children when indiscriminate bombardment began targeting her home and neighbouring houses.
This took place during the first ground invasion of Jabalia in 2023.
"The tanks began shelling homes and everywhere indiscriminately, in an attempt to push residents to leave, leaving them to their fate and what was destined for them," Huda says.
She continues: "When the first shell hit, I did not understand what was happening, but after about the third shell, I realised that we were being bombed. Screaming filled the air, and then I began to feel burns on my body. I had been injured in my back."
As the bombardment continued, Huda pulled her son and daughter Taleen from beneath the rubble, screaming at the top of her voice.
"I do not know how I carried them and got them out. Taleen had lost consciousness in my arms because of her head injury, and for a moment I thought she had been killed. Residents rushed to help me, so they took Taleen, while I returned to the building to rescue Qamar, who had been seriously injured. I pulled her out with one hand and carried her leg with the other, as it had not yet completely separated from her body," she says.
The ongoing Israeli bombardment prevented ambulances from reaching the area, Huda says. Residents tried to help the survivors and transport them to hospitals using a cart and a horse.
Huda's sister and her children were also injured, and one of them later died from his wounds.
Immediately after the injury, Huda was separated from her daughter Qamar, who remained with her father at Al-Awda Hospital, while Huda accompanied her two children, Omar and Taleen, at Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza.
The hospitals were under siege at the time, and some were bombed. Huda recalls how her husband lost a lot of weight, as only small quantities of food were allowed into hospitals, with priority given to the wounded.
It was during this period that Qamar's condition deteriorated. Doctors were forced to amputate Qamar's leg because of a lack of medical supplies, as Israel does not allow many essential materials to enter, citing dual-use concerns.
Huda describes how Qamar's condition deteriorated after her leg was amputated and how her body became frail.
"Qamar's condition worsened because there was no physiotherapy, or even crutches or a wheelchair, and there were no resources in the north as a result of the war and blockade. After months, the muscle in her amputated leg weakened, as did her healthy leg," she says.
Looking back on what happened, Huda says, "We saw a lot and went through a lot, and perhaps we became accustomed to it. I was surprised when I began psychological treatment and was told that if we did not feel like talking, we did not have to. But I wanted to tell our stories, even though they are difficult to hear."
New beginnings
As the situation in northern Gaza became more difficult, Huda was forced to flee again with her three children from the north to the south, without their father this time, fearing that he might be detained and arrested.
The truce that began in January 2025 and lasted until March helped facilitate Huda's departure with Qamar and Omar through the Rafah crossing as part of a medical evacuation in February, with the help of Heal Palestine, a non-profit organisation registered in the US that provides urgent relief and long-term support to Palestinian children and families inside and outside Palestine, including assistance with medical evacuations.
As Huda puts it, the evacuation came after more than a year of waiting for Qamar to receive treatment outside Gaza, with the wider medical evacuation process remaining slow despite an increase in evacuations since the ceasefire agreement, as patients are often sent to countries in the region rather than countries with greater treatment capabilities, particularly for complex cases.
The US has received only a few dozen of these cases, and there are no official statistics on the matter. Although independent humanitarian organisations have covered the costs of Palestinians' treatment and accommodation, rather than the US government, Washington decided in August to stop issuing visas to Palestinians for medical evacuations, without providing any "justification," making Qamar and her family among the few "fortunate" ones.
Upon reflection, Huda notes that leaving Gaza brought Qamar closer to the treatment she needed, but also meant being separated from her husband and daughter.
Healing begins
Going into further detail about the journey to the US, Huda recalls that arriving at a New Jersey airport was not free from bureaucracy, questioning and lengthy checks.
Despite this, she felt relief when she left and saw members of Heal Palestine, the host organisation, as well as members of the Palestinian community and supporters of Palestinian rights waiting to receive them, carrying gifts for the children.
The arrival in the US marked the beginning of a new stage centred around treatment. Huda explains that their lives are filled with doctors' appointments, surgeries, and physical and psychological therapy.
Huda says she is grateful for being able to have Qamar treated, as well as for the attention of the community and the organisation and everyone's commitment to supporting them.
Alongside her treatment, Qamar has also joined a school there and taken part in a summer camp, activities and events, as well as studying a Palestinian curriculum provided by Heal Palestine online.
But the new surroundings have not erased what Qamar experienced in Gaza. Asked whether Qamar remembers the incident, Huda says her daughter suffers from insomnia that is difficult to overcome.
Although her condition has improved significantly, she remains affected by the trauma. Huda says, "For example, Qamar was terrified some time ago because she could not distinguish the sound of thunder from the sound of bombardment.
"I try to strengthen her self-confidence so that she can accept her situation without feeling inadequate because she has lost her leg. But ultimately, she is a child who does not understand the meaning of 'fate and destiny'. She understands us when we tell her that her leg went ahead of her to heaven. But this is not easy at all."
Memories, separation and life in two worlds
The effects of the genocide have not been limited to Qamar's physical injuries. Huda says she initially did not realise that she needed psychological treatment to deal with all the trauma she had experienced.
She also continues to carry the memories of what happened to her family. "We saw a lot and overcame a lot, and perhaps we became accustomed to it," she says, explaining that she wanted to tell their stories even when she was told she did not have to speak about them.
That emotional weight is made harder by the fact that Huda is now living away from part of her family. She says she is living a double life, part of which is in Gaza with her husband and daughter Taleen, who have gone through days when they could find neither food nor shelter, in addition to the bombardment they have endured.
The separation is particularly painful because Taleen believes that her mother left her behind. Huda also thinks about her husband's suffering inside Gaza, away from his wife and two children.
Huda recalls the periods when Israel's forced starvation intensified, and even flour became unavailable while she was still in Gaza with her two children. She remembers the pain she felt when thinking about her husband and daughter Taleen, who were left without enough food.
"The images of starvation being circulated, as difficult as they are to see, do not convey the full reality of what people are experiencing or the extent of their suffering," she says.
The separation has also affected Huda's son Omar. She says, "He tells me that he loves his father, but he does not call him by his name. He believes that his father left him to stay with Taleen, and my heart breaks when I hear him say this.
"He also refuses to say goodbye to anyone, and whenever he sees a plane, he asks me why his father does not come. So I think about how Taleen will feel if she sees a picture of Qamar and Omar playing in the US while she is suffering so much in Gaza."
For Huda, this separation also changes how she experiences ordinary life in the US. Speaking about living in two parallel worlds, she adds, "It is very difficult to go out here and enjoy ourselves while Taleen is in Gaza, suffering from the pain of separation and constantly asking me when she will join us. But I try to stay in touch with her and give her hope that she will see us again, so that she does not feel as though I have left her."
Wanting to return home
Despite everything that has happened, Huda says she still misses her life in Gaza and does not want to live anywhere else or even remain in the US, even though conditions there are better.
"Our country is blessed. Neighbours look after one another, and we grow our own food and eat from the land. The situation is difficult now, but as soon as reconstruction takes place, I want to return. I want to live with my family and children in safety."

Spain advances US extradition of millionaire accused of funneling $7.5M to Hamas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:01:54 UTC
01:01:54 KST

James “Fergie” Chambers’ hopes that Spain’s government would stop his extradition to the United States before the case reached court suffered a major setback Tuesday, after Madrid allowed the American request to proceed to Spain’s National Court.
The Council of Ministers authorized the next stage of the proceedings against the 41-year-old multimillionaire and pro-Palestinian activist, leaving the Audiencia Nacional to determine whether he can legally be extradited to the United States. The Spanish government stressed that the move was procedural and did not amount to a final decision to surrender him.
The government could have halted the process at this stage, including if it concluded that the U.S. prosecution amounted to political persecution, as Chambers’ lawyers argue. Instead, it allowed the judicial phase to begin. If the court ultimately approves extradition, the case is expected to return to the government before any surrender takes place.
The decision came despite opposition from within Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s governing bloc. Sumar and other parties on the Spanish left had urged the government to reject Washington’s request, arguing that Chambers is being targeted because of his support for the Palestinian cause.
Enrique Santiago, a lawmaker associated with Sumar and spokesman for the United Left, has described the case as “political persecution” and argued that Spain should not cooperate with it.
Spain’s government, however, did not accept that argument at this stage. Its spokeswoman emphasized after the Cabinet meeting that the decision merely opens the judicial phase and does not determine Chambers’ guilt or guarantee that he will ultimately be handed over to U.S. authorities.
Chambers is an heir to the Cox family fortune, built through Cox Enterprises, the U.S. communications, automotive and media conglomerate whose holdings include Axios. He separated from his interests in the family business in 2023 in a deal he has said was worth hundreds of millions of dollars.
Since then, he has become an unusual figure among America’s wealthy heirs. Chambers identifies as a Marxist-Leninist, has publicly expressed anti-capitalist and anti-American views and has donated substantial sums to left-wing causes and Palestinian projects.
He was arrested on July 10 in Ibiza, where he had traveled with his wife, Jewish actress Stella Schnabel, and their son. The couple said they were on their way to visit a school as they considered moving to the island when police vehicles blocked their car and Chambers was detained on an international warrant issued at the request of the United States. He has remained in custody in Spain since then.
At the heart of the American case is a $7.5 million transfer from the United States to Tunisia, where Chambers had lived for a period. U.S. authorities allege the transaction formed part of conduct connected to money laundering and support for organizations linked to Hamas.
The case also involves allegations linked to protests targeting U.S. facilities belonging to Israeli defense contractor Elbit Systems. Chambers had supported activists involved in some of those actions, including by paying bail and legal costs, according to reporting on the case.
Chambers and his defense team reject the U.S. account. They say money transferred to Tunisia was used in part for investment in Club Africain, one of the country’s best-known soccer clubs, including debt payments and investment in facilities, while other funds sent to Gaza were intended for humanitarian projects.
His defense team, led by former Spanish judge Baltasar Garzón, argues that the Trump administration has turned Chambers’ pro-Palestinian activism into a criminal case and is portraying humanitarian assistance as terrorism financing. Chambers has also begun seeking asylum in Spain, arguing that he would face political persecution if returned to the United States.
His lawyers still have several avenues to fight the extradition. One issue is Spain’s requirement of dual criminality, under which extradition generally depends on the alleged conduct also constituting an offense under Spanish law. His defense argues that at least one U.S. allegation connected to conspiracy to riot does not have a direct equivalent in Spain.
Money laundering, however, is an offense under Spanish law, leaving the U.S. request with another potential legal basis.
For Chambers, Tuesday’s decision changes the immediate trajectory of the case. His family and lawyers had spent weeks hoping Sánchez’s government, which has repeatedly clashed with the Trump administration and taken a strongly pro-Palestinian diplomatic line, would stop the extradition request before it reached court. Instead, the battle now moves to the Audiencia Nacional, with Chambers still behind bars and the prospect of extradition to the United States a step closer.

Infantino proposed an independent audit of FIFA governance following the scandal
Kyiv • UNN
FIFA President Gianni Infantino is initiating an independent audit of the organization’s governance and consultations on decision-making transparency. His plan to attract investors was withdrawn.
FIFA President Gianni Infantino has proposed conducting an independent audit of the decision-making process in the world football governing body. The move could help him restore support after abandoning a controversial plan to attract private investment, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
"First and foremost, I will ask the Council whether it wishes to commission an independent external audit of FIFA’s current governance system concerning the implementation of major strategic initiatives, as well as receive recommendations on possible improvements," Infantino wrote in a letter to the FIFA Council and the presidents of all 211 national member associations (Reuters obtained a copy of the letter).
He also said he would initiate consultations with confederations, national associations and other stakeholders on improving FIFA’s decision-making mechanisms.
Under these proposals, it is planned to analyze who exactly participates in decision-making on key initiatives (including defining the roles of the president, the Bureau, the Council and the Congress), as well as consider ways to increase transparency and accountability.
Infantino faced sharp criticism over his proposal to sell private investors a 20% stake in FIFA’s commercial rights, including the rights to stage the World Cup. The plan was abandoned in July after opposition and boycott threats; subsequently, UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation and CONCACAF called for changes in FIFA’s leadership.
Infantino’s opponents have so far been unable to find a candidate capable of challenging him in the election, which will be held in March in Rabat. Sources familiar with the discussions told Reuters this month that he still has enough votes to win, prompting opponents to focus on efforts to limit his powers.
Infantino said the rejected plan involved exploring the possibility of raising additional funds for football development by selling a minority stake in a commercial company controlled by FIFA. According to him, this would not have involved losing control over sports-related decision-making.
However, Infantino claims that information about the proposal became public before it had been fully presented to the Council and the national associations.
"I acknowledge that the lack of full context caused concern and created the impression that a decision had already been made. In fact, that was not the case," he wrote in the letter sent on Monday.
"It remained only a proposal, not a final decision, and in any event required approval from the Council and the national associations. The proposal has now been withdrawn, and its implementation has been halted."
Infantino added that he had heard different views on who exactly should make decisions on important strategic issues. Some advocated mandatory unanimity for decisions in the Bureau, while others insisted that such matters be submitted directly for consideration by the Congress and the member associations.
"My task is not to draw preliminary conclusions about this discussion. Those who support a particular model should have the opportunity to clearly set out their position," he wrote.
Proposals received before the Council meeting on October 15 may be discussed during that meeting; later submissions will also be considered, within a timeframe to be determined separately. Any amendments to the FIFA Statutes will require approval by the Congress.
Infantino also noted that member associations’ positions on particular proposals or governance issues would not affect FIFA’s treatment of them, and that development and solidarity programs would continue to be implemented under the existing rules.
"No association’s treatment will depend on its position regarding any proposal or institutional matter," he wrote.
"I remain fully committed to the task of leading FIFA and confident in what we can achieve together."

Russia encircles key Ukrainian defense hub – MOD
Russian forces have completed the encirclement of Dobropolye, a major Ukrainian defensive hub in Russia’s Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR), the Defense Ministry in Moscow has announced.

The cities were transformed into a single fortified zone by a vast system of reinforced trenches, bunkers, and tunnels.
He added that Russian troops had breached a three-tier line of fortifications on the approaches to Dobropolye and claimed that Kiev had no comparable prepared defenses immediately to its north, forcing Ukrainian troops to hastily construct local strongpoints.
The Russian Defense Ministry also said that troops from Ukraine’s 4th and 15th National Guard brigades and the 425th Separate Assault Regiment, known as “Skala” or “Skelya,” were among those trapped in the town. “Operations are underway to eliminate” the surrounded Ukrainian forces, it added.
“Skala” came under scrutiny earlier this year after Ukrainian media reported torture and abuse at its training facilities, as well as 25 non-combat deaths among recruits. Ukrainian authorities subsequently opened an investigation and suspended the regiment’s commander.
As Russian forces continue to advance in Donbass, Moscow has accused Kiev of intensifying attacks on civilian targets, repeatedly describing such strikes as acts of terrorism. The Defense Ministry has warned that the targeting of civilian facilities would be met by intensified precision strikes on military targets in Kiev.
On Tuesday, a major Ukrainian drone raid on the Samara Region left one person dead and four injured, according to Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev. He said private homes and vehicles were also damaged.

Advanced math for whom? Study shows wealth rivals academic readiness in high school tracking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:00:38 UTC
01:00:38 KST

A recent study reveals that while high schools largely sort students into math and science classes based on academic readiness, social pressures from wealthier families also heavily dictate who gets access to advanced courses. The findings illustrate how curriculum tracking operates as both a practical teaching tool and a mechanism that can widen social divides. The research was published in the journal Social Science Research.
Educational tracking is the practice of assigning students to different educational paths based on their past academic performance. In American high schools, this often looks like placing some ninth graders in basic algebra while others take advanced geometry. Teachers and school administrators generally defend this practice by pointing to its practical benefits. When students in a single classroom share similar skill levels, teachers can tailor their instruction to match the pace and needs of the entire group.
Sociologists call this the functional perspective of education. From a functional standpoint, a school acts as a rational organization that efficiently matches a diverse student body with appropriate coursework. If a school has students with vastly different academic backgrounds, a functional tracking system will offer a wide variety of courses to accommodate everyone.
However, sociologists also view tracking through a conflict perspective. This alternate viewpoint suggests that tracking systems are shaped by social inequalities and competition for status. Affluent parents often lobby for highly exclusive academic tracks to ensure their children gain a competitive edge for college admissions. This behavior is sometimes called status competition. Another related concept, opportunity hoarding, occurs when privileged groups attempt to restrict access to premium educational resources, keeping marginalized groups out of advanced programs.
Researchers Shangmou Xu and Sean Kelly wanted to understand which of these opposing theories actually drives the way American high schools organize their science, technology, engineering, and mathematics courses. Xu is a researcher affiliated with both the University of Washington and the University of Pittsburgh. Kelly is a researcher at the University of Pittsburgh.
To test these theories, Xu and Kelly analyzed student transcripts and survey data from four massive national educational datasets. Their final sample included 3,620 high schools, covering student cohorts from 1982 through 2013. The researchers used this data to measure the demographic and socioeconomic makeup of each school, looking at factors like average test scores, family wealth, and racial diversity.
The researchers then built a detailed profile of how each school organized its math and science curriculum. They focused on four specific organizational dimensions of tracking. The first dimension, inclusiveness, measures the sheer volume of rigorous courses a school offers and how many students take them. The second dimension, selectivity, measures how strictly a school relies on past academic achievement to dictate a student’s current course placement.
The third dimension is scope, which evaluates whether a student’s placement in one subject mirrors their placement in another. In a school with high scope, a student placed in an advanced math class is highly likely to also be placed in an advanced English class. Finally, the researchers measured mobility. Mobility tracks how often students move into harder or easier classes as they progress from ninth grade to graduation.
When examining inclusiveness, the researchers found strong evidence for the functional theory of tracking. Schools with higher average achievement scores tended to offer more advanced math and science courses. This suggests that schools rationally expand their rigorous offerings to meet the needs of a high-achieving student body.
At the same time, the conflict theory also proved accurate. Schools with a higher average socioeconomic status offered more advanced courses, even after accounting for academic achievement. This indicates that privileged families exert pressure on schools to create more top-tier academic opportunities for their children. Over the three decades covered by the data, this specific wealth-based pressure on the overall volume of advanced courses grew weaker.
The researchers found a similar split when looking at the strictness and structure of the tracking systems. Schools with a wide range of academic abilities among their students tended to have a wider variety of math courses. They also tended to have highly selective placement systems, where past math scores strongly dictated future math placements. This aligns with the functional approach, showing that schools adapt their course structure to handle diverse skill levels.
Yet, social status again played a major role in shaping these structures. Schools with higher overall social status exhibited a wider gap in course difficulty among their students. These high-status schools were also much more selective in their placement processes. Privileged families appear to push for highly differentiated, strict tracks to maintain an educational advantage for their children.
The researchers did not find strong evidence for the theory of opportunity hoarding. If opportunity hoarding were a major factor, schools with highly diverse student populations would have the most rigid, exclusive tracking systems. The data did not support this assumption. Instead, competition among advantaged students within a school seemed to be the primary social force shaping the curriculum.
When looking at scope, the researchers noticed that affluent schools often linked placements across completely different subjects. In these high-status schools, a student in an advanced science class was very likely to be placed in an advanced English class. This practice restricts learning opportunities by locking students into a single generalized track, rather than evaluating their readiness subject by subject.
The data on track mobility offered a slightly more optimistic view of American high schools. Upward mobility in math and science classes increased gradually between 1982 and 2013. Schools became more flexible over time, providing more students with the chance to step up into harder courses as they progressed through high school.
This upward mobility was more common in schools with high average social status and in schools with diverse student populations. The researchers interpret this flexibility as a functional improvement. As schools open up learning opportunities and allow students to change paths, the tracking systems become more responsive to actual student growth.
There are a few limitations to keep in mind when interpreting these results. The study relied on student transcripts, which show the classes students ultimately took. Transcripts do not reveal the specific school policies, teacher recommendations, or private conversations with counselors that led to those final placements. The mechanisms of how parents lobby for advanced classes remain largely unseen in this type of data.
Additionally, the research evaluates the structure of curriculum tracking, but it does not measure how these systems affect actual student learning. The data cannot show whether placing students in highly tracked math classes improved their standardized test scores or helped them succeed in college. Future research should investigate how the design of science and math programs ultimately impacts long-term student success.
Educators and school administrators are often reluctant to discuss the social implications of how they sort students into classes. They tend to frame course placement as a purely objective, administrative task. This study demonstrates that while academic readiness is the primary driver of course placement, the social wealth of a school community also fundamentally shapes the curriculum.
The study, “Variation and change in high school STEM opportunity to learn in the US: Is the organization of the STEM curriculum functional or conflict driven?,” was authored by Shangmou Xu and Sean Kelly.

Rabbit Is Back, This Time With an AI Agent App
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

Jesse Lyu doesn't think the Rabbit R1 was a flop.
Lyu's gadget was among the first in the gold rush to create dedicated AI hardware that acted as a virtual assistant. You could speak into the R1 and ask it to complete tasks for you—book an Uber; order food on DoorDash. After a buzzy launch at CES 2024, it earned scathing reviews. All the agentic stuff on the R1 just didn't work that well. WIRED gave it a 3/10.
Since those early days, the capabilities of AI assistants have vastly improved, and now the tech is all the rage. So Rabbit is banging the drum again.
On Tuesday, Rabbit announced OS3, a standalone “agentic operating system” designed to run across multiple screens. It also arrives as a software update for the company's R1 gadget, though you don't need an R1 to use it. Instead, you can access OS3 through a desktop browser, Telegram on your phone, or even iMessage.
It’s a striking pivot for a company that once championed the handheld hardware over smartphone apps, but the environment for this type of software has ripened.
Agents that handle tasks for you are all anyone in Silicon Valley talks about. Meta's new Muse agent was just banned from crawling Amazon to shop on a user's behalf using a virtual machine. Lyu smirks as he brings it up, saying, “We've been through all of this a year and a half ago,” calling back to the R1's controversial use of a virtual machine to execute app actions on your behalf. So was Rabbit just too ahead of the curve?
Lyu says from a monetary perspective, the Rabbit R1 was tremendously successful, especially considering the company doesn't offer a subscription for its AI features, unlike many competitors. He claims the company delivered more than 100,000 of the orange-red, Teenage Engineering-designed gadgets worldwide, with return rates of less than 5 percent, and earned roughly a 45 to 50 percent margin on the hardware.
"Internally, from an engineering perspective—we didn't make the wrong bet," Lyu says. “I think the challenge is really being extremely limited in resources, team-wise and money-wise, compared to other AI studios that raised billions of dollars.” He says Rabbit has raised around $60 million in total and currently employs 15 people.
But after dismal reviews upon the R1's launch, the company had to make tough decisions. Rabbit decided against expanding the team and chose to stay lean, but things were dire around this time last year. A planned launch in India was stymied by regulations, putting the company in financial strain, so much so that a handful of employees went on strike and claimed they weren't getting paid. Lyu says he respected their decision, adding that the company secured more funding and is on stronger footing. “There are no issues with the company's health,” he says.
Lyu says the team decided not to rush into new hardware, and instead focused on delivering software updates to polish the R1 experience—to date, Lyu says Rabbit has deployed around 50 updates in the past year and a half. He points to a dedicated Discord community of more than 12,000 users that provide feedback on what new features to add to the R1, like opening up the hardware. For example, you can integrate OpenClaw or Hermes AI agents into the R1 instead of using Rabbit's proprietary models.
“Today, if you look at our R1 device, it's completely different from day one,” he says. “We're more open; the device is yours, you decide what to do with the device.”
And people are supposedly still buying the R1 right now. Lyu raised his phone screen into his webcam to show me four or five orders that came through that morning for the R1 sold through Rabbit's website. (He points out that it doesn't include sales data from Amazon, Target, or Best Buy, where you can also buy the R1.)
For now. Rabbit is no longer manufacturing the R1, and the existing stock is dwindling. The company is focusing on the new OS3 software platform, which is designed to work on the other hardware you already have. If you own an R1, you can use it as an input/output gadget for OS3. Lyu says Rabbit has no plans for an R2. Instead, its next hardware release, slated to arrive within “months,” is what he describes as a Cyberdeck—a dedicated “vibe coding” machine that will run OS3.
So what exactly is OS3? Lyu pitches it as an open, cross-platform agentic system that operates across the devices you already own. The platform lives in the cloud, but connects directly to desktop software, files, and web pages through a local agent node you install on Windows, Mac, or Linux. Using Rabbit’s DLAM (Direct Large Action Model) technology, it can execute local software tasks and autonomously write and debug code. One account links up to five machines, with OS3 determining behind the scenes which device should execute a given task.
The interface is a single, continuous chat stream—no sidebar of disjointed chat threads. Lyu repeatedly calls it a “brain dump” interface: paste your intent, and the system coordinates the models and tools needed to pull it off. It supports universal skill compatibility—paste a public URL for any third-party agent skill into the chat, and OS3 can install it automatically without users needing any technical know-how.
Rabbit uses a “Bring Your Own Key” (BYOK) approach to power OS3. There's no monthly subscription fee, but users supply their own API keys from providers like OpenAI or Anthropic—or link local open source models.
Lyu has been using OS3 to handle plenty of tasks. For example, he says vendors send him an Excel report for R1 sales every week. He'll check it on his phone, but he always returns to his PC to open the document and manually add the data into a master sheet. But with OS3, since the Rabbit agent is deployed on his PC, he can send a message through Telegram on his phone asking it to handle the task, and it'll complete the routine action.
Just the other day, Lyu was heading to a video shoot that would take up most of his day. That meant he wasn't reachable on Slack. So, he asked OS3 to represent him on Slack, and the agent supposedly had a 50-minute conversation with an engineer (it announced itself as Lyu's agent, so the engineer was aware) and could even access files on Lyu's computer to help answer the engineer's questions.
Rabbit says the local agent doesn't store, copy, or sell data. While conversations and memory logs reside on Rabbit’s servers, file contents stay on your machine. The caveat is that when a task requires model reasoning, the relevant prompts pass through Rabbit’s servers to your model provider, which then processes that data under its own terms.
Anyone can try OS3 starting today, which in itself quietly refutes the premise that launched Rabbit into the spotlight in 2024. It turns out people never really needed another gadget in their pocket to chat with AI. They’ve already got the best tool for the job.

Can AI reason without words? A small model puts the idea to the test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

Can AI reason without words? A small model puts the idea to the test
Skipping the words could make some AI reasoning more efficient
AI may be able to reason without putting every step into words.
Many of today’s AI systems tackle difficult problems by generating intermediate steps in lengthy, chains of words before arriving at an answer— a technique often called chain-of-thought reasoning. That approach can improve performance on some tasks, but it also means an AI model may generate many words, or tokens, on the way to a relatively short answer. Each token takes computing power to produce, so longer reasoning can make answers slower and more expensive to generate.
A small, experimental AI system called BDH-CQ takes a different approach. It can solve some reasoning puzzles without spelling out its intermediate thinking, researchers report in a paper submitted August 10 to arXiv.org. The work asks whether AI needs language at every step of reasoning, and whether doing more internally could make some reasoning cheaper.
In training, AI models are often shown a few examples before they try a new problem. Many keep those examples in front of them as they work. But on reasoning tests, BDH-CQ (DH is short for Dragon Hatchling) instead uses each example to update a fixed-size memory, which stays the same size as it takes in more examples, so it does not have to keep going back through everything it has already seen.
“Once the query arrives, the model doesn’t write out its thinking in words at all,” says complexity scientist Zuzanna Stamirowska, CEO of AI company Pathway. Stamirowska says the model works through a problem internally without turning each step into words. “Nothing in between ever converts into language,” she says.
Stamirowska and colleagues said the model solved nearly three in 10 puzzles on the public ARC-AGI-1 evaluation set when given two attempts. The result showed that a small model could solve some new reasoning problems without spelling out its intermediate steps. The benchmark tests ask AI systems to infer visual rules from a few examples and apply them to new puzzles. The tests are like human student exams.
The model did better on some puzzles than others. For example, it handled some tasks involving turning or moving shapes but struggled more with color changes and some combinations of rules. On harder ordering and nesting puzzles, the model did better after seeing an example of similar difficulty.
The process with fewer words may help keep computing costs down, Stamirowska and colleagues say. They estimate that each puzzle query costs about $0.00070 to run, about one-eleventh as much as GPT-5.6 Luna on the same benchmark test, though the two costs were calculated differently. The study has not been peer-reviewed.
The finding is “an interesting efficiency result,” says computer scientist Yuntian Deng of the University of Waterloo in Canada. But he says it does not show that BDH-CQ’s underlying architecture is better than other approaches.
“Specialized small models [like BDH-CQ] are a promising route to efficient reasoning,” Deng says. But more testing is needed to separate the effects of the model’s design from how it was trained, he says. Without written-out reasoning, the model is harder to inspect, Deng says. But even a written chain of thought may not faithfully show how the model reached its answer.
The BDH-CQ model was built specifically for ARC-style problems, which makes it hard to compare directly with general-purpose AI systems, says machine learning researcher Jonas Geiping of the ELLIS Institute Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems in Germany. But he called the approach “neat” and noted that it can tackle test problems without retraining.
For Deng, the study raises a broader question: Does AI need to put all of its reasoning into words?. “Human language is useful for communicating reasoning, but it need not be the most efficient representation for every intermediate computation,” Deng says.

Speaking at the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), US President Donald Trump urged Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war against Ukraine and said he was prepared to use newly granted legislative powers to impose tariffs of up to 100% on Russian energy buyers.
Trump made the remarks on the first day of the high-level general debate on Tuesday, Sept. 22. The annual assembly opened on Sept. 8, and is scheduled to conclude on Sept. 28.

Ahead of his UN address, when a reporter asked what message he had for Putin, he simply said: “Settle the war.”
His comments came ahead of a scheduled meeting with President Volodymyr Zelensky, who previously expressed hope for using the venue to meet with Trump to restore the diplomatic momentum gained by the visits from senior US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow then Kyiv earlier this month.
“Last week, in honor of Senator Lindsey Graham, I signed a powerful new law passed by Congress, providing me with enormous new tariff authorities,” Trump said.
“And, if necessary, I will have to use them. It’s time to stop the killing,” he continued.
Diplomacy resumes in New York
Trump spoke early on the first day, following Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, in keeping with the tradition under which Brazil opens the debate and the US – being the host country – speaks next.
French President Emmanuel Macron, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham were among the other leaders scheduled to address the assembly during its opening day

During his UN address, Trump expressed confidence that Washington could help broker an end to the war, although he did not announce a ceasefire or any negotiating framework between Kyiv and Moscow.
“We’re working very closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine, and we will get that one done,” Trump said, according to Clash Reports.
“It’s going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand. They’ve had it,” he continued.
The president presented his approach as one of direct intervention rather than prolonged diplomacy. “I have no interest in leaving dangers to grow for another day. I do not believe in letting problems fester. They only become harder to solve,” Trump said.
However, no further details about Washington’s resolution to bridge the fundamental differences between Kyiv and Moscow had been offered.
On Monday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that there had been no progress in negotiations, although Moscow hoped trilateral talks would eventually resume.
In July, Bloomberg reported that the Kremlin no longer planned to return any occupied Ukrainian territory as part of a future peace deal. Kyiv categorically rejects any settlement requiring it to surrender territory and maintains that a peace agreement must respect Ukraine’s internationally recognized borders and sovereignty.
Renewed US mediation earlier in September
Trump’s most recent speech follows a renewed US mediation earlier in September.
Special US envoys Witkoff and Kushner met Putin in Moscow on Sept. 5 during talks lasting more than three hours, then traveled to Kyiv on Sept. 6 for their first visit to the Ukrainian capital as Washington’s intermediaries.
Prospects for a direct Trump-Zelensky meeting in New York initially appeared uncertain.
As of Sept. 19, Zelensky was absent from the list of bilateral meetings publicly outlined by US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz, while two senior Ukrainian officials told Suspilne that no meeting had been finalized.
The situation changed following a Sunday, Sept. 20 telephone discussion between the two leaders, who agreed to meet with “ideas for de-escalation steps.” By Tuesday, the bilateral talks had been added to Trump’s schedule, with Reuters reporting that Zelensky was among at least 11 leaders the US president planned to meet during UNGA.
The discussions are expected to center on air defense – particularly US-made Patriot interceptors, the only weapons Ukraine relies on to successfully deter Russian ballistic missiles – as well as energy and security.
Kyiv is urgently seeking additional protection ahead of its fifth winter of war, as the country prepares for intensified Russian attacks against critical infrastructure, such as heating, power and water supplies.

3 Ts Will Dominate the Trump-Xi Summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:58:00 UTC
00:58:00 KST

When Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping last sat down in May 2026, talk was centered on three Ts: trade, technology and Taiwan. Their next summit, due to begin in the United States on September 24, looks set to focus on the same set of issues again. The main difference will be that the technology element has been given added urgency by the sudden and rapid shift in developments in artificial intelligence.
What’s less clear is whether the two sides will be able to come to any sort of transformative agreement on that, or any other issue.
The most urgent issue, but also the simplest to solve, will be on trade. Nearly a year ago at Busan in South Korea, Trump and Xi hammered out an agreement whereby the United States agreed to lift some export controls on high-end technology and to reduce the then three-figure tariffs on Chinese goods. For its part, China agreed not to restrict the flow of critical minerals and rare earths to U.S. users.
That pact – only good for one year – is now up for renewal. Both sides are likely to want a continuation of the current arrangement, and while there may be some tweaking on the side, the new deal will probably be similar to the old one.
Each side has proposed in previous meetings that there should be a new instrument, a Board of Trade, that will assess non-sensitive China-U.S. business interests. However, details about the institution remains vague. Some announcements are likely during the summit, but business leaders will want to know how comprehensive and lasting the arrangements for the board will be.
There is still less information on a proposed Board of Investment, which remains on the drawing board. The Chinese side has proposed bringing major Chinese CEOs to the summit to match the likes of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Tesla’s Elon Musk – both of whom accompanied Trump on the Beijing trip. But the choice of business leaders is likely to turn on which aspects of trade China thinks are likely to develop most effectively in the short term.
Taiwan is a much harder issue to solve, but it’s unlikely that much that is discussed on Xi’s visit will determine its outcome.
Trump has been less willing than his predecessor to commit the United States to defending the island should Beijing invade, instead reasserting Washington’s long-held position of strategic ambiguity.
And although the U.S. is currently distracted from East Asia by the Iran conflict, China still prefers to find methods short of war to bring the island under Beijing’s control.
The island’s January 2028 presidential election is likely to be a more crucial moment for Taiwan’s future, particularly if the opposition – and more China-friendly – Kuomintang (KMT) wins the presidency, or indeed if an isolationist candidate becomes U.S. president later that year. If the next U.S. president opted to change course by taking a less active involvement in overseas issues – as has been floated by early contenders on both the left and right – that would change things all the more.
For now, Beijing will continue to build the People’s Liberation Army’s naval capacity to have the option of military action against the island. But its preference will be to take advantage of changes within Taiwan’s internal politics while combining economic incentives and coercion, squeezing Taipei’s international footprint and hoping for a slackening of U.S. interest in the western Pacific.
Other international issues are likely to gain less attention. China is expected to make clear its unhappiness about the war on Iran, and the U.S. may remind China that it has passed new legislation allowing sanctions on countries that buy Russian oil – of which, China is the largest purchaser. However, neither issue is likely to lead to any major change in practice.
It’s really in the area of tech, and AI in particular, where both sides will be trying to make diplomacy catch up with reality. The May summit surprised many because the question of mutual agreement on regulation of AI came up in a way that had not been on the agenda for the first year of the Trump administration.
However, both sides agreed that talks in principle about regulation might be possible and even desirable because of the growth in the importance, but also unpredictability, of AI. And on September 20, the United States and China mooted the idea of a “hotline” to notify the other over AI national security risks.
Between the May and September summits, fears about AI in the U.S have created an increasingly unfriendly atmosphere toward unregulated AI.
In China, public sentiment about AI is less openly hostile and some of its major benefits in areas such as health care have softened people’s attitudes. Yet there are still plenty of concerns expressed in private about whether China’s troubled economy will definitively benefit from the AI boom. Although many argue it has created new opportunities for consumers, others point to the relatively few jobs that have been created for a workforce that finds itself buffeted by wide-scale job elimination.
Both the U.S. and China have reasons to talk about AI regulation. The alarming prospect of rogue AI companies causing intense social disruptions through their business choices is clearly one such reason, and in the U.S., voters’ more immediate concerns about data centers are another.
There are also China-specific reasons that Beijing may seek restraint. One of the most common concerns about AI is that it may well run out of control. And “out of control” is a kryptonite phrase for the leadership of the Chinese Communist Party. That’s particularly true of Xi who, as a youth, spent years in rural exile after his father fell to a purge just before the Cultural Revolution – an upheaval during which China’s politics turned to anarchy. It was a formative experience for Xi, which has no doubt influenced his tendencies as a leader toward exercising as much control as possible.
AI that undermines the unchallengeable leadership of the Communist Party would be an unwelcome guest in China’s cyberspace, and regulation that solves that problem would not be rejected out of hand.
However, this recognition of mutual concern about AI – albeit for very different reasons – is still not likely to see much progress in the short term. The competition between the U.S. and China on AI is real, and neither governments nor private sector actors in either country are willing to make concessions that could advantage the other side.
Levels of trust between Washington and Beijing remain very low on the issue. Talks about talks seem the most likely public outcome, though what happens behind the scenes may be pursued more discreetly.
The Trump-Xi summit is less important in terms of any major change in policy on either side, and more because it marks part of a commitment to maintain some form of dialogue between the leaders of the world’s two most powerful countries. The leaders may well meet twice more in the near future, at the APEC and G20 summits, to be hosted by China and the United States, respectively.
To meet four times in just over half a year is a good sign; refusal to meet would be much more worrying. But the underlying difficulties of the three Ts, where the leaders seem to have fundamentally incompatible agendas, remain the thread beneath the ostensibly polite and occasionally amiable conversations.

Danish defense startup guarding undersea cables runs on 15 Ukrainian suppliers. Ukrainian fund is putting in €2 million in it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:53:40 UTC
00:53:40 KST

A Ukrainian fund is investing in a Danish defense startup, a reversal for a country far better known for taking in foreign capital than for sending it abroad. Resist.UA is backing BlueShadow, a maritime security firm run by a former US Navy submarine commander but largely engineered in Ukraine, to build defenses for coasts and undersea cables against drones and hybrid attacks.
BlueShadow is registered in Denmark, but almost its entire engineering team works in Ukraine, and it folds gear from more than 15 Ukrainian suppliers of drones, sensors, and communications into a single system.
Resist.UA, which signed a letter of intent to join the company's €2 million pre-seed round, runs a new €50 million fund, Resist 2.0, designed to bring Ukraine's battlefield-proven technology to global markets.
Ukraine engineers the Danish startup
The company was founded in 2025 and is led by Charles Maher, a former commander of a US Navy nuclear submarine, according to Defender Media.
This summer, it registered as a Ukrainian legal entity and builds on Ukrainian components, planning to fit its maritime platforms with M-Fly's RB-220 gimbal, a day-and-night targeting sensor used until now only on flying drones.
The two sides first met in January 2026 and formalized the partnership as BlueShadow raised its round and Resist.UA launched its second fund.
The systems guard the sea
BlueShadow is building two of them. BlueDragon, still in development, is designed to shield Ukraine's coastal cities, ports, and shipping lanes from drone strikes. BlueSentry, which the company plans to launch in October, is aimed at protecting ports, offshore wind farms, undersea cables, and maritime borders from hybrid attack, the kind of sabotage that has repeatedly damaged Baltic Sea infrastructure.
"This partnership will fuel the next phase of our mission to protect people, infrastructure, commerce, and natural resources at sea," the company said.
Ukraine's defense tech turns outward
Ukrainian defense technology, tested in real combat, has drawn growing investor interest, and Ukrainian figures are now building funds to channel it: the former Defense Minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, is raising what he calls the country's largest defense-tech venture fund.

NEW YORK — British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Tuesday an international agreement on AI led by the U.K. will seek to establish “a single set of global principles and standards.”
Burnham told a meeting with business leaders in New York that AI will be “the primary focus” of the U.K.’s upcoming G20 presidency.

Advertisement
It also came shortly before President Donald Trump used his address to the U.N. to assert that the United States “totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme” to control AI, in contrast to Burnham's messaging.
“We want to pick up the initiatives that are beginning to emerge, develop, and bring them into a single set of global principles and standards that are very much about unlocking the full potential whilst guarding against the risks,” Burnham told businesses leaders on Tuesday.
But Burnham said a single set of global standards could “also brings benefits for the U.K. as well in terms of investment.”
Calling AI a “foundational technology,” Burnham said the U.K. will seek to “shape it, work with it, make sure it’s AI for good — understanding the challenges and the risks that come from it.”

Commander Warns Russian Groups Could Reach Zaporizhzhia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:53:00 UTC
00:53:00 KST

Small Russian infantry groups could reach Zaporizhzhia this winter, the commander of Ukraine’s 1st Separate Assault Regiment, Dmytro Filatov, said in an interview with the Real Front YouTube channel.
Filatov, known by his call sign “Perun,” said Russia could intensify offensive operations during the winter and search for weak points in Ukrainian defenses.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I think that this winter we will record the approach and entry into Zaporizhzhia – not of troops, but of individual groups,” Filatov said.
He identified the Stepnohirske area and the Dnipro River’s southern bank as possible directions for such attempts. According to the commander, dense development along the river could help Russian troops infiltrate toward the city.
Filatov said Russian forces had come close to Zaporizhzhia last year. He warned that even the appearance of isolated groups near the city could have a major psychological effect on Ukraine’s partners and encourage the Russian military and President Vladimir Putin.
Filatov warns of wider Russian pressure
Filatov said worsening weather could allow Russian forces to increase pressure across the entire front line.
He said some Russian units had already been transferred to the Dobropillia direction, where they are attempting to advance toward Kramatorsk. According to Filatov, Russia is also trying to shift Ukraine’s attention toward Donbas and force Kyiv to redeploy troops from other sectors.
Russian Ex-Mayor Who Left Prison for Ukraine War Dies From Combat Wounds
“On the Zaporizhzhia front, the number of strikes and sorties has decreased – the intensity has fallen. Yes, we are operating less on this sector. I think the enemy’s redeployment to other directions is part of its strategy in response to our actions here,” Filatov said.
He argued that Ukraine must strengthen its defenses in Donbas while preserving the initiative and continuing to pressure Russian weak points.
Filatov said Russia’s initial objective in the Zaporizhzhia region was to encircle and capture Orikhiv, before advancing toward Zaporizhzhia. Capturing the city would allow Russia to block one of Ukraine’s major industrial centers, which has a degree of energy autonomy because of its hydroelectric power plant. Ukrainian forces, however, managed to stop the Russian advance.
Southern Grouping rejects imminent-entry claims
The Southern Grouping of Ukrainian forces rejected reports that Russian troops are likely to directly enter Zaporizhzhia this winter.
“There are currently no grounds to speak of a high probability of such a development,” Anastasiia Shevchenko, a spokesperson for the Southern Grouping, told Ukrinform.
Shevchenko said the front line is about 30 kilometers (19 miles) from Zaporizhzhia, making a covert advance over that distance highly unlikely. Ukrainian drone systems monitor Russian personnel and direct fire toward detected groups.
She also said there have been no changes in Russian military activity indicating preparations for a direct entry into the city. Russia has not abandoned its goal of capturing Zaporizhzhia, she said, but currently lacks sufficient forces and equipment to advance directly toward it.
Ukrainian forces have recorded attempts by small Russian infantry groups to infiltrate near Mali Shcherbaky, Stepove, and Shcherbaky in the Orikhiv direction. Shevchenko said those attempts had not succeeded.
Similar warnings were made last year
The latest warning echoes reports and forecasts made during Russia’s advances in the southern Zaporizhzhia region last year.
Russia had concentrated assault formations near Orikhiv after advancing through the Hulyaipole area. Russian forces captured Hulyaipole in early 2026 and then pushed toward Orikhiv, increasing pressure on the route to Zaporizhzhia.
Late last year, Russian forces also had intensified attacks around Hulyaipole, including attempts to break through and advance deeper into the region.
A recent Kyiv Post opinion analysis described Russian pressure on Orikhiv from several directions and attempts to use forward positions to threaten Ukrainian supply routes.
However, those warnings did not mean that Russia was certain to capture Zaporizhzhia, rather described a possible military route and potential risks. The same applies to Filatov’s current prediction: individual Russian groups could attempt to approach the city, but there is no confirmation that Russia is preparing or capable of capturing Zaporizhzhia.
For now, the Southern Grouping says the threat is being monitored, while Ukrainian forces continue to block Russian infiltration attempts along the Orikhiv and Stepnohirske sectors.

National Guard of Ukraine Hosts Competition to Determine the Best Tank Crew
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22

00:47:53 KST

The Ukrainian National Guard held a competition to determine the best tank crew.
Thirteen crews participated in the event, performing tasks on T-62, T-64, T-72, T-80, and Leopard 1A5 tanks, according to National Guard Commander Oleksandr Pivnenko.
In particular, the competition featured a T-80 tank, likely from the 12th Azov Brigade, equipped with captured turret armor from a T-90M and side armor from a T-80BVM.
The competition took place in three key categories: Shooting, Driving, and Target Detection. During the live-fire stage, tank crews engaged targets with the main gun and machine gun, which simulated an enemy motorized platoon.
During the driving stage, the tank drivers navigated sections of the route of varying difficulty, and during the reconnaissance stage, they detected camouflaged objects in wooded terrain.
The winner of the competition was the crew of the 3rd Operational Spartan Brigade, named after Colonel Petro Bolbochan.
Second place went to the 1st Presidential Brigade “Bureviy”, named after Hetman Petro Doroshenko, and third place went to the 17th Poltava Brigade.

Iran expands rail routes to China, targets higher-value exports: TPO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22

Iran expands rail routes to China, targets higher-value exports: TPO
TEHRAN- At a press conference, Amir Roshanbakhsh Ghanbari, deputy for international business development at Iran’s Trade Promotion Organization (TPO), said Iran is negotiating with China to develop rail routes for goods transit, with part of Iranian cargo already moving to China via Yazd Dry Port. He said transport is a fundamental trade issue and current conditions impose restrictions.
Last year, Iran exported about 155 million tons and imported about 42 million tons, much of it by sea. With trade routes limited, TPO has divided responses into short-, medium- and long-term measures. Short-term steps include increasing capacity of executive agencies, managing borders, and using border provinces. At Bazargan, he said, higher traffic and truck queues partly stem from limited acceptance capacity on the other side, so not all problems can be managed domestically.
Rail capacity is limited: each train has about 55 wagons and carries about 1,500 tons, compared with about 100,000 tons for a ship. Moving the same amount by truck would require about 3,000 trucks. Therefore, rail and land capacity must be used alongside sea routes. Alternative routes require cooperation with neighbors and trade partners, with infrastructure on both sides.
Ghanbari said recent conditions showed the need to reform trade governance and transport infrastructure after the current period. Otherwise similar import-export problems could recur. Trade finds its way, but when main arteries are blocked, alternatives must exist.
The 30th National Export Day will focus on trade infrastructure and sustainable routes, starting Monday, 20 Mehr. A joint event with the Ministry of Roads and Urban Development will examine transport and sustainable export routes. The second day will address higher export value and services.
For National Exemplary Exporters, 367 applicants entered evaluation; 277 completed files reached final assessment: 235 in goods, 26 in knowledge-based goods, and 16 in services. There are 42 commodity groups and seven service groups.
The average value of Iran’s exported goods is about $300–350 per ton, while some knowledge-based and high-tech products can reach $1,500–2,500 per ton. Services exports reached about $3 billion in 1404, including $1.8 billion in technical and engineering services, up from $790 million in 1403.
TPO also launched an Export Atlas, providing commodity-and-country trade data, competitors, intermediaries, monthly growth charts, and provincial production and export shares. Other planned meetings will cover financing, export management companies, standards, trade laws, diplomacy, and exporters’ demands, including direct importer-exporter transactions.

cast aluminum turns heart forms into sculptural furniture in LOVE collection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:45:32 UTC
00:45:32 KST

LOVE collection translates the heart into sculptural objects
Istanbul-based designer Sami Savatli introduces LOVE, a two-piece collectible design collection comprising the LOVE Chair and LOVE Side Table. Conceived at the intersection of design and sculpture, the collection explores how structure, material, and gesture can transform familiar forms into objects with an independent spatial presence.
The LOVE Chair takes the familiar outline of the heart as its point of departure, but removes it from conventional symmetry and symbolism. Rather than appearing as an applied motif, the form emerges directly from the structure of the chair. Lines extend, divide and reconnect, moving between silhouette and support, while shifts in volume allow the object to read differently from each viewpoint. The LOVE Side Table develops the same language without repeating the heart literally. Its branching structure carries the movement of the chair into a more compact form, connecting the two pieces through proportion, rhythm and construction rather than visual repetition.
Hand-finished cast aluminum shapes LOVE Chair and LOVE Table
Both pieces are produced by designer Sami Savatli in Istanbul in cast aluminum and individually finished by hand. Subtle irregularities in surface, texture and reflection are retained as part of the making process, giving each object its own material character. As light moves across the aluminum, the collection shifts between solidity and visual lightness, reinforcing its sculptural presence. Positioned between collectible design and sculpture, LOVE retains the function of furniture while establishing an autonomous presence within space.

Iran offers to reopen Strait of Hormuz – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:45:26 UTC
00:45:26 KST

Iran offers to reopen Strait of Hormuz – media
The Strait of Hormuz could reopen within seven days if the US eases military pressure and lifts its blockade of Iranian ports, according to media reports citing a senior Iranian official.
The strait is one of the world’s most important energy routes, normally carrying around a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments. Shipping has largely stopped since the US-Israeli war with Iran began in late February, disrupting supplies and driving energy prices higher.
Tehran has proposed that Washington declare its readiness to resolve the conflict through diplomacy and agree on a timeline for further steps, the official told Reuters on Tuesday. The proposal was conveyed to the US through mediators last week as world leaders gather in New York for the UN General Assembly.
The event is a “golden opportunity for the US to return to diplomacy,” the official said, adding that the Iranian delegation had full authority to revive negotiations. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told NBC that the administration was prepared to speak with Tehran if negotiations had the prospect of producing a positive outcome.
The official noted that there were no plans for Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and US President Donald Trump to meet directly at the General Assembly, although Trump signaled on Sunday that he would be open to such a meeting.
Iran has set broader conditions for ending the conflict. Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei said on Saturday that Tehran had conveyed seven demands to Washington through mediators, including an end to hostilities, the release of frozen Iranian assets, and the lifting of the naval blockade.
Previous attempts to halt the fighting have been fruitless. A memorandum of understanding agreed by the US and Iran in June was followed by renewed hostilities, while no face-to-face talks are known to have taken place since July.
US government data show that oil flows through Hormuz fell from 21.6 million barrels per day in the final quarter of 2025 to 4.9 million in the second quarter of this year.
Tensions rose again this week after Trump said he was in “deciding mode” over Iran and weighing further military action, economic pressure, or a deal. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps responded by warning that another US attack would prompt Tehran to expand the scope of the conflict and use different weapons.
Washington has also threatened further economic pressure. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Monday that companies providing Iranian airlines with fuel, airport services, or ticketing could be denied access to the US dollar system.

Austrian ex-billionaire Benko found guilty of insolvency fraud at retrial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Ex-billionaire Benko convicted at Austrian retrial, sentence increased
VIENNA, Sept 22 - An Austrian court found former property tycoon Rene Benko guilty on an additional insolvency fraud charge at a retrial on Tuesday, increasing his prison sentence to 30 months from the original two years.
The case was the first to emerge from a wider criminal investigation into the collapse of the property group Benko founded. Signa's failure in 2023 became Austria's biggest post-war bankruptcy and left investors across Europe nursing losses.
A court in Innsbruck, Benko's home city, convicted him in October on one count of insolvency fraud over a €300,000 ($344,000) transfer to his mother in late 2023, when Signa was already in financial difficulty. The court found the transfer was intended to put the money beyond creditors' reach.
It acquitted him on a second count relating to an advance rent payment of about €360,000 for a house in Innsbruck that prosecutors said made no economic sense. After appeals from both sides, Austria's Supreme Court upheld the conviction and ordered a retrial on the second count.
Benko pleaded not guilty, arguing that he thought his company could avoid bankruptcy when the payments were made.
"Regarding this part of the case that had to be retried, a panel comprising magistrates and a judge at the Innsbruck State Court found the defendant guilty and sentenced him to 30 months in prison," the court said in a statement, adding that the maximum possible sentence was 10 years.
Benko was convicted over the rent payment but acquitted over additional operating expenses for the house that had also been paid in advance, the court said.
His time in custody since his arrest on January 23 of last year would count towards his sentence and he remains in custody in Innsbruck, it added.
Benko was convicted of insolvency fraud in a separate case in December and handed a 15-month suspended prison sentence. REUTERS

- The banned news outlets covered Trump's UN visit using UN-issued media passes, while other major networks suspended White House pool coverage in protest.
- The White House launched a Trump TV stream to replace traditional media coverage, drawing criticism as government propaganda, amid ongoing tensions over press freedom and access.
AI generated
NEW YORK - As CNN, MS NOW and Politico await a court hearing on Sept 23 over President Donald Trump’s decision to ban them from the White House grounds, reporters from the news outlets covered his visit to the United Nations General Assembly on Sept 22 using media passes issued by the UN.
“I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me, you shouldn’t be here,” Trump said on Sept 22 as he entered the United Nations building and addressed a group of reporters. “You said you weren’t going to cover me.”
CNN has not said it would stop covering Trump.
Trump announced the ban on Sept 18 on social media, saying the three news outlets “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States”, and defended it in another post on Sept 21.
The news outlets sued Trump and other members of his administration on Sept 21, saying the action violated the US Constitution’s First Amendment protections for free speech and a free press.
They are seeking a temporary restraining order to block Trump’s action in federal court in Washington, DC, with a hearing scheduled for Sept 23 before US District Judge Timothy Kelly.
Later on Sept 22, Trump was asked by reporters in New York whether he would let the media outlets back into the White House if the court rules against the ban.
Trump said that “this is a judge who’s not a particularly fair judge”.
He added: “But I’m talking about national security. I think we have a right to clean out fake news.”
Trump appointed Kelly to the bench in 2017 during his first term as president. Kelly ruled against Trump in 2018 in a case involving a CNN journalist who sued after his White House press pass was revoked.
Battles with the press
Past presidents have battled with the press, but Trump’s campaign against the media has been unprecedented.
He has upended decades of tradition by denying basic access to many major news organisations, launching personal attacks on journalists for their reporting and elevating media outlets seen as more sympathetic to the administration. He also has filed lawsuits against multiple news outlets.
CNN is one of the five news organisations – along with ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC – that make up the primary White House television pool. They share the costs of covering the president, take turns organising coverage and share the footage with outlets around the country.
CNN had been scheduled to cover Trump’s trip to New York for the United Nations General Assembly on Sept 21, but was not able to provide a pool feed.
In response, the other major TV networks suspended presidential pool coverage.
In an effort to fill that void, the White House launched a Trump TV stream on Sept 21. The White House said the stream will run videos and highlights of what it calls the Trump administration’s achievements. A press freedom advocate said it amounted to “a steady diet of government propaganda.”
During an interview on NBC’s Today show on Sept 22, Secretary of State Marco Rubio did not answer a question about whether he will be making changes to his travelling press pool.
When asked whether media outlets should be banned because the president does not like their coverage, Rubio repeated a sentiment expressed by Vice-President J.D. Vance a day earlier, falsely stating that the outlets were not banned, when they have in fact lost access to the White House grounds.
“They’re not banned... We’re not closing CNN... They’re just not allowed to work from the workspace at the White House,” Rubio said. REUTERS
