Social platforms and police are failing women abused online, report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:27:16 UTC
00:27:16 KST

When Jane* learned that intimate photos of her had been posted on a website without her consent, she expected the police would help her. Instead, she was warned that researching where her photos had been shared might put her at risk of breaking the law.
After she was handed a leaflet on internet safety and told to go to tech companies for help, but to expect little from them, the case was closed.
“The officer called us at all times of day and approached the case in a way that was insensitive, victim-blaming and entirely inappropriate, with misogynistic undertones,” she recalled.
Jane’s Facebook, Instagram and Snapchat accounts had all been hacked, along with those of several other women, and the images extracted from private messages.
The incident was incredibly distressing: on the platform where the images were posted, commenters left derogatory messages, and one stranger used identifying personal data – including names of people and schools and links to social media profiles – to contact Jane directly.
“I felt exposed, harassed, and stalked online by a community of anonymous perverts,” she said. “The experience left me feeling angry, violated and unsafe.”
Like many women who have had similar experiences, Jane has moved more of her life offline and no longer feels comfortable in many online spaces.
A new report from Refuge and End Violence Against Women (EVAW) says: “For many women, abuse, harassment and exposure to misogynistic content have become an ‘accepted risk’ of participating in online spaces.” It says this is despite Ofcom introducing voluntary guidance for tech companies on tackling violence against women and girls one year ago.
Disheartened by the traumatic reporting process, Jane appointed the law firm Leigh Day, which successfully pressed Ofcom into opening a formal investigation into the platforms, and the police into reopening their criminal investigation – though she feels there has been “little to no clarity or transparency” about how long these will take.
Part of the difficulty when looking into such cases is that perpetrators can be based around the world and are able to conceal the IP addresses that identify their locations. But Jane argues this is no different from other online crime and no barrier to action, saying: “We wouldn’t expect the same response when it comes to other serious and complex crimes, such as terrorism.”
Refuge and EVAW’s report found that most women in situations similar to Jane’s did not report their experiences to online platforms or the police, and when they did they often felt the response was poor. In many cases, they felt their complaints were misunderstood or not taken seriously, they were told to adapt their own behaviour, and either no action was taken or it was too slow.
A survey of 2,000 women for the report found that 17% of those who made a complaint to the police did not have their cases investigated at all.
It also found that nearly half (47%) of those surveyed aged 16 to 24 had experienced violence online, with one in four experiencing misogyny or sexual violence.
One in five had been stalked, monitored, harassed or controlled; 18% had experienced image-based abuse, including being sent unsolicited images or having their intimate images shared without consent; and 9% had been doxed, meaning their personal information, such as phone numbers and addresses, was shared online.
For 15% of respondents aged 16 to 24, the level of abuse was so bad they said they had felt suicidal. Nearly one in three of women of all ages had been affected, and one in seven said they had left social media platforms as a result.
The research also found that one in six women aged 16-24 had received dating, sex and relationships advice from an AI chatbot that they considered inappropriate, unhealthy or unsafe.
Gemma Sherrington, the chief executive of Refuge, said that while Ofcom’s guidance was a welcome step, the regulator “must go much further in holding tech companies legally responsible for combating the normalisation of misogyny, holding perpetrators to account, and keeping all women and survivors safe”.
The report also called for enhanced tech abuse training for police and prosecutors, a new online safety commission or ombuds role, ringfenced funding for the specialist services, and for Ofcom be empowered to take “swifter and more robust enforcement action”.
An Ofcom spokesperson said: “Tackling the harms that women and girls disproportionately face online is a top priority for Ofcom. The law is clear that tech firms must take down illegal content – including harassment, stalking, violent threats and abuse – when they become aware of it.
“We’re also cracking down on the spread of illegal intimate images, forcing tech firms to act to stop such content spreading on their platforms, as well as tightening our codes to reflect new quicker takedown timeframes.
“We’ve also shown we won’t hesitate to act where tech firms fall short, with investigations open into three services for suspected failures to prevent individuals from encountering illegal intimate abuse imagery and other illegal content. We’re working to conclude these as swiftly as possible, following a fair, robust and transparent process.”
A government spokesperson said: “This report lays bare the scale of the problem, and it is totally unacceptable. We are taking some of the boldest actions in the world to protect women online.
“Platforms have a legal duty to remove illegal content, and Ofcom has our full backing to take robust action against those who fail to do so.
 “We are also requiring that platforms remove non-consensual intimate images within 48 hours of it being reported and, in some cases, having senior executives face liability.”
*Name has been changed

What We Tell Our Kids About AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:25:11 UTC
00:25:11 KST

Between us, we have six children. The oldest is 12. None of them has a phone yet, and none has asked us whether artificial intelligence is going to ruin their lives.
They will.
They will learn that some of the people building the most powerful AI systems have warned that the technology could become dangerous in ways we cannot yet control. They will hear predictions that many of the jobs they might want in the future may disappear. They will encounter arguments about truth, power, safety, and whether our institutions can possibly keep pace with machines advancing faster than our ability to govern them.
We will not be able to tell them that any of it is nonsense. We don’t think it is.
But another danger looms over this moment. As the conversation around AI grows darker, we risk becoming so consumed by what might go wrong that we stop paying attention to what is beginning to go right.
That is not an argument for complacency. The risks are real and demand immediate action. It is an argument for something we think is becoming equally necessary: pragmatic optimism.
We work in one of the most failure-prone fields there is, trying to understand disease and determine which medicines might work in human beings. From where we sit, on the front lines of investing in and creating medicines, we are beginning to see AI change what is possible.
Drug development has always been a brutal business. Historically, roughly nine out of 10 therapies entering human testing fail. A successful medicine can take a decade or more and billions of dollars to develop. But of course, those statistics obscure the real cost. A failed or missing medicine is a patient still waiting.
For most of modern drug development, scientists have started with a hypothesis about biology, searched for a molecule that might affect it, tested that molecule and, overwhelmingly, discovered along the way that they were wrong. AI is beginning to change that story.
We have had the wonder of watching this shift in human insight and discovery direction being force-multiplied by AI up close. We recently watched a team of researchers use AI to design antibodies from scratch against some of the hardest targets in medicine, unlocking approaches that have stymied some of the most sophisticated groups in pharma. Nearby, another group of only five scientists used an AI-driven experimental system to move from an idea for a challenging new medicine to demonstrating what we believe are unique cancer-treating capabilities in a primate in less than six months. Programs with these ambitions would conventionally require teams of specialists working for years.
What is changing is not simply the tools available to help us make predictions about human biology. It is the speed of the discovery process itself: propose an idea, build it, test it in the physical world, learn from what happened, and begin again. The scientific method itself is beginning to accelerate, and the number of scientific inquiries, opportunities to advance health per dollar spent, is beginning to scale.
Last month, Merck and Moderna reported that a personalized cancer vaccine for melanoma significantly delayed the disease from spreading. The result is remarkable on its own, and studies are already underway in other settings. What we find particularly exciting is how this growing clinical evidence, combined with AI tools and automated labs, can open the field to more competitors. The evidence reduces uncertainty about the approach, while these tools can lower the cost and time required to pursue it. Together, they can bring more teams and more capital into our fight against cancer and expand the number of promising ideas that will be tested at an unprecedented rate.
We are at the very beginning.
Anyone claiming that AI has solved drug discovery is selling something. Of the 117 AI-enabled drug programs in human trials last year across 63 companies. Not one has been approved. Biology has humbled generations of brilliant scientists, and AI will not repeal biology. Models will be wrong. Drugs will fail. Patients will respond in ways nobody predicted.
But we see green shoots and a remarkable new calibration of direction, not a destination. Direction is the whole game in fighting disease and improving human health. AI is beginning to give us better ways of finding it.
That is the source of our optimism. Not the belief that the dangers surrounding AI are exaggerated, or that medicine is about to become easy. We believe neither. It comes from watching a technology begin to alter a field in which meaningful progress has historically been painfully slow.
Our children will inherit all of this. They will live with the disruptions we are debating now and others none of us has anticipated. They deserve leaders who take those risks seriously and institutions willing to act before every consequence is known, and before some of the most dangerous become irreversible.
They also deserve to know what else was happening at this moment.
Diseases we could not understand are now yielding more of their secrets. Machines can now search for possibilities no human mind can find alone. Medicines are being designed differently. Diseases too rare or complicated to command sufficient attention are becoming more tractable.
And if all of that started to compound, the baseline of human health our children inherit started to be different from the one we inherited ourselves.
We don’t yet know what AI will take from our children’s generation. From where we sit, we are beginning to see what it might give.
And that is a story worth telling too.

Dozens of people sue GLP-1 drug companies over alleged vision loss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:23:14 UTC
00:23:14 KST

Can GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic cause vision loss? What we know about the risk
Diabetes and weight-loss medications are believed by some to be the cause of their mysterious loss of vision.
Dozens of people have filed lawsuits in the United States against GLP-1 companies, which make popular weight-loss drugs like Ozempic and Mounjaro, claiming their products caused a rare condition that can cause permanent vision loss, US media outlets report.
The cases and alleged risk could present a significant challenge to a fledgling industry that analysts expected to generate about $100bn in annual sales in the next 10 years after being taken by millions of people in the US and making inroads into combatting widespread obesity in the country.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3WeightWatchers files for bankruptcy amid rise of weight-loss drugs
- list 2 of 3Could weight loss drugs fix UK’s unemployment problem?
- list 3 of 3Wegovy maker Novo Nordisk to slash thousands of jobs
A spokesperson for Novo Nordisk, the pharmaceutical giant that makes Wegovy and Ozempic, said the lawsuits lacked merit and the company was vigorously contesting them, according to The Wall Street Journal, while Eli Lilly, which produces Zepbound, did not comment on the litigation but said it was reviewing the data on potential health risks.
The lawsuits asserted that the drugs cause nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, an eye condition that prevents adequate blood flow and damages the optic nerve, potentially resulting in permanent vision loss.
In one lawsuit filed by a woman in Pennsylvania described to The Washington Post, the patient said that after taking medication for her diabetes, her vision was like looking through a “fishbowl”. Two weeks later, she was diagnosed with NAION.
Scientists have been researching the possible connection between the condition and weight-loss drugs for years, but their findings remained mixed.
What is NAION?
NAION is a condition in which sudden loss of vision happens due to a painless reduction of blood flow to the optic nerve. It is often also referred to as an “eye stroke”.
The damage is usually irreversible and quite rare.
Scientific research has pointed to possible incidents in which patients who have taken GLP-1s end up being more likely to develop the condition.
It remains unclear how or if the drug is the cause of these problems.
Researchers have said, however, that for those who do develop the condition, it happens within the first six to 18 months of starting a GLP-1 medication.
What lawsuits have been filed?
A personal-injury firm in the US called Weitz & Luxembourg has filed more than 90 lawsuits against Novo Nordisk in a New Jersey state court since 2025 on behalf of patients who have developed NAION while taking their products.
Separate lawsuits have also been filed in the US District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, claiming that GLP-1 treatments caused NAION and drugmakers failed to adequately warn of their risks.
A Novo Nordisk company-funded study conducted randomised trials on GLP-1 patients and said they found the drugs do not cause any increase in the risk of NAION.
Dr Tina Vilsboll, a senior medical officer at Novo Nordisk and the lead author of the study, said she sees “no causality” and there are no “indications that we should really be worried about NAION”.
The European Medicines Agency said the eye condition could impact one of every 10,000 GLP-1 users who have diabetes.
The North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society and the American Academy of Ophthalmology said that despite the reports that there is a small possible increase in risk, there are also studies that report no correlation and “the overall magnitude of the risk of NAION remains low.”
Despite the lawsuits, the US has not added any warnings on GLP-1 medications.
The US Food and Drug Administration has been investigating the link after early reports on the connection in 2024.

Zelensky-Trump meeting: Political analyst outlines three key topics but urges against expecting concrete results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:20:00 UTC
00:20:00 KST

Zelensky-Trump meeting: Political analyst outlines three key topics but urges against expecting concrete results
Political analyst Volodymyr Fesenko, chairman of the board of the Penta Center for Applied Political Studies, said this in a comment to Ukrinform.
“As I understand from the context and statements, including those by Trump himself and President Zelensky, this meeting is aimed at preparing for the resumption of trilateral talks between Ukraine and Russia, with the United States acting as a mediator. In addition, there are two obvious key issues that will be decisive for the further negotiating process. The number one issue is the so-called energy ceasefire,” Fesenko said.
In his view, the parties will most likely discuss a symmetrical model: Ukraine would stop striking Russian energy facilities, while Russia would stop striking Ukrainian infrastructure.
“But here, the list of facilities needs to be agreed upon, and this will be the most difficult issue – both sides will have to recognize each other’s lists or agree on them,” the political analyst noted.
The second issue to be discussed, he said, will be a ceasefire in the Black Sea, or the designation of corridors for peaceful shipping from both Ukrainian and Russian ports, as well as the resumption of grain exports from Ukraine and Russia.
“I believe there are currently no grounds for expecting talks on a full ceasefire,” the political analyst said.
In his view, if the United States actively promotes such an agenda, there is a high probability that trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the United States will resume.
“In any case, according to reports from both Moscow and Kyiv, preparations are underway. The only question is when exactly they will take place – this week, for example, or next week. The main thing now is for the United States to act consistently and systematically, in a way that would force Moscow to agree to certain compromises. The U.S. position will be decisive,” Fesenko said.
At the same time, he stressed that concrete results should not be expected from today’s meeting between Zelensky and Trump.
“Either way, further talks with Russia will be necessary, and it is precisely the U.S. position that will have to make an impact there. Today, there may only be preliminary agreements: when and how these talks will take place, what their agenda will be, and what position the United States will promote. That is what is important. Therefore, any agreements reached at this stage will be preliminary and interim. Talks on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly are always working-level, and they do not end with specific decisions,” the political analyst explained.
As reported, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in New York to participate in the UN General Assembly High-Level Week and hold a number of bilateral meetings, including with U.S. President Donald Trump.

LISBON, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- Portugal will sign a joint declaration of intent to join the European Union's cross-border testing network for autonomous vehicles next week, state secretary for mobility Cristina Pinto Dias announced Tuesday.
"Next week I will sign the joint declaration of intent on the creation of an EU cross-border test area for the deployment of automated vehicles," Pinto Dias said, adding that Portugal needs "a very integrated, competitive and above all sustainable ecosystem."
The declaration will be signed during the Connecting Europe Days 2026 alongside Slovakia and Norway, bringing the total number of signatories to 21. Eighteen EU member states had already joined the initiative in June.
The network aims to create a large European testing zone spanning roads and cities across multiple countries, where autonomous vehicles can operate across borders without having to complete separate authorization processes in each member state.
Participating countries commit to adopting common technical requirements for automated vehicles and systems, coordinated type-approval and authorization processes, and shared rules for the circulation and provision of services using autonomous vehicles.
Pinto Dias noted that Portugal's domestic legislation permitting autonomous vehicle tests on public roads entered into force earlier this year, and said the regulatory framework is now in place to attract investment and provide stability for companies, investors and consumers.
The Institute of Mobility and Transport (IMT) confirmed it has already received multiple requests for preliminary meetings from companies seeking clarification on the legal regime for licensing tests of automatic driving systems, describing the interest as evidence of strong sector demand for the new framework. ■

====================================================================================================

Roundup: Record-high fuel prices ripple through Türkiye's economy
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
23:19:50 CST
00:19:50 KST

People refuel their vehicles at a gas station in Ankara, Türkiye, Sept. 22, 2026. Surging fuel prices are increasingly affecting household budgets, transportation choices and the prices of goods and services in Türkiye, after diesel exceeded 100 Turkish liras (2.05 U.S. dollars) per liter for the first time recently. (Mustafa Kaya/Handout via Xinhua)
ANKARA, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- Surging fuel prices are increasingly affecting household budgets, transportation choices and the prices of goods and services in Türkiye, after diesel exceeded 100 Turkish liras (2.05 U.S. dollars) per liter for the first time recently.
The latest increases came amid elevated global energy prices and disruptions to oil supplies. Brent crude rose above 100 U.S. dollars per barrel earlier this month as concerns over supplies through the Strait of Hormuz intensified.
In a country where nearly half of the workforce earns the minimum wage of 28,075.50 liras, the hikes are significant. The impact is particularly significant for Türkiye, a major importer of both oil and natural gas.
Yusuf Koseoglu, a retired architect living in Ankara, told Xinhua that the increases were already affecting households and the wider economy.
"The increases are already affecting us, and we don't know what will happen next," Koseoglu said. "At the moment, it is impossible to live on a pension in Türkiye. I live on my savings."
"There is a direct impact on inflation. A one-lira increase in the price of oil affects everything -- food, drink, transportation. We depend on it for everything," he said.
For some households, higher fuel costs have prompted changes in daily travel habits. The cost of filling a tank has made regular private-car use increasingly difficult, prompting some to limit journeys, use company shuttles or turn to public transportation.
Hilal Onat, a teacher, said that although she owned a car, she had stopped using it to commute whenever possible.
"I drive a car, but now I use the company shuttle whenever possible when going to work because fuel prices have risen so much," she told Xinhua.
Istanbul-based economist Mustafa Sonmez warned that the impact of higher fuel prices extended across the economy.
"People are wondering how they will afford heating fuel for winter and how to cope with higher transportation costs. Fuel prices affect the whole of the economy and will lead to price increases in most goods and services," Sonmez told Xinhua, warning that this would deepen Türkiye's cost-of-living squeeze.
Türkiye's annual consumer price inflation moderated to 31.51 percent in August from 31.75 percent in July, while monthly inflation was 1.84 percent. The recent energy-price increases have added another external pressure as authorities pursue a disinflation process.
Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek said last week that Türkiye's disinflation process had been successful but was moving more slowly than desired, attributing the slowdown to domestic and particularly external factors.
"If there had been no war this year, inflation would be at least 7 percentage points lower as of today," Simsek said.
Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar described the international energy environment as a "perfect storm," citing developments involving the Strait of Hormuz, the Russia-Ukraine conflict and other factors. ■

====================================================================================================

Activists and leaders reflect on Standing Rock a decade on: ‘I would do it again’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:17:47 UTC
00:17:47 KST

Ten years after major demonstrations against the Dakota Access pipeline, tribal leaders and Native American organizers returned to the Standing Rock Sioux reservation this week to honor the movement and its lasting impacts.
In the rural reservation area of Fort Yates, a four-day encampment that centered on the phrase “mní wičóni” – “water is life” – brought together about 150 tribal members and allies for meals, drum circles, sacred ceremonies and memorials.
It opened with the lighting of a sacred fire – “peta waken” – using coals preserved from a fire that burned at the 2016 camp.
The tradition is a significant spiritual unification between the seven councils of the Oceti Sakowin, or Sioux Nation, tribes, typically done in times of historic and political efforts as a symbol of hope. In November 2016, after nearly two centuries had passed without the ceremony, Sioux tribal elders called for the fire to be relit after protesters – concerned that the Dakota Access pipeline (DAPL), which would run within a mile of tribal lands, might pollute the Standing Rock reservation’s water supply and encroach on Native lands and burial grounds – were maced, attacked by dogs and arrested en masse.
Later that winter, thousands more protesters or “water protectors” convened on the Great Plains, and outrage over the pipeline’s construction became a louder, global movement for Native rights and climate justice. But it did not stop Dallas-based Energy Transfer Partners from building the project, and national guard and police cleared the last holdout of protesters in an early 2017 military-style takeover. The pipeline now transports up to 750,000 barrels of oil a day from North Dakota to an Illinois refinery.
In a powerful moment Thursday evening, Manape LaMere – an original headsman from the 2016 council and a member of the Sioux nation – retrieved the original coals and lit the fire as he had 10 years ago.
One of LaMere’s other responsibilities at the Mni Wiconi gathering was to help perform a spiritual healing ceremony to help those who were at the camps find closure from the trauma of what they experienced.
“When we sacrifice in camp the way we did, all that hardship and all that beauty, I always encourage people to call their spirit back,” LaMere said. “But because we got evicted the way we did, a lot of us may not have received that message, and I’ve seen people struggle.”
Reunion attendees, at open mic sessions or around fire pits, reflected on how the often-violent standoffs between protesters and law enforcement in 2016 left many with lingering trauma, like for Candi Brings Plenty, a member of the Oglala Lakota Sioux nation.
But, Brings Plenty said, while the event left scars, the community formed among camps has created lifelong strength. “I got the best knowledge and woksape, which is a Lakota word for wisdom, being at Standing Rock. I got so much empowerment and even though I got the worst-of-the-worst PTSD and everything that came along with it, you know, I would do it again,” Brings Plenty said.
At the Prairie Knights Casino, the inaugural People of the Sun event brought together renewable energy groups, activists and performers for a three-day summit focusing on clean energy solutions.
Speakers and panelists said that the protests 10 years ago underscored the need for Native reservations to build more sustainable energy systems that align with tribal values.
One group making those systems a reality is the Sage Development Authority, a federally chartered corporation formed by the Standing Rock Sioux nation. The group uses grant funding to build wind farms for tribal district buildings, which allows local leaders to then reinvest that money back into their communities.
Joseph McNeil, the CEO of SAGE and an enrolled member of the Standing Rock Sioux nation, said building infrastructure that allows his community to gain energy independence has intergenerational impacts.
“The intergenerational poverty has been so dire, and being forced and your economy purposely depressed has been so intentional, that we can be voices for that and try to think of ways to help folks who aren’t there,” McNeil said. “We’re putting the stuff onto the district buildings, but it’s up to the district. We’re not going to dictate you, have your own choices, make your own decisions, and then live with those.”
In support of the People of the Sun event was the actor Shailene Woodley, whose arrest at the protest 10 years ago spurred additional public discourse around the pipeline.
“Do your research. Learn about the history, the real history of what happened to this country when our ancestors chose to colonize this land. And not from a place of guilt, not from a place of shame, but from a place of empowerment,” Woodley said in an interview.
“If we don’t pay attention and if we don’t educate ourselves on what happened, then we’re going to continue to even unknowingly repeat those patterns and feed into the same cycles.”

EU drops Usmanov from sanctions list after infighting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:15:45 UTC
00:15:45 KST

EU drops Usmanov from sanctions list after infighting
The EU’s 27 member states have agreed to remove Russian businessmen Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from their sanctions blacklist, ending an impasse that threatened the very foundation of the bloc’s anti-Russian penalty regime.
In a deal brokered by Ireland, which holds the EU’s rotating presidency, the member states agreed on Tuesday to remove Usmanov and Fridman from the blacklist. In exchange, the bloc extended sanctions on roughly 3,000 other Russian and Russian-linked entities and individuals by three years instead of the usual six months.
Usmanov, a Russian-Uzbek metals tycoon, was sanctioned by the EU in February 2022 over his alleged ties to the Kremlin. The EU came to this conclusion based on media reports which have been proven false by Usmanov’s legal team over a series of lawsuits, and the billionaire used these legal victories to argue that he had been sanctioned based on false evidence.
However, it was France that pushed for his delisting, having negotiated a deal in which Azerbaijan would free two French citizens – one of whom was imprisoned for espionage – in exchange for the de-sanctioning of Usmanov. A Turkic nation like Uzbekistan, Azerbaijan was one of several countries that lobbied for Usmanov.
Luxembourg lobbied for the delisting of Fridman, as the duchy is currently being sued for $16 billion over its freezing of his assets in 2022. According to Reuters, Luxembourg argued that its case against Fridman would be weakened if Usmanov alone was let go.
If a deal had not been struck by midnight on Tuesday, all of the EU’s anti-Russian sanctions would have expired. An agreement was reportedly reached on Monday afternoon, but Latvia intervened to prevent it taking effect. As one of the EU’s most fervent backers of Ukraine, Latvian Foreign Minister Baibe Braze argued that “EU sanctions against Russia must be strengthened, not weakened. Therefore, Latvia cannot agree to the widely proposed suggestion.”
As negotiations restarted on Tuesday, Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky thanked Braze for “keeping up the legal front against the war of aggression against Ukraine,” and declared that Usmanov and Fridman’s names “must be on the sanctions lists.”
Grateful to our Latvian friends @EdgarsRinkevics, @AndrisKulbergs and other EU partners for keeping up the legal front against the war of aggression against Ukraine. As Russia is escalating the killing of civilians – there have been more attacks overnight and into the day with…
— Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) September 22, 2026
Ultimately, Latvia took a position of ‘constructive abstention’ and allowed the other member states to press ahead with delisting the two tycoons and renewing the remaining sanctions.
Usmanov’s delisting removes a potential legal nightmare for the EU. As RT already explored this week, the billionaire’s repeated litigation has undermined Brussels’ case against him, and an additional lawsuit against the EU threatened to expose the bloc’s secret “evidence packs” used to build the case. Several high-profile Russian businessmen have already been delisted after the shaky evidence in these packs was made public, and a legal win by Usmanov would have cast the legal rationale for sanctions into further disrepute.

Republican calls for Senate investigation of Trump Jr wedding paid for by Russian oligarch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:15:23 UTC
00:15:23 KST

A Republican senator has accused Donald Trump Jr of corruption and demanded a Senate investigation into revelations that a Russian oligarch bankrolled part of his recent wedding in the Bahamas.
John Curtis, of Utah, wrote to the leaders of the US Senate judiciary committee on Tuesday, urging them to subpoena Trump Jr over his business dealings, his relationships with foreign individuals, gifts he has received – and any occasions where his connection to his father, Donald Trump, “was invoked or understood to provide value”.
Trump Jr’s wedding warrants the kind of scrutiny Republicans once trained on Hunter Biden, the son of Joe Biden, Curtis said.
“A toaster is a wedding gift. A private-island party paid for by a Putin-connected oligarch is something else,” he wrote in a social media post accompanying the letter to the committee. “Republicans nearly wore out the subpoena machine investigating Hunter Biden’s foreign relationships. We should not unplug it now.”
The push follows reporting by ProPublica that Umar Kremlev, the Russian boxing official with close ties to Vladimir Putin, helped cover the cost of renting a private island and staging a fireworks display for the wedding of Trump Jr and Bettina Anderson in the Bahamas in May. Bettina Trump later described Kremlev on Instagram as a “dear friend” who had generously hosted two nights of post-wedding celebrations.
Donald Trump, who did not attend the ceremony, defended Kremlev’s involvement but said he was told by Trump Jr that the money would eventually be reimbursed, though explained that giving a wedding party as a gift is “totally allowed” and is also “very common”.
It is not the first time Trump Jr’s conduct has drawn scrutiny over ties to Russia. He was a central figure in the Robert Mueller investigation that followed the 2016 election, after it emerged he had attended a Trump Tower meeting with a Russian lawyer who had promised damaging material on Hillary Clinton.
The call for a formal committee inquiry marks one of the sharper breaks with the president by a sitting Republican senator. Curtis first flagged the wedding payment as problematic on Friday, calling it “corruption” in a video posted online and promising further comment. He was elected to the Senate in 2024, pledging not to shy away from disagreements with Trump.
His letter, addressed to the committee chair, Chuck Grassley of Iowa, and its top Democrat, Dick Durbin of Illinois, lands amid signs of broader unease among Republicans over Trump’s standing heading into November’s US midterm elections, with the party facing pressure over the war in Iran, high gas prices and slipping poll numbers.
Republicans in the House of Representatives spent much of 2023 and 2024 investigating whether Hunter Biden traded on his father’s name in his overseas business dealings, an effort that produced a report alleging a conspiracy to enrich the Biden family, but never resulted in impeachment articles reaching a House vote. The Bidens denied wrongdoing throughout.
“‘Trust us’ was not enough then,” wrote Curtis, “and it is not enough now.”

Iran, Uzbekistan eye AI-driven agricultural co-op as trade delegation aims for $2b
TEHRAN- In a joint meeting and subsequent conference on agricultural cooperation between Iran and Uzbekistan, the two countries' agriculture ministers emphasized joint investment in AI-based modern farming, livestock breeding, and pasture development. With a large Iranian trade delegation present—comprising over 100 companies and heads of provincial chambers—officials outlined plans to boost bilateral agricultural trade from $200 million to $600 million within two years, while broader trade ambitions target $2 billion. Iran also highlighted its transport capacities to provide landlocked Uzbekistan with access to open waters.
The joint meeting between Gholamreza Nouri Qezeljeh and Ebrahim Abdolrahmanov, the agriculture ministers of Iran and Uzbekistan, was held with the presence of Hossein Pirmoazen, Vice Chairman of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, and Mohammad Ali Eskandari, Iran’s ambassador to Uzbekistan. At the meeting, reference was made to the visit of the Iran Chamber’s trade delegation, composed of some heads of provincial chambers, specialized committees, and associations in agriculture and related industries, which signals Iran’s serious determination to expand cooperation.
According to what was raised, Iranian companies are ready to invest in Uzbekistan and have broad capacities for cooperation in areas such as agricultural mechanization, production of agricultural machinery and implements, livestock breeding, fisheries, and veterinary medicines.
Iran’s capabilities in producing poultry and eggs, exporting improved cattle embryos, modern smart irrigation technologies, and producing agricultural drones were among the topics emphasized by Iran’s agriculture minister.
In addition to explaining ways to increase exports between the two countries, the import of agricultural products from Uzbekistan to Iran was also discussed.
At the meeting, the Iranian side stressed the need to activate the joint agricultural cooperation committee with the aim of implementing programs more precisely.
On the other side, Uzbekistan’s agriculture minister, while praising Iran’s achievements in water resource management, combating drought, and improving crop productivity, called Iran’s model in agricultural innovation successful and inspiring for developing countries.
Prioritizing the production of next-generation agricultural equipment in Iran-Uzbekistan agricultural cooperation was another point raised by the Uzbek side, since improving farm productivity is one of the country’s most important agricultural programs.
Later in the meeting, pasture development and the implementation of livestock breeding projects were proposed as key areas of cooperation between the two countries.
According to what was stated at the meeting, Uzbekistan is transitioning from monoculture agriculture and reducing cotton cultivation in favor of developing 400,000 hectares of orchards. Therefore, Uzbekistan’s large market can accommodate Iranian products.
Uzbekistan’s agriculture minister described the activity of Iran’s Innovation House in Tashkent as an effective step for introducing Iran’s modern achievements and expressed hope that the agricultural cooperation development program and regular meetings of joint working groups would make the implementation path of agreements clear and operational for relevant officials.
Iran-Uzbekistan agricultural cooperation conference held to strengthen bilateral ties
At the Iran-Uzbekistan Agricultural Cooperation Conference, while examining ways to strengthen relations between the two countries, the agriculture ministers explained the existing capacities for strengthening ties. Ebrahim Abdolrahmanov, Uzbekistan’s agriculture minister, said at the conference: Iran has taken this major step under special circumstances and has sent a large delegation of activists in agriculture, livestock feed, grains, and agricultural equipment and implements to Uzbekistan. Therefore, we believe that to become stronger, we must expand cooperation, because it is important for Uzbekistan to know how Iran, despite all challenges, has developed to this extent and strengthened its domestic capacities. This issue is noteworthy in all economic and trade areas.
He continued: Despite all economic concerns, Iran’s food security system has been maintained, and we see the high resilience of Iranian industrial units, from which we must learn. Abdolrahmanov, stating that this delegation and the presence of economic activists in Iran is valuable and can be a strong platform for cooperation, emphasized: With my Iranian counterpart, we reached good agreements on cooperation in using modern technologies in the production of meat, milk, and other food and agricultural industries. Food security is an important issue in every country and is a priority in all policies.
He announced the reduction of cotton farms and a move toward producing various orchard products in Uzbekistan and said: In the field of quarantine, there is also the possibility of cooperation between the two countries.
Gholamreza Nouri Qezeljeh, Iran’s agriculture minister, while condemning efforts by enemies against the food supply chain and the security of the region and Iran, said: Despite all these issues, Iran has stood firm and, fortunately, is moving forward. He referred to agriculture and food as the roots of resilience and described cooperation between the two countries in agriculture as growing.
Nouri noted: Iran, relying on indigenous knowledge and achieving knowledge-based principles, seeks the growth of processing industries and agricultural production in its arid and semi-arid region. The agriculture minister spoke about knowledge-based companies in agriculture, modern irrigation methods, and the production of various fertilizers and pesticides based on new scientific procedures in Iran, and said: Given its transport capacities, Iran can provide good access for Uzbekistan to open waters.
Nouri proposed activating joint committees between the chambers of the two countries so that, relying on existing capacities and agreements related to Iran-Eurasia free trade, we witness an upgrade in the level of cooperation between the two countries.
Nouri noted: Establishing a green customs corridor by harmonizing standards with the aim of removing barriers in trade between the two countries, barter models, and using national currencies for trade between the two countries are solutions that should be considered.
The agriculture minister estimated the agricultural trade value between the two countries at $200 million, which could rise to $600 million within two years. According to Nouri, the future of food security lies in synergy and relying on the strengths of both sides, and by accepting this principle, we will pursue the prosperity of relations.
Defining a joint and scientific mechanism in food industry and agriculture cooperation
The head of Uzbekistan’s Food Safety Agency also explained the process pursued in the organization and referred to opportunities for cooperation between the two countries after harmonizing standards. In his view, a unified and scientific mechanism should be defined in agricultural and food industry cooperation between the two countries.
The head of Uzbekistan’s Food Safety Agency spoke about the need to identify capacities to prepare an accurate outlook for relations between the two countries and added: We can also take good steps in defining halal standards, and we are moving forward with this approach. He proposed: To resolve trade challenges and barriers, we must reach a coherent and coordinated mechanism between the two sides.
In another part of the conference, Mohammad Ali Eskandari, Iran’s ambassador to Tashkent, spoke about the importance of turning commonalities between the two nations into trade activities and joint investment and praised the efforts of the private sectors of both countries to double the volume of Iran-Uzbekistan trade. He also highlighted the existence of joint agricultural projects between Iran and Uzbekistan and added: We must use the existing infrastructure in Iran in terms of human resources, natural resources, and knowledge for the benefit of Iran-Uzbekistan relations.
Eskandari announced the readiness of infrastructure by the embassy and the Iranian government to support traders of both sides to strengthen agricultural cooperation and related industries. Iran’s ambassador to Tashkent described Iran’s scientific capabilities in agriculture as significant and added: We must be able to turn bilateral cooperation in agriculture into a model for future cooperation between the two countries.
Duran Vahabov, head of the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Uzbekistan, also said: Supporting traders and their interests is one of the duties we pursue, and we must strive to develop cooperation between the two sides. We must use all our capabilities to consolidate relations and seize opportunities.
From facilitation to reaching $2 billion in trade between Iran and Uzbekistan
Hossein Pirmoazen, Vice Chairman of the Iran Chamber, at the Iran-Uzbekistan Agricultural Cooperation Conference, while explaining what is needed to upgrade the level of trade and investment cooperation between the two countries, asked the private sectors of both countries to benefit from the infrastructure created for the benefit of both economies.
The Iran-Uzbekistan Agricultural Cooperation Conference was held with the presence of the agriculture ministers of both sides, the Vice Chairman of the Iran Chamber, the head of the Uzbekistan Chamber, Iran’s ambassador to Tashkent, the head of Uzbekistan’s Food Safety Agency, and members of the Iran Chamber’s trade delegation, including a number of heads of provincial chambers, specialized commissions of the Iran Chamber, and associations in agriculture and the food industry.
Hossein Pirmoazen, Vice Chairman of the Iran Chamber, said at the conference: More than 100 companies, heads of chambers of commerce, industries, mines and agriculture from 7 provincial chambers, a number of heads of commissions and specialized associations, and 105 active units in areas related to agriculture and the food industry are present in the Iranian trade delegation.
He continued: Facilitation of trade laws, issuance of permits in agreements between the two countries, establishing smooth financial transaction relations, resolving transport-related issues and creating new routes with necessary memoranda of understanding, and increasing the number of coded goods in preferential trade are issues whose handling is highly important and must be placed on the agenda of both sides.
The Vice Chairman of the Iran Chamber, emphasizing that after the necessary facilitation by governments, it is the private sector’s turn to play a role, said: Economic actors must also benefit from the provided infrastructure and develop the level of cooperation. In this regard, let us seize the created opportunity and use the memorandum of understanding to be signed between the two chambers of Iran and Uzbekistan for the benefit of defining joint projects.
Pirmoazen noted: Iran and Uzbekistan have many shared views, and private sector actors must use them so that the trade volume reaches $2 billion and we celebrate this success together.

Suspect in ‘Putney pusher’ case was found dead after missing family meal, inquest hears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:13:52 UTC
00:13:52 KST

The man who was arrested on suspicion of being the so-called “Putney pusher” was found dead at his home after missing a family meal, an inquest has heard.
Nicholas Brandram, 44, was arrested in June in connection with an incident on Putney Bridge on 5 May 2017 in which a jogger shoved a woman headfirst into the path of an oncoming bus.
The former banker was found unresponsive inside his home in Chiswick, west London, on 15 September.
Melanie Lee, the area coroner, opened and suspended an inquest into his death at west London coroner’s court on Tuesday afternoon.
Opening the proceedings, she said: “On the evening of Tuesday 15 September 2026, Nicholas did not attend a family meal as planned.
“His brother-in-law attended Nicholas’s home address and gained access using a spare key provided by a neighbour. Upon searching the house, he found Nicholas in an upstairs room.
“Paramedics attended and despite resuscitation, he was pronounced deceased at 8.58pm.”
The coroner said the death was not considered suspicious and there was “no evidence of third-party involvement”.
Lee said provisional results from a postmortem examination indicated his death was “due to ligature compression of the neck”.
The Metropolitan police has referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) over its contact with Brandram, who was released under investigation after his arrest.
The force said on 17 September that its investigation into the Putney Bridge incident remained ongoing after Brandram’s death.
Lee said on Tuesday: “I have been informed this afternoon that a referral has been made to the IOPC. On that basis, I am suspending the inquest.”
The coroner added that an inquest was not a trial and “nobody and no organisation is on trial”.
Brandram’s sisters, who were present at the inquest opening, have previously accused police of failing him and wider society.
The coroner told the family: “I offer my sincere condolences for your loss. I appreciate today will not be an easy day for you.”
The family have said they believe Brandram took his own life after “months of immense pressure” caused by the Met’s investigation.
In an interview with BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Brandram’s sisters Alexia Hicks and Sophie Voelcker said he did not match the description of the attacker.
Hicks said there had been “urgency” by the Met to arrest Brandram and to have that reported in the press. “I think he couldn’t understand why there wasn’t urgency to help clear his name,” she added.

NEW DELHI: The Delhi government has prepared 81 artificial ponds for people to immerse Ganesh idols at designated sites instead of the Yamuna or other water bodies.The government has also set up 110 collection centres for dignified disposal of old and damaged idols and religious material.The two measures form part of an initiative aimed at balancing religious practices with cleanliness and environmental protection.The initiative will provide designated collection containers at suitable locations, including temples, where devotees can deposit old, damaged idols and other puja material instead of leaving them in public places, chief minister Rekha Gupta said.She said such material is often left under trees, in parks, along roadsides and at other public places due to religious sentiments, creating challenges for cleanliness and the environment.Preparations have also been completed at 81 locations across Delhi for artificial immersion ponds for Ganesh idols. The arrangements cover all 13 revenue districts and include security, sanitation, lighting, medical assistance, emergency response and traffic management, according to a statement.The chief minister has appealed to devotees to immerse Ganesh idols only at designated artificial immersion sites and not in the Yamuna or other water bodies.
She also urged people not to dispose of puja material, flowers, garlands and other religious items in rivers or water bodies and to give preference to eco-friendly idols.The government has advised devotees to avoid idols made of Plaster of Paris, colours containing harmful chemicals and decorative materials that can damage water bodies and the environment.Arrangements have also been made for removal of idol remains and other material from immersion sites after the festivities, followed by cleaning of the locations as per the prescribed process, it said.The initiative is aimed at providing organised and clean spaces for people to follow their religious traditions while reducing pressure on public spaces and water bodies, the statement said.Gupta said religious faith and environmental protection should complement each other and urged Delhi residents to use only designated collection centres for damaged idols and religious material and artificial immersion sites for Ganesh idols.
She said maintaining a clean Delhi was a shared responsibility of the government and citizens, and called for public participation to balance faith, cleanliness and environmental protection.The Ganesh festival began on September 14 and will conclude on September 25, when a large number of idols will be immersed after colourful processions.

Prime Minister Michal’s Opening Remarks at the 20th ABCD Conference in Tallinn

There is a reason for that.
I have visited Kyiv several times during this war. Every visit reminds me of two things.
Russia has not changed its goals. It still believes that it can change borders by force. It still seeks to decide the future of its neighbours, divide Europe and spread discord around the world.
But Ukraine has shown that Russia can be stopped.
Ukraine has changed the way wars are fought. It has learned to adapt fast, use new technology and turn battlefield experience into new capabilities.
“Kyiv in three days?” Ukraine’s answer has been clear: never.
Winning means making sure Russia fails.
Ukraine made the brave decision to fight.
Our job is to help them win. Estonia spends at least 0.25% of its GDP each year on military aid to Ukraine. Russia does not get to decide Ukraine’s future. And it does not get to decide Europe’s security order.
Ukraine will make its own choices. And we will make ours.
We must have the will and resources to defend those choices.
This is what Estonia is working on. Let me make three points.
First, building the defence we need to win.
We are among NATO’s top defence spenders. Over the next ten years, we will invest 26 billion euros in defence. Around half of this will go to weapons and military capabilities.
We are growing our local defence industry.
With public investment support, we are speeding up the production of ammunition, explosives and short-range air-defence missiles.
The turnover of Estonia’s defence sector has increased by an average of 44% a year over the past three years. Our aim is to reach 2 billion euros a year by 2030.
The Estonian Defence Week around this conference shows how far we have come.
Defence is not only about weapons.
We also protect our critical infrastructure, strengthen comprehensive defence and make sure our ports, roads and railways can support our defence.
Lately, we have heard a lot of vague messages about the security situation of our region.
I can assure you there is no reason for panic.
We are informed and we take all possible threats seriously.
When we see a threat, we will say so clearly.
Second, building a Europe and alliances ready to win.
Peace depends on unity and strength. That is what makes deterrence work.
Estonia has long said that Europe must do more for its own defence.
We have led by example. Our core defence spending now stands above 5% of GDP.
Faced with the existential Russian threat, our allies have also stepped up.
Defence spending by NATO allies other than the United States is rising fast. By 2030, it is expected to be higher than US defence spending.
NATO stepped up when critical undersea infrastructure was damaged in the Baltic Sea.
Allied fighter jets have responded fast to violations of our airspace. One shot down a drone over Estonia only recently.
UK, French and US forces are contributing to our security with troops on the ground.
Simply put: NATO works.
The European Union has also raised its game and helps us close critical capability gaps.
Estonia works to make sure the next EU budget matches our security challenges.
Europe now provides most of the support for Ukraine.
Europe’s defence industry has changed gear. Ammunition production has increased sharply since 2022.
But we need more ammunition and more weapons.
We also need drones, air defence, electronic warfare and technologies that may not even exist today.
We need to learn faster. Produce faster. Scale faster.
And we need to do this for less money.
Which brings me to my final point.
Winning the wars of the future.
Ukraine has taught us that a smaller country can defend itself against a much larger enemy. It is possible through innovation and adaptation.
The speed of change, especially in drone warfare, is remarkable.
New solutions appear in weeks and months.
Ukraine has built a direct link between the frontline and production.
It means identifying new needs, collecting data, developing and testing rapidly, and then scaling and implementing quickly.
This knowledge is vital for Europe and for our security.
Learning from Ukraine is a matter of urgency.
Russia and its allies may be slower, but they are learning too.
New drones are being developed to continue spreading terror at night in Kyiv.
Russia’s lessons are also being taken up by Iran, spreading destruction in the Middle East and damaging global energy security.
The free world has some of the most advanced weapon systems in the world.
We cannot spend millions every time Russia spends thousands.
We must work more with Ukraine on defence production.
I took a step in that direction by signing a drone agreement with President Zelenskyy at NATO Summit in Ankara.
The agreement is not only about drones. We will share knowledge, develop technology and produce together.
Now we must make it work in practice. And this is not only a question of production.
It is much more a question of adopting the Ukrainian mindset and approach to defence.
Can we learn and innovate as fast as Ukraine?
Can we test, scale and produce faster?
Can we lower the costs?
Can our defence organisation and industry move at the speed of Ukraine?
We have to - if we want to win.
Thank you.

The expert added that all of this is complemented by the simultaneous destruction of logistical routes, primarily naval military-technical traffic organized by NATO countries to supply components and raw materials to the Ukrainian armed forces, as well as checkpoints to cut off land communications. "Taken together, the elimination of industry, energy, and logistics will guarantee that the Kiev regime is deprived of the capability to launch strikes against our territory," he concluded.

Standoff with Trump administration sidelines UN refugee agency deputy, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:09:17 UTC
00:09:17 KST

Standoff with Trump administration sidelines UN refugee agency deputy, sources say
GENEVA, Sept 22 - The Trump administration is refusing to work with the newly appointed deputy head of the United Nations refugee agency, exposing tensions between the agency and one of its top donors at a time of acute funding pressures, diplomats said.
Tressa Rae Finerty, an American who took up the role of Deputy High Commissioner at UNHCR earlier this month, has taken leave as she seeks a waiver from the US government that would allow her to carry out aspects of her duties, according to seven diplomatic sources.
Her treatment by Washington, which previously considered cutting ties with the agency, is seen by several of the diplomats as a retaliatory response after UNHCR opted against Washington's preferred candidate, Simon Hankinson.
A State Department spokesperson said it could not comment on pending legal issues. "...We work with and through UNHCR when doing so advances US foreign policy interests," the spokesperson said.
Finerty did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The standoff comes as UNHCR grapples with one of its worst ever funding crises following aid cuts by the Trump administration and others, at a time of record global displacement.
Finerty, a career US diplomat who previously served as charge d'affaires at the US Mission to the UN in Geneva, is currently unable to interact directly with US officials because of post-employment restrictions that apply to former US government personnel, the sources said.
Violations of the restrictions, designed to prevent conflicts of interest, could in theory result in a prison sentence.
UNHCR told Reuters that Finerty requested a partial waiver from the US government late last month.
"This relates, in particular, to her participation in multilateral meetings that US Department of State officials attend," UNHCR said in a statement.
"We are hoping for a speedy and favourable resolution to this matter," it said, adding that the agency's operations and reform agenda continued "at full pace".
KEY ROLE FOR DONORS
The failure to obtain a waiver is seen as highly unusual because they are granted routinely for other former US staff entering the global body, diplomats and UN staff said.
The deputy high commissioner is traditionally one of the agency's most important interlocutors with major donors, including the US, diplomats and former officials said, adding Finerty’s situation may make it challenging for UNHCR to fundraise with the US.
The US, which has withdrawn from dozens of other UN entities under President Donald Trump, had long been the agency's largest donor.
According to UNHCR data, Washington contributed more than $800 million in 2025, accounting for nearly a quarter of the agency's $3.6 billion in contributions. That dropped to around $110 million this year. REUTERS

275,000 Missing in Russia-Ukraine War, Red Cross Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:08:00 UTC
00:08:00 KST

About 275,000 people have been reported missing in connection with Russia’s war against Ukraine, while the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) receives roughly 10,000 new tracing requests each month.
ICRC President Mirjana Spoljaric Egger disclosed the figures in comments to Russian newspaper Vedomosti published Tuesday.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The organization does not provide a breakdown of how many missing people are Ukrainian or Russian because information collected during its tracing operations is confidential.
“Over the past four years, we have made significant progress on humanitarian issues,” Spoljaric Egger said, adding that more families had received information about the fate of missing relatives.
The total does not represent only confirmed battlefield disappearances. It includes people reported missing in connection with the international armed conflict, including military personnel, prisoners of war, and civilians whose relatives have lost contact with them.
The sharp rise in the recorded number is also partly linked to a change in the ICRC’s methodology.
Since 2025, the organization has counted both formalized tracing cases and preliminary requests that have not yet completed the documentation process. The change increased the overall number of cases in its system and means the latest figure cannot be directly compared with earlier totals.
The ICRC receives information about prisoners of war through official lists exchanged by Russia and Ukraine. Its representatives may also visit detention facilities and collect oral or written messages for prisoners’ relatives.
Russian Ex-Mayor Who Left Prison for Ukraine War Dies From Combat Wounds
Such visits can allow the organization to confirm that a person previously listed as missing is alive, although the ICRC has repeatedly faced criticism in Ukraine over limited access to Ukrainian prisoners held by Russia.
Separate Ukrainian data indicates that Russian families are searching for large numbers of soldiers who disappeared during Moscow’s invasion.
Ukraine’s “I Want to Find” project said in August that it had received 210,766 requests concerning missing Russian military personnel since its launch in January 2024.
The largest number of requests that included a location was connected to the Pokrovsk district of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region, where relatives sought information about approximately 29,000 Russian troops, primarily reported missing during 2024 and 2025.
More than 12,000 requests were linked to the Bakhmut district, while over 8,000 concerned Russian personnel reported missing in Russia’s Kursk region. Ukrainian forces controlled part of that region from August 2024 until April 2025.
Russian internet users searched the phrase “missing in the special military operation” on Yandex almost 120,000 times in July 2026, according to search data cited by the Belarusian outlet Vot Tak.
The ICRC has warned that determining the fate of people missing during armed conflicts can take decades, even after the fighting ends. The Geneva Conventions require warring parties to record information about detainees and cooperate in efforts to locate missing people.

HAIKOU /China/, September 22. /TASS/. China’s southern Hainan Province plans to use more low carbon technologies based on the experience of the zero carbon demonstration zone of the Boao Forum for Asia (BFA), China News Service (CNS) reported.
According to the news portal, as part of China’s 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), the Hainan Free Trade Port will actively introduce green technologies and efficient waste recycling methods under a government plan aimed at comprehensive optimization of the current urban and rural development model. Sun Shuhua, chief engineer of Hainan’s housing department, said earlier that the province’s authorities added these tasks to the list of priority areas for high-quality growth.
The news portal noted that, under the goals set, Hainan will not only summarize the experience of the zero carbon demonstration zone in the settlement of Boao located on the eastern coast of Hainan Island, but will also find ways to introduce more green technologies used there. The authorities are preparing different scenarios for their application in residential areas and parks, while qualified specialists are studying the related market mechanisms to take the project to the national and even international level.
Hainan plans to improve green building standards for structures that will be primarily characterized by extremely low energy consumption. Such buildings should account for 40% of the total civil construction area in the near future.
According to Sun Shuhua, over the next five years, companies operating in the province or promoting cooperation with it will also improve supply chains for materials and components needed to build high-quality green houses with smart technologies.
Under the 15th Five-Year Plan, Hainan has already launched a pilot project dubbed "Cool City" for Haikou, the province’s administrative center, and Sanya, a leading resort city on the island’s southern coast. One of the main goals is to make life more comfortable in the tropical climate. Urban greening will play a key role in this program that will also cover older neighborhoods. Hainan is expected to see more cozy alleys, parks and shady boulevards.
Boao Forum for Asia’s environmental project
China’s central authorities and Hainan administration have been developing the zero carbon demonstration zone in Boao since 2022. A high-tech system on Dongyu Island at the mouth of the Wanquan River, where the BFA complex is located, provides efficient air circulation and cooling in buildings and uses solar energy to illuminate the surrounding area.
The Boao Forum for Asia was founded in February 2001 and has been held on the eastern coast of Hainan Island since 2002. As many as 29 Asian countries are its participants. This platform for developing multilateral cooperation is often referred to as the "Eastern Davos." The Chinese government is focused on the forum’s development, considering it a tool of soft diplomacy. In 2026, around 2,000 people from 60 countries and regions attended the conference. The next forum will take place from March 24 to 27, 2027.

Metal detectorist finds record-breaking trove of ancient Roman coins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:04:39 UTC
00:04:39 KST

Man's metal detector wouldn't stop beeping, leading to record-breaking trove of ancient Roman coins
An amateur archaeologist who discovered several Roman silver coins in a field in western Germany realized he had stumbled upon something bigger when his metal detector kept beeping.
Oliver Riedl called the authorities for help, and a group of experts who began digging immediately discovered a total of 934 Roman silver denarii. It is the biggest coin treasure ever found in Germany from the time of Roman Emperor Hadrian, the local office in charge of archaeological monuments said Tuesday.
"It was clear to me that there was something bigger buried here," Riedl said, describing how his metal detector continued signaling even after he had found several coins near Wesseling, south of Cologne a year ago.
The hoard of coins, which weighs 3.1 kilograms (6.8 pounds), went on display at the LVR-LandesMuseum Bonn on Tuesday.
The majority of the coins date from the time of the Flavian emperors (A.D. 69–96), and the oldest one was minted in 148 B.C., the museum said in a news release.
The collection of coins was probably buried deliberately in the second quarter of the second century A.D., according to the LVR Office for the Preservation of Archaeological Monuments in the Rhineland.
"Of course, we can only speculate about the motives, but it's very likely that someone wanted to keep this money safe. After all, banks didn't exist back then," Erich Classen, state archaeologist and the director of the office, said in a statement.
Classen said it wasn't clear why the treasure was never recovered before, adding that "perhaps the owner died before that could happen, without being able to pass on the knowledge about the coins."
Treasure troves from ancient Roman times or other distant eras are not uncommon. However, few from the second century are as extensive as the one found in Wesseling, the archaeological office said, adding that it was difficult to estimate the coins' value at the time.
However, the pay of Roman legionaries, which is well documented in written sources, provides a point of reference.
"At that time, an ordinary soldier in the legion earned 300 denarii a year. However, about half of that was withheld for food and equipment," said Rahel Otte, a research associate at the archaeological office.
"A legionary would therefore have had to save all of his disposable income for about six years to amass the Wesseling hoard," Otte said. She added that it remains unclear exactly who ultimately amassed this considerable fortune.
 The Cologne area was under Roman control roughly from 39 B.C. to A.D. 459. The Romans established a presence in the region under General Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa to secure their empire's border along the Rhine River, setting up a military outpost which later became Colonia Agrippina - today's Cologne.
 
Treasures from the Roman era have been found across Europe in recent years.
In February, metal detectorists in Wales found two lead ingots that date back to the Roman era, the first of their kind to be found in the region.
In 2024, a hoard of Roman coins worth over $125,000 was found during a construction project in central England. That same year, metal detectorists in Poland helped discover a large cache of ancient Roman coins.
Also in 2024, a collection of ancient silver Roman coins was unearthed on a small island in the Mediterranean Sea, officials said this week.

Trump announced a “massive” potash deal with Belarus—Lukashenka said the same day there is no spare potash to sell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:04:30 UTC
00:04:30 KST

US President Donald Trump announced a "massive deal" to buy Belarusian potash at prices far below what the US pays Canada, but Belarusian dictator Alyaksandr Lukashenka publicly contradicted him the same day, saying Belarus has no spare volumes to sell.
Washington has spent a year courting Lukashenka with sanctions relief and envoy visits in pursuit of both prisoner releases and trade openings—but the potash episode shows the limits of that courtship when the dictator's own supply chain cannot deliver what the US President has already promised his voters.
Trump promised cheaper potash for American farmers
Trump wrote on Truth Social on 21 September:
"The United States is working on a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus. The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers."
Potash is a key ingredient in fertilizer. Canada is the world's largest supplier—the US takes 53% of Canadian potash exports, and 80% of the potash American farms use comes from Canada. Canadian potash remains exempt from US tariffs despite the ongoing trade war between the two countries.
The announcement came as Trump's trade dispute with Ottawa deepened—he recently called Canada a "terrible trade partner," and on 16 September European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen offered Canada associate EU membership, which Trump said could be a "hostile act."
Lukashenka said all output is contracted
The same day, Lukashenka told officials Belarus cannot deliver. "Even if we wanted to supply potash to other, Western markets, we simply do not have those volumes—everything is contracted," he said during a meeting with the head of Belarus's State Customs Committee, Uladzimir Arlouski.
Arlouski reported that 85% of all Belarusian exports and imports now move eastward—primarily to China, other Asian countries, and Russia. Budget revenues grew almost 3.5% over eight months, and 5.2% so far this month.
A deal built on sanctions relief and prisoner swaps
The potash announcement followed a year-long US effort to engage Lukashenka. Washington lifted sanctions on Belarus's potash industry in exchange for the release of hundreds of political prisoners. US special envoy John Cole has played the central role, meeting Lukashenka last week and securing the release of 25 prisoners—far fewer than the 200 he had previously promised.
Over the course of Cole's effort, at least several hundred people have been freed, among them Nobel Peace Prize laureate Ales Bialiatski and Siarhei Tsikhanouski, husband of the internationally recognized winner of Belarus's 2020 presidential election. But human rights groups and freed prisoners say Lukashenka runs a "carousel"—arresting new political opponents to replace the ones he releases. Lukashenka denied this. "There are no political prisoners in Belarus," he claimed during last week's meeting with Cole.
With US midterms six weeks away on 3 November and the Republican Party struggling in the polls, Trump has been scrambling for wins on fuel and food prices. The same week, he urged Zelenskyy to stop hitting Russian refineries, blaming Ukraine rather than his own war with Iran for record US diesel prices—a move a senior European official told Politico was a search for "scapegoats."

European drugmakers say they are ‘losing ground’ to US and Chinese rivals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:04:10 UTC
00:04:10 KST

Some of Europe’s biggest pharmaceutical companies have said the continent is “losing ground” to rivals including the US and China in developing new drugs and attracting investment.
The chairs of nine companies, including Britain’s AstraZeneca, GSK and Denmark’s Novo Nordisk, wrote to Andy Burnham and the national leaders of other European countries on Tuesday to call for action to “safeguard our companies’ future”.
The letter, entitled Europe is Losing the Pharma Investment Race – But the Comeback is Within Reach, called on governments to treat medicines as strategic infrastructure, secure health sovereignty and act now to restore Europe’s competitiveness.
It argued that the pharmaceutical sector is one of Europe’s great postwar achievements that is supporting millions of highly skilled jobs and generating an EU trade surplus of more than €220bn (£188bn). “But this hard-won inheritance is at risk,” the letter said.
“In our boardrooms, we see Europe losing ground to global competition. Over $600bn in pharmaceutical investment has been announced in the US and China in the last two years alone.
“European governments must create conditions that attract investment in next-generation medicines before it’s too late,” said the letter, which was also signed by the chairs of Germany’s Boehringer Ingelheim, Italy’s Chiesi group, France’s Sanofi and Ipsen, and Novartis and Roche of Switzerland.
Europe’s share of global pharmaceutical research and development has fallen from 43% in 1990 to 31%, according to the European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA).
The continent’s share of commercial clinical trials – where new medicines are tested for safety and efficacy before they are submitted for regulatory approval – has halved to 9% from 18% a decade ago. Only 4% of clinical trials are focused on cell and gene therapies.
China has overtaken Europe in clinical trials, pharmaceutical patents, and the development of new medicines. The country’s share of global clinical trials rose from less than 10% to almost 30% over the same period.
Almost half (49%) of newly approved therapies did not reach European patients last year, up from 46% in 2019; those drugs that do take nearly 600 days on average. This varies hugely from country to country: from a median 56 days in Germany to 1,201 days in Romania, according to data from the EFPIA.
The industry body has said the root causes of unavailability and delay to accessing new medicines range from the speed of regulatory processes to insufficient budgets in some European countries.
Closing the clinical trials gap alone could generate €53bn and create 82,000 jobs in Europe, the nine pharma companies argued in the letter.
“We ask national leaders to work with us to reverse Europe’s declining competitiveness, unleash a new era of medical discovery, and secure health sovereignty. We recognise the fiscal pressures many face. But just like defence or energy, modern medicines should be treated as vital infrastructure and not be left to others to provide,” the letter said.
It was signed by industry leaders including Michel Demaré, the chair of Britain’s biggest pharmaceutical company, AstraZeneca; Jonathan Symonds, his counterpart at GSK, the country’s second-biggest drugmaker; Lars Rebien Sørensen, the chair of the Wegovy and Ozempic maker, Novo Nordisk; Severin Schwan at the Swiss company Roche; Giovanni Caforio at fellow Swiss firm Novartis, and Frédéric Oudéa at France’s Sanofi.
It comes after a public row last year between the industry and the UK government over drug pricing and availability of new treatments to patients. Ministers agreed in December to spend billions of pounds a year extra on medicines supplied to the NHS after pressure from Donald Trump, who argued that high drug prices in the US were subsidising lower prices elsewhere.
