The drone was flying in an area covered by a flight ban, raising questions about how it entered restricted airspace near one of Poland’s most sensitive military installations.
Poland says drone stayed under control
Poland’s Defense Ministry later said the aircraft was monitored throughout the incident and did not approach the base’s critical facilities or fly over the base.
“The drone was detected, and the location from which the operator controlled it was also identified,” the ministry said, according to Onet.
The ministry did not say whether the operator had been detained or whether criminal proceedings had been opened.
According to a report by na:Temat, another Polish outlet, Civic Coalition MP Patryk Jaskulski responded to comments by an Onet reader, who thought the Polish military should have shot down the unidentified civilian drone: “[T]he incident took place on September 15th, not today. The drone was detected approximately 500 meters from the base, the operator’s location was determined, and the authorities were notified. The 112 call was part of the procedure, not the ‘entire defense of Redzikowo.’” he stated in part.
Poland has repeatedly warned about the growing threat posed by small drones to military and critical infrastructure. The Redzikowo incident comes as NATO members strengthen airspace monitoring and counter-drone defenses following repeated drone-related security incidents across the region.
Growing drone risks along Poland’s eastern flank
On Sept. 17, a Russian jet-powered drone fell or was destroyed roughly 4 kilometers from Polish territory, prompting Warsaw to scramble military aircraft and place its air defenses on alert.
Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz has warned that inadequate air defense support for Ukraine could increase the risk to Poland, arguing that more Russian drones could reach Polish airspace if they are not intercepted over Ukraine. The minister described the incidents along NATO’s eastern flank as part of a broader Russian strategy.
Warsaw is concerned that Russia could target border crossings linking Poland and Ukraine. The warnings have added to broader fears that repeated drone incidents could test NATO’s eastern defenses and expose vulnerabilities around military and critical infrastructure.

South Korea’s Air Force takes delivery of its first KF-21 fighter jet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:20:39 UTC
23:20:39 KST

- South Korea's Air Force took delivery of its first production KF-21 Boramae fighter jet, moving the program into operational service.
- Korea Aerospace Industries plans to deliver 40 air-to-air KF-21s by 2028 and 80 more by 2032, with over 100 jets fielded by the early 2030s.
South Korea’s Air Force took delivery of its first production KF-21 Boramae fighter jet, the Defense Acquisition Program Administration and the Air Force said in a joint statement. The aircraft flew from Korea Aerospace Industries’ plant in Sacheon to an Air Force unit in Yecheon, about 165 km (103 miles) to the north, escorted by an FA-50 light attack jet, a TA-50 fighter trainer, and a T-50 Golden Eagle trainer.
The delivery marks the KF-21 program’s shift from development into operational service, roughly four years and two months after the first prototype’s maiden flight on July 19, 2022.
“Overcoming numerous trials and hardships, the KF-21 was handed over to the Air Force today and commenced flight operations. Up until yesterday was the time for the Boramae project’s policymakers and developers. From today onward, it is the Air Force’s time,” said Gen. Son Sug-rag, Air Force Chief of Staff.
“I call upon every service member operating the KF-21 to take immense pride and responsibility in managing our nation’s premier fighter jet, uniting to ensure the KF-21 rapidly establishes itself as the ultimate shield defending the Republic of Korea,” he said.
The KF-21 is a South Korean-designed supersonic fighter meant to gradually replace the Air Force’s aging fleet of F-5 jets. The program traces back to 2001, when then-President Kim Dae-jung first proposed developing an indigenous fighter, though the effort faced repeated budget delays and feasibility reviews before formally launching in December 2015. Indonesia joined the program as a partner nation. Boramae means “young hawk” in Korean.
Korea Aerospace Industries rolled out the first prototype in April 2021 and began mass production in June 2024. The KF-21 completed combat compatibility certification in May 2026 and finished systems development the following month. The Air Force also reactivated its 156th Fighter Squadron in June, roughly 14 years after the unit was deactivated as an F-4E Phantom squadron, to operate the new jets.
Korea Aerospace Industries has said it will build 40 KF-21s focused on air-to-air missions for delivery by 2028, followed by 80 more jets equipped with long-range air-to-ground missiles by 2032. The Air Force plans to field more than 100 KF-21s in phases by the early 2030s. South Korea’s defense budget is set to increase next year, which officials expect will support both the initial production run and follow-on orders for additional aircraft.

US ties Sudanese army leader's UN visa to ceasefire plan, sources say

US ties Sudanese army leader's UN visa to ceasefire plan, sources say
Sept 22 - The United States is withholding a visa for Sudanese army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan ahead of his scheduled UN appearance in a move that Sudanese and other sources say is linked to a US-backed ceasefire proposal that Khartoum has resisted.
The dispute, first reported by Reuters, threatens to deepen tensions between Washington and Sudan's army at a critical moment in the civil war, which the United Nations calls the world's largest humanitarian crisis.
A senior Sudanese source said Burhan had postponed his trip to New York but had yet to receive official notice that the visa had been denied.
"We in the Sudanese government express our deep regret because this is a violation of the UN Convention and international law," the source said. "Sudan's government affirms its stance towards peace."
Sudan's UN ambassador appealed to Secretary-General Antonio Guterres to intervene, arguing in a letter that preventing Burhan from attending the General Assembly would violate the UN's obligations toward member states.
US officials have made Burhan's attendance contingent on his agreeing to a 90-day ceasefire proposed by US Senior Advisor for Arab and African Affairs Massad Boulos, according to a Sudanese diplomatic source and a Western analyst close to American and Sudanese officials.
The US State Department declined to comment on Burhan's visa.
State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said in a statement later on Tuesday that neither the Sudanese Armed Forces, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary nor either of their respective leaders "represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan."
"The United States and President Trump stand ready to work with anyone who is a serious partner for peace in Sudan. In the meantime, we will seek to raise the cost of continued conflict on all belligerents and the networks which fuel the conflict," he said.
The impasse represents a nadir in US-Sudan relations since war broke out in Sudan between the army and the RSF in April 2023, and comes as Burhan was scheduled to address the General Assembly on Thursday.
Another Sudanese source told Reuters that foreign minister Mohieldin Salem would give the address instead.
Sudan's army voiced reservations about the Boulos-proposed ceasefire in July.
Burhan is unlikely to engage with Boulos' efforts further if the visa is not granted, the analyst and diplomatic sources said.
"Burhan rejects this take-it-or-leave-it approach, any proposal is subject to suggestions and changes," the Sudanese diplomatic source said.
The letter dated September 21, addressed to UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and signed by Sudan's UN Ambassador Al-Harith Idriss Al-Harith, asked for the United Nations' "immediate intervention" with US authorities to ensure the issuance of the visa.
"Should this situation persist, it would effectively prevent the Head of State of a Member State of the United Nations from participating in person in the work of the General Assembly," read the letter.
UN 'DEEPLY CONCERNED'
In a statement sent to Reuters, UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said the secretary-general is "deeply concerned that a visa has reportedly not yet been issued to the President of the Transitional Sovereign Council of the Sudan," adding that he is engaging with the US on the issue.
Burhan, the head of Sudan's army, has been the country's de facto leader since 2019, though the African Union and Western powers withdrew recognition after a 2021 coup he led with RSF head Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, against the civilian leadership.
Burhan has spoken at the UN General Assembly on Sudan's behalf since the coup.
Dagalo, known as Hemedti, has set up a rival government that has so far struggled to gain legitimacy.
The United States has made efforts to mediate the conflict within a so-called "Quad" format that also includes the United Arab Emirates, Egypt and Saudi Arabia, countries seen as having the most influence in Sudan.
In a piece in US outlet Foreign Policy published on Monday, Burhan said he would refuse external directives about the war and said previous pauses in fighting had only allowed the RSF and its backers to regroup.
Under the agreement for the United States to host the UN headquarters in New York, it is not supposed to deny visas, though it has denied entry to the head of the Palestinian Authority.
Relations between the US and Sudan's army have already been strained in recent weeks over a US proposal to extend an existing arms embargo over Sudan's Darfur region – the RSF's stronghold – to the rest of the country, a move that Burhan's backers say would disproportionately punish the army.
For his part, in a speech sending soldiers off to battle, Dagalo said "it's time for the rifles to speak."
Sudan's civilian prime minister before the coup, Abdalla Hamdok, is in New York this week as part of the General Assembly, along with members of his anti-war coalition. REUTERS

Türkiye and seven other countries urged Israel on Sept. 22 to fulfill its outstanding commitments under the first phase of the Gaza peace plan, including ensuring aid deliveries and facilitating repairs to critical infrastructure.
The joint statement followed a meeting of the foreign ministers of Türkiye, Egypt, Indonesia, Jordan, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates in New York on Sept. 21, on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.
The ministers called for “immediate, safe and unhindered” delivery of humanitarian aid and recovery supplies, stressing the need to preserve the ceasefire and end all violations.
They said the plan’s roadmap provided the framework for its second phase, including disarmament alongside a full Israeli withdrawal and deployment of an International Stabilization Force.
That phase also includes the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza assuming its responsibilities throughout the territory and the launch of recovery and reconstruction work. All parties must meet their commitments without delay, the ministers said.
They rejected the expulsion or forced displacement of Palestinians and attempts to change the territorial or demographic character of the occupied Palestinian territories.
The ministers condemned settlement expansion, land confiscation, home demolitions and settler violence, calling for the reversal of measures aimed at consolidating Israeli control and annexation.
They also expressed concern over measures undermining the status quo at Muslim and Christian holy sites in Jerusalem.
The statement welcomed British steps aimed at halting trade with Israeli settlements, alongside wider European efforts, and urged stronger action against settlement expansion and settler violence.
Gaza must remain part of the Palestinian territory, the ministers said.
The plan should support the reunification of Gaza and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and a credible path toward an independent Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital.
The ministers praised U.S. President Donald Trump’s leadership and called for sustained American engagement to ensure all parties, including Israel, meet their obligations.
Tangible progress would strengthen the credibility of the Board of Peace and the authority of the plan, they said.

Could you be an ‘autumn spotter’? Public asked to track changing colours of trees in England
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:16:56 UTC
23:16:56 KST

The reds and golds of autumn leaves may be beginning to appear, but exactly when the season arrives is not always as predictable as the calendar might suggest.
Now, Forestry England is asking people to help track the changing colours of forests to create a record of when and how autumn arrives across the country.
The Autumn Leaf Watch citizen science project invites people to become “autumn spotters” using Forestry England’s new autumn colour tracker.
Those taking part can record the most common leaf colour they spot on visits to forests, or search for hues of leaves on specific tree species, including beech, horse chestnut, oak, rowan and silver birch.
By collecting observations over the coming weeks and in future years, Forestry England, which is in charge of the country’s woodlands, hopes to build a picture of how the timing and development of autumn colour varies between regions, habitats and tree species.
Early observations suggest autumn remains in its infancy, Forestry England said, with most reports showing green woodland canopies. But yellow and orange leaves have already been recorded at Wyre Forest in Worcestershire, Haughmond Hill in Shropshire and Delamere Forest in Cheshire.
Silver birch and beech are among the first species showing colour change, while oak has so far remained predominantly green across much of the country.
The timing of autumn is influenced by factors including daylight, temperature, rainfall, soil moisture and the health of individual trees. Forestry England said this year’s extremely hot and dry summer had caused some trees to shed their leaves earlier than usual.
It is too early to say what effect those climate crisis-driven conditions will have on this autumn as a whole, with weather over the coming weeks helping to determine how the season develops.
Chris Sorenson, a forest management adviser at Forestry England, said the UK’s summer of extreme heat made this year particularly interesting to observe. “Some trees have already shed leaves early, but there’s still plenty of autumn to come,” he said. “We want people to get outside, look closely at the trees around them and help us track it.”
The changing of the colours is part of the process by which deciduous trees prepare for winter. With days shortening and temperatures falling, trees stop producing chlorophyll, the green pigment in their leaves, causing yellow and orange pigments already present in the leaves to become visible. Some species also produce red pigments.
The timing and intensity of the change can vary considerably between species and locations, making observations from across the country useful for understanding how autumn develops from year to year.

The online influencer known as Clavicular – who has helped to fuel the rise of the extreme male appearance-improvement trend of “looksmaxxing” – has been charged with rape and drug offenses in Massachusetts.
The 20-year-old, whose real name is Braden Eric Peters, has been scheduled for a 14 October arraignment on Cape Cod, according to legal documents seen by the Guardian.
He faces up to life in prison on felony counts of rape, drugging a person for sexual intercourse, and a misdemeanor charge of providing liquor to a minor.
The offenses are alleged to have taken place in Massachusetts in May 2025. It was not immediately clear if they related to a separate lawsuit filed in April by a teenager in Florida who said that Peters gave her alcohol during a 2025 party at his parents’ home on Cape Cod, then had sex with her while she was passed out. The girl was 16 at the time of that alleged incident.
Peters rose to prominence as a promoter of “looksmaxxing”, which analysts have described as a toxic pursuit by young men of altering or improving their facial looks and physiques, using extreme measures such as bone smashing to achieve more chiseled jawlines, oral and plastic surgeries, and lip enhancement.
The trend, which moved into the mainstream from its roots in the misogynistic “incel” (involuntary celibate) community, has an online following of millions. It has also been blamed by mental health experts for worsening issues of self-esteem, depression, and social anxiety in teenage boys for its messaging that romantic success is tied to physical perfection.
The charges against Peters in Massachusetts were filed in Orleans district court on 8 September, the records show, and a summons was issued the same day. A representative of Peters told multiple media outlets that Bulwark, the online news site that first reported the charges, was “exaggerating” the status of the case “to boost traffic” because, he said, the influencer had not been physically served.
Peters, who has an online following of more than a million, did not respond to the charges directly. But he posted a cryptic message on X on Monday night accusing the teenager who filed the Florida lawsuit of “trying to get my attention in anyway possible, a lawsuit?” and calling her “petty”. It was accompanied by a photograph of a letter allegedly written by the teen – who has publicly identified herself – pledging “you have my loyalty 100%”.
The lawsuit makes allegations against Peters of battery, intentional infliction of emotional distress, fraud, and unauthorized publication of her name and likeness, according to NBC6 South Florida that reported the developments in April. Israeli violence, settlement expansion in West Bank risk 'ethnic cleansing': Guterres at UNGA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:15:16 UTC
23:15:16 KST

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has warned that Israeli violence, displacement and illegal settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank are undermining prospects for peace and raising the risk of “ethnic cleansing”.
“Violence, displacement, and settlement expansion by Israel in the occupied West Bank are bulldozing the path to peace and raising the spectre of ethnic cleansing,” Guterres said on Tuesday in an address to the 81st UN General Assembly in New York.
“We cannot allow the two-state solution to disappear before our eyes,” he added.
Guterres said the devastating situation in the occupied Palestinian territories must not be overlooked amid wider turmoil across the Middle East.
He described the October 7, 2023 attacks by Hamas as “abhorrent”, but said they were followed by “an onslaught on Palestinians in Gaza, with a scale of killing and destruction unlike anything I’ve witnessed in my years as secretary-general”.
‘Comply with international law’
Guterres recalled that the International Court of Justice had issued legally binding provisional measures in the case concerning the application of the Genocide Convention in Gaza.
He also referred to an advisory opinion by the court, saying the UN must be allowed to carry out its mandates in Gaza and that its staff and humanitarian personnel must be protected.
“All parties must comply with international law and the court’s orders,” he said.
Turning to the wider region, Guterres said conflicts were “cascading” across the Middle East, while so-called ceasefires had amounted to “little more than lesser fires”, with civilians continuing to bear the cost.
“I appeal to the leaders in this chamber to maximise this high-level week for de-escalation and dialogue,” he said.
Guterres urged the international community to send a clear message that the fighting must end, humanitarian assistance must be allowed to flow, and navigational rights and freedoms must be fully restored in line with international law.
Ukraine, Sudan and UN reform
On Ukraine, Guterres said Russia’s war had subjected a sovereign country to “a brutal war in blatant violation” of the UN Charter.
He described the conflict in Sudan as “a war on civilians”, citing mass displacement, hunger, attacks on hospitals and homes, sexual violence and ethnically driven attacks.
The UN chief also warned that Myanmar’s crisis risked slipping from global attention.
Guterres called for reform of the UN Security Council, saying the absence of permanent African seats was “unjust and indefensible”.
AI requires global oversight
Guterres said power was increasingly derived from data, computing capacity and algorithms, while control of those resources remained highly concentrated.
“The danger is not technology. The danger is technology without accountability, capability without oversight, decision-making without transparency,” he said.
Countries with the greatest AI capabilities also carry the greatest responsibilities, he said, urging them to share information on emerging safety risks, cooperate on testing and work towards common safeguards.
Guterres called for a multilateral AI risk-management framework backed by credible and independent oversight, while ensuring that no country is left behind.
“Artificial intelligence must be shaped by humanity, with humanity, and for all humanity,” he said, adding that “children must never become the test subjects for unregulated systems.”

Harri Tiido: An idealistic plan for achieving equality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:15:00 UTC
23:15:00 KST

Harri Tiido: An idealistic plan for achieving equality
In his commentary series, Harri Tiido examines an idealistic vision of the future. The part most likely to provoke irritation is the plan to eliminate inequality — a plan that, if implemented, would increase the wealth of the world's poorest fifteenfold while drastically shrinking the share held by the billionaire class, Tiido notes.
Once again, I turn to a highly idealistic view of the future. Some people would probably read it as a nightmare. But if a large group of people has put effort into drafting a plan, why not present it.
The discussion centers on a Global Justice Report compiled by the World Inequality Lab. Forty‑five authors contributed, plus numerous researchers who helped build the global inequality database. The report aims to offer a global vision for the current century.
Starting with the main conclusions, the report identifies the need for change in three areas. First, rapid decarbonization of energy systems. Second, a shift toward sufficiency — meaning a substantial reduction in working hours and material footprints, along with changes in consumption habits and land and forest use. And third, a rapid reduction in inequality in income, wealth, and power.
The plan to eliminate inequality is likely the most provocative. If carried out, the wealth of the world's poorest half would increase fifteenfold, while the share held by the billionaire class would shrink dramatically. Around 90 percent of the world's population would see their income double while working roughly half as much as they do now.
It sounds impressive — working half as much and earning twice as much. But nothing comes without cost; everything comes at someone's expense.
Socioeconomic justice is addressed on two levels. The first is material accounting: working hours, education and healthcare, energy systems, greenhouse gases, land use, forest cover, and temperature levels. The report envisions keeping global temperature rise below two degrees by the end of the century. Reduced working hours would come primarily from productivity gains driven by technological development, plus changes in employment structure.
Labor would shift from manufacturing to services, healthcare, and education. By the end of the century, average annual working hours per person should fall to around 1,000, compared with 2,100 today.
The second level is financial accounting — and this is where many economists, not to mention the wealthy, would likely turn purple with anger. The report examines income and wealth scales both between countries and within them, and also proposes progressive tax rates. By 2100, the suggested average monthly income per person would be €5,000 in all countries.
Currently, the range is €290 in sub‑Saharan Africa and €2,590 in North America. Europe's average is €3,590, and the global average is €1,410.
Global education spending per person would rise to €8,400 annually, compared with today's range of €210 to €4,140, and €2,237 in Europe. Healthcare spending would rise to €14,000 per person, compared with today's €110 to €8,300.
The report proposes compressing the income scale into a range of one to five. The top 10 percent's share of total income would fall from 50 percent to below 20 percent. The middle 40 percent — the "middle class" — would see their share rise from 36 percent to about 44 percent, and the bottom half's share would rise from roughly 15 percent to about 37 percent.
The wealth‑redistribution plan is even more radical. The global bottom half's share of total wealth would rise from two percent to 30 percent, while the billionaire class — 0.001 percent of the population — would see its share fall from six percent to 0.05 percent. In other words, a hundredfold redistribution of wealth.
The report proposes global wealth and income taxes. The wealth tax would depend on the size of one's assets and reach 20 percent for billionaires. The global income tax would peak at 90 percent. Both taxes would apply to one percent of the world's population, based on multiples of the global average income.
Up to seven times the global average income, there would be no tax. At ten times the average, the tax would be five percent; at twenty times, 20 percent. Beyond that, up to five thousand times the average income, the tax would reach 90 percent. As incomes equalize, the tax would gradually decrease and eventually disappear.
Applied to current incomes, 99 percent of the world's population would pay no tax; 0.4 percent would pay five percent; and 0.001 percent would pay 90 percent — a group whose combined income last year was €2.3 trillion.
Applied to Europe, 6 percent would lose income, eight percent would see income rise up to 20 percent, 58 percent would see increases of 20–100 percent, and 28 percent would gain more than 100 percent compared with current income.
Regionally, the biggest winners would be sub‑Saharan Africa and South and Southeast Asia, where 99 percent of people would see income gains of 100 percent or more. The biggest loser would be North America, where 14 percent of the population would see income decline.
The report also proposes creating a Global Justice Fund and a World Sovereign Fund, pooling 10 percent of the world's capital assets. The money would be used to compensate countries for environmental, education, and healthcare costs. The largest expense would likely be reparations for colonial‑era and environmental damage.
In short, this is a proposal for the future that, by all indications, is not destined to be realized. The principle of reducing inequality is sound, but the measures and scale are another matter. Inequality has been rising, with political consequences — and the potential, if tensions grow, to blow the lid off, threatening state stability.
Looking around the world, one finds plenty of countries with enough wealthy individuals who could quickly consign such plans to the trash heap — hiring private armies if necessary. But every researcher has the right to speculate, and the calculations are certainly interesting.
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon

News
Bulgaria records EU’s biggest annual rise in fuel prices in August
Tuesday 22 September 2026 16:21
Tuesday, 22 September 2026, 16:21
PHOTO BGNES
Font size
Bulgaria recorded the EU’s sharpest annual increase in prices for fuels and lubricants for personal vehicles in August, according to Eurostat data. Prices rose 34.5% year on year, compared with an average increase of 23.8% across the other EU countries. The rise in August was the highest since the conflict between the United States and Iran began. The previous high was 33.9% in May.
Bulgaria also posted the second-largest monthly rise in diesel prices. Diesel was 13.5% more expensive in August than in July, compared with an average increase of 8.3% in the other EU countries. Only Czechia recorded a steeper rise, at 14.3%.

US Air Force fighter jet crashes near air base in Germany
September 22, 2026
A fighter jet crashed near the US air base in Spangdahlem, Germany, on Tuesday.
The plane crash occurred at approximately 2:30 p.m. local time (12:30 UTC). The cause of the incident is currently under investigation.
The US military confirmed that the plane was an F-16 Fighting Falcon assigned to the 52nd Fighter Wing and that its pilot was able to safely eject from the aircraft.
"The pilot ejected safely and is receiving medical care," the base said in a statement.
Local authorities in the remote Eifel region also confirmed that one person had been injured.
"Following a plane crash in the vicinity of US Air Base Spangdahlem, fire and emergency response teams from the Eifel District of Bitburg-Prüm were dispatched to the scene," the district said on its website.
"No comments can be made on the further details of the event from the side of the Eifel district at this time."
A NATO operations center
Spangdahlem Air Base is a NATO operations center that was built in the early 1950s. The US Air Force's 52nd Fighter Wing is garrisoned there. The base is home to an F-16 fighter jet squadron comprising around 20 aircraft.
It is located north of the city of Trier in Rhineland-Palatinate, not far west of the border to Luxembourg.
The facility at Spangdahlem is considered one of the most important airfields for the US military in Germany, alongside Ramstein base, outside the city of Kaiserslautern.
Some 5,000 US military and civilian personnel-plus dependents are stationed at Spangdahlem, with around 700 to 800 Germans also employed at the facility.

Could closer Canada-EU ties create a new geopolitical bloc?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:11:55 UTC
23:11:55 KST

Canada and the US share many cultural similarities, from fashion trends to popular culture, partly because of their proximity and the world's longest international border.
Despite these similarities, Canadians have historically resisted becoming part of the US, an idea the Trump administration recently revived by repeatedly referring to Canada as America's 51st state.
More than 250 years ago, when the American colonies revolted against British rule, Canadians refused to join them as a 14th rebellious colony.
During the War of 1812, Canadians again resisted an American invasion. Since then, Canada and the US have largely maintained peaceful relations.
But Washington's repeated statements about making Canada the 51st state appear to have rekindled Canadian nationalism and historical concerns over American ambitions, prompting the country's centre-left Prime Minister Mark Carney to seek new partners, from Europe to China, with "better manners".
While Carney has described his search for new partners as something other than an attempt to build "a third bloc in order to become a great power rival" against the US, he has also made clear that Canada rejects foreign domination.
“We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten territorial integrity or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law,” he said, in a speech to EU lawmakers.
In the same speech, the Canadian leader emphasised that "Europe and Canada are stronger together," adding that "a Canada-EU alliance would create a beacon for other democracies".
Beyond his emphasis on democratic values, Carney's use of the word "alliance" suggests that his pivot towards the EU could extend well beyond economic and diplomatic cooperation, analysts say.
With the Canadian leader also identifying defence as an area for deeper cooperation, the proposed partnership could signal more ambitious strategic plans between the two sides.
A day before Carney's address to the European Parliament, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed the unprecedented possibility of Canada becoming the EU's first associate member.
Although such a status does not currently exist under EU law and its terms remain undefined, the proposal signals Brussels' willingness to explore a deeper relationship with Ottawa.
Carney also broke with Canadian diplomatic tradition by choosing France, an EU member with strong ties to Canada's large French-speaking population, rather than the US, for his first foreign visit.
The Trump administration, however, appeared displeased with Carney's recent manoeuvres with European leaders, warning both the Canadian prime minister and the EU against committing any "hostile act" against the US.
"If it's a good intention, that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe, which is a possibility."
A new geopolitical bloc?
Canada and Greenland, an autonomous region of Denmark, share a land border on the uninhabited Hans Island, established through a 2022 agreement that resolved a decades-long territorial dispute.
Recent talks between European leaders and Canadian officials suggest that Greenland, home to about 55,000 people, could be both a geographic bridge between Canada and Europe and a strategic point of convergence, especially amid the US administration’s ambitions for the world's largest island.
European leaders view the Trump administration’s Greenland claims as a threat to Denmark's sovereignty, while Canada fears US control of the island could set a precedent for Ottawa, which Washington has repeatedly called a potential 51st state.
The dispute has since taken a new turn, with Denmark and Greenland seeking to ease tensions with Washington by allowing a greater US military presence on the island without relinquishing sovereignty.
Greenland occupies a strategically important position between North America and Europe, allowing the US to monitor Russian military activity in the Arctic and detect potential missile threats.
Reuters reported that Washington, Copenhagen and Greenland are set to sign an agreement on September 22, allowing the US to establish two additional military sites on the island.
For Denmark and Greenland, the arrangement offers a way to address Washington's security concerns while maintaining control over the territory.
The agreement's full legal implications remain unclear.
“Undoubtedly, President Trump has played a major role in accelerating this rapprochement. Demands regarding both Canada and Greenland have brought the two actors closer together,” says Muzaffer Senel, an academic and expert in European studies.
According to Senel, the EU's Arctic member states, Denmark, Sweden and Finland, have also pushed for closer cooperation with Canada, itself an Arctic country, amid growing concerns over regional security.
Carney, meanwhile, has cultivated close ties with European leaders, including France's Emmanuel Macron and Germany's Friedrich Merz, as he seeks to strengthen Canada's relationship with Europe.
He also has a particularly close relationship with Finnish President Alexander Stubb, whose country shares a long border with Russia.
But the growing EU-Canada partnership extends beyond their disagreements with the Trump administration and concerns about Russia.
Both sides are also seeking to reduce their dependence on the US and China by diversifying trade, defence industry supply chains, artificial intelligence and critical minerals, according to Senel.
Faced with the Trump administration’s tariff policies, Canada, an energy-rich country that sends roughly two-thirds of its exports to the US, is looking to diversify its economy.
One potential avenue is supplying Canadian gas to European countries seeking alternatives to Russian energy following the war in Ukraine.
“The US is no longer a reliable actor for either party. Both economic and political alliances have been deeply shaken in recent years. Both sides are seeking a reliable, predictable partner that aligns with their own worldviews,” Senel tells TRT World
Long before Carney's recent diplomatic manoeuvres with European leaders, Canada and the EU had already laid the groundwork for closer economic ties through the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA).
A joint study launched in 2007 was followed by formal negotiations in 2009.
The agreement has been provisionally applied since September 2017, but only 17 of the EU's 27 member states have completed their national ratification procedures.
The remaining 10 have yet to ratify it.
Make Canada Europe again
William Earl Weeks, a professor of history at San Diego State University and author of several books, including Building the Continental Empire: American Expansion from the Revolution to the Civil War, calls the “Canada-EU flirtation” a “fascinating” development.
Weeks sees the US administration’s "Make America Great Again" slogan as potentially reviving America's historical expansionist ambitions, driven by both strategic and ideological considerations.
Other experts and some Canadian officials, however, suggest that Washington's approach could push Ottawa in another direction: to Make Canada Europe Again.
“This is Canada turning from looking at itself as a North American nation to a trans-Atlantic nation,” a senior Canadian official told the Wall Street Journal in the paper’s extensive coverage of Carney’s deliberations with Europeans to balance US pressure.
“Canadians, we sound like Americans, we dress like Americans, but as a society we’re much more European,” the official added, referring to Ottawa’s cultural, traditional and political commonalities with Europe.
Unlike the US presidential system, Canada is a constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary system of government, much like the UK.
It is also a member of the Commonwealth, maintaining historical and institutional ties with Britain that distinguish it from its southern neighbour.
Canada's independence from Britain was achieved gradually, beginning in 1867, when the British North America Act united three British colonies into a self-governing dominion.
The Statute of Westminster in 1931 subsequently recognised Canada's legislative independence and equal status with Britain, although London retained certain constitutional powers.
More than five decades later, the Canada Act 1982 ended the British Parliament's remaining authority to legislate for Canada, completing the patriation of the country's constitution.
Yet King Charles III remains Canada's head of state, reflecting the enduring constitutional ties between the two countries.
Although the monarch's role is largely ceremonial, the Crown remains an important symbol of the two countries' shared history.
In March 2025, King Charles III planted a red maple tree in the garden of Buckingham Palace, a gesture some interpreted as support for Canada amid the Trump administration’s statements.
Canada's relationship with Britain has also taken on renewed significance after Andy Burnham was appointed UK prime minister in July 2026, succeeding Keir Starmer.
Burnham has signalled a different approach to Washington, seeking to defend British interests while maintaining the longstanding US-UK relationship.
His government is also pursuing closer economic cooperation with the EU, including participation in its proposed "Made in Europe" initiative.
The Trump administration, meanwhile, has been critical of Burnham, whom he reportedly described as "a mayor of a town", referring to his previous role as mayor of Greater Manchester.
He also called the British leader "extremely liberal", reflecting their political differences.
Despite the US administration’s opposition to closer EU-Canada ties, the emerging partnership could also attract the attention of other countries, including Australia, which is seeking to navigate the growing strategic competition between the US and China in the Asia-Pacific.
"The EU is an actor seeking to enhance its strategic flexibility. It will begin to pursue closer cooperation with actors that share a similar worldview," says Senel.
"Australia could be the next step."

France and the US are preparing a UN resolution to restore traffic in the Strait of Hormuz – media

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
17:11:06 EEST

France and the US are preparing a UN resolution to restore traffic in the Strait of Hormuz – media
Kyiv • UNN
France and the US are drafting a UN resolution on an international mission to restore shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Paris is seeking a compromise with China and Russia.
On Tuesday, diplomats reported that France, in cooperation with the United States, had begun drafting a UN Security Council resolution on establishing an international mission to restore traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Paris had previously made unsuccessful attempts to prepare such a resolution, but this new step resulted from talks between French President Emmanuel Macron and US President Donald Trump, held on Monday evening on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
"Several options were discussed," Macron said after meeting with the American leader at Trump Tower in New York.
"In the coming hours, we will work on diplomatic solutions that would allow us — even in the absence of a comprehensive agreement — to find ways to ensure the passage of more container ships and oil tankers."
According to diplomats, Paris hopes to present the draft resolution to the Security Council soon, although it has not specified a particular timeframe.
Previous attempts at the UN failed to win the support of China and Russia — permanent members of the Security Council with veto power — due to concerns about bias against Tehran.
However, amid a sharp rise in global oil prices and fears that the advance of Houthi rebels in Yemen could threaten the strategic corridor in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, hope has emerged that a compromise can be reached this time.
Diplomats said the resolution would focus on separating the issue of the waterway's security from the broader tensions in relations with Iran, as well as emphasizing the shared interests of all states in preserving freedom of navigation and access to energy resources.
UN member states will coordinate efforts to protect commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz without taking an aggressive position toward Iran, criticizing the United States, or linking the issue to other regional conflicts, diplomats said.
"France seeks to work with the Americans and its partners on a Security Council resolution that would guarantee freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz," a French diplomatic source said.

University in Switzerland receives large donation of diamonds for research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:10:00 UTC
23:10:00 KST

University in Switzerland receives large donation of diamonds for research
The University of Bern will house one of the world’s largest diamond collections for research and teaching purposes. The collection, donated to the university, is intended to aid in the discovery of new minerals and provide insights into the formation of the Earth’s interior.
“Diamonds are more than just jewelry; they are true natural archives and hold unique knowledge about the history of our planet,” the University of Bern explained on Tuesday. The collection was donated by Jeffrey W. Harris and his wife, Francesca Harris.
The Harris Diamond Collection is the world’s largest collection of diamonds dedicated to research and education. It comprises more than 29,000 rough diamonds, with an average value of $10 (CHF8.20) per diamond. The material value of the collection is therefore limited.
More
Deep-sea mining: has Trump unleashed a scramble for the seabed?
The rough diamonds come from Africa, South America, North America, Asia, and Oceania. They were donated by the Diamond Trading Company (DTC) in London to Harris for scientific research purposes. Each donation is documented by the original deed of gift. The collection is housed off-campus.
Time Capsules
Extremely durable and virtually chemically stable, diamonds are like time capsules that preserve valuable information about the conditions of their formation.
The oldest diamonds date back 3.5 billion years, while the youngest are about 55 million years old.
Some diamonds contain tiny inclusions of high-density liquid, molten material, or minerals inside them. By studying these inclusions, scientists can better understand the Earth’s evolution.
More
In pursuit of the crystal hunters
The University of Bern is one of the few universities in the world to have its own diamond grinding wheel, a diamond crushing facility, a state-of-the-art mass spectrometer for high-precision isotopic analyses, as well as other highly specialised equipment and methods for visualising the chemical composition of materials in space.

Recovery of lost capacity at South Pars refineries accelerates
TEHRAN- The Manager of Integrated Planning at the National Iranian Gas Company announced the recovery of part of the lost capacity of South Pars refineries and said: Two phases of the Early Recovery Program have been completed.
According to Mehr News Agency, quoting the Ministry of Petroleum, Saeed Pakseresht said in an interview that during these attacks, 230 million cubic meters per day of the country’s gas refining capacity was taken out of the production cycle, stressing: In terms of the volume of lost capacity, this incident is considered one of the largest attacks on gas facilities in the world.
He stressed: From the outset, reconstruction plans were defined in two parts: the first part was early recovery, aimed at reducing the consequences of the incident and quickly returning part of the refining capacity to the production cycle; the second part was the full reconstruction of the damaged facilities, which requires more time.
The Manager of Integrated Planning at the National Iranian Gas Company continued: The Early Recovery Program was designed in four phases, two of which have been completed so far, and part of the lost capacity has returned to the country’s gas network. Also, the third phase of this program will be commissioned according to the planned schedule.
Pakseresht said: Although the initial schedule for the fourth phase was set until Ordibehesht 1406 (April–May 2027), efforts are being made to return part of this capacity to the production cycle before the beginning of the cold months of the year.
Referring to the process of full reconstruction of the refineries, he stated: Based on the decision of the Ministry of Petroleum, responsibility for the reconstruction of the Third and Fifth South Pars refineries was assigned to the National Iranian Oil Company, and the reconstruction of the Fourth and Sixth refineries to the National Iranian Gas Company, so that by utilizing all the capacities of the oil and gas industry, reconstruction operations can be carried out in the shortest possible time.
The Manager of Integrated Planning at the National Iranian Gas Company, referring to the experience gained from recent attacks on the country’s gas facilities, said: Although in past years various plans and measures had been foreseen for readiness in crisis conditions, this time the gas industry was tested in a real field, and valuable experience was gained in crisis management and increasing resilience.
Pakseresht added: Previously, various measures had been taken to prepare facilities, equipment, and manpower, and this helped us pass through difficult conditions with minimal consequences and secondary effects. However, actually entering such conditions was a different experience, and the damage inflicted was also significant in scope and severity.
He stressed: Using past lessons and previous experiences played an important role in managing this crisis, and the results show that reconstruction and capacity restoration operations have so far proceeded according to plan, and the effects of the incident have been largely controlled.
The Manager of Integrated Planning at the National Iranian Gas Company, regarding the use of technologies and technical know-how in the reconstruction process, said: The country’s gas industry has extensive experience in operating gas refineries, and this specialized foundation has been very effective in carrying out reconstruction operations.
Pakseresht continued: Along this path, maximum specialized capacity, technical know-how, and the experience of experts and specialists in the gas industry were used, and we tried to advance the reconstruction process with appropriate speed and quality by utilizing existing capacities.
Emphasizing the necessity of keeping knowledge and technology up to date in the gas industry, he stated: Iran’s gas industry is a mature, professional, and dynamic industry, and maintaining this position requires continuous use of the latest scientific and technological achievements.

West has ‘misunderstood’ depth of India-Russia ties – ex-foreign secretary (VIDEO)
The West has “completely” misread India’s relationship with Russia by reducing it largely to one over oil, and overlooking the wider geopolitical, economic, and strategic ties between New Delhi and Moscow, former Indian Foreign Secretary Ranjan Mathai told RT.
Russia has historically helped India maintain strategic autonomy and contributed to its economic transformation, and remains important for future supply chains involving critical minerals, food inputs, and other key resources, Mathai told former Indian Foreign Minister Salman Khurshid on the latest episode of RT India’s ‘In Conversation’.
“They have very clearly misunderstood the depth and the scope of India’s relationship with Russia,” Mathai stated. “I think it’s a complete misreading.”
Russia remains a major source of crude for India, with imports tracking at around 1.95 million barrels per day so far in September, according to commodity analytics firm Kpler. India-Russia trade reached $79 billion last year, having grown sevenfold in the last five years, Russian Economic Development Minister Maksim Reshetnikov told RT India earlier this month.
Russia has also recently been buying gasoline and other fuels from India after Ukrainian drone attacks damaged some of its refining capacity.
Mathai was the Indian foreign secretary from August 2011 to July 2013. He noted that the global rules were written by the West at a time when those countries dominated the world economically and politically – and that they want those rules to continue.
He said New Delhi would need to substantially increase its economic and technological heft if it wanted to move from being a “rule taker” to a “rule maker.”
China, he pointed out, is increasingly seen as capable of shaping global rules because of its dominant position in fields including renewable energy, electric vehicles, artificial intelligence, and other emerging technologies.
China and India are both fast-growing major economies but China’s GDP was $19.5 trillion last year, according to World Bank data, compared to India’s $4.5 trillion.
“If we want to be a rule maker, we have to be able to significantly increase our weight in the global economy and particularly in the new technologies which are emerging,” Mathai said.
He added that Indian diplomacy should keep the welfare of its citizens living in Gulf countries top of the agenda amid the Middle East conflict, noting that New Delhi had maintained dialogue with Iran while preserving its relationship with Israel. An estimated 8-9 million Indians live and work across the six Gulf Cooperation Council countries.
The former diplomat called the humanitarian situation in Gaza a “travesty” and said that New Delhi could be “more explicit” about the impact on civilians. Israeli forces in the territory had made babies “special targets,” the chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry, Justice S. Muralidhar, told RT India in an interview in June.

MSCHF bends and twists LEXUS cars into surreal full-scale sculptures in new york
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:07:54 UTC
23:07:54 KST

Brooklyn-based art collective MSCHF has taken two Lexus electrified vehicles and pushed them through radical transformations that feel native to a screen. The team bends one car into a closed ring and torques the other into a long spiral, which gives familiar production bodies the elastic logic of 3D animation. Commissioned by Lexus, MOTOMORPHOSIS opens at Chelsea Industrial in New York from September 24th through 26th, 2026, during Armory Week.
The premise is immediately readable because the distortions borrow from a visual language we already know. Animation uses squash-and-stretch and smear frames to make speed legible between one position and the next. Here, those temporary deformations have been made permanent. Sheet metal appears to behave like soft modeling clay, while windows and lights stretch along with the body.
MSCHF’s Circle Car begins with the Lexus RZ450e and bends its entire length until the nose meets the rear. The vehicle becomes a continuous ring, seemingly caught in an endless drive around its own circumference. Wheels remain distributed along the outside edge while the cabin follows the curve, preserving just enough of the original car to make the art collective‘s transformation feel strangely plausible.
Displayed beside a production RZ450e, the sculpture exposes how strongly a car’s identity depends on proportion and forward direction. Familiar details remain in place, yet their relationship has changed completely. The road has effectively been absorbed into the object itself, which leaves a vehicle whose route begins and ends at the same point.
Circle Car bends the Lexus RZ450e into a continuous nose-to-tail loop
Twisted Car turns bodywork into torsion
Twisted Car takes the Lexus RX450h+ in another direction. The SUV is pulled through a dramatic longitudinal twist, with its body rotating around an invisible central axis. Surface lines follow the spiral and recognizable features are dragged along with them, as though the entire vehicle has been caught for a fraction of a second while being wrung between opposing forces.
MSCHF calls the sculptures ‘Form Cars,’ a counterpoint to the automotive concept car and a useful description of what is happening here. A production vehicle is engineered to move through space. Circle Car and Twisted Car transfer that movement into the body itself. Neither needs to travel anywhere. Speed has already been built into the shape.

You still don’t have the cards: Did Zelensky bring bluff to Trump?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:06:57 UTC
23:06:57 KST

You still don’t have the cards: Did Zelensky bring bluff to Trump?
“You don’t have the cards.”
That was the message US President Donald Trump famously delivered to Vladimir Zelensky during their fiery Oval Office showdown in February 2025. Trump accused the Ukrainian leader of “gambling with World War III” and showing ingratitude for US aid, while pointing out that Kiev’s worsening battlefield position had left Ukraine with few cards to play in peace talks with Russia.
While the clash did not sever US-Ukraine ties completely, the deck has hardly been reshuffled in Kiev’s favor since. Thus the table was set for another Trump-Zelensky game in New York this week on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Even getting a seat at that table was a late deal. Just two days earlier, Zelensky was absent from Trump’s publicly announced list of UN bilaterals, and Ukrainian officials said no meeting had yet been confirmed. In the end they met for 40 minutes.
The hand Zelensky holds is hardly stacked with aces. Instead, it contains an unexpected $27 billion defense shortfall, a desperate shortage of Patriot air-defense missiles, a fresh trail of corruption scandals, and mounting battlefield losses.
Opening bet: The refinery dispute
Trump had already shown his hand before the sit-down. Earlier this month, he blamed Zelensky for the diesel price spike gripping the US and Europe, which the US president said has been caused by Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries.
By the eve of the UN gathering, the US national average had climbed to a record $6.5 per gallon, a topic particularly sensitive for Trump ahead of the midterms.
According to the Financial Times, Trump pressed Zelensky during a weekend phone call to stop striking Russian oil refineries, with the paper’s sources claiming he wanted to ensure Russian supplies could reach the global market.
Trump went so far as to announce that Russia and Ukraine had effectively agreed to stop attacks on energy infrastructure. Neither Kiev nor Moscow confirmed the truce. Speaking to press in new York, Zelensky, who escalated strike intensity and targeting through his so-called 40-day plan, has now demanded that Russia take the first step, though he has continued to attack Russian fuel plants.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has called a prospective truce a “very good idea” and said Moscow was “always on the side of peaceful solutions.” He also argued that protecting refineries alone would not solve the global fuel crunch. The bigger problem, he said, was getting Russian petroleum products onto world markets, which required safe passage for oil tankers – something he said Kiev was not willing to guarantee.
Ahead of the meeting, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also rebuked Ukraine over targeting US-linked ships in the Black Sea, adding that while it did so “probably not deliberately,” “that’s something that needs to be addressed.”
Desperate for Patriot draw
Zelensky has repeatedly sounded the alarm over deliveries of US-made Patriot interceptors, one of the few weapons in Ukraine’s arsenal capable of tackling Russian ballistic missiles. In July, he said the country’s stocks were nearly exhausted and asked Trump for an emergency “winter package” of 300 interceptors, warning that Ukraine needed them “yesterday.” Ukrainian air defenses failed to intercept even a single Russian missile during some recent barrage.
However, multiple media reports have indicated that Washington’s Patriot stocks are also low due to the Iran war, with American Patriot inventories in Europe said to have fallen “beyond critical” levels. While Trump has denied the shortfall, the Pentagon has publicly acknowledged the strain.
Earlier this month, Trump also suggested that Ukraine could receive a license to produce Patriots in a “less sophisticated version,” though no details on the prospective agreement have emerged in the immediate aftermath of the New York meeting. Multiple experts have pointed to numerous obstacles to the program, warning that any production facilities would be prime targets.
Zelensky is almost out of chips
Late summer exposed a glaring weakness in Zelensky’s gamble: an unexpected $27 billion defense budget shortfall expected by the end of the year – a figure that ballooned almost fourfold over the past several months.
Kiev subsequently asked for more money from its European backers – met with a tepid response whereby Brussels even refused to acknowledge the $27 billion figure.
The shortfall arose as a result of Zelensky’s much-heralded 40-day pressure campaign against Russia that involved the very strikes on refineries Trump reportedly asked him to stop. The escalatory attacks also triggered Russian retaliation against Ukrainian military-related logistics, including effectively closing the port of Odessa, which serves as a key hub for agricultural exports.
Ukraine’s $27 billion request “surprised and unsettled” European officials, according to the New York Times, with some of Ukraine’s backers reportedly asking questions about how Kiev is spending the cash and if it actually needs as much as it says it does.
The Trump wildcard
Kiev does have one fresh trump card to hope for – except it lies largely up the US president’s sleeve.
On Friday, Trump signed a new sanctions legislation first proposed by late Republican Senator and Russia hawk Lindsey Graham last year. The measure gives the US president authority to target Russian officials, banks, and the energy sector, and to impose tariffs of up to 100% on leading importers of Russian oil and gas. Zelensky specifically thanked Trump for signing it when the pair arranged their New York meeting.
However, Trump retains authority over sanctions waivers and the scope of restrictions and tariffs, while the bill does not mention China and India, the key importers of Russian energy.
In addition, the Trump administration has a recent history of easing sanctions on Russian oil. During the Iran war, the administration issued temporary exemptions allowing the sale and delivery of Russian crude already at sea to alleviate pressure on energy markets.
A busted flush
Ukraine has faced consistent frontline territorial losses for months, yielding ground to Russian advances while struggling to replenish losses through a brutal and deeply unpopular forced mobilization campaign.
 
Last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, a key Kiev backer, revealed that up to 27,000 Ukrainian troops are killed or wounded every month and that Ukraine could face a “catastrophic” winter. Zelensky claimed in July that 50,000 Ukrainian troops have been killed (in February he claimed 55,000) and 400,000 wounded throughout the entire 4.5-year conflict.
The Russian Defense Ministry, in turn, assessed in February that Ukraine had sustained 1.5 million casualties during the conflict, with more than 500,000 lost in 2025 alone.
Trump himself has repeatedly pointed to Ukraine’s dwindling manpower as a reason for Kiev to stop fighting. During the Oval Office showdown with Zelensky last year, he told him: “Your people are dying. You’re running low on soldiers,” before urging him to accept an immediate ceasefire so that “your men stop getting killed.”
The joker in the pack: Corruption in Kiev
Zelensky’s inner circle has reportedly embezzled millions, and possibly billions, from the war chest, all while asking for more. Trump has also called Zelensky a “dictator without elections” – referring to the Ukrainian leader’s refusal to hold a vote despite widespread unpopularity, and resentment from possible successors he has sidelined.
Zelensky’s inner circle is widely suspected of massive crime, and some have fled the country. The biggest case to date remains the $100 million Energoatom affair, where a network involving Zelensky’s former close associate, Timur Mindich, forced contractors at the state nuclear giant to pay kickbacks of up to 15%. Mindich is in Israel allegedly laundering bags of cash while a former energy minister has been served with corruption-related suspicions and arrested.
Zelensky’s prosecutor general fled the country following accusations he was gathering compromising material on Western-backed anti-corruption agents in Kiev. The head of cybercrime at the same office was exposed for “protecting” a network of scam-call centers, a Ukrainian innovation Zelensky rarely touts abroad but which targets innocent people in the EU with all the contempt one would expect from an enterprise solely focused on profiteering. Ukraine’s scam-call industry is reported to generate up to $1 billion each month.
Zelensky’s current chief of staff, Kirill Budanov, has been pulled into the controversy, with media reports linking him to a money laundering scandal though he has not been charged.
During his first presidency, Trump said Ukraine was known for “tremendous corruption.” Since returning to office, he has also repeatedly opposed open-ended US financial and military support for Kiev.
When will Zelensky’s bluff be called?
That left Zelensky – who insists he hopes Ukraine may still win – heading into another session with Trump carrying a list of critical problems rather than a set of winning cards. The Ukrainian leader is having a tougher time than ever bluffing his way through such widely-known issues as a $27 billion defense hole, thinning manpower, shrinking hopes of securing Patriot interceptors, repeated corruption scandals, and growing pressure to explain how much longer he intends to continue the conflict.
And across from him sat a president who has been reluctant to cut Kiev any slack while treating the weakness as proof that Kiev should sign a deal with Russia. In this vein, Trump has already warned Zelensky: “With us, you have the cards, but without us you don’t have any cards,” adding that if Washington walks away, Ukraine will have to “fight it out” on its own.

Prosecutors demand jail for blast that killed three in drugs lab

Unknown Publisher

Prosecutors demand jail for blast that killed three in drugs lab
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Prosecutors have demanded a seven-year jail sentence for a man who blew up a drugs lab in Rotterdam, causing a blast that killed three people and damaged neighbouring flats.
Jalal O., 37, was renting the garage store on Schammenkamp to produce cocaine when it exploded on the evening of January 29, 2024. One of the victims was his 22-year-old cousin, who was working in the lab at the time.
A forensic investigation found that the blast was caused by vats of acetone, used in the production of the drug, catching fire at the back of the building. A neighbouring block of flats was so badly damaged that five homes had to be demolished.
Prosecutors said O. had “allowed financial gain to prevail over the safety of local residents and others”. They said he had sublet the property via a “shady arrangement”.
O. helped with the search for missing neighbours immediately after the disaster, but was arrested a few days later. He told the district court in Rotterdam he found the events “terrible”, but denied that he was using the garage for drug production.
Prosecutors produces messages between O. and his cousin showing steam rising from barrels of acetone, while residents complained of the chemical smells from the building. The prosecution said the defendant’s denials were “totally unbelievable”.
One woman who was evacuated from one of the flats said the explosion had had a devastating effect on her health.
“I have lost part of my hearing, my hair has fallen out and I have lost my teeth through stress,” she said. “I have flashbacks and sleep badly. I have nightmares in which I fall into the fire and burn to death.”

'I'm done with medical abuse': actor Arnaud Denis dies by euthanasia in Belgium
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:06:45 UTC
23:06:45 KST

The French actor and director had been in unbearable pain since a polypropylene prosthesis was fitted in 2023 after a right groin hernia. Aged 43, he was euthanised this Tuesday in Namur, Belgium.
Actor and director Arnaud Denis, left severely disabled after the insertion of an anti-hernia implant, chose to end his life by euthanasia in Belgium on Tuesday at the age of 43 to put a stop to his suffering, his lawyer Philippe Courtois told AFP.
"The decision taken by Arnaud Denis was made in consultation with three doctors in Namur. His body could no longer carry him. He had lost control of it. Arnaud Denis’s death is the consequence of the intense pain he had been enduring for many months," he added.
Best known for his productions of Choderlos de Laclos' Les Liaisons Dangereuses and Molière's Les Femmes Savantes, Denis had been suffering since a polypropylene mesh implant was fitted on 17 July 2023 after a right groin hernia.
The operation triggered numerous side effects, which eventually drove him to have the implant removed in the United States in April 2024.
The actor was diagnosed with myalgic encephalomyelitis, in the context of ASIA syndrome (an inflammatory reaction linked to exposure to an adjuvant). The implant is thought to have caused persistent inflammation and disrupted his immune system.
"I can no longer leave my home, I have no social life, I have no life at all. I no longer have anything that constitutes the dignity of a man’s life. And it is getting worse and worse. I live like a cancer patient in the terminal phase. The doctors have nothing left to offer me," he confided in early 2026 to the regional daily Dauphiné Libéré (source in French).
'A man knows deep down when he is doomed'
On 5 January 2026, Denis lodged a complaint with the Public Health Division of the Paris public prosecutor’s office for "unintentional injuries", but it was dropped at the end of August "for lack of sufficiently established offence".
Seeing no other way than euthanasia to end his suffering, the actor said at the beginning of the year: "A man knows deep down inside when he is doomed." On 18 March, he was admitted to a palliative care unit in a Belgian hospital, pending approval of his euthanasia request.
His lawyer condemned what he called "a silent public health scandal", arguing that "thousands of patients" are "exposed to high-risk implants, without clear information or informed consent, suffering serious medical complications, most of them irreversible".
"Medtronic has acknowledged in a letter sent to Mr Arnaud Denis that implanting parietal reinforcement devices may be the cause of chronic and acute post-operative pain, an unwanted effect mentioned in the instructions for use of the Dextile device intended for healthcare professionals. Yet these instructions are intended for healthcare professionals and not for patients, who receive no information," Philippe Courtois pointed out.
Denis set up a collective called "French victims of hernia prostheses", which has gathered hundreds of testimonies on social media from people who have suffered adverse effects linked to anti-hernia implants.

Syrian man sets out on foot for 2,000km journey to Mecca
A Syrian man has set out on foot from eastern Syria to Mecca, embarking on a journey of more than 2,000 kilometres across the desert, with Syrian authorities providing assistance along parts of his route.
Abdullah Hammoud al-Nayef began walking from his village of Zughair Jazira in Syria's Deir al-Zour province, heading south through the Syrian Desert towards Saudi Arabia and the Kaaba, Islam's holiest site.
Carrying his belongings and supplies for the road, Nayef is expected to cross Jordan before entering Saudi Arabia.
The journey could take several months on foot, depending on his route and pace.
Syrian security personnel have accompanied Nayef during parts of the journey to help ensure his safety as he crosses long stretches of sparsely populated desert.
When he reached the town of al-Sukhnah, northeast of the ancient city of Palmyra, Syrian road security personnel met him, checked on his condition and offered assistance.
Syrian TV reported that it remained unclear whether Nayef had obtained the permits needed to cross into Jordan and Saudi Arabia.
A journey inspired by a 'recurring dream'
Nayef has said his decision to walk to Mecca was motivated by a dream that he experienced three times.

US-China AI race: Does Trump want to regulate AI by forming a new task force and a special envoy for artificial intelligence in the US?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:04:00 UTC
23:04:00 KST

'AI Force': Does Trump want to regulate AI after all?
September 22, 2026
Developers warning against their own technologies and a government unwilling to take action — that was the situation in the first half of September amid concerns in the US that AI models were becoming too powerful.
Several developers and decision-makers from major AI companies had also called for slowing down the development of the technology.
In response, US President Donald Trump posted one of his typical all-caps tweets on his social media platform Truth Social: "AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX." Trump also asked "Concerning AI, when, in the History of Business, did anyone see the Leaders of an Industry call for Regulation that, if strongly implemented, will drive them into oblivion and bankruptcy?"
Against this backdrop, it comes as something of a surprise that Trump announced over the weekend — following yet another tirade about various alleged Democratic scams — that he would establish an "AI Force" and appoint a special envoy to address the issue.
What exactly did Trump say?
In his post, Trump promised that he would by no means slow down the industry's growth. "However, we will also be looking for BAD, and we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System," he wrote. "To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI 'Czar' — Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" he added.
Trump left open exactly what the individual's duties and powers would be and what resources would be allocated to the position.
Trump's announcement could be an attempt to undermine an initiative by California's Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom. The previous day, Newsom had announced plans to establish a commission to regulate Silicon Valley-based tech companies.
Among other things, Newsom wants to require these companies to build an emergency shut-off switch into their programs, which would allow humans to stop AI agents that have spun out of control. Several states, including some led by Republicans, are pushing for regulation.
US fear of China's dominance
The current "AI race" between the US and China is often compared to the space race between the US and the former Soviet Union in the 1960s. Several US companies are currently considered industry leaders. To ensure this remains the case, Trump intends to continue giving them free rein.
However, this is not just about economic interests. There is concern that Chinese dominance in artificial intelligence could also lead to Beijing's rise as the sole superpower.
In a widely discussed essay, Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, not only warned of the consequences of continued unchecked AI development; he also outlined the potential consequences of the AI competition between the US and China.
"If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance. Therefore any agreement must either have ironclad verifiability, or must be limited enough that defection would not be militarily existential," Amodei wrote.
Does China regulate AI?
In China, technological developments have traditionally been much more closely tied to governmental objectives. As early as 2017, the State Council of China issued a development plan for a new generation of artificial intelligence.
Another strategy paper sets out milestones through which China aims to achieve global dominance in the field of AI by 2030. The regulations are primarily enforced by the Chinese Cyberspace Administration (CAC), which also issues licenses.
Regulation in China ensures that AI models do not run counter to official political doctrine. For example, the Chinese AI chatbot DeepSeek consistently provides answers loyal to the regime when asked politically sensitive questions — such as those regarding Taiwan, the Tiananmen Square massacre, or the oppression of the Uyghurs — as DW previously documented.
The underlying logic of Chinese regulation is thus based on the question: How does an AI system align with state objectives? This represents a clear distinction from the risk-based regulation envisaged, for example, by the European AI Act and now being called for in the US.
Is an AI agreement between the US and China imminent?
On Thursday, Trump will host Chinese President Xi Jinping at a state dinner at the White House. The topic of AI is likely to be very high on the agenda.
The US already proposed establishing a mechanism for exchanging information about serious risks posed by AI. The proposal was discussed at a meeting between Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday in New York.
"We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important," Bessent said.
Whether they actually decide to act on this will likely be left up to the two presidents. After all, for them, potential transparency obligations regarding AI are by no means the only point of contention in the negotiations.
For years, trade restrictions on high-performance AI chips and rare earth elements have been a recurring issue and the extension of a basic trade agreement is also on the agenda.
Whether mutual trust is strong enough to lead to reciprocal concessions on AI will likely only become clear at the meeting.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres sharply criticized Israel during the opening day of the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, warning of what he described as unprecedented killing and destruction in Gaza and a risk of “ethnic cleansing” in the West Bank. The General Assembly’s 81st general debate began Tuesday at UN headquarters.
“We must not lose sight of the devastating situation in the occupied Palestinian territory,” Guterres said. Nearly three years after what he called Hamas’ “abhorrent” Oct. 7 terror attack, he said, Palestinians in Gaza had endured a scale of killing and destruction he had not witnessed during his years as secretary-general.
Guterres also turned to the West Bank, saying violence, displacement and expanding Israeli settlements were eroding prospects for peace and raising concerns about ethnic cleansing.
“We cannot allow the two-state solution to disappear before our eyes,” he said.
The warning echoed comments Guterres made ahead of this year’s General Assembly, when he called for an end to what he described as the “creeping annexation” of the West Bank and said actions that could lead to ethnic cleansing must stop.
Addressing the broader fighting across the Middle East, Guterres said the wars must end and argued that ceasefires in the region had too often amounted to little more than periods of reduced fire while civilians continued to pay the price.
“Enough is enough,” he said.
Guterres also referred to proceedings at the International Court of Justice, noting that the court has issued legally binding provisional measures in South Africa’s case accusing Israel of violating the Genocide Convention in Gaza. The ICJ has not ruled on whether Israel committed genocide; its provisional measures were issued while the case remains pending.
He said all parties must comply with international law and with the court’s orders, and argued that the United Nations and humanitarian organizations must be allowed to carry out their work in Gaza.
Guterres has repeatedly adopted a highly critical position toward Israel’s conduct of the war. In remarks ahead of the General Assembly, he said the suffering in Gaza was “horrendous,” while stressing that determining whether genocide has occurred is a legal question outside his authority. He cited large-scale destruction, civilian deaths, shortages of medical care and continued displacement.
At the same time, Guterres has repeatedly condemned Hamas’ Oct. 7 terror attack and the taking of hostages, while arguing that those crimes do not justify collective punishment of Palestinians. In previous UN remarks, he has called for the immediate release of all hostages, humanitarian access to Gaza and renewed efforts toward a two-state solution.
