Gurugram collapses in rains while Greater Noida planned for 30-40 years: Supreme Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:02:29 UTC
23:02:29 KST

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday said the urban system in Gurugram collapses during rains because adequate investment was not made in infrastructure such as drainage and sewage systems. The court contrasted this with Greater Noida, saying the latter was planned with the next 30-40 years in mind.The observations came while the top court was hearing a plea challenging the Karnataka High Court's decision upholding the state's Premium Floor Area Ratio (FAR) scheme.A bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant, along with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, issued notice on the plea filed by the Citizens Action Forum.The bench, however, clarified that the additional FAR available under the scheme should not be used to regularise illegal construction.
Supreme Court raises infrastructure concerns
Chief Justice Surya Kant said there was no visible improvement or addition to the basic infrastructure of the township, such as roads, sewer lines and bus flyovers, despite the additional construction capacity."We have seen in Gurugram how this system collapses if any natural calamity comes.
Because, without adding to this infrastructure, you are burdening the size of the plot with multiple storeys," the CJI said.He said the situation was different in Greater Noida because the city had been planned keeping the next 30-40 years in mind.The observations came amid arguments over whether Bengaluru's existing infrastructure can support additional construction allowed under the Premium FAR scheme.
What is the Premium FAR scheme?
The Premium FAR scheme allows property owners to purchase additional construction rights beyond the ordinarily permissible FAR by paying prescribed premium charges. The stated objective is to facilitate vertical development and generate revenue for urban local bodies.FAR refers to the ratio of a building's total floor area to the size of the plot on which it stands.Senior advocate Aditya Sondhi, appearing for the Citizens Action Forum, argued that road width had effectively become the main criterion for granting Premium FAR, despite existing pressure on Bengaluru's parking, water, electricity and other infrastructure.Justice Bagchi also referred to Bengaluru's traffic problems, saying the city has a "traffic nightmare" and that this was a serious concern raised by the petitioner.Solicitor general Tushar Mehta, appearing for the state authorities, said the overall additional FAR remained capped at 0.6. He also said existing setback and parking requirements continued to apply and that developers could not simply purchase additional FAR without meeting parking and other regulatory requirements.Mehta said the money collected under the scheme would go into a dedicated fund for civic infrastructure.
Government says Premium FAR cannot regularise illegal buildings
A key issue before the bench was whether the Premium FAR scheme could be used to regularise unauthorised construction.Sondhi questioned how the new scheme differed from the earlier Akrama-Sakrama scheme, under which unauthorised constructions were legalised. He told the court that a provision in the Greater Bengaluru Authority Act allowed Premium FAR to be used for regularising existing illegal constructions.Mehta rejected the contention and gave an assurance that unauthorised construction covered by the Akrama-Sakrama scheme would not be regularised under the Premium FAR scheme."It has nothing to do with that. Kindly record my statement. It is completely different. You can also pass directions to this effect," Mehta said.He argued that urban space was limited and vertical growth was the way forward, adding that cities were increasingly moving towards vertical development.
The Supreme Court asked the Bengaluru authorities to file their response to the plea within four weeks.The case challenges the Karnataka High Court's June 15 judgment upholding the constitutional validity of the Premium FAR scheme. The high court had dismissed petitions arguing that the scheme violated property rights and reduced the value of Transferable Development Rights (TDRs).
The Premium FAR scheme was introduced under Section 18-B of the Karnataka Town and Country Planning Act, 1961. The high court had held that it did not violate Articles 14, 21 or 300A of the Constitution.The NGO had argued that Premium FAR allowed developers to purchase additional building rights at rates significantly below the market cost of TDRs, thereby undermining TDRs secured by landowners as compensation for land.The high court rejected the argument, holding that a state policy resulting in fluctuations in property values would not by itself make the policy violative of Article 300A.

After the ‘wake-up call’: Can a Gulf-Iran security framework take root?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:01:54 UTC
23:01:54 KST

For Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, the US-Israeli war against Iran is a “wake-up call” that should alert Gulf nations and Tehran to the need for a security arrangement in which no country poses a threat to another.
Speaking at the Qatar Economic Forum on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly in New York, Al Thani said the war has tested assumptions about security and stability in the region, which is dotted with US military bases.
The blunt remarks by the Qatari premier came almost seven months after the US and Israel launched a war against Iran with the killing of its supreme leader.
Iran retaliated by hitting Gulf countries in more than 7,000 missile and drone attacks.
Maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway between Iran and Gulf nations that handled one-fifth of global energy supplies before the war, is mostly suspended.
The blockade has stopped oil and gas exports from Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, and Iraq, creating ripple effects in the global economy.
Experts say that the need for a regional security framework is urgent and undeniable, but express doubt whether ground realities would permit it.
Ozcan Akinci, a geopolitical and foreign policy analyst, sees a “genuine interest” in reconciliation between Iran and Gulf nations. However, he notes that a functioning security framework remains a distant possibility, at least for now.
“The war has exposed the limits of relying on outside powers to manage a problem that is ultimately regional,” he tells TRT World.
Iran is not an optional interlocutor, which can be wished away from the region. “The Gulf states have to live with that reality whether they like it or not,” he says.
At the same time, Gulf nations are increasingly looking for extra security insurance.
Akinci points to the Mecca agreement – a trilateral joint defence pact signed among Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan in August under which an armed attack on one is to be treated as an attack on all.
“Doha’s proposal, therefore, comes at a time when the regional security map is already being redrawn,” he says.
The unanswered question is whether Iran will convert the language of dialogue into practical restraint, particularly around Hormuz and proxy activity, he adds.
Mustafa Caner, an Iran specialist and assistant professor at Sakarya University’s Middle East Institute, tells TRT World that neither side benefits when Gulf and Iranian geopolitical visions diverge.
A security framework that reduced that divergence would certainly benefit both sides and contribute to regional security more broadly, he says.
But the architecture of Gulf security has been “outsourced to external powers”, and the war is still the immediate obstacle.
“As long as it continues, and particularly in the face of Iranian attacks, I don’t believe the Gulf states have a solid enough footing, or the capacity, to break away from the US and become founding actors of a security architecture together with Iran,” he says.
Is a GCC consensus possible?
Akinci names Qatar and Oman as the “obvious candidates” to back Al Thani’s idea. That’s because both countries have kept diplomatic channels with Tehran open for years despite setbacks.
Kuwait would probably be comfortable with a broader approach adopted collectively by the six energy-exporting Gulf nations, commonly known as the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), he says.
The UAE and Bahrain are “likely to be more cautious”, given that they have been the frequent targets of Tehran’s backlash in the US-led war on Iran.
How Riyadh reacts to the proposal will be critical because it has come under repeated attacks by Iran-backed Houthis.
“Saudi Arabia wants stability and de-escalation, but it also wants stronger protection against another attack,” he says.
What might convince the sceptics, such as the UAE and Bahrain, is a Saudi decision to treat Qatar’s proposal as part of a wider security strategy, alongside the Mecca agreement with Türkiye and Pakistan, he says.
That packaging of the proposed security framework would make it easier for the UAE and Bahrain to accept. At the same time, Tehran will have to offer something concrete, especially on shipping through Hormuz and the activities of its regional partners, he adds.
But Caner is less optimistic about a GCC consensus.
In principle, many Gulf capitals would view the proposal favourably, he says. In practice though, Doha and Muscat would stand largely alone.
The UAE is likely to “keep its distance”, a posture reflected in Abu Dhabi’s recent trade sanctions against Iran and closer alignment with the “US-Israel axis”.
Caner does not expect Saudi Arabia to take any steps towards diplomatic normalisation with Iran, particularly in light of the Houthi attacks.
He says Riyadh believes Iran is behind these attacks, which is also why it had the foreign ministers’ meeting on Hormuz postponed.
“Doha's proposal is perhaps best understood as a vision of an ideal scenario,” he says.
A layered security system
Yemen is the latest arena where regional divides are most visible. Houthi strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure initially led Riyadh to seek US support. But Washington dithered and has refrained so far from joining the Saudi fight against the Yemeni group.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said last week that Riyadh may have military needs and that Ankara was ready to help meet them under the Mecca pact.
Akinci treats Riyadh’s turn towards Türkiye as evidence that Gulf states are already assembling a “layered system” rather than waiting for a comprehensive settlement with Iran.
Qatar has said that Gulf states cannot rely solely on the US for protection.
US forces maintain their presence in Qatar, Bahrain, the UAE, Kuwait, and Saudi Arabia through bilateral security agreements, military installations, and bases.
Akinci does not see any direct clash between the existing US security umbrella for Gulf nations and the proposed security framework.
That’s because US forces provide capabilities that the Gulf states still need, particularly air and missile defence, intelligence and deterrence, he says.
A Gulf-Iran framework, however, would address how “neighbours manage incidents” before they turn into a full-blown war.
The recent events in the region have made this distinction clearer, he says.
“Gulf states still want the American military presence, but they have also seen that Washington may not want to take responsibility for every regional confrontation,” he says.
Washington would object if a regional framework was used to “push the US out”. But any framework that reduces the number of crises that require US intervention should raise no objection.
“Gulf states are increasingly looking for more than one security backstop,” he says.
But Caner says any Gulf-Iran security arrangement will be in conflict with US objectives in the region.
“It is simply not feasible for the Gulf states to decouple their security infrastructure entirely from the US and pursue a new security understanding with Iran,” he says.
“If anything, the war has shown us the opposite: far from drifting away from Washington, the Gulf states’ security alliance with the US has only deepened,” he notes.
“I don't believe the US will withdraw from the Gulf altogether and leave the region to an independent security arrangement between the Gulf states and Iran,” he adds.

Young Berliners vote overwhelmingly for socialist Left  Party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:01:00 UTC
23:01:00 KST

Young Berliners vote overwhelmingly for socialist Left Party
September 22, 2026
The emphatic victory for the Left Party in last Sunday's state election in Berlin may not have been quite so emphatic if it hadn't been for a significant new rule: This was the first state election in the German capital's history where the voting age had been lowered from 18 to 16.
The actual change was relatively small: It only added around 55,000 voters to the city's electorate of 2.5 million, but it was massively significant to young people themselves: "Of course we talk a lot about politics at school or among our friends," 17-year-old Cecilia told DW's Franziska Wüst on the street outside her school in Berlin on Monday. "We're all very politically engaged; we go to a lot of demos."
Young socialists
That spirit of protest appears to have been reflected in young Berliners' voting habits. While the official exit poll statistics from infratest-dimap don't isolate under-18s, the age-group breakdowns suggest that the Left Party's voters (some 1 in 4 of Berlin voters) skew young. Some 43% of 16-24-year-olds voted for the socialist party — a huge 25-point leap on the last state election in 2023.
That makes sense to 17-year-old Liska, who voted for the socialists: "The Left Party did appeal to me, especially because of the social issues — getting prices down, making rents more affordable." Rents in Berlin are indeed rising at a massive pace — by some 7% in the last two years alone — and first-time tenants are likely to be the hardest hit. Polls also showed that by far the biggest proportion of Berlin voters — 37% — thought that the Left Party was the most likely to create affordable housing.
Cecilia also agreed that rents, as well as the conservative Berlin government's plans to cut education budgets, were the overwhelming concerns among her friends. "We're all getting to an age where we'd kind of like to move out, which in Berlin is almost impossible," she said. "Otherwise, of course it's issues like school, education, so it doesn't get cut everywhere."
Young radicals?
All those answers make a lot of sense to Kathrin Fehse of the German Children's and Youth Foundation (DKJS), which represents the interests of Germany's young people. "It's all the issues that affect them personally," she told DW. "And for that they need to be taken seriously and asked. And the Left Party was one of the parties that mobilized a lot of non-voters, not just young voters — they're people that politicians were not addressing before."
Throughout the campaign, the Left Party had been portrayed as dangerous radicals by the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the party of the incumbent mayor, Kai Wegner — regardless of how true this is or isn't, it did not appear to scare off young voters.
Some argue that young people are more likely to vote for the radical ends of the political spectrum. Cecilia can see that point: "I think that it's generally true that young people are always a lot more extreme than the older generations, and I do see that too, that it's always very extreme opinions," she said.
But there's also evidence that this is something of a stereotype: infratest-dimap statistics show that the biggest age group for the Left Party were the 25-34-year-olds (some 49% of the vote), while the biggest age group for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the Berlin election were 60-69-year-olds (23%). By comparison, only 12% of 16-24-year-old Berlin voters opted for the AfD.
What do young people want?
Gefjon Off, a political scientist who has researched the voting habits of younger generations, said that while it might be generally the case that younger people have more "radical" opinions than older people, the statistical evidence shows that middle-aged men vote for the AfD more than young men. People's age, in other words, "doesn't mean that they are more likely to vote for anti-democratic parties," she said.
What characterizes young voters is not so much radical views, argued Off, but their looser affiliation to any particular party: "In the federal election in 2021, for example, climate protection was a huge issue, and a lot of young people voted for the Greens as the climate was their issue," she told DW. "In this election, affordable housing was a huge issue for the Left Party. That means young people vote more according to issues, and [find it ]easier to move from one party to another."
Off also thinks that young people are less scared off by the stigmatization around the Left Party that still hangs round older generations who associate it with the communist dictatorship of East Germany.
Fehse said that in the DKJS' own study on young people's opinions, named VoiceUp, was that "young people want solidarity, participation, positive prospects for their future, and at the same time they experience these things much too seldom."
She concluded that "at the end of the day, those experiences create the social context in which their political decisions are made."

Muslim police associations accused of undermining police impartiality - Policy Exchange report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:00:56 UTC
23:00:56 KST

Some Muslim staff associations within British policing may be coming into conflict with the principle of police impartiality, a new report by Policy Exchange revealed on Monday.
“Mixed Messages: Police Impartiality & the National Association of Muslim Police” examined the activities of the National Association of Muslim Police (NAMP) and local force-level Muslim Police Associations, finding examples of the organizations becoming involved in highly contentious policy issues and platforming individuals and organizations with “questionable backgrounds.”
The NAMP was established in 2007 at an event held at the British Transport Police headquarters to act as “an umbrella organization [sic] for local Associations of Muslim Police.” By 2021, NAMP claimed to have 1,000 members in police forces across the country. Of the 43 Home Office forces of England and Wales, 20 police forces (43.5%) have a local Muslim Police Association.
A NAMP policy paper, titled “From Past Prejudices to Present Policies: Confronting anti-Muslim hatred and Promoting Human Rights,” dated July 20, 2025, was recently brought to public attention for describing Zionism as “one of the manifestations of anti-Muslim hatred, stripping Muslims of their humanity” and referring to the IDF as one of several “Zionist terrorist groups.”
The paper also defended Hamas against what it described as “alarming and unverified stories about acts of violence” committed during and after the attacks of October 7, 2023.
This policy paper was written by Khaldoun Kabbani, listed as the chair of the Scottish Police Muslim Association and vice president of the NAMP.
NAMP removes controversial policy paper after JLC intervention
Following intervention by the Jewish Leadership Council (JLC), NAMP removed the paper from its website and issued a statement asserting that it did not support terrorism and that the document did not represent its views, even though the paper bore NAMP’s logo, appeared on its website, and was written by its vice president.
Elsewhere on the NAMP website was a 2023 press release claiming that “using terms such as ‘Islamist’ reinforces Islamophobia by creating a higher risk of extreme right-wing radicalization; it also re-enforced a narrative that makes an association between Islam and terrorism, creating a greater risk of radicalization amongst vulnerable Muslims.”
During the recent NAMP Annual General Meeting 2026, held at Greater Manchester Police, attendees heard from speaker Majid Iqbal of the Islamophobia Response Unit.
Iqbal is known for an interview he gave in July 2024 after a violent incident at Manchester Airport where police officers clashed with two men attempting to avoid arrest. Iqbal criticized the “unjustifiable action of the police; the violent actions of the police.” The video circulated of the incident showed only the police response to the two men but not what preceded it: passenger Mohammed Fahir Amaaz assaulting another passenger and then breaking a police officer’s nose.
Policy Exchange said Iqbal’s presence at NAMP’s Annual General Meeting “raises several questions about NAMP’s approach and decision-making.”
“First, how committed is NAMP to contributing to the confidence of the wider public in policing when they are willing to provide a platform to an individual - Mr. Iqbal - who made claims that the police acted in a way which was ‘violent’ and ‘unjustifiable’ following the circulation of clipped social media footage which did not provide the full context of the incident at Manchester Airport?” the paper asked.
The report also discussed the activities of Supt. Hasson Shigdar, a senior West Midlands Police officer and vice-chair of the West Midlands Association of Muslim Police.
Policy Exchange examines conduct of Hasson Shigdar
It argued that Shigdar, also head of Prevent for the West Midlands Counter Terrorism Unit, had shared material online from organizations with questionable history and associations. For example, he tweeted his support for Green Lane Mosque, which had its proposed government funding suspended in 2023 after accusations emerged of hate speech and extremism.
“If policing is to reassure the public that impartiality is not merely a commitment which police chiefs and police officers consider to be an anachronism, they - and government - must act decisively to regulate this arena, which has been allowed to become an ungoverned space for activists,” Policy Exchange said.
It encouraged the Home Secretary to bring forward new legislation - a “Police Impartiality Act” - to set out the impartiality requirements for all chief constables, police forces, and policing-related bodies.
“The recommendations for greater rigor in the governance and operation of Police Staff networks are a key step in maintaining impartiality,” Michael Stewart, a former national security senior practitioner, said. “Senior officers must be prepared to challenge the views of staff networks and their members when those views are unbalanced or too narrowly focused on a particular group.”
“When staff networks in policing publicly involve themselves in matters of policy, which are rightly the preserve of elected governments and ministers, those networks and their leaders are going way over the line,” Chris Donaldson, former police inspector and firearms commander with the Metropolitan Police and founding member of the National Black Police Association, concluded.

Psychologists pinpoint the dividing line between problematic romance and severe love addiction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:00:31 UTC
23:00:31 KST

New research published in Sexual Health & Compulsivity indicates that people with clinical levels of love addiction experience more severe relationship anxiety than those who are simply at risk. The study also found that both at-risk individuals and clinical patients share similar difficulties in regulating their emotions, suggesting that love addiction exists on a spectrum where intense attachment anxiety marks the transition into a clinical problem.
Love addiction is a pattern of obsessive and dependent involvement in a romantic relationship. For someone experiencing this condition, a romantic relationship becomes the absolute center of their life. They tend to constantly seek approval, reassurance, and closeness from their partner, often at the expense of friendships, work, and personal interests.
This intense focus persists even when it causes immense emotional distress or negative consequences in other areas of life. Historically, researchers have debated how to classify this condition, with some viewing it as a behavioral addiction similar to gambling, and others understanding it as an attachment issue rooted in an excessive fear of abandonment.
Because love addiction does not currently have standardized diagnostic criteria in psychiatric manuals, mental health professionals often face challenges in identifying and treating it. This prompted the researchers to adopt a bottom-up approach, meaning they looked at the psychological dimensions, such as emotional, personality, and relational traits, as they naturally occur in people, rather than trying to fit the participants into rigid, predefined diagnostic boxes.
“Love Addiction is increasingly discussed both clinically and in the general public, but there is still considerable debate about what it actually represents,” study author Patrizia Velotti, director of the Emotions, Regulation and Relationships LAB and a full professor of clinical psychology at Sapienza University of Rome, told PsyPost. “Rather than assuming from the outset that it is simply a behavioral addiction, we wanted to examine the psychological processes associated with it from a bottom-up perspective, looking simultaneously at emotion regulation, personality functioning, and relational processes.”
A 2024 study indicated that people at risk for love addiction struggle more with controlling their emotions and forming secure relationships than healthy individuals. In addition, research covered by PsyPost in 2026 suggested that emotional dependence and love addiction feature distinct psychological profiles. Following this, a 2025 meta-analysis found that people struggling with love addiction consistently show high rates of insecure, anxious attachment to their romantic partners. A 2023 study also showed that an overwhelming fear of rejection and abandonment strongly predicts love addiction, especially when paired with low self-worth.
These earlier studies established that love addiction is linked to emotional distress and insecure relationship patterns, prompting researchers to test whether these psychological traits worsen step by step as people move from mild risk to severe clinical dependency. The researchers conducted the new study to examine these emotional, personality, and relational processes across different levels of love addiction severity.
“We were particularly interested in understanding whether people identified as at risk through self-report measures and those identified clinically would show similar or different psychological profiles,” Velotti said.
To investigate these differences, the research team recruited 152 adults in Italy, with an average age of about 33. The participants were divided into three groups based on their relationship struggles. The first group consisted of 70 people with no risk of love addiction. The second group included 53 individuals who were identified as being at risk for love addiction based on their high scores on a self-report questionnaire that evaluates addiction-like behaviors, such as experiencing withdrawal symptoms when away from a partner or having the relationship conflict with daily life. The third group consisted of 29 patients who were actively receiving clinical treatment for difficulties related to love addiction, as identified by mental health professionals.
All participants completed a battery of surveys. To assess emotional regulation, the researchers used a scale that measures how well individuals accept negative emotions, control their impulses, and maintain awareness of their feelings when upset. To evaluate personality functioning, the participants answered questions about their sense of identity, self-direction, empathy, and capacity for intimacy. A strong sense of self-direction involves being able to set and pursue meaningful goals, while intimacy involves maintaining deep and mutually respectful connections with others.
Finally, the researchers measured relational variables by assessing the participants’ levels of attachment anxiety and their ability to recognize and make sense of their emotions specifically within the context of an intimate relationship. The researchers controlled for the participants’ age and gender when analyzing the results to ensure these demographic factors did not skew the findings.
Cavalli and her team found that both the at-risk group and the clinical group reported substantially more difficulty managing their emotions compared to the non-risk group. People in both risk groups struggled to regulate negative emotional states, suggesting that they might use their romantic relationship as a maladaptive way to soothe their own emotional distress.
“One aspect we consider particularly important is that the relationship itself may function as a means of regulating difficult emotional states,” Velotti noted. “In this sense, problematic romantic involvement may be better understood not only in terms of compulsive behavior, but also in terms of what the relationship is psychologically being used to regulate.”
They also showed similar impairments in personality functioning, reporting more difficulties with their own sense of self and their interpersonal relationships than the non-risk group. However, there was no statistically significant difference in general emotional regulation or personality functioning between the at-risk individuals and the clinical patients. Both groups shared these underlying psychological vulnerabilities.
“One particularly interesting finding was how similar the at-risk and clinical groups were on several psychological dimensions,” Velotti explained. “This suggests that the transition toward clinically significant difficulties may not simply reflect a general increase in psychopathology; relational processes, and particularly attachment anxiety, may be especially important in understanding severity.”
The relational measures, on the other hand, showed a progressive worsening across the three groups. The researchers observed that attachment anxiety steadily increased depending on the severity of the love addiction. The non-risk group reported the lowest levels of relationship anxiety, the at-risk group reported moderate levels, and the clinical group reported the highest levels. This indicates that an intense fear of abandonment and an excessive need for reassurance are specific markers of severe, clinical love addiction.
“The most clinically informative finding was not simply that the clinical group showed ‘more problems’ across every dimension,” Velotti told PsyPost. “Emotional dysregulation and personality difficulties were already clearly elevated in the at-risk group… whereas anxious attachment showed a clear progressive increase and was highest in the clinical group.”
In terms of emotional regulation within the relationship itself, both the at-risk and clinical groups showed reduced awareness and clarity regarding their emotions when interacting with their partners compared to the non-risk group. The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2024 and a study covered by PsyPost in 2025, which consistently found that higher levels of insecure, anxious attachment are strongly associated with a greater severity of love addiction. They also align with research covered by PsyPost in 2026, which linked romantic relationship addiction to greater emotion regulation difficulties.
“The main message is that Love Addiction should not simply be understood as ‘loving too much,'” Velotti noted. “What appears to distinguish problematic forms of romantic involvement is a broader pattern involving difficulties in regulating emotions, impairments in self and interpersonal functioning, and, especially, difficulties related to attachment and emotional functioning within intimate relationships.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. “I would strongly caution against interpreting our findings as evidence that intense romantic attachment is itself pathological, or that Love Addiction is already an established diagnostic category,” Velotti said. “The construct remains debated, and our results are better understood as evidence for a dimensional and relational pattern of difficulties rather than for a discrete disorder.”
The study relied on a relatively small number of clinical patients, which makes it harder to generalize the findings to everyone who experiences severe love addiction. The participants were also overwhelmingly female, meaning that the relationship dynamics observed might not fully capture how this condition affects men. Because the research took place at a single point in time, it cannot show whether anxious attachment causes love addiction or if the addiction itself fuels the anxiety.
Future research will need to follow people over time to better understand how these relationship struggles develop. “Our next goal is to move beyond the question of whether Love Addiction resembles other behavioral addictions and develop a more integrated model of the phenomenon,” Velotti said. “Ultimately, this could also help improve assessment and inform interventions that target the underlying psychological and relational mechanisms rather than focusing only on the overt compulsive behavior.”
The study, “Psychological and Psychopathological Features of Love Addiction: A Cross-Sectional Study,” was authored by Roberta Gabriella Cavalli, Arianna Teverini, Viviana Ferrà, and Patrizia Velotti.

UN probe finds Iran committed crimes against humanity in crackdown, cites US and Israel for strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:00:28 UTC
23:00:28 KST

The Islamic Republic of Iran is responsible for gross human rights violations committed in January in response to the widespread outbreak of protests, the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran concluded in a report published Monday, which also condemned the US and Israel for attacks against the regime.
Though Iran failed to fully cooperate with the mission, denying it unhindered access to the country as it did following the crackdown on the 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom protests, the mission concluded that Tehran had violated individuals’ rights to life, freedom from torture and ill-treatment, personal security and liberty, a fair trial, and an effective remedy, as well as the rights to peaceful assembly and association, freedom of expression, equality and non-discrimination, and privacy and health.
The mission sent 47 information requests to the regime, of which only 12 received responses, and none provided the information requested. Despite the Islamic Republic’s failure to cooperate with the investigation and its internet shutdown hindering access to information, the mission gathered testimonies from 73 individuals, and satellite imagery, video, and photographic material, as well as information from credible human rights organizations and forensic and military experts.
After Iran restored internet connectivity to no more than 30% of pre-shutdown levels, access to online spaces and communication remained heavily restricted. A tiered system requiring prior authorization and identity verification prevented unauthorized users from accessing certain systems, which the mission said had “appeared to strengthen its control over digital space.”
The internet shutdown meant that, at the height of the violent repression of the protests on January 8 and 9, Iranian civilians were deprived of the ability to communicate, access information, and seek medical or emergency assistance. Health workers told the mission that the shutdown made it difficult to reach colleagues and coordinate treatment and follow up with sick or wounded individuals. Protesters wounded by security forces also struggled to arrange medical treatment.
Internet shutdown blocked communications to family, emergency services
Families inside and outside the country were unable to learn the fate of their loved ones during the demonstrations, leaving them anxious about their well-being. Additionally, when war broke out between the United States and Israel on February 28, the internet shutdown left the civilian population without access to timely and potentially lifesaving information.
Though the full extent of the regime’s violence was not determined by the mission, the report confirmed that the crackdown on the January protests resulted in at least three-and-a-half times as many injuries and five-and-a-half times as many deaths as the repression of the 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom protests.
This demonstrated, the mission concluded, that the suppression “went beyond a simple continuation of familiar patterns and represented a marked escalation in the use of lethal force and mass arrests.”
Iran acknowledged the deaths of only 3,038 individuals and the wounding of 25,000, more than 50% of whom it said required surgery, while attributing most of the casualties to “terrorists.” However, based on information from credible organizations and discrepancies in figures provided by the regime, the mission concluded that the true death toll was significantly higher than the figures reported by Tehran and that security forces were responsible for the violence.
Security forces routinely fired tear gas before firing shotguns loaded with metal pellets at protesters who did not present an imminent threat, the mission found.
Evidence collected from witnesses and healthcare workers, such as medical records, showed that protesters sustained metal pellet wounds to the eyes, head, chest, and upper body, “suggesting that security forces intended to maximize the damage caused by this type of ammunition.”
Officials from Farabi Hospital in Tehran confirmed that between January 8 and the morning of January 10, more than 700 people had sought treatment for eye wounds, some of which resulted in severe or total loss of vision. One health professional told the mission that the wounds indicated that shotgun rounds had been fired from close range at protesters.
Tear gas, shotguns, automatic gunfire at protesters
Another healthcare worker described treating protesters who were wounded after tear gas canisters were fired directly at their faces from close range.
Medical staff, wounded protesters, and other unnamed sources told the mission that security forces monitored hospitals to search for and arrest those they believed had been demonstrating. In some cases, medical personnel were also arrested for providing the treatment. The apparent presence of security forces also led to many avoiding medical treatment, resulting in several people dying from their wounds as a result.
FURTHER HIGHLIGHTING the pattern of violence, the mission was able to verify a video posted online on January 10, showing individuals firing on fleeing crowds from the roof of a police station in Tehran. They appeared to be firing assault rifles, though there was no evidence to suggest an imminent threat. Another series of verified videos showed individuals firing from a roof outside a police station in Karaj, again where there was no evidence of an imminent threat.
Witnesses also described hearing sustained automatic gunfire during demonstrations in Tehran, Karaj, Mashhad, and Abadan and seeing protesters collapse after being shot, some from the back, suggesting that they had been fleeing when they were killed.
Small children treated for shotgun wounds
Children were not spared the violence. The mission confirmed that a 16-year-old boy was shot in both eyes with metal pellets, resulting in the loss of vision in his right eye, while another boy was blinded in one eye after being shot with metal pellets at close range. The second boy sustained pellet wounds to the upper half of his face and the back of his forearm, “indicating that he likely had adopted a defensive posture before being shot.”
One healthcare professional also told the mission that they had treated children as young as 10 for shotgun pellet injuries, while credible sources told the mission that children as young as five were wounded during the demonstrations.
An unnamed human rights organization also provided the names of at least 221 children who were killed during the protests, including by lethal ammunition. According to the organization, six of the children were under the age of 10, and two were only two years old.
The mission was also able to confirm that at least three individuals were sentenced to death despite being minors at the time of the alleged offense. Two 17-year-old boys were
sentenced to death alongside Hosseinipour Hesarlou, now 19, for allegedly setting fire to the Seyyed al-Shohada Mosque, which allegedly resulted in the death of two individuals. The mission was told the death sentences were upheld, with a lawyer representing one of the defendants complaining that he had been barred by the judge from representing his client.
Witnesses who were detained by the security forces also told the mission about the torture and ill-treatment they had witnessed or experienced.
One individual, who was detained in Karaj, recalled how he had been kicked in the mouth when he questioned why he was being arrested; another described being detained in a continuously lit room in solitary confinement for around one month, where she was deprived of prescribed medication and subjected to regular interrogation sessions lasting up to six hours each, without the presence of a lawyer.
Families of the regime’s victims also told the mission that authorities had refused to release the bodies of their loved ones, in some cases demanding payment or refusing to return the body until the family signed a document with false information that would support the regime’s narrative of the events.

Hidden gem to holiday hotspot: How Albania became one of Europe’s fastest-growing travel destinations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:00:28 UTC
23:00:28 KST

The number of tourists visiting the Balkan nation has doubled in the past decade as more and more people discover its fascinating history, brilliant beaches and awe-inspiring hiking trails.
Albania’s tourism story is unlike any other. Closed off to the world for decades under the rule of dictator Enver Hoxha, foreign tourists began to slowly trickle in after his death and the fall of communism.
Today, the number of visitors has soared – in 2025, arrivals hit 11.9 million, up 3.3% year-on-year but up 93.6% compared to 2019, according to UN Tourism.
There’s no one single factor that has led to this meteoric rise, although we imagine the sheer number of travel publications referring to the Balkan nation as the “Maldives of Europe” (including Euronews Travel) has had something to do with it.
Here, we take a look into the boom, and where you should be heading on your next trip.
Hidden gem to holiday hotspot
Travellers are always looking for the next “hidden gem”: As soon as one place peaks in popularity, people begin to look for off-the-beaten path alternatives.
A decade ago, Croatia – and Dubrovnik in particular – hit the mainstream thanks to Game of Thrones. Then tourists began looking for quieter locales on the Dalmatian coast, landing on Montenegro. Now, people are headed further south still, with the Albanian Riviera earning praise for its clear waters and affordable prices.
The relative ease of moving around the region by bus has brought in plenty of travellers opting for multi-country trips, taking in North Macedonia, Kosovo and other spots in combination with Albania.
For those flying in, the expansion of Tirana International Airport has helped, but a more significant event was the launch of a Wizz Air base here in 2020, bringing with it affordable flights to and from cities across Europe including Barcelona, Budapest, London, Madrid, Rome and Stockholm.
A big part of why Albania is now so popular is also the sheer variety of its offering, whether you’re into history or just want to fly-and-flop.
Tirana: For history buffs
Albania’s capital Tirana is an excellent way into the country’s history and its rapid development over the past few decades.
Begin with a visit to Skanderbeg Square, so named for the statue dedicated to the country’s national hero who resisted the Ottomans in the 15th century.
While the National Historical Museum will remain closed until 2028, the mural on the outside still offers an insight into the country’s past through the figures represented, which include an Illyrian warrior, a fighter from the Albanian National Awakening period, a depiction of Mother Albania and a communist worker.
Communist-era Albanian history piqued my interest, which led me to the House of Leaves, a museum that focuses on the Sigurimi, the country’s secret police. You’ll get to see inside former interrogation rooms, and see first-hand documents, recordings and photos from that time.
Brutalist architecture isn’t the only legacy of Hoxha’s Albania: The country is also covered in bunkers, with 5.7 for every square kilometre. Most are derelict, but near Skanderbeg Square you can visit Bunk’art 2, which also looks at life under the fear of the secret police.
Bunk’art 1, the larger of the two, is on the outskirts of Tirana and covers various periods from the 1930s up to 1990. If you’re planning on taking the Dajti Mountain Cable Car, it’s just moments away from the lower station.
For tourist knickknacks and local food, you can visit Tirana Castle, aka the Fortress of Justinian, which is now the home of many independent restaurants, cafés and shops.
Tirana is known for being a cheaper city break than destinations in neighbouring countries, and it has a thriving nightlife scene as a result.
The Blokku district is a good place to start. For cocktail lovers, try Hemingway, which is known for its live jazz and rum-based beverages, or Radio Bar. For beers, I liked Ruka's Bar 1991.
Wherever you go, be sure to try raki at some point…
Shkodër: For lakeside relaxation
The largest lake in Southern Europe is split between Albania and Montenegro.
Called Lake Shkodër on the Albanian side (and Lake Skadar on the Montenegrin side), you can explore the town by foot and visit Rozafa Castle, but the best thing to do here is rent a bike and make your way around the lake.
This is very much a place to slow down and not do very much at all. I stayed at Hotel Tradita, a boutique property within a building that originally dates back to 1694 and was once the home of poet Filip Shiroka.
Even if you don’t stay there, be sure to pay a visit to the restaurant, which serves up traditional dishes, wine, and raki, and often has live Albanian music, too.
Shala River and Lake Koman are popular day trips from Lake Shkodër, and adventures in the Albanian Alps start from here.
Albanian Alps: For nature lovers
The Valbona Pass is among the most popular hiking routes in the Albanian Alps, and you can read all about our writer Rebecca Ann Hughes’ time exploring the trail in detail here.
The TL;DR version is that the trail from Valbona and Theth is 12 kilometres and takes around seven to 10 hours, and along the way you can expect to see unspoilt scenery, with dramatic peaks and wildflower-strewn meadows.
Albanian Riviera: For beach bums
The place that you’ve probably heard the most about is undoubtedly the Albanian Riviera, aka the “Maldives of Europe”, so called because of its crystal clear waters and soft sandy shores.
Vlorë, Albania’s third-largest city, has seen the biggest influx of visitors, but other popular hotspots along the coast include Dhërmi, Sarandë and Ksamil.
The tourism boom in the country has brought with it plenty of investment in the tourism infrastructure, with five-star hotel options on the coast now including Green Coast Hotel - MGallery Collection (which opened in June last year), Crowne Plaza Durres by IHG (which opened earlier this year), and Miamar Luxury Hotel & Spa.
How to get there
There are direct flights to Tirana International Airport from major hubs across the continent, including London, Frankfurt, Amsterdam and Istanbul, although it should be noted that many of these flights are seasonal.
You can also take buses to Tirana from nearby cities including Skopje and Ohrid in North Macedonia, Podgorica and Budva in Montenegro, or Prishtina and Prizren in Kosovo.

Brussels seeks power to order electricity demand cuts in energy crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:00:09 UTC
23:00:09 KST

The European Commission is seeking more hands-on control to head off power failures during future energy crise, according to plans seen by Euronews.
The European Commission wants new powers to order electricity demand cuts and block national measures that threaten energy supplies elsewhere in Europe during a major crisis, according to draft plans seen by Euronews.
The proposals would give Brussels a more hands-on role in managing energy emergencies, allowing the Commission to declare a regional or EU-wide electricity alarm and require countries to reduce consumption by a specified amount.
The Commission's energy security package was originally due earlier this year and designed largely around lessons from the 2022-23 energy crisis, when Europe lost much of its Russian gas supply following Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
But fresh supply and price shocks emerging from the US and Israeli war against Iran have upended the plans, forcing Brussels to rethink its plans. The draft now seeks to prepare Europe for threats ranging from supply shortages and extreme weather to cyberattacks and physical attacks on critical infrastructure, such as the Nord Stream sabotage and attacks on Germany's power grid.
Under the proposed rules, the Commission could declare a regional or EU-wide electricity alarm if it identifies a substantial risk of a power crisis.
After consulting the Electricity Coordination Group — a high-level group gathering EU countries, industry and EU officials — Brussels could introduce measures including mandatory national demand adjustments, with the Commission deciding what cuts are needed.
“Such measures may include mandatory national demand adjustments (...) The Commission shall specify in the alarm declaration the level of demand adjustments required,” the draft says.
Early warning system in the making
The Commission also wants a clearer escalation system for energy crises.
Countries would first issue an early warning or national alarm before declaring an emergency once market-based measures – including subsidies, taxation or cap-and-trade systems – have been exhausted and electricity supply can no longer meet demand.
Brussels also wants governments to coordinate their interventions and avoid national measures that could restrict cross-border electricity or gas flows, potentially worsening shortages in neighbouring countries.
The Commission argues that unilateral action during a shortage can damage the internal market and create negative spillovers elsewhere. That issue has become increasingly pressing as the bloc is currently grappling with potential fuel shortages – prompting French President Emmanuel Macron to ask Brussels to reassess the EU's joint gas-purchasing mechanism created following the war in Ukraine and the sudden decoupling from Russian gas.
'Strictly limited' gas-fired plants
The draft treats gas and electricity shortages as two sides of the same problem of ensuring adequate gas supplies. It asks EU countries to identify gas-fired power plants that are "strictly limited to the critical gas volumes needed to maintain electricity grid stability".
With a growing push to electrify the bloc's economy, the EU's power system is becoming more dependent on electricity - and with renewable generation dependent on weather conditions, it raises concerns of intermittent power failures.
The draft calls for more detailed short-term and seasonal assessments of power adequacy, including the risks posed by extreme weather, power-plant outages, transmission failures, demand peaks and fluctuations in renewable generation.
Stockpiling critical infrastructure parts
Brussels is also looking beyond energy supplies to stockpile critical spare parts of infrastructure. With growing drone threats near energy infrastructure, the Commission wants to treat the ability to repair the system quickly as part of energy security.
The proposal would create an EU-wide list of essential spare parts needed to keep electricity and gas networks running and quickly fix them after a disruption.
Energy operators would report what equipment they have, while EU energy authorities would set minimum stock levels based on factors such as supply risks, how long it takes to replace equipment and how important each component is for cross-border energy flows.
The Commission could also recommend that countries build shared regional reserves of key equipment.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Fox News on Tuesday, Sept. 22, that Ukraine had repeatedly targeted vessels linked to the United States in recent months, probably unintentionally.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Over the last few months, on a number of occasions, American-linked ships have been targeted, probably not deliberately, but targeted nonetheless by Ukraine. We can’t have that happen. That needs to be addressed,” he said.
Rubio did not publicly name the vessels or clarify whether they were American-owned, US-flagged or connected to the United States through cargo, chartering or energy infrastructure.
Rubio also backed a broader pause in attacks on energy infrastructure during the Fox News interview.
“We think that would be a great idea – an energy infrastructure ceasefire, in which Ukraine’s infrastructure is not being targeted, and Russian energy supplies are not being targeted as well,” he said
What does “US-linked” mean?
The claim appears to refer to vessels using Russia’s Black Sea ports to transport oil connected to the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, which carries Kazakh crude to export terminals.
The Financial Times reported in August that US Vice President JD Vance had asked Ukraine to halt strikes on tankers using the port of Novorossiysk. Washington was concerned that the attacks were disrupting global oil markets and affecting US companies, including Chevron and ExxonMobil.
Ukraine to Charge Russia in UN for Causing Humanitarian Disaster in Occupied City
According to the report, Ukraine agreed not to target CPC infrastructure or non-Russian vessels as long as those ships were not under Ukrainian sanctions and were not carrying Russian oil or other Russian cargo.
That means the vessels could be commercially connected to US interests without being US property. No publicly available report has established that Ukraine repeatedly struck ships sailing under the US flag or owned by US companies.
Ukraine’s attacks on Russian shipping
Ukraine has intensified attacks on Russian-linked shipping and oil infrastructure in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov in 2026.
Ukrainian forces have targeted Russian tankers, cargo ships and other vessels as part of an effort to disrupt Moscow’s energy revenues and military logistics. On Tuesday, the commander of Ukraine’s drone forces said his units struck 300 shadow fleet tankers ferrying Russian oil since July.
The campaigns have also affected commercial navigation. London’s marine insurance market recently expanded its high-risk zone to cover the entire Black Sea after a rise in attacks on commercial shipping by both Russia and Ukraine.
No evidence of repeated attacks on US ships
Reports confirm that Ukrainian strikes have affected vessels and infrastructure linked to Western energy companies, but no public evidence shows that US-owned or US-flagged ships were repeatedly hit.
His comments came as Washington urged Kyiv and Moscow to halt attacks on energy facilities and commercial shipping in the Black Sea. Zelensky was expected to meet Trump at the UN on Tuesday to discuss a possible energy truce.
Russia also attacks commercial shipping
Rubio’s comments come as Russia continues to target Ukrainian ports and civilian vessels in the Black Sea.
In an interview with Kyiv Post, Dmytro Barinov, head of the Ukrainian Ports Association, said Russian forces had damaged or destroyed more than 300 vessels since the start of the full-scale invasion. He said the attacks intensified in July, with Russian forces “hunting for vessels” entering or leaving Ukrainian ports.
The attacks have also disrupted global food supplies.
According to Bloomberg, Russian and Ukrainian wheat exports during the July-September harvest period could fall to roughly half last year’s level. Strikes on ports, grain terminals, storage facilities and commercial vessels have pushed wheat prices to three-year highs and forced major importers to search for more expensive supplies elsewhere.
Russia and Ukraine normally account for more than a quarter of global wheat exports, around two-thirds of sunflower oil shipments and about one-tenth of international corn trade.
Egypt, the world’s largest wheat importer, reportedly received no Black Sea grain for about a month, while buyers in Africa, Asia and the Middle East turned to suppliers in France, Romania, Argentina, India and Australia. Ukraine is also facing a storage crisis as its new harvest accumulates faster than it can be exported, threatening farmers’ incomes and the country’s already strained budget.

TOKYO, September 22. /TASS/. The Japanese government intends to explore the possibility of using humanoid robots for defense purposes, the Kyodo News agency reported.
According to its sources in the government and the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, the plan involves using "physical AI" technology, which enables robots equipped with artificial intelligence to function autonomously.
Authorities plan to use such robots to perform logistical tasks for the country’s Self-Defense Forces - such as guarding bases, transporting cargo, and other support functions. Given the current shortage of personnel in the Self-Defense Forces, the goal is to reduce the need for human resources through the introduction of AI and unmanned systems.
However, the use of humanoid robots directly in combat operations is not currently being considered. Japan’s ruling party points to the lack of an international legal framework and the risks associated with potential errors in a robot’s ability to distinguish between combatants and civilians.
At the same time, the possibility of using such robots in reconnaissance and rescue operations is being examined for the future. According to Kyodo, in about 20 years, the size of the conscript contingent for the Self-Defense Forces will decline by about 30%. Therefore, the Defense Ministry expects that humanoid robots will be "an effective tool to replace or complement operations undertaken by a limited number of personnel."
The government plans to revise key documents on defense and security at the end of the year, regarding the broader use of AI as a key to bolstering the country's defense capabilities, the agency reported.

India is reportedly eyeing a cut in Russian crude imports after the US’s recently introduced new sanctions on Russian oil purchases.
The sanctions, named after late US lawmaker Lindsey Graham, would allow Washington to impose a 100% tariff on imports from nations buying Russian oil.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Bloomberg reported Tuesday that India – the world’s third-largest crude buyer that imports 40% of its crude from Russia – is eyeing a cut in deliveries, potentially starting in November.
The outlet said India’s September Russian crude imports averaged about 1.9 million barrels a day, citing data from commercial analytics platform Kpler. It noted that the volume is the lowest since April.
Those involved in the discussions reportedly told Bloomberg that top refineries in India are already seeking alternatives for fear of US tariffs, with plans to bring Russian crude imports down to 20-30%.
Those sources added that New Delhi would continue to negotiate with Washington over the sanctions and tariffs, while watching for similar measures against other Russian crude purchasers such as China.
China was the top importer of Russian crude in August, according to a report by the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), which gave Moscow total revenue of €8.4 billion ($9.7 billion).
India follows at €4.8 billion ($5.5 billion), followed by NATO member Turkey at €1.5 billion ($1.7 billion). The EU was the fourth-largest buyer of Russian fossil fuels, at €1.2 billion ($1.4 billion).
Moldova Seeks Energy, Water Emergency Over Critically Low Dnister Levels
The US House of Representatives passed the latest sanctions bill on Sept. 17, and US President Donald Trump signed it a day later.
Trump imposed similarly structured 50% tariffs on India in August 2025, but later dropped them to 18% in February, claiming New Delhi had “agreed to stop buying Russian oil, and to buy much more from the United States and, potentially, Venezuela,” according to CNBC.
Kpler data cited by Bloomberg shows Indian imports of Russian crude bounced from an average of 1 million barrels per day that month to 2 million barrels in March, before peaking at 2.83 million barrels daily in July.
India’s gasoline supplies to Russia
India has also been a major supplier of gasoline to Russia amid the latter’s fuel crisis, where Russian crude is sold back as gasoline.
The same CREA report also notes Russia’s unprecedented seaborne energy product imports amid a widening fuel crisis, with Russia importing 172,000 tonnes of oil products by sea – three times the total imports for the whole of 2025 in just one month.
The spike was triggered by regular Ukrainian strikes against its refineries that hampered Moscow’s ability to process its own crude.
The CREA added that 70% of those imports came from India, 94% of which were gasoline.
Considering Russia’s state-owned Rosneft holds a 49.13% stake in Nayara Energy, which refines some of that Russian crude before shipping the fuel back to Russia, Moscow is essentially paying New Delhi to help process crude it cannot refine domestically amid the ongoing automobile fuel crisis.

The renewed fighting came after a dramatic offensive launched by the Houthis three weeks earlier in which the group seized control of much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast from government-aligned forces. They were the most significant territorial gains in the last four years of the civil war in the country. 
 The offensive has upended global energy markets, which are already reeling from the Iranian closure of the strait of Hormuz, and further expanded the regional scope of the US-Iran war, now in its seventh month.
Last week the Houthis took control of Mocha and other strategic cities, which gave them control over the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key shipping lane home to 10% of all global maritime traffic that has gained renewed importance after the closure of the strait of Hormuz.
The clashes have compounded an already dire humanitarian crisis, where about 22 million people need humanitarian assistance and 5.2 million people are already internally displaced.
Yemen’s civil war started in 2014 when the Houthis seized control of the country’s capital and toppled the government. A Saudi-led coalition then intervened in an aerial campaign on behalf of the internationally recognised Yemeni government and allied militias.
A UN-brokered ceasefire was established in 2022, which had largely held until the Houthis launched the current offensive.
In recent days, clashes have focused on the strategic Kahboub mountains near the Red Sea coast as the Houthis seek to consolidate recent territorial gains. Government forces have been trying to hold the line against the Houthi advance on multiple fronts to prevent them from seizing the mountain range.
Control of the mountains would give the Houthis a strategic vantage point over Red Sea coastal areas and would further cut off Aden, the seat of Yemeni government forces, from the western coast. Seizing the mountains would also complicate future government counterattacks.
The Houthis have advanced on multiple fronts, particularly the outskirts of Taiz province and the coastal area of Ras al-Ara, with the greater goal of controlling the Kahboub mountains. Media affiliated with the Houthis have reported gains in the area, while government media said its fighters had successfully repelled Houthi incursions.
Since the Houthi campaign was launched, the group has routed government-aligned forces from western Yemen. The prospect of an Iranian-aligned force controlling Bab al-Mandeb has worried Saudi Arabia as it would place two shipping lanes vital to its energy exports in the hands of Iran and its allies.
Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of strikes on Yemen in recent days to try to stop the Houthis, with little success.
Donald Trump reportedly considered striking the Houthis over the weekend but called them off at the last minute, while the UK said it would assist aerial refuelling of Saudi aircraft engaged in defensive missions, leaving open the prospect of further international intervention.
Members of the G7 have called on Iran to stop arming the Houthis. In a joint statement released ahead of the UN general assembly, member states urged the Houthis to stop their strikes on Saudi Arabia, which have damaged key oil infrastructure and wounded dozens.
“We call on the Houthis to immediately cease all military actions, all threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith,” the statement read.
The clashes have killed about 700 people and displaced more than 100,000 people, pushing some Yemenis to flee the fighting via sea. Civilians have fled westwards across the Red Sea to Djibouti, while aid groups warn conditions for those remaining in Yemen are deteriorating.
Babar Baloch, a UN refugee agency spokesperson, said on Tuesday that displacement inside Yemen could rise to 230,000 people and more than 10,000 could flee to Djibouti if fighting continued.
Saudi Arabia has tried to marshal international support to roll back the Houthi offensive, with the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, asking Trump to strike the Houthis – a request Trump has thus far refused.
Trump held a call with the head of Yemen’s governing body, Rashad al-Alimi, on Monday, with al-Alimi asking the US for military assistance. Trump expressed solidarity but did not promise military support, a source told Agence France-Presse.

Five-party MOU unveiled on business-environment reform, customs levy dispute
