Parents with two daughters report the highest levels of happiness, Chinese study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:00:28 UTC
22:00:28 KST

A study in China found that parents tend to be happier than non-parents. Among parents, those with more children tend to be happier, but only among those aged 60 and above. Parents who only had daughters tended to be happier than those having only boys, particularly those who had exactly two daughters. The paper was published in Acta Psychologica.
Happiness is an important component of quality of life. It can depend on both personal circumstances and broader social conditions. Family structure can play an important role in how happy a person is, particularly through the number of children, their ages, and the kinds of support they provide. Parenthood can make a person happier by creating emotional meaning and companionship, but it can also increase financial demands, daily responsibilities, and work-family conflict. These costs and benefits may change across the life course as children grow older and parents’ needs shift.
Adult children can contribute to parents’ well-being through financial assistance, practical help, emotional support, and maintaining close family relationships. Sons and daughters can provide different forms of support because cultural expectations and gender roles shape how family responsibilities are distributed.
Daughters tend to be more involved in maintaining family contact and providing emotional support, whereas sons may be expected in some cultures to provide greater financial or practical assistance. The relationship between children and parental happiness can therefore depend strongly on cultural norms, economic resources, social security systems, and whether families live in urban or rural settings.
Study authors Zhong Fei and Wenqin Jin wanted to explore how a person’s happiness is associated with the number of children the person has and their gender. More specifically, they wanted to answer the following question: “what kind of offspring composition, in which ways, and for which parents, can improve their quality of life in Chinese society?”
These researchers analyzed data from the Chinese General Social Survey (CGSS). The CGSS is a large, multistage survey initiated by Renmin University of China in 2003. It covers all provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities in China and targets the civilian population aged 18 years and above. Study participants were recruited from 100 counties and five metropolitan areas (Beijing, Shanghai, Tianjin, Guangzhou, and Shenzhen) across China. There were six data collection waves in the study between 2012 and 2021, each involving between 8,000 and 13,000 participants. The dataset used in this analysis included data from 49,752 individuals, 45,108 of whom had children.
From this dataset, the study authors used data about participants’ self-reported happiness (“Overall, do you feel happy in your life?”), the number of children, and their gender (“How many biological children do you have (including deceased children)? How many sons and daughters do you have (including deceased children)?”). They also used data on participants’ gender, age, ethnicity, and various other pieces of sociodemographic information.
Results showed that, on average, parents were happier than non-parents. Participants with a larger number of children tended to be happier than those with fewer children, but only when participants aged 60 and above were considered. Parents with all-female offspring tended to be happier than those with all-male offspring, and this association was strongest among middle-aged parents and those who had exactly two daughters. Parents with a mix of sons and daughters did not report a statistically significant difference in happiness compared to those with only sons.
Additionally, the positive association between the number of children and happiness was more pronounced among men, urban residents, and those with a pension, whereas the happiness advantage of having only daughters was more pronounced among rural residents, middle-aged parents, and those with a spouse.
“It is important to interpret these findings with appropriate caution. As our analyses are based on data from the CGSS, the observed associations – particularly the pronounced positive association of the ‘two daughters’ combination in two-child families – should be viewed as sample-specific evidence within the contemporary Chinese context. The generalizability of these patterns to other cultural settings or time periods remains to be established through future cross-cultural and cross-national research,” the study authors added.
The study contributes to the scientific knowledge about factors associated with psychological well-being. However, it should be noted that happiness was assessed using a single item, so the reliability and particularly the temporal stability of such ratings remain unknown. Additionally, the design of the study does not allow any causal inferences to be derived from the results. Therefore, it remains unknown whether having children makes people happier, whether happier people are more likely to decide to have children, or whether this association is caused by some other factor.
The paper, “Who reports higher happiness? The association between number of children, gender composition of offspring and parental happiness,” was authored by Zhong Fei and Wenqin Jin.

The Patagonia town where Nepal’s deadly glacier flood could be repeated – and what they’ve learned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:00:01 UTC
22:00:01 KST

The images from Nepal stopped Daniela Schmidt in her tracks. A geologist at the University of Buenos Aires in Argentina, she watched the deadly flash floods on 26 August tear through everything in their path, people running for their lives as the water and debris swept over the landscape.
“I had never seen anything like it,” she says. “This was one of the most catastrophic events on a global scale related to these glacial floods.”
The shock deepened as the first geological figures emerged: the volume of glacier ice and rock that had collapsed and the scale of the resulting flow. Schmidt began comparing them with the cases she had studied during her PhD. Very few glacial lake outburst floods, she realised, had reached anything close to this magnitude.
But Nepal also changed the way she saw her own work. Schmidt studies the glacial lake outburst flood (Glof) that could occur at Laguna Torre, in Argentina’s Santa Cruz province, and its potential impact on El Chaltén, a nearby town known as the country’s trekking capital.
The disaster already exists on her computer screen: data, models, flood simulations and maps. According to her studies, if the northern slope of Cerro Solo were to collapse into Laguna Torre, at the base of the Torre glacier, a massive volume of water could travel the 5 miles (8km) to El Chaltén in 20 minutes, sweeping along logs, rocks and sediment.
The discharge could reach 1,769 cubic metres (62,472 cubic feet) a second, rushing down the Fitz Roy River towards the town and inundating its only access bridge and other critical infrastructure. For anyone in the valley, those 20 minutes would be the window to reach safety. “It is the worst-case flood scenario,” says Schmidt, adding that, in the most conservative analysis, the flow would take between 45 minutes and an hour to reach the town.
“You can’t say it will happen on a specific day or at a specific time, but society needs to be prepared,” Schmidt warns. “It is going to happen.”
The threat was already changing how El Chaltén prepared for the future, but the disaster in Nepal has brought these risks to the forefront. Although the scale of that event and the El Chaltén scenario differ, Schmidt sees a similarity in the mechanism: a mass suddenly plunging into a body of water can trigger a flash flood with immense destructive power.
Authorities from Los Glaciares national park and the municipality of El Chaltén, along with local organisations and various scientific institutions, are working to develop the country’s first Glof early-warning system and draft evacuation protocols.
“We are preparing for the worst-case scenario,” says Enrique Rivero, El Chaltén’s secretary of government.
The silhouette of Cerro Solo is unmistakable. The vertical granite peak, rising to 2,121 metres (6,959ft) above sea level, is reflected in Laguna Torre amid floating icebergs. That is where the risk begins.
The Torre glacier is estimated to have lost 4 sq km (1.5 sq miles) of surface area, while its ice thinned by 60-70 metres between 1952 and 2023. As the ice retreats, the balance of the surrounding slopes also shifts – a process researchers describe as a “release of stress”.
This transformation is visible in landslides and rockfalls that leave scars across the mountainside. Between 2002 and 2023, the volume of displaced material increased, while the speed of movement doubled. “It moves slowly, but during heavy rainfall or high temperatures, it accelerates in pulses,” Schmidt says. “As the slopes become unstable, they can slide, dumping a large volume of material into the lake and causing it to overflow. It just needs a trigger.”
Her models contemplate landslides involving between 8m and 13m cubic metres of material. If a mass of that size were to collapse into Laguna Torre, it could generate a wave up to 5.8 metres high. The wave would travel across the lake at approximately 20 metres a second, reaching the Fitz Roy River in just one minute and 40 seconds.
Under the most conservative and the worst-case scenarios, a flood would eventually reach the bridge and render it unusable. The bridge is the only land access connecting El Chaltén to provincial route 41.
The municipality has already ordered the dredging of the river channel and the clearing of the riverbed beneath the bridge. “But now we are being told that the water level could rise by up to 5 metres, which suggests the bridge could be swept away,” Rivero says.
The flood could also affect critical infrastructure located just metres from the riverbanks, including gas and power plants, schools and homes. Discussions have already begun on a contingency plan that considers, among other measures, potential relocation.
“Gas supplies coming from Río Gallegos – the capital of Santa Cruz province – would be cut off, leaving us without heating,” says Paula Chaparro, a member of the El Chaltén Mountain Guides Association. “If the power grid fails, El Chaltén relies on generators running on fuel oil; if they run out of fuel, we lose electricity. It’s a problematic chain reaction.”
If the event were to occur in summer, peaking in December to February, the town would be cut off, with more than 27,000 people – locals and tourists alike – stranded in the town. At present, according to residents, there is no signage indicating evacuation routes or instructions, nor do hotels warn guests about the risk.
The risk has been known for years, but the available instruments could not precisely determine how quickly the slope was moving or, crucially, how much water could be displaced in a collapse. “We’ll have to wait and see if it happens” was a common reaction among locals, says Sofía Bonangelino, a member of Friends of Los Glaciares National Park, an association that manages three campsites.
Even Horacio Pelozo, the park superintendent, acknowledges this: “The initial studies really weren’t alarming, or anything of the sort.”
However, a key new piece of data emerged, Pelozo says, alongside the measurements of the slope’s movement: sustained melting had created a second body of water within Laguna Torre, the depth of which now exceeds 220 metres. Previous estimates had placed the depth at about 80 metres.
Then, in May 2025, an image from the Swiss Alps demonstrated the potential scale of a collapse involving ice and rock: the Birch glacier collapsed on to much of the village of Blatten, burying it in a matter of seconds.
Los Glaciares national park has taken steps to address the risk of a Glof, including relocating the De Agostini campsite, rerouting hiking trails, installing warning signs and establishing an evacuation protocol involving at least 25 personnel to manage potential floods during peak visitor seasons.
The response has expanded to include coordination with local and national agencies, such as the municipality of El Chaltén, in the Santa Cruz province, the Federal Emergency Agency and the Argentine Geological and Mining Service, though no formal contingency plan has been finalised yet.
The El Chaltén city council has passed a resolution to develop an evacuation plan, while a detection system with six monitoring stations – equipped with cameras, sensors and emergency buoys – is in development to trigger alerts via sirens, SMS and email. Yet funding cuts have delayed implementation, with the estimated cost of $220,000 (£163,000) exceeding the park’s current capacity, as noted by Eduardo Marino, a former secretary of government for El Chaltén.
“Let’s not talk about Glofs, because it will scare off tourists” – that concern is circulating around town. And it is not hard to understand why – a large part of the community relies on tourism for its livelihood.
Marino owns a hotel; Bonangelino runs a bookstore, rents out a cabin, and works as a ski instructor. For them, as for so many other residents, protecting tourism also means protecting their own livelihoods.
Marino was asked to drop the subject until the summer season was over. He refused. He knows a day of heavy rain or exceptionally high temperatures could be enough to trigger an event they are not yet prepared for.
For those who work in the mountains, information is key to risk management. “Closing down isn’t the solution,” says Chaparro. The idea, she says, is to offer alternatives: different trails, different activities. “It’s not about being afraid; it’s about staying alert.”
When her colleague Ariel Puntin speaks to local people about the threat he still encounters some who doubt the mountainside could collapse. The problem, he says, is that the gap between “it could happen today” and “it might never happen” is too wide to easily learn how to live with the risk.
For Schmidt, the events in Nepal should serve as a wake-up call, but also as an opportunity to improve the town’s preparedness. “The community and the tourists must be protected and kept safe in the face of this new reality of constantly changing glacial landscapes,” she says.
Bonangelino has noticed a positive shift in recent months. As the studies’ findings have been explained to the community, she says, acceptance has grown that the phenomenon is real and that preparation is necessary.
“We are a resilient, responsible community that cares deeply about its environment,” she says. “We rely on tourism, and we aren’t going to neglect it.”

‘Happy Snacking, Don’t Die!’ is a joyous guide to eating wild plants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Happy Snacking, Don’t Die!
Alexis Nikole Nelson
Simon & Schuster, $35.00
I used to think that foraging for food would involve schlepping myself to a forest far from my urban home, a task that would demand an unpleasant car trip, practical shoes and insect repellent. But when I flipped through forager Alexis Nikole Nelson’s new book Happy Snacking, Don’t Die!, I discovered edible plants right in my neighborhood.
Linden trees, for example, are common across much of the United States, including in cities. They have edible leaves, flowers and fruits, Nelson explains. There’s one just down the block from the Science News office in Washington, D.C. And that is how I found myself, this summer, on tiptoe trying to reach as many green, pea-shaped fruits as I could hold.
And that’s not all. Dandelions, acorns, black walnuts, crab apples, roses, magnolias, serviceberries — all are edible treasures found within walking distance of my home. Nelson explains how to identify these and other plants and provides vegan recipes for dishes unlike anything found in grocery stores.
Awareness of local edible plants helps combat the “plant blindness” that pervades modern society. For many people, plants are a pleasant afterthought rather than a focal point of daily life. “Taking the time to get to know your plant neighbors helps even the most urban neighborhood … seem full of nature and whimsy, even if you have to look close to find it,” she writes.
The book’s cheeky title is a tagline Nelson uses in popular videos posted to her social media accounts, where she sometimes goes by “Black Forager.” (She uses humor to help viewers learn which plants are good for snacking and which ones might make you, uh, “unalive.”) Likewise, the joy Nelson injects into the book makes foraging approachable.
I was nervous about picking unfamiliar fruits from trees in public. Wouldn’t everyone think I was weird? But with Nelson’s encouragement I felt emboldened. While collecting my bounty of linden fruits, I had a few friendly conversations with passersby and had the opportunity to educate neighbors about the tree.
Linden is in the same family as cacao and it can serve as a chocolate substitute, Nelson explains. Following her recipe for linden ice cream, I roasted, ground and sifted my linden fruits. Then, I combined them with sugar, soy milk, vanilla and cornstarch and cooked and froze the mixture. The ice cream tasted like an earthier version of chocolate. Taste testers — some of my Science News colleagues — compared it to brownie batter, cereal milk and tea. But in fact, linden fruits are their own thing with their own incomparable flavor.
It was a fascinating project, but not a complete success. I collected just a fifth of the amount of fruit that Nelson suggested in her recipe, so I was able to make only about a cup of ice cream. And it had an unpleasantly grainy texture despite my best attempts at grinding and sifting.
But at least now I will never overlook a linden tree.

Viture’s Vonder Glasses Are Meant to Map Your Mind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

David Jiang, cofounder and CEO of smart glasses company Viture, tells me about how he used to yell at his kid.
His 10-year-old son played tennis. During tournaments, Jiang says he had a habit of shouting and criticizing his son’s mistakes as he played. He wanted to apply pressure to make him succeed—it was the way he’d been taught to raise kids, after all. It made sense.
But then, unprompted, his smart glasses sent him a message. The AI assistant in his company’s newest wearable had picked up on what he was doing, recognized that his behavior wasn’t helpful, and messaged him about what he should do differently. Stop shouting. Stop criticizing. Just be there, be present, and show that you support your son. That worked, Jiang says, and being called out like that has supposedly made him a better father and improved the relationship with his kid, all thanks to his yet-to-be-released Vonder AI glasses.
“I didn't know this until Vonder could find my pattern,” Jiang says. “This is not only a tool that can summarize your life, but also a tool that can help yourself to be a better person.”
Viture, a San Francisco-based company known for its plug-in virtual display glasses, announced its first pair of spectacles with no virtual display on Tuesday. The glasses instead look remarkably like normal glasses, but aim to map out your memories, ideas, and goals and plop them on a digital vision board, all without embedded cameras.
Now co-headquartered in California and Beijing, Viture has made glasses like the Viture One and the Viture Beast—wearable face computers that connect via USB-C cable to a device to project its screen right before your eyes. The company's products have primarily targeted gamers or anyone interested in big-screen entertainment. They work well for that purpose, but their chunky design means they fall short in comfort and fashion.
The new glasses are a bit of a pivot. They're called Vonder, you know, like “wonder” but with a V, and they don't have cameras. The glasses' arms feature mics and speakers that can play music, dictate map directions, and let the wearer make phone calls. Vonder also features a built-in AI assistant that combines the top large language models. It can trigger OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, Google’s Gemini, or even DeepSeek. Based on the task’s complexity, Vonder AI will source the answer from whichever model is the quickest and most economical.
They cost $299, can be fitted with prescriptions, come in a variety of frame shapes and colors, and can have clear, transition, or shaded sunglass lenses. Preorders launch September 28, and they’ll ship in November.
The company, like other smart-glass brands Xreal and Even Realities, is trying to make it very clear that it is not Meta, distancing itself from the ire Meta’s Ray-Bans have generated for their privacy-encroaching features. Viture says above all else, it wants its smart glasses to be a good pair of glasses. Ones that operate privately—the kind of frames people will willingly wear without worrying about being labeled a creep.
A blue indicator light turns on when the glasses are recording audio. It’s a small dot on the arms of the glasses, less central and less immediately noticeable than the indicator light on the Ray-Ban Meta glasses.
But Viture stands apart because most of the time, the glasses can collect data only when the wearer is speaking. You can trigger a meeting mode, and it will use on-board microphones to record the environment around you, but the rest of the time, they use bone-conduction sensors in the frames that can passively pick up the audio vibrations of the person wearing them all day long. (The Vonder glasses get about 16 hours of battery life.)
Once it collects information about your day and what you talk about, the assistant generates a personal memory graph that tracks your memories—things like what coffee shops you’ve been to, what sports you play, or whatever else you choose to confide in the glasses. As long as you’re talking about something, the glasses will pick that up and try to interpret the context to make a broader picture of what you’re up to. In the app, it displays all those connections in a big web graphic.
In a demo of how the glasses work, Jiang showed that the Vonder glasses he's wearing have kept tabs on his life over the past three months. He can ask it where to find coffee shops based on his caffeine preferences or have it help figure out why he's felt so stressed lately. The tech is also preemptive, pulling up topics he's been thinking about, like help with hiring decisions he's been mulling over and a plan for announcing his new smart glasses a day before Meta Connect. It also pulled up a dossier on me that it presented to him the morning he came to visit. It clearly knew who I was, what I write about, and had suggested some topics for him to prepare for.
“We just want to mimic the way your brain works,” Jiang says. “This is not a transcript or a summary. This is just how your memory organizes in your brain, even better than your memory.”
The Vonder glasses raise a question of how self-indulgent the information you’re collecting across your day is. It only records one perspective, after all—yours. That means you have to be comfortable sharing your thoughts with the glasses if you want them stored in the memory graph or have conversations with others all day.
I ask Jiang about this: how you make sure the information in your mind web considers other factors than your own perspective. Jiang says if he wants something to stick, he tends to repeat what someone else said.
“In a conversation, a human tends to repeat because a conversation is turn by turn—if you have a question, I follow up your question and then AI knows what the question is,” Jiang says, “Even though there's a missing part, it's not 50 percent missing. It's maybe only 10 percent or 15 percent.”
I ask what he’d do if we were arguing right now. If I’d felt one way and he another, and then he went back to his mind web and tried to revisit the conversation. Would it bias him if his own voice was only the information it was given? This is what prompts him to talk about his kid playing tennis. That the glasses had outright told him he was wrong about something.
“The problem right now is that AI has really, really powerful somatic knowledge, but the missing part is the human episodic memory there,” Jiang says. “In the past three months I’ve used these glasses, I feel my life has been changed or improved.”

Adobe Premiere, One of the iPhone’s Best Video-Editing Apps, Is Now on Android
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Nearly a year after releasing Premiere for iPhone, Adobe is finally bringing its redesigned video-editing app to Android. The app has been in beta for several weeks but is now available as the official successor to Premiere Rush, which the company will stop supporting on September 30.
Eric Snowden, senior vice president of design at Adobe, tells WIRED the feedback for the iOS app has been “incredibly positive” (to his credit, it has a 4.8-star rating out of 5 on the App Store with more than 25,000 ratings). The goal with the Android version wasn't just to port the iPhone app experience, but to make it feel really native to Google's platform.
That includes making sure the app works just as well on every kind of Android device out there, whether it's a Samsung foldable or a candy bar Google Pixel. Yes, when you open up a folding phone with the Adobe Premiere app, you can view your footage on the left and see the multi-track timeline on the right, maximizing space. Snowden suggests optimizing the app for Android foldables will help the company with the iPhone app for the upcoming iPhone Duo.
And if you're wondering whether this app will work well on Google's new Googlebook laptop platform, Adobe says its apps—Acrobat, Photoshop, Lightroom, and Premiere—are optimized for the new laptops, meaning they'll take advantage of the larger screen, but can’t quite deliver the “desktop-grade” experience you’ll find on Windows or macOS.
Equally important is ensuring the app runs on lower-power devices, though Premiere has a minimum requirement of 5 GB of RAM (phones will also need to run Android 13 or later).
“We wanted this to run on as many devices as possible, so the team spent a ton of time making sure that this is not just for flagship phones,” Snowden says. “This is for a really broad range of Android devices.”
Launch the Adobe Premiere app and you will see all your footage from your camera roll on the home screen. From there, you can choose creator-made templates—ranging from lifestyle to beauty to templates for foodies—to get started on an edit, or start from scratch if you'd like.
It's easy to add your footage, then opt for the mini editor or the full editor. The former lets you easily trim or replace your footage, and even choose a filter to apply a specific color style to all of your clips. You can export directly to YouTube Shorts without leaving Premiere. The full editor gives you a multitrack timeline for more granular edits, like layering text, music, and effects.
Several AI tools are on board, like Enhance Audio, which can boost the subject's voice and cut background noise. If you want to add a voice-over, you can speak into your phone's mic and see your footage in real time so it all matches up. Adobe says the app has Firefly-powered AI features, like Generative Fill, Image-to-Video, and Generate Sound Effects. However, these require generative credits, aka a subscription, if you run out of your monthly allotment.
Some features are still “coming soon,” like the Continue Editing function so you can wrap up an edit on desktop after starting it on mobile, or support for Adobe Fonts.
Uniquely (for an Adobe product), you do not have to log in or subscribe to Adobe's creative suite to use Premiere on Android. Like the iOS version, the app is free to use.
“What we're seeing with a lot of mobile apps right now is that there are these huge barriers to entry to using it for the first time,” Snowden says. “We really wanted to get away from that, and I think part of the accessibility and simplicity of the app—the onboarding process is part of that—and we just want to get people in and using it."

AI Models Built From Rat Brains Just Got Closer to Reality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

A biological computing startup that uses neural patterns from rat brain cells to build artificial intelligence just got a major boost from Amazon.
Starting Tuesday, select Amazon Web Services customers will gain access to The Biological Computing Company’s “rat brain” AI model as part of a limited preview. The startup’s technology is specifically designed to improve AI for generating videos. Both Amazon and The Biological Computing Company, which goes by the acronym TBC, says they expect the tech to roll out to all AWS enterprise customers soon.
“We figured out a way to code information, like images for example, to the biological material,” says TBC cofounder Alexander Ksendzovsky. “We then observe how the biology processes that information, and then we build a tool that mimics that process.”
This is not the first biologically-derived computing platform that Amazon has made available in its marketplace, says Deap Ubhi, global director of technology for startups at Amazon Web Services. Ubhi says the cloud-computing giant also works with Cortical Labs, an Australia-based company that combines lab-grown neurons with silicon chips to help companies process data. (It calls its products WAAS, or “wetware as a service.”) Cortical Labs also sells a multi-thousand dollar “biological computer,” a low-power device designed for use in laboratories that can supposedly keep neurons alive for six months.
TBC takes a “pragmatic approach,” says Ubhi, which is part of why the company appealed to Amazon. Rather than taking big swings or trying to reinvent the transformer, the core architectural unit of large language models, “they’re working within existing standards of the generative AI space and saying, ‘How can we make the current visual models more efficient?’” he explains.
As AI companies race to find ways to make their models more efficient, a once-fringe field known as biological computing has begun gaining traction. Researchers have long envisioned a world where computer software performs more like the neural networks inside human brains instead of relying solely on math-based algorithms.
But biological computing comes with unique challenges. The field requires running actual biology labs, not just computer labs, in which brain cells, stem cells, or synthetic biomaterials must be kept alive or preserved, carefully monitored, and somehow translated into meaningful digital information. While some startups have made progress in the field, bridging the divide between nature and code remains complicated.
The Biological Computing Company was founded in Baltimore, Maryland four years ago by two neuroscientists and neurosurgeons: Ksendzovsky, now the company’s CEO, and Jon Pomeraniec, who serves as president and COO. Earlier this year, TBC raised $25 million from a group of investors led by Primary Venture Partners, its first significant round of funding.
Shortly after that round closed in March, the company secured an additional $25 million, bringing its funding total to more than $50 million. This new round of capital has not been previously reported.
Last year, the startup opened offices and a small research and development lab in San Francisco. TBC now has about 35 employees, some of whom work directly with rat brain cells as well as human stem cells in the lab. The living cells are placed on multi-electrode silicon arrays made by 3Brain, a Swiss biotech company. Researchers use the arrays to send electrical stimulation patterns into the neurons and record how they respond. TBC then analyzes that neural activity for computational patterns that can be translated into software and used to improve existing AI models, specifically video generation models.
The decision to focus on video out of the gate was both scientific and practical, says Ksendzovsky. One factor was the physical layout of the multi-electrode silicon arrays Biological Computing Company uses. The place where each electrode sits affects how it interacts with the neurons. The company realized images were a natural place to start, since visual information could be mapped onto the grid more readily than text or language.
From there, a potential business use case emerged. The startup theorized that by modeling how the neurons process images, the insights could be used to improve AI models for generating video.
Pomeraniec says that Jeff Dean, a prominent AI researcher and TBC investor, was the person who first suggested that the company try fine-tuning video generation models before trying to apply its neural tech more broadly.
Because there’s already accepted industry benchmarks for video models, the startup could show early on whether its tech represented a meaningful scientific advancement by testing its performance on problems that have been solved already. “Jeff said if we could do that, there’s the promise of doing more complex, interesting things with our AI models down the line,” Pomeraniec explains.
Previously, TBC’s technology was only available through a neocloud provider called Bluesky Compute. The startup is claiming that its AI model, when compared against the open-source AI model it runs on, is up to five times faster at video generation and significantly lowers the cost of inference, the processing or “thinking” part of an AI model versus the training of it. (The company won’t say which open-source AI it is using as a comparison, but claims it’s one of the “frontier” video generation models.)
Now that Amazon is distributing TBC’s software, the ambitious startup could potentially reach a much larger customer base. Amazon’s Ubhi says he’s excited about The Biological Computing Company, but it remains to be seen how well its technology can scale.
“I think with any model like this, the one thing you have to ask is, if you push it to the extremes, will you still see improvements? If you have customers who want to generate longer-form videos, ten minutes, an hour, what’s the potential loss in fidelity over the course of time?” he asks. In other words, a model needs to be able to keep track of what has already happened and maintain consistency as a video gets longer. As TBC enters its next phase, the company will be looking to see whether its technology holds up as new customers try pushing it to the limit.
Update 9/22/26 5:00 pm ET: This story has been updated to clarify that not all of Biological Computing Company's employees work directly with biological cells in its San Francisco lab.

15,000 education professionals participate in teachers' warning strike

15,000 education professionals participate in teachers' warning strike
Around 15,000 education workers took part in Tuesday's nationwide warning strike, according to data received so far by the Estonian Educational Personnel Union (EHL).
More than 400 educational institutions took part in the strike.
"Based on the information we have so far, however, we can say with certainty that today's warning strike showed just how many education workers are prepared to act together to ensure that teachers' salaries finally reach a competitive level," EHL Chair Reemo Voltri said.
According to Voltri, the high level of participation was largely driven by widespread dissatisfaction among teachers, which has grown in recent years.
"This is mainly due to the heavy workload and level of responsibility, which are not matched by teachers' salaries. EHL's latest survey confirmed that 69 percent of teachers in Estonia have considered leaving the profession over the past year. The main factors are precisely the heavy workload and low pay," Voltri said.
The next round of negotiations on the minimum salary for teachers will take place at 3 p.m. Wednesday at the Ministry of Education and Research's Tallinn office.
EHL is seeking to raise the minimum salary for teachers to the projected Estonian average salary in 2027, or €2,312. The current minimum salary for teachers is €1,970.
"I am trying to remain optimistic, although in recent weeks we have seen the government gradually back away from its promise to raise teachers' salaries to 120 percent of the national average," Voltri said.
Tuesday's warning strike lasted one hour: from 8 a.m. to 9 a.m. at preschool institutions and from 9 a.m. to 10 a.m. at general education schools and vocational education institutions.
EHL is continuing to collect data on actual participation from strike organizers and will publish the final number of participants once the data has been compiled.

Estonian MFA official: No reason to free 2 Russian oligarchs from sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:59:00 UTC
21:59:00 KST

Estonian MFA official: No reason to free 2 Russian oligarchs from sanctions
There is no reason to remove Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the EU sanctions list, as France, Luxembourg and Slovakia had sought, MFA Deputy Secretary General Kerli Veski told ERR.
European Union member state representatives agreed Monday to lift sanctions imposed on Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman. This was the price that had to be paid for member states to reach an agreement on extending EU sanctions against Russia.
The decision was blocked reportedly following objections from Latvia, Latvian public broadcaster LSM reported late Monday. Member state representatives must now find a new solution by midnight Tuesday.
The sanctions had already been due to expire a week ago, but member states temporarily extended them for another week in the hope of reaching an agreement with the countries that had made demands regarding the oligarchs.
The proposed agreement emerged after France and Luxembourg each proposed removing one of the men from the EU sanctions list, apparently for domestic political reasons.
"Both of these oligarchs have actually been on the sanctions list since 2022 precisely because they are oligarchs who support the Kremlin regime and support the aggression against Ukraine. None of the circumstances have eased, their position has not changed in any way and their activities have not changed. In our view, and in the view of most countries, there is no reason to remove these oligarchs from the sanctions list. But as for why some countries have now decided to act otherwise based on their national interests, that is a question for those countries themselves," Kerli Veski, deputy secretary general of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said.
Veski said the question ultimately is whether the EU should be in a situation at all where countries seek to have someone removed from the European Union sanctions list based on national interests.
According to Veski, such a loosening of the sanctions regime also poses a major risk going forward because it could send the wrong message to Russia.
"We can also add the question of whether, every time this comes up in the future, another country could come forward with its own national interests. It would set a very bad precedent if this were to go through in this form," Veski added.
Veski said the best solution would be to extend the sanctions regime again for at least six months or even for up to three years.
"From the very beginning, we have actually taken the position, not only alongside Latvia but alongside most countries, that removing anyone from the sanctions list for politically motivated reasons should not even be under consideration at this point. That has been our fundamental position throughout the negotiations and it is the position we have defended," Veski said.
"Now that we are down to the final hours, various questions and solutions are naturally on the table as to how we can ensure that those 3,000 names remain under sanctions. In other words, the most important thing for us is that the entire sanctions regime does not collapse. That is where things stand right now: how do we achieve that? Ideally, of course, without a single name being removed and with the sanctions regime extended for much longer periods instead of having to renew it every six months," Veski emphasized.

UN warns of rising Yemen displacement as thousands flee to Djibouti
Renewed fighting could drive 10,000 across the Red Sea and displace more than 230,000 internally, UNHCR says.
The number of refugees fleeing Yemen across the Red Sea to Djibouti could reach 10,000 as result of renewed fighting in the country, while internal displacement inside Yemen could swell to more than 230,000, the United Nations has warned.
The Iran-aligned Houthi rebels seized control of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline earlier this month in a dramatic offensive that has left hundreds of people on both sides dead, threatened global trade, and pushed up energy prices.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Can the US ban Iranian airlines worldwide – and what would it mean?
- list 2 of 3Why the world should care about the far right’s rise in Germany
- list 3 of 3Palestine weekly: Violent disruptions from olive groves to Al-Aqsa Mosque
The latest fighting between the Houthis and forces loyal to the Aden-based government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, has set off a new humanitarian crisis.
More than 100,000 civilians have been uprooted inside Yemen, while others have risked dangerous sea crossings to escape the violence.
“Intensifying fighting in Yemen could drive more mass displacement,” United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR) spokesperson Babar Baloch told reporters in Geneva on Tuesday.
More than 3,000 people fled across the Red Sea to Djibouti over several days earlier this month, Djibouti state media reported. The UNHCR said it was bracing for that number to rise significantly, especially after mid-October when the current difficult sea conditions are expected to improve.
The agency and its partners are now “planning for more than 10,000 arrivals in Djibouti” in the coming months, Baloch said.
At the same time, the number of people displaced within Yemen by the recent fighting could swell from more than 130,000 today to more than 230,000, he said.
That comes on top of the more than 5.2 million people who were already internally displaced in Yemen before the fighting resumed.
Baloch warned that the renewed conflict was deepening an already dire crisis in the country, where an estimated 22 million people require humanitarian assistance.
He warned that a severe funding shortfall was hampering the response to the emergency, with the UNHCR’s Yemen operation currently just 18 percent funded for 2026.
The agency estimated that $25m is urgently needed to provide approximately 231,000 people with immediate aid.
Meanwhile, the UNHCR’s Djibouti operations are only 15 percent funded, with the agency appealing for $13.5m “to ensure arrivals can access registration, reception, protection, and other essential services”.

EXPLAINER - Morocco heads to polls: What to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:58:21 UTC
21:58:21 KST

Serdar Dincel
22 September 2026•Update: 22 September 2026
- 7,288 candidacies have been registered nationwide, official data shows
- Main parliamentary forces are broadly divided between parties forming current government coalition and those in opposition
Morocco heads to the polls on Wednesday for a parliamentary election that will determine the makeup of the country’s 395-seat House of Representatives and shape the next government under King Mohammed VI.
Some 15.8 million registered voters are eligible to cast ballots in the North African kingdom, where political parties compete for control of parliament but the monarch retains significant powers over the state’s most important political and strategic decisions.
The vote will be Morocco’s sixth legislative election since Mohammed VI took the throne in 1999, and the fourth since constitutional reforms introduced after the 2011 Arab Spring expanded the powers of parliament and the prime minister while preserving the king’s central role.
Here is a look at Morocco’s political system, the main parties competing in the election, the groups boycotting the vote and how Moroccans living abroad can cast their ballots.
How does the election work?
Twenty-eight political parties are vying for 395 seats in the House of Representatives.
A total of 7,288 candidacies have been registered nationwide, averaging more than 18 candidates per seat.
Since Morocco is divided into local electoral constituencies, 305 seats are elected locally and 90 others are elected through regional constituencies.
The Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM), Istiqlal Party, Party of Progress and Socialism and Justice and Development Party each submitted 92 local lists, covering all 92 local constituencies, with 305 candidates each.
The National Rally of Independents (RNI) also submitted 92 local lists with 305 candidates, while other parties submitted fewer lists
Who are the main parties?
The main parliamentary forces are broadly divided between the parties forming the current government coalition and those in opposition.
The coalition consists of the National Rally of Independents, the Authenticity and Modernity Party, and the Istiqlal Party.
RNI, the largest party in the 2021 election, is seeking to maintain its position, while PAM is aiming to emerge as the leading party and head the government for the first time. Istiqlal is also seeking to expand its influence after joining the coalition in 2021.
The main opposition parties include the Socialist Union of Popular Forces, the Party of Progress and Socialism, the Popular Movement and the Justice and Development Party, which are seeking to increase their representation in parliament.
The election will determine the composition of the House and, under Morocco’s constitutional system, the party that emerges with the largest number of seats will be called upon to form the government.
Who is boycotting the election?
Not all political groups are taking part.
The Justice and Charity Association, Morocco’s largest religious movement, and the Democratic Labour Way Party, a left-wing group, are boycotting the election.
Both have criticized the political environment and argued that the conditions do not allow for what they consider free and fair political competition.
Can Moroccans living abroad vote?
The Interior Ministry has launched an online platform allowing Moroccans living abroad who are registered on the electoral rolls to arrange voting by proxy.
Under Moroccan law, eligible voters abroad can appoint a voter registered in Morocco to cast a ballot on their behalf.
The electronic platform allows them to complete the proxy procedure before election day.
Who oversees voting?
Morocco’s Central Election Monitoring Commission, supported by regional and provincial committees, oversees the electoral process.
A total of 3,006 accredited observers, including representatives of 20 international and regional organizations, will monitor the legislative elections on Sept. 23.
Independent and impartial election observation has been regulated by law since 2011.
Observers monitor the process independently and cannot intervene in electoral operations, while state monitoring committees can take action over violations.

Lockheed, Kongsberg test twin-Javelin setup on armored turret
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:55:18 UTC
21:55:18 KST

- The Javelin Joint Venture and Kongsberg completed a simulation demonstration in Norway using a Medium-Caliber Turret fitted with a prototype dual Javelin launcher assembly.
- The companies called it the first phase of an integration effort and have not disclosed a target vehicle platform or timeline for further testing.
The Javelin Joint Venture completed a simulation demonstration in Norway using a Kongsberg Medium-Caliber Turret fitted with a prototype dual launcher assembly for the Javelin anti-tank missile.
The companies described it as the first phase of an ongoing effort to integrate Javelin more closely with vehicle-mounted turret systems.
The Javelin Joint Venture is a partnership between Lockheed Martin and Raytheon, an RTX business, that builds and sells the Javelin missile system. Javelin is a shoulder-fired, fire-and-forget anti-tank weapon that has also been adapted for vehicle-mounted use over the past decade, most often paired with Kongsberg’s remote weapon stations rather than a full turret system like the Medium-Caliber Turret.
The Medium-Caliber Turret, built by Norway’s Kongsberg, is best known in U.S. service as the turret on the Army’s Stryker Dragoon vehicles, where it carries a 30 mm autocannon along with a coaxial machine gun. Kongsberg’s turret family already supports Javelin as an add-on weapon in some configurations, mounted either on a companion remote weapon station or alongside the turret’s main gun. A dual launcher assembly would let a single turret carry two ready-to-fire Javelin rounds rather than one.
Kongsberg and the Javelin Joint Venture have worked together on vehicle-mounted Javelin systems since at least 2012, when the two companies fired Javelin missiles from a Kongsberg Protector remote weapon station mounted on a Piranha V vehicle during winter trials in Norway. More recent demonstrations have shown Javelin firing from robotic and unmanned ground vehicles equipped with Kongsberg’s Common Remotely Operated Weapon Station, including a 2024 U.S. Army exercise in which Javelin fired from two different unmanned ground vehicles at once.
The U.S. Army remains the Javelin Joint Venture’s largest customer. The venture is operating under an indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity production contract with a ceiling of $7.2 billion covering fiscal years 2023 through 2026, and it delivered the first units of a new Lightweight Command Launch Unit to the Army in May. The Army has not said whether it is evaluating the Medium-Caliber Turret dual launcher configuration for its own vehicle fleet.

Latvian information technology group Datlex continues to expand its expertise in business intelligence and data analytics. SIA Digitex, a software development company within the group, is acquiring a 90% stake in SIA InfoStrategy. An existing co-owner of InfoStrategy will retain a 10% stake and continue working at the company.
The transaction marks the next step in the growth of the Datlex Group following the 2025 acquisition of Visma Consulting by Codex, another IT company within the group. Following the acquisition, Visma Consulting continued its operations under the name Digitex. The latest transaction will expand the group’s expertise in developing business intelligence solutions and increase its capacity to deliver larger-scale projects across the Baltic states.
“We do not want to grow simply in terms of numbers—each transaction must bring new expertise and opportunities into the group. InfoStrategy is a small but highly professional team with strong experience in business intelligence and data analytics. By combining its expertise with the technological capabilities of Digitex and Codex, we will be able to undertake larger and more complex projects,” said Uldis Semeiks, Member of the Management Board of Datlex.
With InfoStrategy joining the group, Datlex gains the team’s expertise, accumulated project experience and portfolio of business intelligence solutions. InfoStrategy will continue working with its existing clients and contracts as before. Since its establishment in 2016, the company has specialised in business management and analytics solutions, including management planning, budgeting, cost calculation modelling and data analytics, serving clients throughout the Baltic states.
“Nothing will change in our clients’ day-to-day cooperation with us—they will continue working with the same people they have known for years. What will change is the scale of our capabilities: joining a larger group will give us access to broader technological expertise and capacity that a team of eight could not provide on its own. We will retain our specialisation in business intelligence while gaining the ability to undertake significantly larger projects,” said Romāns Kairovs, Member of the Management Board of InfoStrategy.
Following the transaction, InfoStrategy will continue operating under its existing name and brand. No change to the company’s name or visual identity is currently planned.
Datlex Strengthens Its Group Model Across the Baltic States
The acquisition of InfoStrategy forms part of the Datlex Group’s broader development strategy. The group’s operations are structured around two principal business areas: IT infrastructure solutions and software development.
In the infrastructure segment, the group operates across the Baltic states and Scandinavia. In Latvia, this business area is represented by Datakom, which provides the implementation and maintenance of IT infrastructure solutions, as well as related consulting services. Other companies within the group complement this offering with IT consulting and infrastructure management services. The group’s companies have more than 30 years of experience in this field.
The group’s software development segment comprises Codex, Digitex and InfoStrategy. Codex and Digitex primarily develop customised business information systems for public- and private-sector clients, while InfoStrategy strengthens the group’s expertise in business intelligence, data analytics and data-driven solutions.
“We are developing as a unified group rather than as a collection of separate companies. Our complementary areas of expertise allow us to cooperate freely and make effective use of the knowledge and experience available across the entire group. It is precisely this close cooperation between our software development and infrastructure teams that enables us to offer clients throughout the Baltic states and Scandinavia broader and more technologically sophisticated solutions,” Uldis Semeiks explained.
The Datlex Group will continue assessing opportunities for growth and the acquisition of new expertise in the Baltic market, combining organic development with the integration of professional teams.
The transaction was financed in cooperation with Swedbank, using a guarantee provided by the European Investment Fund under the European Union’s InvestEU programme.

Linell Raud: 43,000 Estonian companies may face tax risk in 187 countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:50:00 UTC
21:50:00 KST

Linell Raud: 43,000 Estonian companies may face tax risk in 187 countries
Do we explain tax risks clearly enough to e‑residents, or do we only whisper about taxes because the topic is too complicated, asks Linell Raud.
For the past decade, Estonia's flagship on the international stage has been the e‑residency program. More and more, however, it has become clear that behind a simple program lie only complicated tax problems. Since Estonia has already had to acknowledge international reputational damage in the Danske Bank money‑laundering scandal and in recently uncovered shell‑round deals, it would be wise to prevent the next blow rather than provide the drama theater with material for another hit production.
The e‑residency program has been successfully marketed worldwide as an easy way to establish a company in Estonia within minutes, bring business profits here, and benefit from our tax system, where profits are taxed only upon distribution. But do we explain tax risks clearly enough to e‑residents both in Estonia and abroad, or do we only whisper about taxes because the topic is too complicated?
So far, 140,000 people from 187 countries have joined the program and established roughly 43,000 companies. In addition to contributing as owners, they participate actively and daily in Estonia's economy as taxpayers and consumers of various goods and services. The direct tax contribution of e‑residents over the lifetime of the program is estimated at about €433 million, and last year alone it was €125 million.
Where does the problem arise?
A more global world brings new problems both in Estonia and in the e‑residents' home countries. Many e‑resident companies operate as one‑person firms, where the owner, board member, and worker are all the same person. There are no employees, no office, clients are generally scattered around the world, and often there are no clients in Estonia at all. The owner does everything remotely, wherever they happen to be.
Like companies founded by Estonians, many e‑resident companies are registered in Estonia as value‑added tax payers. This allows them to freely invoice goods and services sold and purchased, and profit is taxed only upon distribution. But unlike companies operated in Estonia by Estonians, e‑residents face two "buts."
The VAT problem in Estonia
The first "but" is VAT registration. To be registered as a VAT payer in Estonia, a company must conduct business activity in Estonia. If it does not, the Tax and Customs Board (MTA) has the right to cancel the registration. And that is exactly what has happened to many e‑resident companies.
Over the past year, the MTA has focused on checking the VAT numbers of such companies and has requested information about the location of the board, employees, and office. The goal is to assess the companies' real ties to Estonia and the extent of those ties. If it is determined that a company is registered in Estonia and has a VAT number but no actual business activity takes place here, the VAT number is removed.
Once the VAT number is removed, any VAT paid on purchased goods and services becomes a simple expense that can no longer be deducted. The MTA's recommendation in such cases has been that an e‑resident living in another European Union country should explore the possibility of registering as a VAT payer there.
Without business activity in Estonia, the local VAT number will not be kept. Registration abroad may be possible, but unlike Estonia, in most countries it takes a long time.
The income‑tax problem abroad
In addition to VAT, an even more pressing "but" is income tax.
Under the general rule, if a company's activities are managed or carried out daily outside Estonia, the foreign country may have the right to tax the company's profit. The foreign country essentially treats the Estonian company's profit as its own and taxes it as if it had been earned by a local company.
E‑residents are exactly in this situation. They have Estonian private limited companies, but the board member and actual worker — often the same person — are located abroad. Foreign tax authorities are not asleep and are aggressively checking such companies and taxing their profits. Since most countries tax corporate profits annually, the tax obligation is determined for each year, including retroactively.
For example, if a French e‑resident established a company in Estonia in 2023 and earned about €500,000 in profit, the French tax authority has determined that because the board member is located in France, the Estonian company has had a permanent establishment there since its founding.
France has taxed all profits retroactively, and €150,000 in income tax must be paid. In addition, the company owes €100,000 in interest and penalties for not acting correctly from the start.
In some cases, the foreign tax authority has also fined the company's board member personally. In the French example, the personal tax risk was €250,000. So from roughly €500,000 in profit, the foreign tax risk became €500,000. Profit drops to zero, and stress, pressure, and administrative burden skyrocket.
E‑residents understandably ask where the promised tax advantage and simplicity went. The correct answer is that everything promised applies only if the company's board and actual business activity are in Estonia. If either is missing, a profit‑sized tax risk is a real possibility.
Can this risk be avoided?
Measure nine times, cut once applies here as well. Timely notification and reaction would help avoid unpleasant surprises that are indeed mentioned on the e‑residency website but have not reached e‑residents' awareness.
Although company finances are each person's own responsibility, the program could consider stronger communication about risk areas. The mentality of dealing with the problem only once it appears does not work in tax matters. If a company has entered a tax authority's field of interest, it may already be too late to show ties to Estonia or reduce foreign tax risk.
Although the e‑residency website includes an overview of both income‑tax and VAT risks and recommends consulting advisers, this does not seem to be enough. Perhaps it could include specific recommendations, coordinated with the MTA, on bringing the board to Estonia or hiring employees for an office here.
Although such recommendations may bring additional ongoing costs for e‑residents, they would actually create more jobs in Estonia, increase tax revenue, and reduce future misunderstandings with tax authorities on both sides of the border.
E‑residency as Estonia's flagship works only if people participate. To ensure the program continues to bring tax revenue to Estonia, we should speak honestly about both its strengths and weaknesses. If e‑residents feel they learn about real tax risks only through professional advisers or when the tax authority is already knocking, this could become a new ticking reputational bomb or inspiration for another hit stage production.
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon

Due to climate change, Tunisia sees 2026 summer as hottest on record
Tunisia's summer this year was its hottest on record, the country's weather authority said Tuesday, following multiple heatwaves, water shortages and power cuts.
"The summer of 2026 was ranked the hottest in Tunisia since 1950," the year temperature records began, the National Meteorological Institute said.
The average temperature was about 2.9 degrees Celsius higher than the previous record, it added.
Although accustomed to scorching heat, Tunisia experienced a particularly gruelling summer in 2026, with July and August marked by "intense and prolonged heatwaves", the authority said.
Scientists attribute these episodes to climate change.
This summer also saw persistently high nighttime temperatures, the agency added.
The highest temperature was recorded in the central city of Kairouan, which reached 49.7 degrees Celsius in mid-July.

Erdogan Says ‘The World Is Bigger Than Five’ as He Calls for UN Veto Abolition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:49:22 UTC
21:49:22 KST

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has called for the abolition of the UN Security Council’s veto power and an end to permanent membership, arguing that the body’s structure no longer reflects the realities of the modern world.
“The tragedies of recent years, including pandemics, energy crises, disruptions to supply chains and regional conflicts, have demonstrated that leaving the resolution of global crises to the will of a handful of capitals is no longer compatible with the realities of today’s world,” Erdogan wrote in an opinion piece published by Bloomberg ahead of the UN General Assembly’s annual session in New York.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The adaptation of global decision-making mechanisms to today’s circumstances can no longer be postponed.”
The Security Council has five permanent members – China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States – all of which have veto power.
The arrangement was established in the UN Charter in 1945, when the five countries, then including the Soviet Union rather than Russia, were given permanent seats because of their central roles in establishing the UN and maintaining international peace and security.
Russia later took over the Soviet Union’s seat.
The council also has 10 non-permanent members elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms. A substantive resolution requires at least nine votes and cannot pass if one of the permanent members votes against it.
Ukraine, Russia, Hard to Reconcile on Black Sea, Turkish Minister Says
Erdogan said simply adding new permanent members would not address the concentration of power.
“Adding new privileged members to the Security Council would not resolve the problem of decision-making power being concentrated in the hands of a few states; rather, it would expand the scope of the privileged structure,” he wrote.
Instead, he proposed abolishing permanent membership altogether. Under his model, all Security Council members would be elected by the General Assembly on a rotating basis for fixed terms, with countries seeking another term required to win majority support again.
“The powers of the General Assembly should be strengthened, and the representativeness of the Security Council and its accountability to the General Assembly should be enhanced,” Erdogan wrote.
He framed the proposal as an extension of his long-standing slogan: “The world is bigger than five.”
“We must harness the experience, capacity and aspirations of different regions in efforts to address global and regional challenges,” Erdogan wrote. “In this respect, our call that ‘The world is bigger than five’ is a call for a broader understanding of responsibility.”
Reform has been discussed for years
The push for reform is not new, and the General Assembly has been discussing changes to the Security Council for years.
In September 2024, UN member states adopted the Pact for the Future, committing to reform the Security Council and make it “more representative, inclusive, transparent, efficient, effective, democratic and accountable.”
The agreement identified the underrepresentation of Africa as a priority and called for continued negotiations on the council’s membership and the future of the veto.
The General Assembly has continued intergovernmental negotiations on reform, but the council’s basic structure has not changed.
The reform process remains focused on questions including how many members the council should have, which regions should receive greater representation and whether the veto should be limited or otherwise changed.
How the veto can block the UN
The veto gives each of the five permanent members the ability to block a substantive Security Council resolution even if the measure has broad support among the other members.
Russia demonstrated that power in March 2024, when it vetoed a resolution that would have extended the mandate of a UN panel monitoring North Korea’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs, with Moscow and Pyongyang having fostered closer defense ties since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
The other Security Council members did not block the measure, but Russia’s veto was sufficient to prevent its adoption.
The mechanism has also been central to the Security Council’s response to major international conflicts, including Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine, where Moscow’s status as a permanent member has prevented the council from adopting resolutions opposed by Russia.
Erdogan argues that such a system allows a small number of capitals to determine whether the UN can act on major international crises.
“We cannot build the international order of the future by preserving the hierarchies of the past,” he wrote.
“The developments of the last quarter century – a relatively brief period in world history – have demonstrated that no balance of power and no international order are permanent.”
Ankara says it will support efforts to abolish the veto, strengthen the role of elected Security Council members and give the General Assembly greater weight in international decision-making.
“Such a change requires international will on a broad scale,” Erdogan wrote.

Swedish prosecutors probe election fraud allegation casting shadow over vote

Swedish prosecutors probe election fraud allegation casting shadow over vote
STOCKHOLM, Sept 22 - Swedish prosecutors are investigating possible election fraud that could lead to a re-run of the vote in one county, potentially putting 11 parliamentary seats in play and raising uncertainty about the final result of the September 13 vote.
Sweden's parliamentary election saw the opposition narrowly defeat the incumbent right-wing government in a vote widely seen as a referendum on whether the far-right Sweden Democrats should be part of the next administration.
However, the prosecution service has started a preliminary investigation into potential election fraud in Borlange, a town in the largely rural county of Dalarna, central Sweden, that might still affect the final result.
The preliminary investigation was initially closed for lack of evidence, but was reopened this week, prosecutor Oskar Edvardsson said. "New information came in that gave reason to look at this further," he told Reuters.
Swedish media reported that the prosecutor's investigation centred on the election of Mohamed Abdukardir Ali, a Left Party candidate for parliament, who unexpectedly overtook other representatives on the ballot for the party.
In Sweden, voters choose a party but can also pick an individual candidate from a party list. The probe related to the several hundred voters who had checked his name amid reports of pre-marked ballots, Swedish media reported.
Ali told Swedish TV that the allegations were false. "It's completely, completely wrong," he said.
Reuters was not immediately able to reach Ali for comment.
ELECTION RE-RUN WOULD BE A FIRST FOR SWEDEN
The investigation, which was opened on September 1, two weeks before the election, is at an early stage and no suspects have been identified, Edvardsson said. He declined to give further details.
Sweden's Election Review Board could decide on a re-run or recount of the vote in Dalarna, which elects 11 members of parliament, if it decides the result is suspect.
An election re-run would be "a blank slate," said Niklas Bolin, professor of political science at Mid Sweden University.
Sweden has never before re-run a parliamentary vote, he said.
Even if there were a re-run, however, the balance between the two blocs at the national level would be unlikely to change, he said. Voters were more likely to move between parties in the same bloc than across blocs.
"But there is the potential for a different result," he added.
In the September 13 election, the centre-left opposition won 176 seats to 173 seats for the right. In Dalarna, the centre-left bloc won six seats and the right-wing bloc five.
The Election Review Board said it was too early to comment.
A re-run would have to take place within three months of the original election. REUTERS

Sri Lanka court convicts 15 over deadly Easter Sunday bombings

Sri Lanka court convicts 15 over deadly Easter Sunday bombings
Nine people were acquitted, while another defendant was found guilty of only some of the charges, the court said.
Sri Lanka’s High Court has convicted 15 of the 24 men accused of being involved in the 2019 Easter Sunday bombings, which killed 279 people, including 45 foreigners, and injured more than 500.
After a five-year trial, the three-judge bench on Tuesday found that 14 of the accused were guilty on all charges, which included murder, conspiracy to commit “terrorism” and possessing firearms and explosives under the Prevention of Terrorism Act.
A 15th defendant was found guilty of only some of the charges, while nine others were acquitted.
All of the accused are from Sri Lanka’s minority Muslim community. Twenty-five men were originally charged, but one defendant died in custody.
Among those convicted on all charges was Mohamed Naufar, whom prosecutors identified as the ringleader who provided support to the eight-member squad that carried out the bombings.
The presiding judge told a packed courtroom that sentencing would take place later on Tuesday. Dozens of police commandos provided security outside as the verdicts were read.
Sri Lanka’s Roman Catholic Church welcomed the convictions. “Finally, we have justice,” Catholic priest Jude Fernando told the AFP news agency. “It has taken a long time to get to this point.”
Teresa Fernando, a survivor who suffered head injuries, said no one should have to endure what she had gone through. “We came here today as victims of this attack to receive justice,” she said. “Whatever the court says… we will bow our heads and accept it.”
Attack on hotels, churches
The coordinated bombings in April 2019 were carried out at three luxury hotels and three churches – two of them Catholic and one Protestant.
A parliamentary committee found that police and intelligence officials failed to act on repeated intelligence warnings of the attacks.
Two Sri Lanka-based armed groups were accused of carrying out the bombings.
Sri Lanka’s Catholic Church has claimed, without providing evidence, that those identified so far as perpetrators are not the masterminds behind the bombings, and that there was a bigger conspiracy behind the attacks.
In July, a former police chief and a former senior Defence Ministry official were also sentenced to death for failing to act promptly on foreign intelligence warnings of possible attacks.

Royan Institute findings highlight MSCs’ potential for cell-based ASD therapy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:45:34 UTC
21:45:34 KST

Royan Institute findings highlight MSCs’ potential for cell-based ASD therapy
TEHRAN – Researchers from Royan Institute, in a study, have managed to lower the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS) scores and certain inflammatory biomarkers in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) using allogeneic mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) derived from umbilical cord Wharton’s jelly.
The study was conducted as part of the ongoing research by Royan researchers in the field of regenerative medicine and in the investigation of the potential applications of MSCs for cell-based therapeutic approaches across a range of diseases.
According to the Public Relations Department of Royan Institute, five children with Level 2 ASD participated in the study and received three intrathecal administrations of MSCs derived from umbilical cord Wharton’s jelly. Each administration consisted of 20 million cells, with a one-month interval between administrations, royan.org reported.
The preliminary findings of a Phase I clinical trial evaluated the safety and tolerability of three intrathecal administrations of allogeneic MSCs derived from umbilical cord Wharton’s jelly in children with ASD. No serious adverse events or Grade 3 or higher adverse events were reported during the study period, and the intervention was considered acceptable in terms of safety and tolerability.
These findings are of particular relevance from the perspective of Phase I study design, as a primary objective of such early-phase trials is to assess the safety and tolerability of an investigational intervention and to determine whether further clinical investigation is warranted.
The researchers assessed the severity of autism-related symptoms using the CARS and reported a reduction in CARS scores in all participants. Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) also demonstrated reductions in certain inflammatory biomarkers, including tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-a) and interleukin-6 (IL-6). Changes in patterns of cerebral electrical activity were additionally reported based on electroencephalographic (EEG) assessments.
These observations may provide a basis for further investigation into the potential relationships among cellular and molecular alterations, neurophysiological parameters, and selected clinical manifestations of autism spectrum disorder in future studies.
According to the investigators, rigorous evaluation of the potential efficacy of this approach, the durability of the observed effects, and its benefit–risk profile will require further clinical trials involving larger numbers of participants, randomized study designs, and appropriate control groups.
The findings of this study, published in the international journal ‘Stem Cell Research & Therapy’, should not be interpreted as evidence that autism has been treated or cured through cell therapy. Rather, the findings provide preliminary data regarding safety and certain clinical and biological changes observed following the intervention, which may inform the design and scientific rationale of future studies.

Unknown Publisher

Poland's Auschwitz Museum faces US lawsuit over art by Holocaust victim
Heirs of a Jewish prisoner at the former Nazi German concentration camp in Auschwitz have filed a lawsuit with a US court over works created during her imprisonment and kept at the Auschwitz Museum in Poland, US media outlet CBS News reported on Saturday.
Daughters of the late Dinah Gottliebova Babbitt, a Holocaust survivor, demand the return of watercolour portraits of fellow prisoners at Auschwitz that Babbitt was forced to paint for notorious Nazi doctor Josef Mengele.
According to CBS News, the lawsuit is among the first two filed after the US state of California and the Congress passed laws which strengthened the ability to claim artworks forcibly taken from Jews during World War Two. The other one regards the return of two 16th-century paintings stolen by Nazi commander Hermann Goering from the collection of a prominent Dutch-Jewish art dealer, currently held at the prominent Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena, California.
Representatives of both museums maintain they hold legal titles to the artworks and intend to keep them on public display.
Auschwitz Memorial spokesman Pawel Sawicki told CBS News that the portraits of Roma victims must remain at the memorial site to document Mengele's murderous medical experiments on camp prisoners. In Sawicki's view, the watercolours should not be categorised as "Nazi-stolen art" in the traditional sense, as they were created by a prisoner under camp orders and are among the few surviving testimonies of Mengele's crimes.
Spokesman for the Auschwitz Memorial Pawel Sawicki told CBS News that the portraits of Roma victims that Gottliebova Babbitt was forced to paint must remain at Auschwitz to document Mengele's horrendous medical experiments on camp prisoners. In Sawicki's view, the artworks should not be labelled "Nazi-stolen art" as the painter created them as a prisoner and therefore had no ownership over them. He said that the watercolours were among the few remaining testimonies of Mengele's crimes.
"While fully respecting the rights of people who created some of the documents here, we are of the opinion that any loss in the collections of the Memorial will constitute irreparable harm," Sawicki said as quoted by CBS News. "...The loss of even the smallest part of the documentation is an irreparable loss and blemish on the memory of the victims of Auschwitz," he said.
According to CBS News, in the period of 1933-1945, the Nazi regime seized over 600,000 works of art from Jewish families, collectors and museums across Europe. Many of those pieces are held today by prominent institutions around the world. (PAP)
