====================================================================================================

Interview: For U.S. and China, stability means predictability, says U.S. scholar Kuhn
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
18:07:26 CST
19:07:26 KST

by Xinhua writer Yang Shilong
NEW YORK, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- The United States and China have different reasons for seeking a more stable relationship, but both stand to gain from greater predictability even as many differences need to be properly managed, U.S. scholar Robert Lawrence Kuhn has said.
"Each side, the U.S. and China, has a big stake in constructive strategic stability, but for different reasons," Kuhn said in a recent interview with Xinhua.
As long as the outcome is constructive strategic stability, he added, "then everybody wins."
Kuhn, a longtime observer of China who has authored books on the country's development and governance, said the concept should not be taken to mean that differences between the two countries have disappeared. Rather, it points to the need to keep differences under control.
Rather, he said, the immediate value of stability is to prevent those differences from repeatedly disrupting the broader relationship and to make its trajectory more predictable.
STABILITY MEANS PREDICTABILITY
Kuhn said the wording of "constructive strategic stability" itself deserves attention, as such terminology can provide strategic guidance for handling bilateral affairs across various fields.
"When China commits to a certain phraseology or certain words, that's a serious meaning," he said.
The central word, he added, is "stability."
"Stability means something that is predictable, something that maintains a trajectory where you can forecast," Kuhn said. "Stability is broadly important from an economic and prosperity point of view for the world, for China, the U.S. for sure."
Kuhn said "constructive" is also significant because it acknowledges that the relationship needs work. The objective is not to pretend that disagreements no longer exist, but to create a framework in which they can be managed, he added.
For Washington, Kuhn pointed to a fierce midterm election environment and multiple international challenges. China, meanwhile, places a premium on a stable external environment as it pursues its economic and development goals.
THE WORLD ALSO HAS A STAKE
From artificial intelligence and climate change, public health and the fight against drug trafficking, China and the United States are involved in many of the major issues confronting the international community.
Kuhn said the benefits of a more predictable relationship would extend beyond the two countries.
"There's no question that U.S.-China relations are the single biggest factor in the world, in terms of giving the world confidence in the future," he said.
He cautioned, however, against confusing stability with reconciliation.
Rather than expecting Washington and Beijing to suddenly work together perfectly, the more immediate objective should be to prevent disputes over tariffs, critical minerals and other issues from repeatedly escalating.
WHY THE STATE VISIT MATTERS
Against that backdrop, Kuhn said an upcoming meeting between Xi and Trump in Washington could be consequential even without dramatic breakthroughs.
"Whenever President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump meet, it is good for U.S.-China relations and for the world," he said.
Kuhn said there is "a good chemistry between the two presidents" and that Trump places considerable weight on personal relationships with other leaders.
A visibly constructive meeting, he said, sends a signal through government and business circles that legitimate engagement with the other country is acceptable. That matters because political uncertainty can itself discourage economic and social ties.
"It's easier not to do something than to do something," Kuhn said. "When there's uncertainty, you just do nothing. That's the safest thing to do."
The same applies to people-to-people exchanges. Kuhn said scholars, healthcare professionals, cultural institutions and others have increasingly worried that engagement could be interpreted as "aiding the other side, the competitor."
Clear support from the top can help create political space for such contacts, he said. Of sustained people-to-people engagement, Kuhn said, "I think it's the single most important thing the world can do on a long-term basis." ■

Century-old sea cucumbers highlight overfishing risks: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
18:07:25 CST
19:07:25 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- Endangered black teatfish sea cucumbers can live for more than 100 years, far longer than previously thought, highlighting the species' vulnerability to overfishing, an Australian study finds.
The findings suggested black teatfish sea cucumber populations recovered much more slowly from fishing pressure than previously thought, with implications for commercial fishery catch limits, according to a statement released Tuesday by the Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS).
In a genetic mark-recapture study, researchers compared DNA samples from black teatfish collected in a no-take zone of Australia's Great Barrier Reef Marine Park in 2000 with samples from the same location 24 years later.
Small biopsies were taken from the animals, which were then returned, while modelling was used to estimate their lifespan. Of 55 animals sampled, 33, or 60 percent, were identified as the same as those sampled in 2000.
The findings showed the sea cucumbers lived for at least 24 to 27 years on average, while some survived for more than a century, said Sven Uthicke, a senior principal research scientist at the AIMS and lead author of the study published in iScience.
"Most of the recaptured animals had grown very little over the 24 years, and many had become smaller," Uthicke said, calling for more conservative harvesting to avoid possible extinction and preserve the species' ecological functions.
Sea cucumbers play a vital role in tropical marine ecosystems by recycling nutrients and mixing sediment, and healthy populations can also enhance coral health, researchers said.
Black teatfish are classified as Endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature and listed under Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species. ■

Meanwhile, risks to the outlook include the possibility of a pullback in AI-related investment that could harm growth prospects and impact corporate profitability, another round of trade tensions, or a further energy shock arising in the Middle East, said the MAS.
Although asset quality could come under some pressure in these scenarios, credit risk is expected to stay under control.
Its stress test also affirms that Singapore banks have sufficient capital buffers to weather an adverse scenario driven by a downturn in the AI-led global growth cycle amid tensions in the Middle East. ■

Trump's White House media ban faces long odds in court, legal experts say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:04:40 UTC
19:04:40 KST

Trump's White House media ban faces long odds in court, legal experts say
NEW YORK, Sept 22 - US President Donald Trump’s move to ban several news outlets from the White House over his dislike of their coverage likely runs afoul of US legal prohibitions against viewpoint discrimination by the government, four legal experts told Reuters.
Trump’s announcement on Friday that he would ban CNN, MSNOW and Politico for reporting what he deemed “FAKE NEWS” was the latest move by his administration to curtail press access, part of the Republican president’s wider pressure campaign against news coverage he dislikes. Trump said on Saturday that he might ban other outlets as well.
The president’s justification for the ban could be its undoing in a legal challenge because US courts have long held that the government cannot condition press access on favorable coverage once it has opened a space to the media, according to legal experts.
"They don’t have to allow anyone in, but once they do, they cannot decide who gets in based on viewpoint or content”, said University of Maryland journalism professor Lucy Dalglish.
The White House said in a statement that the news outlets were completely capable of reporting from outside the White House.
“The Fake News has no place demanding a spot in the President’s Oval Office. The lies they smear are a disservice to the American public and tear at the very fabric of our Democracy,” the statement said.
In a lawsuit filed in Washington D.C., federal court on Monday, CNN, MSNOW and Politico said the ban was unlawful retaliation for legally protected speech under the First Amendment and violated their rights to due process.
“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the outlets said.
US District Judge Timothy Kelly, who blocked Trump from banning a CNN reporter during his first presidency, scheduled a Wednesday hearing on the outlets’ request for a temporary restraining order blocking the move.
The press does not have unfettered access to the White House, and presidents have more discretion over access to tightly controlled spaces with limited capacity, such as the Oval Office and Air Force One.
It is longstanding practice for the White House to select so-called pool reporters who follow the president while he travels and disseminate coverage to other media. CNN is a member of the TV pool, which suspended coverage on Monday.
A Washington D.C., appeals court held in June 2025 that Trump likely had the right to bar the Associated Press from certain spaces including the Oval Office, but not White House press facilities writ large. Trump had banned the AP from the pool of reporters that cover his movements because it did not adopt the name Gulf of America, his preferred name for the Gulf of Mexico. A final ruling is still pending.
PRESS PASSES DEACTIVATED
CNN, MSNOW and Politico said in their lawsuit that their reporters had been denied access to the White House grounds on Saturday and were told their so-called hard passes, which are given to vetted and credentialed media representatives, had been deactivated.
The outlets said they were given no advance notice of the ban or opportunity to contest Trump’s decision, which they said violated their right to due process under the Fifth Amendment's protections against unfair treatment by the government.
The government is permitted to restrict reporters if they are deemed security risks but must have a clear basis for doing so and follow established procedures that give reporters the chance to dispute their designation, according to First Amendment lawyer Douglas Mirell.
“There has to be a non-arbitrary and compelling reason to restrict access, and to say that you disagree with someone’s opinion has never been a compelling reason under the First Amendment,” Mirell said.
In March, a federal judge blocked the US Defense Department from implementing regulations that would allow officials to revoke reporters' Pentagon press credentials if they sought information that was not authorized for public release.
The department said the new rules were aimed at protecting national security. But the New York Times said in a lawsuit that the changes would permit the Pentagon to ban news outlets over coverage the department viewed as unfavorable.
US District Judge Paul Friedman granted the Times' request for an initial order blocking the policy, saying it violated the First and Fifth Amendments because it was vague, overly expansive and "makes any newsgathering and reporting not blessed by the Department" a possible basis for revocation of a journalist's pass.
The Trump administration is appealing the ruling. REUTERS

As resistance mounts, Trump reaches for a familiar shield: national security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:04:19 UTC
19:04:19 KST

As resistance mounts, Trump reaches for a familiar shield: National security
WASHINGTON – As US President Donald Trump’s agenda has increasingly encountered resistance, he has turned to a familiar strategy: invoking national security.
Just this weekend, Trump declared that his planned 250-foot triumphal arch near Washington would also serve as a “military complex” to ensure national security, outfitted with snipers, drones and ammunition.
On Sept 21, Trump wrote on social media that the news outlets he has banned from the White House – CNN, MS NOW and Politico – represented a “threat to our National Security”.
The twin declarations represented the latest efforts in the President’s broader campaign to use national security concerns to justify presidential actions in the face of legal roadblocks, political defiance and popular opposition.
During his second term in office, Trump has cited the nation’s security to advocate for his planned US$400 million (S$509.9 billion) White House ballroom; the cancellation of offshore wind farm projects; the dispatching of National Guard troops to Democratic-led US cities; and many of his tariffs on foreign goods.
In each case, the security claim was aimed at bolstering presidential authority in the absence of formal congressional approval.
While US presidents have long used national security as a potent legal and political justification, legal experts said Trump is applying it more broadly and frequently than his predecessors, including for issues that have little clear connection to security matters.
The reliance on such claims is no accident, according to a senior White House official with knowledge of the matter, who said the administration sees security justifications as a useful way to strengthen Trump’s position when his priorities run into legal challenges.
The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said expanding national security into an all-purpose defense is “not ideal”, but doing so changes “the legal and political terrain of a dispute”.
“It’s working,” the official said.
In response to a request for comment from the White House, a second senior administration official said it is the president’s prerogative as commander-in-chief to protect national security.
The official said the ballroom project includes security enhancements developed with the White House Military Office and Secret Service, and that journalists who solicit classified information and disclose sensitive details can act against US national security interests.
Trump’s latest moves coincide with his approval rating hitting the lowest level of his political career at 32 per cent, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Sept 21. Just 17 per cent of Americans approve of his handling of the cost of living, voters’ top concern, and the war in Iran is broadly unpopular.
Series of setbacks
In the span of five days last week, the Supreme Court rejected Trump’s bid to limit mail ballots; diesel fuel prices hit a new record high; and a federal judge blocked adding his name to the facade of the Kennedy Center, prompting Trump to threaten to cancel planned renovations unless the ruling is overturned.
Trump’s argument for the arch appeared to be following the playbook he used for the ballroom, which includes upgrades to an underground bunker at the White House. In both cases, the President pivoted to describing the project as a “military complex” and an urgent security priority only after each was slowed by lawsuits and a lack of support from Congress.
In a social media post on Sept 20, Trump said the US military had requested the changes to the planned arch. It would now feature snipers on the roof and plaza as well as drones and “large quantities of sniper ammunition”, he said, despite its location on a busy traffic circle less than a mile from the Pentagon.
Critics said the move seemed aimed at countering opposition to the monument.
“He knows aviation safety experts, Veterans and the American people are against building this golden arch – and so naturally, the President wants to exploit our military as a political shield to proceed,” said Democratic Senator Tammy Duckworth of Illinois.
The ballroom case, the White House official said, showed that adding a security dimension can deter courts from intervening, after the administration failed to prevail in lower courts on presidential authority alone. The Supreme Court in August allowed construction to proceed, citing in part national security concerns.
The official said the same logic could apply to disputes over press access, noting that courts are more likely to defer to the president in matters of national security rather than a First Amendment dispute.
Courts could become less willing to accept Trump’s national security claims if he continues to broaden them, legal experts said.
If an administration strains credulity, that jeopardises “the traditional deference presidents of the nation have received from the public, from courts, and from allies when invoking national security and doing so in good faith”, said James Baker, director of the Syracuse University Institute for Security Policy and Law and a former federal judge.
Courts and Congress have especially given presidents latitude on the issue since the Sept 11, 2001, attacks, said Elizabeth Goitein, an expert on national security at New York University’s Brennan Center for Justice.
But it becomes “a hard sell” when Trump invokes security concerns on matters with little obvious nexus, such as the arch, she said.
Framing negative White House media coverage as a security issue, she added, was “so transparent” that “I can imagine it backfiring.” REUTERS

Ukraine Knocks Out Pipeline Supplying 50% of Russian Forces’ Diesel in Occupied Luhansk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:02:30 UTC
19:02:30 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Knocks Out Pipeline Supplying 50% of Russian Forces’ Diesel in Occupied Luhansk
Ukraine’s Third Army Corps destroyed a fuel pipeline that supplied around half of the daily diesel requirements of Russian forces in the temporarily occupied Luhansk region, forcing Russian troops to move fuel supplies farther from the front.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Militarnyi on September 21, the pipeline ran from Russia’s Voronezh region into the temporarily occupied Luhansk region and served Russian forces operating in the area.
The Third Army Corps said Ukrainian forces targeted both the pipeline’s initial and final fuel reception points, as well as Russian fuel trucks involved in the supply network.
“It provided about 50% of the enemy’s daily diesel fuel needs. The headquarters and brigade general Andrii Biletskyi set the task of stopping the operation of this pipeline,” the corps told Militarnyi.
The strikes ultimately forced Russian forces to stop using the facility, according to the Ukrainian military. “This forced the Russians to completely shut down the facility,” the corps said.
The operation disrupted fuel logistics for Russia’s Zapad grouping of forces, according to Militarnyi. Russian fuel trucks now have to travel roughly 400 kilometers to collect supplies directly from Russia.
Third Army Corps commander Andrii Biletskyi previously said disrupting Russian logistics was among the objectives of Operation Vivaldi. As a result of Ukrainian actions, he said, Russian forces were forced to relocate fuel and lubricant supplies across the border into the Voronezh region.
The resulting fuel shortages have also affected equipment used by Russian frontline units, according to the corps. Ukrainian military personnel said Russian forces have faced difficulties fueling generators used to recharge drone batteries, while some electronic warfare systems have been operating on a limited basis.
The pipeline strike was part of the broader Operation Vivaldi, during which Ukraine’s Third Army Corps has targeted Russian command posts, communications, supply routes, crossings, and reserves while conducting offensive operations in the Donetsk region.
Across the operation, Ukrainian forces have returned 125 square kilometers to Ukrainian control, including 50 square kilometers of previously occupied territory.

Statistical Model Shows Putin’s Party Won Just 34% of Real Vote in Russian Elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:02:04 UTC
19:02:04 KST

- Category
- World
Statistical Model Shows Putin’s Party Won Just 34% of Real Vote in Russian Elections
Russia’s ruling party United Russia secured an actual vote share of only 34% once fraudulent ballots were removed, based on analysis by Novaya Gazeta Europe, ASTRA reports.
This figure stands 1.7 times lower than the officially reported outcome, which placed the party at nearly 58%.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The findings rely on a statistical approach created by physicist Sergey Shpilkin, which calculates genuine voter participation by studying how party choices align with turnout levels across individual polling stations.
Valid polling stations form a balanced core when mapped against turnout data, whereas stations impacted by fraud create an elongated tail, according to ASTRA.
In the most recent election cycle, honest precincts centered around a 34% baseline for United Russia, forming a clear, symmetrical cluster. The statistical study suggests this number represents the likely outcome of the vote in the absence of manipulation.
The calculations operate under the premise that votes cast for competing parties remained genuine, meaning the leading party's performance should naturally follow turnout patterns similar to other candidates.
Analysts at Novaya Gazeta Europe noted that two electoral experts reviewed and validated these findings. To maintain data accuracy, researchers excluded Moscow due to the widespread usage of electronic voting, which alters physical paper ballot metrics.
According to Central Election Commission data gathered after processing 96.95% of protocols, United Russia officially earned 57.83% of the vote.
The Communist Party received 13.76%, the Liberal Democratic Party gathered 9.01%, and New People won 7.96%. While A Fair Russia initially appeared to miss the 5% threshold required to enter parliament during morning counts, the Central Election Commission later stated the party successfully passed the required barrier.
As reported by ASTRA, voters at specific Moscow polling stations were coerced into using the electronic voting system. Meanwhile, Ramzan Kadyrov secured 99.85% of the vote in the Chechen head elections.
Official figures show United Russia is set to hold its largest parliamentary delegation in history following a record official turnout of 59.32%.
As stated by Central Election Commission head Ella Pamfilova, authorities registered only two cases of physical ballot stuffing across the nation.
Pamfilova asserted via the official commission website: “The percentage of reports of committed violations is minimal — if calculated in figures, it will not even be a hundredth of a percent across 91 thousand election commissions! This is many times less than during the elections in 2021.”
In contrast with official claims, analyst Boris Ovchinnikov stated in a conversation with ASTRA that fraudulent votes accounted for approximately 55% of the total tally attributed to United Russia.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy previously stated that the Kremlin intended to use the orchestrated vote to manufacture the appearance of public support for the war before rapidly conscripting several hundred thousand additional troops by the end of the year.

Türkiye, US deepen nuclear cooperation with next-generation reactor deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:01:58 UTC
19:01:58 KST

Türkiye and the United States have taken another step towards deeper cooperation in nuclear energy, with Türkiye Nuclear Energy Inc. (TUNAS) and the US Trade and Development Agency (USTDA) signing a grant agreement to assess small modular reactors (SMRs) and fourth-generation reactor technologies.
The agreement was signed at Türkevi in New York during President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s visit for the UN General Assembly.
On Tuesday, Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said the project will examine the technical, economic and regulatory feasibility of next-generation nuclear technologies for Türkiye.
Bayraktar said the cooperation would support Türkiye’s goal of reaching net-zero emissions by 2053 while strengthening energy independence and diversifying the country’s power mix.
“In addition to our large-scale nuclear power plants, we will continue with determination to build a robust and modern energy infrastructure,” Bayraktar said.
Deal builds on closer US-Türkiye nuclear ties
The agreement comes months after Turkish President Erdogan and US President Donald Trump met in Ankara during the NATO summit on July 7, where the two leaders discussed strengthening bilateral ties, including economic and energy cooperation.
The latest nuclear agreement also builds on a broader framework for cooperation. In September 2025, Türkiye and the United States signed a Strategic Civil Nuclear Cooperation Memorandum of Understanding aimed at supporting potential partnerships between Turkish and US companies in the sector.
The timing also comes as Washington is promoting wider international deployment of SMR technology.
On the sidelines of the July NATO summit in Ankara, the United States, Japan and South Korea signed a memorandum aimed at accelerating SMR deployments in other countries.
Türkiye weighs next generation of nuclear power
Türkiye is already pursuing large-scale nuclear projects, with the Akkuyu plant under construction and plans for additional plants in Sinop and Thrace.
TUNAS has said the country is also targeting as much as 20,000 megawatts of nuclear capacity by 2050, including SMRs.
For Ankara, the effort represents another avenue for expanding nuclear power beyond conventional large reactors as it seeks a broader and more secure energy mix.

Ukrainian Drone Attack Sparks Fire at Major Rosneft Refinery in Russia’s Samara Region
A fire broke out at the Kuibyshev Oil Refinery in Samara following an overnight Ukrainian drone attack on September 22, with preliminary analysis indicating that one of the facility’s processing units was hit, according to Russian media outlet ASTRA.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Residents of Russia’s Samara region reported hearing explosions overnight. An analysis of eyewitness footage by ASTRA indicated that the Kuibyshev refinery had been struck, with a fire subsequently breaking out at the facility.
Samara region Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev confirmed the attack, saying that an industrial facility had been targeted.
“The enemy targeted industrial enterprises. Civilian facilities were also damaged, including private homes and vehicles,” Fedorishchev said.
Separately, Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi, citing its analysis of available footage, reported that the refinery’s AVT-5 unit was preliminarily identified as the site of one of the strikes. Several other fires were also observed across the refinery’s territory.
The Kuibyshev Oil Refinery is one of the leading refineries in Russia’s Volga region. Located in Samara, the facility is part of Rosneft’s vertically integrated structure.
According to Militarnyi, together with the Novokuibyshevsk and Syzran refineries, it forms Rosneft’s Samara group of refineries. The facilities within this refining hub process oil produced by the company, including crude extracted in Western Siberia and the Samara region.
The Kuibyshev refinery has a design capacity of around 7 million tons of crude oil per year, although its actual processing volumes have remained lower in recent years. In 2024, the refinery processed 4.7 million tons of crude oil, equivalent to approximately 94,400 barrels per day.
The reported strike comes a day after Ukrainian drones attacked the Bashneft refinery complex in Ufa on September 21, targeting a major Russian oil processing hub approximately 1,600 kilometers from the Ukrainian border.

Does exercise really slow brain aging? A new study complicates the narrative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:00:19 UTC
19:00:19 KST

Physical activity is widely believed to protect the aging brain, but recent evidence suggests the relationship might actually operate in the opposite direction. A new analysis of a large group of German adults found no statistically significant evidence that exercise leads to better cognitive performance or a younger-looking brain, indicating instead that having a healthy brain might make a person more likely to stay physically active. The findings were published in eLife.
The concept of a physically active lifestyle preserving cognitive health rests on a large foundation of prior research. Animal studies have frequently indicated that running and other movements boost the production of brain-fertilizing chemicals, helping neurons survive and form new connections. Based on these mechanisms, human studies often look at brain structures that are vulnerable to aging, such as the hippocampus. The hippocampus is a seahorse-shaped ridge of tissue deep in the brain that manages memory and learning.
Another common way to assess brain health is by calculating a Brain Age Gap Estimate, or BrainAGE. This measurement uses a machine learning algorithm to estimate a person’s age based purely on the physical structure of their brain. Subtracting their chronological age from this estimated age yields a score, where a positive score means the brain appears older than it actually is.
Despite the popularity of the idea that exercise builds a younger and larger brain, some recent large-scale population studies have found contradictory results. For instance, a 2023 study of middle-aged and older adults found that physical activity had almost no effect on cognitive test scores. This discrepancy raised the possibility of reverse causation, the idea that early, unnoticed declines in brain health might cause people to feel fatigued and stop exercising, rather than a lack of exercise causing the brain to decline.
To explore this dynamic, Polona Kalc and colleagues at Jena University Hospital analyzed data from the LIFE-Adult Study, a large project tracking the health of residents in Leipzig, Germany. The research team wanted to see if they could detect a positive effect of physical activity on brain structure and cognitive performance when looking at a broad slice of the general population, rather than relying on a small group of volunteers who signed up specifically for an exercise program.
The researchers evaluated baseline data from 2,576 participants. To measure physical activity, the team relied primarily on a standardized questionnaire that asked participants how much time they spent walking or engaging in moderate and vigorous physical tasks over the previous week. Because people are often inaccurate when recalling their own habits, the researchers also collected objective data from a subset of 227 participants who wore an armband accelerometer for a week to track their actual physical movements.
To measure brain structure, participants underwent magnetic resonance imaging scans, which use strong magnetic fields to create detailed pictures of the inside of the body. The researchers used these scans to calculate overall hippocampal volume and BrainAGE. To measure cognitive function, participants completed the Trail Making Test. In the first part of this test, participants draw a line connecting scattered numbers in chronological order as quickly as possible, providing a measure of basic mental processing speed. In the second part, they alternate between connecting numbers and letters, which tests executive function, a category of higher-level mental skills that includes cognitive flexibility and working memory.
A smaller subset of the original group returned for a follow-up visit several years later. About 340 participants completed the cognitive tests again, and about 250 provided a second magnetic resonance imaging scan. During this follow-up, participants also answered questions about their physical exercise capacity, estimating how much effort they could exert before becoming fatigued. In all of their statistical models, the researchers adjusted the data to account for the participants’ age, smoking history, alcohol intake, and socioeconomic status.
When analyzing the baseline data, the research team found no statistically significant positive effects of total or moderate-to-vigorous self-reported physical activity on hippocampal volume or BrainAGE. In fact, higher self-reported physical activity corresponded with slightly worse scores on the executive function test.
The objective accelerometer data yielded a similar outcome. The researchers found no statistically significant relationship between accelerometer-measured movement and the size of the hippocampus or the BrainAGE score in the general adult sample.
The analysis did reveal a notable age-related bias in how people report their own exercise habits. Older adults, particularly those over age 60, tended to overestimate how much physical activity they engaged in compared to what the armbands actually recorded. When the researchers isolated a small group of 70 participants between the ages of 30 and 60, they did find that higher accelerometer-measured activity was associated with a younger-appearing brain. This effect did not appear in adults over 60, who made up the majority of the sample.
The longitudinal data, which tracked participants over time, provided evidence for reverse causation. The amount of physical activity a person reported at the beginning of the study did not predict whether their brain would look younger or older years later. Instead, the participants who had an older BrainAGE at the start of the study tended to report a lower physical capacity at the follow-up visit. The researchers suggest that underlying age-related issues, such as cellular energy problems or low-grade inflammation, might silently diminish a person’s brain health and simultaneously cause the physical fatigue that makes them less active.
“The most important takeaway is that this study did not find consistent evidence that people who reported being more physically active had better brain structure or cognitive function, at least for the specific outcomes examined,” Ben Singh, a Research Fellow in Health at Adelaide University who was not involved in the research, told PsyPost. “That is important because physical activity and brain health are often discussed as though the causal direction is straightforward. This study suggests the relationship is likely more complicated and potentially bidirectional.”
These results stand in tension with several previous findings. For example, the findings contrast with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which indicated that structured exercise interventions consistently boost general cognition and executive function. That prior review synthesized controlled exercise programs, whereas the current study assessed habitual, everyday physical activity in an observational cohort.
The new results also stand in tension with a 2025 study linking objectively measured exercise to larger hippocampal gray matter. That previous research focused specifically on isolated subregions of the hippocampus in young adults, which might behave differently than overall hippocampal volume across a broader, older population.
“I would describe it as challenging part of the existing observational literature rather than overturning the broader evidence for physical activity,” Singh noted. “Importantly, this study examines habitual physical activity in an observational cohort. That is not the same question as whether a structured exercise intervention can improve particular aspects of cognition or brain health. Randomized exercise trials remain especially important when we want to determine whether exercise itself is causing a change.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting the results. The reliance on self-reported questionnaires for the bulk of the sample introduced measurement errors, as demonstrated by the older participants overestimating their activity levels. The objective accelerometer data bypassed this issue, but the subset of people who wore the devices was relatively small and generally exhibited low activity levels. It is possible that the participants simply did not exercise intensely or long enough to trigger the biological mechanisms that improve brain structure.
“The main thing I would caution against is interpreting this as ‘exercise does not benefit the brain.’ That would go well beyond what the study can establish,” Singh said. “It is also important to distinguish between no statistically detectable association and proof of no effect.”
The study also focused exclusively on hippocampal volume and BrainAGE. Physical activity might still benefit the brain in ways these specific measurements cannot capture, such as by improving the integrity of the brain’s white matter tracts or enhancing the functional connectivity between different brain regions. Additionally, the longitudinal analysis compared physical activity at baseline to physical capacity at follow-up. Because these two surveys measured slightly different concepts, tracking exact changes over time is difficult.
“The next step I would most like to see is a large, well-powered longitudinal study beginning in midlife that repeatedly measures physical activity objectively and repeatedly assesses both brain structure and cognitive function over time,” Singh explained. “Rather than asking simply whether ‘more activity equals a healthier brain,’ the more useful question may ultimately be what type of activity, how much, at what age, and for whom?”
The study, “The effect of physical activity on brain structure and cognitive function in the population-based cohort of LIFE-Adult Study,” was authored by Polona Kalc, Robert Dahnke, Christian Sanders, Frauke Beyer, Andrea Zülke, Steffi Riedel-Heller, A Veronica Witte, and Christian Gaser.

Trump to address U.N. General Assembly as he navigates Iran, Gaza, Ukraine conflicts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:00:07 UTC
19:00:07 KST

In U.N. speech, Trump threatens to "annihilate" Iran and defends handling of global conflicts
Washington — President Trump defended his handling of conflicts around the world in a speech before the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, saying he could "annihilate" Iran while predicting that its leaders would make a deal to end the war after the U.S. midterm elections.
He framed his approach to foreign policy over his first two years back in office as deploying American power to solve "decades of intractable challenges" that previous U.S. leaders have failed to address.
"I do not believe in letting problems fester. They only become harder to solve. So while others have talked, I have acted," he said.
The roughly 35-minute speech came before Mr. Trump is set to meet with other world leaders on the sidelines of the annual U.N. gathering, including the prime minister of the U.K. and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He is navigating several ongoing international conflicts beyond the war with Iran, which will hit its seven-month mark next week. Mr. Trump is also seeking to close a peace plan for the Gaza Strip between Israel and Hamas, and has struggled to bring Russia's invasion of Ukraine to an end.
In his remarks, the president justified his decision to begin the war with Iran, framing it as an effort to prevent Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. After recounting the run-up to the war and the failed negotiations to end the fighting over the past several months, Mr. Trump said he has "a big decision to make."
"Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world?" he said. "Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?"
"But I believe we'll make a deal, right after the election," he continued. "Because it doesn't make sense for them not to. They're waiting to see how I do on the midterm election. What they don't realize is that I'm not running."
Later Tuesday, Mr. Trump indicated that his son-in-law Jared Kushner and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff met with the Iranians on the sidelines of UNGA. He said they "had a very good meeting, and we'll see how it turns out."
In his speech, the president said "the United States and Iran will definitely get it done — we will get it done, one way or the other." Mr. Trump also dismissed reports about diminished U.S. munition stockpiles, saying "we have more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using." The Pentagon's own inspector general said last week that the war in Iran has led to "strategic inventory shortfalls" of munitions.
The president insisted in his speech that he has brought about peace in a way other world leaders could not, while settling years of "unfinished business."
"While others have talked, I have acted," he said. "While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace. While others have ignored threats, I have confronted them. While others have talked of courage, America has shown it. While others have promised strength, I have used it to make America the most powerful country in the world."
The president also emphasized the United States' influence in the Western Hemisphere, particularly touting U.S. intervention in Venezuela and procurement of billions of barrels of Venezuelan oil.
"To the victor belong the spoils, you've all heard that," he said. "Our actions in Venezuela are proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere, and if necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States."
The president also touted the new security agreement the U.S. reached with Greenland and Denmark, calling Greenland the "northern frontier of North America." The U.S., which already has a military presence in Greenland, will be able to add new "defense areas" in Greenland, according to the deal. Mr. Trump and the leaders of Greenland and Denmark signed the security agreement later Tuesday. Disputes over Greenland, trade, defense spending and Mr. Trump's push for NATO members to assist with the Iran war have frequently brought him into conflict with Canada and European states over the last year.
The president also continued his tirade against critics of the acceleration of artificial intelligence, while saying he's going to try to rebrand "AI" as "superintelligence" or "SI."
"Every major new technology brings challenges. And superintelligence is no exception," he said. "Yet, the very same people who said we'll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming … and nobody was dead. These are the same people that are now saying that AI is going to kill us all, that robots are going to attack us, and that everything is going to be a total disaster."
"I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution," he added, insisting the U.S. will continue to lead the world "safely and responsibly."
Trump at the U.N. and Xi's visit
Mr. Trump is scheduled to meet with a number of leaders on the sidelines of the General Assembly, including U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and various Gulf state leaders. He met with French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday. He's also expected to have a pull-aside conversation with acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodriguez, about whom Mr. Trump has spoken positively since U.S. forces removed former leader Nicolás Maduro from power.
Mr. Trump is preparing to welcome Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday for a high-stakes state visit. The tenuous U.S.-China relationship is lingering in the background of the General Assembly. American and Chinese negotiators have sought to mend their economic relationship after last year's tit-for-tat trade war, and have discussed opening up communications on the risks posed by artificial intelligence.
The U.S. president has praised Xi in spite of questions about Chinese entities assisting Iran and buying Russian oil. China is the world's largest buyer of Russian crude oil, potentially putting Beijing in the crosshairs of a law signed by Mr. Trump last week threatening heavy tariffs against Russia's largest energy customers.
Mr. Trump dismissed a report by the Wall Street Journal that Chinese entities provided Iran with satellite imagery of a base in Jordan used by U.S. troops before Iran killed three Americans there.
"I think he's behaved reasonably well, and we behave reasonably well," Mr. Trump said last week of Xi's conduct during the war with Iran.
The president's movements and meetings at the U.N. won't be nearly as accessible for viewers as in past years.
After the White House banned Politico, CNN and MS NOW from the White House, the presidential network pool — consisting of ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC — suspended pool coverage of the president. That means there likely won't be television coverage of the president's meetings with foreign leaders. Politico, CNN and MS NOW announced they're suing the Trump administration, citing First Amendment concerns, in an effort to restore access.
Other cameras, however, are covering UNGA as a whole, and captured Mr. Trump on camera as he entered the building.
"You should not be here covering me," the president told a CNN reporter.

Revisiting Childhood Hobbies Is a Way to Learn Who You Are as an Adult
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

I swept my arm overhead, forming a half-moon shape as my body bent into a side stretch. I could almost hear the ballet instructors of my childhood calling out steps: Plié first position. Keep your heels down. Legs straighten, lift your kneecaps. Stretch toward the barre.
When I started experimenting with ballet as an adult, it had been well over a decade since I last took a class. I started alone with no mirrors, clutching my kitchen counter in tennis shoes. It was as if this routine had been lying dormant in my muscles and my memory. I still knew the steps. I could still hum music that had been paired with certain exercises. But now, this melody was accompanied by my knees snapping, crackling, and popping.
In addition to being floored by what I could recall (even if my body couldn’t quite execute it), I was taken aback by how an activity that defined my childhood and young adulthood felt like an opportunity for my preteen self to tell me something about who I was now.
Dan P. McAdams, professor of psychology at Northwestern University, focuses on narrative identity. Part of that entails “this business about going back to the past, sometimes the distant past, and bringing something forward,” he said. While he hasn’t studied that exact process with a childhood hobby, he said that bringing something back that you feel good about “can be a very positive experience and make you feel like you're kind of integrating your life around something that was once really important to you.”
For some, revisiting these activities brings up memories. Kristen Martin, author of The Sun Won’t Come Out Tomorrow, grew up in a multigenerational household, and her grandmother was constantly knitting. She was known for making everyone slippers in different color combinations of stripes, in addition to full-sized blankets.
She taught Martin to crochet as early as kindergarten, and by fourth grade, they made a blanket for Martin’s childhood dog together. “I always think about her sitting and knitting,” Martin said. “I think that she did it as a way to keep her hands busy throughout the day as her mind worked.”
When Martin picked up knitting and crocheting again in adulthood, she noticed something similar in herself. She typically practices her hobby at night with the TV on, a wind-down activity. “I find it very relaxing as something that I can focus on, but without my full attention,” she said. She loves making things for other people, just as her grandmother did.
Benjamin Vigeant, 40, who works as a social media manager in Chicago, grew up with a pinball machine in his basement. He stopped playing until his late 20s, when he and a friend would play when they spotted pinball machines at bars, getting competitive with each other.
Eventually, he started a pinball league in Chicago. “I really enjoy competing, and now there's a bunch of people competing with me,” Vigeant said.
In a 2023 Teen Vogue article, Aiyana Ishmael interviewed Gen Zers who revisited hobbies they loved earlier in life, from swimming to fashion, as a means of “healing their inner child.” Revisiting childhood activities, in particular, can feel like a chance to reclaim part of your own story.
According to Hollen Reischer, visiting assistant professor of psychology at the University at Buffalo, narrative identity refers to the “internalized, evolving story of the self,” including the past as we remember it, the present, and the future we imagine.
“Returning to a hobby abandoned in childhood has the potential to engage all three of these temporal selves at once: It draws on our reconstructed memory of what the activity meant to us then, it alters what we are actually doing in the present, and it gestures toward some version of ourselves we hope to become,” she said.
The more frequently I took myself through basic ballet steps, the more I noticed glimmers of my younger self present-day: The preteen who wanted to show up early and stay late at the studio, trying to get a step just right, became an adult who painstakingly fiddles with sentences to find the right words, reaching for the same “ah-hah!” moment. I wondered about my younger self’s fearlessness—her willingness to throw herself into steps that were too hard, even if she stumbled. I no longer leap across studios, but I yearn for more of that freedom to try in my adult life.
As I talked about my own return to a beloved childhood activity, I heard from others revisiting theirs, like someone who recently retired and went back to piano lessons, or the parent who started playing pick-up basketball games again after his kid expressed interest in playing, too.
There are plenty of conversations around how hobbies provide fulfillment and build community, and endless debates about what hobbies can be monetized. But by revisiting childhood hobbies specifically, we can discover how much we’ve changed, or how the parts of us that once loved this thing remained all along.

Press review: US may impose sanctions on ICC as AfD may push for early elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

MOSCOW, September 22. /TASS/. The opening UN General Assembly High-level Week 2026 may help revive Ukraine talks, and the United States is considering sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court. Meanwhile, the opposition Alternative for Germany party is planning to call for an early parliamentary vote in Germany. These stories topped Tuesday's newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: UNGA High-level week to attempt and reboot talks on Ukraine, Iran
On September 22, the UN General Assembly High-level Week 2026 alongside marathon negotiations commence in New York. The heads of state and their representatives will primarily focus on resolving the crises in the Middle East and Ukraine. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres is planning to hold meetings with US President Donald Trump, Gulf leaders, and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, Izvestia has learned.
The upcoming talks between Russia’s top diplomat Lavrov and his US counterpart, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, are among the most anticipated events. The meeting will help clarify if not the contours of future peace agreements, then at least Washington's stance, especially ahead of potential contacts between Russia, the United States, and Ukraine. So far, there has been no progress, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, while commenting on the prospects for the Ukrainian settlement and the possible resumption of trilateral talks.
The main issue of the dialogue is that the American side does not offer Russia any specifics on the Ukrainian track, Bogdan Bezpalko, a member of the Russian Presidential Council for Interethnic Relations, told Izvestia.
According to him, even potential criticism from Rubio of Ukraine's position at the UNGA session would not be a radical shift. The US is seeking at least a declarative or framework truce deal to present it as its own foreign policy success in the run-up to congressional elections. According to the expert, a proposal from Washington to at least partially lift anti-Russian sanctions and recognize Russia’s sovereignty over its new regions might bring a trilateral meeting closer.
Alongside Russia-US contacts, other meetings will also occur. Vladimir Zelensky will attempt to coordinate efforts to enhance Ukrainian air defenses with Trump and French leader Emmanuel Macron on the sidelines of the UNGA session.
The French president also has something to discuss with his US counterpart. Paris fears the US might monopolize the talks and sideline the EU. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin directly described Brussels as a key obstacle to peace, stating EU leaders are seeking to join the talks only to disrupt the balance for Kiev. Bezpalko dismissed any attempts by Brussels to interfere as futile unless Europe proposes at least some options for resolving the conflict.
However, meetings on the sidelines of the UNGA session may fail to bring the parties closer to any resolution at all, Konstantin Blokhin, a leading researcher at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Center for Security Studies, argued. A diplomatic breakthrough requires a significant advance on the battlefield that will give one of the sides a clear advantage. Even as the Russian Army has regularly liberated localities, its pace has not yet compelled Kiev to request peace. Ukraine still controls part of the territories, and its gradual loss of positions may last for several years, Blokhin maintained.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Russian expert comments on potential US sanctions against ICC
The US plan to impose sweeping financial sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC) reported by The Wall Street Journal on Sunday may significantly complicate matters for this judicial body. However, they cannot lead to its closure, at least as long as the ICC enjoys the support of major European countries, Anatoly Kapustin, who heads the Center for International Law and Comparative Legal Studies at the Institute of Legislation and Comparative Law under the Russian government, told Rossiyskaya Gazeta in an interview.
The United States is not a party to the Rome Statute, which gives ICC judges and prosecutors privileges and immunity in ICC signatory states. The document does not have any legal force in the US, so Washington is free to impose any restrictions on the Court or at least those that affect mechanisms controlled by the Americans, Kapustin maintained.
The ICC has already felt the effect from overcompliance as companies are scaling back cooperation with it for fear of sanctions. ProcoliX, a Dutch cloud and email hosting provider, has decided to stop accepting new orders from the ICC, fearing US restrictions, sources told TASS.
Kapustin views the threat of secondary US sanctions as quite real for businesses seeking to limit their cooperation with the ICC. And the Court will need to look for ways to respond to these threats, including the possibility of moving its headquarters in The Netherlands to another jurisdiction.
Over the past few years, an increasing number of ICC signatories have either withdrawn from this organization or are at least considering such an option. This shows how countries, primarily in the Global South, treat the ICC. However, even as such steps do undermine the credibility of this tribunal, they cannot bring about its closure for it is the brainchild of major Western European countries, such as Germany, France, and Britain, the expert explained. And it is these countries that will have to change their policies for the ICC to cease its operations, he concluded.
Izvestia: AfD may push for early parliamentary election in Germany
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party intends to raise the issue of an early parliamentary election in the Bundestag, Rainer Rothfuss, an AfD parliamentarian, told Izvestia. The reason was the outcome of voting in the state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Berlin and Saxony-Anhalt, where the ruling Christian Democratic Union (CDU), led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz, recorded its worst results in Germany’s history. Currently, 28% of voters are ready to vote for the AfD, while the CDU enjoys a nationwide support rating of roughly 19%.
The poor election results for the ruling CDU party in the three German state elections may trigger a change in power in Germany. "Under the current Red and Black government (a CDU/CSU and SPD coalition), Germany has found itself in a dangerous impasse affecting not only fiscal policy, characterized by an astronomical €203 billion in new borrowings, but also the course in the energy sector, the economy, and, in particular, a hostile policy toward Russia," Rothfuss said.
Holding an early election would serve the vital interests of citizens as the new composition of parliament should reflect the fundamental changes in public sentiment shown in opinion polls. According to them, about 28% of the electorate are ready to vote for the AfD, making it the most popular political force in the country. It is followed by the CDU/CSU bloc with a support rating of about 19%. Only approximately 14% of citizens approve of the performance of Merz who himself has a record low personal rating, according to sociologists from INSA.
"I believe that the current chancellor can no longer remain in power for long and hopefully Germany will hold an early election as the country’s citizens are suffering from the latest economic developments and the policy course pursued by the federal government," Markus Frohnmaier, a member of the German Bundestag and deputy leader of the AfD parliamentary faction, told Izvestia.
The results of the regional elections have had quite a negative impact on Merz’s position, Maria Khorolskaya, a researcher at the World Economy and International Relations Institute under the Russian Academy of Sciences, noted. According to her, discontent has intensified in regional offices of his party, especially in eastern Germany, as Merz’s fellow CDU members view him as a toxic personality that stands in the way of attracting new electorate. Nevertheless, Merz should not be expected to resign for now for much will depend on the outcome of landtag elections in western German states of Saarland, Schleswig-Holstein and North Rhine-Westphalia slated for April 2027, she added.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Saudi Arabia halts oil supplies to Europe, India
Saudi Arabia has cut oil shipments to Europe and India. The country’s state-controlled oil giant, Saudi Aramco, has told its European customers they will receive no Saudi crude in October. Even as no such announcement regarding India was made, The Economic Times, India’s leading business daily, reported that Saudi Aramco has stopped crude oil supplies to Indian refineries. Unless exports are resumed soon, this will worsen fuel shortages in Europe.
Overall, the global market may lose between 2.5 million and 6 million bpd of Saudi oil and petroleum. So far this year, Saudi crude has accounted for 9% of Indian oil imports and around 6.5% of European purchases.
Valery Andrianov, an associate professor at the Russian Financial University, told Rossiyskaya Gazeta that approximately 577,000 bpd of supplies to Europe will be halted, with basically no major alternative supply routes available.
However, Viktoria Trifonova, a senior analyst at the Yakov and Partners think tank, said that attempts to substitute Saudi crude are being made anyway. Poland’s Orlen has purchased additional North Sea oil volumes and it is also considering supplies from the United States, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Guyana.
Given the low fuel inventories in Europe, the region may face a local fuel crisis at gas stations and airports as early as October-November, while petroleum production will be least affected, Andrianov predicts.
According to Maxim Malkov, a partner and the head of the Oil and Gas Practice at Kept, diesel and jet fuel shortages that have persisted for months and are exacerbated by the loss of Saudi crude for European oil refineries, rather than a crude deficit, may pose the largest risk to markets. Unless Saudi Aramco restarts the East-West pipeline in the next six weeks, as scheduled, an even more challenging fall and winter may await the European fuel market, he warned.
Kommersant: Bitcoin going north on news about new regulation for US market
Bitcoin has risen to a new eight-month high of above $86,000 amid investor optimism in the wake of statements from US regulators that they could establish their own regulation for the cryptocurrency market without the Clarity Act. Exchange-traded funds (ETFs) reported a major inflow, and the mass closing of short positions only drove token prices higher. If the comeback of large capital to ETFs continues, and positive signals from US agencies remain in place, Bitcoin may soar to $90,000, analysts say.
Against this backdrop, investors significantly boosted their Bitcoin ETF purchases: according to CoinMarketCap, on September 17-18, ETFs attracted a total of around $600 million in investments, while an outflow of more than $1 billion was recorded in the previous week.
Bitcoin purchases by large institutional investors demonstrated to the market that there is still demand for the cryptocurrency and that "big capital is ready to increase its Bitcoin positions again," Guzel Protsenko, CEO of Alfa-Forex, told Kommersant.
If big capital returns and US agencies send more positive signals, Bitcoin will continue to rise, analysts say. If the price stays above $85,000, a rise to $90,000 may happen soon, Vladimir Zernov, a financial analyst at Bitbanker, argued.

The Priest Preparing to Care for 31 Children If ICE Detains Their Parents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

When a mother returned to Maryland earlier this year after four months in Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention, her children, ages one and four, did not recognize her at first. In her absence, they had lived with Vidal Rivas, an Episcopal priest who had agreed to be their temporary guardian if immigration authorities took her into custody.
Rivas’ wife slept beside the children to soothe them while their mother was gone. When his wife became sick, Rivas took on more of the childcare.
The experience was demanding. But Rivas, 62, stands ready to do the same for 29 other children whose immigrant parents have named him as their standby guardian. Two more families are making similar arrangements with him, he says.
“I feel a lot of responsibility, and a very heavy weight,” says Rivas, who has served at St. Matthews Episcopal Church in suburban Washington for nearly two decades.
Inside the church hangs a sign bearing the same message in English, Spanish and Haitian Creole: “We love migrants.” For Rivas, the words have become a commitment to the families who fear an immigration arrest could suddenly separate them from their children.
Rivas began encouraging families to name him as a standby guardian last year, shortly after President Donald Trump returned to office. Nearly all of the parents are Salvadoran, like him, and have been bracing for the Trump Administration to end Temporary Protected Status, or TPS, for roughly 170,000 immigrants from that country.
“It's not easy for parents to know that they could be arrested and their children could be left [in the U.S.] without them,” says Rivas.
How standby guardianship works
Under Maryland law, parents can designate a standby guardian in the event they are arrested by immigration authorities. The designated guardian automatically becomes the child’s legal guardian for six months, with the possibility to extend if approved by a judge. Rivas says some parents have talked to him about contingency plans in case they remain in a detention center for longer.
Maryland was among the first states to revise its guardianship laws to help prevent the children of detained immigrants from entering foster care. During Trump’s first term, state lawmakers passed a law allowing families to name a temporary guardian if detention or deportation separates their family. In July, Massachusetts made a similar change in state law, joining Virginia, New York, California, Nevada, and Washington, D.C. to streamline such arrangements.
Salvadorans await TPS decision
After the mother of two young children was released, Rivas and his wife remained close to the family. “We now feel like the children's grandparents, because we still have a close relationship with her, looking after her and looking after the children,” he says.
Caring for the two children made Rivas acutely aware of the scale of what he has agreed to. If immigration enforcement ramps up in Hyattsville, a small city where more than a third of the population is Hispanic, he could be called upon to care for many children at once.
Such fears have been further exacerbated by the uncertainty surrounding TPS, a program Congress created in 1990 to protect immigrants who cannot safely return to countries affected by armed conflict, natural disasters, or other extraordinary conditions. El Salvador was the first country designated for TPS in 1990 due to its civil war, and that protection was renewed in 2001 after the country endured a pair of earthquakes. Since 1990, more than 170,000 Salvadorans have been granted TPS status, becoming one of the largest groups protected by the program.
The Trump administration has recently rolled back TPS protections for more than a dozen other groups—including Haitians, Hondurans, and Nicaraguans—fueling fears that El Salvador could be next.
In early September, hours before the TPS designation for Salvadorans was set to expire, the Department of Homeland Security released a notice that suggested it would remain in place for now. The short notice said Salvadorans under TPS would continue to “retain protection including work authorization,” but added that an announcement on the program’s future “will be made at the appropriate time.”
The statement offered little reassurance. Reports quickly emerged of Salvadorans in Hyattsville and elsewhere losing their jobs amid confusion over their immigration status. Even those still employed worry that the Trump Administration’s reprieve is only temporary.
“Many people have left the church for other cities, and some have returned to their country,” Rivas says. “People are in fear and become insecure.”
Maryland is home to many Salvadorans who fled to the United States in the 1990s or the early 2000s. Around that time, El Salvador was just rebuilding itself from a brutal civil war, before a powerful hurricane and two earthquakes hit the Central American country.
For those who have been in the United States for more than 20 years, returning home may no longer feel like a viable option. More than 27% of El Salvador’s population lives below the national poverty line, according to the World Bank. It also has the highest imprisonment rate in the world, according to data from the World Prison Brief, a database compiled by the Institute for Crime & Justice Policy Research (ICPR) at Birkbeck, University of London. President Nayib Bukele has overseen an aggressive crackdown on gang violence as well as critics of his administration. The strategy is credited with reducing the country’s crime rate, but rights groups accuse his government of arbitrary detention and abuses in prison. Last year, Trump sent hundreds of deported Venezuelan migrants to El Salvador’s CECOT, a maximum security jail designated for gang members.
"A moral obligation"
Rivas grew up in El Salvador during another tumultuous era. A military coup in 1979 led to a deadly decade-long civil war between the U.S.-backed Salvadoran government and a left-wing guerrilla group backed by Cuba.
Rivas decided to become a Catholic priest at age 27. He says the military viewed Catholic clergy who advocated for social justice and human rights as communists. He was detained, beaten and hospitalized, he says.
Rivas came to the U.S. in 1998 to work at a Catholic Church in Washington, D.C., where his advocacy work put him at odds with the church’s leadership. He eventually converted to the more liberal Episcopalian Church, and joined St. Matthews in 2008.
As the church’s Hispanic membership has grown, Rivas has felt an increasing responsibility to help parishioners struggling with immigration issues. Watching parents cry as they discussed what might happen to them—and their children—convinced him that he had to do more.
Rivas says the support from the community over his guardian commitments has been overwhelming. Many have donated clothes and toys, and other churches and immigration organizations are also helping parents with standby guardianship arrangements.
If he ultimately takes in more children, he intends to open a bank account in the church’s name to accept donations to cover the costs of childcare. “I know that there are also other churches that are willing to support us,” he says.
Rivas acknowledges that caring for so many children at once would be an enormous challenge. But in the current political environment, he sees it as “a moral obligation.”
“I'm going to keep doing it as much as I can,” he says.

Patti Harrison Had Dreams of a Tech Utopia. Silicon Valley Smashed Them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Patti Harrison, like every great comic, knows how to use her face. If you’ve seen her stealing scenes in TV shows like Tim Robinson’s I Think You Should Leave or Hulu’s Shrill, you know that she often starts out a bit demure, or pouty, before walking audiences into the deep end. She’s a bit innocent, until she’s deranged—and you’re gasping for air.
It’s that quality in Harrison’s work that WIRED borrowed for our own rather unhinged cover concept. Harrison plays five (well, actually six) of the current masters of the universe—Elon Musk, Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, Mark Zuckerberg, and Jeff Bezos (with Lauren Sánchez Bezos by his side). Combining her farcical sensibilities with our commentary on the man-heavy leadership of Silicon Valley worked perfectly—and she was happy to lampoon the people behind the platforms she used to enjoy. (RIP Harrison’s Twitter account.) We caught up with Harrison in London, where she had just finished a sold-out run of her show, Just Ironing Some Things Out!, and a week of performances at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
KATIE DRUMMOND: When we were putting together our WIRED Women cover, we knew we had to put the best possible woman on it. You immediately came to mind, and I can’t stress enough how much you nailed the assignment.
PATTI HARRISON: That’s such a nice intro. I want to argue with a bunch of it.
You do?
I was coming in today like, oh, I guess I didn’t really check to see what the interview was about. Then I had this natural creeping anxiety. What if this is some sort of ambush, like a transphobic takedown piece—and then it was going to launch into me having to define what a woman was.
Oh my God. Thank you for being here, Patti. You are our WIRED Woman.
I appreciate that so much. It’s very affirming.
To be honest, when we were thinking about this cover and who would be perfect for it, I knew you, and I knew you were hilarious. I had no idea that you were a trans woman. It wasn’t part of the calculus. We were just so thrilled at the idea of imagining you and your really over-the-top absurdist approach to comedy embodying these characters. That was the whole joy of it for us.
From the start, I’ve been pretty outspoken about being transgender. I just don’t talk about it a lot in my work explicitly. Or when I do acting stuff, I’m not always playing a character that’s said to be trans.
Nor should you have to.
It’s fun to kind of leave that open and nebulous, especially if it's not important to the content of the work or the jokes I’m making. So, it is meaningful to me to get to do this on the basis of you guys liking how much I’m online talking about jism and kissing my dog on the mouth, that kind of discourse.
I mean, the kissing-the-dog-on-the-mouth discourse is so important. You are so, and I mean this as a compliment, conventionally funny. You’ve talked before about feeling pressure to incorporate politics into your work and how you don’t necessarily want to. You’ve also talked about how those things can’t really be separated. I’m curious about that line for you, because obviously sometimes we just want to make jokes about jizz and poo and kissing dogs.
I think there’s a balance. I think in our current climate of social media access, the kind of social media we have access to and how it’s been monopolized, we have been corralled Temple Grandin–style humanely into choosing to be in this very limited silo where our speech is heavily censored.
Right.
I have strong moral views that I’m connected to. I definitely feel that it’s important to pay attention to what’s going on politically, but I think in terms of my ability to articulate, I have very scattered speech, and I forget stuff. So I have never felt that I was the right person to be speaking explicitly about those things.
But I think when you live an intrinsically politicized life, your experience is political. I don’t think people can separate morals from politics. Comedy is sat in your understanding of the truth of the world and how you either speak on that or you subvert that. So making the choice to make a bunch of comedy that’s about anything other than what’s happening in the world in and of itself is political, because it’s a reaction to wanting to escape from a reality that is giving you existential dread.
There is so much right now that just isn’t funny. How do you gesture to those more horrific realities of the news when there’s no punch line?
I feel like people en masse are being traumatized in such a specific way by what they’re seeing on a daily basis, and that juxtaposed with AI slop, I feel like it creates a high probability for people to experience a cataclysmic kind of cognitive dissonance about what they’re seeing, how their feelings are spiking from it, and what they are to believe is real and what’s not real. I think people get overwhelmed, so then they opt out.
I think a large part of that has to do with the fact that we have conflated our news intake with social media, which is horrific. I remember when Twitter was, like, comedy. It was just people tweeting, and then when they integrated the news it created this really toxic dynamic of incentivizing people to have really inflammatory political takes to get shares or retweets or whatever.
Yes.
You can talk about something horrible happening without making fun of that horrible thing. Good comedy, good art in general, is based in truth. The less filtered something is, the more raw it is, the more unabashed it is, the higher the likelihood it will connect in a deeper way, even if that means it connects with less people.
We see a lot of comedy now that is people really afraid to engage with what’s happening, and I think the lowest-hanging fruit in a lot of ways, to try and be edgy or whatever, is taking digs at transgender people or using the R-word.
People want to be shocking in their humor, and I think I’m one of those people. I’ve always been drawn to shock humor, and I think it’s just because of the way I was brought up and the way that my childhood played out. You can read all about that in my book that I’m also pushing today, sponsored by Darpa, which is so awesome that they gave me the money to self-publish this book.
The Defense Advanced Research Project Agency?
Mm-hmm.

Why they need to be able to carry a human amount of weight, why they need to be able to grab someone from under a bed, why they have to have that sort of prehensile grip, and why those things are necessary. All that time is wasted. Our lives are wasted, and then we fund evil people who make the quality of everything worse, because it’s all interconnected. But then there’s the disillusionment that comes with realizing that capitalism will sour everything. Capitalism reveals grifters. Capitalism reveals the rot and shows you how quickly people will fold against their proclaimed morals to make money or to make a name for themselves.
These companies, when they’re developing these robotics that have the potential to really hurt people, they promise these aren’t gonna be used in combat. We see them using these robot dogs in Gaza. I don’t have a way to reconcile that at this point, because it makes you lose faith in this community that I have always seen as intrinsically progressive, because it’s science, it’s progressive by nature.
I think the idea behind capitalism is that it creates positive competition so we get innovation.
