With Limitations apartment reveals unvarnished glimpse into life as a London designer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
09:45:55 UTC
18:45:55 KST

With Limitations apartment reveals unvarnished glimpse into life as a London designer
A lack of money, materials or equipment shaped every object in this mock apartment, which has taken over the basement of London shop Aram as part of an exhibition by guerrilla design collective Design Everything.
With Limitations, which debuted as part of the London Design Festival, takes the form of an imagined designer's apartment to offer a glimpse behind the curtain at how young creatives are managing to survive in one of the world's most expensive cities.
Every piece in the show was made by one of 102 emerging designers and reflects not just the hurdles they faced in the making process but also the weird, wonderful and ingenious ways they've found to overcome them.
"We hope this will enable you to peek behind the veneer of the design industry – the glossy photographs and Instagram reels – to see an honest portrayal of life as an emerging designer today," Design Everything wrote in the exhibition's introductory text.
In total, the exhibition features 130 objects organised into three distinct rooms – a kitchen, living room and bedroom. And although each was born from different constraints, a lack of funds seemed to be at the root of most limitations faced by young designers.
Stuck for time between her two part-time jobs, designer Symran Shah took to knitting during her commutes as a way of rapid prototyping. Once she was happy with the shape, she sand-cast one of her creations to burn away the cotton yarn and leave behind a deceptively soft-looking metal tray for the bedside table.
Faced with skyrocketing material costs, others resorted to creating new objects from off-the-shelf components, scavenged objects and offcuts.
Among them is a bow-shaped light in the kitchen, made by Design Everything co-founder Lewish Duckworth using an old tent pole and a tensioning guy rope. Nearby, another lamp was assembled from found nitrous oxide canisters by Absolute Beginners, a factory in Park Royal that teaches young people how to make everyday products.
"Funnily enough, NOS canisters came up a lot in the open call," Duckworth laughed.
South London designer Felix Fried lent out his own bed, cobbled together using offcuts from a fabrication job, for the sake of the exhibition and is currently sleeping on a mattress on the floor until the show finishes on 10 October.
Unable to access expensive industrial equipment, others turned to creating improvised production lines in their own homes and hacking their existing machinery.
The speckled backsplash in the apartment's kitchen was made by Royal College of Art student Olivia Webb using wilted flowers from local supermarkets and a DIY tile factory she set up in her flatshare.
In the absence of a welding machine, Jake Robertson instead made a floor lamp by cutting and bending an aluminium tube "like peeling a banana", and Sam Braid created his Pylon lights from craft wire and masking tape.
"It's almost like a prototype that is so beautiful in its execution, it becomes the final thing," Duckworth said.
Design Everything has made a splash at LDF in recent years by hosting guerrilla shows that offer young and emerging talent a space to exhibit their work for free.
It's a radical departure from existing participation fee models, where even dedicated emerging designer exhibitions, such as Isola, can allegedly charge around £900 per square metre.
"It's very, very inaccessible," explained Design Everything co-founder Tabatha Pearce Chedier, who is exhibiting a series of lights made from wall mouldings.
"I never thought I could show at LDF at all," she admitted.
Instead of a conventional exhibition, last year's LDF saw Design Everything show 36 chairs by emerging designers from the back of a travelling van. The year before, Duckworth turned the renovation of his friends' record shop into an opportunity to commission work from other young designers he admired.
"The whole point of that show was that you saw the work being used, which became the basis of a lot of what Design Everything is now," he remembered.
"It's about being interactive and playful, about bringing people together, making design feel accessible, and trying to build a community."
This year's show at Aram – a stalwart of the London design scene since 1964 – marks the first time that the collective has gone mainstream.
"They kind of liked our 'punk energy'," Duckworth said.
It's an energy that's very much alive in the Aram show, which doesn't charge a participation fee and encourages visitors to interact with the designs on show instead of placing them on a plinth.
At any given time during the exhibition, Design Everything members, designers and visitors could be found playing with a flat-pack cardboard chess set by Maja Rowecka, perched on sofas made from road signs and bales of cardboard boxes by Charlie Boyden and Max Hayward.
There's also a Jenga set, although this game can't be played since designer Hao Chen has reimagined it as a tiny chest of drawers for holding incense and matchsticks.
In the kitchen, heated conversations about the state of the design industry could be overheard around a dining table assembled from off-the-shelf materials by David Searcy, surrounded by a mishmash of chairs by Jamie Reed, Abby Ghent, Cam Rowley and Gloriana Valverde.
The soundtrack was provided courtesy of a stereo speaker, which designer and DJ David Chen assembled from two £15 IKEA work lamps, 3D-printed adapters and a set of Beyma tweeters.
"I think a lot of us create quite wacky objects," Duckworth said. "And I think being able to engage with them, like actually spend a day with that object, you're like: oh, I actually really like this, and I can see how it would fit within my life."
Throughout the week, the exhibition also hosted live making sessions with some of the designers.
Oliver Linnell assembled a candelabra of nuts and bolts from B&Q's pick-and-mix section, Polly Jennings showed how she slip-casts cups using DIY cardboard moulds, and Anna McAllister used a vegetable steamer and an electric hob to mould balsa wood into a minimalist wall clock, using a process she developed in her own kitchen.
In total, the exhibition features 130 objects by 102 designers, which might sound like a lot but is only a fraction of the 520 submissions that Design Everything received to its open call – more than three times as many as last year.
"I hope it's because we feel accessible that people apply with stuff that they've made and feel like there's an opportunity there instead of being intimidated and put off," Duckworth said.
The Design Everything team – Jacob Marks, Eleanor Murphy, Sammi Cherryman, Izi Thexton, Duckworth and Pearce Chedier – went through each project and developed a points system to rank them based on how well they fit the theme and what was needed for the apartment.
Duckworth also interviewed each of the 102 participants about the limitations they face and photographed their workshops, with the results collated in the final part of the exhibition.
In total, the process of organising the exhibition took around six months, during which the members also created their own contributions to the show and held down their day jobs.
"Everyone's kind of got their bread and butter," Duckworth explained. "It's a bit of a passion project for now. But we're hoping that we can get some funding soon."
The photography is by Kane Hulse.
With Limitations is on show from 11 September to 10 October 2026 as part of London Design Festival. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

Barcelona FC faces backlash over 25-year deal with Israel-linked Babylon Park
Barcelona has faced criticism from supporters after approving a 25-year agreement with entertainment company Babylon Park to establish a family entertainment centre inside the Camp Nou.
Club members approved the agreement ahead of Barcelona's match against Sevilla, granting Babylon Park Spain SL a concession to develop a 900-square-metre interactive entertainment centre at the stadium.
Although the company involved in the deal is registered in Spain, corporate records cited by Spanish media link it to the wider Babylon Park group, owned by Israeli businessman Efi Malka, who lives in Tel Aviv.
The agreement was approved by 252 votes, or 57.15%, compared with 158 votes against and 31 invalid ballots, while 10 members abstained.
The deal had already faced political opposition before the vote. Jaume Asens, a Catalan member of the European Parliament from the Comuns party, wrote to Barcelona president Joan Laporta calling for the agreement to be withdrawn from the general assembly agenda.
Asens called on the club to investigate the company's ownership and investors and determine whether its parent company or other businesses within the group have activities or economic links to Israeli settlements, the occupied Palestinian territories or institutions accused of contributing to the continuation of the occupation.
He proposed that, if the deal was not withdrawn, the vote should be suspended pending an independent assessment of its potential legal, institutional, reputational and human rights implications.
The agreement has since prompted criticism from some Barcelona supporters on social media.
One fan posted on Reddit that they were "so disappointed in the club", writing that the agreement went against what Barcelona and Catalan identity represented and drawing parallels between Palestinian and Catalan struggles.
"Lliure Palestina, lliure Catalunya," the supporter wrote, meaning, "Free Palestine, free Catalonia".
Another Reddit user criticised the commercial considerations behind the agreement, writing: "Disappointing seeing this from a fan-owned club, unfortunately seems like that matters less these days than pure commercial interests pushed by the board."
Barcelona has long promoted the slogan "Més que un club", or "More than a club", reflecting its historic association with Catalan identity and its role beyond football.
The latest agreement has led some supporters to question whether the partnership is compatible with those values, while also drawing attention to the balance between the fan-owned club's identity and the commercial interests pursued by its board.
The controversy comes amid heightened scrutiny of sporting institutions and clubs over their commercial relationships with Israeli companies amid Israel's genocidal war on Gaza, expansion of illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and continued occupation of southern Lebanon and southern Syria.

Russian missile and drone strikes across Ukraine killed at least four people overnight, officials said Tuesday, while a Ukrainian long-range strike damaged another Russian oil refinery.

Zelenskyy was due to meet other world leaders, including U.S. President Donald Trump, at the U.N. General Assembly in New York. The Ukrainian leader is hoping to recruit their help to end Russia's more than 41/2-year-old full-scale invasion of his country.
Russian President Vladimir Putin isn't due to attend the annual event.
The war, which Western officials say has killed more than 500,000 Russian troops, has had global repercussions.
The repeated attacks on Russian refineries, following Moscow's strikes on Ukraine's power grid, have caused international shortages of diesel and price spikes, according to Trump. However, the global crunch also came after the Iran war led to curtailed oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
Zelenskyy also wants help to ensure the flow of Ukrainian grain and other farm products to world markets through the Black Sea. Russian attacks on cargo vessels have severely disrupted Kyiv's exports, hurting its economy and threatening global supplies.
French President Emmanuel Macron said Tuesday that his country would provide Ukraine with more radars to help protect its power grid.
He said on social media that he discussed with Trump the possibility of a truce between Moscow and Kyiv on strikes on energy infrastructure and a "moratorium" on Black Sea attacks.
Zelenskyy began his New York visit by meeting with U.S. senators, thanking them for what he called strong bipartisan support for Ukraine and for recently passing a tougher Russian sanctions bill that Trump has signed into law.

Zelenskyy said on social media that he briefed senators on his proposals for de-escalation measures that he intends to discuss with Trump later Tuesday.
The Ukrainian leader also plans to again press Trump to send more U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems that Kyiv desperately needs to stop Russia's ballistic missiles.
Ukraine said that it struck the Kuibyshev oil refinery in Samara, southeast of Moscow, in an overnight attack.
Several drones hit their targets, sparking a large fire at the facility, according to a statement from Ukrainian special forces.
The refinery, owned by Rosneft, is a key fuel supplier for central Russia, producing gasoline, diesel, fuel oil and other petroleum products, the statement said. Ukraine said that it struck the same refinery last June.
One person was killed and four others were wounded in the Samara attack, regional Gov. Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said. He said that "the enemy targeted industrial facilities," but didn't specify which ones.
The Russian Defense Ministry Tuesday said that its forces downed 297 Ukrainian drones over 14 Russian regions overnight, as well as the illegally annexed Crimean Peninsula.
Russia's overnight attack on Ukraine included anti-ship missiles, ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and more than 200 drones, Ukraine's air force said.
The strikes killed four people in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro, said Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk regional military administration.
The strikes across Ukrainian regions damaged homes, businesses and storage facilities, wounding at least five people, authorities said. Five people were wounded in the capital, Kyiv, according to officials.
The Russian Defense Ministry said Tuesday that its forces struck metallurgical and chemical industries, the fuel and energy sector, and the military-industrial complex, as well as port infrastructure facilities in four regions of Ukraine.
They included a Fire Point plant in Kyiv producing components for long-range cruise missiles and a tobacco factory in the central Poltava region used to make small arms ammunition, it said.

Italy registered 1,189 work-related
deaths in 2025, Inail said on Tuesday in its annual report.
Although this was 37 fewer than in 2024, a drop of 3.02%, it
still means that Italy is averaging over three work-related
deaths every day.
The workplace-accidents-and-occupational-illness agency said
nine students died in situations related to their educational
activities in 2025, four fewer than in the previous year
It said it received 600,000 reports of injuries in 2025, an
increase of 1.2% on 2024, including 519,000 regarding workers
and 81,000 regarding students.

Two men who registered 14 Starlink terminals for the Russian military were detained in Lviv

Unknown Publisher

12:38:39 EEST

Two men who registered 14 Starlink terminals for the Russian military were detained in Lviv
Kyiv • UNN
Two Lviv residents registered Starlink terminals under the names of nominees for the Russian military. All illegally connected terminals were blocked.
Two Lviv residents, aged 26 and 20, organized the illegal registration and verification of 14 Starlink terminals using the details of front persons so that the terminals could be used by representatives of the Russian Federation. This was reported by the Office of the Prosecutor General, UNN reports.
Details
According to the investigation, in May 2026, the men contacted via Telegram an individual who offered them money for cooperating with the aggressor state. Their task was to ensure the registration of Starlink satellite communication terminals in the names of front persons.
To do this, they involved 14 citizens who were unaware of their intentions. Starlink terminals were registered using their personal details, and the required verification was completed. All that was needed was to provide a photo of the device’s box showing its serial number. In this way, the actual users of the terminals remained outside the official registration procedure. Subsequently, these communication devices were used by representatives of the Russian Federation to conduct combat operations against Ukraine
At the same time, the terminals themselves were located in temporarily occupied territory, where restrictions on their use are in effect. According to the available information, the men received payment for their services after transferring the authorization data for the terminals to the handler.
Under the procedural guidance of the Lviv Regional Prosecutor’s Office, they were served notices of suspicion under Part 2 of Article 28 and Part 1 of Article 111-2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.
All illegally connected terminals that were identified have been blocked. The legality of the verification of more than 40 additional devices is also being checked. At the request of the prosecution, the suspects were remanded in custody without the right to bail
Recall
The Russian company "Bureau 1440," which is creating the low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation "Rassvet" as an analogue of Starlink, said it was ahead of schedule amid reports of problems with the launched spacecraft.

TJO Youth-Galilee, a delegation from the Jerusalem Orchestra East & West, is in New York this week for a series of performances, including an appearance Tuesday evening at an event marking the opening of the annual United Nations General Assembly session.
The ensemble, conducted by Maestro Tom Cohen, is expected to be the only musical act performing at the event.
Before taking the UN stage, however, the young musicians fulfilled another ambition: playing with veteran Israeli singer-songwriter David Broza, one of the most beloved Israeli artists of all time.
The orchestra members, ages 14 to 23, include Jewish, Muslim, Christian, and Druze musicians from communities throughout the Galilee. They joined Broza in a New York rehearsal room for an informal jam session featuring songs drawn from a wide range of Eastern and Western musical traditions.
A Jewish businessman and philanthropist invited the youth ensemble to New York to show how musicians from different backgrounds can come together through music.
Group's UN repertoire intended to bridge cultures
At Tuesday evening’s performance, the group is scheduled to present a repertoire intended to bridge cultures, including Zohar Argov’s “Yam Shel Dmaot” (“A Sea of Tears”), Abdel Wahab’s “Khayy Khay,” and a closing performance of Leonard Cohen’s “Hallelujah.”
Tom Cohen described the meeting with Broza as particularly meaningful for both the young musicians and for him personally.
“During this trip to New York, the soloists of our youth orchestra had the privilege of meeting an artist they admire, and the person who helped me, as an enthusiastic child full of dreams, become the mature musician I am today,” Cohen said.
“The same generosity David showed me two decades ago, he gave with endless patience and love to our young musicians, who eagerly absorbed everything they could from this special encounter.
“Together, we experienced once again that when you follow the path of music – particularly the musical paths of David and of our orchestra – there is the potential for a colorful and exciting future in the meeting between East and West.”

Iranian children to be recruited for Islamic Republic’s ‘self-sacrifice’ campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
09:38:08 UTC
18:38:08 KST

Children under the age of 15 will soon be given training to join the Islamic Republic of Iran’s Janfada (self-sacrifice) campaign, spokesperson Sasan Zare confirmed to the Iranian Labour News Agency last week.
Acknowledging that individuals as young as 15 have already begun training, Zare said that, due to high demand, “special training appropriate for younger ages will also be arranged.”
Zare, however, asserted that only male children would be provided with training; girls will only be able to enlist after reaching the age of 18.
The planned recruitment of children comes despite international humanitarian law, including the Geneva Conventions, prohibiting the recruitment of minors under the age of 15 by both state armed forces and non-state armed groups. The regime has nevertheless admitted to recruiting children as young as 12.
In March, Rahim Nadali, the cultural and artistic deputy of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ Mohammad Rasoulollah Corps, admitted to Iran’s Defa Press Agency that the minimum age for joining the homeland defense fighters had been set at 12. Days after Nadali’s announcement, 11-year-old Alireza Jafari was killed at a military checkpoint, according to Iranian state media. The Basij Teachers Organization confirmed that the minor was killed “on duty.”
The Jerusalem Post has contacted the Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict for comment on the planned recruitment of minors for the Janfada Campaign.
Military training set to begin this week in Tehran
Military training for the campaign is set to begin in Tehran this week. Training exercises will be carried out at military centers and in “high-traffic squares,” Zare said, noting that the major public Imam Hussein Square would be converted into a “fully equipped military training pseudo-camp.”
Those who sign up will be trained in “ensuring local security, general war preparations, observation, surveillance, and intelligence measures” and in “guiding micro-aircraft [drones], which are used in military operations,” as well as training in “the possibility of using shoulder-launched weapons.”
“The training platform is the Basij community, and the content is approved by the Basij organization, and the training capacity of all armed forces will be used,” he said. “There is also full preparation to ensure the security of the training sites.”
Zare further alleged that of the 31 million Iranians he said had enlisted in the campaign, 26% had signed up for military and security duties.
Zare: campaign centered on slogan: 'We have one life, and we give it for Iran'
He said the campaign was centered on the cultural slogan “We have one life, and we give it for Iran,” which he said had drawn international criticism.
Zare also alleged that a large number of Iranians living abroad had signed up for the campaign and would soon be included in “cultural and educational events.”

Türkiye's Erdoğan proposes stripping permanent UN Security Council members of veto power
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:37:00 EEST
18:37:00 KST

Türkiye's Erdoğan proposes stripping permanent UN Security Council members of veto power
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has said that abolishing the veto power of the permanent members of the UN Security Council should be a key objective of its reform.
Source: European Pravda, citing Erdoğan's op-ed for Bloomberg
Details: Erdoğan said that the "tragedies of recent years" had demonstrated that entrusting the resolution of global crises "to the will of a handful of capitals is no longer compatible with the realities of today's world".
"The adaptation of global decision-making mechanisms to today's circumstances can no longer be postponed. The United Nations Security Council still reflects the structure of the post-World War II era," he said.
Erdoğan believes that a more "effective, equitable and accountable" approach to representation has become an urgent necessity.
He said this requires not only broader representation but also a fair distribution of leadership responsibilities.
In this context, Erdoğan stressed that abolishing the veto should be both the starting point and the main strategic objective of any meaningful reform.
He also believes that a broad coalition should be formed within the UN General Assembly based on the principle that no state "should have the power to permanently obstruct the will of the majority of the international community".
In his view, the balance between the Security Council and the General Assembly needs to be restored.
Background:
- In spring, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul criticised the UN Security Council for its inability to make decisions due to the vetoes of individual members.
- Later, Germany's bid for a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council was unsuccessful.

Attempts to expand the “gray zone” and armored vehicles for the autumn — the Defense Forces revealed the Russians’ tactics near Dobropillia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:36:52 EEST
18:36:52 KST

Attempts to expand the “gray zone” and armored vehicles for the autumn — the Defense Forces revealed the Russians’ tactics near Dobropillia
Kyiv • UNN
Russia is trying to expand the “gray zone” in the Dobropillia area, but the Defense Forces are holding back the attacks. Ukrainian intelligence is preventing the enemy from deploying armored vehicles.
Despite the occupiers’ attempts to expand the "gray zone" in the Dobropillia sector of the front, it would not be entirely accurate to speak of any major gains by the enemy, as the Defense Forces are stopping and neutralizing the adversary to the maximum extent. Meanwhile, against the backdrop of the beginning of the autumn campaign, increased activity by enemy armored groups is expected, but it is extremely difficult for the occupiers to transfer equipment to the Dobropillia area amid the development of Ukrainian reconnaissance capabilities. This was reported by Ihor Yaremenko, chief of staff of the artillery reconnaissance division of a separate artillery brigade of the National Guard of Ukraine, during a national telethon on September 22, UNN reports.
Details
"We clearly see and understand (...) that the enemy is, in principle, periodically expanding the ‘gray zone,’ since there really are a great many assault operations taking place. But, for their part, the Defense Forces are stopping and neutralizing the enemy to the maximum extent, and great importance is attached to infiltration groups, which are constantly being detected and neutralized. Therefore, to say that the enemy has made any major gains does not quite correspond to reality. But because there is a constant and large number of assault operations, plus we should not forget that the enemy continues to employ a scorched-earth tactic. That is, constant artillery shelling, constant raids by large numbers of UAVs, and, most importantly, strikes with guided aerial bombs, which simply destroy and wipe off the face of the earth all infrastructure in any cities and settlements that the enemy can reach," Yaremenko said.
"The Defense Forces are actively fighting not only infiltration groups, but many plans for counteroffensive actions are also being developed. We clearly see that the Defense Forces are also achieving success in this regard. Therefore, we are holding the line," the serviceman emphasized.
At the same time, he noted that "the enemy is not going to end the hostilities. It constantly changes its plans and deadlines for capturing the entire Donetsk agglomeration, but (...) I believe these plans are unattainable. The enemy is losing an enormous number of personnel."
The serviceman also noted the beginning of the autumn campaign, with the appearance of dense fogs.
"We clearly understand that we have already entered the autumn campaign, (...) and it is precisely in this weather that the enemy is trying to transfer equipment. And I think that in the near future we will see activity specifically by armored groups, which the enemy barely used during the summer campaign. But I emphasize that during the summer campaign, the Defense Forces developed their reconnaissance capabilities very actively," Yaremenko said.
"Therefore, it is extremely difficult for the enemy to transfer equipment specifically to the Dobropillia area, since with the help of such means as optical reconnaissance systems and radar systems—and we should not forget the active work of UAVs—it is extremely difficult for the enemy to move its armored vehicles undetected and transfer them to any sector or area of the front. Plus, we should not forget that the so-called Middle Strike assets are actively operating—systems that constantly destroy both the enemy’s logistics routes and the depots where the enemy concentrates and stores its equipment to the greatest extent," Yaremenko noted.
"Therefore, the enemy is making attempts, but realistically, it has almost no positive movement," the serviceman emphasized.
Additional information
In its report for September 21, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine noted that the Pokrovsk sector remains the hottest area of the front, with enemy assaults also recorded in the Dobropillia area.
On the Pokrovsk sector, Ukrainian troops repelled 33 enemy attacks over the past day, out of 248 across the front.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — A Greenpeace Taiwan poll found that 87.5% of respondents supported establishing marine sanctuaries, the group said Tuesday.
Such a proposal would influence the voting behavior of 57.1% of politically neutral voters in the Nov. 28 local elections, per CNA. Greenpeace called on the major parties to make ocean conservation a core part of their election platforms.
Greenpeace activists dressed as a hammerhead shark, parrotfish, and tilefish gathered outside the DPP and KMT headquarters Tuesday. The three species face threats from bottom trawling. The group urged the parties to work with local governments to establish marine sanctuaries.
The poll found that 62.2% of respondents were either dissatisfied with or did not rate their local governments’ work on ecological restoration, enforcement against illegal activity, and pollution prevention. Greenpeace called on candidates to disclose their positions on ocean conservation and said it would publish a review of their stances closer to election day.
Focus Survey Research conducted the landline poll from July 31 to Aug. 3, collecting 1,502 valid responses from adults in 19 coastal cities and counties. Samples in Keelung, Yilan, Taitung, Pingtung, and Penghu were expanded to 100 respondents each, Greenpeace said. The results were weighted by demographic data and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.53 percentage points at a 95% confidence level.

NTUH opens new building to expand patient capacity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
09:36:06 UTC
18:36:06 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — National Taiwan University Hospital said Tuesday that its new Health Building has officially opened, per CNA.
The hospital spent more than 20 years planning the building and eight years constructing it. The facility had a soft opening on July 27 before beginning full operations Tuesday.
Located next to the hospital’s pediatric facility, the building has 14 aboveground floors and four basement levels for medical care, teaching, research, and administration. It has capacity for 330 general beds and 10 intensive care beds, along with 16 operating rooms, 24 postsurgical recovery beds, 69 consultation rooms, and a 30-bed chemotherapy area.
Several departments formerly based at the west campus, including otolaryngology, dermatology, and urology, have moved into the building. Head and neck ultrasound services from the east campus have also relocated, providing patients with one-stop care.
NTUH Superintendent Yu Chong-jen (余忠仁) said more than 190 beds are currently in use, with additional beds expected to open later. He said the expansion would ease congestion and allow the hospital to admit new patients each day.
Yu said the hospital has also taken steps to alleviate emergency department congestion ahead of the fall and winter. The emergency department lobby is now free of patients awaiting beds more than 90% of the time, he said.
The relocation of several departments has freed space for a post-emergency admission ward, Yu said. He added that reducing traffic at the historic west campus would also ease pressure on its 105-year-old building.

Pepe Losada joins Iran football team coaching staff
TEHRAN - Following the departure of Andranik Teymourian and Aliasghar Ghorbanalipour from the Iran national team coaching staff, head coach Amir Ghalenoei has bolstered his backroom team with the additions of Mehrdad Khanban and Pepe Losada.
The Football Federation of Iran began negotiations with several candidates identified by Ghalenoei to complete the coaching staff, eventually confirming the appointments of Khanban and Losada as the national team prepare for the next stage of their campaign.
Khanban, 44, is a familiar figure within Iranian football and has extensive experience with the national team. He began his professional coaching career with Persepolis club and later worked under Carlos Queiroz with Iran. His first spell with the national team lasted until 2018, when he left the coaching staff ahead of the FIFA World Cup in Russia.
Following Dragan Skocic’s appointment as Iran head coach, Khanban returned to the national team setup. He subsequently spent several years at Persepolis, working alongside coaches including Gabriel Calderon, Yahya Golmohammadi and Osmar .
Khanban was part of the Persepolis staff during their title-winning campaign before moving to Tractor. Last season, he worked on the coaching staff under Dragan Skocic and Mohammad Rabiei. He also took charge of Tractor on an interim basis during their AFC Champions League Elite clash with Al-Gharafa.
Khanban will now return to the national team, although in a different capacity, joining Ghalenoei’s staff as one of his assistant coaches.
Meanwhile, Spanish fitness coach Pepe Losada has been appointed as the national team’s new conditioning coach.
The 50-year-old has extensive experience in physical preparation and has previously worked in Iranian football with Persepolis, Nassaji Mazandaran and Gol Gohar.
Losada enjoyed one of the most successful spells of his career at Persepolis. During the 2022/23 season, he was part of the squad that won the Iranian Pro League, Hazfi Cup and Iranian Super Cup. The following season, he remained with the club as Persepolis again lifted the league title and Super Cup.
According to Spanish club Balompédica Linense, Losada has more than two decades of experience in physical preparation. Earlier in his career, he also spent around 12 years working within the Cádiz setup in Spain.
With Khanban and Losada now joining Ghalenoei’s staff, Iran have reshaped their coaching team as preparations continue for the next stage of the national team’s campaign and the 2027 AFC Asian Cup.

‘Apartheid 2.0’: South Africa condemns US refugee program
Unknown

‘Apartheid 2.0’: South Africa condemns US refugee program
South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola has denounced US President Donald Trump’s program for resettling Afrikaners, a white ethnic minority in South Africa, as refugees, describing it as “Apartheid 2.0.”
Lamola made the remarks at an African Diaspora Forum in Washington, according to footage posted on Sunday by South Africa’s Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO). The minister argued that the program gives preferential treatment to white South Africans while excluding other racial groups.
“Only white Afrikaners from South Africa are allowed to be refugees here. And all of you or any other race is not allowed. It’s a race-based policy, which we call the Apartheid 2.0,” he said.
The Democratic Alliance, the second-largest party in South Africa’s coalition government, welcomed Lamola’s condemnation and urged him to oppose race-based policies at home. It called for economic justice and opportunity “without permanently reducing citizens to arbitrary racial categories.”
Afrikaners are a predominantly white, Afrikaans-speaking ethnic group descended mainly from Dutch, German and French settlers who began arriving in southern Africa during the 17th century. Afrikaner-led governments instituted apartheid, the system of racial segregation that ended in 1994.
Trump established the resettlement initiative through an executive order signed in February 2025, alleging that Afrikaners faced state-sponsored racial discrimination, violence, and farmland confiscation under South Africa’s Expropriation Act.
There is no genocide against white people in South Africa. #UnityInDiversity#SouthAfrica@UbuntuRadioZA@GovernmentZApic.twitter.com/ROLKbFHqkD
— DIRCO South Africa (@DIRCO_ZA) September 20, 2026
Pretoria has rejected the allegations, insisting that the legislation is intended to address land inequalities inherited from apartheid and that no private property has been confiscated under it.
Trump expanded the initiative in May 2026, raising the annual US refugee admissions ceiling from 7,500 to 17,500 and reserving the additional places for Afrikaners, citing an “unforeseen emergency refugee situation.”
AfriForum, which had lobbied Washington over alleged discrimination against Afrikaners, said it “does not have information” about the claimed emergency. The group said its priority was creating conditions that would allow Afrikaners to remain in South Africa. More than 13,000 South Africans have since been resettled in the US, according to State Department figures, even as Washington sharply restricted refugee arrivals from most other countries.
Applicants must establish past persecution or a credible fear of future persecution and undergo security screening. Dozens have reportedly received rejection notices that provide no detailed explanation and cannot be appealed. Cases examined through information requests included denials linked to criminal records and public-safety concerns.

CorkVector Panel by Gencork
Dezeen Showroom: Portuguese brand GenCork combines one of the world's most sustainable natural materials with customisable algorithmically generated design, creating an insulating wall cladding that makes a strong visual impression.
GenCork's CorkVector Panel is made using the Corkvectors algorithm – created by creative director and designer Le Brimet – which blends organic patterns inspired by nature with geometric structure to create a dynamic 3D surface design.
The panels make use of cork, which is a highly renewable material, harvested from trees without cutting them down and so allowing forests to continually regenerate.
GenCork's owner and producer Sofalca lowers the environmental impact even further with its expanded black cork, which is made using a zero-waste process where steam from waste biomass from the cork's cleaning and milling bonds the material together with only its natural resin.
This process also gives the panels their distinctive rich colour, darker and earthier than raw cork, while CNC milling gives it its precise relief.
The computational design system allows the pattern to be customised to the dimensions of the wall or other parameters, while cork's strong thermal and acoustic insulating properties make the product as functional as it is aesthetic.
"Corkvectors [is] a bridge between nature and design, evoking the beauty of both," said GenCork.

EU split over Russian tycoon pushes entire sanctions regime to the edge
The EU is at an impasse over the proposed de-sanctioning of Russian businessman Alisher Usmanov, with Latvia flat out rejecting demands by fellow states to lift the restrictions during an ambassador meeting on Tuesday.
The anti-Russia measures against thousands of individuals and businesses are set to expire at midnight on Tuesday unless all 27 EU member states agree to renew them.
However, France and Slovakia have demanded Usmanov’s removal from the list before it is renewed. Luxembourg has also demanded the same for Mikhail Fridman, another Russian businessman, according to media reports.
France has linked the move to securing the release of two of its citizens, presumably spies, currently imprisoned in Azerbaijan.
After extended deliberations over the de-sanctioning of the businessmen, Ireland, which holds the EU’s rotating presidency, proposed a compromise. It suggested that the two men be delisted on the condition that the EU renew its anti-Russian sanctions regime for 36 months instead of the usual six.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, who has held office for just over 100 days and faces a general election next month, rejected the proposal, taking to social media overnight to insist that he would not allow “one of Putin’s oligarchs” to be de-sanctioned, insisting that the EU’s “pressure must become stronger.”
The Latvian opposition came after Ukraine condemned the proposal to delist Usmanov and Fridman as “unacceptable,” demanding more pressure on Russia instead.
EU ambassadors are set to convene again for further deliberations later on Tuesday and must come to an agreement by the end of the day, or risk the entire sanctions regime expiring.
Commenting on the delisting proposals, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov stressed that Moscow considers all Western sanctions illegal, and demanded that they be lifted from Usmanov, Fridman, as well as all other Russian businessmen and citizens.
Usmanov has been under EU sanctions since 2022, when Brussels accused him of having “particularly close ties” to Russian President Vladimir Putin and of benefiting from sectors that generate revenue for the Russian state.
The businessman has repeatedly denied the allegations. His lawyers have argued that the case against him was built on sketchy media reports, most of which have already been legally proven false. More than 3,200 articles concerning Usmanov have been corrected since 2022, while another 1,300 have been deleted entirely, his lawyers reportedly claimed in a letter to the European Council. At least 18 documents have also reportedly been removed from the EU’s own evidence file.
The businessman has also won legal cases against several major European media outlets over claims about his supposed links to the Kremlin, including Germany’s Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung and public broadcaster ARD.

====================================================================================================

A New Chatbot Wants to Unlock the Secrets in Tattered Ancient Greek Records
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Academic libraries across the globe are stuffed with hundreds of thousands of Ancient Greek papyrus fragments. Though many are so damaged that their meaning is probably lost, scholars have the ability to restore the rest by methodically filling in missing words or phrases. To accelerate that laborious task, researchers have turned to artificial intelligence.
On Wednesday, the Austrian Academy of Science will release “the world’s first advanced large language model for Ancient Greek,” developed in partnership with French AI lab Mistral and technology services firm Sail Reply. The model, Apollo, is trained on roughly 600 million historical Greek words drawn from manuscripts, papyri, and inscriptions.
The model will be freely available to academics through a chatbot interface. The ambition is to help scholars to more rapidly identify papyrus fragments relevant to their specific sub-disciplines, as well as promising new avenues of research. Where documents are tattered and torn, Apollo is built to fill in the blanks with the most statistically likely words or passages, potentially revealing hidden details about historical events and practices.
Dimitris Vlitas, partner at Sail Reply, tells WIRED that unlocking knowledge in this way “was unthinkable a year ago.”
Until now, restoring a tattered piece of papyrus has required a skilled academic to first identify the word divisions—there are no gaps in Ancient Greek writing—then accurately date the document, weigh the appropriate socio-political contexts, and consult reference materials to help choose suitable words to fill in the gaps. “There are very few people in the world who are that good at Greek history,” says Stephen Colvin, a professor of classics and historical linguistics at University College London.
But all of that specialized knowledge is baked into Apollo. “When it sees Homer, it supplements Homeric Greek. When it sees an inscription in Doric dialect, it uses Doric dialect,” says Anna Dolganov, a historian and papyrologist at the Austrian Academy of Science.
Academics who find themselves bogged down in painstaking reconstruction work expect Apollo to accelerate things, allowing them to focus on the implications of historical documents, rather than figuring out what they say.
“I think it’s very exciting,” says Armand D'Angour, a professor of classical languages and literature at the University of Oxford, home to the world’s largest ancient papyrus collection. “If I had a machine telling me, ‘Here are the three possible words that could fit into that gap,’ it would speed up matters considerably.”
Apollo is unlikely to change the broad-strokes understanding of the ancient world; many papyri are yet to be restored precisely because they are mundane—personal letters, marital contracts, civil service papers. “If you were a layperson, you might think suddenly we’ll get a few new plays by Sophocles, but that’s not going to happen,” Colvin says. However, the model could help to uncover new details about life in antiquity and substantiate existing scholarly assumptions. “Every time something is produced, it adds a tiny element of knowledge about the ancient world,” D’Angour says.
If Apollo is a success, says Vlitas, the same technique could be readily applied to other ancient languages—Latin or Egyptian, say—or any other academic discipline that would benefit from the distillation and indexing of a large corpus of material. AI has had notable success in some areas; OpenAI recently said its AI models solved a 200-year-old math problem, while Google DeepMind released a vast dataset that maps how genetic mutations affect molecular biology, which it compiled using AI.
One concern might be that relying on a language model—which deals in probabilities—to fill in gaps in ancient documents risks polluting the historical record with errors. But to head off that issue, Apollo is built to propose a selection of word options for a scholar to select between. “The crucial point is that human competence needs to remain,” says Dolganov. “If we become totally reliant on AI transcriptions and interpretations of historical material, that’s when the problems start.”

gaetano pesce foundation launches to preserve and continue the architect’s practice

gaetano pesce foundation to continue the architect’s work
The Gaetano Pesce Foundation carries forward the work of Italian architect and designer Gaetano Pesce (1939–2024), extending a practice that treated design as a way of thinking. Announced alongside Gaetano Pesce Studio: Continued at Salon 94, the nonprofit will safeguard his archive of objects, drawings, prototypes, and documentation while supporting exhibitions, publications, scholarship, and authorized editions.
Pesce’s work repeatedly moved between art, design, architecture, performance, and social commentary. The foundation positions that refusal of strict categories as a central part of its mission, carrying forward an approach in which objects and projects functioned as vehicles for experimentation. The foundation was established according to a vision Pesce set out before his passing. Its board is responsible for preserving his archive and legacy while guiding research, educational initiatives, institutional partnerships, and the continued production of authorized editions.
original UP chair | image courtesy of Gaetano Pesce
a board built around Pesce’s collaborators
Giulia Tosciri serves as director after working closely with Pesce for many years, including on the complex operations surrounding his practice. Glenn Adamson, the design historian, author, and curator who was a close friend of Pesce and a scholar of his work, serves as president and oversees the foundation’s academic direction and institutional partnerships. ‘On the occasion of Gaetano Pesce Studio: Continued at Salon 94, we’re excited to announce the creation of this new non-profit dedicated to the legacy and vision of the maestro. Radical, poet, and provocateur, Pesce is one of the most influential figures in art and design of the past century,’ he shares, announcing the launch of the foundation with a post on his Instagram account.
Michael J. Greenberg serves as secretary and brings his experience as counsel to the Gaetano Pesce Estate since 2023. Edward Secker, a longtime friend of Pesce, is treasurer and oversees the foundation’s finances. Alessandro Byther joins the board as director while continuing as creative director and head of production at Gaetano Pesce Studio, the artist’s original workshop at the Brooklyn Navy Yard. Byther has worked alongside Pesce for more than a decade and continues to oversee the hand-produced realization of his edited works. For Adamson, Pesce’s resistance to fixed categories was fundamental to his practice. In one of their last interviews, Pesce described this freedom in direct terms: ‘To be free means to be incoherent.’

British robot sailboats test submarine picket line
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:22:40 BST
18:22:40 KST

A British maritime technology company is testing a distributed anti-submarine surveillance network made up of six small robotic sailboats at the multinational REPMUS26 exercise in Portugal, with each vessel carrying a hydrophone and operating as part of what Oshen describes as an “acoustic picket line”, according to the company.
The 1.2-metre C-Star uncrewed surface vessels are being used together against live targets for the first time, with the boats spread across an area of water to create a passive listening network rather than concentrating sensors on a single ship or towed array. Oshen says the arrangement could allow operators to change the shape and density of the network as conditions change, while observations from several positions could help determine the location of a contact rather than simply its bearing.
Traditional passive anti-submarine warfare systems can use long towed arrays carrying large numbers of hydrophones behind surface ships. These provide sensitive local detection and bearing information but can be affected by noise from the towing vessel and are tied to the movement and position of a comparatively small number of platforms. Oshen’s approach is instead based on deploying a larger number of inexpensive autonomous sensors across a wider area, with the company suggesting a future network could be used to monitor areas such as the GIUK Gap and cue other anti-submarine assets once a contact is detected.
Each C-Star taking part at REPMUS is fitted with a hydrophone supplied by Systems Engineering and Assessment. Oshen says the vessels can hold station under sail for extended periods and have been designed for operations in difficult weather. The company has previously demonstrated C-Star operations in a Category 5 hurricane and argues that the small size and low profile of the boats could make a distributed network harder to identify and disrupt than a smaller number of larger sensor platforms.
Gordon Jones, Defence and Oceanography Lead at Oshen, said: “A defensive network built from a host of individual hydrophone platforms behaves very differently to one built from a handful of expensive towed arrays. It is wider, more resilient and harder for an adversary to characterise. REPMUS is the first real test of that model against live targets, and it points the way to how persistent undersea surveillance can be evolved.”
A significant part of the exercise is also concerned with command and control. REPMUS brings together maritime systems ranging from small autonomous craft to crewed warships, requiring data and tasking to move between equipment developed by different companies and nations. Oshen said its engineers worked with naval personnel before the exercise to integrate the C-Star command software with NATO systems and to limit the volume of data being pushed across communications networks. Sensor information from the vessels is being fed into a central database before processed information is shared with participating forces.
Anahita Laverack, CEO of Oshen, said: “REPMUS embodies what our technology is designed to do: take a capability that normally depends on a handful of expensive assets and turn it into something that can be deployed at scale, cheaply and continuously. There are many potential applications, including an acoustic picket line to help protect the GIUK Gap.”
The Plymouth-based company is already working on three projects with the Royal Navy, including work through the UK Defence Innovation accelerator programme, and has a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with the US Navy covering single-beam sonar applications. Oshen plans to take eight C-Stars to the Maritime Big Play exercise in San Diego next month, where the same acoustic picket-line concept will be tested in a US setting.

Hilltops to houses: A new phase of Israeli settlement expansion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
09:22:20 UTC
18:22:20 KST

Breadcrumb
From hilltops to houses: A new phase of Israeli settlement expansion
On August 9, 2026, Israeli settlers surrounded three houses in the Ras al-Ain area of Qusra, a Palestinian village southeast of Nablus in the West Bank.
The settlers pitched a tent just outside the homes, then cut their power lines and broke their water pipes. Fifteen people were living in the homes, including at least two children, at the time of the attack. Alarmingly, a month later, the families remain trapped in their homes.
One of the besieged houses belongs to Loui Ridi, a Palestinian American who runs a gas station and car wash business in Toledo, Ohio. He has spent nearly a million dollars building the home, though the project remains unfinished. From his Ohio home, he watched the settlers surround and attack his unfinished house in Ras al-Ain on the security cameras he had installed.
Ridi has reached out to the US embassy for assistance, and the White House was reportedly in contact with the Israeli government regarding the situation. So far, nothing on the ground has changed.
Qusra has lived with settler violence for more than a decade. What happened in August 2026, however, differed from these previous acts of violence in one significant respect. In this case, the settlers came from an outpost right at the edge of the village itself.
Established in November 2025, the settler outpost lies within Area B, the region of the West Bank over which the Palestinian Authority (PA) formally holds civil jurisdiction. This time, the settlers deviated from their usual attacks on outlying farmlands and instead targeted homes and the people living inside them. The siege in Qusra is not simply an anomaly, but points to a dangerous escalation in Israeli settler activity in the West Bank.
For most of the past three decades, Israeli settlement expansion has been overwhelmingly concentrated in Area C, which is the 60 percent of the West Bank under full Israeli control. However, since October 2023, settlement activity has expanded into Area B - including places like Qusra - and, increasingly, into Area A. Israeli settlers no longer appear to limit their seizures to agricultural land and hilltops in the West Bank, as they did in the past. Now they are occupying Palestinian houses on the edge of villages.
More than a failure of Israeli government enforcement or a wave of vigilantism, the recent escalation reflects implicit cooperation between the settlers and the Israeli state: settlers create facts on the ground, the military turns those facts into conditions that Palestinian residents cannot reverse, and the Israeli government legally seals the outcome. In practice, the systemic cooperation among these three forces accelerates the Israeli annexation of the West Bank, without any need for a formal policy declaration.
Beyond Area C
The 1993 Oslo Accords signed by Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization divided the West Bank into three zones as a transitional measure before the PA would assume full control. Area A contained the main Palestinian cities and was directly under the PA; Area B was under the civil administration of the PA with Israeli security control; and Area C fell under full Israeli control.
After Oslo, Israeli settlements mostly expanded in Area C following a fairly consistent pattern. Existing settlements extended their boundaries through planning approvals and construction, while settlers independently established new outposts on surrounding hilltops and agricultural land.
The Israeli government would then support these expansions with infrastructure and military protection, in some cases designating surrounding areas “state land,” restricting Palestinians’ access to their own property, and gradually bringing nearby grazing areas under settler control. Some outposts were later legalized as new settlements, or were retroactively folded into existing ones as “neighborhoods.” Yet although settlers took land around Palestinian communities, the outposts themselves were overwhelmingly kept inside Area C. This pattern intensified after the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, and crossed the geographic boundaries that had previously constrained settler activity.
This shift was enabled by the right-wing Israeli government that took office at the end of 2022, which placed political representatives of the settler movement in positions with direct authority over the West Bank. In February 2023, the Israeli government approved ten outposts in the West Bank and created a new category of “sites under legalization,” allowing other outposts to receive government funding and infrastructure support even though they were still unauthorized.
That same month, the Israeli military-run Civil Administration transferred significant powers over settlement planning to a new Settlements Administration under the authority of far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.
Since October 7, 2023, Israeli settlers have built 152 new outposts, at least 22 of them in Area B and at least one in Area A, on some 25,000 acres inside Areas A and B. As the outposts have multiplied, so has the number of settler attacks. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported that in 2023, settlers carried out 1,291 attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank that caused injury or property damage.
In 2024, the number of attacks increased to 1,449 and in 2025, jumped to 1,836. In 2026, OCHA estimates an average of six settler attacks are carried out every day across more than 275 communities in the West Bank, higher than in any year on record.
The village of Jalud in Area B illustrates this pattern of violent escalation. In 2023, Israeli settlers first took the land surrounding the village and then repeatedly attacked its residents. By 2026, the settlers were entering the residential edge of the village. One Palestinian house was occupied while still under construction. Another family endured weeks of settler violence, culminating in a siege during which settlers cut off the family’s water and electricity before brutally attacking them. The residents eventually escaped their homes, which settlers soon occupied.
The new strategy of settler expansion has reached Area A as well. On July 14, 2026, settlers took over a Palestinian house under construction in Beit Imrin, north of Nablus, in territory under full Palestinian Authority control. By the time of the attack, Israeli settler seizures of Palestinian houses were no longer isolated occurrences.
Settlers have increasingly changed their targets from unfinished buildings to inhabited homes, such as those in Jalud and Qusra, taking dozens of Palestinian structures, in some cases after repeated attacks and sieges had forced the occupants to leave.
Although the number of houses seized by Israeli settlers in Areas A and B is small relative to the tens of thousands of acres they have taken across the West Bank, the expanding geographic scope and the trend toward seizing homes mark a turning point.
The move toward taking Palestinian houses, in particular, effectively extends the Israeli frontier into the heart of the West Bank. Israel has already begun to use administrative reforms to register Palestinian land as Israeli property in Area C. What is happening in Areas A and B is a similar annexation pursued by occupancy rather than by statute; or put differently, de facto rather than de jure annexation.
The Qusra timeline
The process of de facto annexation has unfolded in less than a year for the roughly 6,350 residents of the Palestinian village of Qusra, close to which Israeli settlers established an outpost in November 2025. Settlers reportedly built the outpost by taking over five unfinished Palestinian houses, then brought in tents, water tanks, and livestock. According to the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), settlers have escalated their attacks on the village ever since the outpost was created.
In May 2026, settlers began to attack Ras al-Ain on the outskirts of Qusra, which occupies high ground and offers a potential strategic advantage. The mayor of Qusra, Abdul Azim Wadi, counted eight separate attempts to establish a settler outpost there.
On August 9, 2026, settlers surrounded local homes, cutting off food and water supplies to their 15 residents. On August 13, Israeli military forces arrived in Qusra ostensibly to end the settler siege and dismantle the unauthorized outposts. Instead, they declared the Ras al-Ain area around the occupied homes a closed military zone. Wadi reported that Israeli forces seized 16 Palestinian homes in Qusra, converted them into military posts, and ordered the residents of two of the besieged houses to leave, forcing them into the remaining building.
They also turned back a group of Peace Now activists and Italian volunteers carrying food and water for the besieged Palestinians, though local residents said that they allowed around 15 settlers to enter the village despite the closure. Israeli soldiers permitted limited food to reach the besieged families, but blocked a water tanker. Israeli forces also detained several settlers who were among those attacking PA municipal workers trying to repair the severed water and electricity lines.
Israeli forces were filmed praying alongside the settlers rather than removing them, though the Israeli army later claimed that it had disciplined those soldiers. At the time of publication, Palestinian families were still trapped inside the siege.
A division of labor
On August 13, 2026, Ophir Falk, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s foreign policy advisor, described the settlers at Qusra as “vigilantes” and said that such incidents were only sporadic. Aryeh Eldad, a West Bank settler and former member of the Israeli Knesset, argued that these kinds of attacks happen outside of state authority.
In a narrow sense, their claims are defensible. No Israeli minister specifically selected Ridi’s house to be occupied or issued orders for the siege. But the settler strategy for annexing land in the West Bank does not depend on a single chain of command or clear policy decisions. Israeli settlers, the military, politicians, and non-government institutions operate independently, yet their actions reinforce one another and collectively support settlement expansion.
Settlers may choose where to move, for example, but they do not build outposts on their own. Amana, the settlement movement’s development organization, had reportedly established more than 30 farms in the West Bank by February 2021, and in June 2023, its secretary-general, Zeev Hever, said that agricultural farms occupied more than twice the area of all settlements combined.
Legally, Amana is a private cooperative association, not a government agency. But in practice, it has long operated within the broader framework of the Israeli state. The Israeli government’s West Bank regional councils have transferred tens of millions of shekels in public money to the organization, and Amana has also appeared as a party to land-allocation agreements with the Settlement Division of the government-funded World Zionist Organization.
The Israeli military can then turn unauthorized settlements into protected areas. As was the case in Qusra, by creating closed military zones - often under the guise of removing settlers - Israeli forces can bar Palestinian owners from returning to an area, leaving the settler presence effectively undisturbed without officially transferring ownership of the land. The result is an ostensibly temporary measure that produces new facts on the ground.
How Israeli law 'legalizes' settler seizures
The State of Israel can give formal recognition to such unauthorized outposts. On February 8, 2026, the Israeli security cabinet widened the reach of Israeli administrative authority in the West Bank, expanding the Israeli Civil Administration’s enforcement powers inside Areas A and B, publishing previously classified land registries, repealing the Jordanian-era prohibition on non-Arab land purchase, abolishing transaction licenses, and transferring authority over building permits for the Israeli settlement in Hebron from the Palestinian municipality to the Civil Administration’s Higher Planning Council.
The Yesha Council—the umbrella organization for Jewish settlements in the West Bank—called the package one of “the most significant decisions” since the 1967 War. The United Nations (UN) Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, Francesca Albanese, condemned the move as yet another step toward the permanent Israeli annexation of the West Bank. In March 2026, the government secretly used its expanded powers to approve more than 30 additional outposts and farms in the West Bank.
The full scale of settler and military incursions into Areas A and B is difficult to measure because international monitoring does not treat them as a distinct category. Both OCHA and OHCHR track settler violence but do not systematically separate incursions from Areas A and B from those in Area C. Without such differentiation, it is difficult for independent observers to quantify the most consequential changes underway in the West Bank.
Nevertheless, the reports already show a clear pattern in which Israeli settlers are effectively making dispossession permanent by seizing houses rather than fields. Albanese has said that Israel is “using [settlers] to advance ethnic cleansing.” Local Palestinian residents are being forcibly displaced without the need for an expulsion order or demolition permit.
The Trump administration has largely framed settler violence as a problem of individual perpetrators, echoing the language of Israeli officials. But this characterization misses the vast network of actors and government institutions that supports the outposts. Washington should address this gap by targeting the financing and construction of settler outposts, not just individual settlers. Sanctioning such groups is not a new idea.
Under Executive Order 14115, issued by President Biden in February 2024, the United States sanctioned violent settlers and the organizations behind them, including Amana. On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump revoked the order, and four days later, the US Department of the Treasury removed the resulting designations. The US should now restore these sanctions against settler groups.
In the meantime, the Israeli outpost overlooking Qusra remains standing as the military refuses to carry out eviction orders against settlers there. The siege on Palestinian homes has entered its fifth week and the families inside are still trapped.
Their fate will indicate whether the seizure of Palestinian homes remains an exceptional tactic or becomes an established instrument of ethnic cleansing on the West Bank.

EU fails to agree on Russian sanctions, voting to continue on 22 September
The Committee of Permanent Representatives of EU member states (Coreper) held a meeting in Brussels on the morning of Tuesday 22 September, and was unable to adopt a decision regarding the extension of sanctions for violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity and sovereignty (the so-called "sanctions against Putin"), postponing the attempt to vote via written procedure.
Source: European Pravda, citing European diplomats familiar with the proceedings
Details: The European Union has thus far been unable to extend sanctions against Russians for violating Ukraine's territorial integrity.
"Coreper convened for a meeting this morning to discuss extending the sanctions lists. No agreement was reached. The Irish presidency decided to extend the voting time under the written procedure," one of European Pravda's interlocutors reported.
He added that the voting will continue until 15:00 Kyiv time.
Background:
- An attempt to adopt a compromise decision via written procedure was launched on the evening of 21 September.
- Ireland, with the support of the EU's most influential states, proposed a compromise: to extend the sanctions regime for violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity and sovereignty (the so-called "sanctions against Putin") immediately for 36 months (rather than six, as is customary) in exchange for removing Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the lists.
- The removal of the two Russian oligarchs is a demand of Slovakia and France. It is worth noting that Paris is insisting on the removal of only Usmanov's candidacy.
- The vote was not completed on 21 September due to the position of Latvia, which publicly "blocked" removing Russian oligarchs from the sanctions lists.
- The current sanctions regime, the list for which the EU began compiling back in 2014, covers individuals and legal entities responsible for actions that undermine or threaten the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine.
- Since 2022, it has included Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin, Russia's ruling elite and leading oligarchs, as well as former Ukrainian president Viktor Yanukovych.
- Currently, personal sanctions against Putin, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, former Ukrainian MP Viktor Medvedchuk, Viktor Yanukovych and roughly 3,000 other individuals and legal entities responsible for the war against Ukraine remain in force until midnight on 22 September.
- As reported by European Pravda, on 14 September, Coreper extended the sanctions regime for violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity and sovereignty for seven days as Slovakia and France continued to insist that the two Russian oligarchs be removed from the list.
- European Pravda sources in French diplomatic circles explained why Paris wants to lift sanctions on Usmanov. It later emerged that France plans to "exchange" Usmanov's delisting for the release of several French citizens who are currently in prison in Azerbaijan.
- The last extension of personal sanctions took place on 14 March. On that occasion, too, Slovakia pushed until the last minute for Fridman and Usmanov to be removed from the list.

europe’s largest carbon capture facility sends CO₂ from the netherlands to norway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
09:19:09 UTC
18:19:09 KST

EUROPE’S LARGEST CARBON CAPTURE FACILITY OPENS AT YARA SLUISKIL
Europe’s largest industrial carbon capture facility has officially opened at Yara’s ammonia and fertilizer plant in Sluiskil, the Netherlands. Designed to capture and liquefy up to 800,000 tons of CO₂ every year, the facility marks the beginning of a complete cross-border carbon capture and storage chain connecting Dutch industry with permanent geological storage beneath the Norwegian North Sea. Instead of releasing the gas into the atmosphere, Yara is effectively turning one of its largest by-products into cargo — although this particular shipment comes with no return journey.
The system targets emissions generated during ammonia production at Yara Sluiskil, Europe’s largest ammonia and fertilizer plant. Once captured, the CO₂ is liquefied and temporarily stored on site before being loaded onto vessels operated by Northern Lights. The ships then carry it north to Norway, where the carbon enters a storage network developed to serve industrial emitters across Europe. For sectors such as fertilizer, cement and waste management, where eliminating process emissions remains particularly difficult, the project offers another route towards reducing their footprint without dismantling the industries themselves.
Yara’s carbon capture facility in Sluiskil | all images courtesy of Yara
CO₂ BECOMES CROSS-BORDER CARGO
After arriving at Northern Lights’ facilities in Øygarden, the liquefied CO₂ is transferred into the company’s storage infrastructure before being permanently injected around 2,600 meters beneath the seabed. In this sense, the project is as much a logistical system as a piece of climate technology: capture equipment, storage tanks, ships, terminals and underground reservoirs are stitched together across national borders to move emissions away from the atmosphere and into geological formations.
That geography is key. Rather than requiring each industrial plant to sit directly above an appropriate storage site, shipping allows capture facilities across Europe to connect with shared offshore infrastructure. The Yara project establishes the first complete cross-border chain of its kind at this scale, turning the North Sea into the final destination of emissions produced hundreds of kilometers away. Carbon, once an invisible exhaust, now acquires an itinerary, infrastructure and — rather unusually for waste — a carefully planned permanent address.
the facility captures CO₂ from ammonia production
TWELVE MILLION TONS, FIFTEEN YEARS
Over the next 15 years, Yara and Northern Lights expect the system to capture and permanently store approximately 12 million tons of CO₂. The facility also allows Yara to lower the carbon footprint of products manufactured at Sluiskil, including fertilizers and ammonia used across agriculture, industry, energy and shipping. The company positions CCS as part of a broader effort to maintain European industrial production while reducing emissions from processes that cannot yet be fully electrified or replaced by renewable alternatives.
The Sluiskil facility was officially inaugurated on September 7, 2026, bringing together representatives from the Dutch and Norwegian governments, the European Commission, Yara and Northern Lights. Beyond the ceremony, its significance lies in making carbon capture visible as actual industrial infrastructure rather than an abstract climate target: pipes, tanks and ships now connect one of Europe’s largest fertilizer plants to a reservoir deep below the sea. Whether CCS ultimately serves as a bridge or a longer-term fixture of heavy industry, Sluiskil shows just how much architecture, engineering and logistics can be required to make 800,000 tons of carbon disappear from view each year.

Israeli jailed 4.5 years for spying for Iran, gathering intelligence on Yoav Gallant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
09:19:00 UTC
18:19:00 KST

Israeli citizen Fares Abu al-Hija, a resident of Kaukab in northern Israel, was sentenced to 4½ years in prison Tuesday after he was convicted of spying for Iran, including gathering intelligence on former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant and traveling to Gallant’s home in Moshav Amikam, where he was arrested.
Abu al-Hija, 32, was convicted in a Haifa Court under a plea agreement of contact with a foreign agent. According to the indictment, filed in February, he was in contact from October 2025 to January 2026 via Telegram with a person who called himself “Martin” and carried out a series of tasks for him in exchange for payments transferred through the Binance app.
According to the indictment, Abu al-Hija carried out the assignments despite “suspecting that the person was a foreign agent and refraining from investigating that suspicion.”
As part of the tasks he was given, he purchased and concealed mobile phones and a charger at several locations in Haifa and Kiryat Haim, activated the devices, installed communication apps on them, documented the hiding places and sent the documentation to his handler.
He was later asked to deliver an envelope containing an access code to a cryptocurrency account at a location in Zikhron Ya’akov and to photograph a cafe in Tel Aviv.
The prosecution, represented by attorney Yaniv Zohar, asked the court to set a sentencing range of five to eight years in prison, arguing that the offenses were committed for financial gain during wartime and that the potential harm was significant.
Defense attorney Adel Dabbah argued that the acts were not at the highest level of severity, that his client did not know the location in Amikam was connected to Gallant and that he had not acted out of ideological motives.
In explaining the sentence, Judge Avi Levy said the defendant had acted in a planned and sustained manner and that the potential harm was high because the activities were intended to gather intelligence and harm state security.
The judge noted that Abu al-Hija received a total of about $3,600 for the assignments and chose not to investigate his suspicions regarding the identity of his handler.
At the same time, the judge took into account Abu al-Hija’s confession, remorse, lack of a criminal record and his parents’ medical condition.
“The defendant has no criminal record, took responsibility and expressed remorse for his actions. I took into account the defendant’s family circumstances, including his parents’ serious health conditions and the effect of their son’s arrest on their mental state,” the judge said.
In addition to the prison term, Abu al-Hija was also sentenced to two years’ suspended imprisonment.
