SEOUL, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- A South Korean appellate court on Tuesday reduced the prison sentence for Kim Keon-hee, wife of former President Yoon Suk-yeol, to five years, cutting two years off a lower court's seven-year ruling for corruption, including the sale of government posts.
The Seoul High Court handed down the lighter sentence, acquitting her of some counts. The court ordered the confiscation of gifts offered to her, along with a forfeiture fine of 24.4 million won (about 18,000 U.S. dollars).
The team of Min Joong-ki, an independent counsel who led investigations into corruption allegations involving the former presidential couple, demanded a seven-year sentence for Kim for selling public offices in exchange for high-priced jewelry and luxury goods.
The court overturned a conviction regarding a luxury wristwatch, which Kim received from a robot dog entrepreneur in September 2022 in return for business favors.
The court also acquitted her of charges that she received a replica of a famous painting in exchange for personnel solicitation, citing a failure to prove the charges.
However, the court upheld all other corruption charges from the initial trial.
Kim was found guilty of accepting luxury jewelry, including a necklace, a brooch and earrings, from a businessman between March and May 2022 in return for the appointment of his eldest son-in-law to a government post.
She was convicted of receiving a designer bag and other luxury goods from a pastor between June and September 2022 in exchange for favors, and a gold turtle from a former chief of the national education commission in exchange for an appointment favor in April of the same year.
The court upheld the finding that Kim received a painting from a former prosecutor in February 2023 in return for political nomination favors.
Kim, who was indicted under detention in August 2025, became the first wife of a former South Korean president to be tried under detention. ■

Around 40 industrial parks currently operational in Ukraine – MP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:25:00 UTC
17:25:00 KST

Around 40 industrial parks currently operational in Ukraine – MP
Deputy Chairman of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Economic Development Dmytro Kysylevskyi said this in a comment to Ukrinform.
"There are currently slightly more than 120 industrial parks registered in the industrial parks register. At the same time, the number of parks is not an indicative figure – it is like counting the number of individual entrepreneurs or limited liability companies. Much more important is the dynamics of active industrial parks – those where industrial infrastructure and industrial enterprises are being built or have already been built. If there were only two such parks in 2021, there are now almost 40," the MP said.
For the third year in a row, the government has been allocating around UAH 1 billion for the development of industrial infrastructure in industrial parks. The funds are provided on a 50/50 co-financing basis. In addition to contributing its share of the financing, the applicant undertakes to commission at least 5,000 square meters of industrial real estate within three years and attract at least two industrial enterprises to the industrial park. Thus, for every UAH 1 of state investment, the recipient undertakes to attract UAH 5-6 in private investment.
"By the end of last year, 37 plants had been built or were under construction at these industrial sites. Construction of most of them began during the full-scale invasion. We now have more than 300 MW of substation capacity in industrial parks, as well as more than one million square meters of industrial real estate. Overall, nearly UAH 46 billion in investment had already been made in industrial parks by the beginning of 2026," Kysylevskyi said.
According to him, the number of such plants is expected to reach around 50 by the end of 2026.
Under the program to stimulate the development of industrial infrastructure in industrial parks, an average of 15-17 applications are currently considered each year. The first assessment of how the state funds have been used will take place in 2027, when the three-year period for the provision of the funds expires.
"The first funds were disbursed at the end of 2024, which means that the first assessment will take place at the end of 2027. In other words, the parks that received funds in 2024 will have to report on the fulfillment of their commitments," the MP said.
Recently, the Verkhovna Rada adopted Law No. 12117, aimed at creating clearer and more effective conditions for attracting industrial investment through industrial parks. Kysylevskyi said the law does not contain any revolutionary solutions, but instead technically improves legislation governing the operation of industrial parks and addresses 20 issues, each of which helps remove a specific local obstacle to attracting investment.
"For example, we have regulated the procedure for adding and removing land plots from an industrial park. We allowed the status of management company and industrial park initiator to be held by the same entity. We granted management companies the right to take out loans under the '5-7-9%' program, among other things," he said.
The amendments are expected to accelerate investment processes, simplify the work of management companies, which serve as ambassadors for attracting industrial investment to Ukraine, and encourage communities to more actively develop industrial infrastructure.
As reported, Ukraine has launched a program to stimulate industrial parks that have been damaged by Russian shelling. Under the program, the state covers up to 80% of the cost of restoring infrastructure, but no more than UAH 200 million per park. For the construction of new infrastructure, the co-financing rate is 50%, with funding of up to UAH 150 million.

Istat said Tuesday that Italy's deficit-to-GDP ratio for 2025 was 3.1%, confirming the provisional figure it gave in April. Russia Delays Civilian Spending as Soaring War Costs Widen Budget Deficit
The Russian Finance Ministry was forced to delay a portion of scheduled government expenditures to later periods to maintain its "everything for the front" priority and keep the budget balanced.
Finance Minister Anton Siluanov announced these measures during the Moscow Financial Forum, as reported by The Moscow Times on September 21.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"The most important thing for us right now is defense tasks, the tasks of the front," the minister stated, adding that resolving budget challenges this year required "digging around somewhere" and adjusting both expenditures and the resource base.
From January through August, the federal budget deficit expanded to 5.8 trillion rubles ($72.5 billion), representing 2.5% of GDP. Siluanov noted that this deficit will continue to grow, explaining: "During the execution of the budget, additional needs for financing and expenditures arose.
Additional sources of funding for these costs will also be provided for this purpose. We expect the deficit to be larger than planned, but it will remain within 3% of GDP." He added that the government intends to cover the shortfall using accumulated account balances and borrowing on the debt market, according to The Moscow Times.
In the 2026 budget law, the Russian government originally allocated 12.9 trillion rubles ($161.25 billion) under the "national defense" item.
However, actual spending related to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, including adjacent budget categories, reached 10.687 trillion rubles ($133.58 billion) in the first half of the year alone, according to calculations by Janis Kluge from the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, The Moscow Times reports.
Compared to the same period last year, military and arms production expenditures grew by another 30%. They rose by 65% compared to January–June 2024, and have increased more than fivefold compared to pre-war 2021. Cumulative spending on the military since the beginning of 2022 has exceeded 57 trillion rubles ($712.5 billion).
This stagnation aligns with a previous report, which warned that severe labor shortages and intense military spending have pushed Russia to its absolute productive limits.
It notes that the Kremlin is rapidly exhausting its current human and financial resources, leaving Putin with a fundamental choice: either scale back his military ambitions in Ukraine or implement deeply unpopular domestic measures, such as forced conscription and a Soviet-style command economy, to sustain the invasion.

Red Cat’s maritime arm hits a one-year milestone in Georgia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:17:27 UTC
17:17:27 KST

- Blue Ops, the maritime arm of Red Cat Holdings, marked one year since opening its uncrewed surface vessel plant in Valdosta, Georgia.
- The company built its first prototypes with Hodgdon Shipbuilding in Maine before shifting production to the 155,000-square-foot Valdosta facility.
Blue Ops, the maritime division of drone maker Red Cat Holdings, marked one year since it opened a manufacturing plant in Valdosta, Georgia, the company said. The state of Georgia recognized Sept. 21 as the inaugural Blue Ops Day in the city, according to a company statement.
Blue Ops builds uncrewed surface vessels, small autonomous boats used for military and national security missions. The company leased a 155,000-square-foot former boat factory at 601 Gil Harbin Industrial Boulevard in Valdosta, the site of an earlier Regal Boats plant, and announced the move in April with plans to invest about $30 million and create more than 200 jobs. Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp announced the facility in April, and state officials said the company planned to hire up to 100 workers in 2026, with more roles to follow as production increased.
Blue Ops president Barry Hinckley said at the time the investment was meant to build “a modern, scalable, and domestic USV manufacturing base from the ground up.”
The company built its first prototype vessels elsewhere. Blue Ops partnered with Hodgdon Shipbuilding, a Maine boatbuilder founded in 1816, to construct its first five uncrewed surface vessel prototypes at facilities in Boothbay and Damariscotta, Maine, before shifting full-rate production to Valdosta.
In April, Blue Ops also partnered with HADDY, a robotic 3D printing company, to add large-scale 3D printing and robotic production systems to the Valdosta plant. The companies said the partnership would roughly double the facility’s manufacturing capacity by using robotic systems to build vessel hulls before workers complete final assembly.
Red Cat Holdings, based in Salt Lake City and traded on Nasdaq under the ticker RCAT, also makes small drones through its Teal Drones and FlightWave Aerospace subsidiaries. The company has positioned Blue Ops as its expansion into uncrewed maritime systems, alongside its existing air-domain drone business.
Blue Ops has not disclosed how many vessels it has built at the Valdosta facility over the past year or named specific government customers for its USV line. The company said in its anniversary statement that it intends to keep expanding production capacity at the site.

Libya’s NOC says armed group shuts oil pipeline valve, sharply reducing main field output
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:13:28 UTC
17:13:28 KST

Muetaz Wannes and Mohammad Sio
22 September 2026•Update: 22 September 2026
An armed group has shut a valve on a crude oil pipeline linking Libya’s Sharara field to the western port of Zawiya, causing a sharp drop in production at the country’s main oil field, the National Oil Corporation (NOC) said late Monday.
The NOC said the armed group closed Valve No. 7, halting the flow of crude from the Sharara field, operated by Akakus Oil Operations, to Zawiya Port in western Libya.
The closure caused pressure to build up in the crude pipeline, resulting in a “significant reduction” in production at Sharara, it added.
Located in the Murzuq Desert, around 800 kilometers (500 miles) south of Tripoli, Sharara is Libya’s largest oil field, with production capacity of around 340,000 barrels per day.
The NOC said it contacted the southwestern branch of the Petroleum Facilities Guard and urged it to carry out its duties, but the appeals “had produced no results.” Technical teams had also been unable to reach the area around Valves 6 and 7.
The corporation warned that the continued shutdown would halt production at the Sharara field as well as oil transport and export operations, directly harming Libya’s economy by causing a decline in state revenues.
It also warned that the oil transport system and its facilities will be exposed to technical and operational risks, anticipating that the shutdown will cause the Zawiya oil refinery to cease operations, thereby further increasing the cost of importing fuel from abroad.
It called for the immediate reopening of the pipeline and demanded the relevant authorities secure oil installations and keep them away from protests and other disruptions.
The corporation said it “may be compelled to declare force majeure” if the closure continues.
Force majeure is a contractual provision that suspends liability when extraordinary circumstances prevent parties from meeting their obligations.
The NOC did not identify the armed group responsible for shutting the valve.
The incident comes a week after members of the Petroleum Facilities Guard closed the main Hamada-Zawiya oil pipeline on Sept. 15, causing production and operations to stop at the Hamada and Al-Tahara fields and Station NC5. The NOC also warned at the time that it could declare force majeure if the closure persisted.
The Hamada field is located in the Hamada al-Hamra area of the Ghadames Basin in western Libya, about 400 kilometers (250 miles) south of Tripoli. It is considered one of the key oil and natural gas fields in western Libya and produces around 700 barrels per day.
Members of the Petroleum Facilities Guard have been demanding higher salaries amid a broader wave of labor protests in Libya.

U.S. Army orders more M270A2 launcher upgrades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:09:31 UTC
17:09:31 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Lockheed Martin $200 million in September to rebuild more M270 rocket launchers to the M270A2 standard.
- The upgrade adds a new engine, an armored cab and a fire-control system shared with HIMARS, letting both launchers fire the same precision munitions.
The U.S. Army has awarded Lockheed Martin $200 million to rebuild more M270 Multiple Launch Rocket System launchers to the M270A2 standard, the company said. The September award is the latest in a series of contracts that began in 2019 to modernize the tracked rocket launcher.
The recapitalization strips down existing M270 launchers and rebuilds them as close to new, with a new engine, an armored cab and the Common Fire Control System, the same fire-control system used on the wheeled HIMARS launcher. That shared system lets the two launchers fire the same family of precision munitions, including GMLRS, Extended-Range GMLRS and the Precision Strike Missile, and lets crews trained on one system move more easily to the other.
The Army has awarded similar M270A2 recapitalization contracts nearly every year since 2019, including a $362 million award in 2019, a $226 million award in 2020, a $451 million award in 2024 and a $214 million award last year. Lockheed Martin has said the goal is to keep the M270 fleet in service through 2050. The Army’s fleet includes 225 M270A1 launchers being upgraded to the A2 standard, along with about 160 older, decommissioned M270A0 launchers slated for the same overhaul.
The M270A2 is a tracked launcher that carries more armor and cargo capacity than the wheeled HIMARS, while HIMARS offers greater mobility on roads. Both can fire the Extended-Range GMLRS, which reaches out to 150 km (93 miles), and the Precision Strike Missile, a longer-range weapon still being fielded across the Army. Lockheed Martin has said only the M270A2 and HIMARS can fire those newer munitions, which older, unmodernized M270 launchers cannot use.
The recapitalization work is split among Lockheed Martin’s Camden, Arkansas, plant and facilities in Grand Prairie and New Boston, Texas, with the Army’s Red River Army Depot handling part of the overhaul. Recent contracts have carried completion dates stretching into 2027 and 2030, reflecting the scale of the work needed to rebuild dozens of launchers at a time.
The Army has fielded more than 220 M270-series launchers, and international partners that operate the M270 or HIMARS, including NATO members, are also eligible for the upgraded fire-control system under foreign military sales.

U.S. Army laser weapon shown defeating drones at border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:05:04 UTC
17:05:04 KST

- Newly released footage shows an Army Multi-Purpose High Energy Laser, built with AeroVironment technology, defeating drones at the southern border.
- The system engaged and defeated three hostile drones over two nights in late August under Joint Task Force Southern Border.
The U.S. Department of War has released new footage showing an Army Multi-Purpose High Energy Laser, built with directed-energy technology from AeroVironment (AV), defeating drones along the U.S. southern border, according to a report by Army Verification Alliance (AV).
The laser is deployed under Joint Task Force Southern Border, a U.S. Northern Command unit that supports U.S. Customs and Border Protection. In late August, task force personnel used the system, known as AMP-HEL, to engage and defeat three drones over two nights, Aug. 25 and 26, near the border. The U.S. Army said the aircraft were judged hostile based on their use in direct support of activity that threatened U.S. military personnel and CBP partners.
“Cartel networks are increasingly employing unmanned aircraft systems to facilitate illicit human-smuggling and actively spy on our personnel and law enforcement partners,” said Army Maj. Gen. Curtis Taylor, commander of Joint Task Force Southern Border. “By integrating layered countermeasures alongside advanced directed-energy capabilities like this laser system, we have made it clear that we will not tolerate hostile surveillance.”
The Army has not disclosed exactly where the drones were engaged or confirmed who was flying them, though officials have linked similar incursions to cartel surveillance. AV told Breaking Defense the system used is the product of the Army’s AMP-HEL program but did not say which specific configuration was deployed or whether it was vehicle-mounted.
AMP-HEL is a 20-kilowatt-class laser weapon built to defeat Group 1 and Group 2 drones, the U.S. military’s category for smaller, slower unmanned aircraft. AV delivered the first two prototypes, mounted on Joint Light Tactical Vehicles, to the Army in December 2025 as part of the AMP-HEL prototyping effort. The company markets the underlying laser weapon system as LOCUST, which it says pairs an electro-optical tracking system, a laser rangefinder and a targeting laser with the high-energy laser itself. AeroVironment says the system uses a common gaming controller for weapon control and is designed to plug into a range of sensor types and radio-frequency bands, as well as existing command-and-control networks.
About 8,000 service members are currently deployed under Joint Task Force Southern Border, the Army said. Officials have said hundreds of drones fly near the border each day, and Northern Command leaders have described the border as a proving ground for technology meant to counter them. Weeks after the August engagements, the Army awarded AV a production contract for the laser under a separate program called Enduring High Energy Laser; DefenseScoop reported the deal is worth $464.8 million and covers dozens of additional LOCUST-based systems over the next several years.

Four Corners episodes breached ABC's editorial standards, ombudsman finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:04:59 UTC
17:04:59 KST

Four Corners episodes breached ABC's editorial standards, ombudsman's investigation finds
In short
The ABC breached four editorial standards in stories by sacked reporter Mahmood Fazal, its ombudsman found.
The episodes involved have already been withdrawn by ABC News.
What's next
The ABC has said it accepts the report's seven recommendations and has started to implement them.
The ABC's Four Corners program had insufficient verification and fact-checking and a culture of "limiting knowledge" about anonymous sources, its independent ombudsman has found, identifying breaches of editorial standards in two stories by sacked reporter Mahmood Fazal .
The ombudsman's report, released this afternoon, found two episodes failed to meet editorial standards for accuracy, fair and honest dealing, and independence.
"Audiences were given a misleading impression of who key contributors were, the basis on which the ABC was relying on them and the level of confidence that could reasonably be placed in their claims," the report said.
The ombudsman made seven recommendations, which include amending the ABC's editorial standard on anonymity, further legal and editorial training for the Four Corners team and more support for less experienced reporters.
The ABC says it accepts the recommendations in full and has begun implementing them.
ABC News had already removed the two episodes covered by the ombudsman's review — Cocaine Nation and Meth Highway — after its own investigation into the anonymous interviewees.
In total, three episodes of Four Corners and two of Background Briefing by Fazal have already been withdrawn by the ABC, with a short segment edited out of another Four Corners episode.
Last month, the ABC said its own review found verification policies on anonymous interviewees were "not followed to a level that meets our editorial standards".
"The ABC is committed to journalism of the highest standard. Maintaining the trust of Australians depends on upholding those standards and we take any concerns about our journalism seriously," it said.
Fazal, a former member of the Mongols bikie club, had his employment terminated in May after an ABC investigation into his appearance on a podcast with a former underworld figure last year.
He had launched an unfair dismissal claim in the Fair Work Commission, but his hearing was removed from the schedule. The ABC said it was aware Fazal was no longer pursuing his claim.
In a social media video post last month, Fazal said he felt like the ABC was "trying everything in their power to stop me from ever working again".
"Even though all my work was approved across different teams and departments, cross-checked and met the standards before broadcast, they've decided there's now different standards that are retrospectively being applied to all of my stories," he said.
"They want to make me a scapegoat? Don't give a s***. I won't stop."
He has previously said he was hired by the ABC for his access to certain sources, but that proximity had then been used against him.
Previously, Fazal's reporting appeared in VICE, The Guardian, Rolling Stone, The Sydney Morning Herald, The Monthly and The Saturday Paper.
Last month, the ABC announced its head of investigations and current affairs, Jo Puccini, was leaving the public broadcaster after a 25-year career.
She had oversight of Four Corners and Background Briefing.
Other senior managers at the ABC at the time of Fazal's reporting, including news director Justin Stevens, have already left the broadcaster. The ABC's incoming news director Simon Robinson started in the role on September 14.
Last week, ABC managing director Hugh Marks rejected an Australian Communications and Media Authority finding that the public broadcaster breached impartiality obligations in an unrelated Four Corners program about the redevelopment of the Australian War Memorial.
ACMA said on Thursday it had found the program's March 2025 episode, Sacrifice, had "unduly favoured one perspective".
The ABC says it "stands behind the team" that created the episode.
"If this interpretation of the code is applied, including more widely across the industry, it could have a chilling effect on the body of investigative journalism that delivers the important stories that serve the public interest," Marks said in a statement.

Why young people are paying to get hired

A US congressman urged Monday for Israel to end its airstrikes on Syria, saying the attacks “shouldn’t be done,” in an interview with Anadolu on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
“I’m really grateful the president’s envoy, Tom Barrack, has expressed opposition to the Israeli air strikes, and it just shouldn’t be done,” said Rep. Joe Wilson, a Republican from South Carolina.
Asked whether he was calling on the Israeli government to end the strikes on Syria, Wilson responded: “Absolutely.”
“I appreciate the leadership of President Donald Trump, at the request of Türkiye, at the request of Saudi Arabia, to give Syria a chance. And Syria will succeed, and then it’s beneficial to every country in the Middle East,” he told Anadolu.
Wilson also said the “liberation of Syria” — referring to the collapse of Syria’s Bashar al Assad regime in late 2024 — was important for other countries in the region, including Iran and Lebanon.
Barrack, the US special envoy for Syria and Iraq who also serves as ambassador to Türkiye, said in August that Washington was “deeply concerned” over Israeli air strikes on the Abu al-Duhur Airbase in northern Syria, calling them an “unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability.”
Wilson backs Türkiye’s return to F-35 programme
Wilson, who co-chairs the Congressional Caucus on US-Türkiye Relations and Turkish Americans, also underscored the depth of ties between Washington and Ankara, pointing to their cooperation since the Korean War.
“I’m very grateful that Türkiye led the effort for the liberation of Syria, and Syria now having an opportunity of stability, peace and prosperity, it’s going to benefit all of the Middle East, but particularly Türkiye,” he said.
Asked about efforts by Trump and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to address the dispute over Türkiye’s purchase of Russia’s S-400 air defence system and Ankara’s possible return to the F-35 fighter jet programme, Wilson said he was “hopeful.”
Wilson said he supported US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth working with Türkiye, adding that cooperation between Washington and Ankara would contribute to “peace through strength.”
Asked whether he supports the sale of F-35 fighter jets to Türkiye, Wilson replied: “I do. Yes, I do.” He also said he supported removing sanctions on Türkiye, imposed under the Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act (CAATSA).
“But the bottom line, let’s go back: Türkiye is a great ally of America, America is an ally of Türkiye, and we want mutual benefit,” he said.
The US suspended Türkiye from the F-35 fighter jet programme in 2019 after objecting to its purchase of the Russian S-400 air defence system, claiming the system would endanger the fighter jets and is inoperable with NATO systems. Türkiye has said repeatedly that there is no conflict between the two and proposed a commission to study the issue.
Several Turkish defence entities were sanctioned under CAATSA.
During his meeting with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Türkiye in July on the sidelines of the NATO summit, Trump said he would “certainly” consider allowing Ankara to buy F-35 fighter jets and wants to remove the CAATSA sanctions on the country.

I IN contrasts concrete architecture with bright colours in Andersson Bell Tokyo store
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:00:21 UTC
17:00:21 KST

I IN contrasts concrete architecture with bright colours in Andersson Bell Tokyo store
Local studio I IN drew on the existing architecture when creating fashion brand Andersson Bell's flagship store in Japan, which is filled with glossy, reflective surfaces and warm red and yellow hues.
Located in Tokyo's Aoyama neighbourhood, the original building from 1993 has an exposed concrete interior that heavily influenced I IN's design for the store.
"It is quite rare to find such a magnificent space in Tokyo, and we were fortunate to have the freedom to take a bold and radical approach to the design," I IN co-founder Yohei Terui told Dezeen.
"Especially, the building's strong composition of mass and void became a major source of inspiration and guided us throughout the spatial planning."
The studio aimed for the interior to be contrasting but not competing with the architecture.
"The idea was to translate the brand's identity of 'contrast' into space design," Terui continued.
"The existing architecture, built in Tokyo in the 90s, already had a very strong character and presence, so rather than competing with it, we wanted to introduce a strong modern layer that would create a beautiful contrast with the existing architecture."
To do so, I IN, which Terui founded with Hiromu Yuyama, introduced warm, saturated colours across the building's three storeys.
Bright red, orange and yellow hues contrast against the boardmarked concrete walls throughout the space, with the red section also visible through the store's large front window.
"The red comes from the brand's signature colour and became the introduction of the store," Terui said.
"As guests move through the space and step upstairs, they experience a gradual transition from red to orange and then to yellow," he continued.
"Rather than simply applying colour to each floor, we wanted this transition to become part of the spatial experience, giving each level a different atmosphere and creating a sense of progression as guests move through the building."
Terui and Yuyama also added pipes that "extend through the existing architecture as if piercing its structure", the studio said.
As well as contrasting the concrete's grey hue with more colourful details, I IN juxtaposed its raw tactility with plenty of glossy and mirrored details, including a glass floor, steel pipes and tables and display cases with shiny, lacquered surfaces.
The furniture pieces used in the 309-square-metre store were tailor-made by the studio and designed to feel like a part of the existing architecture.
"All of the furniture was custom-made for the store," Terui said.
"We followed the same idea of creating a bold presence, taking inspiration from the powerful character and scale of the existing architecture," he continued.
"Rather than treating the furniture as separate elements placed within the space, we designed each piece as a part of the architecture, as if it had always been there, so that the furniture and the space ultimately merge into one."
I IN has previously also designed a tile-clad store for designer Nigo's Human Made brand and a glossy purple lounge for department store Matsuya Ginza.
The photography is by Tomooki Kengaku.

China eyes chip-industry foothold with a tiny Han Xin code to challenge US standard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

08:00:09 UTC
17:00:09 KST

China eyes chip-industry foothold with a tiny Han Xin code to challenge US standard
After failing to unseat the QR code years ago, Beijing is betting that a “micro” version of its home-grown barcode can gain a foothold in the global semiconductor supply chain
China is attempting to breathe new life into its nearly 20-year-old Han Xin code by promoting a miniaturised version to use on semiconductors, marking the latest chapter in Beijing’s long-running attempt to secure a foothold for its home-grown standards in global industrial supply chains.
The State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) said on Monday that the “Micro Han Xin” code – a scaled-down iteration of the 2007-era symbology – had entered the formal international standardisation process. The effort aims to mark components that are too small for conventional labelling, specifically computer components.
These ultra-compact codes give unique identities to sensors, microprocessors, controllers, memory units and other components, allowing them to be tracked across complex fabrication, packaging and testing workflows.
The move reflects a strategic recalibration as China looks to challenge the established foreign technologies being used in high-specification industrial applications. The SAMR acknowledged how the domestic semiconductor sector currently relies heavily on foreign systems such as Data Matrix, which was created in the United States nearly 40 years ago and is already the global standard for marking and tracking semiconductors, silicon wafers and electronic components.

Ukraine hits Russian oil refineries in Samara and Ufa
Units from the Ukrainian defence forces struck two key oil refining facilities in Russia on the night of 21-22 September.
Sources: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine; Special Operations Forces (SOF)
Details: The Kuibyshev oil refinery in Samara was struck.
The Special Operations Forces said the attack was carried out by Special Operations Forces' Deep Strike units jointly with the Unmanned Systems Forces and Defence Intelligence of Ukraine. Several drones reached their targets, causing a large-scale fire at the facility.
The Kuibyshev oil refinery is one of the largest oil refining facilities in Russia's Samara group and is part of the Rosneft structure. It has a refining capacity of around 7 million tonnes of oil per year. The refinery produces petrol, diesel fuel, fuel oil and more than 30 other petroleum products.
The Bashneft-Ufaneftekhim oil refinery in Ufa, Republic of Bashkortostan, Russia, was also struck, with a fire reported on the premises.
Bashneft-Ufaneftekhim has a refining capacity of around 7.5 million tonnes of oil per year. The facility carries out deep oil refining and produces petrol, diesel and boiler fuel, liquefied gases, sulphur and other petroleum products.
Products from both refineries are used to meet the needs of the Russian military.

There's the inroads of the far right, but also the broader desire for change. Introducing Berlin's answer to Zohran Mamdani: Elif Eralp, who led the far-left Die Linke party's historic win in Sunday's municipal elections in Berlin. We ask if the 45-year-old daughter of Turkish political exiles can push through her promises of rent freezes and nationalisation of private real estate companies. Just like in New York last year, affordable housing was a hot-button issue. It didn't hurt that her party ran a social media-savvy campaign.

The result in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg–West Pomerania is also a pain point for Germany's other historic big tent party: yes, the Social Democrats limited the damage, but the far-right AfD won more votes.
A capital city that goes red, a rust belt region that's turning increasingly far right – it's all part of a pattern. Is it about winners and losers of globalisation, a generation gap with younger voters sick of all the boomers who cling to power, some even say a gender gap with younger women voting left and younger men far right. How fast and how deep is the change in our politics?

China on Tuesday released the 2026 list of the country's top 500 private enterprises, with 110 companies reporting operating revenue of over 100 billion yuan, underscoring robust growth in the country's private sector.
JD.com, Alibaba (China) and Hengli Group retained the top three positions, according to the 2026 China Top 500 Private Enterprises list unveiled by the All-China Federation of Industry and Commerce in Tianjin.
The 28th large-scale private enterprise survey conducted by the federation took in a total of 6,350 companies, each with operating revenue of over one billion yuan in 2025, with the top 500 companies by revenue making up the list.
The survey showed that China's private enterprises continued to improve their innovation capacity, operating efficiency and core competitiveness, demonstrating an overall trend towards new and higher-quality development.
The top 500 private enterprises reported total operating revenue of 44.93 trillion yuan in 2025, up 4.35 percent.
They also saw a combined net profit of 1.83 trillion yuan, with 17 companies each posting over 20 billion yuan in net profit.
Manufacturing companies on the top 500 list recorded total operating revenue of 32.22 trillion yuan, up 8.73 percent.
The top 500 companies are actively positioning themselves in strategic emerging and future industries.
Of those that provided relevant data, 311 companies invested in 679 strategic emerging industry projects, and 82 launched 112 future industry projects.
In innovation, the top 500 companies that provided relevant data reported total research and development spending of 1.26 trillion yuan, with R&D investment averaging 2.95 percent of revenue.
In addition, they paid 1.3 trillion yuan in taxes last year, with 254 companies each paying over one billion yuan. (Xinhua)

India sees rise in both overweight and underweight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
07:55:31 UTC
16:55:31 KST

Sedentary lifestyles are often blamed for rising obesity. It is perhaps the most obvious explanation, repeated ad nauseam in this digital age, where often the entire world stays within our six-inch screen. But data from the government's latest pan-India health survey (NFHS-6) suggest something quieter, and potentially more complicated for policymakers. Below-normal BMI has stopped retreating in India even as overweight and obesity rise.The National Family Health Survey (NFHS) is the government's main source of data on health and nutrition, run by the International Institute for Population Sciences for the Union health ministry. Its sixth round, NFHS-6, covered about 6.79 lakh households across 715 districts, with fieldwork running from May 2023 to December 2024. It reports 101 indicators for India and every state and union territory except Manipur.Among women aged 15-49, the share with below-normal BMI rose marginally from 18.7% in NFHS-5 to 19.7% in NFHS-6, while the share classified as overweight or obese rose steeply from 24% to 30.7%.
Hence the calculated share of women in the normal-BMI range fell from 57.3% to 49.6%, a decline of 7.7 percentage points.Men aged 15-49 are moving in the same direction. Below-normal BMI rose from 16.2% to 19.7%, while overweight or obesity increased from 22.9% to 27.3%. Hence the share of men in the normal-BMI range shrank from 60.9% to 53%, a decline of 7.9 percentage points.
The dual problem
BMI is weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared. For these indicators, NFHS classifies BMI below 18.5 as below normal and BMI of 25 or above as overweight or obese. It does not publish the normal range in between; TOI calculated that middle by subtracting the two published shares from 100.The NFHS-6 fact sheets are provisional, and without unit-level data it has not been tested whether the changes are statistically significant.Trend reversal in low BMIComparable figures for both sexes begin with NFHS-3, and below-normal BMI fell in each round until now. Among women it went from 35.6% in NFHS-3 (2005-06) to 22.9% in NFHS-4 (2015-16) and 18.7% in NFHS-5; among men, from 34.2% to 20.2% and then 16.2%.
Trend reversal
NFHS-6 is the first of these rounds in which the below-normal share rises for both sexes, and men's share, lower than women's in each earlier round, now matches it at 19.7%. Overweight has risen in every round, from 12.6% to 30.7% among women since NFHS-3 and from 9.3% to 27.3% among men.How states faredBelow-normal BMI increased from NFHS-5 in 20 of the 35 state/UT comparisons among women and 27 of 35 among men. Overweight or obesity rose even more widely, in 33 of 35 among women and 28 of 35 among men. Both rose together in 19 of the comparisons for women and 20 for men.
State-wise comparison for men
Among women, just seven of the 35 states and Union territories in the NFHS-6 release had a calculated normal-BMI share below 50% in NFHS-5; in NFHS-6, that number has risen to 16. So in 16 states, more than half of women in the 15-49 age group are either overweight or underweight. Among men, only one of the 35 — Puducherry — was below 50% in NFHS-5. In NFHS-6, 11 are below 50%.Rajasthan recorded the sharpest increase in below-normal BMI for both sexes: from 19.6% to 27.3% among women, a rise of 7.7 percentage points, and from 14% to 24.7% among men, up 10.7 points. Other large increases in low BMI among women were in Jammu & Kashmir, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Jharkhand; among men, the sharpest increases were in Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Tripura and Delhi.At the other end, Lakshadweep saw the largest increase in overweight or obesity among women, from 33.5% to 50.1%, followed by Sikkim, West Bengal, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka. Among men, the biggest increase was in Chandigarh, from 34.4% to 48.5%, followed by Goa, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat and West Bengal.
State-wise comparison for women
The state numbers show this is not confined to a few pockets.Urban-rural divideAmong urban women, 13.2% have below-normal BMI and 42.8% are overweight or obese. Among rural women, below-normal BMI is much higher at 22.5%, while overweight or obesity stands at 25.5%. Against NFHS-5, below-normal BMI among rural women has risen from 21.2%, while the urban estimate is unchanged at 13.2%. Overweight or obesity rose in both, from 33.2% to 42.8% in urban areas and from 19.7% to 25.5% in rural areas.Men show a similar urban-rural divide. Among urban men, 14.9% have below-normal BMI and 36.3% are overweight or obese. Among rural men, 21.9% have below-normal BMI and 23% are overweight or obese. Compared with NFHS-5, low BMI among urban men rose from 13% to 14.9%, while among rural men it rose more sharply, from 17.8% to 21.9%. Overweight or obesity increased from 29.8% to 36.3% in urban areas and from 19.3% to 23% in rural areas. Among men, the rise in low BMI was larger in rural India, while the increase in excess weight was sharper in urban India.
Contrasting trend in urban and rural areas
Dr Sadajit Banerjee, a Kolkata-based internal medicine and geriatrics specialist, says that as an urban doctor he has been seeing mostly a shift towards overweight. Patients increasingly arrive asking about semaglutide and tirzepatide, having read about them; those whose BMI is still within acceptable limits are advised on lifestyle change instead.Most urban Indians, he says, do not seem motivated enough to exercise or change how they live, while others are frightened of the side effects of those drugs. The patients who take up either route readily are usually the ones who already have diabetes or another metabolic disorder. At population level, the coexistence of low BMI and overweight or obesity is consistent with what the World Health Organization calls the double burden of malnutrition. Low BMI is one marker of undernutrition rather than a complete measure of it.India not following global pattern?Most of the world has been moving in one direction. A 2024 Lancet analysis by the NCD Risk Factor Collaboration, covering 200 countries and territories, found obesity rising almost everywhere between 1990 and 2022 and more than a billion people living with obesity, while adult underweight fell in most countries.That is what makes the NFHS-6 reading unusual: India's overweight share is rising in line with the global pattern, but its below-normal share is not falling. A Global Burden of Disease study put India second only to China, at 180 million adults aged 25 and older with overweight or obesity in 2021. That is a modelled estimate on a different age base.The district-level analysisThe fact sheets report these BMI measures only for women, so the district picture is a picture of women. The female BMI indicators exclude women who were pregnant or had given birth in the preceding two months.Of the 713 district records in the release, 680 can be compared with NFHS-5, where both BMI figures are available for both rounds. In 372 of those 680, or 54.7%, both ends grew at once: more women with below-normal BMI, and more women overweight or obese. All districts in Punjab, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Delhi and Goa fall below 50% on the calculated female normal-BMI measure. So do the overwhelming majority in Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Haryana and Karnataka.A normal BMI can hide muscle loss and excess fatBMI can also conceal what it is measuring. With the elderly population growing, Banerjee says he is seeing patients whose BMI is skewed by sarcopenia — too little protein and too little exercise producing muscle loss on one side and fat gain on the other. The number on the chart often stays in the normal range. Such patients may have low muscle mass and excess body fat despite an apparently normal BMI, risks that BMI alone can miss.Blood sugar also climbedNFHS-6 also tested blood sugar, on a different age base of 15 and above, against 15-49 for BMI. The share of women with high or very high blood sugar, above 140 mg/dl, or taking medication for diabetes rose from 13.5% to 17.8%; among men, from 15.6% to 20.9%. Urban prevalence is higher on both counts, at 21.9% among women and 23.9% among men, against 16.2% and 19.7% in rural areas.
The fact sheets do not establish cause and effect.Overweight and obesity are rising fast, and low BMI has stopped retreating. Across much of the country both are now visible at the same time, which leaves public-health programmes carrying two problems rather than watching one give way to the other. For Banerjee, they are not two problems at all. "Overnourished or undernourished, both fall in the malnourished category," he says. Much of the chatter is about improving urban lifestyles. How rural India gets proper nutrition is the question policymakers will have to answer.

Details
Authorities are investigating the circumstances of a suspected workplace accident that occurred on the evening of Monday, September 21. According to police, visitors were not in danger.
The incident occurred at a "free-fall tower" attraction, where passengers are lifted high into the air before the gondola rapidly descends.
Police said the worker was apparently in an area where he should not have been, and was then struck and possibly crushed.
The 52-year-old man was resuscitated at the scene and taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries, but later died.
A crisis response team provided support to witnesses of the incident. The area around the attraction was cordoned off during a large-scale emergency response operation.
Additional information
The 191st Oktoberfest began on Saturday and will run until October 4. More than 6 million people visit the world-famous beer festival every year.
Around 600 police officers and hundreds of security personnel have been deployed around the festival.

Taiwan power chipmakers see firmer prices through 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
07:51:07 UTC
16:51:07 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s power semiconductor manufacturers are expected to benefit from stronger AI demand and improving prices from the fourth quarter through 2027, CTEE reported Tuesday.
Domestic power semiconductor companies reportedly plan to raise prices for some non-contract products by around 10-15% beginning next month. The companies include Panjit International Inc., Taiwan Semiconductor Co., Eris Technology Corp., and Niko Semiconductor Co.
Analysts expect rising power consumption by AI systems to drive higher sales volumes, firmer prices, and demand for more advanced products. Actual price adjustments are expected to vary by product, customer, and contract terms.
Power semiconductors control and convert electricity within power systems. Price increases by major international suppliers are also supporting the market. Industry leader Onsemi announced that it would adjust prices beginning in October, while Renesas Electronics plans to follow early next year, according to MoneyDJ.
Meanwhile, the reallocation of 8-inch wafer capacity and growing AI server demand for power-management chips and protection devices are tightening supply for mature-node products.
AI servers are also driving demand for metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistors (MOSFETs), which regulate electricity flow and help manage power in electronic systems, according to Pocket Securities.
Panjit has already reported stronger AI-related demand. AI applications accounted for around 11% of the company’s revenue in the first half of the year, while shipments of power MOSFETs and small-signal products are expected to increase in the second half. New customer projects are also expected to begin contributing to revenue in the fourth quarter.
Eris Technology expects demand for power-protection devices to grow as AI servers and edge AI systems move toward 800V power architectures. The company said the shift would increase demand for components that protect systems from voltage spikes and other electrical disturbances.
Eris currently offers products for 800V direct-current applications and is developing products for 1,000V and 1,200V systems. The company also said its automotive MOSFET packaging and testing orders were fully booked for 2026 and 2027.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) pledged Tuesday to improve teachers’ working conditions, reduce administrative burdens, and help schools adapt to changes in education.
Speaking at an annual awards ceremony for teachers and educators, Lai thanked teachers for their dedication. He also acknowledged the growing pressure they face from staff shortages, communication with parents, student discipline, and administrative duties.
Lai said the government would work with teachers and parents to improve conditions in schools. The goal is to eliminate unnecessary burdens and allow teachers to focus more on teaching, he said.
Lai said all children should have access to education regardless of their family background. Government support should allow students to pursue further education or vocational training based on their interests and abilities, he added.
The president also highlighted the growing impact of artificial intelligence on education. The education ministry’s AI Talent Ark Project will invest NT$11.76 billion (US$389 million) from 2026 to 2029 to improve digital and AI learning, strengthen teachers’ skills, and expand the use of AI in schools.
Lai said AI can assist teachers and help analyze information but cannot replace their role in guiding and supporting students. Trust, communication, and personal interaction will remain central to education as technology develops, he added.
Taiwan continues to face teacher shortages in elementary and junior high schools. The education ministry said 6,464 permanent positions were available for the current school year, but only 5,676 were filled, while 614 substitute positions remained vacant shortly before schools opened, per CNA.
A September online survey by the National Substitute Teachers Union found that about 90% of 136 respondents had been asked to teach extra classes. About 40% described themselves as extremely fatigued.
The education ministry said extra teaching hours should be used only as a last resort while schools continue recruitment.

Taiwan develops water-softening process that turns waste into reusable material
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
07:50:46 UTC
16:50:46 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan Water Corporation said Monday that it had developed a new water-treatment process with the Industrial Technology Research Institute, according to a press release.
Some raw water sources used to produce tap water contain relatively high concentrations of minerals such as calcium and magnesium, which can affect the water’s taste. Existing softening methods produce lower-purity crystals with limited applications, some of which must be removed off-site, adding to operating costs.
The company and research institute developed a new fluidized-bed reactor that uses smaller quantities of chemical agents while promoting more stable crystal growth. The process raises the calcium carbonate purity of the resulting crystals from about 80% to between 96% and 98%.
The higher-quality byproduct can be used to manufacture plastics, paper, coatings and building materials.
Taiwan Water plans to expand testing of the process and assess its introduction at water purification facilities. The crystallization and separation technology could also be applied to industrial wastewater recycling, including wastewater from semiconductor manufacturing in areas such as the Southern Taiwan Science Park, according to ITRI.

Israel enters Sukkot on high alert as West Bank attacks fuel fears of wider escalation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
07:48:53 UTC
16:48:53 KST

A recent string of terrorist attacks in the West Bank has shaken the security picture and reinforced the IDF’s assessment that the area still contains large numbers of weapons, terrorists and, above all, people willing and intending to carry out attacks.
Following the shooting at Ein Raya spring in Binyamin, where Netanel Shukrun was killed shortly before Yom Kippur, the IDF increasingly believes the terrorist acted alone. His interrogation by the Shin Bet is expected to focus on how and where he obtained the weapon and whether anyone helped him before or after the attack.
The IDF and the broader security establishment are now entering the Sukkot holiday at one of their highest levels of readiness in recent years. Thousands of visitors, hikers and families are expected to travel through tourist sites, settlements and major roads across the West Bank in the coming days.
Within hours of the spring attack, IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir ordered major reinforcements across the sector. The goal set by Central Command and the General Staff is to prevent the current violence from developing into a broader escalation.
The IDF has been warning for weeks of a significant deterioration in the West Bank. The issue has featured prominently in security cabinet discussions and led to a series of large-scale exercises involving regular and special forces.
One of the clearest signs of the heightened preparations is the decision to position an additional division headquarters as reinforcement. In the event of escalation, the extra headquarters would assume responsibility for the sector from Jerusalem southward, allowing the West Bank Division to concentrate its personnel and resources on the most volatile areas.
Raids, drones and attack prevention
Even during Yom Kippur, the IDF said forces acting on Shin Bet intelligence thwarted a significant attack planned by two Hamas-affiliated terrorists in Qabatiya.
In a separate brigade-level operation in Biddu, the town from which the terrorist who carried out the spring attack emerged, forces searched 100 buildings, questioned 90 suspects and found a hunting rifle.
Duvdevan troops operating in Beit Ur al-Tahta located what the military described as a weapons-production workshop, two improvised Carlo submachine guns and additional weapons. In the Menashe sector, Paratroopers Reconnaissance Unit troops questioned suspects, arrested wanted men and found materials intended for manufacturing explosives.
The West Bank Division is also placing increased emphasis on the threat posed by drones. Forces are confiscating drones and have instructed Palestinian security forces to take action on the issue as well.
In Southern Command, pressure on Hamas and efforts to target senior figures are expected to continue, based on incoming intelligence and resources allocated by the Air Force, Military Intelligence and the Shin Bet.
Northern Command, meanwhile, is maintaining preparations along the Yellow Line following the demolition of underground infrastructure on the Ali Taher Ridge. IDF forces have already conducted drills and prepared positions from which they will secure the area. Commanders assess that the immediate period of heightened tension surrounding the demolitions has passed, but forces remain prepared for any Hezbollah violation.
‘Thank you for giving me my life’
Hundreds of people gathered overnight at the cemetery in Alei Zahav to bury Netanel Shukrun, who was killed at Ein Raya spring in Binyamin hours before Yom Kippur began.
Shukrun, a high-tech worker employed as an information systems analyst at Hachshara Insurance Company, is survived by his wife, Merav, and six children. His eldest son, an 11th-grade student, had accompanied him to the spring. His youngest child is 4.
At the graveside, the family stood together during the traditional tearing of garments.
Yoav, Shukrun’s 16-year-old son, who escaped the attack after his father warned him, thanked him in his eulogy.
“Dad, I want to say thank you for 16 years together,” he said. “Thank you that during the attack, when the terrorist came in, you shouted to me. I don’t remember what you said, and I ran. Thank you for giving me my life, thank God I survived, and I want to tell the family that we will keep going together and it will be OK.”
His daughter Talia recalled realizing through news reports that her father and brother had been at the spring.
“At 11:36 I heard on one of the channels that there had been an attack at a spring near Neve Tzuf,” she said. “At first I didn’t make the connection, but then I realized it was the spring you were at. I went to Mom and asked her to check where you were, and you didn’t answer. From that moment our lives changed.”
Merav, Shukrun’s wife, described him as the person who would normally help prepare her before she spoke in public.
“I’m supposed to be used to speaking in front of an audience, but not one like this,” she said. “Before I give a lecture I’m prepared, and Nati would go over the presentation and make sure I knew the material. I don’t have that possibility now.”
Shukrun had gone to Ein Raya spring with his 16-year-old son to immerse before Yom Kippur. After returning to his vehicle, the terrorist opened fire, killing Shukrun. His son was unharmed.
According to details emerging from the investigation, the terrorist, Qadri Samara, a 37-year-old Hamas terrorist, had passed through the area of the spring the day before the attack. Investigators suspect he took advantage of the large number of people who come to immerse there before Yom Kippur, arrived by car and opened fire at Shukrun’s vehicle.
A tracker from the Binyamin Brigade who was nearby in an armored vehicle returned fire and wounded the terrorist, preventing him from continuing the shooting and saving Shukrun’s son.
The attacker fled and reached a clinic in Ramallah for treatment. Duvdevan troops later entered the clinic, found him lying in a bed and arrested him.
The initial investigation indicates that he acted alone.

Turkish environment minister launches COP31 in New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
07:47:01 UTC
16:47:01 KST

Turkish Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Minister Murat Kurum said Monday that Türkiye aims to turn climate targets into measurable and actionable steps through the UN Climate Change Conference COP31, to be held in Antalya in November.
Kurum launched COP31 during his visit to New York for the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.
Speaking at the "Launch of the COP31 Action Agenda -- High-Level Event" held at the UN Economic and Social Council Chamber, Kurum, in his capacity as COP31 president, said: "We are here today not only to introduce the COP31 Action Agenda, but also to discuss together how we can accelerate the transition from targets to implementation in climate action."
There is now a strong common understanding of the urgency of the climate crisis, he said, noting that common targets have been set and that workable solutions are available in many parts of the world.
He stressed that the key issue was how these solutions could be put into practice.
Pointing to challenges, including access to finance, capacity gaps, and matching technology and investment with needs, Kurum said these questions would be addressed at the COP31 conference in Antalya in November.
"Our approach in this process is based on three fundamental principles: Dialogue. Consensus. Action. Through dialogue, we listen to different needs and priorities. Through consensus, we identify areas for joint action. Through action, we want to turn this partnership into concrete results," he said.
Kurum stressed that their work was not simply about announcing more commitments, but about turning existing commitments into measurable results on the ground.
"Our Action Agenda brings common priorities together with measurable targets, concrete initiatives and implementation tools," he said.
Kurum briefed representatives of countries party to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change on the 10 priority themes, six global targets, 11 initiatives, and 13 supporting outputs of the COP31 Action Agenda, which is built around the principles of "Dialogue, Consensus, Action."
He said they had established an "implementation architecture" to move from targets to implementation, adding that the Action Agenda had been developed through an extensive consultation process involving countries, international organizations, financial institutions, the private sector and civil society.
"We want to turn climate targets into measurable, actionable steps through our Action Agenda," Kurum said.
He said 10 priority themes had been identified under the Action Agenda, ranging from energy and industry to cities, food, oceans and health.
Kurum also said global targets had been set for 2035 in areas including energy consumption, waste, recycling and carbon dioxide reductions.
"We aim to increase the share of electricity in final energy consumption to 35% by 2035. Through the COP31 Global Electrification Initiative, we will accelerate electrification on a global scale," he said.
Kurum outlined examples of COP31 targets, ranging from climate-resilient cities and action in oceans and seas to food security and dynamic, resilient health systems.
During the launch, participants also shared their views. In his closing remarks following the question-and-answer session, Kurum said: "We did not only introduce our Action Agenda here. We listened to you. We assessed the barriers to implementation, the needs and the areas where we can move forward together. We will reflect the views and recommendations you put forward today in our work in the process leading up to Antalya."
Kurum said they would be pleased to welcome everyone to Antalya in November, adding: "However, we do not see Antalya as the final destination. We want Antalya to be a turning point where implementation accelerates in a visible and measurable way."
UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell, UN Assistant Secretary-General Selwin Hart, COP30 President Andre Aranha Correa do Lago, Azerbaijani Deputy Foreign Minister and COP29 Lead Negotiator Yalcin Rafiyev, Australian Assistant Minister and COP31 Executive Director Kushla Munro, and World Meteorological Organization Secretary-General Celeste Saulo also addressed the event.
Representatives of international financial institutions, as well as ministers and deputy ministers from around 20 countries, also took part in the launch.
COP31, under the presidency of Türkiye, will be held on Nov. 9-20 at the Expo Center in Antalya.
Kurum also met with European Commissioner for Climate, Net-Zero and Clean Growth Wopke Hoekstra in New York.
He said they discussed Türkiye-EU climate cooperation and preparations for COP31 during the meeting.
“We see COP31 as an important opportunity to take Türkiye-EU climate relations to a more strategic and results-oriented level. We are ready to work closely with the European Commission for a COP31 that translates our climate targets into implementation and commitments into concrete action.
"We would like the European Union to make an active contribution to COP31, the initiatives we have developed under our Action Agenda, and our Global Implementation Goals. I hope our meeting will further strengthen our cooperation,” he added.

French Army gets upgraded Jaguar with new anti-tank missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
07:46:44 UTC
16:46:44 KST

- The French Army has received 21 Jaguar armored vehicles built to the fully operational R3 standard as of Sept. 4.
- The R3 standard adds full integration of the Akeron MP anti-tank missile, and existing Jaguars will be retrofitted to it by the end of 2027.
The French Army has received its first Jaguar armored vehicles built to the R3 standard, the fully operational configuration for the reconnaissance and combat vehicle, KNDS France said. Twenty-one vehicles had reached French forces as of Sept. 4, following deliveries that began this summer.
France’s defense procurement agency, the DGA, qualified the R3 standard on April 8, and the French Army approved its use on July 20, before the first vehicles arrived at units.
The Jaguar is a six-wheeled, 25-tonne armored vehicle built under the French Army’s SCORPION modernization program to replace the AMX-10RC and other older reconnaissance vehicles. It carries a 40 mm cannon and, on the R3 standard, full integration of the Akeron MP medium-range anti-tank missile, made by MBDA. The missile can hit targets up to 4 km away and penetrate more than 1,000 mm of armor with its tandem warhead, according to manufacturer specifications.
KNDS France, Arquus and Thales jointly design, build and support the Jaguar under a temporary industrial partnership. Final assembly takes place at KNDS France’s plant in Roanne. Safran supplies the vehicle’s optical and sighting systems, CTA International makes the 40 mm cannon, and MBDA supplies the Akeron MP.
Jaguar vehicles already in service will not be replaced. Instead, KNDS France is retrofitting them to the R3 standard under a campaign due to finish by the end of 2027.
France has ordered 300 Jaguar vehicles to equip seven armored cavalry regiments, with deliveries planned through 2030 and the full fleet in place by 2035. The Jaguar first entered service in 2022, when an earlier standard allowed mobile firing from its digital turret; the 1st Foreign Cavalry Regiment became the first unit to field it, deploying a platoon of six vehicles to Estonia in 2024 as part of a NATO mission.
The SCORPION program overall is valued at roughly €11 billion ($12.65 billion), with about €2 billion ($2.3 billion) earmarked for the Jaguar’s 300 vehicles. The Jaguar’s unit cost, initially targeted at €3 million ($3.45 million), has since risen to around €6 million ($6.9 million).
KNDS France did not say how many more R3-standard vehicles are due to reach units this year or give a date for the retrofit of the rest of the existing fleet beyond the 2027 deadline

The U.S. ambassador to the UN explained the reason for Trump's concern over Russian oil refineries
Kyiv • UNN
Mike Waltz linked Trump's concern to Russia's role in the global diesel market. Fuel prices affect inflation and the economy.
U.S. Permanent Representative to the UN Mike Waltz explained U.S. President Donald Trump's remarks about problems in Russia's oil refining industry following Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries. This was reported by UNN, citing Waltz's statement.
Details
Waltz explained that the U.S. president's reaction was related to Russia's role in the global diesel fuel market.
Russia was a net exporter of diesel fuel. Diesel is used in tractors, trucks, and, obviously, in our aviation and fleet as well. We are not a country where products go directly from the farm to the table. In our case, there is a chain from the farm to the truck and then to the table. And one of the factors behind global inflation is diesel
According to him, diesel fuel is necessary not only for road transport. It is widely used in agriculture, freight transportation, aviation, and shipping. As a result, changes in its price affect prices in other sectors of the economy.

Undermining the UN is not a new US policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
07:42:37 UTC
16:42:37 KST

Undermining the UN is not a new US policy
While acting as the official host for the UN, the US has sought to weaken it for decades.
The annual general debate of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) starts on Tuesday morning in New York amid dire circumstances. Besides traffic gridlock and overpriced hotel rates, cavalcades of motorcades and successive dignitaries delivering calibrated speeches, this session will hear Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’s last speech on the state of the UN.
Guterres headed the UN for 10 years, and during that time, he repeatedly failed to defend it when it came under attack. He passes on his post at the top of a world organisation on the verge of financial collapse and more marginalised than ever before.
Paradoxically, Guterres has the United States, the host government of the UN, and its mercurial president, Donald Trump, to thank for this dismal state of affairs.
Earlier this year, the Trump administration withdrew from dozens of UN agencies and organs and, in an extraordinary move, ceased all payments of its dues to the regular and peacekeeping budgets of the UN. But these drastic policy decisions did not spring out of nowhere. Trump’s unhappiness with the UN is multifaceted, and his decision to stop fulfilling Washington’s legally binding financial obligation may well be the logical culmination of decades-long US policy.
In the mid-1980s, the Reagan administration accused the UN of being a third-world, anti-US forum. To compel the organisation to better serve its interests and under the guise of the ubiquitous need for reform, which all secretaries-general fell for, the US started to withhold a share of its assessed contribution, which accounted for a quarter of the regular budget and a third of the peacekeeping budget back then.
By 1987, the US relaxed its payment withholding policy, but the precedent was set. Washington continued to use the threat of withholding payment to maintain its grip on an organisation it viewed and continues to view as a vehicle serving its national interests rather than a multilateral agent serving the whole of humanity.
Ever since the Reagan years, the US has kept the UN on a short financial leash, and to this day, has been deliberately accruing arrears. It currently owes an estimated $4.2bn – that is equivalent to 120 percent of the regular UN budget for 2026.
Trump has readily embraced this policy of financial blackmail. His administration has slow-walked mandatory payments, although earlier this month it paid $827m towards its outstanding dues so it could preserve its voting rights in the UNGA.
The president’s ambivalent view of the UN may be rooted in a lesser-known detail. In 2001, Trump, then a real estate developer, lobbied then Secretary-General Kofi Annan to be awarded the billion-dollar renovation project of the UN headquarters, but he did not get his way. That was probably not forgotten.
But just like during the Reagan years, there is another major factor driving Trump’s assault on the UN: US congressional politics. As Israel faced growing backlash at the UN for its genocide in Gaza, pressure from the Israeli lobby in Washington mounted. The Iron Dome diplomatic cover the US provided to Israel in the UN Security Council (UNSC) was no longer sufficient.
By 2025, two years into the genocidal campaign, Guterres’s tepid and overdue criticisms of Israeli policies, critical UNGA resolutions and scathing reports by special rapporteurs of the Human Rights Council – including Francesca Albanese, whom Washington placed under sanctions in violation of its host country obligations – became too much for Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the US Congress.
In the 1980s, Washington deemed the UN a third-world anti-US forum; today, it is deemed anti-Israel and anti-Semitic. The US’s blind and unconditional support for Israel has brought it growing isolation at the UN, as has its decision to launch a war of aggression against Iran.
Against the backdrop of these developments, the selection of the next secretary-general is dominating the behind-the-scenes agenda. Guterres’s lacklustre tenure at the helm of an organisation on the verge of financial bankruptcy and political demise will soon be forgotten. But what should be remembered is that his appeasement policy vis-a-vis Washington since the first Trump administration has evidently failed.
The new secretary-general will inherit the modus vivendi under which all secretaries-general since Javier Perez de Cuellar have had to operate — chronic cash flow problems due to US arrears.
That should motivate the new UN leadership to consider an overhaul of how the UN budget is put together and how member states’ contributions are allocated. Leaving the power of the purse in Washington’s hands is a self-inflicted perpetual wound that could prove lethal for the organisation.
Another fundamental question is whether the UN would be better off had its headquarters not been in the US. For too long, Washington has seen the UN either as a vector of its national interests or in adversarial terms. It has even used its position as a host to exclude world leaders it has viewed as hostile or undesirable, such as PLO Chairman Yasser Arafat and today Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas.
Evidently, those are decisions only the UNGA can take. But a secretary-general with foresight and political backbone ought to provide views and leadership on those seminal questions to save the organisation from further marginalisation and possible demise.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

German engine maker teams up on U.S. autonomous vehicle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
07:42:01 UTC
16:42:01 KST

- DEUTZ and Hypercraft are expanding their partnership on the Razorback autonomous ground vehicle to include hybrid, battery and energy systems.
- DEUTZ already supplies Razorback's combustion engines and is weighing final vehicle assembly for Europe at one of its own production sites.
German famed engine maker DEUTZ has signed an agreement to expand its work with Hypercraft, a Provo, Utah, defense technology company, on the Razorback, an autonomous ground vehicle, DEUTZ said Monday. DEUTZ already supplies the combustion engines for Razorback and will now study adding hybrid, battery and other energy systems to the platform.
DEUTZ Business Unit Defense CEO Marco Herre said the companies’ strengths complement each other, with Hypercraft’s software architecture paired against DEUTZ’s engine and hybrid-electric experience.
“DEUTZ contributes extensive experience in engines, hybrid-electric systems, and defense vehicle integration at scale. Together, we will develop innovative and reliable solutions for defense customers globally,” said Marco Herre, DEUTZ Business Unit Defense CEO.
The two companies are also weighing joint development of future platforms and considering final assembly of Hypercraft vehicles for the European market at a DEUTZ production site, according to the memorandum of understanding. Hypercraft would contribute research and development resources and its military customer network; DEUTZ would provide its global service network, which spans more than 1,000 sites in over 180 countries.
The agreement builds on a partnership that started with engines and is now moving toward a broader defense business for DEUTZ, which is establishing defense as a fourth core segment alongside its engines, energy and new-technology divisions.
Hypercraft launched the Razorback in April. The vehicle carries a 2,400-pound payload, covers up to 280 miles on a diesel hybrid-electric powertrain and exports up to 38 kilowatts of power, enough to charge drones, run directed-energy weapons or sustain a forward command post. Four independent electric motors combine for 300 horsepower and a top speed of 60 mph, and the Defence Blog reported the redundant motor design lets the vehicle keep moving if one or more motors are damaged. Hypercraft demonstrated the vehicle at South Valley Regional Airport in Utah in early August for government and defense officials.
The Razorback is built to run without a crew on missions including contested resupply, casualty evacuation, electronic warfare relay and countering small drones. Its low-signature design is meant to give it 360-degree protection against Group 1 and 2 unmanned aircraft, the U.S. military’s classification for smaller, slower drones. Hypercraft has separately partnered with Fortem Technologies to mount Fortem’s TrueView radar and drone-mitigation system onto the platform.
“Razorback isn’t just a vehicle, it’s the new tactical standard,” said Brian Bowers, Hypercraft CEO.
DEUTZ’s move into Razorback comes as the company pursues a larger defense push. It recently raised about €179 million ($206 million) through a share sale and won German antitrust approval for a separate acquisition, moves the company has linked to building out its defense business.
