ISIL-linked detainees report night raids, extortion, violence at Roj camp
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
07:13:01 UTC
16:13:01 KST

ISIL-linked detainees report night raids, extortion, violence at Roj camp
Over 2,300 women and children are still held in what UN experts and human rights groups describe as open-ended detention.
When the shooting starts, Sara tells her children to lie flat on the ground; the bullets, she said, can go straight through her family’s tent.
Sara, who asked that her real name not be used, has been arbitrarily detained for nearly a decade in Roj camp in Syria’s far northeast, which holds more than 2,300 children and mothers, many of whom are held on the basis of alleged family or other associations with ISIL.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Analysis: ISIL attacks could undermine US-Syria security collaboration
- list 2 of 4Australian ISIL relatives sent back to Syria’s Roj camp after release
- list 3 of 4Women and children remain trapped in Syria’s Roj camp
- list 4 of 4‘Just ask Grok’: How ISIL is using Big Tech’s AI to build bombs
Her children have grown up behind guarded fences topped with barbed wire and tangled with rubbish that often blocks the view of the barren, windswept landscape beyond.
United Nations experts and human rights groups describe open-ended detention in camps such as Roj as a breach of international law.
In recent months, women in the camp told Al Jazeera that the situation has steadily escalated: gunfire at night, stones thrown by guards and a boy left with a serious head injury.
Complaints to the administration, they say, bring promises but little else. “Every cry for help results in another wave of aggression,” one mother said.
Al Jazeera cannot independently verify their accounts, but they match reports by UN investigators and NGOs.
On September 8, the UN Independent Commission of Inquiry on Syria told the body’s Human Rights Council that conditions in Roj had worsened over the past year, with regular night raids, extortion and violence by camp security.
It described the camp as the world’s largest site of mass arbitrary detention of women and children on security grounds.
Who really controls the camp?
The violence comes amid sweeping change in the region.
On August 25, the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), once a key US ally in the fight against ISIL, announced it would dissolve as an independent military force under an agreement with Syria’s central government in Damascus.
After a government offensive in January, the SDF lost much of the territory under its control and agreed to merge with the national army.
Its commander, Mazloum Abdi, has since been appointed a presidential adviser.
Roj, which the SDF had controlled until last month, is now the Syrian state’s responsibility.
But inside the camp, detainees said the transition has been anything but smooth.
One woman described to Al Jazeera a divided security presence, with those who accepted integration with the government on one side and holdouts who refused or were rejected on the other, and tensions between them that play out over the heads of the women and children.
In an open letter published on Monday, 11 mothers in Roj wrote that many of the same guards remain.
“While individuals’ [affiliations] may have changed,” one woman told Al Jazeera, “the people themselves remain the same”.
No legal basis for detention
Children from more than 50 countries remain stranded in Syria.
None has been given an individual legal process to determine why they are held, or for how long.
Fionnuala Ni Aolain, who served as UN special rapporteur on counter-terrorism and human rights from 2017 to 2023 and now sits on its inquiry commission, visited the camp in 2023.
Upwards of 70,000 people were once detained in al-Hol, another larger camp in the northeast holding the families of alleged ISIL fighters. In 2023, more than 52,000 people – mostly Syrians and Iraqis – were held in al-Hol and Roj, including an estimated 12,000 foreign nationals.
She found that conditions met “the threshold for torture under international law”. The violence women and children face now, she told Al Jazeera, is worse.
“It is utterly unacceptable that women and children who have never been convicted of any crimes, who have never been subject to any legal process, are being detained in this way,” she said.
There is no legal basis for their arbitrary detention, she said, adding that the remedy is release.
In January, order at al-Hol collapsed in chaos. The fate of thousands who had been held there remains unknown.
Beatrice Eriksson, a spokesperson for the Swedish branch of the rights organisation Repatriate the Children, which has been in contact with hundreds of mothers in the camps since 2019, told Al Jazeera that boys have been taken from their mothers as young as 12 or 13 and initially held in so-called rehabilitation centres.
Some have since been transferred to Iraq, she said, while others have been transferred to a makeshift prison for adult alleged ISIL fighters in northeast Syria.
Eriksson argues that integrating former SDF-controlled forces and administrative structures into the Syrian government could provide an opportunity for change.
She said responsibility for the families has shifted from a non-state group to an internationally recognised government with which most of their home countries have diplomatic relations.
However, some detainees told Al Jazeera that they feel trapped. Governments tell them to reach out to an embassy, but their detention makes that impossible.
Ni Aolain said the responsibility does not just lie with the Syrian government, which is “doing its best to manage the massive post-conflict needs of the population as a whole”.
Instead, she said part of the blame clearly lies with foreign governments, “who have remained persistently stony-faced and unwilling to accept responsibility for their nationals”.
“It is not consistent with solidarity and support for a transitional state, and it’s an abdication of both their human rights and their security responsibilities to Syria”, she said.
For the women and children in Roj camp, the current situation is not sustainable.
“We want the next steps to begin where we’ll see an end to the suffering of our children,” one woman told Al Jazeera, “even if that means going to prison back home.”
At the time of publication, Syria’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates had not responded to Al Jazeera’s request for comment on the reports of violence at Roj as well as the government’s plans for the camp and its detainees.
The camp administration also did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has urged member states to deploy additional warships and air assets to reinforce the bloc’s maritime security mission in the Red Sea, warning that the current force is insufficient to meet rising threats.
Speaking in New York after an EU foreign ministers’ meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Kallas said Operation Aspides needs to expand as shipping risks increase around the Bab al Mandab Strait.
“The operation needs more naval assets and more air assets to address the increased level of threats in the region,” Kallas told reporters.
She said the Black Sea, Strait of Hormuz and Bab al Mandab are critical maritime chokepoints whose disruption could have consequences well beyond their immediate regions.
Mission faces growing pressure
Operation Aspides was launched in 2024 to help protect commercial shipping from attacks by Houthis in Yemen. The defensive mission operates in the Red Sea and surrounding waters, escorting and protecting merchant vessels.
Kallas said the operation would need more than 10 warships to adequately respond to the current security environment. Reuters reported that the mission currently has six warships, with Italy and Greece among its main contributors.
The appeal comes as Italy has separately pressed EU partners to increase their contributions. Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto has called for more ships, warning that existing assets are insufficient to respond to requests for protection from commercial vessels.
Despite the calls for reinforcement, EU member states have yet to commit to a major expansion of the mission.
Kallas said the original planning for Aspides envisaged at least 10 ships, adding that the security situation has since become more serious.
The renewed push highlights growing European concerns over the vulnerability of a maritime corridor linking the Indian Ocean with the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal, with disruptions potentially affecting shipping, supply chains and energy markets.

RBA governor's final speech before board meeting cements rate rise bets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
07:12:11 UTC
16:12:11 KST

Rates set to rise as RBA governor says 'heat' needs to be taken out of job market
In short:
All four major banks and the bulk of money market traders believe the Reserve Bank will raise interest rates next week.
RBA governor Michele Bullock said Australia's jobs market was still putting upwards pressure on wages, business costs and inflation.
What's next?
The RBA Monetary Policy Board meets on September 28-29.
All four major banks and the bulk of money market traders believe the Reserve Bank will raise interest rates next week and governor Michele Bullock did nothing to dissuade them in her last public appearance before the meeting.
Speaking at a Committee for Economic Development of Australia (CEDA) event in Sydney, Ms Bullock said Australia's jobs market was probably still a bit too tight and putting upwards pressure on wages, business costs and inflation more generally.
"Between 4.5 and 5 [per cent unemployment] will probably take enough heat out of the labour market that eases pressure on inflation," she said.
The latest August unemployment data will be released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Thursday and is the last major piece of economic data before the RBA Monetary Policy Board meeting on September 28-29.
Echoing comments she made at a federal parliamentary hearing on Friday, Ms Bullock said it was critical that imported inflation from the global energy price shock was not allowed to translate into rounds of domestic price increases.
"We need to be very careful to ensure that policy is set in a way that minimises the second round and indirect effects which might perpetuate ongoing inflation," she said.
"I think monetary policy really just needs to continue to focus on making sure that we limit indirect effects and we try to keep inflation expectations anchored."
Major banks hike fixed mortgage rates
After Friday's testimony the three major banks that had been forecasting the Reserve Bank would stay on hold in September changed their forecasts to predict a rate hike at the meeting next week.
The economics team at NAB was already anticipating a September move, while CBA and Westpac now expect the RBA to lift rates once more in September, with the risk of a second move in November.
ANZ's economics team has added a September rate rise while maintaining their forecast of a November hike as well, which would take the cash rate to 4.85 per cent, the highest level since late 2008.
Futures pricing on Bloomberg suggests a 90 per cent chance rates will rise next week, with about a 50/50 chance of a follow up hike in November.
The bank and market predictions are already having a real effect on interest rates, with fixed mortgage pricing rising dramatically in recent days.
Today the Commonwealth Bank lifted its two-year fixed home loan rate by 0.48 of a percentage point to 6.82 per cent, and other fixed rates by between 0.15-0.3 of a percentage point.
Comparison website Canstar said that follows similar moves of up to 0.2 of a percentage point by the other three major banks last week.
The lowest one or two-year fixed home loan rates offered by the big four of 6.49 per cent are now noticeably above their lowest variable rates of between 5.99 to 6.25 per cent, indicating an expectation that rates will increase.
AI 'great white hope' or massive financial bubble?
Ms Bullock's wideranging economic discussion also touched upon the issue of artificial intelligence.
She noted that, over the longer-term, as people and businesses found the best uses and workflows for the technology, it would add to productivity, putting downward pressure on inflation.
"AI is the great white hope to improve productivity," Ms Bullock said.
"When I talk to colleagues around the world about this, I think everyone thinks that."
However, that potential longer-term benefit is coming with a short-term headache, as AI providers scramble to build data centres and other enabling infrastructure.
"But I think everyone also agrees that there are very few signs yet that AI is actually influencing the supply side of the economy," Ms Bullock said.
"There's lots of evidence that it's influencing the demand side of the economy.
"So we've got this sort of awkward sequencing event at the moment where, in Australia at least, we are in a situation of excess demand and the AI boom is adding to that demand ahead of any potential supply impacts that it might have going forward."
Ms Bullock also acknowledged the risk that investment enthusiasm and the valuation of companies was running ahead of their realistic earnings potential.
"All central banks are a little bit worried about that," she said.
"You know, it might not be a bubble, but it might be.
"And if it unwinds in a disorderly manner, then that could have implications for the financial system and also for the real economies."
She said it was an area the RBA was keeping an eye on, with its twice yearly Financial Stability Review out next week.
"Some people think it's a bubble, some people don't. I don't have a particular view one way or the other, but it's a risk that I think we're watching," Ms Bullock said.

Film studios shun women but men make them less money, report shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
07:11:35 UTC
16:11:35 KST

Film studios shun women, but men make them less money, report shows
In short:
A new report shows films written by women make the most money but the budget often goes to male filmmakers.
The Frontiers in Communication paper analysed 200,000 films released between 1994 and 2023.
What's next?
Experts say creative women should be given more chances, and government screen agencies could do much more to pursue fairness and stamp out discrimination.
Barbie was an undeniable hit, raking in $US1.45 billion ($2.03 billion) at the worldwide box office.
Avatar: The Way of Water grossed more than $US2.3 billion ($2.85 billion) globally and is the third highest-grossing film in history.
These films have something in common.
Women played a role in co-writing the films and, in the case of Barbie, directing.
A new analysis, Women in Directing and Screenwriting: The Capital Allocation Puzzle in Commercial Film, has found movies with a female screenwriter returned higher median profits than male-only productions.
The Frontiers in Communication study covered 30 years of film, including theatrical and non-theatrical releases.
"Films with a woman screenwriter but no woman director had 34 per cent higher median profits than films with only men in those roles, despite similar budgets," said Anja Huwiler, the study's author and a researcher at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz.
"Yet 39 of the 44 films in the top 1 per cent of production budgets were male-only productions, and none involved a woman director."
Films written but not directed by women with budgets comparable to male-only productions generated the highest median profit.
Movies written but not directed by women also generated a higher return on investment.
Films in which women had both screenwriting and directing roles achieved a similar return on investment to male-only films when operating on half the budget.
While films written by women made more money, movies with higher budgets were male-dominated.
"The extreme uncertainty of film financing can make familiar people and established ways of working feel safer, especially when decision-makers are risk- or loss-averse," said Ms Huwiler.
"This can reinforce the status quo even when the financial evidence points elsewhere."
The report also found that the share of films crediting at least one woman as a director or screenwriter was growing at a sluggish pace.
After the #MeToo movement in 2017, women's participation rose, but the study found no lasting acceleration in the rate of growth.
Men hold privileged position 'not earned'
Senior lecturer in screenwriting at the University of Melbourne Radha O'Meara said the findings of the report were in line with what she sees in the Australian screen industry, despite the international focus.
"Gender discrimination in the Australian screen industry is often couched in the language of financial risk, and this report confirms that men screenwriters and directors are actually the greater financial risk," Dr O'Meara told ABC News.
"Sexism is alive and well in the Australian screen industry, sometimes blatant, often veiled or subtle."
Dr O'Meara said the data shows that men hold a privileged position in the screen industry that they have not earned.
"The films they write and direct are less commercially successful than those created by women.
"Men are allowed to fail in their creative pursuits — write or direct a film that flops — and are given another chance to prove themselves.
"Women who create a project that flops are condemned and ostracised.
"This is a clear double standard."
Dr O'Meara said government screen agencies could do much more to pursue fairness and stamp out discrimination but are often too closely aligned with the industry to push back on faulty logic.
"Government screen agencies seem quick to celebrate a minor improvement rather than work to address the glacial pace of change.
"This data shows that, even in purely commercial terms, creative women should be sought out and given more chances to create stories and develop careers in the screen industry."

Türkiye’s average home sale price rose to 5.3 million Turkish Liras ($109,000), according to Emlakjet’s August 2026 Housing Value Report prepared using Endeksa data.

U.S. Army drone-defense vehicles shield artillery in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
07:09:59 UTC
16:09:59 KST

- U.S. Army air defense crews used the Stryker-based SGT STOUT system to protect artillery units from drones during Saber Junction 26 in Hohenfels, Germany.
- The exercise's opposing force fielded about 1,900 autonomous systems against roughly 2,300 U.S. paratroopers and more than 2,100 allied troops.
U.S. Army air defense crews used a Stryker-based system called SGT STOUT to shield artillery units from drone attack during Saber Junction 26, a training exercise that ran Aug. 15 to Sept. 13 at the Joint Multinational Readiness Center in Hohenfels, Germany. A platoon from Alpha Battery, 5th Battalion, 4th Air Defense Artillery Regiment, part of the 52nd Air Defense Artillery Brigade, operated the vehicles in support of the 173rd Airborne Brigade.
SGT STOUT is the Army’s name for what was formerly called the Maneuver Short-Range Air Defense vehicle, or M-SHORAD. Built on a Stryker A1 chassis, it carries a 30 mm cannon, Stinger missiles and a 360-degree radar that lets a crew track threats in every direction. The radar and sensors are meant to spot drones early enough for a crew to act before the drones reach their target.
That early warning was the point during the exercise. Bravo Battery, 4th Battalion, 319th Airborne Field Artillery Regiment, towed howitzers into firing positions at Hohenfels on Aug. 28. Setting up a howitzer position normally means splitting a small crew between operating the gun and watching for drones, which slows both jobs. With SGT STOUT crews handling the watch, the artillery battery could keep working the guns.
“The [SGT STOUTs] are a tremendous asset for us,” said 2nd Lt. Gordon Turner, platoon leader assigned to Bravo Battery. “The more help that we have from these [M]-SHORAD guys to focus on the UAS threats, we can enable our guys and use them most effectively to shoot artillery.”
“With the incorporation of air defense on this kind of rotation right here, it allows us to see how a maneuver [unit] would employ us,” said 1st Lt. Christopher Barkley, executive officer for Alpha Battery. “Our [SGT STOUTs] are emplaced in order to provide the most applicable early warning as it applies. With our Sentinel [radar] we’re able to forecast over this entire terrain so that essentially everyone is informed of what threats are currently going on.”
“If we do receive any contact, and that can come from a UAS threat, we have to pick up and move to the next location,” said Turner. “But if we can deal with that threat before it affects us then we can stay at our firing point and continue to provide fires to the maneuver unit.”
The exercise put those systems against a heavy simulated drone threat. The opposing force at Saber Junction 26, the 1st Battalion, 4th Infantry Regiment, fielded about 1,900 autonomous systems against the roughly 2,300 paratroopers of the 173rd Airborne Brigade and more than 2,100 allied troops from 10 nations, Stars and Stripes reported. Brig. Gen. Terry Tillis, who leads the 7th Army Training Command, called that drone count large even by the standards of a training center built to stress modern threats.
SGT STOUT has been in limited Army service since 2024, when it was renamed for Sgt. Mitchell W. Stout, an air defense artilleryman who received the Medal of Honor for actions in Vietnam. The Army began delivering the vehicles to air defense units in early 2025 and plans full-rate production starting in fiscal year 2026.
The 52nd Air Defense Artillery Brigade, based in Europe, is built to defend critical assets and maneuver forces and to counter unmanned aircraft, rotary-wing and fixed-wing threats across the European and African theaters.

According to the survey, 32 percent of members plan to maintain their existing number of stores and employees, while 21 percent intend to enter 2027 on a smaller scale by closing underperforming stores and reducing headcount, Öncel added.

Putin plans to visit China for Xi Jinping’s summit but will skip the G20 with Trump - Bloomberg
Kyiv • UNN

Russian dictator Vladimir Putin plans to travel to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, which will be hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping, but will likely skip the Group of Twenty (G20) summit in the United States, where Donald Trump will be present. Bloomberg reports this, UNN writes.
Details
According to people close to the Kremlin, the Russian president plans to personally attend the APEC meeting for the first time since 2017. They noted that the likelihood of his attending the G20 summit in Florida together with President Trump is extremely low. The sources asked not to be named because the matter is not public.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov did not respond to a request for comment.
Xi Jinping will host APEC leaders in Shenzhen, China, on November 18–19. Russian officials had suggested the possibility of an unprecedented trilateral meeting of the leaders of the world's three largest nuclear powers on the sidelines of the summit.
As Bloomberg notes, Putin largely avoids multilateral forums where there is a risk of encountering Ukraine's Western allies from Europe, as well as representatives of countries such as Canada, Japan, South Korea, and Australia. In addition, there is a risk that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy could make an unexpected appearance at the G20 summit.
At the same time, attending the APEC summit would give him the most prominent international platform since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022.

French victims of clerical abuse hope Pope's visit can deepen Church reform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
07:04:14 UTC
16:04:14 KST

French victims of clerical abuse hope Pope's visit can deepen Church reform
LOCTUDY, France, Sept 22 - Ghislaine Magoarou, 65, was 9 years old when her teacher, Brother Gabriel Girard, pulled shut the curtains of their classroom in a fishing town in northwest France and raped her.
That incident marked the start of a months-long cycle of abuse at the now-shuttered Catholic school that eventually led Magoarou to attempt suicide by throwing herself into the sea.
"I had gone swimming with friends and simply let myself sink," Magoarou recalled during a walk along the beach in Loctudy with three other survivors. "I let the waves carry me away, and I had absolutely no desire to come back up. I felt at peace in the water, as if I were being cleansed."
POPE DUE TO MEET FRENCH SURVIVORS
Magoarou is one of at least 330,000 French minors who were abused between 1950 and 2020 by priests, religious figures, or laypeople working in Church institutions. Those figures were revealed in a landmark 2021 report that found France's Catholic Church had ignored the issue for far too long.
Pope Leo will seek to redress some of that harm during a visit to France, when he will meet next Sunday with seven victims of Church sexual abuse in Lourdes, some of those involved said in a press release.
During a visit to Spain in June, in which he met Spanish survivors of clerical abuse, Leo told bishops they must listen to survivors and offer them reparations.
In meeting with survivors, Leo is carrying on the work of his predecessor, Pope Francis. He took steps to address clerical abuse, although some groups have criticised them as insufficient.
Girard abused an estimated 50 to 70, 8-to-9-year-olds at the school in Loctudy, a pretty seaside town in Brittany, from 1969 until 1972. Survivors recounted how he would summon a child to the front of the class and abuse them while ordering the rest of the class to keep their heads down.
He died in 1979, by which time he had assaulted an estimated 170 children across France, without ever facing justice.
The Frères de Saint-Gabriel, the religious congregation that operated the school, did not respond to a request for comment. It has previously recognised and condemned all acts of physical and sexual abuse committed by its members, including Girard.
HOPES FOR LASTING CHANGE
Magoarou, who met Pope Francis at the Vatican in 2023, said she could "almost forgive" Girard as "there was something wrong with him", but still struggled to understand the other adults who had enabled or turned a blind eye to his actions.
Fellow survivor Michèle Le Reun-Gaigné said her life was ruined by Girard's abuse, leading to her dropping out of school and losing faith in adults. Still, she remained optimistic that she and others like her could help engender a change in how the Church handles such cases.
"Change won't happen overnight; we might not even live to see it," she said. "But what we are trying to do, in our own modest way, is to lay down small stepping stones to try and improve things, especially for future generations."
Alain Esquerre, 66, a spokesperson for victims at the Notre-Dame de Bétharram Catholic institution, said he wanted a genuine mea culpa from the Pope and the Church.
"I believe Leo bears the immense responsibility of 'declaring enough is enough' - of putting a stop to this so that children across the globe will no longer be raped by priests," he said.
NEW COMPENSATION MECHANISM UNDER SCRUTINY
The 2021 report by the Independent Commission on Sexual Abuse in the Church led to the creation of the Independent National Body for Recognition and Reparation (INIRR), which offers compensation of up to €60,000 for victims of abuse.
Over five years, 1,969 victims contacted INIRR, according to INIRR President Marie Derain de Vaucresson. Both Magoarou and Le Reun-Gaigné were among those who received a payout.
The French Bishops' Conference says the INIRR will cease operations on October 1, after which previously undeclared victims will have to contact local parishes to seek compensation, recognition and support.
The Bishops' Conference has described the new system, in which victims' first point of contact would be the local parish, as a continuation of its efforts to compensate people who have been abused.
Ampaseo, a victims' association, said the new scheme lacks the independence and judicial oversight that made the previous system a success.
"How could victims entrust their journey to an institution that failed in its duty of protection?" it said in a statement.
Véronique Margron, 68, a Dominican theologian who has supported many victims of clerical abuse, said she hoped Leo would mandate obligatory processes across the entire Church to aid victims in speaking out, adding that highlighting abuse was particularly difficult in Africa or India.
"All victim advocacy groups say - and rightly so - that not enough is being done," she said. "The response must be systemic." REUTERS

US military leaders divided over striking Yemen’s Houthis, opening a second warfront - report
The debate comes as Saudi Arabia pushes Washington for direct military action following a series of Houthi attacks
US military leaders are reportedly divided over whether US President Donald Trump should get involved in the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis, according to two US officials who spoke with NBC News. Saudi Arabia has been pressing Trump for US military action against the Houthis, a request that intensified after the rebels claimed to have shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet and advanced on Marib province, where one of Yemen's largest oil and gas fields is located.
Some military leaders argue that opening another front in the region is unwise given the Pentagon's dwindling supply of defensive and long-range weaponry, noting the Houthis are not targeting US ships. Others argue the US should help Saudi Arabia retaliate, warning that failing to act more forcefully would betray an important regional ally.
According to the report, Trump had ordered strikes to begin at 5 pm EST on Sunday, but the military was notified around 2 pm that the order was canceled. One official said Trump has not ruled out military action in the future.
The officials also said that one senior US military leader in the region warned that striking the Houthis could create risk to US troops involved in the Iran war mission, including the naval blockade and security operations in the Strait of Hormuz. The same leader said US forces could carry out both the Iran mission and strikes on the Houthis while mitigating some of that risk.
Suggested articles
Trump had shown little interest in acting until Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman told him by phone last Thursday that the kingdom could not succeed alone. The Houthis said Saturday they struck sites in Riyadh and an Aramco facility in Yanbu, while also advancing to control the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another key oil chokepoint.
Trump said earlier this month that the Houthis "don't want to fight" with the US.

Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson’s Disjointed But Endearing Brothers Coasts on Charm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
07:00:04 UTC
16:00:04 KST

As a nation still mourning Dolly Parton is all too aware, there aren’t many entertainers left who are embraced by Americans across demographics and ideologies. Among the few A-listers with bipartisan appeal are Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson, separately but especially as longtime best friends and occasional co-workers—two sons of Texas who, as you’ve probably heard, might also be sons of the same biological father. So it makes sense that Brothers, an Apple TV comedy that casts them as exaggerated versions of themselves, seems built to satisfy as broad a range of their fans as possible. Disjointed but breezy, it coasts on the chemistry between its leads.
Premiering with two episodes on Sept. 23, Brothers bills itself as being “based on a true rumor” whose plausibility Harrelson acknowledged in 2023: that McConaughey is the product of a tryst between his mom, Kay McConaughey, and Harrelson’s dad, the notorious contract killer Charles Voyde Harrelson, during her second divorce from James McConaughey. (Genetics aside, both families evidently have a flair for off-screen drama.) That’s certainly a big part of the show, supplying a central mystery and fueling tension between the stars after Kay, a.k.a. Ma Mac (Holland Taylor, playing delightfully against buttoned-up type as a hard-drinking, straight-talking, tanned-to-a-crisp matriarch), blurts out her secret to Woody. Can he bear to wound his bestie with the knowledge that Matthew might not share DNA with the late father he idolized?
But there are a lot of other things going on. Too many, really. When Woody, his wife Joy (Brittany Ishibashi), and their two daughters roll up to the McConaugheys’ Austin estate in a psychedelic bus, it’s because Joy refuses to let her husband abandon their eldest child, Olive (Highdee Kuan), as she heals from a broken engagement. Matthew has his own family and challenges, writing a speech for a public event honoring his dad while trying to nurture a bond with his kids, especially timid teenage son Wyatt (Nolan Almeida). Brothers is most generic in these double-family-sitcom storylines, with the two wild, larger-than-life leads constantly testing the patience of their more grounded, long-suffering, emotionally intelligent wives. A subplot for, perhaps, True Detective fans, in which two sickly old-timer crooks (Jeff Kober and Barry Corbin) try to extract from Woody a debt his dad owed them, feels like excerpts from a different show.
What actually works is, not surprisingly, the buddy-comedy stuff—the sillier, the better. Matthew and Woody squished into a rideshare with too many rowdy, young fans? A treat. Woody and Matthew donning ridiculous Sunset Strip rocker disguises, complete with facial prosthetics, to play an acoustic set at a coffee shop? Classic. Showrunner Lee Eisenberg (Stick, The Office), who created Brothers alongside McConaughey, Harrelson, and Schitt’s Creek alum David West Read, understands his leads’ personae, and they’re more than game to laugh at themselves. The series opens by showing us the versions that live in the public imagination; Woody enters smoking a joint and holding a surfboard, while Matthew roams the sun-dappled fields of Texas, sipping whisky in a cowboy hat as he recites an excerpt from his megahit memoir Greenlights in voiceover. He plays the charismatic, image-conscious, golden-boy straight man to Woody’s free-thinking hippie, a guy who doesn’t let fame stop him being as weird as he wants to be.
Then it pushes those archetypes without fully puncturing them. Woody’s discovery that they might literally be brothers from different mothers adds some useful pressure—though, truth be told, the storyline is less effective as a driver of plot than it is as a showcase for Taylor, who disappears into her role, making Ma Mac a spitfire but never a cartoon. Brothers gets more juice out of another ripped-from-the-headlines narrative: McConaughey’s political ambitions. While in real life he decided, after months of speculation, not to enter the 2022 Texas gubernatorial race, the show puts Matthew on the campaign trail. (What it carefully doesn’t do is align him with any party or cause. But boy does he love Texas!) It’s a fun reality check for a guy who’s great at kissing babies but can’t answer a simple question about housing policy. His jaded campaign manager, played to the hilt by Lisa Gilroy, gets the series’ most self-aware jokes (“Your Achilles’ heel is that you have been a celebrity for so, so long that your brain has turned into a big old sloppy pile of goo”). A cynical, Type A Armando Iannucci character in the land of alright, alright, alright, she’s deployed sparingly enough to add some edge without killing the laid-back vibe.
Really, though, the campaign could have been the whole show. It’s the perfect context for contrasting the stars’ personalities, pitting Matthew’s traditionalism and discretion against Woody’s unapologetic outlandishness. When the former announces he’s running, his old friend doesn’t mince words. “I’m a f-cking anarchist, and I think this is the stupidest, craziest f-cking idea you ever had,” Woody exclaims. But will he support Matthew on the trail anyway? Of course he will. Because, regardless of what any DNA test says, that is what makes a brother.

Europeans are exercising more. But who gets to take part?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
07:05:25 UTC
16:05:25 KST

More Europeans are playing sports and doing so more often than four years ago. However, disparities remain across countries, from how regularly people play sports to how well their cities support active living.
The European Commission's Eurobarometer survey on sport and physical activity shows that Europeans are, overall, doing more sport than they were in 2022. Yet significant differences remain between countries and socio-economic groups, even as many Europeans say physical activity benefits their physical and mental well-being.
“More Europeans are getting active, but the opportunity to take part still depends too much on income, age and education,” said Roxana Mînzatu, Executive Vice-President for Social Rights and Skills, Quality Jobs and Preparedness.
Nearly half of the 26,508 people surveyed, representing a range of social and demographic groups, said they exercise or play sport daily or several times a week. Meanwhile, 39% said they never exercise or play sport, down from 45% in 2022.
Finland and Denmark top the charts for daily exercise, with 21% and 20% of respondents respectively saying they exercise every day. In both countries, a further 59% said they exercise several times a week.
At the other end of the scale, 68% of respondents in Portugal said they never exercise or play sport, while Greece and Romania followed closely, both at 66%.
The reasons people give for exercising — whether for less than an hour a week or more than three hours — ranged from maintaining physical health to relaxing and improving mental well-being.
Nearly all respondents believe that being active contributes to improving mental health. Most also agree that it helps to build communities and improve the wellbeing of marginalised groups.
However, for those who don't exercise as much as they would like, time is the biggest barrier, cited by 37% of Europeans. Others named lack of motivation or interest 26% and health problems or injury 15%. Cost is also a factor for 12% of respondents.
Education and financial circumstances track closely with participation.
Some 59% of people who continued their education until at least age 20 exercise or play sport several times a week, compared with 23% of those who left education at 15 or younger. Those who have the most difficulty paying their bills are also twice as likely to say they never exercise as those who rarely or never struggle financially — 54% versus 26%.
“Everyone should have access to affordable sport and safe places to exercise, close to home," said Mînzatu. "This means opening doors to children whose families cannot afford club fees, older people and people with disabilities.”
The age divide is stark. Nearly three-quarters of 15- to 24-year-olds exercise or play sport at least several times a week, compared with just 25% of those aged 75 and over. Among the oldest respondents, health problems or injury is the most commonly cited barrier, while younger and middle-aged Europeans are much more likely to point to a lack of time.
The survey also looked at how often people engage in physical activity for other reasons, such as for commuting or gardening.
The share of people actively commuting increased the most across all surveyed categories, from 24% in 2022 to 37%. Walking for at least 10 minutes at a time is now reported by 72% of citizens, a significant increase compared to 16% in 2022.
However, not all Europeans feel that their neighbourhoods are well suited to walking or cycling, potentially limiting opportunities for active commuting.

Leaders push for stronger AI safeguards at UN as Trump touts 'Super Intelligence'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
03:54:49 UTC
12:54:49 KST

AI has become a major topic at the UN General Assembly after incidents of the technology falling out of the control of humans and warnings by company insiders drew global alarm and calls for better government supervision of the industry.
Visions for the future of AI are playing out at the United Nations as world leaders talk about the threat — or promise — of artificial intelligence.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres kicked off the parade of world leaders speaking at the General Assembly by calling for more oversight of AI, warning in vivid if not ominous terms of what could go wrong.
“Let us resolve that life-and-death decisions must never be surrendered to machines. Killer robots must have no place in our future,” Guterres said in his farewell address to world leaders. He also warned about AI in his first General Assembly address a decade ago.
With Guterres saying the world needs to “advance the conditions for the responsible pacing of AI and the additional safeguards needed to address risks,” the UN Security Council on Wednesday will address how to place some kind of controls on the technology and it will feature some of the biggest names in the field.
US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, stood by his firm opposition to regulating AI, while arguing the word "artificial" undersold the technology and voicing hope the rest of the world would adopt the new term.
Super Intelligence "sounds much better" and "it's much more accurate," he said.
also compared the warnings of AI safety advocates to warnings about climate change, whose human causes are affirmed by the overwhelming consensus of the scientific community.
"The United States totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control... artificial intelligence," he said.
"Every major new technology brings challenges, and superintelligence is no exception," he added.
"The very same people who said we'll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming... are now saying that AI is going to kill us all, that robots are going to attack us, and that everything is going to be a total disaster."
Other nations call for safeguards
Ahead of the UN assembly, leaders of more than 20 mostly European countries urged binding safety measures for advanced AI, warning that the technology's development could outpace the ability to control it.
AI superpowers China and the United States did not endorse the idea.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain would launch an effort to establish global AI standards during its 2027 G20 presidency, while announcing an AI defence partnership with Washington to detect cyberattacks on critical infrastructure.
"We will work towards agreeing a single set of global principles and standards to ensure the transparency and access we need to increase our preparedness and to ensure that AI development is safe," he said.
He earlier revealed London plans to use Britain's role as host of the Group of 20 next year to push for a "single set of global principles and standards" around AI.
French President Emmanuel Macron proposed building AI technology independent from the great powers.
"I don't want anyone to become the vassal of one of the great powers," Macron told the UN General Assembly, apparently in reference to China and the US.
"Our investment capabilities must be pooled to build a cutting-edge open-source AI model, which we will share. We should not depend on somebody else."
The US-based AI giants themselves are increasingly asking for global coordination on AI safety, with OpenAI's Sam Altman set to address the UN Security Council on Wednesday.
France, which holds the Security Council presidency this month, initiated the meeting and believes AI's threat to international peace and security has not been sufficiently discussed at the UN.

"Grain from Ukraine feeds people all over the world": EU urges Russia to stop attacks on Ukrainian food exports
Kaja Kallas, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, has urged Russia to stop attacks on Ukrainian grain in the Black Sea to restore grain exports and prevent a global food crisis.
Source: Kallas's speech at the opening of a UN General Assembly event on the Black Sea and global food security
Quote from Kallas on X (Twitter): "Grain from Ukraine feeds people all over the world. But Russia is blocking exports through the Black Sea and is deliberately causing global food insecurity.
The EU is calling for attacks to stop and grain to flow again. Food must never be used as a weapon of war."
Details: Kallas said that the consequences of Russia's military aggression do not just affect Ukraine, since it is one of the world's most important agricultural exporters.
Ukraine accounts for 15% of global maize exports, 10% of wheat exports, 15-20% of barley exports and around 50% of sunflower oil exports. Almost 90% of these products are transported through the Black Sea corridor.
To help address the problem, the EU is looking for new grain storage options in Ukraine, supporting farmers and small and medium-sized agricultural businesses and facilitating the cross-border movement of goods.
Background:
- Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha also discussed global food security, including Russian attacks on Ukraine's maritime corridor, with Carl Skau, Acting Executive Director of the World Food Programme.
- Sybiha stressed that the consequences of Russian strikes will be felt far beyond the Black Sea region, as Ukraine supplies a significant share of grain and sunflower oil to global markets.
- He therefore described ensuring freedom of navigation in the Black Sea, protecting Ukrainian ports and holding Russia accountable as urgent global priorities.

Russia considers new fee on airline passengers to fund purchases of Russian-made aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
07:04:13 UTC
16:04:13 KST

Russia considers new fee on airline passengers to fund purchases of Russian-made aircraft
Russia’s Transport Ministry, Industry and Trade Ministry, and state corporation Rostec are considering a passenger fee to subsidize the leasing and operation of new Russian-made aircraft, sources familiar with the proposal told Kommersant.
The amount has not yet been determined. Most of the newspaper’s sources said the fee could be as much as 500 rubles per ticket for domestic flights and 1,000 rubles for international flights. One source said the fees could be as high as 700 rubles for domestic flights and 2,000 rubles for international flights.
The Transport Ministry could administer the fee, distributing some of the revenue to leasing companies to cover the difference between the aircraft’s production cost and the subsidized price charged to carriers. Initially, another portion would go to airlines to offset the higher cost of operating the aircraft compared with foreign-made models.
Kommersant estimates that, at current passenger volumes, the fee could raise 200–250 billion rubles between 2027 and 2030. After that, the newspaper’s sources said, the fee may no longer be necessary as the aircraft become less expensive.
Work on the proposal has only just begun, and “no final decisions have yet been made about the amount or how the fee would be collected,” a government source said.
Analysts interviewed by the newspaper warned that higher ticket prices would reduce passenger traffic, airline and airport revenue, and tax receipts. They proposed covering the initial costs of operating the new aircraft with government funds.
Since September 2025, airline passengers have already been charged 150 rubles each to fund airfield renovations. The fee is to be adjusted annually for inflation.
The MC-21 is estimated to cost 8.9-11 billion rubles to produce, while Airbus A320-200s and Boeing 737-800s sell for 3.4-4 billion rubles. The production cost of the Russian-made SJ-100 is estimated at 5.4 billion rubles, while a comparable Embraer E190 sells for about 3 billion rubles. The Tu-214 is estimated to cost 8.9 billion rubles and the Il-114 4 billion rubles.
Since 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine and Western countries imposed sanctions, Western aircraft can be delivered to Russia only through unofficial channels, via intermediaries and at higher prices.

Russia tried to interfere in the 2019 election, says UK
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:04:27 BST
16:04:27 KST

Britain has evidence that Russian agencies tried to interfere in the 2019 general election, the Prime Minister has told the United Nations General Assembly, as he tasked the country’s security chiefs with building a new National Centre for Information Defence.
Andy Burnham used his first address to the assembly, delivered in New York on Monday evening, to set out what he described as an industrial-scale assault by hostile actors on the information environment in Britain and among its allies.
He said: “Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people’s fears. They’ve used bots and fake websites. Falsified newspaper articles. Forged the branding of 28 British organisations, including universities and the BBC. They’ve amplified far right narratives. And we have evidence that they tried to interfere with the 2019 General Election.”
He added that Russian agencies had also tried to stoke tensions and unrest in the wake of what he called horrific events, saying the idea that anyone would use such things to their advantage is repulsive but is what they do.
Putting a figure on the effort, the Prime Minister said the Kremlin spends around £1.3 billion each year on manipulating information, describing “an insidious campaign that reaches into people’s homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community, creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair. We have tiptoed around this for too long. Over the last decade we have given too much ground to those who want to run a negative, corrosive narrative about life in Britain, which bears no resemblance to reality. Well, no more.”
He then announced a new body, to be built by the security services, with three functions attached to it. “Today I am tasking our security chiefs to begin work on a new National Centre for Information Defence, to detect, attribute and disrupt these kinds of hostile state information attacks. To support and defend our democracy,” he said.
Governments have generally been slower to name the source of an information operation than to acknowledge a cyber intrusion, partly because the evidence is circumstantial and partly because saying so publicly invites a demand to act on it.
Mr Burnham linked the threat directly to conditions at home, saying that someone struggling with the cost of living, or a young person not in employment, education or training, would be more vulnerable to that kind of influence, and that “faced with this information warfare, security starts in every home”.
Britain intends to share what it has learned with others facing the same problem, and the Prime Minister said the country had already supported Moldova in protecting its elections from Russian interference, and that with more elections approaching across Europe it stands ready to share its understanding of how these actors work and how they can be countered.
Cyber attacks on British companies and institutions were cited alongside the information campaign, with Mr Burnham warning that artificial intelligence will multiply the threat.
The commitment is part of a considerable body of work already under way across government, with ministers having committed to rewriting the War Books by the end of the year under an accelerated Home Defence Programme, and a national resilience public awareness campaign is due to launch later this year, while the Defence Secretary told the Commons this month that he would report back to Parliament with plans for a national conversation about the threats the country faces.

Britain forms squadron to strike threats in orbit
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
07:54:49 BST
15:54:49 KST

The Royal Air Force is today forming No. III Space Effects Squadron, the first British unit dedicated to disrupting, degrading and denying hostile activity in space, the Ministry of Defence stated.
The squadron is being announced by the Chief of the Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, at the first UK Space Power Conference today, and will bring together specialist personnel from across the armed forces to counter hostile activity in orbit and defend the satellites the country depends on.
Sir Harv will say: “Space no longer supports operations from the sidelines. It’s a domain of direct competition, where our military advantage can be won or lost. No. III Space Effects Squadron will safeguard the vital benefits that space gives to our integrated armed forces, and will be capable of denying those benefits to our adversaries.”
The new unit completes a trio of squadrons, since No. I Space Operations Squadron gives the Royal Air Force the ability to watch what is happening in orbit and No. II Space Warning Squadron provides warning of threats, while according to the department No. III will act against those threats using advanced technology including electronic warfare. It will support both offensive and defensive space operations and is expected to expand as new capabilities enter service.
The department describes the formation as contributing to developing British capabilities for space warfare, including electronic warfare and countermeasures against anti-satellite weapons, and delivering the Control of Space Requirement set out in the UK Space Strategy published earlier this month. That requirement covers maintaining freedom to operate in space while denying adversaries the same freedom.
Britain has formally ruled out destructive anti-satellite missile testing, the kind that generates long-lived debris fields, and the department says it continues to work through the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space to promote norms and principles of responsible behaviour in orbit. The government describes itself as committed to the peaceful and sustainable use of space while protecting critical infrastructure.
Alongside the announcement, the department restated an £880 million investment between 2026/27 and 2029/30 in space-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance and in space control activities.
The squadron numbering follows Royal Air Force practice of reusing historic numberplates, with the space squadrons formed in recent years as the service has built out UK Space Command, which was established at RAF High Wycombe in 2021 and brings together military space operations alongside existing assets including the radar at Fylingdales.
The Strategic Defence Review stated that the ability to operate in, from and through space underpins British security, prosperity and daily life, and the Defence Investment Plan committed to the Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability, a trilateral programme with the United States and Australia whose British site is due to begin construction in April 2027 and which will provide continuous radar coverage of geostationary orbit.

U.S. puts Ukraine-tested interceptor drones through border tests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
07:10:12 UTC
16:10:12 KST

- U.S. Northern Command tested Perennial Autonomy's Bumblebee interceptor drones during Falcon Peak 26.2 at Yuma Proving Ground, focused on Southern Border counter-drone challenges.
- Perennial Autonomy, founded by Eric Schmidt, holds a $500 million Pentagon contract for drones already credited with over 4,000 intercepts in Ukraine.
The U.S. Northern Command tested Bumblebee interceptor drones from Perennial Autonomy during Falcon Peak 26.2, a counter-drone experiment underway at Yuma Proving Ground, Arizona, through Sept. 25.
The command said on Sept. 22 that the exercise is pulling lessons directly from Joint Task Force-Southern Border to sharpen how the military detects and stops unauthorized drones used for smuggling and surveillance along the U.S.-Mexico border.
Falcon Peak 26.2 is the fourth iteration of the recurring experiment and the first held at Yuma Proving Ground, run jointly by U.S. Northern Command and the Pentagon’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401. This round is focused specifically on the counter-drone challenges unique to the Southern Border, testing systems for detection, tracking, and low-collateral ways to bring drones down.
“Gaining and maintaining operational control of low-altitude airspace requires complete unity of effort across government partners,” U.S. Northern Command said. “At Falcon Peak 26.2, USNORTHCOM and JIATF-401 are integrating operational lessons directly from the Southern Border. By testing counter-drone systems alongside Joint Task Force-Southern Border and interagency partners, our teams are identifying the exact tools required to detect and interdict unauthorized drones used for illicit surveillance and smuggling. Developing shared tactics and integrated communications ensures our forces maintain decisive domain awareness along the nation’s borders.”
Bumblebee is a semi-autonomous quadcopter built to destroy small drones through direct collision, with a secondary role in reconnaissance and target tracking. Perennial Autonomy has said the system achieves a direct-hit rate above 70 percent using onboard artificial intelligence for terminal guidance, letting the drone stay locked on a target even if the target aircraft’s own operator loses control of it.
That AI-driven guidance is the common thread across Perennial Autonomy’s product line, not just the Bumblebee. Ukrainian forces have used different Bumblebee variants against Russian FPV drones and reconnaissance drones, while Merops has been credited with thousands of intercepts against Shahed-series one-way attack drones and Gerbera decoy and reconnaissance drones. Ukrainian officials and military bloggers have circulated numerous videos of Bumblebee interceptors downing Russian tactical strike drones and FPV drones. Ukrainian units have pointed to that autonomy-first design, more than any single platform, as the reason the company’s equipment has earned their trust.
Perennial Autonomy, founded by former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, began under the names Project White Stork and Project Eagle before adopting its current name. The company built its flagship product, the AS-3 Merops interceptor, for Ukrainian forces fighting off Russian Shahed-series attack drones, and Ukrainian officials credit the system with more than 4,000 intercepts since mid-2024. The company’s Hornet strike drone has also seen use in Ukraine.
The Pentagon has moved to bring that combat record into U.S. service. Joint Interagency Task Force 401 awarded Perennial Autonomy a $5.2 million contract for the Bumblebee V2 system in January, followed by a three-year, $500 million ceiling contract in May covering the Merops, Bumblebee, and Hornet platforms across the joint force. U.S. forces in Central Command have used Merops interceptors against Iranian-designed Shahed drones, and the Marine Corps’ 2nd Marine Division trained on all three systems in August at the Marine Corps Air Ground Combat Center in California.
Falcon Peak 26.2 runs through Sept. 25. U.S. Northern Command has not said which specific technologies from the exercise, including the Bumblebee, will move toward operational use along the Southern Border or on what timeline.
